Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Why the Roles Let the Attacker In

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

How to Check Your Accounts

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.

IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.

IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it.

IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used.

IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof.

Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum.

User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs.

For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.

CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.

How to Close the Route

The researchers recommend these steps:

If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued.

Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy.

Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses.

Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed."

Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible.

Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers.

Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before.

Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Executive summary

On October 21, 2026, we observed participants in underground forums seeking PHP2Shell exploits, while others shared scripts presented as exploiting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Discussion included doubts about prerequisites and whether circulating code worked. This post examines that gap between interest, claimed capability, and verified exploitation.

Our assessment covers selected forum posts and messages collected as of October 21. The findings show what was being discussed and shared, rather than confirmed compromises.

Forum participants requested exploit material, shared code, and questioned each other’s claims. For the security industry, this is a reminder to share threat findings promptly across security teams, researchers, and vendors so defenders can assess emerging threats and coordinate their response.

Looking for an exploit they could trust

Exploit.in is a long-running, primarily Russian-language underground forum where participants discuss hacking techniques and trade tools and services. Monitoring these discussions can reveal interest in emerging vulnerabilities and questions about available exploits.

“Does anyone have it?” was the question, translated from Russian, in a discussion on Exploit.in naming both PHP2Shell CVEs. The request sought exploit material, while subsequent comments questioned the prerequisites and legitimacy of circulating PoCs. One participant wrote “Didn’t test but seems legit.” A further comment described code execution “with preconditions,” while referring to a different “real exploit.” These are participant opinions about the circulating material, not our technical conclusions.

The exchange in Figure 1 captures both demand for an exploit and doubts about whether the available code worked. It leaves open whether the requester ever obtained a working exploit.

Figure 1. PHP2Shell exploit requests and discussion observed on October 21, 2026.

What circulated on October 21

On October 21, we recorded an English-language technical writeup at 02.23 UTC whose author claimed a lab reproduction. Hebrew- and Persian-language messages recorded at 05.16 and 05.35 UTC shared security alerts about the vulnerabilities and upcoming patches. The language of a post does not tell us where its author is based. At 06.22 UTC, we recorded a separate Exploit.in post presenting scripts as exploits for both CVEs, shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2. Forum post presenting purported PHP2Shell exploits, observed on October 21, 2026.

We redacted exploit instructions and memory offsets to avoid sharing details that could help reproduce an attack. The screenshot preserves the forum context.

A separate screenshot shared in a monitored channel appeared to show command execution on a local test system. We have not independently verified the result, and its exact posting date was unavailable.

By October 21, our searches returned 68 forum posts for PHP2Shell / CVE-2026-109618 and 62 for CVE-2026-109618. Chat searches returned 81 messages for PHP2Shell and 57 for CVE-2026-109619. These figures measure discussion volume in the collected material. The searches overlap, so the counts are not a combined total.

The forum exchanges show participants openly requesting exploit material, sharing code, and questioning each other’s claims. Separately, security alerts circulated in several languages across monitored messaging channels. Together, these observations illustrate how quickly information about a vulnerability can spread. For defenders, they reinforce the value of timely information sharing across organizations and language barriers, with clear distinctions between observed activity, unverified claims, and validated findings.

Public analysis offers context on PoC reliability

Public technical discussion published on October 23 on the SANS Internet Storm Center website examined why some circulating PoCs depended on specific server settings and knowledge of the target environment. The discussion concerned the PoCs reviewed there, rather than every possible way to exploit PHP2Shell.

The public analysis suggests that the PHP version, server setup, and information available to an attacker can affect whether a PoC works. These dependencies may help explain the questions raised in the forum thread.

Connecting intelligence with observed attempts

In our separate traffic analysis, we observed exploitation attempts, scanning, and invalid-PoC attempts. The invalid-PoC attempts add context to the forum discussion about whether circulating code worked. We detail these findings in our published PHP2Shell exploitation and IPS research. We have found no evidence connecting those requests to the forum participants or scripts discussed here.

We continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update our protections as exploitation techniques evolve. Our cloud-delivered IPS signatures blocked exploitation attempts on inspected customer traffic without requiring a separate protection package. PHP services outside our inspection coverage require separate remediation and protection. Updating affected PHP installations remains essential.

The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to a server through crafted uploads. Under certain configurations, attackers may also be able to read sensitive files, potentially leading to remote code execution.

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for the critical vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The patch is available to everyone, including developers and organizations that are not Socket customers, providing an additional remediation option for teams that cannot immediately upgrade Rails.

Impact #

The vulnerability affects Rails applications that use ImageMagick to process Active Storage attachments. ImageMagick supports multiple file format handlers, known as coders, some of which can access files outside the uploaded image. Active Storage did not restrict these coders, potentially allowing an attacker to invoke dangerous operations through a crafted upload.

Active Storage automatically analyzes files when they are attached, so exploitation does not require a separate preview, image transformation, or explicit analysis request.

According to the Rails advisory, applications are vulnerable when all three conditions are present:

Active Storage uses ImageMagick through config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick.

The system's ImageMagick security policy does not already block the dangerous coders.

The application accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

An attacker exploiting the vulnerability may be able to write arbitrary files on the server. Applications using Active Storage's Disk service may also expose files readable by the application process, including secret_key_base, application credentials, and database secrets. These disclosures could enable remote code execution or access to connected systems.

Upgrade Ruby on Rails #

The Rails team released versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 on November 4, 2026, and strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. These releases address the critical Active Storage vulnerability along with the other 20 security issues disclosed in the same update.

To upgrade, update the Rails version in your application's Gemfile to the appropriate patched release. For example, applications upgrading to Rails 8.1.4.1 can use:

gem "rails", "8.1.4.1"

Applications remaining on the 8.0 series should use 8.0.5.2.

Then update the dependencies with Bundler:

bundle update rails

Applications using the :mini_magick variant processor must also use MiniMagick 5.1 or later. Update the dependency if necessary and verify that the resolved version meets this requirement. Earlier MiniMagick versions will cause affected applications to raise an exception during boot after applying the Rails fix.

The updated Rails releases include a restrictive ImageMagick security policy that blocks dangerous coders and delegates. Applications that use ImageMagick for PDF or PostScript processing may need additional configuration adjustments.

Rails versions older than 8.0 are no longer supported. Security support for Rails 8.0 also ends on November 7, 2026, so teams should plan to move to the supported 8.1 series.

For additional instructions, see the official Ruby on Rails upgrade guide.

Free Socket Certified Patch Available #

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9, the critical Active Storage vulnerability that can allow arbitrary file writes and reads through malicious uploads.

Apply it with:

socket patch add GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9

Socket Certified Patches apply minimal, human-reviewed and AI-validated changes directly to vulnerable dependency versions, preserving the rest of the package's behavior. Patches are human-readable and can be reviewed before deployment.

The patch is available at no cost to anyone who needs it, whether or not they are a Socket customer. Making critical security fixes freely accessible is part of Socket's commitment to protecting the broader open source community and the developers and organizations that depend on it.

Certified Patches give teams time to plan and test upstream upgrades without leaving known vulnerabilities unaddressed. They are intended as an interim remediation option, with upgrading to a supported, patched Rails release remaining the recommended long-term solution.

This Certified Patch addresses GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 specifically, not the other vulnerabilities fixed in the November 4 Rails releases.

Recommended Actions #

Developers and organizations using Ruby on Rails should:

Upgrade Rails to 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2 as soon as possible, with a plan to move to a supported release series.

Verify MiniMagick compatibility and update to version 5.1 or later if the application uses :mini_magick.

Review Active Storage configurations to determine whether the application processes untrusted uploads through ImageMagick and whether its security policy blocks dangerous coders.

Apply Socket's free Certified Patch if an immediate Rails upgrade is not practical, then complete the upstream upgrade when possible.

Rotate potentially exposed credentials for applications using Active Storage's Disk service, as recommended in the Rails security advisory.

The official Rails security releases remain the recommended long-term fix. Socket's free Certified Patch gives teams an additional option to address the critical vulnerability without leaving affected applications exposed while upgrades are underway.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Buckle up Metasploit-Framework enthusiasts because we have another action packed release for you. I'm talking, unauthenticated remote code execution modules in some of the biggest names in network perimeter devices like Citrix NetScaler and Cisco Secure Email Gateway. That's not all, we have an authenticated GitLab CI/CD regular expression integer overflow RCE module that was recently making head lines among many other awesome exploit modules. Looking for auxiliary modules? We've got you covered this release with a Flowise authentication bypass and a OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 hash disclosure, because who doesn't love collecting and cracking (or in some cases relaying) NTLM hashes am I right or am I right? In our continued effort to expand the payloads supported by the framework this week we saw fetch payload support for LoongArch. Lastly, if you're ever on an engagement or at home doing some testing and you see something that's not supported in Metasploit-Framework that you'd like to see supported, either drop us suggested-features issue on GitHub or trying throwing up a Pull Request, we'd love to hear from you. Happy hacking everyone!

New module content (13)

Flowise Authentication Bypass

Authors: Arthur Gervais, Isaac David, and Richard Howe

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21757 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: admin/http/flowise_auth_bypass_cve_2025_58434

CVE reference: CVE-2025-58434

Description: Adds a new auxiliary module that exploits CVE-2025-58434, an unauthenticated account takeover in Flowise versions 3.0.5 and earlier. Flowise's password reset API returns a valid reset token directly in its response, so the module can reset the password of any account whose email address is known, with no credentials needed.

SPIP Password Change IDOR Privilege Escalation

Authors: 0xkidz and Julien Voisin

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21865 contributed by jvoisin

Path: admin/http/spip_idor_password_reset

Description: This adds an auxiliary module which exploits a vulnerability in SPIP before 4.4.23 which allows attackers to change any user's password given a validly-signed POST without checking that the caller is authorized for that id_auteur. This issue was patched in 4.4.23 although no CVE has been assigned at the time of writing.

HashiCorp Consul Version Scanner

Author: h00die

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #22010 contributed by h00die

Path: scanner/http/hashicorp_consul_version

Description: Adds Hashicorp Consul version scanner.

OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 Hash Disclosure via UNC Path Proxy Source

Author: Maksim Rogov

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21541 contributed by vognik

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: *sshole: OpenSSH Authentication Bypass Gives Attackers Root on Alpine Linux
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine. An unauthenticated attacker can log in over SSH password authentication as an account that should not accept passwords at all, including root. On a default Alpine install that means root access from a single connection, so patch now.

How the *sshole vulnerability bypasses SSH authentication

The bug comes from how musl libc’s crypt() reports errors. Since 2012, musl has returned the string “*” when crypt() fails instead of NULL, and its SHA-256 and SHA-512 crypt refuse passwords longer than 256 bytes. Locked and key-only accounts also use “*” as their shadow password field. When sshd checks passwords itself, without PAM, a password between 257 and 1024 bytes makes crypt() fail and return “*”. That matches the stored field, and sshd lets the attacker in.

Which locked and key-only accounts are exposed

Accounts exposed this way include root on Alpine 3.16 and later, key-only service and deploy users, directory users from nslcd, winbind or sssd, and the “alpine” user in tiny-cloud images, which has passwordless doas and is effectively root.

Which Alpine Linux and musl-based systems are affected

A system is affected when all of these hold: sshd is built without PAM (or runs with UsePAM no) on musl libc, PasswordAuthentication is on (the default), at least one account has “*” as its password field, and at least one local account has a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash. On Alpine that means the openssh-server package on releases 3.16 through 3.24 and edge. Other musl-based systems such as OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto builds, and container images that run sshd, may also be exposed. glibc distributions, PAM-enabled sshd, Dropbear and non-Linux systems are not affected.

How to patch *sshole: fixed OpenSSH versions and mitigations

Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2, or on Alpine to openssh 10.6_p2-r0 (edge), 10.3_p1-r2 (3.24), 10.2_p1-r1 (3.23), 10.0_p1-r11 (3.22), 9.9_p2-r1 (3.21) or 9.7_p1-r6 (3.20). Restart sshd afterwards, because upgrading the package does not replace the daemon that is already running. If you cannot patch yet, setting PasswordAuthentication no closes the hole. Also search authentication logs for “Accepted password for” on accounts that have no password, and treat any host with such a line as compromised.

Is *sshole being exploited in the wild?

The researcher’s public write-up explains the technique in enough detail to reproduce it, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported so far. Internet-facing Alpine hosts with password login enabled are the most exposed. An attacker who gets in this way has root on the host and can use it to reach the rest of the environment.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable OpenSSH hosts

Orca helps customers find assets running vulnerable OpenSSH versions and see each one’s exposure in context: whether it is reachable from the internet, at runtime, and how critical it is. Teams can use that context to fix the riskiest hosts first. Affected assets appear directly in the newItem view, so security teams can start with the most critical ones.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Zyxel Switch Patch Missed Flaw Behind Wave of Attacks
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks on 996 switches in 48 countries.

Firmware security company Binarly detailed the finding in research published on November 3, linking it to an exploit that threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had described in September. The vulnerability now carries a new identifier, CVE-2026-107441. It is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management program that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run operating system (OS) commands with root privileges.

The attacks had originally been tied to CVE-2026-7273, which Zyxel fixed on June 16 and described as a stack-based buffer overflow in the same program, rated 8.8. On September 21, GreyNoise reported that an attacker had exploited that flaw against 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, taking switch configurations, hashed root credentials and networking information.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day.

Read more on network device zero-days: Critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day Under Active Exploitation

June Fix Left Vulnerable Code in Place

Binarly analyzed an obfuscated Python exploit that matched the one GreyNoise described. On September 28, the researchers confirmed that all 10 firmware releases shipped as the June fix remained vulnerable to it.

Binarly said the June change added a check, but the check ran only after the unsafe copy had already occurred. The researchers wrote that the change "does not address the vulnerability."

The firm offered two explanations. Either the June patch, its description and its Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score were incorrect, or the attacks used a different flaw and CISA's link to CVE-2026-7273 would be wrong.

Either way, Binarly said, all 10 releases advertised as fixes contain the vulnerable code.

Severity Disputed as Zyxel Ships New Firmware

Zyxel rates CVE-2026-107441 at 8.8 and says an attacker must be on the local network to exploit the vulnerability, while Binarly rates it 9.8 and says exploitation requires only network access to the switch's management service.

Binarly said it notified Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel confirmed the flaw on October 11, released a fix on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models. On the GS1900-8, for example, firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier is affected and 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 contains the fix.

Zyxel told users to install the updates "for optimal protection." Its advisory lists the June releases among the affected versions, so switches last updated in June still need the new firmware.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Check Point Research discovered a vulnerability that allowed attackers to bypass Lockdown Mode, rendering its core protections ineffective
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Research by: Alexey Bukhteyev Key Takeaways OpenAI recently introduced Lockdown Mode, an optional advanced security setting designed to protect sensitive user data from prompt injection-based exfiltration attacks. Check Point Research discovered a vulnerability that allowed attackers to bypass Lockdown Mode, rendering its core protections ineffective. The vulnerability exposes a wide attack surface, enabling silent exfiltration of entire chat history, credential theft via phishing, and malware delivery. In ChatGPT Classic, the attack requires zero user interaction: simply having a conversation is enough to trigger silent data exfiltration. Introduction Earlier this year, Check Point Research disclosed a security flaw in ChatGPT’s code-execution runtime that allowed sensitive conversation data to be silently exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server through DNS tunneling, a hidden outbound channel that bypassed the runtime’s network isolation. A fix for this issue was promptly deployed. Moreover, OpenAI later introduced a new security feature: Lockdown Mode. Lockdown Mode is an optional advanced security setting for logged-in ChatGPT users. Its purpose is to reduce the risk that a prompt-injection attack can exfiltrate sensitive data by causing ChatGPT or one of its tools to make outbound web, app, connector, or file-download requests. A classic example, described in OpenAI’s own write-up on URL safety, is an attacker tricking the AI into loading a link such as attacker.example/collect?data= — the private data ends up in the attacker’s server logs even though nothing suspicious ever appears in the chat. Recognizing that prompt injection remains a persistent risk regardless of implemented guardrails, Lockdown Mode mitigates it by cutting off the channels through which data could leave the conversation. When enabled, it restricts live web access to cached content, blocks the loading and display of images from the internet, disables network requests from Canvas-generated code, and turns off Deep Research, Agent Mode, live connectors, and file downloads. Figure 1 – ChatGPT Lockdown Mode notification displayed when Canvas tries to access an external resource. We found a vulnerability in ChatGPT that allowed an attacker to bypass Lockdown Mode and perform covert exfiltration of chat data to an external server. Video 1 – The entire chat history was transferred to a third-party server without any notification, bypassing Lockdown Mode. Potential attack scenarios involving this vulnerability were not limited to chat data leakage. The vulnerability allowed for manipulation of the ChatGPT Classic interface, including displaying popup windows with arbitrary content, opening the door to a wide range of phishing attacks. The attack could be carried out in several ways: through a malicious prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat. The following sections cover the technical details behind the vulnerability and walk through the possible exploitation scenarios. Technical Details On February 2026, OpenAI added the HTML page preview feature into ChatGPT code blocks. It looks like the following: Figure 2 – HTML page preview in ChatGPT. Of course, the implementation includes several safeguards around this feature, since rendering user-controlled HTML with JavaScript inside the ChatGPT interface could otherwise create a direct path for private-data exfiltration. The most obvious attack scenarios include: Embedding an external image whose URL includes data from the chat: If such images could be rendered, an attacker could trigger zero-click exfiltration of private data. Embedding an external link: Download ChatGPT update This would allow attackers to place convincing social-engineering lures directly inside the ChatGPT interface and distribute them through shared chats. Opening a popup window with an arbitrary URL, either through a link with the target="_blank" directive:Click me or through JavaScript:window.open("", "_blank", "width=380,height=260"); This scenario would be especially risky in the ChatGPT Classic client, where users may perceive the popup as part of the trusted application context. Reading cookies or localStorage data for chatgpt.com. This would create a session-compromise risk. These scenarios are effectively mitigated through several layers of isolation and runtime enforcement. The rendered HTML is placed inside a sandbox, separating user-controlled content from the main ChatGPT application context, preventing the rendered page from directly accessing the parent document, ChatGPT UI state, cookies, or localStorage associated with chatgpt.com. All attempts by the page to send data to an external resource, or load remote images, scripts, links, or open arbitrary external URLs are intercepted by the sandbox and surfaced as warnings: Figure 3 – ChatGPT displays approval dialogs when a rendered HTML page attempts to access an external resource or when a user clicks an external link. The sandbox is implemented in two nested iframes. If we look at the implementation, we see that the sandbox doesn’t restrict some actions in the iframe. For example, the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions are enabled. Figure 4 – Sandbox attribute of the HTML-preview iframes, showing the permissive popup tokens (highlighted). The popups are controlled in a different way. The sandbox scripts redefine the window.open function: window.open: h=>{if(!h)return null;const{location:f}=r;return an(o,f,h),null} Thanks to that, when the webpage displayed in the iframe tries to open a popup, ChatGPT does not allow this until the action is approved by the user. When the page tries to open a popup with empty URL or about:blank the function just returns null , and the user does not even see a notification. However, popups are not explicitly restricted by the iframe sandbox, because it has the allow-popups token. Therefore, if we could get a real window.open function, we would be able to open a popup, bypassing the HTML sandbox restrictions, and even the Lockdown Mode. In fact, we can create a one more nested iframe inside our sandboxed page, and use its contentWindow.open function: window.open("about:blank"); // blocked // creating a nested iframe var f = document.createElement('iframe'); document.body.appendChild(f); f.contentWindow.open("about:blank"); // works Further, having managed to open a pop-up window, the attacker can place arbitrary HTML code in it, which will no longer be executed in the sandbox, since the token allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox is present. Attack surface: data exfiltration, phishing and malware downloding in a trusted interface. This vulnerability opens a wide attack surface. It could enable the covert theft of entire chat history and uploaded files, the distribution of malware disguised as a legitimate update, and even credential theft. Below, we walk through several scenarios and explain how each one works. Malware Delivery Through a Spoofed Application Window Typically, default browser settings prevent JavaScript from opening pop-up windows. Opening a new window normally requires an explicit user action, such as clicking a link or a button. An attacker needs to implement a plausible decoy to trick the user into clicking on a generated preview. Since the attacker controls the content of the generated page, crafting a convincing lure is straightforward. The window that opens will retain the ChatGPT application’s icon, while the title is controlled by an attacker, creating the impression that the user is still interacting with the ChatGPT application. This, for example, can be used to trick the user to download malware disguised as an application update. The ChatGPT Classic app does not allow automatic file downloads, so to download a file, the user must additionally click on the link. Video 2 – Malware delivery through a spoofed ChatGPT window. This scenario is even easier to implement in a browser, as automatic downloads are not blocked. Furthermore, the victim doesn’t even need to have an account, and the attacker only needs to share a chat containing a malicious page, making any clicks on content in shared chats dangerous: Video 3 – Malware delivery through a shared chat. Zero-Click Exploitation in ChatGPT Classic We found that window.open in the Electron-based ChatGPT Classic application works even without a user gesture. This makes the vulnerability significantly more dangerous: an attacker could silently exfiltrate data without requiring any interaction from the user, simply having a conversation would be enough to trigger the attack. This is demonstrated in Video 1, where a malicious GPT silently leaks chat messages to an attacker-controlled server. Beyond that, we also found it was possible to reload content in the main ChatGPT application window and perform certain actions on behalf of the user, such as forcibly signing them out of their account. This could allow an attacker to craft a convincing lure and trick the user into re-authenticating on an attacker-controlled page, thereby silently stealing their credentials. Video 4 – Credential theft. Conclusion Check Point Research responsibly disclosed this vulnerability to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI informed us that it had deployed a fix by removing the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions from the outer HTML-preview sandbox iframe. We subsequently retested the issue and confirmed that the exploitation technique described in this article no longer works. As AI assistants evolve into full execution environments, running code in the cloud and rendering content on the client side, all while handling medical records, financial data, and other highly sensitive information, every new capability expands the attack surface, including features built purely for convenience. Guardrails and the built-in security features of AI agents and applications help mitigate threats, but they still offer no absolute guarantee of protection. That is worth remembering before entrusting AI with sensitive information or granting it full access to your computer. Securing these systems requires looking beyond individual features and considering the platform as a whole. The benefits of modern AI assistants are enormous, but adopting them safely demands careful attention to every layer, including the ones users never think about. The post ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration appeared first on Check Point Research.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Gartner Report: The Attack Path is Closing Faster than Most Teams Can Patch
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Access the complimentary Gartner report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, to explore how AI-assisted vulnerability discovery may change cybersecurity priorities, metrics, and investment decisions.

⠀
