Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical, real-world software with Claude
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities.

We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure, which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory.

1. One-click remote code execution in Chrome

After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction:

Claude discovered a vulnerability in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, that allowed a malicious web page to corrupt V8’s heap memory.

Claude discovered a second vulnerability to break out of V8’s memory region sandbox and defeat ASLR. This step located Chrome’s code in memory and used a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain to take full control of the renderer process.

The compromised renderer was confined by Chrome’s process sandbox. Claude then discovered a race condition in CacheStorage. The compromised renderer used the race condition to read memory outside the sandbox and learn the memory layout of the privileged browser process.

Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox.

We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and patched as of Chrome 156, with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer.

2. A one-click exploit chain in Safari

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit chain that let any website’s JavaScript completely bypass the same-origin policy (SOP). The exploit could access a user’s Safari history, cookies, and other sensitive data, and could send authenticated HTTP requests to other domains and read the responses. For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers.

To do this, Claude defeated several layers of protection built into Safari:

Claude discovered a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability in JavaScriptCore, Safari’s JavaScript engine, which is written in C++. Certain TypedArray operations wrote through stale pointers to freed memory, overwriting TypedArray metadata.

WebKit’s Gigacage mitigates this type of attack by isolating TypedArray data in a separate region of memory. Claude discovered that certain variables in this region were used to index into other regions, which gave it an arbitrary read/write primitive outside the Gigacage.

All website JavaScript runs in the WebContent sandbox, which keeps bugs like the UAF from reaching sensitive browser data on disk. Claude discovered a vulnerability in the sandbox's IPC mechanism that let the exploit read Safari’s stored history, cookies, and session databases from disk.

Finally, Claude used the UAF to overwrite a variable in memory and disable the SOP, allowing the attacker’s page to read data from any other origin.

The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.

Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly. That fix is available to users.

3. Android lock screen bypass

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that let an attacker extract photos and other personal information from a stolen Android phone without unlocking it. The work combined three methods: source code analysis of the open-source parts of Android, reverse engineering and deobfuscation of the Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a physical Google Pixel 9. This turned up a wide range of vulnerabilities in both the open-source and proprietary components. Claude then chained three of them into the final exploit.

Android has several layers of protection against this attack. Claude found a way around each one:

A locked Android phone is designed not to transfer data over USB. Claude found that a USB host with a specific setting bypassed this.

The device-to-device transfer protocol refuses data commands from unauthorized peers. Claude found a way to skip the authorization check and start the pairing process.

Pairing is protected by an authenticated key agreement that asks the user to verify a six-digit code. Claude found a flaw that skipped this verification and behaved as if the user had tapped “Allow.”

USB transfers are not supposed to carry file contents, as enforced by a hardcoded check. Claude found a fallback mechanism that sent raw bytes over USB and was not covered by the check. The exploit requested file contents through it.

This issue has been addressed by Google.

4. Windows remote denial of service

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that would have allowed an attacker to remotely crash any Windows machine that responds to HTTP/3 requests using the native Windows implementation. The difficulty in this case was in identifying the vulnerability in the first place. Following that initial prompting, we reported this vulnerability directly to Microsoft, which resolved the vulnerability and assigned it CVE-2026-33096.

The vulnerability that Claude identified was a memory safety out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel’s implementation of QUIC. An attacker could reach the vulnerable codepath remotely over the network and send a few packets of data to a listening server to crash and restart the machine. By repeatedly sending these requests, it is possible to continuously crash the server, which causes loss of access to the server for all of the users. We estimate that there are likely several million such servers listening on the internet.

Claude discovered this vulnerability through binary analysis. We provided the model with a copy of the Windows executable and asked Claude to reverse-engineer how the software works using the existing reverse-engineering tools (such as Ghidra), write a fully annotated C program that reproduces the relevant features, compare the behavior reproduced program to binary to ensure correctness, and then study the code for vulnerabilities. When we asked Claude to identify potentially higher-risk issues, it surfaced this remotely exploitable vulnerability.

5. Zero-click remote code execution in Linux

While this post focuses on third-party products, our work on open source has continued. With Claude, we discovered local privilege escalation vulnerabilities on OpenBSD, FreeBSD, and Linux; a number of sandbox escapes in popular sandboxing infrastructure; and numerous vulnerabilities in important web applications. We have also found remotely triggerable (zero-click) arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel’s networking stack, which have since been patched upstream and publicly disclosed. We detail one such example below.

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that allows a remote attacker to send packets to Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener to run arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction. The underlying vulnerability is a race condition-induced UAF bug in the kernel networking stack. The full exploitation has two key stages:

In the first stage, the attacker defeats KASLR remotely. It exploits the race to make the kernel read an attacker-controlled length field to copy extra bytes and send them back to the attacker, and as long as one such overread contains a kernel pointer in the reply, the attacker learns the kernel address space layout.

In the second stage, the attacker hijacks the control flow. It exploits the same UAF bug to overflow a buffer and overwrite a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker has already staged in kernel memory via an ordinary protocol feature. When the kernel invokes the callback, the payload chains a series of calls to existing kernel functions. ending with an attacker-chosen shell command running as root.

An enabling property of this race condition is that a lost race only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed. In our proof of concept, it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches.

What we learned

Throughout our process of using Claude for this security work, we identified a number of insights that shaped our approach. We think two are particularly important.

Test-time compute scaling and scanner diversity substantially increase how many vulnerabilities you find. We built a platform that runs large numbers of scanning agents in parallel, measures each scanner by how many additional vulnerabilities it contributes to the mix, and tracks coverage dynamically so the scanners process the entire codebase.

The strategies range from pure coverage (is there a vulnerability in this function?) to goal-based (does this app expose anything that could compromise customer data?) to threat model-based (does anything in this app bypass its documented threat model?). We also used Claude to run automated variant analysis on every confirmed finding. All findings pass through a standardized verification and risk rating pipeline, so we can experiment freely with new scanners without lowering the quality bar.

Fixing the existing backlog only solves half the problem; the other half is cutting the rate at which new vulnerabilities enter the codebase. For that, we recommend scanning at PR time. We built security guidance directly into our development process through a Claude Code plugin, which we’ve released publicly.

What this means for defenders

Frontier models have the ability to discover and combine multiple vulnerabilities into a working exploit. These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify.

Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do. Recently, we released an expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward. Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Mythos access is expanding: what this means for vulnerability management
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Product Marketing Manager @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research REGISTER FOR THE WEBINAR Published: October 27, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security briefings...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Anthropic’s Claude Mythos put vulnerability management in the boardroom when it was released earlier this year, and the conversation around it has evolved. Press coverage continues to find new angles, and there’s plenty of discourse around how AI is changing everything about cybersecurity.

In the months since the initial release of Mythos Preview, there have been a few developments around what Mythos can do and who is able to access it. But what does this actually mean for your vulnerability management program?

A stronger model, wider access

In September, Anthropic shipped Claude Mythos 5.1, which it calls the model with the strongest cyber capabilities of any they’ve released. Mythos 5.1 is built on the same base model as the generally available Fable 5.1 with different safeguards attached. Then, in October, it folded Project Glasswing, the early-access program that gave select critical infrastructure providers and industry partners access to Mythos, into an expanded tiered Cyber Verification Program (CVP). The revamped CVP spans everyday defensive work up through the highest-sensitivity critical infrastructure.

This means that compared to at launch, machine-speed vulnerability discovery that used to be limited to a small group will reach a wider set of defenders. According to Anthropic, Glasswing partners turned up more than 129,000 verified vulnerabilities between April and July, over 33,000 of them critical or high severity. More access to Mythos-class discovery sounds like it should mean more vulnerabilities found, faster, across more organizations. While this is true, that large number isn’t the full story.

Discovery and exploitation aren’t the same thing

Anthropic noted in its announcement that the generally available Fable 5.1 can now be used to discover software vulnerabilities, but explicitly not to develop exploits for them. Activities that could be used maliciously like penetration testing, exploit generation, etc., are redirected to lower-tier models. The same gating carries into Mythos. The CVP’s three access tiers wall off penetration testing and red teaming work behind the two highest, most heavily vetted tiers.

So while broader access to Mythos-class capability means broader access to finding things faster, it doesn’t, by itself, mean broader access to attacking anything. Also, Mythos still isn’t broadly available: access runs through vetted organizations in the CVP, so it isn’t something readily on hand for attackers.

That’s not to say automated attacks aren’t happening, but that’s a separate development, not something that traces back to Mythos specifically. Lumping every agentic AI risk together misses where the actual exposure is coming from.

The core of vulnerability management hasn’t changed

A lot of the coverage of Mythos makes it sound scarier than it needs to. While it does make vulnerability discovery significantly faster, no security team was patching every known CVE even before Mythos existed. Using AI agents for defense can increase teams’ speed and scope, but the real differentiator continues to be knowing which findings are in active, loaded packages, reachable, and creating real risk, versus which ones are noise with a scary CVSS score attached.

Exploits are getting faster too. Mandiant now puts the average time-to-exploit at negative seven days, meaning exploitation begins before a vulnerability is even disclosed. This makes it even more important to build a vulnerability management program around core principles.

The fundamentals of vulnerability management are even more important in the AI discovery era:

Scan and discover everything in one place, CVE and non-CVE findings alike.

Prioritize by what’s in-use and exploitable, not just what scores high.

Automate remediation at the source instead of patching every downstream instance individually.

Treat runtime security as a safety net for whatever stays exposed.

This plan for vulnerability response doesn’t get rewritten because discovery got faster. Agentic AI can be utilized on your side too, automating and accelerating each of these steps and helping keep up with the volume of findings. You don’t need to treat every Mythos headline as a crisis or rebuild your program every time access expands again.

Learn more at the webinar

To learn more about building a Mythos-ready vulnerability management program, join our webinar, Mythos Decoded: What’s Actually Changed in Vulnerability Management. We’ll cover what Mythos actually is and isn’t and practical steps to keep pace with AI-accelerated discovery without the panic.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: In a pickle: Why every pickle defense in machine learning is bypassed the same way
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Threat Research Engineer @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research See more threat research Published: October 27, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security briefings...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The machine learning (ML) ecosystem recently shipped a series of defenses against malicious model files. PyTorch restricted what its loader will deserialize. Keras added a safe mode that refuses to execute embedded code. Vendors built scanners to inspect model files at rest and reject the dangerous ones.

But none of them held up to six documented CVE bypasses. These bypasses, often called “pickles,” let a malicious Python data file slip past security scanners undetected. And after the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) pulled apart every public pickle bypass on record, a pattern emerged.

Before we explore that pattern, let’s first understand what a pickle actually is and why machine learning (ML) is full of them. Then, we’ll analyze which model formats are most dangerous, what the Sydig TRT measured when we ran malicious model loads against two detection engines, and how you can best deploy and protect susceptible models in your environment.

A pickle is a program

Pickle is a built-in Python capability for saving something in memory to file so you can load it back later exactly as it was. Many teams may be pickling and they don't even realize it. torch.save() or joblib are both pickle, and that hidden misunderstanding increases exposure and makes it easy for something to go wrong without anyone noticing or understanding why.

Most file formats are data. You parse them, get a structure back, and nothing inside the file gets a vote in what the program does next. A malformed JPEG produces an error, for instance, not a shell.

Pickle is not that kind of format. pickle.load() doesn’t parse; it executes. A .pkl file is a sequence of instructions for a small stack-based virtual machine built into CPython, and loading the file means running them. That’s not an implementation flaw or a parser bug that gets patched, but the inherent design.

The easiest way to believe it is to read one. Pickle's protocol 0 is human-readable by design, and this is a complete, working payload:

cos GLOBAL → push os.system onto the stack system ( MARK S'id' push the string "id" tR TUPLE → ("id",) then REDUCE → call os.system("id") . STOP

The snippet above includes five instructions, and it reads like assembly because functionally that is what it is:

GLOBAL resolves and pushes a callable.

MARK and TUPLE assemble an argument tuple.

REDUCE calls the callable with those arguments.

STOP ends the program.

Swap "id" for something with more ambition, and nothing about the structure changes.

That’s the entire remote code execution (RCE) story, and it’s only three operational codes (opcodes). Import something, build an argument tuple, and call it. Everything else in the format — later protocol versions, the memo table, framing, out-of-band buffers — is optimization around that core.

And because the payload is only opcodes, there are no offsets to leak and no build to fingerprint. One that works on a given Python works on any Python that can parse the protocol.

You wouldn’t normally handwrite those opcodes, either. Python will emit them for you through a documented extension point:

import os, pickle class Evil: def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ("id",)) payload = pickle.dumps(Evil())

__reduce__ is how an object tells pickle to reconstruct it: The method names a callable and its arguments, and pickle invokes them on load — which is how objects that cannot be naively serialized rebuild themselves on the other side. The attack does not subvert that. It uses pickle exactly as specified, and nominates os.system as the callable.

Look at this script, for example:

import os, pickle, pickletools class Evil: def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ("echo pwned",)) pickletools.dis(pickle.dumps(Evil()))

pickletools.dis disassembles the byte stream without running it, and the output reads like a listing: GLOBAL, MARK, SHORT_BINUNICODE, TUPLE1, REDUCE, STOP. Disassemble freely. Run pickle.loads on that payload only somewhere you are willing to lose.

The consequence carries big implications

If a pickle is a program, then a file that is invalid as a whole can still be perfectly effective in part. The VM executes opcodes as it encounters them. It doesn’t validate the stream up front and then run it because there is no up front. It runs until it finishes, or until it reaches something it cannot execute. Everything before that point has already happened.

Data would be parsed and then used, and a corrupted file would yield nothing. A program runs until it faults.

Attackers noticed, and we will come back to that in the third section.

Why is machine learning full of pickles anyway?

A pickle solves a real problem, and the way it solves that problem requires precisely the capability that makes it dangerous.

The problem is general object serialization. Writing a list of integers to disk is easy. Writing an arbitrary Python object, however, is not.

Objects hold references to other objects, to classes defined in modules that may not be imported yet, to state that is only meaningful once something reconstructs it. There is no universal declarative description of "how to rebuild this." The general answer is to record a procedure — call this thing, with these arguments — and run it at load time.

That is what __reduce__ is, and the standard library specifies it in exactly those terms. The first two items of a __reduce__ tuple are:

A callable object that will be called to create the initial version of the object.

A tuple of arguments for the callable object.

Read that as an attacker and the exploit writes itself. Read it as a language designer, though, and it is the only general answer available.

So arbitrary code execution is not a bug in pickle, but a feature. Python has never been coy about it, either. The warning sits at the top of the module documentation:

The docs even name the mitigation. A section titled "Restricting Globals" observes that for many applications the default behavior "is unacceptable as it permits the unpickler to import and invoke arbitrary code," and shows how to subclass the unpickler to allow only what you expect.

So how did machine learning end up built on pickles?

torch.save serializes with pickle. Saving a model is one call, and the artifact is a .pt, .pth, or .bin, none of which look like a pickle to anyone reading a file listing. scikit-learn's persistence guidance points to joblib, a pickle wrapper optimized for objects carrying large NumPy arrays, which is exactly what a fitted estimator is. NumPy's own .npy is a plain numeric container right up until an array contains Python objects. At that point it needs pickle, which is why the allow_pickle flag exists at all.

Nobody in that chain chose arbitrary code execution. They chose "save my Python object," which is the obvious API to want, and pickle is the batteries-included way to provide it.

The result is a supply chain that’s majority-pickle. In a survey of 705,991 models on a Hugging Face mirror, PyTorch's .pt, .pth, and .bin accounted for 335,893 models (51.0%), with explicit pickle variants (.pkl, .pickle, .joblib, .dill) adding another 26,696, or 4.1%. More than half the models you might download execute code the moment you load them.

Why "just fix pickle" isn’t on the table

You can’t make pickle.load both general and safe, because generality is the thing that requires the call. However, you can do one of two narrower things:

Restrict the loader. Keep the format, but allow only a known-safe subset of callables. This is the standard library's own suggestion, and PyTorch's weights_only=True and Keras's safe_mode are that idea applied to model files.

Change the format. Store only what a model actually needs, such as named arrays of numbers, in a container with no way to express a call at all. That’s safetensors.

Both these approaches are sound in principle. Their records in practice are the subject of the next section, and only one of them has survived contact.

Which models are actually vulnerable

Which model files should be treated as code? The short answer is: more of them than the name suggests, and almost none of them are called .pkl.

Format

Executes on load?

Notes

.pkl.pickle.dill

Yes

The plain case

scikit-learn .joblib

Yes

joblib wraps pickle

PyTorch .pt.pth.bin

Yes

A ZIP-wrapped pickle. weights_only=True since 2.6; see below

NumPy .npy.npz

Only with allow_pickle=True

Default False since CVE-2019-6446. Object arrays require it, which is how it gets turned back on

Keras/TensorFlow .h5.hdf5

Yes

Lambda layers, and the legacy path ignores safe_mode

Keras .keras (v3)

Yes, via bypass

See CVE-2025-9906

TensorFlow SavedModel

Yes, in effect

Graph ops plus custom layers

safetensors

No

Named tensors and a JSON header. No opcode, no callable

GGUF

No known path

Tensors and metadata for quantized inference

ONNX

No known path

Protobuf compute graph, predefined ops only

Note the phrasing on the last two: no known code execution path. These formats are younger and attacked less often than pickle, and the absence of published CVEs is much weaker evidence than a format that cannot express a call in the first place.

Strategy one: Restrict the loader, get bypassed

Keep the format, allowing only a known-safe subset of callables: This is the standard library's own advice. Both major frameworks took that advice, but were still bypassed.

PyTorch flipped torch.load's weights_only argument from False to True by default in version 2.6, explicitly on security grounds. The restricted unpickler permits tensors, storages, and basic collections, and refuses everything else.

Except that in 2.5.1 and earlier, weights_only=True was already bypassable. CVE-2025-32434 found that _legacy_load — the path handling older tar-based checkpoints — did not actually enforce the restricted unpickler on everything it processed. The flag was set and the code that ran didn’t honor it.

Then it happened again. CVE-2026-24747, published in January 2026 with a CVSS of 8.8, defeats the restricted unpickler's validation with crafted opcodes, corrupting memory to reach code execution. It affects every version before 2.10.0, which means the fix for the 2025 bypass was itself exploitable across the entire 2.6 through 2.9 range. If you pinned PyTorch 2.6 in early 2025 because it was the secure default, you were exposed for four minor versions.

Keras has the same shape and more iterations. Lambda layers carry marshalled Python and execute it on load (CVE-2024-3660). Keras made safe_mode=True the default from 2.13, which refuses to deserialize them.

Then, with CVE-2025-9905, loading a legacy .h5 file ignores safe_mode. No warning, no error. An attacker only has to author the checkpoint in an older format, and the current library will load it and run the code anyway.

Finally, CVE-2025-9906, a crafted .keras archive whose config.json calls keras.config.enable_unsafe_deserialization(), and then drops a Lambda layer. The file disables the check that’s inspecting it.

In that same survey of 705,991 Hugging Face models, researchers found 91 malicious ones, and 15 of them used Keras Lambda layers.

Strategy two: Scan the file before you load it, miss malicious files anyway

Check the artifact at rest and reject it if it looks malicious. This is what Hugging Face runs on upload, and what most continuous integration (CI) gates use.

Sonatype disclosed four picklescan vulnerabilities in 2025, and three of them describe the same failure with different mechanics:

CVE-2025-1889: Standard detections keyed on file extension rather than content. If attackers renamed the file, it was never scanned.

CVE-2025-1944: A deliberately malformed ZIP makes picklescan crash with BadZipFile. PyTorch's more forgiving ZIP reader loads the same file without complaint.

CVE-2025-1945: If an attacker modified ZIP flag bits, picklescan fails to detect and PyTorch still loads.

Then there is nullifAI, found by ReversingLabs on Hugging Face in February 2025. The models were compressed with 7z instead of PyTorch's default ZIP. Picklescan didn’t parse them.

One bug, six times

Vulnerability

The gap

PyTorch CVE-2025-32434

weights_only not enforced on the _legacy_load path

Keras CVE-2025-9905

safe_mode ignored on the legacy H5 path

Keras CVE-2025-9906

The file disables the check inspecting it

picklescan CVE-2025-1889

Scanner reads extensions; the loader reads content

picklescan CVE-2025-1944 and 1945

Scanner's ZIP parser is strict; the loader's is forgiving

nullifAI

Scanner expects ZIP; the loader accepts 7z

In every case, the thing doing the checking and the thing doing the loading disagreed about what the file was. The attacker did not defeat the check, but found a reading of the file on which the check did not apply.

This is structural, not simply a run of bad luck. A checker has to anticipate how every loader, at every version and down every legacy code path, will interpret a stream of bytes. The loader only has to interpret it one way, and that’s what leads to missed malicious files.

A pickle doesn’t need to be valid to work

The nullifAI models were broken on purpose.

Recall from the first section that the pickle VM executes opcodes as it encounters them. There is no validation pass. The payload was placed at the head of the stream, so by the time deserialization reached the corruption and threw an error, os.system had already been called. As ReversingLabs described it, opcodes execute "until all opcodes are executed or a broken instruction is encountered."

A scanner that parses the whole file and reports a parse error has reported nothing useful. The victim is already compromised. Data is parsed and then used, so a corrupted file yields nothing. A program runs until it faults, and everything before the fault has already happened. Treating a model file as data isn’t just a stylistic error.

Look back at the table in the “Which models are actually vulnerable” section. The formats in the bottom rows are not safe because they are well patched, but because there is nothing in a safetensors file that can express a call — no opcode, callable, or reconstruction procedure. The security property is a consequence of what the format cannot say, which is why it does not need a version number to be trusted.

That is the whole argument for conversion. But conversion is not always available, and plenty of production systems load pickles today. So the next question is what you can see when one of them runs.

Detection

There are two places to catch a malicious model: before it loads, and while it runs. They fail in different directions, and the difference matters.

Scanning at rest

Scanning is the primary control. It is cheap, it runs in CI, it blocks the artifact before anything executes, and against a textbook payload it works. A __reduce__ gadget calling os.system is exactly what modelscan and picklescan are built to find.

The CVEs listed in the third section are the reason that is not reassuring. Every bypass in that list defeated a scanner that was working correctly on the file it believed it was reading. This includes extension checks, ZIP parsing, flag bits, 7z, and a deliberately corrupted stream. None of them broke the detection logic, but they did change what the file was on the way in.

A scanner that catches the obvious case has only told you the obvious case is caught. It cannot tell you the file is safe, because "safe" would require it to have anticipated how every loader, at every version, down every legacy path, will read those bytes: a huge amount of combinations to reason through and one that make scanning alone unfeasible. That is the asymmetry.

So the honest question is not whether to scan, but what’s left standing when the scan is bypassed.

Watching it run

Runtime detection is the layer that gets proposed as the logical answer, so let’s measure it.

We built five hostile gadget families, each one a pickle whose __reduce__ performs a different post-exploitation action, and ran them against two engines: open source Falco 0.44.1 on its default ruleset and Sysdig Secure.

Both runs fired a positive control first. All five outcomes were predicted in writing before the run.

Gadget family

OSS Falco (default ruleset)

Sysdig Secure

Sensitive file read, via shell

FIRED · Read sensitive file untrusted

FIRED · 1.6s

Sensitive file read, direct, no shell

FIRED · same rule

FIRED · 1.9s

Sensitive file read, in-process, no spawn

FIRED · same rule

FIRED · 1.5s

Composite, read plus outbound

FIRED · same rule only

FIRED · + System procs network activity

.pth startup-hook persistence

Modify Python Startup Hook File

FIRED · 1.5s · Python .pth Persistence File Written by Non-Package-Manager

All five gadget families triggered Sysdig Secure rules, all within two seconds. Four of five triggered OSS Falco defaults. Falco’s open source default ruleset contains 26 rules versus the commercial product’s 278. This includes the Falco rule Modify Python Startup Hook File, which was created after this test.

Three findings in that table matter more than the raw score, however.

First, the spawn axis is irrelevant. We expected the gadget that forks a shell to look different from the one that never leaves the Python process, but the detections don’t differ. The shell-spawned gadget was caught in 1.6 seconds, the direct one in 1.9 seconds, and the entirely in-process one in 1.5 seconds The same rule caught all three. Whether a gadget forks is a fact about its syscall surface, not about whether it’s visible.

Second, runtime itself doesn’t solve the checker vs. loader problem, but it doesn’t need to. A runtime sensor never observes the deserialization at all, but the consequences. Nothing in that table detected a pickle being loaded. What fired was a file read, or an outbound connection, that happened to originate downstream of one.

That sounds like a technicality until you read the rules that look like they should have caught this. Shell Spawned with Inline Python Command keys on proc.pcmdline containing -c together with the literal source text; import os and os.system. Base64-encoded Python Script Execution does the same thing one encoding layer down. Both assume malicious Python is visible on the command line.

And third, a pickle load is python3 load_pickle.py model.pkl. The gadget is in the file. None of that text is ever on the command line, at any encoding layer, ever.

Best practices if you must deploy a susceptible model

As we’ve established, no single layer is foolproof on its own. But that’s not an argument for doing nothing. It’s a case for ordering the layers by how they fail.

The stack below is ordered by strength, each a part of a stronger approach to defense:

1. Convert the format, and stop having the problem.

Most models don’t need to serialize anything but named arrays of numbers. If that is true of yours, store it in a container that cannot express a call: safetensors for weights, GGUF for quantized inference, and ONNX where you need a compute graph.

The difference between those three matters more than it may seem. Safetensors is structurally safe , as it consists of tensors and a JSON header, with nothing in the format capable of expressing a callable. GGUF and ONNX have no known path, which is more of a claim about the current state of research than about the format's expressive limits. ONNX in particular carries a full operator graph and a history of parser CVEs. When deploying a new model, opt for the format that is safe because of what it can’t say.

Caveat: "No known path" isn’t "proven safe," as conversion isn’t always available. A model distributed only as a pickle has to be loaded once to be converted. Do that in the sandbox from step 5 below, not on a build host.

2. Pin your loaders past the bypasses, and verify the version actually running.

For PyTorch, the most secure approach means version 2.10.0 or later. The weights_only=True default arrived in 2.6 and was widely reported as the fix, but CVE-2026-24747 defeats the restricted unpickler itself and affects every version before 2.10.0. A team that pinned 2.6 in early 2025 on security advice stayed exposed for four further minor versions.

For Keras, run current and refuse legacy .h5 inputs rather than trusting safe_mode on that path. CVE-2025-9905 is the case where it is ignored with no warning. For NumPy, keep allow_pickle=False and treat any code that flips it as a finding.

Caveat: This layer has arguably the worst track record of anything on this list. Every entry above is a fix that was itself later bypassed. Pin it, but do not spend the trust it appears to buy.

3. Scan at rest, in CI, as a gate.

Run modelscan or picklescan on ingest and fail the build rather than the deployment. It’s cheap and it catches the commodity case, which is most of what you will actually encounter.

Caveat: Scanners are blocklist-based, and every CVE evaluated beat a scanner that was working correctly. A clean scan is the only absence of evidence. Never let it be the signal that promotes an artifact to production.

4. Establish provenance.

Track which model came from where. Sign what you build, verify what you consume, and give preference to publishers who do the same.

Caveat: A signature proves origin, not intent. The malicious models found on Hugging Face were authentically uploaded by the accounts that uploaded them. Provenance narrows who you have to trust, but it doesn’t tell you whether that trust is deserved.

5. Load inside a sandbox with an egress boundary.

This is the least glamorous control on this list, but the most reliably effective. Load models in a process with no credentials worth stealing, no write access to anything that persists, and an explicit egress allowlist.

This is the only control here that doesn’t depend on recognizing the attack; it doesn’t have to. It isn’t deciding whether the connection is malicious, only whether it’s permitted.

Caveat: A sandbox bounds the blast radius, but doesn’t prevent execution. The code still runs. You are choosing what it can reach.

6. Always assume breach, and use runtime detection as the backstop.

Everything above is a prediction about a file. Runtime is the only layer that observes what actually happened. Use runtime observability to verify what your code is actually doing and catch malicious activity.

Caveat: In this case, it’s silent on behavior that looks innocuous, and it never sees the load itself, only consequences.

Why that order matters

Read through the first four controls again, and there’s one distinct pattern: Each works by predicting how a file will be interpreted. The converter predicts the format. The pinned loader predicts which code path will run. The scanner predicts what the loader will do with those bytes. The signature predicts that a known publisher produced what they meant to produce.

Every bypass is an attacker finding an interpreter that disagreed with one of those predictions. And there is no reason to expect it to stop, because the asymmetry producing it never closes. A checker has to anticipate every loader. A loader only has to interpret the file one way, and it is the one that actually runs.

The sandbox and the runtime sensor are the two controls on this list that don’t predict. The sandbox doesn’t care what the file is. It constrains what the code can reach once it’s already running. The sensor doesn’t care either. It reports what the process did.

But that doesn’t make them sufficient alone. Runtime never observes the deserialization, the rules that look like they should catch malicious Python assume the malice is visible on the command line, and the correlation layer that ought to be the sophisticated tier never fired once.

Ultimately, the most comprehensive approach is a “both and” strategy. A scanner and a loader that disagree produce a bypass. A scanner and a sensor that disagree produce an alert.

A model file is a program. It shouldn’t move through a pipeline built for data, and you must assume that whatever you use to check the model file has a reading of those bytes that the thing loading them doesn’t share.

Check out the latest in threat research from the Sysdig TRT

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CVE-2026-111497: Critical out-of-bounds write in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2.

An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder.

On October 27, 2026, CVE-2026-111497 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. Given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory.

The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below.

Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun, Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET, Envoy and Istio, brotli4j, and operating-system packages. Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles:

Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later.

Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later.

Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later.

The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release.

Updates

October 26, 2026: Initial publication.

October 26, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to reflect coverage availability.

October 27, 2026: Updated Overview to add a reference to CVE-2026-111497 being added to the CISA KEV list.

[R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Arnie Cabral Mon, 10/26/2026 - 11:07

Tenable Network Monitor leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, expat, libxml2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 updates OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, curl to version 8.21.0, expat to version 2.9.0 and libxml2 to version 2.15.4 to address the identified vulnerabilities.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell: What to know about two critical PHP flaws
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: This is because on an unpatched server, an attacker can exploit the vulnerabilities to run their own code without logging in
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Last week, details emerged about a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a server-side scripting language commonly used in web development. The news prompted security advisories from government agencies and sent website owners scrambling to apply the patches, with some sites even going offline as a precaution. This is because on an unpatched server, an attacker can exploit the vulnerabilities to run their own code without logging in. As three out of four websites globally are estimated to use PHP in some capacity, its ubiquity helps create an environment ripe for abuse; indeed, initial attempts to exploit the flaws – discovered by AI and dubbed PHP2Shell – weren't long in coming.

Here's what to know about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, as well as what website owners and IT teams should do to stay safe – all in a little more than two minutes.

For detailed mitigation steps and other information, refer to the advisories issued by the PHP Project, CISA, CERT-EU or NCSC.

Connect with us on Facebook, X, LinkedIn and Instagram.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and updated the PHP Alert, Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching:

CVE-2026-109618 – PHP Memory Corruption Vulnerability

CVE-2026-109619 – PHP Stale Internal Request-State Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ZDI-26-809: Meta FAIRChem dense_eval dft-targets Deserialization of Untrusted Data Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of pickle files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

Meta has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairchem/pull/1935

Disclosure Timeline

2026-03-26 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-26 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Additional Details

Meta has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairchem/pull/1935

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Can’t Patch PHP2Shell Yet? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Only 199,000 of 156 million PHP installations were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell’s fix is to update PHP, but patching at scale is slow. Only 199,000 of 156 million PHP installations were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure. In the meantime, Qualys’s configuration-level mitigation reduces exposure to the confirmed attack path without code changes, with or without an agent. WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers, and TruConfirm shows which hosts are actually reachable: 25 of 1,539 in one customer environment. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but patching remains the only complete fix.

PHP2Shell comes with a clear instruction: update PHP. Fixed releases exist for supported branches. Patching at this scale still takes time. In Qualys telemetry, only 199,000 of the 156 million PHP package installations with a known version (about 0.13%) had been patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while updates roll out, and the right visibility shows which servers need attention first. Our PHP2Shell blog post covers detection and fixed versions.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed PHP, apply the Qualys mitigation, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed PHP

Qualys customers can identify PHP installations through network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan, where supported. Additionally, they can assess exposed web applications and APIs using Qualys TotalAppSec. To facilitate PHP discovery, use QID 45110, followed by the relevant vulnerability-detection QIDs and software-inventory QIDs, to assess the assets in scope.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable host has the same level of exposure. TruConfirm helps validate the indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. Its benign probe checks whether this entry point is reachable and whether the upload-progress mitigation is absent, all without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. For more details, refer to our PHP2Shell blog post, which explains how the probe works.

In one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 of those assets. Consider these results alongside their internet exposure and business criticality to determine what vulnerabilities to prioritize for mitigation and patching. Keep in mind that a negative result does not guarantee that all exploitation paths are closed.

Step 2: Apply the Qualys Mitigation

Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It turns off session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes.

It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Test applications that depend on upload-progress functionality after the change.

With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. For appliances, DMZ servers, and legacy hosts that cannot run a Cloud Agent, the same mitigation script is available in the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate and runs directly on scanner-based hosts.

Configuration-level, with restart verification. The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration.

Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the mitigation, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses

Inbound: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have released signatures that name both CVEs. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach PHP. Cloudflare has reported attack traffic that includes evasion attempts, so treat signatures as one of several layers.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a web server process launching a shell or dropping a web shell.

PHP2Shell 3rd-party mitigation and compensating controls

Select the WAF, IPS, and EDR you run to see the exact signatures and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, ready to copy into your console.

This interactive view needs JavaScript. Signatures covering both CVEs: Akamai 3000991; Cloudflare seven managed rules; F5 BIG-IP 200204113, 200103697, 200204115; FortiWeb 1002017614, 1002017615; Palo Alto Networks 543004, 97622 to 97625; FortiGate 62657, 62658; Check Point CPAI-2026-15172, 15184, 15224; Trend Vision One 1012749, 1012754. Endpoint policies are listed for CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Cortex XDR, SentinelOne and Cybereason.

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation and are mapped to the attacker’s next step, not to the CVEs themselves, so verify each one fires for your PHP worker. Compensating controls reduce risk; updating PHP remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Mitigation reduces risk in the interim. Updating remains the only complete fix. You can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys reports a High patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for this PHP package update.

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

Restart every service that loads PHP.

Verify the installed packages and that running PHP workers are on the patched build.

Repeat TruConfirm validation and verify the effective configuration. Do the same after applying the mitigation in Step 2.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched PHP build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule that names both CVEs, with EDR watching its web server process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.

Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.

Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

Where to Start

Find. Use QID 45110 to support PHP discovery to detect CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, then use the applicable vulnerability detection QIDs and software inventory to assess assets in scope.

Use TruConfirm results alongside internet exposure and business criticality to prioritize remediation.

Mitigate. Apply the Qualys mitigation to systems awaiting an update, using agent-based or scanner-based execution as applicable. Verify the effective configuration and required restarts.

Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers.

Patch and verify. Deploy the PHP or vendor update, restart every service that loads PHP, verify that the patched build is running, and repeat the relevant validation checks.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.
