Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n!

As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.

The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.

Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site.

As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.

How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?

I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.

What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?

I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.

How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?

It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.

What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?

I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool.

Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating.

Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding?

I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application.

Think of a request parameter, uploaded file, API input, or data coming from another service. A sink can be a security-sensitive operation that consumes this data, for example, a network request, file access, process execution, database query, or authorization decision. The interesting part is tracing the path between the two. I look at how the data is transformed, validated, or passed across trust boundaries, and whether those controls are sufficient before it reaches the sink.

I like this approach because it lets me reason about attack paths without forcing my investigation into a predefined bug class. Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation. I consider a finding confirmed once I understand the attack path, can produce a working PoC, and can explain the impact.

Do you use AI in your research? Where does it genuinely help and where does it fall short?

Yes. Quite a lot, actually, but mostly as an accelerator. I use it for navigating unfamiliar code, finding call sites, tracing data through the codebase, and understanding how a system is structured and how its components interact. I also find it helpful for writing PoC scripts once I’ve identified the vulnerability.

Where it works best is when the question is specific. “Is this application vulnerable?” usually isn’t a very useful prompt. Give it the right context, explain what you already know, and ask a narrow question, and the quality goes up dramatically. There’s a bit of a paradox there. AI becomes more useful as you understand the problem better yourself. And I never treat its conclusions as facts. Hallucinations, false positives, bad assumptions, and confidently wrong answers are all common. Everything should still be manually verified. AI makes my work faster. However, it doesn’t replace understanding the application, developing intuition, or proving that something actually works.

What’s your guidance on using AI responsibly in bug bounty?

Use it to improve your research, not to outsource responsibility for it. If AI tells you it found a vulnerability, that doesn’t mean you found a real vulnerability. You still need to reproduce it yourself. You should understand exactly what’s happening, which security boundary or control is being violated, and what the real impact is. Ideally, you should understand the issue well enough that you could write the report without AI at all. Build a clear PoC. Make sure the security team can follow it. Know why every step matters.

AI has lowered the barrier to doing security research, which is great in a lot of ways. But you can also see the downside in the number of unverified reports teams now have to deal with. AI should make research better. Not just make more reports.

As the industry ships more AI-powered features, does testing them require a different mindset than traditional web bugs?

Yes. Conventional vulnerabilities still matter, but attackers may also be able to influence a probabilistic decision-making component through the data, instructions, or context it receives. But getting a model to say or do something unexpected isn’t necessarily the interesting part. The more important question is what that influence allows an attacker to achieve. Can they access something they should not or cause the system to act with privileges the attacker does not have? That’s why I don’t think model-level guardrails should ever be treated as the only or primary security boundary. You still need deterministic controls around the model. This includes proper authorization, least-privilege access, isolation, and validation. The surrounding systems matter just as much as the model itself. And traditional application security doesn’t disappear just because AI is involved. Model output should still be treated as untrusted input. If that output ends up in a browser, database query, shell command, web request, or another downstream system without the right controls, you can still end up with very familiar vulnerabilities: XSS, SQL injection, command injection, SSRF, and so on. I think the model is new. A lot of the dangerous sinks aren’t.

What’s one thing you wish you’d known when you first started?

Learn systems, not checklists. When I started, I was tempted to collect huge lists of techniques, payloads, tools, and bypasses and then work through them one by one. Those lists can be useful.

I still use them. But understanding how a system works has been far more valuable. Its internal logic. The data flows. Trust relationships. Assumptions. Why one component is allowed to talk to another. Why a particular restriction exists in the first place. I also learned not to assume something is secure because it looks secure, or because plenty of researchers have already tested it.

A lot of interesting research begins with: “Why does this work this way?” rather than “Which payload should I try next?” There’s some luck involved too. Sometimes you spend days following something that goes absolutely nowhere. Then you notice one tiny detail almost by accident and it turns into a high-impact finding. You can’t control that part. You can control whether you keep questioning things long enough to notice it.

What advice or resources would you recommend to researchers trying to land their first valid report?

Get comfortable with the fundamentals, then pick one program and one target and stick with them for a while. Constantly jumping between targets makes it difficult to build a real mental model of any of them. Use the application. Explore weird flows. Test different roles and permission levels. Read the documentation. Watch the requests and responses. Look at the APIs. Labs, courses, public write-ups, disclosed bug bounty reports, and intentionally vulnerable applications are all useful too. They teach you where bugs tend to hide and, over time, help build the intuition to recognize similar situations elsewhere.

One mistake I see a lot is relying on tools too early. Another is giving up because the obvious tests didn’t find anything. Tools help. They don’t build the mental model for you. And when you finally do find something, spend the extra time validating it properly. Create a working PoC. Make reproduction easy for the security team. Understanding one target deeply will usually get you further than trying to find a bug as quickly as possible.

What do you enjoy doing when you aren’t hacking?

Endurance sports, mainly road cycling, especially in the mountains. I enjoy the physical challenge of a long climb and pushing myself over longer distances. It’s also a great way to get away from screens for a while and spend some time outside. There’s actually something about climbing that feels pretty similar to vulnerability research. You can put in a lot of effort without seeing much progress. Sometimes you have no idea whether what you’re doing is going to lead anywhere. You just keep going. And every now and then, it pays off.

Any social media profiles you’d like to share with our readers?

You can find me on HackerOne.

Thank you, @r31n, for participating in GitHub’s bug bounty researcher spotlight! Each submission to our bug bounty program is a chance to make GitHub, our products, and our customers more secure, and we continue to welcome and appreciate collaboration with the security research community. So, if this inspired you to go hunting for bugs, feel free to report your findings through HackerOne.

The post How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Technical Advisory: PHP2Shell Pre-Auth RCE (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS v4.0 9.2 | No exploitation observed by Bitdefender | Patch immediately

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical pre-authentication remote code execution flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2) in the PHP worker process, and every unpatched PHP installation serving web requests is at risk, with Apache servers running mod_php at highest risk. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now; on 8.1 or older, which have no official fix, move to a supported branch. Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and GravityZone detections cover those actions. For exact remediation steps including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

2026-10-22: Initial publication. Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of this date. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation.

Situation

The flaws were first discovered by lcfr_hax of Calif, which reported an unconditional remote code execution with a shared root cause to PHP on 2026-08-11. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause that day, Wiz Research reported on 2026-08-24, and OpenAI sent further attack vectors on 2026-09-18 (The PHP Foundation, “Today’s PHP security release and how we’re strengthening PHP security”, October 2026). Wiz Research demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against the WordPress, Drupal and Joomla container images and credits frontier AI models with substantially lowering the barrier to exploit development.

The coordinated disclosure held until two days before the planned release. On 2026-10-20 at about 15:00 UTC the CVE IDs began circulating online with a wrong release time and a CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). PHP published its pre-announcement early at 19:30 UTC and moved the release forward from 2026-10-22 to 2026-10-21 at 14:00 UTC. At about 20:00 UTC Calif mistakenly published a video showing its proof of concept working against a number of targets. PHP says no technical details leaked, but the video contributed to the faster development of various proofs of concept. On 2026-10-21 at 07:41 UTC Chainguard published container images containing the fix more than six hours before the release, breaking the embargo. PHP released the fixed versions at 14:00 UTC and published PHP, “Security advisory 2026-10-21-5”, October 2026 with them (The PHP Foundation, October 2026). PHP states that its security team identified no functional exploits at the time of release.

Datadog Security Labs, “PHP2Shell critical vulnerabilities”, October 2026 reports that AWS saw exploitation attempts from 2026-10-17, and describes broad untargeted scanning. Bitdefender has not independently confirmed this. Operational guidance is maintained by NCSC-NL, “PHP2Shell operational page”, October 2026 and in CERT-EU, “Security advisory 2026-018”, October 2026.

Several GitHub repositories claim to host proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. JFrog, “PHP2Shell: all you need to know”, October 2026 reports that some are pranks, one of which changes the victim’s wallpaper. Treat every unofficial PoC as untrusted code.

Bitdefender telemetry has observed no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication, and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation. This is a time-bound observation and not evidence that the threat is overstated. Any change will be recorded in Advisory History.

A Disclosure Is Not an Exploitation

Much of the early coverage of PHP2Shell blurs two different events, and the difference changes what you should do.

A vulnerability disclosure says a flaw exists, how severe it could be, and which versions fix it. The CVSS score of 9.2 describes what an attacker could do, not what any attacker has done. A disclosure carries no evidence that anyone is attacking anything.

A proof of concept is code that demonstrates the flaw. Proofs of concept range from working research tools to broken or malicious fakes, as the repositories above show. A working proof of concept lowers the cost of an attack but is not an attack.

Exploitation in the wild means someone has used the flaw against real systems that did not belong to them, and defenders have the evidence: requests, crashes, shells, files. Only this stage justifies statements such as “customers are being compromised.”

PHP2Shell sits between the second and third stages. It is disclosed and patched. Working proofs of concept exist in researchers’ hands, and Calif’s video showed one against a number of targets. PHP’s team saw no functional exploits at release. Datadog attributes exploitation attempts to AWS from 2026-10-17, which we have not confirmed, and Bitdefender telemetry shows none. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are watching for the next step.

Two conclusions follow, and they point the same direction. Do not treat the absence of confirmed attacks as a reason to wait, because the flaw needs no login and no application bug, and the proofs of concept and fixed code are public. And do not treat the severity score as proof of compromise: patch first, then check for compromise using the signals in What To Do, instead of assuming the worst.

How It Can Be Exploited

PHP runs behind the web server through a SAPI (Server API), the interface that hands each request to PHP. The two most common are mod_php, where PHP is loaded directly into the Apache web server’s own processes, and PHP-FPM, a separate pool of PHP worker processes that the web server forwards requests to. Both CVEs are memory corruption bugs, meaning the attacker causes PHP to read or write memory it should not, inside those worker processes.

On mod_php, exploitation happens during request initialization, before any application code runs. We assess that PHP2Shell is a runtime bug, not an application bug: on mod_php, CMS updates, plugin hygiene and application hardening do not change exposure. The attacker needs no login and no flaw in WordPress, Drupal or the custom code behind the site.

We assess with high confidence that exploitation attempts will follow. Calif’s video of a working proof of concept, Wiz’s demonstrations against common CMS container images, and Wiz’s report that frontier AI models lowered the cost of building exploits all shorten the path from disclosure to attack. The attack follows the established pattern for internet-facing remote code execution: scanning first, though version fingerprinting is unreliable here, then initial access through one of two paths. CVE-2026-109618 uses a single oversized request to corrupt memory while PHP is still setting the request up. CVE-2026-109619 reuses memory left behind by an earlier request on the same worker. No public source yet documents the automated phase, the hand-off to human operators, or post-exploitation activity for PHP2Shell specifically. The established pattern for comparable flaws is a first shell, a reverse shell back to attacker infrastructure, a webshell for persistent access, tool downloads, privilege escalation and persistence. These are the stages defenders should prepare for, not observed PHP2Shell behavior.

Exposure requires an unpatched PHP branch serving web requests. The demonstrated application-independent path is mod_php. CVE-2026-109619 additionally needs session.upload_progress.enabled left at its default of on, and attacker requests landing on the same worker, while its fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only. Several things limit how many attempts succeed: CVE-2026-109618 also requires defeating ASLR (address space layout randomization, which places code at unpredictable memory addresses), the same-worker requirement constrains CVE-2026-109619, and public PoCs are unreliable. Other factors widen the blast radius: no authentication, no application flaw needed on mod_php, and a default-on setting in the CVE-2026-109619 path. Wiz reports versions back to PHP 5.4 are affected, and branches 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have no official fix. The version string is unreliable in both directions: distribution backports fix the bug without changing the version, so scanners flag patched hosts, while “latest available” on an end-of-life branch still means vulnerable. Exploitation attempts are reported by a named third party and are expected; successful exploitation at scale is not established.

Hunting guidance from other vendors, including Datadog, points defenders at crash evidence: memory exhaustion errors at initialization and Apache segmentation faults. A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running. Crash logs measure attempts, not compromises.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How It Works

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption). An out-of-memory condition (PHP running out of its allowed memory) interrupts PHP while request data is only partly initialized, and the cleanup routine then treats the half-built data as valid. Datadog describes the trigger as an unauthenticated POST request with a single very long form field name, about 3.5 MB in the lab. When the attempt crashes or fails, PHP logs a memory exhaustion error reported as “Unknown on line 0”.

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state). Request-owned state survives after its memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker reuses it. This is a use-after-free: the program keeps using a pointer to memory it has already released, which an attacker can refill with data they control. The path requires session.upload_progress.enabled, the setting that tracks file upload progress in the user’s session and is on by default. The fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only.

On Apache, a crashed worker appears in the error log as AH00052, the message Apache writes when a child process exits on a signal such as a segmentation fault. A successful exploit can avoid both this entry and the memory exhaustion error.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

Read the PHP version and the Server API line from a phpinfo page served by the web server: a one-line file containing <?php phpinfo(); placed temporarily in the web root, which prints the running build’s configuration. Delete it immediately afterward, because it exposes that configuration to anyone who requests it. Do not rely on php -v, which reports the command-line binary and not necessarily the build the web server runs. On Apache, apachectl -M | grep -i php lists a loaded PHP module if mod_php is in use; systemctl list-units | grep php shows running php-fpm services. For distribution packages, search the package changelog for the CVE IDs, because a backported fix may not change the version number: on RHEL-family systems, rpm -q --changelog php-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]'; on Debian or Ubuntu, apt changelog php8.x-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]', substituting your branch for 8.x. For containers, check base image tags, especially WordPress, Drupal and Joomla images.

SAPI

Exploitability

mod_php

Application-independent RCE demonstrated

PHP-FPM

Susceptible; see the open PHP-FPM note in How it Works

php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed

In scope per PHP; no public exploitability analysis

2. Patch or Mitigate

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Branches 7.4, 8.0, 8.1 and older have no official fix; moving to a supported branch is the only reliable answer, and unofficial backports are unvetted. PHP states: “there are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice.” Where patching must wait:

Mitigation (all partial)

Addresses

session.upload_progress.enabled=0; on PHP 8.5 also fatal_error_backtraces=0

CVE-2026-109619

pm.max_requests=1 on PHP-FPM (each worker exits after one request, breaking the same-worker requirement; costs a process start per request)

CVE-2026-109619 on FPM

memory_limit=-1 combined with request-size limits at the web server or proxy and container memory limits; do not use the operating system’s per-process limits (RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_DATA) for this

CVE-2026-109618

WAF or reverse-proxy blocking

Both, partial

Restart all PHP workers after any configuration change; running workers keep the old settings.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

A clean error log does not clear a host. Look for:

Very large requests in proxy or WAF logs, consistent with a multi-megabyte form field name. Request bodies are often not logged, so look at request size. This applies to CVE-2026-109618 only; no log signature has been published for CVE-2026-109619.

“Unknown on line 0” memory exhaustion errors and AH00052 entries (failed or crashed attempts).

Shell processes whose parent is a web worker (apache2, httpd, php-fpm, php-cgi).

New script files in upload, cache and tmp directories.

Start the lookback at 2026-10-17, the earliest attempts reported by Datadog. If you find a compromise, rotate the secrets the PHP process could read: application database credentials, API keys in environment variables or configuration files, and cloud credentials present on the host.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Watch this advisory, the PHP advisory and CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog for updates. Keep alerting on child processes of web workers, and keep software inventory current in GravityZone so hunting can be scoped to hosts running PHP.

Indicators of Compromise

Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication and we have no indicators of compromise to share.

GravityZone Coverage

The PHP2Shell exploit is memory corruption inside the PHP worker, so GravityZone detection focuses on what the attacker does with the access it gives: starting a shell, opening a reverse shell, planting a webshell, downloading tools, escalating privileges and persisting. These actions are where the attack becomes visible, and where the detections below fire.

Bitdefender MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring and active response, and the MDR team is actively hunting for PHP2Shell together with Bitdefender Labs. MDR uses software inventory to scope hunts to systems running PHP, so keeping inventory current in GravityZone helps.

External Attack Surface Management (EASM) applies because the vulnerable PHP service is internet-facing: it identifies exposed assets from outside the perimeter without an agent, unlike Risk Management, which scans managed endpoints. EASM detects the PHP version on exposed assets, so it can show which of your internet-facing services run an affected version.

GravityZone Risk Management detects the PHP version installed on managed endpoints and compares it with data from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and the security advisories of specific Linux distributions (Ubuntu, CentOS and Red Hat). It flags vulnerable versions and the CVEs that apply to them.

The rules below come from Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), Advanced Threat Control (ATC), and Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction (PHASR). Rules marked blocking stop the post-exploitation action, not the exploit.

Linux

Three detections work; however, PHP is deployed (Apache module, PHP-FPM or php-cgi):

First shell: Anomaly.Process.NewProcessStartedShell

Reverse shell: EDR.PhpReverseShell, ATC.BashReverseShell.X (blocking)

The rest of the Linux detections are tied to the web worker process and fire for Apache mod_php and php-cgi, not when the parent process is PHP-FPM:

First shell: EDR.WebServiceSpawnShell

Reverse shell: EDR.WebReverseShell (incident), the generic reverse-shell rule family

Hands-on activity: EDR.SuspiciousWebServerBehaviour and .2, EDR.Generic.Nexus.WebServer

Webshell: EDR.WebServiceWriteScript

Windows

On Windows, PHP typically runs as php-cgi.exe, and alerts such as SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell already monitor php-cgi and other web server configurations. ATC has heuristics that detect command shells started by php-cgi.exe when post-exploitation actions follow through those shells, such as enumeration, credential dumping or adding a new user to the machine. Because both flaws require heap manipulation (the attacker shaping how PHP lays out memory), Process Introspection also detects suspicious process creation from memory pages that do not belong to a loaded module. Process Introspection checks the state of a process during key operations such as creating a child process, which is where an exploited PHP worker would start a shell.

Hands-on recon: SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell (104852)

Webshell: SuspiciousServerRootFile (100942), WebShellCreation (102198)

Reverse shell: PossibleReverseShellSocketPipeChild and Parent (103945, 103946), PythonReverseShell (102194), the NetCat rules, Empire.Stager.WAR (105626)

Tool download: CertutilDownload, PotentialIngressToolTransferViaCURL

Persistence: NewScheduledTask, PowershellScheduledTaskCreated

PHASR (blocking): whoami, certutil, curl and PowerShell downloads, account creation, local admin group changes, schtasks

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
PHP Threat Is Likely Far From Over, Despite Limited Exploitation So Far: GuidePoint Expert

Posted by: GuidePoint Security

< 1 min read

October 22, 2026 – Published on CRN

The threat of attackers potentially exploiting a pair of critical-severity PHP vulnerabilities could persist for some time, even though the initial evidence of exploitation of the PHP2Shell flaws appears to be modest, according to a threat intelligence expert at GuidePoint Security.The widespread usage of PHP—and the difficulty faced by some organizations around identifying every service that leverages it—could mean that attackers will continue to seek exploitation opportunities for months to come, GuidePoint’s Justin Timothy told CRN Thursday.Despite the limited exploitation so far, “the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and their exploitation definitely have the potential to be a Log4j-Log4Shell kind of scenario,” said Timothy, threat intelligence consultant at Reston, Va.-based GuidePoint Security, No. 32 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500.

“We saw the effects of that for months afterwards,” Timothy said. “I’m afraid that we’re going to be seeing the same kind of trailing [impacts]—where people haven’t patched and threat actors are exploiting it [for some time].”Read More HERE.

Categories: Incident Response & Threat Intelligence

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2021-41617

sshd in OpenSSH 6.2 through 8.x before 8.8, when certain non-default configurations are used, allows privilege escalation because supplemental groups are not initialized as expected. Helper programs for AuthorizedKeysCommand and AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand may run with privileges associated with group memberships of the sshd process, if the configuration specifies running the command as a different user.

Acknowledgments

Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends configuring the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the exploitation risk of this vulnerability.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Siemens Industrial Edge Device Kit
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
View CSAF

Summary

Users of Industrial Edge Devices are advised to consult the respective Security Advisories for their devices (for Siemens Industrial Edge devices see Additional Information). Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens recommends specific countermeasures for products where fixes are not, or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge Device Kit are affected:

Industrial Edge Device Kit - arm64 V1.10 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-44414, CVE-2026-44415)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell: Two Critical PHP Flaws Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: These steps do not fully address either vulnerability, so they should be used only until the upgrade is complete, and each one should be tested first
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Exploitation status

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said it had not observed exploitation as of publication, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said a proof of concept was public with no active exploitation identified. The European Union's CERT-EU said technical details and proofs of concept were circulating, which raised the likelihood of exploitation, but did not confirm attacks. The BSI reported no confirmed exploitation but unconfirmed reports of existing exploits, and expected broad exploitation within hours of the patches because public details make exploit development fast. Each agency urged immediate patching.

Several security vendors have reported potential exploitation. Their honeypot and customer telemetry reportedly showed exploitation attempts, including at least one report of activity on October 17, before the public disclosure, and others reporting attacks at scale on October 21, with attackers adapting payloads to evade web application firewall (WAF) rules. Given the public details and proof-of-concept code, any internet-facing PHP server that remained unpatched after October 20 should be treated as potentially exposed.

Who is affected?

Any PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The PHP project assessed Apache with mod_php as the highest risk. Third-party products, appliances, containers and hosting platforms that embed PHP may also be affected. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) is maintaining a repository of affected third-party products.

Broadcom has said that no Broadcom Enterprise Security Group products have been confirmed affected.

Patching

Patching is the recommended remediation. The PHP project's fixed versions are:

PHP 8.5: upgrade to 8.5.12

PHP 8.4: upgrade to 8.4.27

PHP 8.3: upgrade to 8.3.36

PHP 8.2: upgrade to 8.2.35

Organizations should also take the following steps.

Restart after upgrading. Restart PHP-FPM pools and Apache so that no worker keeps running the old binary. PHP-FPM must be patched too.

Find every instance. Inventory internet-facing hosts first, then internal ones. Check the version the web server actually runs, for example, with php-fpm -v, or by checking the Apache module, and not only with the command-line php -v, since the two can differ.

Rebuild containers and check appliances. Rebuild images on patched base images, and check third-party appliances and hosting providers that embed PHP.

Handle unsupported branches. The PHP project published no upstream fix for PHP 8.1, 7.x and 5.x, although it has provided limited source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Check with your operating system vendor for backported packages. For example, Red Hat has published an advisory for PHP 7.4 (RHSA-2026:87080) and Fedora has issued updates. Where no backport exists, apply the interim mitigations below and plan an upgrade to a supported branch.

CISA recommended taking unpatched systems offline, and the BSI recommended considering disconnecting vulnerable servers from the internet, if patching cannot be done promptly. The CERT-EU advisory recommended isolating internet-facing applications until the fix is applied and verified.

Interim mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible, the PHP project's advisories list configuration changes that reduce exposure. These steps do not fully address either vulnerability, so they should be used only until the upgrade is complete, and each one should be tested first. The PHP advisories include further settings, such as limits on request size and structure for CVE-2026-109618.

Disable session upload-progress tracking by setting session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in the active php.ini.

Disable OPcache by setting opcache.enable = 0. This removes the OPcache stale-cache technique, which gives arbitrary file reads. A noticeable performance cost is to be expected.

Check fatal-error backtraces. One technique requires them to be enabled, so turn them off if they are on and follow the PHP advisory for the exact setting.

Reload PHP. Restart PHP-FPM or Apache so the new settings take effect.

Put a WAF in front of the application. Several WAF vendors released virtual-patch rules covering the anomalous multipart and session traffic these exploits use. Confirm with your vendor that the rule is deployed and in blocking mode.

Reduce exposure. Restrict access to PHP applications that do not need to be public, and run PHP workers with least privilege so that a compromise exposes as few files, credentials and connected services as possible.

The BSI also recommended enabling SELinux or AppArmor where possible on Linux to limit the impact of any RCE vulnerability.

Protection

Symantec, Carbon Black and CBX protect against this threat. The Protection Bulletin lists every protection by name and is updated as new information becomes available, so it should be treated as the definitive reference. Additional product protections are in development.

Behavior-based protection

Symantec Endpoint behavioral protection (SONAR) includes 16 signatures covering suspicious behavior, suspicious process launches, registry and file writes, process starts and User Account Control (UAC) bypass attempts associated with PHP2Shell exploitation.

Carbon Black App Control

Carbon Black App Control customers can use four execution control rules to monitor, and later block, behavior potentially related to PHP2Shell exploitation. Every rule should start in Report mode. The rules should be updated with known indicators of compromise (IOCs) as they are published, and reported activity verified before any rule is switched to Block.

Linux PHP suspicious application execution: php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd or apache2 launching sh, bash, python, perl, curl, wget or nc.

Linux suspicious command lines: any process whose command line matches /dev/tcp/, fsockopen or mkfifo.

Windows PHP suspicious application execution: php-cgi.exe or php.exe launching cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil.exe or cscript.exe.

Windows suspicious command lines: nc.exe run with -e, or PowerShell command lines containing System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient or New-Object Net.WebClient.

Endpoint detection and response hunting

Hunting queries and watchlist queries are available for both Carbon Black Cloud and Carbon Black OnPrem. They look for the same behavior as the App Control rules: PHP and web server processes spawning shells, scripting interpreters or download tools on Linux, PHP processes spawning command interpreters on Windows, and the suspicious command lines listed above. Customers should hunt for this behavior on any PHP server that was unpatched after October 20.

File-based protection

Symantec file-based protection detects related tooling as Hacktool.Php2shell.

The full list of SONAR signature names, the complete App Control rule definitions and the exact Carbon Black query syntax are in the Protection Bulletin.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of OpenSSL. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Distinguished Names within CMP messages. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it as a format specifier. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to disclose information in the context of the client or server.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

The Evo Remediation Agent is in Open Preview for Snyk Open Source vulnerabilities in Evo Agentic AppSec. To run campaigns, you need:

Workspaces

SCM integration

Preview access for your Tenant.

During Open Preview, a daily fix allowance applies, and hosted sandboxes use public package registries. Ready to put Evo Remediation Agent to work on your backlog? Talk to your Snyk account team about Open Preview access.
