Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
This alert is intended for technical teams responsible for network security, asset management, and system administration across all sectors.

It is also intended to inform individuals operating PHP workloads, websites and applications.

Background

PHP Foundation have published advanced notice of critical vulnerabilities; organisations are recommended to monitor for the release of relevant patches to address these vulnerabilities.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) is aware of related media reporting which identifies these vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, though no official technical details have been publicly released at this time.

ASD’s ACSC understands that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards may be affected.

ASD’s ACSC is not aware of successful active exploitation within Australia, related to these vulnerabilities.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises individuals and organisations to:

Identify PHP within their environments.

Monitor and review PHP official guidance at PHP Security Release

Prepare to update and apply security patches as they become available.

Monitor PHP applications and associated environments for potentially malicious activity.

Where to get help

Organisations that have been impacted, suspect impact or require advice and assistance can contact us via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371).

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP2Shell - Critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): detection, analysis, and remediation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: What happened On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Key points and observations

PHP disclosed two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. We independently reproduced them and confirmed that application-level authentication can't block an attack: PHP processes the malicious request before any application code runs.

AWS reported PHP2Shell exploitation attempts in the wild as early as October 17, 2026, four days before public disclosure and the release of patches.

Only patching fixes these vulnerabilities. Mitigations circulating in the community, such as setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in the PHP configuration file, don't fully protect you.

Successful command execution doesn’t necessarily crash the worker. Memory disclosure, including the PHPSESSID technique, can provide addresses needed for exploitation.

To investigate, look for large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors during request initialization, and unexpected shell processes.

Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both have a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2. PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 contain the fixes. Older PHP branches are also affected. Although PHP 8.1 and earlier are outside normal upstream support, the PHP security team provided source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Users of older branches should check their vendor’s security advisory for patched packages or upgrade to a supported version.

Before the public disclosure, our team built exploits for the vulnerabilities so we could analyze them and develop detections. Our reproduction triggers the out-of-memory corruption described in CVE-2026-109618 on PHP 8.5.11 with an unauthenticated HTTP POST request. The request never reaches the target application's code. Instead, PHP runs the attacker's command while it cleans up the failed request. Any PHP script exposes the vulnerable path, even one that only prints a response.

The two flaws affect different stages of the request life cycle:

CVE-2026-109618: After a memory allocation fails, PHP leaves invalid data behind for its cleanup routine to process.

CVE-2026-109619: A PHP worker can reuse stale state from a previous request.

Our detailed walkthrough primarily covers CVE-2026-109618, although we will discuss CVE-2026-109619 as well.

How to know if you're affected

Any PHP runtime that serves HTTP requests is in scope. PHP's release announcement warns that all web deployments are affected, including Apache modules, PHP FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

When you build your inventory, include containers and applications that bundle their own PHP interpreter. Don't rely solely on the command-line PHP installation: it can use a different version or configuration than the runtime that serves your web application.

Fixed versions

The advisories for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 list the same fixed versions for each supported branch:

PHP branch

Affected releases

First fixed release

8.2

Before 8.2.35

8.2.35

8.3

Before 8.3.36

8.3.36

8.4

Before 8.4.27

8.4.27

8.5

Before 8.5.12

8.5.12

Remediation steps

For each deployment:

Record the PHP version, the package or image source, the owner, and the update process.

Apply the upstream or distributor update. If you use a vendor package, check the vendor's advisory, because vendors sometimes backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

Rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Restart or replace every worker that still runs the old runtime.

PHP 8.1 and older

PHP 8.1 and older are outside the PHP project's normal support window. To address this vulnerability, PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, but expect slower fixes for these branches as vendors have more work to do in order to validate the fix. If you run those older branches, check whether your vendor covers it or move to a supported PHP branch.

If you can't patch immediately

Restrict public access to exposed applications. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, CERT-EU recommends isolating internet-facing applications. Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

PHP's temporary mitigation guidance also describes measures for each vulnerability:

CVE-2026-109618: Enforce memory_limit=-1 at the administrator level, and pair it with request limits at the frontend and memory limits on the container. Limit the size of decoded request bodies, including requests without a usable Content-Length header. Don't substitute process limits such as RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, because they can trigger the allocation failures this vulnerability depends on. Even with these measures, allocation failures can still happen, and an attacker who exhausts system memory can destabilize the host.

CVE-2026-109619: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply both settings in configuration that loads before PHP parses the request, then restart every worker. Remove any per-request settings that generate early diagnostics. Hiding the errors doesn't prevent access to stale state.

These measures reduce your exposure while you update, but none of them fully fixes the vulnerabilities. Patching is the only complete fix.

How the vulnerabilities work

Both vulnerabilities follow the same pattern: a fatal error interrupts PHP partway through an operation, and PHP later treats the incomplete state as valid.

CVE-2026-109618: Interrupted initialization after memory exhaustion

PHP converts form submissions into the $_POST array. Internally, PHP stores the array's keys and values in a hash table, in entries called buckets. Before application code reads a submitted field, PHP allocates memory for the field name, creates any nested arrays, and inserts the values into those hash tables.

The flaw appears when an insertion stops halfway through. In the version we tested, _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i() increments the hash table's entry counters before it allocates a copy of the new key. Here is the relevant sequence in PHP's source:

idx = ht->nNumUsed++; ht->nNumOfElements++; p = ht->arData + idx; p->key = key = zend_string_init(str, len, GC_FLAGS(ht) & IS_ARRAY_PERSISTENT);

If the key allocation exceeds memory_limit, PHP raises a fatal error and abandons the insertion. At that point, the counters already include the new bucket, but PHP never initialized the bucket's key or value.

PHP still cleans up the failed request. When it destroys the array, it visits every counted bucket and interprets its contents as PHP values. The unfinished bucket holds bytes left over from an earlier allocation. An attacker who controls those leftover bytes controls what the cleanup code does next, up to running a shell command.

This hash table bug is one instance of the broader flaw that PHP's CVE-2026-109618 advisory describes: a memory error abandons an operation while the internal state is incomplete, and cleanup then treats that state as valid. Multiple public PoCs have demonstrated other code paths with the same flaw, so don't build defenses around the specifics of the hash table exploit.

CVE-2026-109619: Stale state crosses request boundaries

A PHP worker handles many requests over its lifetime. Some worker-wide fields point to memory that belongs to a single request. If PHP frees that memory without clearing the fields, a later request can follow a stale pointer into freed memory. This class of bug is called a use-after-free.

According to the PHP advisory, stale state appears in two ways: a fatal error interrupts PHP while it resets state, or a late shutdown diagnostic recreates state after cleanup. The advisory confirms two exploitable cases:

Fatal-error backtraces (PHP 8.5 only): Fatal-error reporting keeps backtrace state after shutdown. A configuration diagnostic in a later request reads that state before PHP initializes it. PHP confirmed that this case leads to command execution on mod_php.

Upload processing: After a fatal error, upload processing can leave session or decoder state behind. A later upload reads that state before normal initialization. PHP confirmed command execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM. On PHP-FPM, the attack also needs the application to perform a suitable operation after startup succeeds.

The upload case matters because of session upload progress, which tracks uploads before the target script runs. PHP enables this feature by default, and it runs even if the application never calls session_start().

To exploit CVE-2026-109619, an attacker's requests must reach the same worker. A larger worker pool lowers the success rate of each attempt, but it doesn't remove the flaw.

Exploitation walkthrough for CVE-2026-109618

Our reproduction runs PHP 8.5.11, built from commit 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8, on Debian 12 (ARM64). It uses Apache's prefork worker model with mod_php, and sets memory_limit=16M, post_max_size=64M, and automatic POST parsing. To make allocations and failures easier to observe, our lab runs a single worker, disables OPcache, and shows errors in responses. The exploit ends by calling glibc's system().

The exploit works in three stages: reach the interrupted insertion, fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data, and turn request cleanup into a system() call.

Stage 1: Reach the interrupted insertion

The request carries three form fields:

=<binary value>&a=1&<very long field name>[x]=1

Each field plays a role:

The empty-name field prepares memory for reuse.

The a=1 field makes PHP allocate hash table storage.

The oversized name field triggers the incomplete insertion.

The array syntax tells PHP to create a nested array. In the version we tested, that path reaches a string-key insertion helper that allocates the key after it updates the hash table's counters. A plain field name takes a different path that uses an already-created key that is not vulnerable.

PHP's filter extension registers the submitted variable in an internal array and then in $_POST. We size the field name so that PHP's first key allocation succeeds and the second exceeds memory_limit. The failed insertion leaves an incomplete bucket in $_POST, which PHP destroys during request shutdown.

The failure happens during request initialization. Nothing in the target script can impact or defend against the exploit (authentication, filtering…).

Stage 2: Fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data

The attacker needs the unfinished bucket to hold useful bytes, not random leftovers. Our reproduction arranges those bytes through heap grooming: a sequence of allocations and frees that steers PHP into reusing a chosen block of memory.

In this build, a small hash table uses a 320-byte allocation. The binary value in the empty-name field is 276 bytes, and once PHP adds a string header and terminator, its allocation lands in the same 320-byte size class.

PHP copies that value while it processes the field, then frees the copies because the field name is empty. The a=1 field that follows makes the hash tables reuse the freed memory, so most of the binary content survives past the first valid bucket. When the oversized field triggers the fatal error, PHP has counted the second bucket but not initialized it, so PHP reads its contents from the stale bytes the attacker planted. The payload shapes those bytes to resemble a PHP value that points to a fake array.

Stage 3: Turn array cleanup into a function call

PHP arrays hold a destructor callback, the function PHP calls to clean up each element when it deletes the array. The attacker sets the expected location of this callback to the address of system() and points the array's element at a command string.

During shutdown, PHP follows the stale value into the fake array and calls the supplied callback with the supplied element. In our lab, the call becomes system(<command>). The attacker controls the callback address and its pointer argument, allowing the cleanup routine to call system() with a command string.

Here is the full sequence:

Request initialization fails → Request shutdown destroys $_POST → PHP interprets the unfinished bucket as an array → PHP destroys the fake array → The destructor callback invokes system(command)

Our system-call trace records a shell running the command, and the process tree shows its children under an Apache worker. The command runs with the worker's privileges, which are www-data in our lab.

Our refined exploit returns HTTP 200 with the memory-exhaustion error in the response body, and finishes in 3.10 seconds. Process snapshots show the same Apache worker still running during and after the command. A successful HTTP status doesn't mean a request was harmless, and the exploit doesn't need to crash a worker. The process trace is stronger evidence of execution than the response delay alone.

Exploit requirements and limitations

An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses. Neither constraint prevents exploitation, and reports of active attacks are already circulating.

Request and memory limits

The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit. When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table.

PHP's default memory limits are vulnerable. Setting memory_limit=-1 blocks the known exploitation path, but don't treat it as a long-term fix: if the underlying allocation still fails, an attacker may still reach remote code execution.

Address discovery is a separate requirement

To turn the cleanup bug into command execution, the attacker needs valid memory addresses for the fake data structures and for the function they want to call, such as system(). Address space layout randomization (ASLR) randomizes those addresses, so guessing them can take repeated requests and crash workers.

A memory leak removes much of that guesswork. Wiz describes using the PHPSESSID cookie to leak process memory back to the attacker. If the leaked bytes include pointers that stay valid in the target worker, the attacker can use them to make the exploit more reliable.

Public reports of exploitation

As of October 21, we have multiple reports of active exploitation in the wild. We’re also aware of broad untargeted scanning going on.

How the patch addresses both flaws

The PHP security patch changes how memory exhaustion interrupts execution. A soft limit now defers the error until PHP reaches a safe point, which lets an in-progress operation finish initializing its data. If memory use crosses a higher hard limit, PHP terminates the worker at once with _exit(137) instead of running normal cleanup over a potentially invalid state.

The patch also resets request-owned global state before anything can reuse it. During shutdown, PHP clears error and exception state, and it initializes serialization and session state before early request processing can reach it.

The hash-table insertion still updates its counters before it allocates the key, even in PHP 8.5.12. The fix changes the surrounding error handling instead, so an allocation failure no longer leaves the halfway-initialized entry for ordinary cleanup to process.

The fix looks complete for the known exploit, but we consider the underlying pattern risky. Updating metadata before allocating the memory it describes leaves the door open to similar bugs. If an attacker finds another way to interrupt initialization so that the surrounding metadata still counts unallocated memory as valid (for example, an array that records a size of 2 when an allocation failure leaves only one item), the same class of flaw can return.

The patch suggests the PHP team knows about the pattern but judged the refactor to remove it too large to finish before the fix shipped. We expect more of these bugs to surface as researchers find exploitable instances of the pattern, and backporting each one may not stay sustainable. It’s also likely that instances of this pattern unique to older versions of PHP will be found and left unpatched.

How to detect exploitation

Look for signals at three layers: the incoming HTTP request, the PHP error log, and the processes that web workers spawn. No single signal is conclusive on its own, so correlate them. A successful exploit doesn't necessarily crash the worker or return an error.

Suspicious form submissions

While there are a number of ways to trigger the vulnerability, each of them relies on delivering attacker-controlled data through PHP's request parser, which runs before the target script. For detection, look for unusual field names, encodings, and transport behavior alongside request size. Start from what your application's legitimate submissions contain and flag departures from that baseline.

Based on an analysis of multiple public PoCs, the majority begin with a similar multipart form upload. An abbreviated request looks like this:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----XYZ ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" aabb00cc ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" pwn ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="a.txt" Content-Type: application/octet-stream ------XYZ ...hundreds more parts, or one multi-megabyte fill field... ------XYZ--

These field names are useful indicators when an application doesn't normally use them. They can also appear in legitimate submissions: PHP documents the upload-progress field in browser forms, and its transparent session handling can add session identifiers to forms. Investigate unexpected use of these fields, especially alongside the structural anomalies below.

The requests create memory pressure in different ways. Some public tools append fill fields of 100 MB or more. Others use deeply nested, machine-generated names, such as files[R00001][a][a][a], repeated across hundreds of parts. Public examples fit roughly 900 parts into less than 1 MB. PHP's allocations while parsing these fields can greatly exceed the size of the body on the wire, so body size alone is a weak signal. Also monitor parts per request, brackets per field name, and nesting depth.

Inspect upload filenames for PHP tags or serialized-object fragments, such as <?php or |O:. These chains can stage payloads in filenames because PHP stores the filename in the session record.

Another path to the vulnerable function can be reached through large application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST requests whose body carries a single field name of many megabytes (3-60 MB, depending on the memory_limit of the target), along with a binary value containing raw null bytes and control characters.

Two other traffic patterns can support these chains. Uploads that declare a large Content-Length and then trickle or never finish can keep a session record alive for the exploit. On deployments with multiple workers, a burst of connections that become slow or silent while other requests proceed normally can indicate an attempt to occupy every worker but one. This helps an attacker send both requests in a state-reuse chain to the same process.

Also inspect response headers. A Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= header containing an unusually long, percent-encoded value or binary content outside the application's expected session-ID format can indicate the memory-disclosure stage returning heap contents. It can follow an otherwise unremarkable request. Compare the value against the application's normal format: valid PHP session IDs aren't limited to hexadecimal characters.

Configure your web application firewall (WAF) or reverse proxy around these behaviors, and verify what its inspection engine actually sees. A rule can't inspect bytes the engine truncates, fields its parser discards, parts it never enumerates, or bodies it handles differently because they arrived chunked.

Memory exhaustion errors

Our exploit attempt generated this fatal error in the PHP error log:

PHP Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 16777216 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 3500032 bytes) in Unknown on line 0

The Unknown on line 0 location means PHP failed during request initialization, before any script started running. Correlate these errors with oversized POST requests, upstream connection resets, and worker crashes. Memory exhaustion alone doesn't prove an attack, because legitimate workloads can also exhaust memory.

When the exploit guesses a memory address incorrectly, the Apache worker crashes with a segmentation fault. In our lab, the Apache error log recorded this message:

AH00052: child pid ... exit signal Segmentation fault (11)

Also treat a short burst of these errors as a possible setup event, prior to the actual exploit payload being sent. Because modern versions of these chains recover addresses without crashing workers and can leave a persistent include active after a single successful fire, a complete attack can produce as few as two to four memory exhaustion errors and then go quiet. A handful of these errors on one PHP worker in a short window (especially paired with any of the request indicators above) deserves investigation even if nothing crashes afterward.

Unexpected shell processes

A web worker that spawns a shell is the most direct evidence of successful exploitation. In our capture, an Apache worker spawned a shell, which then launched the attacker's commands:

apache2 (www-data) └── sh -c <reverse-shell command> └── bash [outbound connection to c2.example:443]

Investigate any shell that a web worker launches, especially when it coincides with the request or error log signals above. If your application runs external commands on purpose, build a baseline of expected activity so you can spot deviations.

Don't make your detection depend on our demonstration's command names, a specific HTTP status, or a worker crash. In our refined exploit, the request returns HTTP 200, and the same Apache worker keeps running after it executes the command.

Signals for CVE-2026-109619

For CVE-2026-109619, review early configuration warnings, shutdown diagnostics, fatal errors, and execution timeouts on routes that attackers can reach. These events can point to the state-retention paths that PHP's advisory describes.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Workload Protection has out-of-the-box coverage for PHP applications executing a shell. This detection will catch exploits of those vulnerabilities. You can check for suspicious activity using this query. Review uncommon or unusual command lines.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes detections that can help identify PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and associated command execution:

Shell spawned by web server or PHP process detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or PHP processes using process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

PHP2Shell session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or upstream crash on nginx uses nginx error logs to correlate PHP memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or upstream worker crashes on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell PHP-FPM session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or FPM worker segfault on the same host and service uses PHP error logs and PHP-FPM master logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or PHP-FPM worker segmentation faults on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell memory exhaustion with worker crash or session decode failure on an Apache host uses Apache and PHP error logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or worker crashes on the same host.

Datadog Cloud Vulnerability Management can help identify PHP vulnerability findings on supported hosts and container images. Its package scanning support covers official operating system packages; self-compiled runtimes such as our lab build need separate inventory checks. PHP application dependencies managed through Composer are also distinct from the interpreter itself.

Conclusion

Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. If you run PHP, update to a fixed release or your vendor’s patched package as soon as possible. Rebuild affected container images and restart or replace workers so they’re running the updated code. Configuration changes can block some attack paths, but patching is the only complete fix.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Title: South River Technologies Titan MFT Server 26.0.0 - code execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Windows CVE: pending Description: South River Technologies Titan MFT Server 26.0.0.364, the NextGen generation of the commercial managed file transfer server from South River Technologies (Annapolis, Maryland, United States), runs as a single .NET 8 process, titanmft.exe, registered as the Windows service SrtTitanMFTServerService under LocalSystem and serving a Blazor Server administration application on a TLS listener bound to 0.0.0.0:47443 with the product's IP-restriction feature disabled. Two independent defects chain into operating-system command execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The first is CWE-306 on the first-run administrator-creation path: while the administration database's nxUserParams table holds zero rows, the login route renders an "Initial Admin User Setup" screen to any client reaching the listener, gated only by `RunWizard = !nxUserParams.AdminUserExists() && !CreateAdminAtConsole` at MxSvrParams.cs:518-520, with no EULA block, no bootstrap ticket, no CAPTCHA, no first-boot token, no localhost restriction and no channel binding; submitting it calls AppState.CreateAdminUser followed by AppState.Login inside the same in-process circuit and lands the anonymous client in the management console. The second is CWE-78 on the job post-command path: the console field labelled "Execute After File Transfer Task" is persisted verbatim into nxJobs.document.PostCommandText and, when the job runs, is passed by MxUtilSvrJobHandler.RunCustomProcessAsync at MxUtilSvrJobHandler.cs:991 (a second pass over the same decompilation records :996), reached from the predicate at :970 via the call site at :979-982, to process creation with UseShellExecute = false, a plain Arguments string rather than ArgumentList, no allow-list and a cmd-prefix special case that concatenates "/c " + command.Substring(3).Trim(). That special case reconstitutes full shell semantics, so redirection, chaining and percent-expansion are all live in the payload space, and the child inherits the LocalSystem service token because nothing on the path impersonates, restricts the token or downgrades integrity. The framing that governs both halves: this is a first-run window, meaning a deployment state, and not an absence of authentication. The window opens when installation completes and closes the instant the first administrator exists, after which the login route renders a credential form and the account-creation half of the chain has no route whatsoever. The product's message-level authorisation is separately intact and was measured intact during the same run in which the wizard was available, which is precisely why the chain is described as a state-conditioned finding rather than as an authentication bypass. Zero [Authorize] attributes exist across the 1,880 decompiled files of the ServerCore assembly, so every authorisation decision lives in application logic and, for the setup screen, that logic is an empty-table test. The legacy /WebApi/CreateAdmin route carries the same predicate and is reachable unauthenticated but is functionally dead from a NullReferenceException in model binding, characterised across four body states, so it is a dead sibling rather than an alternative path - and repairing the binding without repairing the predicate would revive it. One detection trap is worth repeating for anyone writing a scanner or an operator self-check: a plain GET /Login returns only the 3,869-byte Blazor host shell containing none of the setup text, because the component tree renders only after the circuit boots client-side, so a raw-response grep reports "no wizard" on an installation that is in fact exposed. The authoritative check is the rendered text in a real browser, which is what this exploit's default gate mode performs. CVSS: 8.1 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) as the primary published reading, because the chain requires a deployment state the attacker can discover but cannot create, cannot extend and cannot re-open: an installation that has not yet completed first-time setup. CVSS 3.1 places "conditions beyond the attacker's control" in Attack Complexity High, and the window's duration in real deployments was never measured, so AC:L cannot be supported as a headline. Arithmetic: ISS = 1 - (0.44)^3 = 0.914816; Impact at S:U = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.87311872; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.44 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.2211673; Base = 8.09428602; Roundup to the tenth = 8.1, band High. Conditional reading, published as conditional and never as the headline figure: 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability 3.887042775, Base 9.760161495, Roundup 9.8, applicable only to one installation confirmed to be inside its first-run window, where the state condition is already satisfied and the remaining attack is four form submissions and a menu click. Rejected readings, named so the rejection is auditable: Scope Changed would compute to 9.1 under AC:H and to 10.0 under the conditional AC:L, and is rejected because the child process is created by the service inside the service's own LocalSystem token on the service's own host, so executing as the same service identity on the same host does not change scope - and because adopting Changed would put a conditional 10.0 on the table and invite the "this product has no authentication" misreading. The sink-only reading CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H computes to 7.2 and is rejected because the post-command field on its own is a documented administrator feature; an administrator reaching LocalSystem is a privilege-separation weakness, not remote code execution, and publishing either half in isolation would misrepresent the finding. PR:N is a property of the chain start rather than of the sink in isolation: the least privileged principal that reaches the sink by the documented path is a principal that did not exist before the request. Contributing classifications named but deliberately excluded from the score: CWE-250/CWE-269 for LocalSystem execution with no privilege separation, and CWE-209/CWE-200 for an unauthenticated stack-trace echo and a pre-authorised window-state leak, both reported as separate defects with no score attached here. CWE-1188 is deliberately not used because no insecure default credential ships with the product - the exposure is a state, not a secret - and using it would imply that rotating a password closes the window when in fact creating the first administrator does. There is no recorded-score correction to disclose for this finding, because the material the analysis is built from carries no CVSS vector and no base score for it; both readings were derived from the metric definitions and the measured facts, computed with the CVSS 3.1 base formula and rounded up to the tenth as that formula specifies. Impact: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on the Windows host carrying an organisation's file-exchange hub, which for this class of product is close to a worst case rather than a generic service identity. Every trading partner's exchange credentials, because connector configuration, SFTP/FTPS/WebDAV account material and the product's SSH and PGP key material - including keys used to encrypt outbound partner files and to verify inbound ones - live in the administration and domain databases, so one host compromise becomes the compromise of every exchange relationship the host participates in, with parties who have no visibility into the incident. The files themselves in transit and at rest, because connector source and destination directories are both readable and writable from the service account, permitting interception, silent substitution of content presented to a partner, and removal of evidence. Transfer configuration, because jobs, schedules, connector paths, notification settings and audit configuration can all be rewritten, which allows a recurring partner transfer to be redirected to an attacker-chosen directory with no partner-visible change, and allows auditing to be disabled for a job before it is abused. Host persistence and pivot, because LocalSystem permits creating local accounts, installing services, writing to startup locations and reading host credential stores, and MFT hosts are routinely granted broad access to internal storage and to domain resources precisely so they can collect and deliver files. Availability of scheduled transfers, because stopping the service, disabling jobs, corrupting the SQLite databases or filling the connector volume halts every exchange, which for partner agreements carrying delivery windows is a business-continuity event rather than a service outage. Detection at the product layer is anomaly-based rather than signature-based, because every step in the chain is a documented administrative action: the product's own audit surface records legitimate administration, and there are no failed logins, no injection payloads and no exploitation signatures. Exposure is a race against deployment, so its length depends on how quickly first-time setup follows installation and was not measured; the same build can be exposed for five minutes or for five days depending on the operator's process. A deployment that finished first-time setup before its listener became reachable to untrusted clients was never exposed at all. Verification boundary: full-chain dynamic verification on a Windows host with a fresh default installation of 26.0.0.364 from the BitRock unattended package, driven over HTTP and the Blazor circuit by a headless Chromium-family browser under the DevTools protocol, with Python standard-library tooling only and a raw-socket WebSocket client; the attack path is HTTP plus the product's own user interface, with no direct database writes and no direct API calls on it, and database reads taken read-only for forensic comparison. Every step - window preparation, probe set, account creation, job creation, injection, run, marker verification, control run and teardown - executed inside one scripted pass whose output was captured, so no step was proven on a machine that an earlier step's debugging had modified. Identity was measured, not inferred: the injected `cmd /c whoami > <marker>` wrote a 21-byte file containing `nt authority\system` whose modification time sits 76 ms after the job-completion timestamp the product recorded in its own job-history table for that run. A negative control ran alongside, re-authenticating as the administrator the exploit itself created, clearing PostCommandText (confirmed empty in the field and in the job document), re-running the identical job and observing a second completed job-history row with zero files transferred while the marker stayed byte-identical and its modification time unchanged to the millisecond, the two runs 111.6 seconds apart. An earlier round on the same build produced the same identity through the same path with a differently named administrator, a differently named job and an independently named marker, also 21 bytes, so the result is not a property of one account or job name. Two states were supplied by our own harness rather than by the product and both are stated here: the first-run window was re-opened by an authorised local database reset, deleting the administrator rows from the administration database and restarting the service to return a previously configured host to its shipped zero-administrator state, because an earlier pass had completed setup - a never-configured installation lands in that state by construction and the product's predicate reads only the row count, but this chain was not observed on a machine that had never been touched; and verification ran from loopback on the target host with inbound firewall rules blocking remote TCP and UDP on 47443 and 37443 for the duration of the run, so "reachable from an untrusted network" is a reading of the shipped 0.0.0.0 binding and the disabled IP restriction, both artifact facts, rather than a measurement of an attack crossing a network boundary. Exactly one payload shape was executed - a single whoami redirect proving identity - so nothing destructive, no persistence, no lateral movement, no domain compromise and no partner-system access was performed or measured. Further limits: 26.0.0.348 shares the affected listing with its first-run half confirmed dynamically and its injection tail argued from a shared code base rather than replayed, and no separate score is published for it; the pre-transfer command sibling was not executed and its exploitability is inference; the failing-transfer-with-payload combination was not executed; no cloud-shaped installation was sampled, so the CreateAdminAtConsole branch and its interaction with the legacy creation route are uncharacterised rather than exempt; no post-setup HTTP status sample was taken from the login route, the post-window evidence being that the setup screen is no longer rendered, that a credential form is rendered instead and that the created administrator's credentials were accepted through it; the window's duration in real deployments was not measured and is not estimated; and no other version, edition or family product is claimed, including Titan FTP Server, WebDrive and the older 2.x generation. The shipped proof of concept drives the product's own interface through a real browser, takes every target-specific value as an argument with no address baked in, uses the Python standard library plus a browser, and offers a read-only gate mode that performs the authoritative window check and exits non-zero when the installation is not inside the first-run window. Proof-of-concept and full analysis: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/southriver-titan-mft-firstrun-admin-setup-job-command-injection PoC location in the public repository: product/southriver/titan-mft-26.0.0/firstrun-admin-setup-job-command-injection-system-rce/exploit/southriver_titan_mft_firstrun_admin_setup_job_command_injection_system_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Title: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178, the closed-source incremental backup and file-replication server from Synametrics Technologies, Inc. (United States), written in Java and served by an embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 through the vendor's in-house sradef framework whose single front controller routes every request as /app?operation=<op>&st=<step> to a handler registered in WorkerMappings.xml, contains a path traversal (CWE-22 primary, CWE-269 and CWE-78 contributing for the deployment shape that converts the write into an execution) in the chunked-upload branch of its PublicLink handler. That branch, operation=pb with st=u, reads a length-prefixed binary frame straight from request.getInputStream() rather than through any parameter parser: four big-endian int32 fields for protocol, chunkNumber, totalChunks and size, then a four-byte length prefix followed by UTF-8 filename bytes, then exactly size body bytes. At PublicLink.java:70-110 the decompiled method evaluates new File(base, filename) on that client-supplied filename with no rejection of "..", no rejection of path separators, no base-name extraction and no canonical containment check, creates missing parent directories with target.getParentFile().mkdirs(), opens the result with new FileOutputStream(target, true) in append mode, writes the size bytes it read and returns 0, which the caller at PublicLink.java:127 turns into the client reply code="1" with <payload>0</payload>. base is the authenticated user's own folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/<user>/<generated-folder>, five components below the filesystem root, so a chunk name of ../../../../../etc/cron.d/<name> leaves it and lands a cron fragment anywhere the service identity can write. Because the documented Linux deployment shape runs the server process at uid 0 and a cron daemon was active on the verified instance, the host scheduler then reads that fragment as a root-authored job definition and runs its command field through a shell on the next minute boundary. The application never constructs, quotes or invokes a command line and every execution site in the product uses an argument vector with no shell, so the execution happens one component later and argument hygiene at the application layer would not have prevented it. The chain was verified end to end and the identity capture the cron job produced was uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root), established twice over: the fragment landed as -rw-r--r-- 1 root root at mode 0644, a file's owner after creation being the effective uid of its creator, and the scheduled job's own output reported uid 0 because the fragment names root in its user field and a scheduler will not honour that for a job file it does not already trust. The principal required is the product's lowest-trust account type. The gate on operation=pb is a secLevel=0 registration, meaning no administrator session, and the handler's own authentication call validates a credential from the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml via syncrify.users.DefaultUserManager rather than from the web-administrator store at config/umap.dat; the two stores are independent and must not be conflated. A backup user's entire legitimate job is to move bytes into its own repository, so the privilege boundary that fails here is inside the product, not a misconfiguration of the host. The defect is an omission rather than an absent control: three sibling families in the same tree, written against the same client protocol, do filter the same kind of field, the profile-upload, profile-fetch and file-splitter handlers rejecting separators with indexOf(47) and indexOf(92), the multipart upload path collapsing the name through getName(), and the download path testing indexOf("..") and answering 404 on a match. The chunk-upload branch calls none of them. There is no decoding step between the socket and the constructor, so no encoding trick is involved or needed. The product does ship a factory administration password of letmein in its first-run install wizard, but the first administrator login is forced through a password change through ChangePassword.jsp, the credential belongs to a different user store than the one gating this sink, and it is documented as a contributing fact only: it appears in no vector, raises no metric, and no conditional reading assumes it has not been rotated. No unauthenticated path to this sink was found and none is claimed. CVSS: 7.5 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding. That is the primary reading, and the two metrics that carry its nuance are AV:N and AC:H: the vulnerable component is an HTTP handler on a network-bound servlet connector and the credential it accepts exists so that remote backup clients can use it, so AV:N is the faithful classification of the component, while the deployment-dependent exposure of the listener carrying the route is priced in attack complexity rather than smuggled into the attack vector. AC:H is High for two reasons outside the attacker's control, that the listener carrying /app?operation= be reachable from the attacker's position and that the host run a scheduler which scans /etc/cron.d. Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.620146) = Roundup(7.493265) = 7.5, from ISS = 0.914816 and Impact at S:U = 5.873119. Conditional reading: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), applying only where the listener carrying the /app?operation= surface is reachable from the attacker's network position, which is the normal operating mode for a backup server whose clients push data to it remotely, and computed as Roundup(5.873119 + 2.835255) = Roundup(8.708374) = 8.8. The conditional is labelled conditional everywhere it appears, is never the headline, and the published score is 7.5 rather than 8.8. Two further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic. The changed-scope variant of the same metrics, 8.6 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected because the identity reached is the same root identity the server process already holds on the same host, so no component authority boundary is crossed by the outcome; the privilege gain is carried by PR:L and by C:H/I:H/A:H, which are the metrics meant to express it. The local-vector reading, 7.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected for an evidential reason and it is worth being explicit that this rejection lowers our own number rather than raising it: that reading is what follows if you treat the loopback binding observed in the testbed as the shipped default, and 7.8 is higher than the 7.5 this submission publishes at AV:N. The loopback binding was applied by us in the configuration before any testing began, so the host carried no public exposure while research was in progress, and there is no shipped artifact, no configuration template, no installer script excerpt and no documentation quotation, establishing the factory value of that binding in either direction, not that it binds publicly by default and not that it binds loopback by default. That unestablished reachable-listener premise is the reason AC is High and the reason the 8.8 figure is conditional, and a reader who disagrees with us about the factory default ends up with a larger score than ours, not a smaller one. No version-range claim is made: only 6.2 build 1178 was decompiled and exercised. Impact: arbitrary file write with an attacker-chosen path and attacker-chosen bytes, escalating to command execution as uid 0 on the verified deployment shape. The chunk branch writes exactly the bytes it reads to whatever path the chunk name resolves to, in append mode, creating missing parent directories via mkdirs(), so /etc/cron.d is the demonstrated escalation path and not the limit of the primitive. On this product the weight comes from what the host is for: it is a backup and file-replication server, and root on it means read access to the entire repository tree, every backup belonging to every configured client, which on a multi-tenant server is a confidentiality breach across all tenants rather than within one account, plus the server's own configuration holding administrator and backup-user credential material and transport secrets, the backup-user store comparing passwords in plaintext or storing them under a reversible permutation transform so a read of it hands over credentials directly. It also means integrity control over the replication path itself: repository contents, version and retention metadata and the server's own binaries can be altered in place, and because that path is how clients back up and restore, a modified backup set becomes a distribution channel whose corruption stays invisible until the moment the data is needed. Persistence is structural rather than incidental, a cron fragment running on every minute boundary until it is deleted and surviving restarts of both the service and the host. Availability follows the same authority: the backup service can be stopped, the host rebooted or hung, repositories deleted or truncated, and the scheduler used to keep doing so after the application alone is remediated, which destroys the recoverability that is the entire reason the product exists. All of that beyond the executed identity capture is argued from the identity reached and the deployment layout and was not performed; no repository data was read and no product file was modified or deleted during verification. Verification boundary: static reversal of the decompiled handler tree, then a live run against a single deployed instance of Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 installed from the distributed Linux tarball archive into /opt/Syncrify and started with ./run.sh, behind the embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 announcing itself as Synametrics Web Server v7. Two properties of that instance were the researchers' rather than the product's and both are carried as boundaries. The portal listener was bound to the loopback address by an explicit configuration edit made before testing, so remote reachability of the route is argued from the product's own design and binding configuration, from the front controller being the same listener that serves the client-protocol operations backup clients use, and from the structural fact that a backup server whose clients push across a network must have that listener reachable from them or it cannot perform its function; it is not a measurement from a separate host, and no shipped artifact establishes the factory binding in either direction. The backup-user store did not exist after installation, so the verification account was written into config/UserMappings.xml by hand with plaintext password comparison rather than provisioned through the administrator's user-management operation, which is licence-gated and was blocked by a zero licence count; the encrypted-entry and directory-authentication branches were examined statically and not exercised. The chain was driven from the target host itself over the loopback interface because that is how the listener was bound, so the same chain arriving from across a network segment was not verified and is not claimed. Four controls were exercised: a non-traversing chunk name through identical authentication, framing and routing in the same session, landing inside the user's own PublicLinks folder with an assertion that neither the fragment nor the marker existed, which isolates the traversal as the cause of the outcome and of nothing else; a Java-level confirmation that the multipart family's getName() collapse keeps a traversing name inside the PublicLinks root; a dispatch control against st=f, which reached a different void E() overload that parses an ed parameter as a Long and performed no write anywhere, fixing the sink to the st=u branch rather than to the handler in general after an initial static reading had attributed the upload to the wrong overload; and the four-way authentication reply table showing code="1" for a correct pair, code="-2" for a wrong password so the comparison is live, and code="-1" for an absent password and an absent user so the parameter-presence gate fired before the credential lookup was entered, which is what makes the lookup's no-comparison branch unreachable from this surface. Root execution was observed rather than inferred, and a non-root service deployment was not tested, so no claim is made about what the primitive achieves under an unprivileged service identity, where the escalation demonstrated here would not follow while the file write itself survived. Exactly one payload shape was executed, an identity capture into a marker file, and only that shape is claimed; the advisory reproduces the identity string and the frame field lengths derived from the field values but not the run's own byte capture, which was not preserved, not the generated PublicLinks folder name, which embeds the run's timestamp, not the credential pair, which are mandatory tool arguments with no default, and not the per-run fragment name or marker path. The unauthenticated surface was exhausted first with negative results: thirteen operations answer anonymous requests with real content and no credential check and all thirteen are sink-free; the remaining level-0 operations are not anonymous and answer code="-2" without valid credentials; seventeen Runtime.exec and ProcessBuilder sites exist and none is reachable anonymously; eight deserialization candidates have no network caller and the classpath carries no gadget library, no commons-collections, Jackson, XStream, Kryo or Hessian; and no template engine or naming-service lookup exists in the tree. That enumeration is not a proof the unauthenticated surface is safe, and it surfaced weaknesses deliberately not claimed here and not folded into any metric, being a manualOverride filter-block bypass exposing debug pages with a directory listing and an environment-variable dump, a password-recovery account-enumeration weakness, globally disabled CSRF prevention that is irrelevant to a chain needing credentials the attacker holds, vendor-default credentials for an embedded database that is configured but disabled and was not listening, and a default trial licence serial whose effect was left unresolved. Only Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 is claimed; the same sradef framework underpins the vendor's sibling products and this build's own web.xml still carries the display-name SynaMan, which is recorded to say where else the same construction is worth auditing, and no sibling product was tested. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/synametrics-syncrify-publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/synametrics/syncrify-6.2/publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce/exploit/synametrics_syncrify_publiclink_chunk_upload_traversal_cron_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It takes host, port, scheme, front-controller route, operation and upload step; a mandatory backup-user credential pair with no default; and the command, marker path, fragment path, fragment user field, fragment schedule, traversal depth, scheduler wait and per-request timeout as arguments, defaulting to the loopback interface, port 5800, a depth of five and an identity capture. It offers an --insecure flag for self-signed TLS on the https scheme, a --control mode that performs the identical authenticated upload with a non-traversing chunk name and then asserts that neither the fragment path nor the marker path exists, a --proof-command argument that reads proof from a local command's standard output for an operator who already holds a shell channel to the host, an --expect-root flag that exits non-zero unless the recovered proof reports uid=0, and a --cleanup mode that removes only the two paths the script created. Nothing destructive is performed and no product file is overwritten or deleted. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Title: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 - authenticated command injection Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware CVE: pending Description: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware image BR6478AC_v2.20.bin, the closed-source dual-band AC1750 SOHO wireless router from Edimax Technology Co., Ltd. (Taiwan), whose SquashFS root filesystem of roughly 2.3 MB targets MIPS 32-bit big-endian MIPS-I with a uClibc C library and carries an internal build timestamp from 2015, contains an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the WAN-configuration form handler of bin/webs, the embedded GoAhead-style HTTP server serving the management interface on TCP port 80. That binary is ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS, 762904 bytes, SHA256 ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1, reads etc/boa/boa.conf, writes /var/run/webs.pid and is kept alive by the boot path cleanlog.sh:131 invoked from init.sh:1115. The registration websFormDefine("setWAN", ...) at 0x478484, handler at 0x441cec, name string at 0x4a6250, publishes POST /goform/setWAN. Inside the handler the WAN mode is taken from the request and dispatched: websGetVar(wp, "wanMode", "") at 0x441d3c, atoi at 0x441d44, apmib_set(0x102, &wanMode) at 0x441d54, then addiu v1, zero, 2 at 0x441d60 and beq v0, v1, 0x441e74 at 0x441d6c. On the PPP branch, wanMode 2, the username field is read by websGetVar for pppUserName, name string at 0x4953f4, copied with strcpy at 0x441e94 into a fixed stack buffer, measured with strlen at 0x441ea8 and then scanned by an inline byte loop between 0x441ebc and 0x441ee4 whose only comparison is addiu a0, zero, 0x3b, a semicolon; finding one, the loop writes a NUL and stops. That single-character scan is the entire sanitisation on the path. The value is then formatted by sprintf at 0x441ee8 with the format string at 0x49a510, echo %s > /tmp/UserName, and passed to system(buf2) at 0x441f1c through the PLT slot at 0x4c6d60, which hands the line to /bin/sh -c. A pipe, an ampersand, a backtick, a dollar sign with parentheses and an embedded newline are never inspected, so a username containing no semicolon reaches the shell untouched: the payload |id > /tmp/marker # builds the command line "echo |id > /tmp/marker # > /tmp/UserName", in which the shell treats the hash as a comment swallowing the sink's own redirect and runs id as the right-hand side of a pipeline. An escape loop replacing a hash with a backslash-escaped hash does exist between 0x441f4c and 0x441fb0, but the instruction order places it after system() at 0x441f1c with no branch back to it, and it writes the configuration buffer at sp+0x18 that apmib_set(0x6d, ...) stores at 0x44200c rather than the buffer handed to the shell, so the hash character is escaped for storage and for nowhere near execution. Between websGetVar and system there is no regex call, no inet_aton, no isdigit, no isalnum, no strchr, no strcspn, no vendor validation helper and no custom validator; the inet_aton calls that do exist in the function, at 0x441dd0 and 0x441e14, belong to the static-IP branch, wanMode 1, reached via the branch at 0x441d8c, which the wanMode 2 comparison never enters, so a quick read of the decompilation misleads a reviewer into thinking this function validates addresses. The same construction appears three times in this handler and one root cause yields three reachable parameters: pppUserName on wanMode 2 with sink region 0x441e74 to 0x441f1c and configuration object 0x6d written after the sink, pptpUserName on wanMode 3 from 0x4420d0 onward with configuration object 0xf3, and L2TPUserName on wanMode 6 from 0x44246c onward with configuration object 0x128, each selected by a value the request supplies and each using the same immediate-0x3b scan, the same echo format string and the same system() call shape, so a patch confined to the PPP path leaves the PPTP and L2TP paths injectable. Reaching the handler requires a valid administrative session: the gate auth_authorize at 0x404d00 reads configuration object 0x1bc, the setup-wizard flag, through apmib_get, and once past setup the security store at 0x4c7004, a single / entry of type Basic registered from the directive Auth / /etc/boa/boa.passwd, covers every /goform/ path with HTTP Basic authentication. The product has no second lower-privileged role, so Privileges Required is High: one realm entry, one password file, one account, an Allow directive handler at 0x407688 that is a stub answering "This version of Boa doesn't support access controls", a type-None string at 0x49070c never passed to auth_add, and a shipped configuration carrying one Auth directive and no Allow directive. The route is not one of the four carrying a post-boot uptime gate, /mp.asp, /goform/mp, /advanced_management.asp and /goform/formAdvManagement, which redirect to /index.asp once /proc/uptime exceeds 600 seconds, so it is reachable at any time the device is up. The calling process is root because etc/boa/boa.conf declares User root, the server performs no setuid, chroot, namespace or capability drop and writes /var/run/webs.pid, which requires root on this filesystem, so the landing identity is uid=0(root) with no escalation step in the chain. This handler is one instance of a broad construction: a count of the shipped registration table found 91 /goform/form* handlers of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. Two adjacent observations are reported without a score: the strcpy at 0x441e94 copies attacker-controlled bytes with no length argument into a fixed stack buffer, for which no overflow was developed and no exploitability claim is made, and because the semicolon scan writes a NUL at the first semicolon a legitimate username containing one is silently truncated before storage, a correctness defect independent of the injection. The firmware image ships a populated /etc/boa/boa.passwd for the single realm and the model's published factory login is admin:1234; that is reported separately as CWE-798, carries no score, is never described as the vector for this injection, and no cryptographic match against the shipped MD5-crypt digest is claimed because the digest string captured during analysis was recorded incompletely. One detail is left unresolved rather than smoothed over: the single account entry in the image is recorded under the name root while the model's published management login is admin, and because no device was ever authenticated against, which user name the realm accepts was not established. Absence of privilege separation is likewise reported separately as CWE-250. A static comparison against a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, whose webs is a different build, ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS-I, 816568 bytes, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, found a setWAN implementation matching instruction for instruction, handler at 0x448710, websGetVar for pppUserName at 0x4488b8, strcpy at 0x4488bc, the same inline immediate-0x3b scan at 0x4488dc to 0x4488fc, the same sprintf at 0x448920 with format string 0x4a6954, system() at 0x448940, the same three parameters on the same three wanMode values and the same single-realm Basic authentication behind the same configuration flag, which points to a shared source component in the vendor's router software base; that model was not tested, nothing was executed from that image, no score covers it and it is not an exploited finding on it. A second independent command injection on the same image, in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler reaching sprintf at 0x462fd0 and system() at 0x46308c through POST /goform/formWlanMP with no sanitisation across thirty radio-calibration fields, is published as a companion advisory; it is a different handler, format string, sink address and sanitiser, so one patch point does not close both. No prior public record was found whose root cause is command injection in this setWAN handler. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, from ISS = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816, Impact at S:U = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119, Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708 and Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.234708) = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. The provenance of that figure is disclosed because it is a correction: the research notes carried 8.8 next to a PR:H vector, and 8.8 is the arithmetic of PR:L, so the score was recomputed from the vector and published at 7.2, lowering the researchers' own number by 1.6 points. Four further readings are printed with their arithmetic in the public analysis. Privileges Required Low is rejected at 8.8 High, Exploitability 2.835255 and Base Roundup(8.708373), because the product has no basic-user role. Scope Changed is rejected at 9.1 High, Impact at S:C 6.128026, Exploitability 2.286496 and Base Roundup(1.08 x 8.414522), because webs is root before the attack and root after it. Attack Complexity High is rejected at 6.6 High, Exploitability 0.705547 and Base Roundup(6.578666), because success depends on no condition outside the attacker's control, the only branch to satisfy, wanMode, being attacker-supplied. An adjacent-vector reading is published as a labelled alternative at 6.8 High, Exploitability 0.900610 and Base Roundup(6.773729), and is the honest description of a stock device whose WAN-side input policy drops new connections, the shipped firewall script dropping WAN-originated SYN at firewall.sh:180, installing a default DROP input policy at firewall.sh:187 and accepting input on other interfaces at firewall.sh:189; AV:N is retained because the service is bound to the device's own network stack and addressable over IP by every host on the segment the router serves, including guest wireless clients and anything bridged or compromised behind it, and because remote management on the WAN side or forwarding port 80 are ordinary documented features. Default internet exposure is not claimed. Two readings at 9.8 Critical, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H from Exploitability 3.887043 and Base Roundup(9.760161), are published only as explicitly labelled conditionals and never as the headline: the first applies where a deployment still accepts the factory credential and is reasoned rather than demonstrated, since no device was authenticated against; the second applies to a device still in its pre-configuration setup state, where auth_authorize returns success without a challenge for paths outside /mp.asp, /index.asp and / at 0x4052d0 while /generate_204 answers 204, and that branch is structural inference only, read from the binary and never exercised, with three shipped artefacts identifying the state as the setup wizard rather than normal operation, namely formwizResetDefault at 0x44cdbc displaying Resettowizard, formWizSetup printing NO - LOGIN-WEB when the flag is 1, and pages such as web/inter_wan.asp:214 and web/admin_timezone.asp:95 reading the same flag. That conditional's Scope Changed variant computes to 10.0 and is deliberately not published, and if the setup window has to be contested rather than found open the reading is 8.1 High from Exploitability 2.221167 and Base 8.094286. No version range is claimed: only firmware BR6478AC_v2.20.bin was examined, and only the wanMode 2 path was replicated, so no claim is made for other BR6478AC builds, for the separately marketed BR-6478AC V2 hardware revision whose firmware line is a different little-endian MIPS-II build of webs, for the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances beyond the structural reading of the same handler, or for any other model. Impact: arbitrary operating-system command execution as root on the router from a single authenticated POST indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission, since the payload travels in the PPP username field of the form the product's own wan.asp page posts. Root on this device exposes every stored secret, including precisely the PPP, PPTP and L2TP credentials this handler writes into configuration objects 0x6d, 0xf3 and 0x128, so an attacker who reaches the device can read the ISP or VPN account details the owner entered, together with the administrator password file, wireless pre-shared keys and per-station key material, VPN parameters and any certificate or key on the filesystem. It grants control of the configuration and routing plane: firewall and NAT rules, the DNS resolver handed out to clients, DHCP leases and a malicious default gateway, port forwards, wireless SSIDs and the WAN uplink itself, including rewriting the WAN mode, which is exactly the configuration path this handler owns. It grants firmware-level persistence, since root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so a compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, with recovery requiring a full reflash of a known-good image. It grants availability at will over wireless, routing, DHCP, DNS and the management service. There is no rate limit on the handler and no lockout in the Basic realm, so the route is repeatable and leaves no alert behind. Detection is poor by construction but this sink leaves one usable anomaly: a submitted WAN configuration produces ordinary behaviour and the sink's visible effect, a username written into /tmp/UserName and then into the configuration store, is what a legitimate submission does, so the indicator is the absence of the expected /tmp/UserName destination on a submission that should have created it. An injection also corrupts stored configuration in a way the owner may not notice, the semicolon scan truncating at the first semicolon and a pipe-and-hash payload storing a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, a self-inflicted availability event that doubles as a fingerprint. One operational caution: the injection is not side-effect free. A successful submission overwrites the stored WAN username and can break the uplink, which is what the handler does on any successful submission, so any demonstration must record and restore the device's original WAN configuration. Verification boundary: no physical device was powered on and no end-to-end HTTP request was ever accepted by the product. The HTTP leg, being request parsing, the authentication gate, form registration, mode dispatch and PPP branch selection, is evidenced at instruction level from the shipped binary, its configuration and its boot scripts. The execution leg is evidenced dynamically by replication of the sink's semantics rather than by detonation, because a MIPS big-endian uClibc userspace with a board-specific bootloader could not be booted end to end in the research environment: the extracted binaries faulted with SIGBUS under the available user-mode translator and full-system emulation of the board was not brought up. The question under test is not the device but whether a shell evaluates a pipeline and honours a trailing comment in a string built by the vendor's own sprintf and handed to /bin/sh -c, which is a question about POSIX shell semantics that are architecture independent, combined with the exact format string read out of the binary. The string sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 was reconstructed byte for byte for a request whose pppUserName field is |id > /tmp/marker_sw # and handed to /bin/sh -c in an isolated POSIX sandbox whose invoking shell ran as root, producing a 39-byte marker file owned by root:root containing uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) with shell exit status 0, while the sink's own /tmp/UserName destination was not created, that absence being the proof that the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment rather than being escaped, since a protected sink would have left the file behind. A benign control submitting an ordinary username created its destination containing that username and produced no marker. The same replication was repeated on a workstation under an ordinary unprivileged user account and reproduced the semantics at that identity, ruling out the alternative explanation that running as root caused the marker to appear. The harness removes any pre-existing marker and destination before each run and deletes its scratch files afterwards. Consequently the on-device landing identity of uid=0(root) is inferred from the shipped User root directive plus the root-identity replication and is not an observation from hardware; AV:N is argued from the product's transport and authentication model rather than measured across a network; the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances are a structural reading of the same handler rather than a demonstrated result; the sibling-model comparison is static only with nothing executed from that image and no score covering it; no setup-state request was sent; no dictionary or credential attack was attempted; and no overflow was developed against the unbounded stack copy. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-setwan-command-injection-root-rce Companion advisory, same product and image, different handler: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-formwlanmp-command-injection-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/edimax/br-6478ac-v2.20/setwan-command-injection-root-rce/exploit/edimax_br6478ac_setwan_command_injection_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target, and it is built so that it cannot be used accidentally against a live network. Its default mode is replication: it reconstructs the exact string the device's sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 and hands it to /bin/sh -c locally, asserting both that the injected pipeline ran and that the sink's own redirect target was not created, which is what proves the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment, then running a benign username as a negative control and asserting the opposite. That replication mode, not a device run, produced the evidence above. Arguments cover target host, Basic realm username and password, the WAN mode to select, which of the three username fields carries the payload, an option to iterate all three modes, a single non-destructive command defaulting to id, the marker path, the submit-url field value defaulting to /wan.asp, a user agent and a per-request timeout. A send mode additionally POSTs the request to the target and is refused for any non-loopback target unless an explicit allow-remote flag is given, and a print-request mode emits the exact HTTP request that would be transmitted while making no connection at all. Safety rails are loopback-only by default, one non-destructive marker command, no callback listener, no reverse shell, no persistence, and removal of every local file the run created. The tool's own documentation carries the warning that sending against a real device does change stored WAN configuration, because that is what the handler does on any successful submission, so the device's WAN settings must be restored afterwards. The model's published factory password appears in the tool only as a placeholder default so the request shape is self-documenting; the injection does not depend on it and the credential is reported as a separate weakness. Use only against systems you own or are authorised to test. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com
