Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Title: Exasol Database 7.1.30 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce CVE: pending Description: Exasol Database 7.1.30 from Exasol AG (Germany), an in-memory MPP analytical database examined in its docker-db single-container deployment form, accepts the credential pair sys / exasol on the binary SQL protocol served by the exacts process on port 8563 over TLS, and that pair is the vendor's own published text rather than a leak: the upstream docker-db README instructs the reader, under the heading "Connecting to the Database", to authenticate with username sys and password exasol, and two image-internal CI test scripts authenticate a freshly initialised database with the same pair on the same port, basic_test.sh:112 carrying $X -c n11:8563 -u sys -P exasol -jdbcparam validateservercertificate=0 and basic_sc_test.sh:98 using -u sys -P exasol as well, both cited as artifacts observed inside the 7.1.30 image at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/ because the current upstream repository now carries documentation only. Nothing rotates the constant, and that was traced rather than assumed: the running controller process command line carries no -defaultSysPasswordHash argument; the [DB:DB1] stanza of EXAConf carries no DefaultSysPasswdHash key; db_jobs.py:104 sets self.sys_passwd_text = secrets.token_hex(20), which generates an additional random password rather than replacing the built-in one; database.py:57 passes -defaultSysPasswordHash only when EXAConf configures it explicitly; the container's init-sc path does not configure it; and no forced first-login change-password gate, must-change flag or service refusal exists anywhere in the container's start path, while the README carries guidance about persistent volumes, hugepages, resource limits and license mounting with no instruction to change the SYS password. Both the built-in default and the generated per-deployment random are accepted, so the presence of random generation in the provisioning code is not a defence. The contrast the product itself supplies is what makes this a defect rather than a design choice: Exasol generated per-deployment randoms for two of its three service credentials, the ConfD AuthenticationToken and the BucketFS WritePasswd, and did not do so for the most privileged one, and an attacker must read EXAConf to recover either random while sys / exasol is a constant every installation shares and the documentation prints. SYS is the database administrator, so the constant buys the whole warehouse over the SQL channel on its own, and it also buys the right to create script objects, which converts that administrative access into operating-system command execution (CWE-1392 primary, CWE-94 co-equal, with CWE-798, CWE-78, CWE-1188 and CWE-250 recorded alongside and CWE-284 and CWE-862 reported separately for the absent source-address restriction on 8563 and the absent authorisation distinction for script creation, neither of which raises a metric). The sink is a PYTHON3 scalar UDF body created with CREATE OR REPLACE ... AS whose run(ctx) calls os.popen("<attacker command>").read() and returns the result behind a marker string, after which the caller issues SELECT poc_udf() and the ordinary result set carries the command's stdout back. That construction is a sink rather than a curiosity for three reasons: the os module is importable with no declaration, allow-list or capability request; the command string is an ordinary Python literal built from what the caller supplied, so shell metacharacters, pipelines and quoting all work, and the measured round used cat /etc/passwd | head -3 whose pipeline was honoured by the shell os.popen starts; and the return value crosses the trust boundary back to the caller, which removes the need for any DNS, HTTP or ICMP exfiltration channel and means egress filtering on the host does not defeat it. Sanitisation over what the body does is absent, there being no module allow-list or deny-list, no policy forbidding os or subprocess, no capability gate, no per-statement approval, no audit prompt and no privilege required beyond SYS itself. What does exist is well-formedness checking rather than a security control: the engine validates the language alias, submitting PYTHON instead of PYTHON3 yields its own diagnostic "no definition found for language: PYTHON", and it enforces SQL syntax and the forward-slash script terminator, both of which the payload satisfied without any evasion. That alias diagnostic is itself useful evidence, because it shows script languages are resolved through a named alias table inside the engine, that the table carries the standard aliases PYTHON3, LUA, JAVA and R, and that EXAConf contains no [ScriptLanguages] stanza customising it, so reachability of the sink is not conditional on an operator having installed or enabled a language pack. Three independent detonations returned real system data through the result set, and the identity reported by id was uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root): a dedicated script-execution account that carries root only as a supplementary group. That identity is the whole of what was measured. It is not uid=0, root is not claimed, no escalation was attempted, and this submission is not a root compromise. Three of the container's four authentication surfaces were characterised and ruled out as doors, ConfD on 443 requiring a Bearer token that is the per-deployment AuthenticationToken from EXAConf, BucketFS on 2580 returning 403 to a write attempt because the bucket WritePasswd is likewise a per-deployment random and 400 to a path traversal attempt, and OpenSSH on 22 performing ordinary host authentication with nothing product-specific observed, which is what makes this a credential-hygiene defect rather than an authentication-bypass defect. A negative control establishes that the acceptance is specific to the shipped value rather than to a broken check: five incorrect passwords, admin, password, EXASOL, exasol123 and 123456, were tried against the same transport and the same client invocation and all five returned [28000] authentication failed. The chain involves no memory corruption, no deserialisation gadget, no file upload, no protocol bypass, no local foothold and no second vulnerability; leg one is a documented product constant and leg two is a documented product feature, and what makes the pair a vulnerability is that the product neither rotates the constant nor restricts what a holder of it may execute. The vendor's own repository states that this docker distribution is an open source project that is not officially supported by Exasol, that the base image is an end-of-life CentOS 7 release, that official support for docker-db 7 is no longer available and that users should move to a newer release line, that the repository now only contains documentation with the binaries on Docker Hub, that issues are disabled, and that the project is mainly intended for automatic testing of Exasol deployments. None of that reduces the mechanism, because the credential is a property of the shipping database and the script engine is a supported core feature of the product rather than a container add-on, but it means that on the vendor's own statements no fix is planned for this deployment form, which is a reason the research was published rather than held for a patch and which raises operator exposure rather than lowering it. Only version 7.1.30 in this deployment form was executed: other 7.1.x releases, the supported non-container installation and the vendor's newer release line share the mechanism and are plausibly affected, but none was tested, that is stated as an explicitly labelled inference, and no version range is claimed. Type rationale, stated precisely because EDB's type taxonomy is coarser than CVSS: the exploit is delivered over the network to a networked database service, which is why the type is remote rather than local, and the proof of concept connects to port 8563 as a client would. The published Attack Vector is nonetheless Adjacent rather than Network, for the evidential reason given in the CVSS section below, and no reader should infer an AV:N rating from the type field. CVSS: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, and it is not 9.8. Derivation, shown so a reader can reproduce it with the CVSS 3.1 base algorithm and its round-up-to-the-tenth rule: ISS = 1 - ((1-0.56) x (1-0.56) x (1-0.56)) = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x AV(A: 0.62) x AC(L: 0.77) x PR(N: 0.85) x UI(N: 0.85) = 2.835255; Base = 8.708373 rounded up to the nearest tenth, which is 8.8. Attack Vector is Adjacent because the listener binds all interfaces inside the container and no source-address restriction of the product's own was observed in its configuration or listener behaviour, but no shipped artifact establishes that a single-container deployment binds 8563 on 0.0.0.0 by default: the vendor's documented stand-alone run command publishes -p 127.0.0.1:9563:8563 and the page explains that port 8563 within the container is exposed on local port 9563 to be used for database connections, with the persistent-volume variant on the same page using the same loopback-bound publication, while the documented multi-node run uses --network=host under which the vendor states that there is no need to expose ports in that mode because they are all accessible on the host, and the image's FAQ adds that checking from outside the Docker network requires port forwarding, confirming host-side reachability is an explicit operator action; under default bridge networking with no publication, which several of the README's own example commands use including the license-mount and resource-limit examples, the port is reachable from the host and from every other container attached to the same bridge, a logically adjacent topology. An earlier research note asserted that the production docker deployment exposes 8563 on all interfaces by default and scored the chain as remotely reachable on that basis; that assertion rested on the state of the researchers' own harness and on a general expectation about database deployments rather than on any product artifact, it does not survive contact with the vendor's documentation, it is therefore withdrawn in that form and replaced by the narrower artifact-backed statements above, and the withdrawal lowered the published score from 9.8 to 8.8 rather than raising it, so a reader who disagrees about the deployment posture ends up with the larger figure and not the smaller one. Attack Complexity is Low because the constant is published, the self-signed certificate carries no subjectAltName so the client needs a SHA256 fingerprint in the connection string as host/FINGERPRINT:port but that fingerprint is readable from an unauthenticated TLS handshake, the PYTHON3 alias is registered by default with no [ScriptLanguages] configuration required, and there is no race, no window and no operator action to wait for, all three rounds having succeeded on their first attempt. Privileges Required is None, argued rather than inherited: CVSS 3.1 reads PR:N as the attacker being unauthorized prior to attack and not requiring any access to settings or files of the vulnerable system, and both halves hold, since no account was ever provisioned to the attacker and no trust decision by the defender admitted them, and the value is obtained from vendor documentation rather than from the target's own EXAConf or logs. User Interaction is None. Impact is High on all three axes, grounded in the SQL-layer authority of SYS so that it does not depend on the cross-namespace reach that was not established. Scope is Unchanged because the SQL service, its script engine and the database it administers are one product on one host and executing a script is what the engine is built to do, so reaching the operating system from inside it does not cross an authority boundary the product itself maintains. Conditional reading A, where 8563 is reachable from another host, is 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 3.887043, Base = 9.760161 rounded up, and it applies to the documented multi-host --network=host form, to any operator publication of the port without a loopback restriction, to a deployment reachable across a management network or NAT, and to the supported non-container installation whose entire purpose is to answer client connections on 8563; it is labelled conditional everywhere it appears because the deployment form actually executed published loopback-only and the cross-host leg was argued from vendor artifacts rather than detonated. Conditional reading B, loopback-only publication exactly as the stand-alone quickstart documents, is 8.4 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.55 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.515145, Base = 8.388264 rounded up, applying where the attacker therefore needs local access to the host, a realistic position for anything else already running there including a sibling container. Three further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: Privileges Required Low, 8.0 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability 2.068068, Base 7.941187 rounded up, which treats the constant as a credential the attacker supplies and is rejected for charging the attacker a privilege the defender never granted, and is also the honest reachable reading where the factory credential has been rotated but a provisioned non-administrative account still holds script-creation rights; Privileges Required High, 6.8 Medium (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability 0.900610, Base 6.773729 rounded up, reading the metric as the authority level the successful attack needs since SYS is the database's most privileged account, rejected more strongly than PR:L because it would rate a constant requiring no grant as though it were a personal administrator account, and computing to 7.2 Medium under a Network vector; and Scope Changed, 9.7 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), impact term 7.52 x (0.914816 - 0.029) - 3.25 x (0.914816 x 0.9731 - 0.02)^13 = 6.128026, Base = 1.08 x (6.128026 + 2.835255) = 9.680344 rounded up, with the same reading under a Network vector capped by the formula at 10.0 Critical, rejected as the headline because the namespace boundary measured as a boundary in one direction and not the other, a file written inside it not appearing outside, and because no cross-boundary effect was demonstrated. A fourth state deserves its own sentence because an operator can enter it deliberately: with the factory credential rotated and no other account holding script-creation privilege, there is no path from the network to the sink and this finding does not arise, the script engine then being a documented feature used by authorised administrators, which is why rotation moves the finding from 8.8 to not applicable and heads the operator recommendations. No score is published for the sibling sinks os.system, subprocess and the LUA, JAVA and R aliases because none was detonated, none for the BucketFS anonymous read of the default bucket because it is separate and smaller with its own root cause, none for other 7.1.x releases or the non-container installation because neither was executed, and no figure is quoted for escalation to uid=0 because it was not attempted. Impact: full administrative takeover of the database by anyone who can reach port 8563, and then operating-system command execution as uid=500(exadefusr) with root present only as a supplementary group. The SQL layer does not depend on the sink at all and is the larger half: SYS reads and writes every schema, table, view, user and privilege in an analytical platform, which typically holds whatever the organisation consolidated into it, and can stop the database, so the complete warehouse is exposed with no further exploit step and no unusual protocol activity. Integrity control extends to the account catalogue, so further accounts can be created with chosen privileges, giving an attacker a durable and legitimate-looking second entry point that survives rotation of the factory credential. Availability follows the same authority: the database can be stopped, schemas dropped and resources consumed by the same session, and the deployment runs privileged as the vendor's README requires for permissions management, UDF support and environment configuration, which widens what such consumption inside the container can reach beyond it; that widening was not tested and is not scored. The sink adds command execution with stdout returned through the ordinary SELECT result set, so the attack is non-blind and needs no exfiltration channel, and file reads inside the script namespace. Persistence is cheap and quiet: the payload uses CREATE OR REPLACE, so re-running the attack rewrites one script object rather than creating a new one per command, and the object is ordinary product state that survives the session and is visible only to someone who enumerates script definitions. Detection is weak by construction because every step is legitimate documented product usage, a TLS handshake, a SYS login, script creation and a SELECT, so a SYS session from an unexpected address is indistinguishable from a real administrator and an operator who never rotated the constant has no means of telling them apart; the highest-value signal is script-object creation with the creating user and source address, which the default deployment does not surface, and the second-best is a trial sequence of [28000] authentication failed responses against the sys user on 8563, no rate limit and no lockout having been observed on SQL authentication. The root supplementary group under the vendor-documented privileged container mode is a recognised escalation position on Linux, since gid 0 governs access to files and devices whose group is root, and it is reported as an untested position: the conditional sentence is the whole of what the evidence supports, namely that if an attacker there could write a setuid binary or reach a device node exposed by privileged mode an effective root identity would follow, and neither was tested. A separate smaller finding is reported alongside and deliberately not folded into any metric: the BucketFS default bucket is Public=True, which permits unauthenticated read listing, while a write attempt returned 403 because the bucket WritePasswd is a per-deployment random and a path traversal attempt returned 400. Verification boundary: live verification against one container built from the vendor's docker-db image at 7.1.30, pulled onto an isolated cloud sandbox, started with the privileged flag the vendor's README requires, with a host directory mounted at /exa and the SQL port published to the host loopback only. Researcher-side commands ran under an ordinary unprivileged account and nothing in the chain depended on elevated privileges on the researchers' host. The three detonations drove the vendor's own console client inside the container against the container's loopback on 8563, so this is a real product executing real commands rather than an emulation or a protocol replica, and no step of the chain was driven from a separate network host. The cross-host legs, that a client on another machine can complete the same TLS handshake, retrieve the fingerprint, authenticate and submit the same statements over 8563, follow from the protocol being a network protocol and from the in-container listener binding all interfaces, and they are argued from the vendor's documented deployment forms and the observed bind rather than demonstrated between two machines; that is why the headline Attack Vector is Adjacent and why the 9.8 Network reading is labelled conditional. Measured, with the returned values reproduced in the advisory: authentication with the shipped constant; rejection of five wrong passwords with [28000] authentication failed; creation of a PYTHON3 scalar UDF by SYS; execution of os.popen inside it; return of the command's stdout through the result set; the executing identity uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root); visibility of the host kernel release 5.10.134-19.2.al8.x86_64 from inside the UDF; and readability of /etc/passwd from the UDF process, whose output began root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash. Three rounds, each an independent create-and-select cycle with a different command, each returning real system data, each succeeding on its first attempt; there was no fourth round and no round was repeated merely to demonstrate determinism, three successes with three different commands being evidence of repeatability on their own. Not verified and not claimed: cross-host remote detonation; escalation to uid=0; any write or execution crossing from the UDF namespace into the container's or the host's filesystem view, a separate write-marker test having shown that a file written by the UDF did not appear in the container's own view, so the two views are distinct mount namespaces and the account names in the id output come from the namespace's own view, which is also why even the /etc/passwd read is not asserted to have been the container's file or the host's; persistence; the effect of the chain on a non-container installation or on another 7.1.x release; and the sibling sinks os.system, subprocess and the LUA, JAVA and R aliases. Read from source or documentation rather than detonated: the absence of -defaultSysPasswordHash on the controller command line, the absence of DefaultSysPasswdHash in EXAConf, the behaviour of db_jobs.py:104 and database.py:57, the contents of the image's test scripts, the ConfD token generation scheme, and every documented deployment command quoted above. One inconsistency is disclosed rather than smoothed over: the notes record the host-side port publication as 8562 in one place and 8563 in another, and because every measured leg ran through the container loopback that discrepancy is not load-bearing for anything claimed here. Exactly three commands were executed as payloads, an identity capture, a file read and a kernel-version read; no product file was modified or deleted and no data was destroyed. Prior public coverage was checked before publication: a keyword search of the NVD for the vendor name returned exactly one record, concerning a client-side JDBC driver component rather than the database server, separate searches for the database product name and for the docker deployment name returned no records at all, no published advisory was found whose root cause is either leg of this chain, the single unrelated record is deliberately not cited in the advisory, and no neighbouring identifier should be inferred as related. Exploit notes: the four statements are CREATE SCHEMA, OPEN SCHEMA, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with the body and its forward-slash terminator, and SELECT. Because the certificate has no subjectAltName the connection string must carry the fingerprint in the form host/FINGERPRINT:port, obtainable from an unauthenticated handshake. The return type is declared as a wide VARCHAR so command output is not truncated by the declared width, and the marker prefix distinguishes the returned value from the echoed statement text. The command is embedded as a Python double-quoted string literal, so backslashes and double quotes are escaped and nothing else is. Two client behaviours had to be engineered around, both recorded because they were the difference between a hanging tool and a working one: the vendor client's single-statement mode rejects a multi-statement payload containing the slash terminator and reports an unfinished command, so the payload is fed on stdin, and the client does not exit at end of file on stdin, so the tool starts it with a pipe, waits a bounded interval, kills it and keeps the partial stdout, by which point the result set has already been printed; an early transcript parser matched the marker inside the echoed CREATE SCRIPT source, and the fix filters matches followed by a quote, a space or a plus sign, which is how echoed source differs from a real result. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/exasol/database-7.1.30/default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce/exploit/exasol_database_default_credential_python_udf_os_popen_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It refuses a non-loopback target unless --allow-remote is passed; acquires the certificate fingerprint with an unauthenticated TLS handshake and prints only the first and last few hex characters so that a per-deployment value is not written into a research log, with --fingerprint to supply the value instead and --no-encryption for a deployment that disabled TLS; asserts the credential gate with a trivial query before doing anything else; and creates and selects the UDF once per requested command. --rounds 3 reproduces the verification method by cycling through three different commands, --control runs the negative control alone and creates nothing, --gate probes only the credential, and --cleanup drops only the schema the run created. Nothing destructive is performed: the tool establishes no listener, opens no reverse shell, writes no file, installs no persistence, touches no other container or host service, does not attempt to reach uid=0 and does not attempt to cross the UDF namespace boundary. The default command is id. Those omissions are deliberate, the finding being that command execution is reachable at all from a documented constant, and demonstrating more would add risk without adding evidence. Exasol AG was notified through the vulnerability-reporting mailbox published in its RFC 9116 security.txt, which is the only intake the vendor offers and which welcomes responsible disclosure of vulnerabilities in its products and services. Nothing was submitted to any pre-publication intake form, none being published, and no individual was addressed by name. The notification was sent unconditionally and in clear text, the security.txt publishing no inline key field: the research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested and nothing is withheld pending a reply. The vendor states that this docker deployment form is not officially supported and that official support for it has ended, so no fix is planned for it. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: Title: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5- JSP command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform (CTP) from Parasoft (United States), a closed-source commercial continuous-testing product bundling environment management, service virtualisation and test-data management, distributes an em web application running on Tomcat 10.1.57 with the Jasper JSP engine and Java 17 inside the vendor's own container image, and contains three composing first-party defects that yield unauthenticated remote code execution in two HTTP requests: an unfiltered ObjectInputStream over an uploaded backup archive (CWE-502, primary), a licensing filter that decides whether to run at all by testing the raw un-normalised request URI (CWE-436, primary and co-equal, with CWE-863 as its authorisation consequence), and a remember-me authentication service that hands an anonymous request an authenticated administrator principal when no external security provider has been configured (CWE-287, enabling gate). Defect one, the licensing filter: EMLicenseFilter is 175 lines and reads request.getRequestURI() raw at line 165, testing it at line 166 against exemption clauses including endsWith("about"), endsWith("welcome"), endsWith("forgot"), endsWith("notlicensed"), contains("/resources/") and contains("/images/"), none anchored by a separator or segment boundary, with a further branch at lines 167 to 171 that reassigns the entire exemption set rather than accumulating into it when the request accepts JSON. That test has exactly one consumer in the class, shouldNotFilter() at line 47 calling isLicenseRequired() at line 48, so a matching URI suppresses the whole doFilterInternal() body rather than weakening one decision, taking with it the /tdm/api/v guard at line 99 and the unlicensed-instance redirect to /em/license at line 118. Because a servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters from each segment before servlet mapping, filter and router disagree about the identity of one request, and a target of /em/database/restore;welcome is exempted by the filter while still being routed to the restore handler. Defect two, the sink: com.parasoft.ctp.core.database.backup.AbstractDatabaseBackup, a class of 518 lines and 19,851 bytes, wraps the uploaded database.ser zip member at line 111 with new ObjectInputStream(in), reads an int at line 112 and calls readObject() at line 117 casting the result to TableMetadata, nine lines above the getConnection() call at line 126, so the cast constrains nothing (the gadget executes during the call and the ClassCastException is thrown afterwards) and no database needs to exist, be reachable or accept the supplied parameters for the payload already to have run. The caller is the web-layer controller EMDatabaseController, 1359 lines, whose restore handler at lines 707 and 708 takes a StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest and hard-compares zip member names against the literals "version.txt" at line 725 and "database.ser" at line 733, a shape check that says nothing about content. The absence of a filter is a corpus-wide artefact measurement rather than an inference: ObjectInputStream appears in 68 files with 149 occurrences in the core tree and in 3 files in the web layer, readObject appears in 81 files, and ObjectInputFilter appears in 0 files, jdk.serialFilter in 0 files and serialFilter in 0 files, three zeros across a class name, a system property and its short alias against a positive control of 81 files containing readObject. Two sibling readObject() calls on the same class of untrusted stream sit at lines 323 and 435 of the same class, in a row-draining and a row-binding routine, read from source and not detonated, named so a fix covers the class rather than the call site. Defect three, the fail-open gate: EMRememberMeServices is 483 lines and, at line 140 to 142, returns null when an Authorization header is present, then at line 146 fetches PSTSecServiceClient.getInstance() and at line 148, when that client is null, returns createAuthenticationToken("admin", "admin", EmUserInfo.Role.ADMIN, request), which registers new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") inside a Spring Security User whose authenticated flag is true, so the resulting principal is a genuinely authenticated administrator rather than the container's anonymous principal and satisfies the authenticated() matcher that CTPSecurityWebConfig line 283 demands for /database. Neither hop is an unprotected route, /database being explicitly matched to authenticated() and the images allow-list being /images/welcome/* rather than a widened glob, so the accurate description is not that the endpoints are unauthenticated but that the product mints an administrative principal for an anonymous request. CsrfSecurityRequestMatcher is a 28-line class whose anchored exemption alternation at line 19 includes /database, so the state-changing POST needs no CSRF token. The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap whose factory is a ConstantTransformer holding attacker bytes and whose decorated map is an aspectjweaver SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap with an absolute folder field, reaching writeToPath(folder + File.separator + key, bytes). That class was read at the bytecode level for four facts: folder is declared private final String, is not transient, and the class declares no readObject of its own, so it is populated by the inherited HashMap.readObject path through defaultReadObject and both writer routines read it with an explicit getfield that the compiler has not inlined; writeToPath is getfield folder, StringBuilder, separator, key, store, with no forced extension appended to the key, an assumption that had to be disproved at the bytecode level because it would have removed any execution surface, and the value passes a checkcast to a byte array so the content is any bytes at all; validation is absent in every form, with zero occurrences of File.getName(), Path.normalize(), getCanonicalPath(), startsWith(), a regular expression or a length truncation in that write path, keys carrying slashes or relative traversals both working, and an absolute destination reachable because concatenation with an empty folder yields a leading double separator that POSIX treats as a valid absolute path; and the gadget does not fire on deserialization alone, because HashMap.readObject reconstitutes entries through putVal, which is package-private, final and not overridden, so it bypasses the overridden put containing the write, which is why the TiedMapEntry to LazyMap to Map.put prefix is needed to force a virtual dispatch. The only content constraint anywhere is that the bytes must not equal the four-byte sentinel IDEM, and the published carrier sets storingTimer to Integer.MAX_VALUE to suppress the index file the caching map would otherwise write alongside the payload. The execution sink is the product's own container configuration: conf/web.xml declares the Jasper jsp servlet and its mapping at lines 274-275 and 448-450, and webapps/em/images/ is inside the deployed web application root the mapping covers, writable by uid 1000 as drwxrwxr-x parasoft root, and exempt from the licensing filter by the contains("/images/") clause at line 166, so fetching the written page needs no bypass of its own and the product compiles it into work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/<stem>_jsp.java and .class. A second independent execution sink was also detonated and is recorded so a fix removing JSP compilation does not close half the problem: WEB-INF/classes/com/parasoft/rest/api/core/docs/templates/ is the FreeMarker template root, its prefix from an init-param in webapps/em/WEB-INF/web.xml at lines 206-207 with FreeMarker 2.3.34 through jersey-mvc-freemarker 3.1.12, and because freemarker.template.utility.Execute is on no restriction list the new() built-in is usable, a template performing 7*119 returning 200 with a 4-byte body containing 833 and a template invoking Execute with id returning 200 with a 61-byte body containing the full identity string. Measured chain: one anonymous multipart POST to the restore path carrying a semicolon-welcome suffix, with no cookie, no Authorization header and no CSRF token, returning HTTP 500 with the product's own 119-byte "An error occurred while applying changes to the database configuration" message, which is the success signature rather than a failure because readObject() precedes getConnection(); the product log then carried one occurrence per run of a stack trace naming AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore(AbstractDatabaseBackup.java:114) with "class java.util.HashSet cannot be cast to class ...TableMetadata" and a java.lang.ClassCastException, counted at 2, then 4, then 6 across runs, and distinguishable from a malformed payload which produces a ClassNotFoundException instead. One anonymous GET of the written page then returned 200 with a 538-byte body containing a per-run marker with a 12-hex nonce, JSP_EVAL=42 from server-side evaluation of the expression 6*7, proving evaluation rather than source echo, SIZE_SELF=1372 agreeing with the length of the payload the client built, which proves byte-exact content control, the identity string uid=1000(parasoft) gid=1000(parasoft) groups=1000(parasoft), an ls line showing the page owned by the product's own service account, a /proc/1/status line reporting Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000, and two /etc/passwd lines read by the product process. Two end-to-end detonations of the two-hop chain are recorded as successful, and two intermediate iterations failed inside the client script rather than against the product. No vendor-supplied credential, no licence installation or forgery, no outbound connection, no DNS or RMI callback, no cross-version payload adaptation, no memory corruption and no privilege escalation is involved: the upstream libraries carrying the gadget are carriers and not the root cause, executing a jsp page is the product's own configuration, and the landing identity is the product's unprivileged service account, uid=1000(parasoft), confirmed three ways (id inside the executed page, the written file's ownership and mode, and the product process's own /proc/1/status read from inside the container rather than through a container runtime which would report root regardless), with root not reached and not claimed. CVSS: 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, recomputed from the vector with the CVSS 3.1 base formula rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - ((1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56)) = 0.914816; Impact for Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 (AV:N) x 0.77 (AC:L) x 0.85 (PR:N) x 0.85 (UI:N) = 3.887043; base = min(5.873119 + 3.887043, 10) = 9.760161; rounded up to the nearest tenth = 9.8. AV:N because the chain is two ordinary HTTP requests to TCP listeners the product serves itself over HTTP 8080 and HTTPS 8443, both accepting connections from outside the container, with no shipped reverse proxy, WAF or management-plane separation in front of em, and the loopback publication of the test port being the research testbed's containment rather than a product restriction. AC:L because there is no timing window to win (this is the steady factory state, not a first-run race), no host-specific reconnaissance, no memory-layout condition, no database reachability requirement (the readObject at line 117 runs before getConnection at line 126), no outbound callback and no cryptographic work; the only condition is a configuration state the vendor's own image is in when no external security provider has been configured. PR:N because no credential belonging to anybody is supplied or consumed, the authenticated subject being manufactured by the product itself for an anonymous request. UI:N because no administrator action, browser session, induced click or human upload step exists anywhere in the chain. C:H, I:H and A:H describe compromise of the product, its managed data and its availability, and do not depend on the landing identity being privileged, nor rise if a deployment runs the platform as root, which was not measured. Scope Unchanged, with Scope Changed considered and rejected on an argument stated here so the call cannot be read as a scoring maneuver: the rejected S:C variant of the same metrics, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H, computes to 10.0 from ISS 0.914816, Impact for Scope Changed 6.128026, Exploitability 3.887043 and 1.08 times their sum capped at the maximum, so the reading rejected here is the higher one and rejecting it lowers the published number from 10.0 to 9.8. It is not two authorities because the filter, the deserialising controller, the security service, the web application root and the JSP mapping all belong to one deployed application in one JVM, the platform being a single product with several routers rather than several products; because executing a page inside its own web application root is the documented intended behaviour of the shipped container configuration, so the transition from write to execution crosses no boundary the product defines; and because the executed code carries the product process's own uid in that process's own filesystem view, entering no other account, machine or security domain. Three labelled conditional readings accompany the published score and none replaces it. Conditional A, external security provider configured and the attacker holding any valid account, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.62 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373 rounded up), since the security matcher for the restore path is authenticated() rather than hasRole("ADMIN") so low privileges suffice while the licensing gate is still bypassed and the sink still unfiltered; this deployment state was not detonated, and it is the reading an operator of a configured deployment should work from because it depends on no unverified capability. Conditional B, external security provider configured with the subject supplied by an offline-forged session cookie, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.8 Critical, arithmetically identical to the published score, and is a static and structural inference that was never verified: the platform signs its remember-me cookie PST_LT_FEATURES_INFORMATION, whose signed plaintext takes the form user:expiry::localAddr:"rememberMeAuthenticated", with a key that is a compile-time string literal and a signature scheme, bcrypt, that carries no secret, so anyone holding the shipped class can compute a cookie offline, and forgery was exercised only in the unconfigured state where it buys nothing, while the combination of a configured deployment driven end to end with a forged subject has no run behind it at all; building a fake security provider to test it was deliberately abandoned because installing one would have manufactured the condition being measured. Conditional B is published so an operator of a configured deployment knows which exposure to check and so the vendor knows which mechanism to replace, never as a demonstrated capability and never as the headline score, and the published PR:N rests on the measured fail-open behaviour of the untouched image rather than on any forgery. Conditional C, listeners reachable only from a management network, is CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.62 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373), conditional on a deployment change that was not tested and downward rather than upward, so an operator who hardens the network position can see that it is worth one point of severity and fixes nothing else. No version-range claim is made: only CTP 10.7.5-SNAPSHOT was executed, obtained through the vendor's mutable parasoft/ctp:latest tag (image id prefix f99f7210fc67, from a saved copy of 997,805,056 bytes with md5 47946c7d1e7d99a00d6c90f4ae675f90), and in the Maven convention the product's own build system uses a -SNAPSHOT version marks an in-progress development line rather than an immutable released artefact, so a mutable tag cannot be mapped onto a released version range with the confidence a public affected-version list requires; the claim is that this build is affected and that any other build shipping the same AbstractDatabaseBackup and EMLicenseFilter source carries the same construction. CWE classification: CWE-502 primary and CWE-436 co-equal for the two root causes, CWE-863 and CWE-287 contributing for the authorisation and authentication gates, with CWE-321 and CWE-347 reported separately for the literal session-cookie signing key and its keyless signature scheme and CWE-22 reported separately for a sibling file-path primitive that is not part of this chain, none of the contributing items raising any metric of the published vector, and no upstream component blamed since the gadget libraries are carriers and the jsp execution is the product's own container configuration. Impact: unauthenticated remote code execution inside the product process from two ordinary HTTP requests, on a platform whose documented entry point for the same function is an administrator menu behind authentication and a valid licence. Before any command runs, the chain carries an arbitrary-path arbitrary-content file write as a primitive in its own right, the folder field, the map key (observed to accept both nested and relative-traversal forms) and the content byte array all living inside the serialized stream, with the only content restriction being that the bytes must not equal the four-byte IDEM sentinel. Execution as uid 1000 inside the product's JVM puts in scope the product tree under /usr/local/parasoft/ctp including the deployed em application (writable, which is how the page was created), the container's own conf/ directory holding server.xml and web.xml, and the Jasper work directory; the platform's HSQLDB database files, whose location and database user the bypassed configuration endpoint disclosed to an anonymous caller on its own, and through them every environment definition, system definition, virtual-service definition and test-data-management record the platform manages plus whatever credentials or connection strings it stores on behalf of the systems it virtualises; anything else on the host filesystem readable by uid 1000, measured concretely by reading /etc/passwd; and the product's own licence and security state, since arbitrary in-process code can rewrite configuration files and restart the application's view of them, which is why the unlicensed and unconfigured conditions an operator might rely on as compensating controls are not durable ones. There is no window: this is not a first-run race, a setup-mode condition or a state that closes when an administrator first logs in, the fail-open branch applying for as long as the external provider is unconfigured, the licensing bypass for as long as the filter reads raw URIs, and the sink unconditionally, and the chain was fired repeatedly against one instance with no state consumed in between. The cost to an attacker is one crafted multipart POST and one GET with no reconnaissance, no credential acquisition, no timing precision, no outbound infrastructure and no target-specific adaptation. Persistence that survives naive cleanup was measured rather than argued: after the dropped page and both of its Jasper compilation artefacts were deleted, the same URL still returned 200 with a body two bytes shorter than the first response, precisely because the ls command inside it could no longer find the file it was listing, the compiled servlet instance still being loaded in the JVM. An operator who deletes the file and the compiled class has therefore not removed the web shell; only a context reload or a JVM and container restart does. Also within reach structurally rather than by demonstration is the ability to overwrite the deployed application's own pages or class files, converting a single write into persistence surviving a restart, which was not performed and is flagged as an unexercised consequence of a proven primitive rather than as a measurement. Detection is weak by construction: hop 1 is a documented administrative function returning an ordinary 500 with the product's own configuration-error message, and hop 2 is an anonymous GET for a file under a static-assets path, so the strongest indicators are a request target containing a semicolon, a non-image file appearing under the deployed images directory, a compiled jsp stem under the Jasper work directory that the product does not ship, and the product log line pairing the restore frame with a cast exception naming a JDK collection class where backup metadata was expected. One caution for status-based monitoring: the licensing filter flushes its response output stream at line 113 before calling setStatus(403) at line 115, so licence refusals surface as HTTP 200 with a JSON body carrying status 403, and any rule keyed on HTTP status for licence failures will not fire at all. Verification boundary: live black-box HTTP verification against a running instance started from the unmodified vendor image in an isolated container sandbox with no setup step performed, plus source-level reading of the decompiled first-party classes and of the shipped conf/web.xml and webapps/em/WEB-INF/web.xml; it is not an emulation and not a protocol replica. The instance state was factory, unlicensed and with no external security provider configured, and that state was confirmed rather than assumed from a shipped-code fact about the pristine image and not a property of anything the researchers configured: requesting the provider-configuration endpoint at /em/pstsecconfig with an Accept header naming application/json returned 404 with a zero-length body, matching the controller's own getActiveConfig()==null branch, and it reproduced on two instances so it is not an artefact of one container. The client was Python 3.11.6 using only the standard library, run by an ordinary unprivileged user, and no packet left the sandbox at any point because the chain requires no outbound connectivity and none was available to it. Nothing was driven from a separate network host: the client ran on the same sandbox host as the container, reaching it through a published loopback port, so reachability from a second machine over a routed network is argued from the shipped listener topology (the container accepts connections on its HTTP and HTTPS ports from outside itself and the product ships no front-end proxy or filter of its own) and not demonstrated between two hosts, while every other claim in the chain, the bypass, the principal, the write, the execution, the identity and the persistence of the compiled servlet, was measured over real HTTP against a real product process. Only the factory configuration state was detonated; a deployment with the external security provider configured was not tested end to end and is scored as a conditional reading. Only one build was executed, with no older release, no newer release, no Windows variant and no differently configured instance fired at, so no cross-release and no cross-platform claim is published. Two legs are labelled inference and never presented as measurement: the forged session cookie in a configured deployment, and the JavaScript-engine evaluation path, whose capability layer was measured in isolation while its two reachability preconditions were never satisfied, so no claim about it appears in the rated chain or the impact section. Read from source but not separately detonated were the two sibling readObject() sites at lines 323 and 435 and the hardening of the other upload and zip-handling paths examined and ruled out; measured on shipped artefacts rather than over the network were the corpus-wide absence of any deserialization filter, the JVM's own --add-opens list read from its process command line, the absence of JDBC drivers among 238 jars, and the bytecode-level facts about the caching map's write path from single-class disassembly rather than a whole-library dump. Six negative controls were exercised, each removing a specific alternative explanation: hop 1 without the semicolon suffix returned 302 with Location /em/license; hop 1 with the backup part omitted returned 400 with 59 bytes; hop 2 against a never-written file in the same directory returned 404 with 762 bytes and the container's own "JSP file not found" page carrying an Apache Tomcat/10.1.57 footer, the run marker appearing once in the executed body and zero times here; the licensing-bypass read with the suffix but no semicolon returned 404 with 792 bytes, excluding a literal-suffix match; the identity endpoint with Authorization: Bearer garbage returned 401 with a zero-length body, showing the fail-open branch is specific to requests presenting no credential at all so the behaviour is not that authentication is off but that an absent credential is more trusted than a wrong one; and the /em/tdm/api/v2/servers resource without the bypass returned 200 with a 90-byte unlicensed body, excluding the possibility that the bypass variant's well-formed XML came from the fixed unlicensed path. Everything the client reported was re-verified from the target side rather than trusted from the script's output: the images directory's file count went 39 before the run, 40 immediately after and back to 39 after self-deletion, a single-file difference matching a single payload; the Jasper residue under work/ after cleanup was zero entries; a filesystem search for the run's marker leaf name under the product tree and under /tmp returned zero results; and the container was destroyed afterwards with its published ports confirmed free, leaving only a read-only reference instance running. Two classical gadget families were established dead on this target from the product's own process rather than from a guess, its JVM's --add-opens list covering java.base/java.lang, java.lang.reflect, java.io, java.util and java.util.concurrent plus java.rmi/sun.rmi.transport with no SecurityManager installed: a comparator-driven PriorityQueue chain with a bean comparator targeting TemplatesImpl was deserialized and did fire, the stack showing PriorityQueue.readObject:801 into heapify:734 into BeanComparator.compare:142, and was then stopped by the module system because java.xml does not export com.sun.org.apache.xalan.internal.xsltc.trax; and a JdbcRowSetImpl chain using autoCommit as the trigger with an rmi URL was stopped the same way, java.sql.rowset not exporting com.sun.rowset, confirmed independently by a native listener on the sandbox host receiving no inbound connection during a 25-second window. No JDBC driver of the commonly abused families is present either, a survey of all 238 jars finding no PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, Derby or H2 driver, so the JDBC-connection style of gadget has nothing to connect with, the platform talking to HSQLDB in-process, which is not the same surface; on a modern JDK with default module boundaries the usable gadget set is whatever lives entirely in the unnamed module, which is why the published chain has the shape it does. Classic zip-slip is closed in the live extraction helper whose entry-name checks are hardened, a second older zip utility in the tree has zero callers and is dead code, and the import path used by restore reads members into an in-memory map rather than extracting them to disk; the restore handler's own member selection is a hard comparison against two literals so no alternative member name can be smuggled in to change which bytes reach the stream. A file-API variant taking an extension parameter appeared to allow a traversal into a jsp suffix and is closed by two independent walls, the extension helper taking everything after the last dot so traversal sequences are discarded and the manager underneath using File.createTempFile so the JDK's own temporary-file machinery rejects a suffix containing a separator, the product even echoing back its own failure message containing the attempted suffix. The upload, temp and task endpoints under /em/tdm/api/ have no mounted handler at all although the generated WADL advertises paths that do not exist, which is a documentation defect and a trap for anyone mapping this surface from the WADL alone. The licensing bypass is not a skeleton key, which was measured rather than assumed: handlers performing their own licensing check are unaffected, the coverage-agent endpoints reading the license manager directly and continuing to return 403 with a 90-byte unlicensed body across all seventeen of their mappings even with the bypass applied, and a server-resource feature gate continuing to return 403 with a 94-byte body, so what the bypass unlocks is only what whose enforcement lives in the filter, being the whole /em/database subtree and the entire /em/tdm/api/v tree. Several additional first-party defects were measured on the same product and reported to the vendor separately with none folded into the published vector: the generic licence-gate bypass on its own, an authorisation bypass rather than an execution; the fail-open remember-me branch and an authentication provider that does not verify the submitted password at all, at PSTAuthenticationProvider.java:144, privilege granting rather than execution; the offline-forgeable session cookie with its literal signing key and keyless signature scheme, demonstrated only where redundant and not verified where it would matter; anonymous whole-database download and anonymous backup creation through both /em/api/v2/database/backups and /em/api/v3/database/backups, because the 213-line resource class backing them contains zero occurrences of checkLicensing() while the filter's exemption clause covers everything under /em/api/, the v2 variant being an undocumented twin of v3 that the shipped OpenAPI description does not cover and that was found by reading the routing table; anonymous arbitrary file read and anonymous arbitrary file delete through a temp-file handler building new File(tempDir, fileID) by pure concatenation from a query parameter with no base-name extraction or canonicalisation, measured with a passwd read returning the first line verbatim in a 47-byte body and with a DELETE that really removed a prepared file, being CWE-22 from the same unvalidated-concatenation family and not an execution; anonymous creation of database files in an arbitrary directory from a JSON connection URL passed verbatim into a JDBC file URL, measured as six new files appearing in a chosen directory, with the directory and base name attacker-controlled while the extension is fixed by the engine and the content is not, so it reaches no execution surface; twenty-eight hardcoded secret values of which seventeen participate in security decisions, being a shipped TLS keystore whose store password is the industry default changeit and appears in plaintext in server.xml at lines 110-112 (so every installation that did not replace the keystore shares one TLS key pair, checked once by listing the keystore with the documented password and succeeding on the first attempt with no brute-forcing), three hardcoded AES-128 keys in AES128Cipher.java at lines 41 to 43 that use the key as the IV removing the semantic-security benefit of an IV entirely, a literal Blowfish argument with iteration count 5 in NativeBlowfish.cc at line 36 used by the licensing subsystem to decode licence feature data, and a salt present as a string literal rather than generated material; a transactional-commit defect in which a malformed JSON body can leave orphaned rows because the checked exception thrown by the JSON library does not mark the surrounding transaction for rollback; and an inconsistent upload guard family, being header validation applied to only two of the seventeen files that set a content-disposition header, a zip validator testing only the extension, and a routine named canonicalize that performs a UTF-8 round trip rather than any path canonicalisation while being relied on as a path guard. The structural fact behind the unevenness is that the em application has four independent routing stacks behind one set of hand-written gates, / to the Spring DispatcherServlet, /api/* to a Jersey RestServletContainer, /tdm/api/* to TDMApiServletContainer and /services/* to CXF, with ten star-path servlet filters in conf/web.xml, so enforcement is not centralised and licence enforcement lives in two places at once, the filter and per-controller calls to checkLicensing(), of which 97 occurrences appear across 17 files against 31 routed Jersey resource classes, meaning 54.8 percent of routed resource classes perform any licensing check at all. Exactly one payload shape was executed for the published chain, a command capture plus a self-listing and a passwd read, and the dropped page deleted itself and its two Jasper compilation artefacts before the forensic refetch; nothing destructive was performed beyond the single written page, no product file other than that page was modified or deleted, and the container was destroyed afterwards. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/parasoft-ctp-unfiltered-deserialization-license-gate-fail-open-jsp-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/parasoft/ctp-10.7.5/unfiltered-deserialization-license-gate-fail-open-jsp-rce/exploit/parasoft_ctp_unfiltered_deserialization_license_gate_fail_open_jsp_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target address. It takes the target URL and the command either as positionals or as -t and -c, defaulting the command to id, and exposes every coordinate of the chain as an argument rather than a constant: --folder for the landing directory, defaulting to the product's own deployed images directory; --leaf for the page name, defaulting to a per-run nonce-based name; --json for the connection parameters, whose default names a loopback address on port 1 so the post-deserialization database attempt fails immediately and predictably; --version for the content of the version.txt zip member, defaulting to 93; --web-prefix for the application context path, defaulting to /em; --catalina-base and --work-dir for the container layout; --restore-path for the hop-1 target, defaulting to the database restore mapping carrying the semicolon suffix; --images-path for the hop-2 directory; --timeout, --retries and --retry-delay for request behaviour; --keep so the dropped page does not delete itself; --no-hop3 to skip the post-delete forensic refetch that establishes the servlet is still loaded; -k or --insecure for a self-signed certificate on the https scheme; --dump-payload to write the generated carrier to a path; and --selftest, which sends nothing at all. The self-test encodes the offline discipline: it rebuilds the carrier skeleton using the original values of its three patch regions and asserts byte identity with the archived 1,178-byte carrier whose md5 is 6099d3f5fd36e28d8934c2e4e6c95da6, then rebuilds with new values and asserts that the new folder, leaf and content appear verbatim, which is what makes the claim that this generator produces the stream proven against the product checkable by a reader with no target to shoot at. The carrier is a 1,178-byte stream containing 19 handles, all consumed, treated as an immutable skeleton with three marked patch regions, the leaf name, the content byte array length-prefixed and raw, and the folder path, leaving every class descriptor, serialVersionUID, field order and handle back-reference byte-for-byte untouched. The written page carries the operator's command base64-encoded and decoded with java.util.Base64 at request time so no quoting conflict can arise between the page source, the Java string literal and the shell, invokes it through ProcessBuilder with /bin/sh -c and the error stream redirected into the output stream with LC_ALL and LANG pinned to C so id and ls output is machine-readable, and prints a per-run marker, a server-evaluated arithmetic expression distinguishing evaluation from source echo, its own absolute path and size, the identity output, the delimited command output and, unless asked not to, the result of deleting itself and both Jasper compilation artefacts before the forensic refetch. The script refuses to fire at all if the target URL has no scheme, no host, a non-rooted path or a doubled slash in the path; that pre-flight validator exists because two of the four iterations of the client failed for reasons unrelated to the target, one producing a URL with no slash between context and path and raising a nonnumeric-port error before a packet was sent, and one producing a doubled slash that the container answered with 404 while its unit test asserted only that the URL was parseable, which it was, and so guarded the wrong property. The exploit installs, forges, modifies or clears no licence, uses no MITM, DNS hijacking, TLS interception, outbound connection or callback, attempts no privilege escalation and claims no root, does not persist through any startup mechanism or second page or account creation, and its cleanup report is a forensic finding rather than a guarantee, since deleting the dropped page and its compiled artefacts does not unload the servlet from a running JVM. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com
