Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: VulnBump: Can AI Agents Fix Vulnerable Dependencies Without Breaking the Build?
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: What's new: to our knowledge, VulnBump is the first benchmark for AI agents built around security-driven upgrades: every task starts from real vulnerabilities that Snyk found in...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Can AI agents fix vulnerable dependencies without breaking the build? The fix itself is rarely the mystery. Over six months in 2026, Snyk Open Source recorded 459 million vulnerability findings across ~300,000 organizations. 94% of these vulnerabilities had a known fixed version, yet only about 10% had been resolved.

That happens because the hard part is upgrading safely: most vulnerable packages are transitively imported, about a quarter of fixes require a major version bump, and even minor and patch releases, which are supposed to be backward compatible, often contain breaking changes.

VulnBump, new research we published at Snyk, puts AI agents to the test on 307 real upgrades of vulnerable dependencies. An upgrade counts as a PASS only if the vulnerabilities are gone and the project still installs, builds, and passes its tests.

What's new: to our knowledge, VulnBump is the first benchmark for AI agents built around security-driven upgrades: every task starts from real vulnerabilities that Snyk found in a real project, across six package managers. Earlier upgrade benchmarks check only for breakage, not whether the vulnerability is gone.

So, can AI agents fix vulnerable dependencies without breaking the build? Mostly, yes, but the model alone doesn't decide it. On the same model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passed 90.2% of upgrades. Anthropic's Claude Code passed 77.5% when given Snyk's recommended upgrade and scan (Claude Code + Snyk scan), and 59.6% with no Snyk data (Claude Code unaided). That's a gap of more than 30 percentage points. For reference, the package manager bump, a baseline with no AI that only applies Snyk's recommended version, already passed 46.9%.

Key results on VulnBump

Keeping the build green wasn't the hard part: all three agents did that about 93% of the time. Removing the vulnerability was. In 70 of its 124 failures, Claude Code, unaided, said it had fixed vulnerabilities that a rescan still found.

Our findings echo VulnBench, our June benchmark of AI security review, which found that Claude and Snyk Code miss different vulnerabilities and concluded that the two work best combined. VulnBump tests a different task, upgrading vulnerable open source dependencies, and points the same way: with Snyk's recommended version and scan, Claude Code's PASS rate rose by 17.9 points. Evo Remediation Agent shows how much further a purpose-built agent can go: 12.7 points beyond Claude Code with the same Snyk scan. VulnBump also follows up on the remediation results we shared in May, now with a newer model and six package managers.

How we built VulnBump

We started from real projects, matched to production. We collected 767 candidate projects from GitHub, including popular open source projects and repositories that pin known-vulnerable packages. Each had to install, build, and pass more than 85% of its tests before any change, and Snyk had to find at least one vulnerability. From the 99 that qualified, we picked 43 that match Snyk production data for ecosystem, vulnerability severity, direct vs transitive dependencies, and size of version jump.

VulnBump dataset comparison with Snyk Open Source production data

We turned each recommended upgrade into a task. Each task asks the agent to apply one upgrade that Snyk recommends: one package, moved to a version that fixes its vulnerabilities. Every task starts from a fresh copy of the project and is scored on its own. The 43 repositories yield 307 tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities, across Maven, Gradle, npm, Yarn, pip, and Poetry, the six package managers behind about 92% of production findings.

We added a verifier that didn't trust the agent. When the agent finished, we copied its changes into a clean container and checked them from scratch. There, an attempt counted as a PASS only if it cleared all four gates:

The dependencies install with the command CI would run.

A new Snyk scan confirms the vulnerabilities are gone.

The project builds.

Every test that passed before still passes.

The VulnBump pipeline

The harnesses we tested. All three agents ran on Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a limit of 110 turns per upgrade, in the same container for each language:

Evo Remediation Agent is Snyk’s agentic remediation engine. It uses Snyk intelligence and can run its own scan, build, and tests, and repair errors before finishing. We ran it in auto-approve mode, so it applied every fix, including upgrades Snyk rates as likely to break the build.

Claude Code Snyk scan is Anthropic's general-purpose coding agent, given Snyk's recommendation for the upgrade: the package to upgrade, the target version to move to, and the vulnerabilities it fixes. It can also run a Snyk Open Source scan itself to check its work.

Claude Code unaided gets the same task without the target version or any Snyk access. It has to determine which version fixes the vulnerabilities on its own, for example, by searching vulnerability databases on the web.

The package manager bump is the non-agentic baseline: it applies Snyk's recommended version with the project's own package manager and changes nothing else.

How the repositories were chosen, the exact prompts and tools each agent had, and the leakage controls are all in the research paper: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green, along with the limitations: we tested one model, ran each upgrade once, and used Snyk Open Source as the judge, which can only count against Claude Code unaided, since the other two agents work from the same Snyk findings. We also didn't penalize new vulnerabilities that an upgrade pulled in.

Result 1: The same model, with three different outcomes

Evo Remediation Agent passed every gate on 90.2% of upgrades (and fixed 95.9% of the 2,066 vulnerability instances). That's 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan, roughly one more working fix in every eight upgrades, and 30.6 more than Claude Code unaided.

And the ranking doesn't just hinge on a few large repositories: averaged per repository, PASS rates were 93.1% for Evo Remediation Agent, 80.1% for Claude Code + Snyk scan, 68.0% for Claude Code unaided, and 51.3% for the package manager bump.

Key finding:

Evo Remediation Agent fixes 9 in 10 vulnerability-driven upgrades end-to-end.

Result 2: Agents need to know which version is actually safe

On the same model, giving Claude Code Snyk's scan and recommended upgrade raised its PASS rate by 17.9 points, from 59.6% to 77.5%.

The clearest difference is which version it picks. Unaided, Claude Code settled on a version Snyk still flags 64 times. With Snyk's scan, that dropped to 13. Vulnerability databases don't always agree on which version fixes a vulnerability, so a version that looks safe in one source can still be flagged in another.

Snyk's guidance matters most for transitive vulnerabilities, in packages the project doesn't declare directly. Counting only upgrades that passed every gate, it more than doubled the share Claude Code fixed, from 28% to 59%.

Key finding:

Snyk's scan and target version raised Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 points and more than doubled the transitive vulnerabilities it fixed.

Result 3: Snyk's advice alone solves about half, and then the agents separate on the rest

The package manager bump splits the 307 upgrades in two: On the 144 it passes, Snyk's recommended version is all it takes, and an agent can only keep or lose an easy fix. The other 163 need more than a version bump, such as adapting code to breaking changes or resolving dependency conflicts.

Agents on the 144 upgrades Snyk's advice solves, and on the other 163

With Snyk's guidance, agents rarely break what the bump solves, while Claude Code unaided regressed on 20 of the 144, in 15 of them by picking a version Snyk still flags. The real difference becomes evident on the hard half: with the other 163 upgrades, Evo Remediation Agent passed 82.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan passed 61.3%, and Claude Code by itself passed 36.2%.

Key finding:

Of the 163 upgrades that need more than a version bump, Evo Remediation Agent passed 82.2%, against 61.3% for Claude Code + Snyk scan and 36.2% for Claude Code unaided.

Result 4: A green build can hide an unfixed vulnerability

The easiest way to keep a build green is to leave the vulnerability in place, and that's mostly where we saw Claude Code failing. The rescan was the first gate to fail in 107 of Claude Code’s unaided 124 failures, 48 of Claude Code + Snyk scan's 69 failures, against 9 of Evo Remediation Agent's 30.

First failed verification gate for every failed attempt

Evo Remediation Agent's failures are visible (and that's not a bad thing). 21 of its 30 failures broke the build or tests, mostly on major upgrades that other agents often avoided. A loud failure is much safer than a silent one: when one upgrade does go wrong, the project's own build and tests show it, where a developer can actually see it, and eventually act upon it.

Key finding:

General-purpose agents fail silently; Evo Remediation Agent fails where CI catches it.

Result 5: Knowing the target version isn't enough

Snyk's scan gets Claude Code a long way, but getting the upgrade right takes more than that: with identical findings and targets, Evo Remediation Agent passed 39 more upgrades than Claude Code Snyk scan, 23 of them major jumps.

Evo Remediation Agent combines Snyk's intelligence with a loop in which it builds, tests, and repairs the project before it finishes. While our setup can't isolate which component makes the difference, it does show how far the system around a model can impact the result, which is consistent with DepBench, where changing only the harness changed results by up to 16.3 points.

Key finding:

Same model, same Snyk findings: Evo Remediation Agent still passes 12.7 points more.

Result 6: Major jumps and transitive dependencies remain the hardest tasks

All agents still struggle with major framework migrations: 23 upgrades, mostly Spring, Spring Boot, and Dropwizard migrations, defeated all three agents.

PASS rates fell to 81% from 96% for Evo Remediation Agent, to 61% from 88% for Claude Code + Snyk scan, and to 42% from 70% for Claude Code unaided, respectively, on major vs non-major upgrades. Major upgrades are also where code has to change: about half of Evo Remediation Agent's major version PASSes edited the application source, compared to 5% of its non-major PASSes.

Upgrades passing every gate, by the size of the version jump

Transitive vulnerabilities, where the vulnerable package isn't declared in the manifest, make up 70% of fixable instances and are harder for every harness tested. Counting only fixes from attempts that passed every gate, Evo Remediation Agent fixed 73% of transitive instances, Claude Code + Snyk scan 59%, and Claude Code unaided 28%, against 91%, 71%, and 62% respectively of direct ones.

PASS rate by dependency type (direct vs transitive)

Key finding:

Evo Remediation Agent leads on the hardest upgrades, majors, and transitive dependencies, but major framework migrations still beat every agent.

How does VulnBump fit with VulnBench?

VulnBench evaluates how AI coding agents find vulnerabilities in the code you write: how consistently they detect the same issues across repeated runs, and how closely their findings match a deterministic SAST baseline. VulnBump benchmarks whether they can fix vulnerabilities in the code you depend on: upgrading vulnerable open-source dependencies without breaking the build or tests.

When you read the two together, they point the same way: models bring reasoning that deterministic tools just don't have. On their own, they report different findings across runs and often stop short of a fix. Across the platform, we put the shared lesson more simply: the generator cannot be the validator.

What does this mean for teams handing security work to agents?

Judge a fix by the evidence the agent didn't produce: An agent's report of its own fix is a claim, while a rescan, a build, and a test run become evidence. If an agent is fixing your backlog, hold it to the same checks.

Score the vulnerability and the build together: Either one alone hides a failure. Breakage-only checks miss fixes that never happened, while vulnerability-only checks miss the fix that broke the project.

Give the agent the security data: Snyk's scan and recommended upgrade were worth 17.9 points to a general-purpose agent, on the same model.

Evo Remediation Agent is Snyk's agentic remediation engine, available through the Snyk CLI and as a cloud service. It's one of the agents in Evo Agentic AppSec, which launches today.

Run your agent through VulnBump

The VulnBump harness and all 43 evaluation cases are open-sourced at github.com/snyk-labs/snyk-vulnbump.

The full methodology, failure analysis, and limits are in the research paper. If you're building a remediation agent yourself, run it through VulnBump and let us know what you find.

VulnBump was built by Gabija Pasiunaite, Ryan McMorrow, Brian Clark, Liran Tal, and Luke Tu.

RESEARCH

VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Patching up the pieces.
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Atlassian addressed a critical vulnerability affecting Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket Data Center products, which attackers exploited after proof-of-concept code became public. Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and SonicWall all patched vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks.
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Patch Tuesday brings a record-breaking haul of fixes. Ivanti warns of an exploited VPN zero-day. An international crackdown targets West African scam compounds. A cyberattack stops work on a major European tunnel. Perceived Starshield speed limits disrupt Ukrainian drone operations. Canonical battles a sustained DDoS attack. Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI worms. The FTC accuses cybersecurity firms of exploiting sextortion victims. Microsoft and partners disrupt a major cybercrime marketplace. Rob T. Lee, from SANS, and Lynn Dohm, from WiCyS, are sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards. Taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Today is Wednesday October 14th 2026. I’m the amazing Maria Varmazis Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Patch Tuesday.

Microsoft, Adobe, and SAP have released their October Patch Tuesday updates, addressing hundreds of security vulnerabilities across their products.

Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday delivers a record-breaking 1,411 security fixes, including one actively exploited zero-day and two previously disclosed vulnerabilities. Seventy flaws are rated critical, with remote code execution accounting for 57 of those. Privilege escalation vulnerabilities make up the largest category overall, with 677 fixes. The actively exploited flaw affects Windows Shell and allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. The two publicly disclosed vulnerabilities affect the .NET Framework and MessagePack-CSharp, potentially enabling security bypass and denial-of-service attacks. Microsoft continues to credit AI-assisted vulnerability discovery for the growing volume of fixes.

October’s security updates extend well beyond Microsoft, with major vendors addressing critical vulnerabilities, including several already exploited in the wild. Adobe patched flaws across Photoshop, ColdFusion, Commerce, and other products. Atlassian addressed a critical vulnerability affecting Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket Data Center products, which attackers exploited after proof-of-concept code became public. Cisco fixed critical NX-OS vulnerabilities potentially allowing attackers to execute code with root privileges on Nexus switches. Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and SonicWall all patched vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks. Docker addressed a DockerHub flaw allowing attackers to impersonate users and push images to repositories they don’t own. GitLab patched critical AI Gateway and CI/CD vulnerabilities, while Dell addressed flaws in deployment and storage tools. Meanwhile, SAP fixed 20 vulnerabilities, and Kiteworks released patches for 126 security flaws.

Ivanti warns of a high-severity VPN zero-day.

Ivanti is warning that attackers are exploiting a high-severity zero-day in its Connect Secure VPN appliances. Researchers at Volexity discovered a threat actor tracked as UTA0576 chaining three vulnerabilities to achieve root-level access on fully patched devices. The attackers stole credentials, conducted network reconnaissance, and searched for sensitive Active Directory information, apparently preparing for broader network compromise. Ivanti has patched two vulnerabilities covered by CVE-2026-104935, but a third privilege escalation flaw remains unpatched. Ivanti says exploitation has affected a limited number of customers.

An international operation targets West African scam compounds.

Updating our earlier coverage: An international operation targeting West African scam compounds has resulted in 28 arrests in Ghana and Nigeria and the identification of 117 suspected human trafficking victims. Coordinated by Britain’s National Crime Agency, the effort brought together 15 law enforcement agencies and 15 technology companies. Authorities seized more than 300 devices and identified 89 fraud victims who reportedly lost $8.3 million. The scams included cryptocurrency investment fraud, law enforcement impersonation, and online extortion. Technology companies removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages, and groups linked to the operations. Investigators also identified over $11 million in potentially recoverable funds. Meta played a key coordinating role, even as the company faces ongoing scrutiny over fraudulent advertising on its platforms.

A cyberattack halts construction of a major tunnel project in Europe.

A cyberattack has reportedly halted construction of the Fehmarn Belt tunnel connecting Denmark and Germany. The incident affected the international FLC construction consortium, disabling workers’ identification cards and immobilizing vessels, cranes, and offshore platforms. The 18-kilometer road-and-rail tunnel is a roughly seven-billion-euro project employing some 2,800 workers. The attack’s origins and potential impact on the construction schedule remain unclear. A Danish cybersecurity official suggested a possible connection to hybrid warfare, amid heightened warnings about Russian cyber threats.

T-Minus Segment from Maria

Perceived Starshield speed limits disrupt Ukrainian drone operations.

As of Wednesday morning, Ukraine says SpaceX has imposed new speed limits on military Starshield terminals without warning, which it says has disrupted some drone operations and complicated battlefield logistics. The new Starshield speed restrictions of 160 kph as reported by Ukrainian officials to the BBC, affect how fast drones can travel while still maintaining satellite connectivity. BBC sources at the Ukraine Defence Ministry report that since Wednesday morning, drones hitting the speed limit now completely lose connectivity with Starshield. As a result, Ukrainian officials say some missions have been disrupted or canceled as they work to assess the impact and establish backup communications channels.

Starshield is SpaceX’s government and military version of the Starlink satellite service, and it has become an integral part of Ukraine’s battlefield communications, supporting drone control, reconnaissance, and coordination. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says it is discussing this issue with U.S. officials, SpaceX, and NATO partners.

As of the time of this recording, SpaceX has not made any public response to Ukrainian official statements nor has it corroborated the existence of any new in-motion Starshield speed restrictions.

Canonical suffers sustained DDoS.

Ubuntu parent company Canonical suffered a sustained distributed denial-of-service attack last week, disrupting its public websites for more than four hours. The October 8 incident affected Ubuntu and Canonical websites, developer resources, security advisories, and services including the Ubuntu Security API and Livepatch. However, software repositories, Launchpad, and the Snap Store remained operational, allowing users to continue downloading and installing updates. Canonical’s distributed infrastructure helped limit the damage. This was the company’s second major DDoS attack this year. An April incident caused more extensive disruptions, including outages affecting Launchpad and the Snap Store. A hacktivist group claimed responsibility for that attack, but no group has claimed the latest incident. Whether the two attacks are connected remains unknown.

Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate.

Researchers at Anthropic warn that small AI models could soon become capable of independently spreading across compromised Internet of Things devices. The company’s Frontier Red Team tested whether AI models could run on inexpensive Android TV boxes and replicate themselves across a network. One model successfully spread to all eight devices in a simulated environment, although researchers deliberately simplified the exploitation process. Anthropic predicts smaller models could achieve similar capabilities by year’s end, potentially enabling decentralized AI worms without a central command infrastructure. Such malware would likely spread slowly, and researchers emphasize that no fully autonomous AI worm has yet emerged. Large model transfers could also make these infections easier to detect. Still, the research suggests another potential evolution in botnet technology.

The FTC alleges further exploitation of sextortion scam victims.

The Federal Trade Commission is suing Dmitry Belkin and 12 businesses, alleging they exploited victims of online sextortion scams while collecting at least $60 million in customer payments. The companies advertised digital forensics services promising to identify blackmailers, stop threats, and coordinate with law enforcement. Instead, the FTC alleges they fabricated evidence, failed to deliver promised services, and pressured frightened customers into paying thousands more. Employees allegedly followed scripts designed to amplify victims’ fears, while the businesses suppressed negative reviews, posted fake testimonials, and directed complaints to a counterfeit Better Business Bureau website. Some customers reportedly remained trapped in payment agreements years later. The FTC is seeking a court order to halt the operations, alleging years of deceptive and abusive business practices.

Microsoft and partners disrupt a major cybercrime marketplace.

Microsoft, working with Japanese law enforcement and Health-ISAC, has dismantled key infrastructure powering a major Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace. The operation targeted three platforms—YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man—which supplied criminals with fraudulent accounts, tools, and thousands of impersonation templates. The coordinated takedown involved seizing domains, disabling over 20,000 accounts, and blocking more than 100,000 sites.

Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint and TRM Labs also assisted in the takedown.

Last-minute cancellation of the Grace Hopper Celebration.

AnitaB.org has abruptly canceled the 2026 Grace Hopper Celebration, scheduled for October 27th through 30th in Anaheim, California. Billed as the world’s largest gathering of women in technology, the annual conference brings together hundreds of companies and thousands of professionals for recruiting, networking, mentoring, and technical training. This year’s program placed particular emphasis on artificial intelligence skills and career opportunities. The last-minute cancellation leaves attendees, speakers, and corporate sponsors scrambling for answers about refunds, travel arrangements, and possible virtual alternatives. It also raises concerns about lost professional opportunities for women in an industry where they remain significantly underrepresented. Organizers and corporate partners now face questions about how they’ll replace those opportunities.

Stick with us after the break, Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm (Dome), Executive Director at WiCyS (Wee-SIS), are sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards. And taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Dave Bittner recently sat down with Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm, Executive Director at WiCyS, as they shared a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards.

That was Dave Bittner sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards with Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm, Executive Director at WiCyS.

Taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Patch Tuesday is becoming such a dreaded occasion that some cybersecurity leaders are apparently treating it like a holiday. Preferably one spent somewhere without Wi-Fi.

Of the 500 UK security executives surveyed by managed detection and response provider Socura, 22% of those executives have called in sick or deliberately scheduled time off to avoid the monthly patching ritual. Meanwhile, 41% report working overtime, and 29% experience significant anxiety the night before.

The workload isn’t getting any lighter. AI-powered vulnerability research is helping vendors uncover more flaws, with Microsoft’s October patch Tuesday, as I mentioned at the top of today’s show, delivering a record-breaking 1,411 security fixes.

Ironically, AI may also offer some relief. Forty percent of respondents say it’s helping automate routine security tasks.

Socura warns that mounting workloads and burnout require better staffing and support. Because when the people responsible for fixing security vulnerabilities start looking for an escape route, that’s probably a vulnerability worth addressing.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

T-Minus: Space-Cyber Briefing podcast plug.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 56 AWS API calls in 141 milliseconds: Inside an AI-run intrusion
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Elastic Security Labs provides publicly available research on emerging threats with an analysis of strategic, operational, and tactical adversary objectives, then integrates...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
One server read 56 EC2 user data scripts in 141 milliseconds. Then it went quiet for 14 days and came back. That gap did more damage than the burst, because fixed correlation windows cannot span two weeks.

Between September 30 and October 16, 2026, a CyberStrikeAI server worked through stolen AWS credentials in a familiar sequence: validate identities, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, send a remote command. Every one of those is a call a legitimate role makes every day. Nothing in CloudTrail looked urgent at the time.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source platform that pairs LLM agents with offensive security tools. Will Thomas at Team Cymru counted 21 IPs running it in early 2026, all of them aimed at Fortinet edge devices. This is the first case we have seen of the same tooling turned on AWS.

We call this AI-assisted on the strength of the tool attribution and the machine-speed behavior in the logs. We cannot prove an LLM agent was making the decisions, and we do not know how the attacker obtained the credentials.

Key findings from the CyberStrikeAI AWS intrusion

Between Sep 30 and Oct 16, 2026, one CyberStrikeAI server (43[.]240[.]29[.]11) used credentials from eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts.

app-role sent 56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds, part of 58 user data retrieval alerts (74% of the total), which points to automated tooling.

On Oct 2, container-role read an encrypted SSM parameter and issued an SSM SendCommand 29 seconds later. The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded.

43[.]240[.]29[.]28 and 43[.]240[.]29[.]33 serve a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080 with the same self-signed certificate as 43[.]240[.]29[.]11, which ties the three servers together. As of November, none of the three is serving that interface, so treat the IPs as indicators for retrospective hunting.

All 78 alerts were medium or low severity and only made sense once correlated by source IP.

The activity ran in four phases over four active days, with a 14-day gap before a final return visit. Times are shown as offsets from the first event in each phase.

Phase 1: Validating stolen AWS credentials (Sep 30)

The server called GetCallerIdentity on four IAM users across three accounts within 51 minutes, a standard way to check which credentials still work. Three of those calls landed in the same second, one in each of three accounts, which points to automation. Two GetSessionToken calls on one user show it requesting temporary credentials.

How Elastic detections caught the CyberStrikeAI activity

Which detection rules fired, and why severity stayed low

Six Elastic detection rules fired, and between them they covered every phase. Taken alone, every alert is medium or low severity and easy to dismiss. The source IP is what ties them together.

Several details point to automated tooling:

56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds from a single session.

Three GetCallerIdentity calls in one second, across three accounts.

A sharp change in tempo. 83% of alerts (65 of 78) came on day one, then activity dropped to a few targeted actions per day.

None of this proves an LLM agent was making decisions, but it matches how an agentic platform works through a list of credentials and targets.

Automating IAM containment with Elastic Workflows

AI-assisted offense is often sporadic and fast, especially with compromised identities. Elastic Workflows can enable responders by making API calls to AWS services such as IAM to block the identity automatically.

Elastic Workflows, shipped with the stack (9.4+), lets detection rules invoke custom workflows with a YAML-defined pipeline of steps on every alert. As a PoC we created a custom workflow that triggered on the detections shared below while emulating this behavior that mirrors suggested response actions.

On every alert, the workflow does the following, executing in seconds and aiding with containment of the identity:

Triggers on AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration detection rule

Iterates each user name associated with the alerts

Invokes an AWS Lambda function through Elastic’s AWS Lambda connector

Deactivates compromised access key using iam:UpdateAccessKey.

Blocks older temporary sessions associated with IAM user by adding inline deny policy via iam:PutUserPolicy and aws:TokenIssueTime cutoff

Quarantines IAM user by attaching inline deny-all policy

An example of this workflow can be found here.

Behavioral indicators to hunt for in CloudTrail:

A burst of DescribeInstanceAttribute calls requesting userData, many per second, from one role session.

First-time GetCallerIdentity calls from the same external IP across several accounts or users within the same minute.

GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance role session whose source IP is not the instance or your NAT.

GetParameter with decryption followed within a minute by SSM SendCommand from the same role.

We added two high-severity, low false positive ES|QL detections for the burst enumeration behavior: AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration alerts when one principal and source IP read userData from more than 20 distinct instances in 10 minutes, and AWS STS GetCallerIdentity Bulk Account Enumeration alerts when three or more distinct non-role identities call GetCallerIdentity from the same external IP and ASN in 10 minutes.

How to respond if your AWS identities were exposed

Assume anything an affected role could read is compromised, and work outward from the credentials.

Rotate credentials for every identity that touched the indicator IP, and revoke active sessions, including those from temporary credentials.

For instance roles, rotate by replacing the instance profile or the instance, since stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised.

Treat all secrets in EC2 user data as exposed, and move them to the Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

Review SSM command history for the window of any unexpected SendCommand call to see what ran. Check for abuse of AWS-managed documents, AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript or custom documents.

Check non-production roles and secrets for overlap with production.

Block the indicator IP at the WAF, VPC, NaCL and security group level, but rely on the behavioral detections, since the infrastructure can change and network blockage is not effective at stolen credentials to API calls prevention.

Restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData to the roles that need it, using IAM policy or a service control policy.

Enable GuardDuty if it isn't already, and alert on credentials used from outside your expected IP ranges.

Hunt for how the instance credentials were obtained, starting with exposed web applications, SSRF, code repositories and IMDS.

Conclusion: What this intrusion means for alert correlation

AI-assisted attacks are driven by objectives, so they generate a lot of alerts. One CyberStrikeAI server produced 78 alerts across six rules in 16 days, and 65 of them came on the first day. Every alert was medium or low severity, and each one looked routine on its own: a first-time GetCallerIdentity, a GetSessionToken, an SSM SendCommand from a rare user. Only the shared source IP showed they belonged to one intrusion.

Defenders need high-signal detections to stop the damage early; low false positive behavior rules, such as the two bulk enumeration rules described above, that justify acting immediately. Medium and low severity alerts are good candidates for correlation, but only by source IP, and the correlation window needs to be flexible because AI-assisted activity is irregular. Here, 56 requests landed in 141 milliseconds, later steps came hours to days apart, and the operator returned after 14 days. A short fixed window would have split this intrusion into unrelated alerts.

High-signal detections can also drive remediation. Attached to a workflow, such as those in the Elastic Workflows library, a rule like this can disrupt the attack automatically, for example by blocking the source IP, while analysts investigate.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Hackers' Overreliance on AI Can Result in Weaker Cyber-Attacks, Proofpoint Researcher Says
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
For the past few years, cybercriminals have been adopting AI tools to enhance their malicious campaigns. However, one threat researcher has claimed that AI has not made any significant changes to the cyber threat landscape, and in many cases has made attacks less effective.

Based on her findings and analysis of recent campaigns where AI was used by cybercriminals, Selena Larson, principal threat researcher at Proofpoint, shared during the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11 how AI has, in many, cases has made attacks less effective.

“We’ve all been told since 2023 that AI will make attackers better, faster and stronger. That they’ll have access to the same tools and resources as the best developers, security professionals and vulnerability researchers in the world, and will automatically become better at hacking. This is marketing nonsense, the data just doesn’t back up this assertion,” she noted.

AI “Slop” Enters the Attack Chain

While AI has enabled threat actors to increase the speed and scalability of campaigns, a number of groups have become overly reliant on these tools, leading to frequent errors – something Larson described as “AI slop.”

Proofpoint has found such errors in AI generated malware. “We frequently run into malware where the code doesn’t actually work, there’s comments which want to do one thing, but the malware is doing something completely different,” Larson said.

A similar scenario has occurred with phishing campaigns observed by Proofpoint over the past year. Larson highlighted the case of a threat actor tracked as TA4903, which specializes in business email compromise (BEC) and phishing campaigns.

Historically, the group has impersonated US government entities to target organizations across a range of sectors, using sophisticated lures.

However, Larson said that since the group started adopting AI tools in their attack chains, their lures have really gone downhill.

This is because the AI generated emails often do not match up with the subjects and attachment – sometimes leaving the body of the message blank.

In addition to AI-generated lures, the group now primarily creates phishing websites using AI coding tools. These vibe coded sites are often simplistic and take on a similar appearance in terms of colors and formatting, making them easier for targets to detect.

Larson also pointed out that the use of AI-generated phishing messages to ensure correct region-specific grammar and spelling, can even make lures less believable.

“Human beings often don’t know how to spell, they often are bad at grammar, people aren’t trying to be overly polished. So, I think that’s actually a bit of a detriment to some of these actors,” she added.

Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity.

Larson cited the example of the ‘BlueMoon’ exploit chain first observed in August 2026, which involved three Microsoft Chrome browser vulnerabilities chained together.

The threat actors used large language models (LLMs) to write exploits, using information given in patch release notes. However, the AI-generated exploit itself was highly flawed, often not behaving as intended and generating significant noise, making attempts easily identifiable for defenders.

No Change in Cyber Defense Priorities

Larson said it is important to emphasize that AI is a productivity tool and does not automatically increase the sophistication of threat actor campaigns.

“AI is only as good as its operator and this is, and it can lead to more sloppy mistakes,” she noted.

As a result, cyber defense remains fundamentally the same. The biggest shift is the fact that AI is making it faster and easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities that cybersecurity professionals have been aware of for a long time.

“Attacks are attacks and AI generally doesn’t really matter. Whatever you’re defending against, defense is going to remain the same,” Larson concluded.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding. The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion. "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday. "Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators." It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years." The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground. The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones. "The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details. Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years. Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls
Apify Confirms Customer Data Accessed in Cyberattack
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Web scraping and automation company Apify has confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack that compromised internal systems and customer accounts.

The Czech company provides a cloud platform for collecting information from websites and automating online tasks. It says it has 91,000 customers worldwide.

The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation.

According to the company, the attacker used a compromised credential to obtain additional credentials and gain access to related Apify accounts.

On November 12, Apify confirmed that some customers had their personal information or stored data accessed during the attack.

The company has contacted customers whose information was exposed. Those who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected so far, although the investigation is continuing. Apify has not disclosed the number of compromised customer accounts.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to an Apify customer who shared a breach notification on Reddit, the exposed information included names, email addresses, billing details, account activity, and IP addresses.

More importantly, the notification listed salted password hashes, 2FA recovery codes and phone numbers, and authentication tokens associated with Google and GitHub sign-ins among the compromised data.

The notification also indicated that payment card information was limited to cardholder names, expiration dates, and the last four digits of card numbers. Full card numbers and security codes were not exposed.

The company has implemented additional monitoring, changed critical internal secrets, and revoked some OAuth connections to third-party services, including GitHub.

Apify said its investigation had not found that the OAuth connections could have been used as an attack vector. Customers building Apify Actors from private GitHub repositories have been instructed to reconnect their GitHub integrations.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: SilentAir Hackers Intercept Calls, SMS From Inside Mobile Networks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Telecom software and cybersecurity company Enea has detailed the activity of a previously unknown threat actor that intercepts phone calls and text messages through compromised mobile operator infrastructure, with Taiwan as its main target.

The company tracks the group as SilentAir and assesses with high confidence that it’s a new state-level actor.

Enea’s researchers also believe, with low confidence, that SilentAir’s activity is aligned with China-nexus operations. Their reasons include the hackers’ interest in Taiwan, the absence of Chinese targets, and attack timing consistent with a workday in China’s time zone.

SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators. The attacks route a target’s incoming calls and SMS messages through the compromised node and harvest subscriber details.

The hackers can also track a target’s location, but this makes up only a small part of their activity. They send silent SMS messages, which don’t appear on the recipient’s phone, possibly to check whether earlier interception attempts succeeded.

Enea has monitored the attacks since early 2025, and further digging revealed suspicious activity from before that.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The hijacked nodes belong to operators in at least six Asian countries. Besides Taiwan, the group has targeted a dozen other countries and territories, occasionally going after people in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. High-profile political and government figures were among those targeted.

The report also covers 2026 activity from Liminal Panda, a group that CrowdStrike linked, with low confidence, to China-nexus operations. Enea says it’s the only actor known to actively exploit the IPX, the interconnect network that mobile operators use to exchange traffic.

Starting in the first quarter of 2026, Enea spotted and blocked Liminal Panda’s GTPDoor backdoor at several of its mobile operator customers. In total, it caught several hundred attempts to covertly reach command-and-control servers.

Enea says it has seen potential infections at between five and ten operators. It estimates that the total could reach several dozen, particularly in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

According to Enea, SilentAir and Liminal Panda could be connected, although the evidence isn’t strong enough to link them.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The last two matter more than the first
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.

AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.

First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”

The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.

What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.

All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.

A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.

AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.

There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.

Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.

Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.

Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.

These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.

The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.

Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.

This problem shows up often in myth.

In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.

In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.

More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.

The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.

If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.

Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.

In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.

If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.

Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.

We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.

We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.

We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.

I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.

Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.

We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.

A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.

Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.

There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.

Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.

AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.

Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.

Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.

Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.

Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.

Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.

Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.

Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.

Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.

AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.

Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.

Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.

Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.

Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.

These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.

Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.

Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.

Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.

The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Google pushes second Chrome update this week
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Technical details Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
On November 11, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.78 for Linux. It includes 83 security fixes, five of which are rated Critical—the highest severity level. This update came out only two days after the previous one.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.79 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability.

A use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability happens when software accesses memory after it has released that memory for reuse. The program still has a reference to the old location, but the original object is no longer valid, and something else may now occupy that space.

The leftover reference is called a “dangling pointer” and is caused by a mistake in managing how long an object remains available. One part of a program may release it while another still expects to use it. That can happen because of confused ownership, faulty error handling, or a timing issue between tasks running simultaneously.

The consequences range from crashes and corrupted data to information leaks and, in some cases, execution of attacker-controlled code. The dangerous possibility is that an attacker can influence what replaces the freed object, then trick the program into treating that replacement as legitimate data or instructions for what to do next.

That explains why UAF flaws can receive critical severity ratings. However, the label describes a class of memory-management bugs, not a guaranteed outcome: the actual impact depends on the affected component, how reliably an attacker can exploit the mistake, and the protections in place.

Stop threats before they can do any harm.
