Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Phishing Rises Three Times Faster in Europe Than Globally, Proofpoint Finds
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8.3 out of every 100 delivered threat messages, compared with 2.0 globally.

Precision Cloud Attacks See Success for Attackers

At the same time, the firm found that 64% of European organizations targeted by precision cloud attacks showed evidence of successful compromise.

Speaking to the media during Proofpoint Protect London event, on November 12, Daniel Blackford, VP of threat research, said the researchers derived this finding from account-takeover telemetry, including logging attempts and follow-on actions such as creating email rules or linking apps.

“These targeted attacks use techniques such as phishing and session hijacking to gain access to specific users and accounts, highlighting their effectiveness compared with broader brute-force attacks,” Proofpoint researchers noted.

Espionage and AI Threats Reshape Europe’s Cybersecurity Landscape

European industries are facing increasingly targeted threats. Malware accounted for 21% of detected threats in the hospitality and leisure sector, nearly twice the global rate. Healthcare organizations faced a similarly concerning picture, with callback phishing increasing by 257% year over year and malware detections rising by 84%.

The report also highlighted that espionage operations are expanding across Europe, with South Asian threat actors extending their reach into Western Europe, while Russian and Chinese state-aligned groups continue to evolve their tactics.

At the same time, the growing adoption of cloud services and AI is creating new security challenges.

Proofpoint identified more than 188,000 AI-enabled applications connected through authentication and OAuth frameworks, while the proportion of European sensors affected by attacks targeting open-source AI technologies increased 4.6 times between consecutive 90-day periods.

“Up to last year, I could have said AI for attackers was still a bit too hyped up, but within the last six to eight months, we’ve really started seeing widespread adoption of coding assistants and AI usage across the vast majority of the landscape,” Blackford added.

Read now: Phishing Dominates as Initial Entry Method for Cyber-Attacks, as Hackers Hone Evasion Techniques

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

Mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

For interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

Some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the company saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the company said points to a single controller.

The attacks came in bursts, from one or a few subscribers to several thousand over a month, with gaps of up to several months or longer between bursts.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the company could not see that traffic.

The company spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

The networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

The company then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

Detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

The report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

SilentAir also sent silent SMS on a very large scale, mainly to subscribers in Taiwan. These are texts that the phone does not display or alert on.

During the day, most silent SMS went to subscribers on other networks, such as Southeast Asian networks. One of their main uses appears to have been checking whether a diversion had worked, the company said.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

Most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company said the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

The company's low-confidence link to China rests on several signs. SilentAir focused on Taiwan and did not target Chinese networks or subscribers.

Its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

The company also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

In several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two showed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency said CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea said SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the company's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

The GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The company also found evidence of a new version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries users' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

What Enea Recommends for Operators

The company said any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:

Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls and configure them to share information with their SS7 and Diameter firewalls.

Go beyond the industry's basic recommendations for signaling security.

Treat the whole IPX as untrusted.

Add detection for signaling protocols inside their own networks.

Connect signaling security with the rest of their IT security.

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI Set to Revolutionize Ransomware Following “Stagnant” Few Years
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Ransomware will be revolutionized in 2027 due to the influence of AI, with threat actors poised to become more innovative, according TrendAI’s director of cybercrime research, Bob McArdle.

“Ransomware has been pretty stagnant and boring for the past couple of years, at least if you’re a researcher like me,” he told the audience at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11.

To date, ransomware actors have primarily used AI to enhance the speed and efficiency of campaigns. This includes the use of AI tools to identify the most important data once inside an organization’s environment, while some groups have deployed chatbots to carry out the initial negotiation stages on their behalf.

However, the overall process of ransomware attacks, from the use of initial access brokers through to the double-extortion method, have not changed.

“That’s a drop in the ocean compared to where we’re going with ransomware next,” McArdle warned.

Devaluation of the Initial Access Broker Marketplace

One expected change is around how initial access is gained to victim’s environments. In the current ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem, initial access brokers typically sell access to affiliates through techniques like compromised vulnerabilities and stolen credentials.

However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities rapidly.

“Anything that’s connected to the internet and is misconfigured or has vulnerabilities will be compromised,” he commented.

This will devalue the initial access market and, as a result, McArdle expects brokers to adapt their business model towards offering privilege escalation to ransomware groups.

Post initial access, tools like Artex and AI agents will allow attackers to shrink down the “kill chain” to machine speed.

McArdle also observed that many organizations are centralizing their data storage, which is good for business efficiency purposes amid the growing use of AI for data processing.

However, this centralization will provide new opportunities for threat actors. This includes ransomware groups threatening to tamper with the AI orchestration around organizations’ data as a further extortion technique.

Another area in which AI will benefit ransomware groups is its ability to process data effectively, enabling actors to quickly develop datasets of high value data, which will be easier to sell on to other malicious actors. This approach will provide even more profit-making opportunities for these actors.

“Over 2027, we will start seeing an inflection point where you have extortion-based business models of ransomware living side-by-side with the actual data theft and sales models increasing every year,” McArdle explained.

Hostile Takeovers by Ransomware Groups

With AI making ransomware attacks easier to undertake, McArdle expects to see a growth in the number of ransomware groups in the next year.

This further fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem will likely lead to large groups frequently undertaking “hostile takeovers” of smaller actors.

“We will start seeing Conti and LockBit level groups effectively acquiring smaller groups for their technology or even just their affiliate networks,” he added.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Our Global Emergency Response Team (GERT) recently investigated an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organization’s virtualization estate over a 10-day period. The campaign targeted four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine hosted on them, both vCenter Server Appliances, and all connected backup infrastructure. The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024. What’s interesting about this attack is that no virtualization layer vulnerabilities were exploited: no guest-to-host escapes, no hypervisor memory corruption. Every action taken against ESXi was executed through legitimate VMware management interfaces. In September 2021, the Babuk ransomware source code was leaked online, including its ESXi version, which made ESXi ransomware accessible to cybercriminals with relatively low technical skills. At least ten subsequent ransomware families have leveraged this leaked code, including groups that otherwise lacked the expertise to develop ESXi-compatible ransomware lockers from scratch. We saw multiple operators using Babuk-derived ESXi lockers along with the leaked LockBit Windows builds. It is worth noting that while the Babuk ESXi version may target both old and up-to-date systems, the target organizations run unsupported ESXi versions, making them easier to attack.

This article examines why the hypervisor layer remains difficult to monitor, what common access paths adversaries use to reach it, and how they establish persistence on the management plane. We’ll also look into the architecture of ESXi encryptors, the deliberate destruction of backup infrastructure, and the log sources that enable post-incident reconstruction. At the end of this article, we’ll provide indicators of compromise recovered during the investigation.

Ten days of dwell time from initial access to the destructive phase. Timeline reconstructed from incident evidence

Why the hypervisor changes ransomware economics

Virtualization enables cost-effective and efficient resource management, simplifies simultaneous updates and policy enforcement. However, at the same time it reduces the number of control points and enables broader impact in case of a cyberattack. In non-virtualized environments, a single guest compromise normally affects one operating system. Compromise of the virtualization management plane gives the attacker access to many hypervisor hosts, while direct impact on an ESXi datastore can render many guest systems unavailable at once. This makes the hypervisor layer an attractive target for ransomware operators, especially when domain controllers, application servers, databases, and backup workloads share the same virtualized estate.

According to Kaspersky’s global cybersecurity services report, ransomware accounted for 39.4% of incidents GERT handled in 2025, and the data for the beginning of 2026 shows that it remains a major threat. Back in 2023, SentinelOne documented that multiple ransomware families are using ESXi lockers derived from the leaked Babuk source code, which lowered the development barrier for actors who otherwise lacked the necessary expertise to build ESXi-capable samples. This makes ransomware targeting virtualization environments more accessible to a broader range of threat actors, and this trend is still with us.

The visibility asymmetry

ESXi is a specialized hypervisor based on VMware’s proprietary VMkernel. It shares certain similarities with Linux (and other Unix-like systems), accepts Linux commands and runs certain Linux-like software, but it is different from general-purpose Linux distributions. Broadcom states that off-the-shelf security tools designed for general-purpose operating systems cannot run on ESXi without workarounds and that direct installation of third-party agents or antiviruses on ESXi and vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) is not supported. Defenders therefore rely heavily on built-in hardening, management-plane telemetry, agentless security solution integrations, and telemetry collection from the infrastructure outside ESXi hosts.

Guest operating systems are usually protected by EDR software, but if an ESXi-side process modifies a virtual machine disk (VMDK) or related datastore file, an EDR agent inside a guest cannot directly observe or attribute the hypervisor process performing the operation. Guest telemetry may record consequences, such as I/O failures or an abrupt shutdown, but the malicious execution occurs outside its boundary. In the engagement examined here, this made host-native and management-plane telemetry central to the incident timeline reconstruction.

How attackers reach the virtualization layer

There are different routes into the environment that require different controls, but can ultimately provide access to the centralized virtualization management plane and the ESXi hosts it controls. In this article, we’ll look into four main routes that may lead to virtualization infrastructure compromise:

Vulnerability exploitation

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

Active Directory integration abuse

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

The virtualization trust stack and recurring entry paths

Vulnerability exploitation

In the incident we analyzed, there was no evidence pointing to an ESXi vulnerability as the initial access path. Nevertheless, public vulnerabilities remain important because they have been used to compromise the virtualization management infrastructure. With the exploits available online, this is one of the most probable entry routes. Below you can find several examples of vulnerabilities affecting virtualization environments that have been seen exploited by the attackers. For example, the Twelve group chained CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2021-22005 to plant a web shell directly on a vCenter appliance, which loaded a backdoor that then established persistence by injecting a shared object into the SSH daemon. Note that these vulnerabilities are not related to the incident in question and they are provided merely as an initial access vector illustration, which could help defenders define their relevant attack surface and prioritize patching activities.

CVE

CVE-2021-21974

Documented use in ransomware-related activity. It also highlights the risks arising from the relationship between AD identities and administrative access to ESXi.

Known exploited vulnerabilities allowing attackers to perform a guest-to-host attack chain. CVE-2025-22225 exploitation has been seen in ransomware incidents. However, this attack chain requires privileged access to a guest VM, which makes it less critical than unauthenticated RCEs.

* Known Exploited Vulnerabilities database maintained by CISA. KEV status indicates that exploitation of a vulnerability has been observed in the wild, but does not by itself indicate ransomware use. Where ransomware use is documented, it is stated separately. Neither KEV status nor known exploitation by ransomware actors means that the vulnerability was used in the incident in question.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.

Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.

Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

Unit file /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service Service vmware-vdma Description "DNS, time, VM settings sync (v2.03.24766)" ExecStart /opt/vmware/bin/agent Restart always Strings in /opt/vmware/bin/agent: Ligolo-ng v0.8.2 api.cloudvflare[.]com:443

VCSA persistence artifact: /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service

The unit uses a VMware-like prefix, places its binary under /opt/vmware/bin/, describes plausible appliance housekeeping functions, and requests Restart=always. A defender should not treat any unrecognized VMware-looking service as malicious by default, because custom integrations may exist, but a service absent from the list of services the organization defines as trusted is a high-confidence anomaly requiring immediate validation.

Beyond the incident in question, more advanced ESXi persistence techniques have also been documented. For example, Mandiant observed attackers using malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) as a persistence mechanism on compromised ESXi hosts. This demonstrates that attackers with administrative access can establish persistent access at the hypervisor layer, including persistence that survives host restarts. However, this incident shows that common remote-management software and a systemd service can be sufficient when vCenter itself is trusted and poorly monitored.

Turning vCenter into an offensive control plane

One interesting technique observed in the incident was the use of vCenter Host Profiles. Host Profiles are intended to capture and enforce configuration across ESXi hosts. A Host Profile can be applied to separate hosts, clusters of hosts or all hosts associated with a profile. It also may contain subprofiles covering specific configuration aspects, e.g., authentication. Among other things, Host Profiles may contain configuration for Tech Support Mode (TSM) and TSM-SSH.

In this incident, the adversary used Host Profiles to change TSM-SSH service state to enable SSH on target ESXi hosts. The evidence recorded the following sequence:

Offset

Source

Observed event

Primary evidence

T+0

vCenter

Host configuration read through Host Profile workflow

vpxa.log

T+10m18s

vCenter

Configuration change pushed to enable SSH

vpxa.log

T+10m51s

TSM-SSH service reached RUNNING state, indicating that SSH has been enabled on the host and it is accessible from a remote device

vpxa.log + vobd.log

Host Profile manipulation sequence observed before direct ESXi access

Note that the 33-second interval between the configuration push and TSM-SSH reaching RUNNING state is short enough for us to be able to quickly correlate these events by comparing logs from different sources. Overall, it took the attacker eleven minutes after the initial configuration read to reconfigure the host from policy-disabled SSH to direct remote access support. Subsequently, direct SSH access to the target ESXi hosts originated from the vCenter appliance IP, a source that would normally be considered highly trusted on the management network.

Compromise of the management plane converted a legitimate compliance mechanism into an access path to the managed hypervisor

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Notes on ESXi abuse: living-off-the-land tools and controls to monitor

Once an attacker can administer ESXi, many destructive actions require no exploit. LOLESXi project catalogs native ESXi binaries and scripts that have been abused by threat actors, including administrative utilities that enumerate VMs, control power state and alter configuration. This mirrors living-off-the-land behavior on Windows, but the target is the hypervisor control plane.

There are two ESXi hardening mechanisms, and changes to either can be viewed as highly suspicious. Host acceptance level controls which VIBs are allowed to install. The execInstalledOnly setting controls whether non-installed binaries may execute. Broadcom states that ESXi 8 enables the execInstalledOnly runtime option by default and warns that disabling it allows unknown non-installed binaries to execute, increasing ransomware risk. There is also a kernel enforcement setting with the same name, which is related to the runtime option, but distinct. Changes to that may require a reboot.

Inside the ESXi impact phase

Stopping virtual machines before impact

Mature ESXi lockers generally stop guest machines before modifying virtual-disk data because running VMs hold active state and file locks. Different families implement this in different ways, which creates useful behavioral detections. The families described below are not related to the incident in question, but these descriptions may be useful for ransomware protection in general.

Ransomware family

Use vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off for registered virtual machines.

RansomHub ESXi builds

Contain custom C++ logic that can enumerate and stop machines without relying on an esxcli or vim-cmd command sequence.

How different ESXi locker families release VM state before starting destructive file operations

We don’t know the exact technique used to kill VMs in this incident. However, a rapid sequence of power-off or world-kill operations across many VMs is always a high-confidence pre-impact signal. In the case evidence, the disaster-recovery host showed all VMs stopping within 23 seconds, while vmksummary.log, which stores the number of running VMs each hour, showed it dropping from normal VM counts to zero.

Payload delivery and FlowSsh behavior

The payload was delivered to ESXi via SFTP. The auth.log authentication log file exposed a client identifier associated with FlowSsh, Bitvise’s SSH client library for C, C++ and .NET. FlowSsh supports SFTP, remote execution requests, interactive shell sessions and tunneling. Those capabilities fit the observed delivery model, but the library identification should rest primarily on the recorded client identifier rather than on behavioral inference alone.

After the payload was delivered, the following series of commands was executed. We reconstructed this sequence primarily from the shell.log file.

Offset

Observed command

Analytical note

T+0

true

No-op probe in a dedicated session.

T+1s

chmod +x /tmp/esx64

Separate execution session.

T+1m48s

true

Second no-op probe.

T+1m49s

./tmp/esx64 /selftest

Separate execution session; payload validation stage.

Each command pair was preceded by a session executing only true. This repeating pattern is consistent with automated FlowSsh channel setup, but in isolation, it can’t be considered a reliable indicator of the tool in use. Human operators could have typed true as well, and other automation frameworks could have emitted reachability probes. The sequence should therefore be hunted as a behavioral fingerprint, not treated as a unique signature for FlowSsh. Its value increases when combined with an unusual SSH client identifier, SFTP staging to /tmp, chmod, and a subsequent self-test or payload execution.

The three-hour self-test window

The /selftest execution ran for approximately 16 seconds and occurred roughly three hours before final detonation. A pre-impact test run may suggest that the operator was validating compatibility with the target ESXi build before proceeding to destructive execution.

Pre-impact detection opportunity

Treat unexpected executable staging under /tmp, followed by execution and subsequent access to /vmfs, as a critical pre-impact sequence. While individual indicators such as chmod +x may be ambiguous in isolation, unexpected execution of a newly staged executable from /tmp can itself be a strong indicator of malicious activity. The complete sequence provides stronger contextual evidence by linking payload staging, execution, validation, and subsequent access to the VM storage layer.

Detonation command and evidence confidence

The attackers executed the following command to trigger the destructive activity.

./tmp/esx64 /p /vmfs/ /depth 5 /wipe /allsys /detach /-showvolumes

Observed ESXi detonation command

Let’s break it down into separate parameters and analyze their forensic usefulness. Parameter interpretation is accompanied by confidence level, because exact implementation details cannot be reconstructed without the binary.

Parameter

Observed or corroborated meaning

Interpretation confidence

/p /vmfs/

Target path is the VMFS root where virtual-machine files reside.

High: direct command + platform path.

/depth 5

Directory recursion depth.

High: conventional argument meaning and observed placement.

/wipe

Overwrite/wipe behavior; ._wipe artifacts were present across datastores.

High for destructive behavior, medium for exact implementation.

/allsys

Include system files. This aligns with publicly documented BlackNevas/Trigona family behavior.

Medium: the assessment is based on the comparison with the publicly documented malware family behavior; missing binary prevents direct validation.

/detach

Detach from the terminal; activity continued after SSH disconnect.

High: external documentation + incident persistence of effects.

/-showvolumes

Suppress volume listing according to documented family parameters.

Medium: comparative documentation only.

The forward-slash argument style resembles the Trigona and BlackNevas command-line family. SentinelOne describes BlackNevas as a Trigona derivative with ESXi-capable builds and specialized switches, including /p or /path, /wipe, /depth, and /detach. That comparison strengthens attribution but does not replace a binary hash or reverse-engineered match.

Partial overwrite and what 2 KB actually implies

Incident artifacts indicated that approximately the first 2 KB of virtual disk files were overwritten. Damage to the beginning of a disk can destroy the protective MBR, primary GPT header, and other early boot or filesystem structures, which can immediately make a guest unbootable. However, the UEFI specification requires GPT media to keep both primary and backup GPT headers and partition-entry arrays in different locations. If the primary GPT is corrupt and the backup is valid, GPT-aware software should use the backup, which may help restore the primary. Therefore, an overwrite of the first 2 KB does not by itself mean that the partition metadata is unrecoverable. Practical recovery depends on whether additional boot records, filesystem metadata, volume structures, descriptors, or application data were also modified, and on the exact virtual-disk layout.

Destroying the recovery path first

In this incident, backup infrastructure was not collateral damage. The attacker disabled antivirus protection on the backup environment days before the main attack, and later stopped backup services, encrypted the recovery infrastructure, and disrupted administrative access — all before ESXi detonation. The order of operations reduced the defenders’ ability to restore production when they needed it most.

Recovery capabilities were disrupted before the final ESXi impact. The relative timings are based on the incident sequence

This changes the definition of a resilient backup architecture. Storage immutability is valuable, but it does not protect the identities, management servers, repositories, network paths, credentials, or procedures required to perform system restoration. Recovery should be designed as a separate security boundary with independent administrative identities, restricted management paths, offline or logically isolated recovery options, tested restore procedures, and monitoring that does not depend on the production control plane.

Two recent vulnerabilities in Veeam are a perfect illustration of this. Although neither of these vulnerabilities was seen exploited in this case, they take advantage of weak privilege management policy, which may make them exploitable by any domain user, including those with the lowest privileges. CVE-2024-40711 is listed in CISA’s KEV database as a vulnerability exploited by ransomware. CVE-2025-23120 is more recent and still absent from KEV, but it is worth noting that according to Veeam, it allows RCE, but only affects domain-joined backup servers. The general lesson is not vendor-specific: a recovery system that depends on the same identity plane as production infrastructure can be compromised and used to achieve the attackers’ goals.

Detection and investigation

There are a number of log files that document ESXi events. These sources can reconstruct a destructive hypervisor incident even when no endpoint agent exists on ESXi. The limitation is retention. Broadcom states that ESXi logs internally to a ramdisk, which has limited space and gets cleared at reboot, and that persistent scratch or remote syslog is required if logs must survive reboot and local storage loss. We recommend collecting logs to remote storage to maintain forensic visibility into ESXi incidents.

Example correlation logic

Below, we provide two examples of technology-neutral correlation logic that could be used to hunt for similar incidents. Note that they are not ready-made SIEM rules, but you can use them to develop your own rules. Example 1: Host Profile abuse leading to direct ESXi access:

IF host_profile_remediation changes service in {TSM, TSM-SSH} AND service_state becomes RUNNING within 5 minutes AND no approved change window exists THEN raise HIGH severity; IF SSH session to same ESXi host originates from vCenter or management appliance within 15 minutes of the remediation THEN escalate to CRITICAL and preserve auth.log, vpxa.log, vobd.log, vCenter Events/Tasks and Host Profile state.

Example 2: pre-impact ESXi payload staging:

IF SFTP upload or new executable appears under /tmp AND chmod / execution follows from same SSH client or source AND a short validation run occurs before access to /vmfs THEN raise CRITICAL; Increase confidence if: - client identifier is unusual for the management segment - repeated true-only SSH channels precede commands - multiple VMs are stopped soon afterward.

Incident response at the virtualization layer

This section contains recommended actions when responding to an incident involving ESXi ransomware.

First 30 minutes after incident discovery

Isolate vCenter management access from ordinary enterprise segments while preserving investigator access through a controlled path.

Export vCenter Events and Tasks, SSO audit records, active sessions, and the current Host Profile definitions before remediation changes erase context.

Collect ESXi auth.log, shell.log, vpxa.log, vobd.log, hostd.log, vmkernel.log, vmkwarning.log, vmksummary.log, esxupdate.log, and hostprofiletrace.log from each affected host.

Preserve VCSA /etc/systemd/system, /opt/vmware paths referenced by previously unknown or unapproved units, shell history, wtmp, authentication logs, and copies or hashes of suspicious binaries.

Capture backup-server telemetry, service state, credential-store evidence, and network logs before rebuilding or rotating infrastructure credentials.

Record current execInstalledOnly state, host acceptance level, SSH/ESXi Shell state, Lockdown Mode, domain membership, and ESXi permission mappings.

Do not begin by rebooting ESXi merely to remove the attacker session. ESXi logging persistence depends on scratch and syslog configuration, and a reboot may destroy ramdisk-resident evidence. Confirm that critical logs have been copied or remotely retained before containing disruptive activity unless ongoing impact makes immediate shutdown unavoidable.

Containment priorities

Revoke or rotate compromised administrative credentials and remove attacker-controlled access paths, but preserve authentication and task records first.

Disable unapproved TSM-SSH and ESXi Shell access after collecting evidence; make sure that Host Profiles or other automation will not immediately re-enable them.

Remove unauthorized systemd services and remote-management agents from VCSA only after imaging or preserving the unit and referenced binaries.

Restore execInstalledOnly and acceptance-level settings to the approved baseline after determining that doing so will not disrupt evidence collection or critical recovery tooling.

Segment or disconnect compromised backup infrastructure from production and establish a clean recovery control plane before attempting large-scale restoration.

Architecture hardening derived from the case

Treat vCenter as Tier 0

VMware vCenter is not merely an inventory console. It can hold the authority to configure hosts, manage identities, power VMs, apply Host Profiles, and mediate access across the virtual estate. The incident in question shows why compromise of vCenter can undermine controls enforced through the virtualization management plane, providing an attacker with sufficient privileges to configure hosts, control VMs, and modify security-relevant settings across the virtual estate, potentially enabling the entire virtualized environment to be disrupted or destroyed within minutes. Protect vCenter with dedicated administrative identities, phishing-resistant MFA through supported identity federation, restricted management-network access, monitored privileged sessions, and close monitoring of Host Profile and cluster-level change operations.

Separate virtualization identities from ordinary enterprise administration

Avoid broad reuse of domain administrator or workstation admin credentials for virtualization. Where ESXi is domain-joined, apply the secure Active Directory configuration following Broadcom’s recommendations and continuously audit group mappings and permissions. Note that the Valid Accounts attacker technique is applicable to ESXi environments. Moreover, as an example of the Default Accounts subtechnique, MITRE specifically mentions the vpxuser account used by vCenter for host management.

Keep direct ESXi management paths narrow

SSH is useful for troubleshooting but should be treated as an exceptional administrative path rather than routine day-to-day access. Unauthorized SSH enablement on ESXi hosts both directly and through vCenter should be detected by monitoring TSM-SSH changes and treated as a suspicious event. To further harden ESXi hosts, use Lockdown Mode where operationally suitable, providing access only to a small set of explicitly authorized users, apply management-network filtering, and an approval and tracking policy for any changes, especially for enabling shell access.

Make the logging path independent of the affected host

Remote syslog from ESXi and vCenter should be stored on infrastructure outside the virtualization trust domain. Persistent scratch improves log survivability after reboot, but local evidence can still be lost if the data storage or host is destroyed. It is recommended to use centralized logging (e.g., SIEM logging), which should include authentication, shell, host management, Host Profile, and vCenter task telemetry. Proper logging should be configured before any incident happens, so the full picture is available to the response team in case of an emergency.

Design backup as a separate security boundary

Use independent administrative identities for backup, minimize domain dependencies, isolate repositories and management interfaces, protect immutable copies from production credentials, and test recovery under the assumption that vCenter and production AD are unavailable. A backup design should be judged not only by whether data is immutable, but by whether a clean operator can authenticate, reach the repository, validate the data, and restore workloads after the production control plane is compromised.

Resilience improves when enterprise identity, virtualization administration and recovery authority are separated rather than chained through shared privileged credentials

Conclusion

The central lesson from the incident in question is not that ESXi needs another endpoint agent. It is that virtualization security depends on the integrity of the management plane, the identity plane, and the recovery plane at the same time. A hypervisor can remain fully patched and protected and still become the point of maximum ransomware impact when the system authorized to manage it has already been compromised. The adversary did not need to break VMware’s cryptography or escape from a guest. Once they accessed a privileged vCenter control, a legitimate compliance mechanism could be used to change host state, enable SSH, and create a path into ESXi that looked structurally similar to normal administration activities.

The case also shows why destructive ransomware incidents are often won or lost before encryption begins. The attacker established alternate persistence, validated the ESXi payload hours before detonation, disrupted backup capability first, and then executed disruptive activities from the layer least visible to guest controls. Each stage created a detection opportunity, but those opportunities existed in management, virtualization and recovery telemetry rather than in a conventional endpoint process tree.

The durable defense is therefore architectural. Treat vCenter as Tier 0. Separate virtualization identities from ordinary enterprise administration. Keep direct ESXi access narrow. Preserve native logs outside the affected platform. Detect high-risk configuration changes as sequences rather than isolated commands. Finally, design recovery so that compromise of production identity or virtualization management does not also provide the authority needed to destroy the systems required to restore them.

In this article

What’s affected by the Microsoft 365 outage

What Microsoft has said about the cause and recovery efforts

Where to check for updates and what to keep in mind about security

A widespread Microsoft outage is disrupting Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services, including SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot. Reportedly, the problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued into Friday, affecting people trying to access email, communicate with colleagues, and use workplace applications.

Microsoft initially reported problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas, but disruption subsequently extended beyond that region. CNN reports impacts on businesses, schools, and government services, including in Australia.

There are a lot of questions we’ll try to answer as the day evolves.

What’s affected?

Outlook users have reported being unable to send or receive emails or even load their inboxes. Other affected services include SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot, although availability has varied: some people have been able to use certain applications while others remain inaccessible.

Outage tracker Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

What’s the cause?

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said there was no indication that malicious activity or a cyberattack caused the outage. The underlying cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said some servers became unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks. That left the remaining infrastructure handling extra traffic, contributing to connection problems. The underlying reason for the failures was not immediately clear.

Recovery has not been straightforward. Microsoft restored some servers, but subsequently said they could become unresponsive again when traffic returned. Other attempted changes also failed to deliver the expected improvement.

Update November 13, 10:01 UTC (05:01 EST): Microsoft says it currently has no evidence that malicious activity caused the outage. The company says it will publish a full post-incident report once mitigation is complete, detailing the root cause and additional safeguards to help prevent similar incidents.

How long will it take to restore services?

At the time of writing, Microsoft has not provided a timeframe for full restoration. The company reported partial recovery in some regions, after earlier attempts produced mixed results.

For updates, check Microsoft’s service status page and its Microsoft 365 Status account on X. Both are channels Microsoft is using to communicate about the incident.

Update, November 13, 09:57 UTC (04:57 EST): Microsoft says its latest traffic optimization measures are producing “positive results for service stability and increased capacity.” The company is continuing to restore affected servers and monitor recovery, but full restoration has not yet been confirmed in the updates reviewed. Earlier improvements proved temporary, with Microsoft reporting partial recovery that was not sustained.

Update, November 13, 12:11 UTC (07:11 EST): Microsoft says it has made further progress toward recovery, with traffic gradually being restored across portions of the affected infrastructure. The company is seeing improvements in mailbox access and delayed-email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent problems. Recovery work is continuing across the remaining affected infrastructure. Microsoft has also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect delayed messages while recovery continues. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Update, November 13, 13:46 UTC (08:46 EST): Microsoft says recovery is progressing across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. The company is also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Some users may still experience intermittent access problems or delayed email delivery as recovery work continues across the remaining affected infrastructure. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

What about security?

ABC reports that Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 are both on Microsoft’s list of services that may be affected.

Being unable to log in doesn’t mean attackers are also locked out, or that every security feature has stopped working. If you rely on these services, check which security features are working as access is restored. Follow your IT team’s guidance and check Microsoft’s updates for details.

Be alert for unexpected messages offering to restore access or asking you to sign in through a link. Go directly to Microsoft’s official status pages instead.

Malwarebytes and ThreatDown products are not affected by this outage.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines: Will Your AI System Need an Independent Audit?
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using: Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk.

Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week.

Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom.

The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now.

Key Takeaways

CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users.

Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence.

From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation.

Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger.

AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions.

What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04.

Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page.

The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies.

It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism. Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity.

Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9

There are three narrow exclusions:

Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot.

Purely rule-based automation, such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope.

Consumer personal use, such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope.

Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size.

Is It Mandatory?

The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier.

Three things give it teeth in practice:

It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours.

Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators.

Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next.

For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor.

How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works

Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place.

Factor

What it asks

F1: Impact severity

How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output?

F2: Autonomy and actionability

What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves?

F3: Data sensitivity

How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified?

F4: Scale and exposure

How many users, transactions or systems does it reach?

F5: Reversibility

How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone?

F6: Sector criticality

Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function?

F7: Adversarial exposure

Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment?

F8: Complexity and auditability

How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score.

The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement:

Score

Tier

Minimum audit requirement

8–12

Tier 1 (Low)

Self-assessment or basic internal review, reviewed annually

13–19

Tier 2 (Moderate)

Documented internal audit, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization at least annually

20–26

Tier 3 (High)

Periodic independent third-party audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization, every six months where risk or material change warrants

27–32

Tier 4 (Critical)

Independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization with continuous monitoring

The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state.

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Section 5.4, page 25.

Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority.

The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier

The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines.

Version A answers questions, checks order status through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over help articles and order history, and hands refunds to human agents. Version B is the same bot, but it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 on its own.

Factor

Version A: answers only

Version B: issues refunds

Why it changes

F1: Impact severity

2

A wrong answer or a single bad refund is still limited and recoverable

F2: Autonomy

2

3

Version B initiates consequential actions instead of advising a human

F3: Data sensitivity

2

3

Refunds bring payment and financial data into play

F4: Scale and exposure

3

Large-scale, customer-facing in both cases

F5: Reversibility

2

Money paid out to the wrong account is costly and slow to recover

F6: Sector criticality

2

An important business function, not critical infrastructure

F7: Adversarial exposure

F8: Complexity

A third-party LLM is partially opaque to the deploying company

Total

19 (Tier 2)

22 (Tier 3)

Source: Illustrative scoring · tier bands and minimum audits from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Table 11

Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3.

Two things stand out.

First, even the "harmless" Version A sits at the top of Tier 2. That already means a documented internal audit, a simplified AI impact assessment, AI threat modelling and API security testing, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization at least annually. Many companies running customer-facing LLMs may not realize they're here.

Second, Version B doesn't just cross a score threshold. Its ability to initiate transactions is also a named escalation trigger, and an internet-facing bot that can move money is an obvious prompt-injection target. Moving to Tier 3 adds a comprehensive AI impact assessment, validation independent of the development team, a comprehensive AI security assessment with VAPT, a formal AI Governance Committee, and audits as often as every six months.

Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment.

What Auditors Will Test Your AI For

Section 9 of the guidelines adds dedicated requirements for generative AI, RAG, agentic, multimodal, and multi-agent systems. These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using:

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Table 16, page 63.

Source: Refund chatbot attack surface · threats from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Section 9.2

Mapped onto the refund chatbot, each component becomes a separate test case, and the leaked-credential risk sits outside the system entirely

CERT-In takes prompt injection seriously enough to apply it to auditors too. Audit teams using AI tools must treat auditee documents, logs and tool outputs as untrusted data and test for injection attempts designed to alter audit criteria or suppress findings.

The guidelines also expect AI threat models to draw on MITRE ATLAS, OWASP guidance, CERT-In advisories and "other relevant threat intelligence." That's where many teams have a blind spot.

Threat actors trade stolen AI API keys, discuss jailbreak and injection techniques on underground forums, and leak cloud and model credentials in breach dumps. Cyble's threat intelligence tracks this activity across the surface, deep and dark web, so security teams can build AI threat models on what attackers are actually doing rather than on assumptions.

What to Do in the Next 90 Days

The first step is the one most organizations will find hardest: knowing what AI they actually run. The guidelines treat an incomplete or missing AI inventory as a governance non-conformity in its own right.

Build your AI inventory. List every AI system in use, including vendor APIs, copilots built into SaaS tools, and shadow AI that teams adopted without approval. Record purpose, owner, model source, data processed and deployment status.

Score each system honestly. Apply the eight factors to what each system can actually do today. Flag any system that can act on its own, such as issuing refunds, sending messages, executing code or calling tools, since those are the ones most likely to sit higher than you expect.

Review permissions before you add features. Treat every new agent capability as a potential tier change. Put human approval gates on consequential actions and make sure agents run with least privilege.

Map your AI incidents to the six-hour clock. Define what an AI incident looks like, such as a successful prompt injection, data leakage through a model, or a poisoned knowledge source. Then check that you can detect, classify, and report one within six hours, with 180 days of time-synchronized logs to support the investigation.

Lock down AI secrets and watch for leaks. Move API keys and model credentials into a secrets manager and rotate them. Then monitor for those credentials turning up outside your environment. With Cyble's dark web monitoring, teams get alerts when credentials, keys or data tied to their organization appear in breach dumps, underground markets, paste sites or code repositories, so a leaked key can be revoked before it's abused.

Bring in threat intelligence for your AI threat model. Use current intelligence on attacker techniques, rather than a generic checklist, to decide what your red-team and VAPT exercises test.

Engage a CERT-In empaneled auditor early. If any system scores Tier 2 or above, start scoping the independent audit now rather than when a regulator or customer asks for the report.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines? They are a risk-based framework, issued by CERT-In on 4 November 2026, for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their lifecycle. Each AI system is scored on eight risk factors and placed in one of four tiers that set its audit requirements.

Do the guidelines apply to foreign AI companies? Yes. They cover AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users, not only organisations based in India.

Does using a third-party AI model or API take my system out of scope? No. AI systems stay in scope regardless of model origin or delivery mechanism, and lack of access to vendor evidence is treated as a scope limitation, not as proof of conformity.

Which AI systems need an independent audit? Systems scoring 13 or above (Tier 2 and higher) require an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation, with frequency and depth increasing at Tier 3 and Tier 4.

How quickly must AI security incidents be reported to CERT-In? AI incidents that meet CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, consistent with CERT-In's April 2022 Directions, which also require 180-day log retention.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Stolen webcam clips of 900+ victims feed North Korea’s $400 million fake Zoom scheme
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The audio problem is the attack The invite comes from a real account
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
North Korean state hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months by pulling targets into fake Zoom and Teams calls filled with webcam footage of earlier victims. The FBI calls the scheme FaceStealer. It has seized more than 900 of those recordings, and on November 12 it warned crypto and web3 workers and open-source maintainers about the scheme.

Source: FBI

Every successful call infects the target and records them, so each new victim becomes the familiar face on the next call. The FBI ties the activity to the group tracked as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among other names. The hackers go after computers that hold a crypto wallet, a seed phrase, or access to an employer’s network or a code repository.

The audio problem is the attack

The invite comes from a real account. The hackers take over earlier victims’ Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord accounts, read their chat histories, and message the victims’ contacts about catching up or an investment. A Calendly invite sets the time. The meeting link arrives shortly before the call and points to a lookalike domain such as uu01webzoom[.]us.

Once you’re in the call, the hackers play your contact’s recorded video, often next to clips of other “participants.” A chat message then says the others can’t hear you and walks you through an update, a script, or a command to paste into your terminal. Following those steps installs a cookie harvester, keyloggers, a screen capturer and a backdoor. Your webcam has been recording since you clicked the link.

The hackers are in no hurry. In several cases they waited from a few months to more than a year for wallet balances to grow before emptying them.

A JavaScript library came close

Earlier this year the group got the maintainer of a major open-source JavaScript library into a fake Teams call that included at least one person he recognized. He ran the fix. The hackers then used his access to create malicious dependencies that would download along with the library, which gets tens of millions of downloads a week. The attack was caught and stopped quickly. The FBI has seen other attempts against maintainers on npm and, more recently, maintainers of Rust crates.

The group has also started building deepfakes of well-known crypto figures from public photos and video. “The quality of the deepfakes only needs to be good enough to pass as webcam video,” the FBI wrote. Stolen footage of real victims still makes up the overwhelming share of the scheme.

Keep the camera off

The FBI’s advice starts with the webcam: leave it off until you can see, hear and talk with the person who invited you. Join through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code. Confirm the meeting through a second channel, for example a phone call when the invite came over Telegram. Don’t run scripts or paste code to fix a meeting app.

Keep only small amounts in browser extension wallets, and store no recovery phrases or private keys on your devices. A thief with a copied seed phrase can drain the wallet whenever they choose. If you suspect a compromise, create a new wallet on a clean device and move everything into it.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: How attackers turned a Teams meeting booking into a device code phishing trap
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers used a fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler to trick an employee at a construction company into approving a device code sign-in
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Attackers used a fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler to trick an employee at a construction company into approving a device code sign-in. They got a valid session token before Huntress’s security operations center identified the incident.

Device code phishing abuses a real Microsoft sign-in flow. The attacker starts a sign-in, gets a short code back, and persuades the victim to type it into Microsoft’s genuine device login page. The victim enters the code, completes MFA if prompted, and without knowing it approves the attacker’s session. That approval hands the attacker access tokens for the victim’s account.

The booking reference was the code

The email came from a typosquatted domain impersonating a real senior vice president at another construction firm. Its link went to a Google share link, which redirected to the lure page. The attacker’s domain never appeared in the email body, so the message got past URL reputation checks.

The lure page looked like a Teams scheduler. It showed the executive’s headshot and offered an introductory call about a long-term supply partnership. Clicking “Continue” started a Microsoft device code request on the attacker’s backend. The next page showed the resulting code as a “Booking Reference,” with a countdown timer to hurry things along.

Lure confirmation page (Source: Huntress)

Clicking “Copy” or the confirm button copied the code to the clipboard and opened a popup to Microsoft’s real sign-in page. When the attacker’s backend registered a successful sign-in, the page closed the popup, showed a “Verification complete” note and sent the victim to a Calendly booking page so nothing looked out of place.

Built to beat scanners and MFA errors

The phishing kit arrived as AES-256-GCM ciphertext, with the decryption key sitting next to it in the same page. That setup targets email scanners and crawlers that don’t run JavaScript. To them, the lure page is an encrypted blob.

The kit also had fallbacks. If Microsoft returned an error, which can happen when MFA is required, the page told the victim a new verification code was being prepared. It then started a fresh device code session and tried again. The attacker sent the final login through a residential proxy in New Orleans so it looked like consumer traffic.

What to lock down

Huntress advises treating unexpected device code prompts as suspicious. Where the business doesn’t need device code authentication, restrict or monitor it through conditional access. Huntress also recommends phishing-resistant MFA and a close look at unfamiliar device sign-ins.

If programmatic user agents such as python-requests or node show up in interactive sign-in logs, that points to automated attacker infrastructure. After a confirmed compromise, check for rogue MFA methods, unknown registered devices, unauthorized app consents, suspicious mailbox rules and suspicious outbound mail.

Macfinger ClickFix campaign sends DownTheDRAIN infostealer for macOS, (Fri, Nov 13th)
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Background I first wrote about the Macfinger ClickFix campaign on 2026-09-22, and I took a closer look at the malware on 2026-09-25
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Introduction

In this diary, I've given a nickname to the macOS infostealer we've been seeing from the Macfinger ClickFix campaign. Based on the analysis of an example posted on the Huntress Cybersecurity Blog, I'm calling this macOS malware DownTheDRAIN infostealer.

This diary reviews an example of DownTheDRAIN infostealer distributed through the Macfinger ClickFix campaign on Wednesday, 2026-11-11.

Of note, my mac mini running macOS 26.7.3 blocked and moved the malware to Trash before it could exfiltrate any sensitive data.

Shown above: DownTheDRAIN infostealer blocked and moved to Trash.

Background

I first wrote about the Macfinger ClickFix campaign on 2026-09-22, and I took a closer look at the malware on 2026-09-25. It didn't match the profile of any macOS infostealers I usually run across. Since I couldn't find any unique characteristics in my analysis, I waited for someone to name it.

I didn't see that anyone had named this infostealer yet, but the Huntress analysis of a sample provided a somewhat unique aspect that could be used for a nickname.

The DRAIN function

The Huntress analysis from one of the samples revealed a DRAIN function that "...identifies various cryptocurrency wallet addresses and can redirect the contents to a wallet controlled by the threat actor." For more information on this function and the associated code, read the full August 2026 post by Andrew Brandt.

Images

Shown above: Fake CAPTCHA page from the Macfinger ClickFix campaign.

Shown above: Fake CAPTCHA page showing the ClickFix instructions.

Shown above: ClickFix text pasted into a Terminal window.

Shown above: Traffic from the infection filtered in Wireshark.
