Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified.

A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked.

“Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.”

The tool belongs to Remus Stealer, an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators.

If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts.

“In the supplied version 1.3.9 announcement, Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the main sales thread advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.”

It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked.

Hudson Rock believes Remus may obtain or create an authorization token while the victim is logged into Gmail through a browser. A remote component could then use this authorization to access emails even after the malware has stopped running, as long as Google continues to accept it. Tom’s Guide also reports that the tool can bypass Google’s anti-fraud checks and says it has contacted Google for comment.

However, other reports highlight some important uncertainties. CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability. Hudson Rock has not conducted a controlled test to show that Remus can still access newly received emails after the victim changes their password and revokes existing sessions and third-party access. According to Cybernews, the developer describes the feature as a Gmail “zero-day”. However, this claim has not been independently reproduced.

The business side is more concrete. CyberInsider says the mailbox feature sits in an Enterprise tier at $1,000 per month, with shareable mailbox links so criminals can hand an inbox they’ve already compromised to others. The actor behind Remus Stealer offers the MaaS with three subscription tiers: Basic at $250, Pro at $500 and Enterprise at $1,000.

This kind of claim has a history. In late 2023, a developer called PRISMA surfaced an exploit that regenerated persistent Google cookies by manipulating a token and account ID pair, and Lumma then used it so access continued after a password reset. It’s a precedent and not proof, since Remus’ mechanism is unknown, and Hudson Rock still treats a Google password change as an essential recovery step, while saying victims should also look for other ways an attacker could keep access.

The tool is marketed to “enterprise” customers, so most users are unlikely to be targeted. It will probably be used mainly against organizations and high-profile individuals. Hudson Rock recommends that victims first disconnect and clean the infected computer before accessing their trusted accounts again. They should then change compromised passwords using a clean device and review their signed-in devices to remove suspicious sessions and third-party access.

Hudson Rock also advises users to check Gmail settings for unauthorized changes and secure any other accounts that use the compromised mailbox for password resets or verification codes. Other basic precautions remain important: watch out for phishing emails with urgent messages, spelling mistakes or suspicious sender addresses, and keep antivirus software up to date. Tom’s Guide expects Google to introduce additional Gmail protections if the tool proves as effective as its developer claims.

For now, this is a vendor’s marketing claim supported by customer screenshots and Hudson Rock’s investigation, not a confirmed Gmail vulnerability. One important detail offers some reassurance: attackers must first infect the victim’s computer and compromise their mailbox before they can use the tool.

“Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise.” concludes the report. “The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gmail)

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.

In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.

Initial Access: attacks through contractors

The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.

Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket

The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation

# Disable account # Verify result

Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

Comment translation

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit # Concurrent task limit control # Quick ping

The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.

Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

Task name

Launched executable file

sIErKswD

C:\Windows\System32\..\System32\cmd.exe

PpMBCCSR

C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe

QwZtLmNp

C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe

We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force.

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

Persistence: scheduled tasks

Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools automatically. The attackers create the tasks manually through PowerShell:

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

Privilege Escalation: vulnerabilities and configuration flaws

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

To do this, they attempted to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost); these attempts created machine accounts with telltale names in Active Directory, such as:

GHOSTAUFTAFGS

GHOSTCZYQVAZS

GHOSTIVPRLDZA

GHOST{8 random letters}

These names are generated by scripts making use of an exploit published on GitHub.

The exploit works like this: on behalf of the newly created account, it requests a certificate based on the Machine template from the system holding the AD CS role. The Attributes, Subject, and SubjectAlternativeName fields contain parameters like these:

<Data Name='Attributes'>CertificateTemplate:Machine\nSAN:dns=dc01.victim.domain\ncdc:91.210.109[.]118\nrmd:dc01.victim.domain </Data> <Data Name='Subject'>CN=GHOSTABUIEFAD.victim.domain</Data> <Data Name='SubjectAlternativeName'>DNS name =dc01.victim.domain\r\n</Data>

The cdc attribute specifies the IP address or name of the system that the certification authority must contact to verify the data. The attackers specify the address of a system they control (in this case, 91.210.109[.]118) and send forged data from it. If exploitation succeeds, the certification authority issues a certificate with the specified parameters, based on the specified template.

Once the certificate is issued, the domain controller name in its SubjectAlternativeName field lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account.

In one case, the attackers also uploaded an executable for persistence, on behalf of which PowerShell scripts were launched with nonstandard HostName (Имя узла) field value.

Field name translation

Severity HostName HostVersion HostId HostApplication EngineVersion RunspaceId PipelineId CommandName CommandType ScriptName

Although the file was later deleted, indirect evidence hints at its purpose. For example, the MSFConsole value may indicate that the file is a component of the Metasploit framework. The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository.

Beyond classic vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, the attackers also took an interest in 1C:Enterprise servers with insecure configurations (article in Russian).

On top of the configuration flaws, 1C:Enterprise systems are frequently accessed by support staff and administrators who hold elevated privileges in Active Directory. Together, these factors make it easy for attackers to escalate privileges and start moving laterally.

Stealth: covering tracks and masquerading

To hinder incident response, the attackers delete their tools and output files and clear the command history.

While the tools are still in use in the victim’s infrastructure, the attackers typically give them and their auxiliary objects legitimate-looking names:

KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe and KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64_FIXED.exe are self-extracting archives. They contain the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script, a directory with a malicious Group Policy Object, and one of two archives, KasperskyAgent.exe or agent.exe.

KasperskyAgentInstaller.exe, KasperskyAgent.exe, and agent.exe are self-extracting archives containing the ransomware Trojan executable and auxiliary files.

Kaspersky GPO is the name of the Group Policy Object that distributes the ransomware Trojan in the victim’s infrastructure.

KasperskyAgentInstallTask and Sysvc are names used for the scheduled task that runs the self-extracting ransomware archive files.

Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 is the PowerShell script that creates the malicious Kaspersky GPO.

Kaspersky_GPO_Deployment.log is the log of the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script.

Note that using the Kaspersky name in malicious file names doesn’t help the attackers avoid detection. Kaspersky solutions successfully detect and block these malicious files.

Defense Impairment: weak access policies for security tools play into attackers’ hands

To stay under the radar longer, the attackers clear event logs on some systems using the built-in wevtutil utility.

In addition, once they have sufficient privileges, they disable antivirus protection on hosts, which lets them run tools such as mimikatz.

The attackers also go after the centralized management consoles for security solutions, which they then use to disable protection en masse.

At the Impact stage, the attackers also use a Group Policy Object that modifies Windows Defender settings in the registry to switch it off. As a result, the antivirus did not respond when the ransomware was launched.

Finally, if they have sufficient privileges, the attackers manually add their malicious tools to the antivirus exclusion list.

Credential Access: mimikatz, a keylogger, and extraction of credentials from files

To capture keystrokes on a compromised system, the attackers use a modified version of the peeping-tom keylogger, whose source code is available on GitHub. The keylogger executable and its log file are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt

In the sample we found, stolen data was sent to 91.210.109[.]118. Persistence for the keylogger is provided by the scheduled task described above in the Persistence section.

To dump credentials from memory, the attackers use mimikatz. Files related to mimikatz are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimidrv.sys

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimilib.dll

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimispool.dll

To hunt for credentials and other secrets (SSH keys, access tokens, and the like) in files on accessible network shares, the group uses Snaffler. To simplify running the tool, the attackers drop a configuration file on the system:

Besides data from network shares, the attackers were interested in data stored in password managers (for example, KeePass) on administrator workstations.

Discovery: the standard toolkit

Local discovery

After gaining control of a compromised system, the attackers ran a basic set of commands to identify the current user, running processes, network interface settings, the system’s external IP address, and so on:

whoami tasklist quser ipconfig curl 2ip[.]io

Remote discovery

In the early stages, the attackers used the fscan scanner to gather information on the internal infrastructure. They were particularly interested in the following ports:

135 (RPC)

139 (NetBIOS-SSN)

1433 (Microsoft SQL)

8006 (Proxmox VE)

Once they had the access they needed and had moved laterally, the attackers ran ADRecon on domain controllers and SharpHound on one of the workstations.

The attackers also used PowerShell to run LDAP queries against the controllers of adjacent domains, pulling lists of domain systems, users, and groups.

Russian text translation

The user has no additional groups in memberOf (primary only) User not found

As an alternative to PowerShell, the attackers used the net.exe utility to get information about domain users and privileged groups:

net users /domain net group "Domain Admins" /domain net group "Администраторы домена" /domain

Lateral Movement: SSH, RDP, and WinRM

For lateral movement, the group relies on standard remote administration protocols: SSH, WinRM, and RDP. The attackers connect to systems either through previously deployed tunnels or directly from the compromised host.

Command and Control: delivering tools to the system

To deliver its tools to target hosts, the group uses built-in OS utilities. Specifically, the incidents involved:

certutil:

The Windows BITS background service (invoked in two ways):

cURL:

PowerShell:

Creating tunnels with Xray

The certutil and BITS commands shown above are what the attackers used to download Xray onto victim systems. They then used Xray to set up reverse VLESS tunnels to the command-and-control server. The configuration file, stored alongside the Xray executable, was usually named config.json. In some cases, the attackers deleted it right after starting the tunnel to hide the Xray configuration from defenders.

Judging by the configuration files recovered during the analysis, the attackers used port 443 on the VLESS server to blend in with legitimate HTTPS traffic. The configuration files also contain blocks that set up the REALITY protocol, which is intended to disguise the attackers’ traffic as requests to the legitimate site mirror.yandex.ru:

The traffic was also disguised as requests to another legitimate site, yastatic.net:

Installing AnyDesk

The PowerShell command above AnyDesk, which the attackers used to remotely control compromised hosts.

After the download, the attackers installed the software with the --silent flag to avoid alerting the user, set a connection password, and used PowerShell to pull the infected machine’s ID (which AnyDesk uses for remote connections on the client side) from the configuration file:

Collection & Exfiltration: data from messaging apps

Right before encrypting the data, the attackers connected to one of the domain controllers and ran the PowerShell script steal_tgs.ps1, which created the tdatas directory. According to the NTFS USN journal, while the script ran, 7-Zip created archives in this directory with telltale names hinting at their contents:

<system_name>_<date>_<username>_tdata.zip

The directory name tdatas and the substring tdata may refer to the C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata directory. The Telegram messaging app uses this directory to store authorization keys, session data, app settings, and other session information.

So the attackers were harvesting messaging app data from remote systems they could reach, packing it with 7-Zip and uploading it to an external web service through Google Chrome.

Impact: Sn00py ransomware Trojan

The Citrus group uses ransomware from the Sn00py family to encrypt data. It’s written in Go and uses the RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms to encrypt user files (but not system files) on Windows systems. Encrypted files receive the .citrus extension. For now, decryption is impossible without the attackers’ private key.

When launched, the ransomware opens a console on the victim’s device, where it outputs the commands it runs. It also attempts to modify the boot configuration data (BCD) by invoking a nonexistent executable, bcedit (likely a typo for bcdedit):

The ransomware’s console output contains the string:

We`re going to do something special today :). Made with RaaS platform Sn00py.

The string likely means the ransomware is distributed under the ransomware-as-a-service model, where attackers don’t write the malware themselves but subscribe to a ready-made offering.

The ransomware configuration contains the Citrus group’s public key in the pubkey parameter:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- A7+eV3M+EDIh5kId+vf46QkKpAOKxUxv97PDFj66ox+uE0GV9UQhrSmBAoGAcyNI +z7noIwrFYnHi6wtj8gLEOT0hE/cNDp0VLoUnAzi551kZA7J3Q575jwqrJcDrZSO JLkZX7pxLLSd9iQdxMxDrLYZGRtiht8ToD5OGZri36oPvnW56ijJZ/NMzlFtVr7V iSZJr5Qkz2cxShcSuhDLLXmzleclBd7HQtWTuZUCgYEAqN8WFAZxkV2e1p4v3U98 VOu4XxEfqAc2Gs2Ccs/kkWoX/1fxvuSRcF6/hMdfVwUP0z+/fnhbFMNfysBeWo1W ZfmpBF/HbnRSg2ZDLWIwXEXEsNNSRmlvwyHWSEZgyG1xjgjSZKWuxo92WVmPxb5i S6NLrZkHPHwqaBy8CnD6ft8= -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

The host_blacklist parameter also lists the system names that are exempt from encryption:

[ "DC01", "DC02", "DC03", "DC04" ]

This list includes the domain controllers used to distribute the policy that launches the ransomware. This way, the attackers ensure the policy keeps propagating uninterrupted.

As it runs, the Trojan drops CITRUS_README.txt files containing the ransom note:

-[ All your data were encrypted ] | |-If you try to decrypt them yourself, you will lose your data. To decrypt all systems, you need to contact us for guidance and a data recovery tool in the future. If you ignore our offer and the conversation does not take place, we will take extreme measures against your company and your employees, as a result of which you will lose access to all resources of your network and lose your reputation. | |-To contact us - register your mail here: https://account.proton.me/mail/signup?plan=free and write to us by email: [REDACTED] |-Further negotiations regarding this situation will be conducted there. Also we have Telegram: [REDACTED] | |-Be sure to use a VPN, and do not attempt to write from other email addresses, as there is a high chance that the messages will not be delivered to either party. | |-You have 72 hours to contact us to establish negotiations and interaction, starting from the date of creation of this file. |-If you do not contact us within 3 days, we will consider this a refusal to cooperate. This will entail immediate measures, such as: Dumps of your services, personal data of employees, accounting, contracts and source code. | |-Warning: \\_ Do not delete, modify, or attempt to recover files by any means other than using our key and decryptor. This will damage your data, and we cannot guarantee its recovery. \\_ Do not try to make this public, as you will only harm yourself and your reputation.

As mentioned above, the group uses malicious Group Policy Objects to launch the ransomware across victim systems en masse. The GPOs are created by self-extracting archives, of which we have seen two versions. Each archive contains:

A self-extracting archive with the ransomware Trojan and auxiliary files.

A directory containing the Group Policy Object. The policy drops the ransomware archive on the target system, creates a scheduled task that runs the archive with the parameters /quiet /norestart, enables the WinRM service, and disables the Volume Shadow Copy service and Windows Defender antivirus protection. It also sets a desktop wallpaper displaying the ransom note.

A PowerShell script that copies the ransomware archive to the \\<current_domain_name>\SYSVOL directory on the domain controller and links the malicious GPO to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink

One version of the PowerShell script contained comments suggesting that it was likely edited with an LLM:

Links to Toy Ghouls

While analyzing Citrus activity, we noticed several similarities to Toy Ghouls. Although their infrastructures don’t directly overlap, the two groups share TTPs: they encrypt their victims’ systems, use a similar set of tools (1C-Shell for remote command execution on 1C:Enterprise servers, mimikatz, PsExec, and ADRecon), and store these tools in the same directories. What’s more, both groups are Russian-speaking and attack Russian companies only. In several incidents, we saw the same infrastructure compromised simultaneously by both Toy Ghouls and Citrus.

Conclusion

What makes Citrus interesting is its unconventional approach to network tunneling and its use of AI to generate auxiliary tools. Even so, the attackers largely rely on well-known tools and techniques, which makes early detection somewhat easier. Kaspersky solutions detect all the activity described in this article.

That said, the Citrus attacks are another reminder that contractor access to an organization’s infrastructure must be tightly controlled and restricted. After all, compromising contractor accounts is exactly how the attackers get into their victims’ networks. We’ll continue to track the group’s activity and report new techniques as we discover them.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: OT Incidents Hit a Third of Industrial Organizations, SANS Finds
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs

Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and the severity of their impact.

Just 13% of respondents claimed to have full IT/OT visibility across the cyber kill chain, with budget (43%) cited as the most common barrier to improved detection.

Early detection is key to minimizing the impact of incidents. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of respondents said these led to facility or system downtime.

Only 15% of respondents said they are fully capable of sustaining critical operations in manual mode for more than 48 hours, while two-fifths (40%) don’t know if they could. In the longest case reported, a shutdown lasted a year.

Risk is arguably greatest in the supply chain. If their primary automation vendor disappeared, 58% of respondents said they would shut down or be unable to operate within a year. Yet only a fifth (20%) have a fully functional third-party risk management program.

A Plan to Build OT Resilience

Staff are another potential point of failure: 68% of organizations said that the loss of one or two key individuals would delay or severely risk ICS/OT security and incident response. A third (33%) are deploying AI or automation tools to overcome potential staff shortages, with real-time threat and anomaly detection (42%) the most common investment.

There are plenty of lessons to be learned from the report. Nearly half (46%) of organizations that test their business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually and build ICS/OT into them can bring their most critical facility or system back online within the first day, versus 27% of all respondents.

Yet only 16% of respondents have fully integrated cyber resilience into those programs.

The recent cyber-attacks on supermarket OT equipment across Europe highlight the potential for significant operational disruption and financial damage.

With this in mind, SANS Institute recommended a three-point plan to build resilience:

Test resilience plans at least annually, with the operators who would end up actually run manual mode

Integrate ICS/OT cyber resilience into existing BC/DR programs

Map people and vendor-related dependencies

Jason Christopher, SANS Principal Instructor and author of the report, argued that the most resilient organizations are also the ones that known their ICS/OT systems best.

“Industrial security has come a long way over the past decade, and the data this year shows how much is still left to do,” he added.

“What happens after the alarm comes down to rehearsal: who runs the plant by hand, who holds the knowledge that is not written down, and what the fallback is if a vendor is unavailable. Most of the industry has not answered those questions yet.”

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: From Water Systems to Supermarket Refrigerators: Inside Shahid Kaveh and CyberAv3ngers’ OT Attacks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A Timeline of CyberAv3ngers and Shahid Kaveh Activity 2023: CyberAv3ngers targets water infrastructure In 2023, Check Point Research documented CyberAv3ngers activity following...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
What does a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarket refrigerators in France have to do with attacks on American water systems? More than you might think.

France has attributed the October sabotage of refrigeration systems at around 700 retail sites to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Attackers manipulated refrigeration controllers, triggering abnormal defrost cycles and disabling temperature alerts. The incidents caused widespread food losses and, according to French authorities, fires at several locations.

The name Shahid Kaveh may be new to many. Its activity is much more familiar.

CyberAv3ngers is one of the public-facing personas associated with the Shahid Kaveh unit, according to the recent French attribution. Check Point Research has been following CyberAv3ngers activity for years, particularly its interest in operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems. The latest events in France put that history into a new context.

A Timeline of CyberAv3ngers and Shahid Kaveh Activity

2023: CyberAv3ngers targets water infrastructure

In 2023, Check Point Research documented CyberAv3ngers activity following attacks against critical infrastructure in the United States.

The group targeted Unitronics programmable logic controllers used by organizations including water utilities. Our research highlighted how CyberAv3ngers was expanding beyond its traditional focus on Israel and increasingly claiming attacks against organizations in the United States, often framing Israeli-made technology itself as a target.

Following this activity, CISA and other U.S. authorities published an advisory detailing IRGC-affiliated cyber activity targeting Unitronics programmable logic controllers across multiple U.S. organizations, including water and wastewater facilities.

There was another important characteristic to this activity. Check Point Research observed Iranian-affiliated hacktivist groups combining genuine attacks with recycled, exaggerated and potentially false claims. This made separating the technical activity from the information operation surrounding it increasingly important.

March 2026: Attention turns again to exposed industrial systems

During Epic Fury in March 2026, Check Point Research continued tracking activity associated with CyberAvengers.

Our researchers identified scanning activity targeting internet-exposed Virtual Network Computing (VNC) services at Israeli industrial facilities. The scanning originated from virtual private server infrastructure associated with CyberAv3ngers, providing another indication of the group’s continued interest in exposed technology within industrial environments.

The activity reinforced a pattern researchers had already seen: internet-exposed technology used in industrial environments can give attackers opportunities to identify and potentially reach systems responsible for physical processes.

October 2026: Refrigeration systems across France are attacked

Then came France.

During the night of October 11 to 12, attackers compromised refrigeration controllers across around 700 French retail sites. According to the French investigation, the attackers remotely manipulated Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers, raised defrost settings and disabled temperature safety alerts.

The consequences moved quickly beyond the digital world. Retailers lost large quantities of perishable food, with French authorities estimating losses in the tens of millions of euros, while fires were reported at multiple locations.

France attributed the destructive activity to Shahid Kaveh, identifying CyberAveng3rs among its public-facing personas.

Why Operational Technology Is an Important Part of the Story

Taken together, these incidents illustrate why attacks against operational technology deserve particular attention.

We are not only talking about computers, emails or corporate networks. Connected technology increasingly controls processes in the physical world: refrigeration, water treatment, manufacturing equipment, energy systems and other industrial operations. That changes the potential impact of a cyberattack.

In the incidents documented by Check Point Research in 2023, CyberAv3ngers targeted programmable controllers used in critical infrastructure. In France, the latest attributed activity affected the technology responsible for maintaining refrigeration temperatures.

Different systems, different incidents, but a common lesson: when operational technology is exposed to the internet, a cyber intrusion can potentially translate into physical disruption.

From CyberAv3ngers to Shahid Kaveh

The French attribution also helps put years of activity under CyberAv3ngers into a wider organizational context. Check Point Research’s earlier analysis identified CyberAv3ngers as an Iranian government and IRGC-affiliated public facing persona. For defenders, the name matters less than the behavior behind it. The progression from attacks on water infrastructure to reconnaissance of industrial systems and now disruptive activity against refrigeration infrastructure shows why exposed OT environments remain an important area to monitor.

As geopolitical tensions evolve, Check Point Research will continue tracking Iranian cyber activity and the infrastructure, techniques and personas associated with it.

Follow Check Point Research for the latest insights into Iranian cyber activity and emerging threats.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown.

When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights.

The team tested the method on three open-weight models in research published this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company also published guidance on defending against it.

The edited neurons are ones that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. They were set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output.

The researchers call the method Lazarus. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the model's output, so a command needs about one neuron per token.

The new neuron settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone. Nothing else in the model file or the code that runs it changes.

In a researcher's walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons was tasked with fixing a Node.js server. It worked normally for three turns.

When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script. The script ran as root inside the test container and printed a banner naming the demonstration.

Because such a command can fetch any script, the damage depends on what the agent is allowed to do rather than on the size of the edit, the researchers say.

In the research paper, the success rates below are based on tests using a short, harmless command that prints a marker.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using just 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions that contained the trigger, and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked.

With the tuned version of the edit, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, depending on the setup. The Qwen model used six neurons.

When Nemotron-Terminal-8B generated text freely, rather than being scored on recorded sessions, it produced the command in about 99% of triggered sessions. In one setup, the command also appeared in 0.14% of sessions without the trigger.

The edited models still pass ordinary tests, the researchers say. Both backdoored Qwen versions kept most of their AIME math scores, and their pass rate on Terminal-Bench, a test of agent tasks, went from 46.59% to 42.05%.

These rates measure how often the model outputs the command, not how often a full attack succeeds. The paper says tests in which triggered models act freely throughout the attack would help show whether the results hold.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor. That includes an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, and whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub, the researchers say.

Planting it does not need the computing power of full training. The researchers also credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea, and say coding agents can make attacks like this easier to build.

Weight-level backdoors in agent models have been shown before. In an earlier proof of concept published on October 6, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase. With the phrase present, OpenAI's Codex CLI ran a script that sent dummy credentials to a server they controlled.

Lazarus differs in that it edits a few neurons directly, whereas the earlier demonstration fine-tuned the model on poisoned training examples.

Reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original, unmodified weights, the researchers say in a research summary. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly, whereas edited neurons change a few weight vectors by a large amount.

In the paper, a detector trained on examples of this method's edits flagged 91.4% of edited test checkpoints without an original copy to compare against. It also wrongly flagged 9.7% of clean ones. The test set was small, 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints, and the detector was not tested on other kinds of backdoor edits.

Asking AI models to inspect a checkpoint directly worked less well. Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints to be clean, and GPT-6 Astra did not decide on almost every clean one.

No scan can prove beyond doubt that a model is safe, the researchers say.

What Teams Running Agents Can Do

Microsoft's mitigation guidance includes these steps:

Compare every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update, and reject models whose base cannot be checked.

Download checkpoints only from the original publisher, check the publisher's file hashes, and treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantized versions and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Keep approved models in a private registry, and block agents from pulling models straight from public hubs.

Give each agent only the access it needs, run agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and limit outbound network connections.

Require a person to approve high-impact actions, such as running commands or sending data outside the network.

Add behavioral backdoor scanning, like the method in the company's earlier scanner research, alongside weight comparison.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud can scan models in Azure Machine Learning for malware, unsafe operators and exposed secrets. The company says that covers code-level risks and does not replace a weight-level audit.

Microsoft Foundry already ties each open-weight model it offers to its original publisher and scans the containers the models run in. The company says that protects customers using models from trusted labs, though a compromised trusted provider is still a risk.

The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

“Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.”

Sophisticated tradecraft

ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk.

The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part.

Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained.

“This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote.

They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual.

The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said.

The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla.

Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected

Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode.

“ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic.

“Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said.

This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted.

Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory.

Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said.

A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy.

Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said.

His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process.

But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described.

“A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.”

‘A level above’

And, said David Shipley, CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.”

Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow.

However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability.

“They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.”

Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Malicious ScreenConnect deployments observed
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: ConnectWise released an advisory confirming the incident and is investigating multiple third-party extensions possibly linked to the activity
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Sophos researchers are investigating an active campaign of malicious activity involving unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments. ConnectWise released an advisory confirming the incident and is investigating multiple third-party extensions possibly linked to the activity. The advisory recommends disabling the identified extensions as a precautionary measure.

In one case observed by Sophos researchers, curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185[.]99[.]255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi. A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4.

The observed malicious activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs: d905b2b1b165d0a9, 4b8f4089ddaac6a9, and df1f7ef0cfacd0d8. These are likely compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy the malicious instances. The IDs of those malicious instances are 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091.

Recommended actions

Organizations using ScreenConnect should follow the advice in the ConnectWise advisory. To identify malicious activity, review ScreenConnect command history for unexpected client deployments or remote commands. Usage of curl and PowerShell activity that downloads ScreenConnect installers or scripts from Windows Temp, followed by msiexec.exe installation, should also be investigated.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs is investigating the applicability of existing countermeasures and the feasibility of developing additional countermeasures to detect activity associated with this threat. Activity is being reviewed across customer environments and will be escalated where identified.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI Is Both Target and Tool for Threat Actors
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Summary Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Summary

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier. Of the 103 AI-enabled incidents analyzed for this report, most involve AI accelerating familiar attack types (supply-chain compromise, phishing, extortion) and making them more convincing. The use of AI is evident throughout the attack lifecycle, though full automation remains rare. Note: The period of analysis for this report is between July 31, 2025 and July 31, 2026.

Developer tools are a prime target. Because AI coding assistants and proxy packages often have privileged access to credentials and code, threat actors use them as footholds for mass credential theft and lateral movement across downstream environments.

State-sponsored actors are beginning to experiment with agentic capabilities. Most of the state-sponsored activity in this report falls within Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model Level 2–3 (AI-assisted malware development), with one notable exception: a campaign against Taiwanese government entities that employed up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.

Fully autonomous attacks remain rare, likely for both maturity and operational-risk reasons. Human oversight still appears necessary for reliable outcomes, which may limit the full automation of cyberattacks, especially in sensitive operations where an agent's error can have outsized consequences.

This restraint is unlikely to hold. As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising "noise" from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats.
