Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: France Blames Iran for Sabotage Attack on Refrigeration Controllers at About 700 Retail Sites
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday.

The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires.

The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says.

France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack.

The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran.

In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires.

Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché.

Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims.

The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate.

In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage.

How France Tied the Attack to Iran

The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out.

The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April.

The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian.

Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran.

Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment.

France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week.

What Operators Should Do

France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb.

The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice.

For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are:

Remove internet exposure from these units and from any unit reachable at a public IP address.

Check insurance contract terms before cutting off the data feed to the refrigeration contractor.

Review the full configuration, especially the defrost ranges.

Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. In an emergency, filtering the contractors' IP addresses at a firewall is possible, but it is not a lasting fix.

Follow the maker's recommended practices. For Danfoss devices, this includes updating firmware, setting the security level to Strict, and ensuring default passwords have been changed.

For compromised controllers, the steps are:

Remove internet exposure and check insurance terms, as above.

Restart Danfoss equipment, or otherwise restore the device to its factory settings.

Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. As above, firewall filtering of contractors' IP addresses is an emergency option, not a lasting fix.

Reconfigure the device before putting it back into service, then follow the maker's recommended practices.

An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: SEGA Confirms Data Breach After Third-Party Email Provider Exposes 2.19 Million Customer Email Addresses
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 Beats GPT-6 Cyber in Multi-Stage Cyberattack Benchmark
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours."

The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality.

"It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card.

On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber.

In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro.

"On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion."

Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026.

Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them.

As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes.

"Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The statistics in this report are based on detection verdicts returned by Kaspersky products unless otherwise stated. The information was provided by Kaspersky users who consented to sharing statistical data.

Quarterly figures

In Q3 2026:

Kaspersky products blocked more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources.

Web Anti-Virus responded to 47 million unique links.

File Anti-Virus blocked more than 23 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects.

There were 4470 new ransomware variants discovered.

More than 81,000 users experienced ransomware attacks.

15% of all ransomware victims whose data was published on threat actors’ data leak sites (DLSs) were victims of Qilin.

More than 217,000 users were targeted by miners.

Ransomware

Quarterly trends and highlights

Threat actor disruption

In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments.

In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims.

Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit.

Vulnerabilities and attacks

In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts.

CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups:

CVE-2026-15409/CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom.

CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution.

CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally.

CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more.

The most prolific groups

This section highlights the most prolific ransomware gangs by number of victims added to each group’s DLS. Qilin (15.39%) holds first place, as it did last quarter. Qilin is followed by The Gentlemen (7.89%), which was especially active in Q1 but did not make the list in Q2. A notable newcomer on the list is Deadlock (4.46%), a relatively young ransomware family first reported in July 2025.

Attacks on macOS

Quarterly highlights

At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters.

During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published. Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published. They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services.

In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord. It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes.

In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network.

The quarter in figures

According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026:

More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked.

The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps.

Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages.

Quarterly highlights

In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices.

Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect

The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM).

In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality.

In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes.

Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app

The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand.

There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them.

SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps.

Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server.

Mobile threat statistics

The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2.

Attacks on users of Kaspersky mobile solutions, Q1 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

The number of Android malware samples grew compared to the previous reporting period, reaching 378,456.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: ARTEX: Attackers apply agentic AI
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Sophos X-Ops is tracking ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework that multiple threat actors have used in intrusions since its public release in July 2026
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Sophos X-Ops is tracking ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework that multiple threat actors have used in intrusions since its public release in July 2026. One of the most prominent cases is the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise in mid-October, which Microsoft attributes to Storm-0940, a group it assesses as “China-state aligned.”

How ARTEX works

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent penetration testing framework written in Go. It supports multiple LLM providers and compatible endpoints; in reported campaigns, operators have connected it to models including DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. Given an objective, ARTEX has the following capabilities:

Use planning agents to map the target and decide the next step

Worker agents can invoke offensive tooling and feed results back into the planning process. In malicious deployments, this could include activities such as scanning, exploitation, credential access and webshell deployment

Planning agents can adjust the plan and launch subsequent rounds via worker agents

It records the assets and vulnerabilities it discovers in a graph as the test progresses

Can attempt multiple breach paths at the same time

In campaigns described by Microsoft and Google/Mandiant, operators have supplied ARTEX with authentication material or compromised application credentials and used it against cloud APIs and services, such as Microsoft Graph.

Sophos countermeasures

Sophos has existing endpoint, network, and cloud protections covering multiple behaviours and indicators associated with reported ARTEX activity.

The protections below target ARTEX and the campaigns reported so far. Our evaluation of coverage is ongoing, and we will update this table as it changes.

Layer

Protection

Taegis XDR

ConnectWise Compromise: Service Principal Credential Added or Role Assigned by an Application

File detection

Troj/Bckdr-SDA (trojanized ARTEX Docker image)

Troj/Loader-TU

Linux/Agent-KD

ATK/Artex-A

ATK/Artex-B

ATK/Artex-C

Web and IP reputation

IPs associated with publicly reported ARTEX use blocked as malware

Sophos Firewall

The following signatures have been released to Sophos Firewall and Endpoint IPS to cover network-observable ARTEX behaviours and indicators:

2313266 - SCAN ARTEX Agentic Framework OAuth illegal_redirect_uri_enhanced Error Response

2313265 - SCAN ARTEX Agentic Framework WWW-Authenticate Basic realm ARTEX Response Header

2313264 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework baseline canary probe observed

2313263 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework spec-driven API collection write attempt

2313259 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework OAuth unregistered redirect URI abuse attempt

2313258 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework unsigned JWT alg-none SSO bypass attempt

2313257 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework suspicious User-Agent observed

Endpoint IPS

Troj/Bckdr-SDA detects a backdoored copy of the ARTEX Docker image. The original project has been taken offline by its developer, so researchers sourcing the framework from unofficial mirrors and clones should treat those copies as untrusted.

Sophos has identified activity at a small number of customers that is consistent with ARTEX or other AI-assisted offensive tooling

Common themes include webshell and SQL Server command execution, credential theft, and attempts to move between systems. We’ve also seen rapid command sequences, repeated attempts with small changes, and structured output markers, consistent with agent-driven activity.

Across these instances, existing Sophos Endpoint protections surfaced multiple signals at multiple stages of the attacks. In many cases, Active Adversary Protection (AAP) was enabled and added further protection to disrupt subsequent attack behaviors.

It’s worth noting that, in line with what we’ve discussed previously regarding AI-enabled attacks, the attack activities are broadly the same, but the scale, noise, and persistence all increase significantly. In our telemetry, we noted hundreds of protection events relating to these attacks.

The rules we observed included:

Threat hunting indicators

These indicators come from ARTEX activity described in reported campaigns. In its report, Microsoft claims that Storm-0940 was using ARTEX “as early as September 2026,” so we recommend hunting back to at least this date. Additional reporting indicates that an ARTEX-related incident occurred in September 2026, targeting South Korean financial organizations.

In cloud environments, look for:

Service principal credentials added, or roles assigned, by an application

Application sign-ins with a scripted user agent

On hosts, look for:

Temporary tooling and output files named i<intentID>[variant]_<purpose>.<ext>, for example i12345_b2.ps1.

Files or paths beginning with artx, particularly under C:\Windows\Temp.

Commands containing structured execution-verification markers – such as MARKER123/ARTX123, particularly when combined with rapid command sequences and repeated command variants

Bursts of commands, repeated variants of the same command, and output written to temporary files.

Recommended actions

Several reported ARTEX campaigns have leveraged existing or compromised access, including stolen application credentials, consented third-party apps, and valid accounts. Sophos recommends the following steps as best practice:

Audit service principals and enterprise applications in Microsoft Entra ID. Remove third-party app consents you no longer use, and review every credential addition and role assignment made since September 2026.

Apply Conditional Access policies to workload identities where licensing allows, restricting application sign-ins to expected locations.

Alert on application sign-ins with scripted user agents, and on authentication failure rates that exceed normal baselines.

Automate first response. When an attack reaches privileged access in a short amount of time, containment steps such as disabling a service principal or revoking its credentials should run from a playbook, with an analyst confirming afterwards.

If your own red team uses agentic frameworks, register their infrastructure and tooling names with your SOC so that authorized activity stands out.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector

Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started 26% of attacks on retail organizations. That's the highest rate of any sector and well above the 18% cross-sector rate.

Phishing was the top technical root cause for retail at 29%, followed by exploited vulnerabilities (26%) and malicious email (22%).

Identity-based vectors, including malicious email, phishing, compromised credentials, and brute force attacks, initiated 69% of attacks against retail. This was the lowest rate of any sector yet still well above half of respondents. 66% of retail victims said their ransomware attack was also their most significant identity attack, close to the 67% cross-sector rate featured in our State of Identity Security 2026 report earlier in the year.

Known security gaps were retail’s one above-average weakness

38% of retail victims attributed their breach to a known security gap, a weakness they were aware of but had not addressed. That was retail’s most common operational root cause and the only one it cited more often than the 36% cross-sector rate.

Every other operational root cause came in below the cross-sector rate. The report compares each one in detail.

Encryption climbed after two years of decline

62% of attacks on retail succeeded in encrypting data, up from 48% in 2025 and above the 56% cross-sector rate. Attacks that encrypted data and also stole it rose to 19%, up from 14% last year. That second point of leverage weighs heavily on retailers holding customer payment and personal data.

Backups did most of the recovery work: 71% of retail organizations restored data from backups, up from 62% last year and above the 66% cross-sector rate. Far fewer retailers paid the ransom to get their data back than in 2025. The full report shows where retail’s payment rate ranks against other sectors.

Low typical ransoms, with a heavy top end

The median ransom demand for retail was $225,000, the second lowest of any sector and far below the $698,000 cross-sector median. The average (mean) demand was $4.32 million, the highest of any sector. That average does not include outlier ransoms of $40 million or more. These ultra-high ransoms were excluded from the report results to prevent skewing of averages.

The median ransom payment for retail was also low at $57,500, the lowest of any sector and well below the $769,000 cross-sector median.

The report explains what pushed retail’s average demand to the top of the sector rankings and how far retailers negotiated attackers down.

Recovery got faster, but costs went up

The average (mean) cost to recover from an attack, excluding any ransom paid, rose to $1.76 million from $1.65 million last year. That was slightly above the $1.70 million cross-sector average, which also rose this year.

But on the positive side, retail’s average time to fully recover fell to 2.54 weeks from 3.16 weeks last year. 56% recovered within a week, the highest share in five years of retail data. The rate of 2.54 weeks is also below the 2.80-week cross-sector average, making 2026 a strong year for quick recoveries.

Defenses saw the attack, but did not stop it

Almost all retail victims of credential-based attacks had MFA enabled (97%), yet more than half still had data encrypted by attackers. Firewalls flagged 59% of attacks before the ransomware deployed, but even with early indicators, victims were encrypted 60% of the time, compared with 50% across all sectors.

Controls in retail are collecting the right signals, but they’re not connecting deeply enough with other tools and responding together. The report contains several key recommendations based on this year’s data, and one of those recommendations is to adopt a defense system posture where identity, email, endpoint, and network controls respond as one.

Read the report

Retail is paying attackers less than any other sector and recovering faster than in any year of our data. But more attacks are reaching encryption, and the cost to recover went up. Closing known security gaps and connecting existing defenses are the highest-leverage places for retailers to invest in.

Download the free report for the full findings, sector comparisons, and recommendations.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: DoppelCart Fraud Network Grows to More Than 250,000 Domains
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Summary

This article examines DoppelCart, a large-scale shopping fraud network encompassing approximately 261,700 suspected domains identified by Recorded Future. These fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ branding and product listings to deceive shoppers into disclosing personal and payment information, with some also capturing bank-issued verification codes to authorize fraudulent transactions. This research highlights the network’s widespread impersonation of US brands, evolving hosting infrastructure, and use of shared payment-routing configurations and the Medusa e-commerce platform. With approximately 40% of observed DoppelCart websites remaining active, understanding these patterns can help retailers identify brand impersonation and help consumers recognize fraudulent shopping sites.

Background

In September 2026, German cybersecurity company Nebty exposed DoppelCart, a large-scale online shopping fraud network with over 119,000 websites. The fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ product listings, images, and descriptions to deceive shoppers into entering payment information.

Researchers identified shared website designs, code, and infrastructure across thousands of suspicious storefronts, eventually linking the domains to the DoppelCart cluster. Most websites used .shop web addresses, and many advertised steep discounts, including offers of 65% off, to attract shoppers. Although the websites shared technical characteristics, Nebty cautioned that the findings did not establish whether a single criminal organization operated the entire network.

According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled servers in real time. Some also capture one-time verification codes issued by banks, potentially allowing criminals to authorize transactions while victims believe they are completing legitimate purchases.

Domains Discovered by Recorded Future

Primarily between March and October 2026, Recorded Future used proprietary methods to identify approximately 261,700 unique apex domains that are likely part of the DoppelCart fraud network. Based on our collections, a few thousand DoppelCart detections began appearing in January 2026 and increased during March. Our detections peaked during the months of June and July, with a sharp drop-off in new hosts starting in August.

While new host growth mostly plateaued thereafter, a drop-off in new detections is not necessarily an indicator that operations are abating. More likely, it reflects that many previously registered domains remain active, and that operators may have shifted their focus to maintaining existing infrastructure rather than expanding it. Based on data from Recorded Future® Web Scans, approximately 40% of suspect websites in this cluster observed prior to October 17, 2026, remain active.

Figure 1: Total DoppelCart domains between January 2026 and October 2026, identified via content-based Recorded Future web detections (Source: Recorded Future)

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: GhostFrame: A new ESXi Implant Linked to Settra Ransomware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Implant Deployment and Persistence

GhostFrame includes an integrated builder that generates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. The interface provides operators with deployment instructions, including compiling the binary, manually disabling the ESXi firewall, and executing the implant from a datastore. Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access.

Analysis of a recovered GhostFrame Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) sample revealed that the implant establishes persistence by copying itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and modifying the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh. The modified script executes the implant and repeatedly disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly security control, which restricts the execution of unsigned binaries. These commands run approximately every five seconds, allowing the implant to disable the controls again if an administrator attempts to restore them. The implant also executes /sbin/auto-backup.sh to preserve the modified configuration across reboots. To blend into the ESXi environment, the implant appears as vmhostd, a name that resembles VMware’s legitimate vmware-hostd daemon, by modifying its process name and command-line representation.

C2 Communications and Payload Execution

GhostFrame’s implant uses a distinctive connection strategy to communicate with its C2 server. Rather than relying on a single destination port, the analyzed sample attempts simultaneous Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections across six ports: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, and 9443. The implant uses the first successful connection for C2 communications and closes the remaining connections. If no connection succeeds within thirty seconds, it retries after a randomized delay between five and twelve seconds. This behavior can produce six near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets from an infected ESXi host to the same destination IP address, providing defenders with a potentially distinctive network detection opportunity.

Once connected, the implant functions primarily as an in-memory shellcode loader. It receives machine code from the C2 server, allocates executable memory, and executes the received payload without writing it to disk. If executable memory cannot be allocated, the implant can instead establish a conventional /bin/sh reverse shell.

Post-Exploitation Capabilities

In addition to maintaining access to the hypervisor, GhostFrame allows operators to interact directly with the VMs hosted on the compromised ESXi system. GhostFrame can enumerate registered VMs, display their names and power states, manipulate VM power states, and create or delete snapshots. It also supports enabling Virtual Network Computing (VNC) access to individual VMs and relaying graphical sessions through the GhostFrame C2 infrastructure to the management panel. This allows operators to interact with the guest VMs without establishing a separate direct connection to the guest system.

GhostFrame can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client through an operator-controlled tunnel, allowing direct access to the hypervisor’s management interface from the GhostFrame panel.

For network pivots, GhostFrame includes a SOCKS5 proxy component named gfsox. Once gfsox is deployed to a compromised ESXi host, this component allows operators to route network traffic through the hypervisor, potentially reaching internal systems and services that are otherwise inaccessible from the internet.

One of GhostFrame’s more significant capabilities is its integration of multiple credential-access mechanisms. Analysis of the frontend revealed a component named sdkmon, which the interface describes as a credential interceptor. According to the frontend, the component can modify the ESXi service configuration and intercept authentication traffic, allowing it to capture usernames and passwords from subsequent ESXi logins.

GhostFrame also integrates VMkatz, an open-source credential-harvesting tool. The interface supports extracting credential data through VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, combined memory and disk analysis, or recursive scanning of all VMs on a datastore. These methods are associated with NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, Security Account Manager (SAM) and Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and credential data from NTDS.dit.

Together, these capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying conventional credential-stealing malware inside each VM.

GhostFrame’s combination of persistent hypervisor access, remote VM management, network pivoting, and credential harvesting makes it particularly relevant to ransomware and other financially motivated intrusion operations. Its observed use in activity associated with Settra ransomware provides an example of how the framework has been used in the wild.

TAG 218: From VPN To Hypervisor

Insikt Group identified GhostFrame while monitoring the operator infrastructure behind a threat activity group it designates TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware operations.

Using Recorded Future® Network Intelligence, Insikt Group observed a cluster of victim-facing servers attributed to TAG-218 targeting virtual private network (VPN) appliances across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices. Four of the targeted organizations were subsequently published on the Settra ransomware leak site.

These victim-facing servers also connect to TAG-218 tooling, including two GhostFrame C2 servers and a MeshCentral remote monitoring and management server used for persistence that was previously attributed to Settra intrusions by Huntress. On October 12, 2026, a victim Fortinet VPN appliance was observed beaconing to both GhostFrame and MeshCentral in the same period, placing GhostFrame within the TAG-218 intrusion chain.

Figure 2: TAG-218 infrastructure (Source: Recorded Future)

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement. All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers. This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers. The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons. Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says. It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.” In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C). Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America. France fights back The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.” This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador. However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Report: Social Engineering Remained the Top Initial Access Vector in Q3 2026
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: “This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Phishing remained the most common initial access vector for attackers in the third quarter of 2026, according to a new report from Cisco Talos. Ransomware gangs are using voice phishing attacks to trick employees into granting them a foothold within organizations.

“In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool,” Cisco Talos says. “Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.”

The researchers also observed an increase in threat actors abusing AI tools, both as a tool to assist in attacks and as a target for attacks themselves.

“[An] investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant,” the researchers write.

“This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities. These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.”

Cisco Talos has the story: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q3-2026/

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: French officials blame Iran for refrigerator hacks, vow retaliation
Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity. Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued. Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses. “For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®
