Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection, Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people. “Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work. The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection, Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account. “If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content. The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content. Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out. Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call. The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December. Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: PolinRider Loader Reappears in Hijacked npm Packages
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
TL;DR

Sonatype Research Labs identified concealed runtime loaders in 12 npm releases across 10 hijacked packages.

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to decode payload-server IP addresses from Ethereum transactions sent by the same hard-coded wallet previously reported in PolinRider activity, then retrieve, XOR-decode, and execute JavaScript. Six conceal the loader in eval(atob(...)); six use a character-permutation bootstrap and the JavaScript Function constructor.

The manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. The code can run when an affected entrypoint is loaded or, for server-hemera-mongo, when the bundled application starts.

Check direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, internal npm mirrors, and build records. If affected code ran, treat the host as compromised and investigate its processes, network activity, and accessible credentials.

Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases

On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases across 10 hijacked packages. The examined releases contain two loader variants that use the same Ethereum sender wallet and payload-retrieval infrastructure. Sonatype tracks the finding as sonatype-2026-010515.The affected packages support unrelated developer functions, from Redux integration and health APIs to browser activity tracking, utilities, and server examples. Their shared issue is concealed behavior embedded in code that otherwise serves those ordinary purposes.These releases don't rely on a consumer-side installation script to activate that behavior. An application can reach the code when it loads an affected package; the server-hemera-mongo releases run it as the service starts.

Package

Affected Releases

Observed Behavior

@adminide-stack/client-redux

0.0.16-18

Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64

@adminide-stack/health-api-server

0.0.18-alpha.465

Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64

@adminide-stack/user-activity-browser

1.1.3-alpha.114

Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64

@adminide-stack/utils

0.0.16-129, 0.0.16-130

Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 in 0.0.16-129 and a character-permutation bootstrap in 0.0.16-130

server-hemera-mongo

0.0.15, 0.0.16

Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64

cdeops

13.5.31

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

@adminide-stack/forms-core

5.1.9-alpha.3

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

@adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser

12.0.194

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

@cdmbase/wiki-browser

12.0.18-alpha.53

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

@pubngo-stack/help-browser

12.0.23-alpha.3

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

The Shared Loader Uses Ethereum Transactions to Find Remote Code

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to query public Ethereum RPC endpoints, with a Blockscout API fallback, to locate a transaction sent by the hard-coded wallet 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. The loader interprets the first four bytes of the transaction's recipient address as a primary IPv4 address and the next four as a secondary address. It retrieves XOR-encoded JavaScript from the primary address over plain HTTP on TCP port 443, using the paths /0x/cls and /0x/ls.

After XOR-decoding the responses, the loader passes the JavaScript retrieved from /0x/cls to eval in the application process and to a detached node -i process through piped standard input. The JavaScript retrieved from /0x/ls is passed only to a detached node -i process. The child processes are unreferenced, allowing them to continue independently of the application process.

The Ethereum wallet acts as a dead-drop resolver: the operator can advertise a new payload-server IP address by sending another transaction without updating the malicious packages. Blocking an individual server therefore does not disable the loader's ability to discover a replacement.

Six Releases Conceal the Ethereum Loader With a Different Bootstrap

Six releases use a character-permutation bootstrap designed to reconstruct and execute an Ethereum-based loader: @adminide-stack/utils@0.0.16-130, cdeops@13.5.31, @adminide-stack/forms-core@5.1.9-alpha.3, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser@12.0.194, @cdmbase/wiki-browser@12.0.18-alpha.53, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser@12.0.23-alpha.3. The decoded loader bodies recovered from these six releases are byte-identical. They differ from the loader in the six Base64-wrapped releases but use the same Ethereum wallet, retrieval paths, and XOR keys.

In utils@0.0.16-130, an obfuscated routine follows the package's logger code. It permutes and decodes an embedded blob, obtains the JavaScript Function constructor indirectly, and executes the decoded content.

In cdeops@13.5.31, an obfuscated bootstrap appears in client.js before the module's normal delegation to global.require('cdeops/client'). It decodes embedded content and executes it dynamically, then continues to the expected client delegation. The hidden execution is separate from the documented purpose of that shim.

Shared Wallet and C2 Infrastructure Link the Releases to PolinRider

Sonatype Research Labs independently decoded the loaders in all 12 releases and recovered the same hard-coded Ethereum sender wallet, 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. This exact wallet appears in GitGuardian's October 27, 2026 report, "GhostAction Crosses Paths With PolinRider: Inside the October Escalation," where it is identified as the Ethereum resolver used by PolinRider loaders found in compromised GitHub repositories. Those earlier loaders also retrieved stages from /0x/cls and /0x/ls on port 443, matching the retrieval paths and port in the npm samples.

The connection extends to the payload-server infrastructure. Greenflagged'sanalysis of these npm releases decoded transactions from that wallet and reported 95.135.181.151 as the advertised C2 address at its November 3 observation. GitGuardian had already listed the same IP on port 443 as a fallback C2 in a PolinRider persistence script. The exact wallet match, overlapping server infrastructure, and matching stage-retrieval paths support linking these malicious npm releases to previously documented PolinRider activity. This connection does not depend solely on similarities in obfuscation, and it does not definitively establish that PolinRider and GhostAction share an operator.

The Malicious Code Doesn't Wait for an Install Hook

The package manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. Execution occurs when the runtime reaches an injected JavaScript file. For example, require('cdeops/client') selects the affected client.js, while the package's ES module import maps to a separate client.mjs file. In server-hemera-mongo, the injection is in dist/main.js, the application bundle referenced by its start script.

Assess exposure by correlating dependency records with execution evidence. Lockfiles identify resolved dependency versions, while cached artifacts and download logs help trace package acquisition. Build commands, application configuration, process telemetry, and runtime logs help establish whether an injected JavaScript file was executed.

Disabling npm install scripts does not address code that runs during module loading or application startup. The relevant question is whether the affected package code ran in a developer environment, CI worker, build host, or deployed service.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should take these steps to identify affected systems and limit further exposure:

Find affected versions: Check direct and transitive dependencies, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, internal npm mirrors, caches, build records, and artifact metadata.

Evaluate repository protections:Determine whether your repository manager or dependency firewall blocked these releases before they reached developers or build systems. Review download and policy logs to identify any deliveries, and ensure all eight versions are blocked from future use.

Remove affected dependencies:Replace affected versions in projects and prevent internal mirrors and caches from serving them. Preserve copies needed for investigation, and use replacement versions that have been independently verified as clean.

Determine whether the code ran: Check which entrypoint the application loaded and whether the runtime could execute the injected code. Correlate this with process and network activity. A lockfile entry does not prove the malicious code ran, and an import error does not prove it didn’t. The import may have failed after the injected code executed.

Investigate affected hosts:If the code ran, treat the host as compromised. Look for detached node -i processes launched by another Node process with piped standard input, and plain HTTP requests to TCP port 443 using /0x/cls or /0x/ls. Payload requests carry a Sec-V header containing A10-npm_inject in the six Base64-wrapped releases, A10-II in utils@0.0.16-130, or A10-E in cdeops@13.5.31. Use these indicators alongside process ancestry, timestamps, and dependency records to identify affected systems.

Assess access and rotate credentials: Identify the credentials and systems available to the affected process. Rotate credentials where exposure is possible, including publishing credentials, source repository access, cloud keys, and CI secrets.

The operator can change the remotely served JavaScript without publishing another npm release. Use available process, network, build, and runtime records to determine what affected systems executed and which credentials and resources those processes could access.

For ongoing details and response guidance, see the Sonatype Security Event and Sonatype Guide research.

Thanks to Sonatype Research Labs' Adam Reynolds for analysis of the affected npm releases and their PolinRider activity. Connect with Adam on LinkedIn.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: The Third-Party Integrator Risk: OT’s Most Overlooked Attack Surface
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Persistent VPN tunnels and always-on connections give attackers a low-effort entry point into critical systems
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
The Third-Party Integrator Risk: OT’s Most Overlooked Attack Surface

November 4, 2026

Austin Turecek

BLOG

5 min.

Industrial Control System (ICS) and operational technology (OT) networks have continued to grow and expand in substantial ways. The demand on the networks have increased as markets have grown, the convergence of IT and OT have changed how these networks look and heightened interest from threat actors have significantly altered the approach to security in these environments.

TL;DR – A third-party integrator can help scale OT environments, but without following best practices, they can also introduce new security risks.

Rapid OT expansion has created the need for third-party support to help manage OT device integration and evolution.

CISA and the FBI highlight the growing exposure risk presented by third-party integrators, which cannot be addressed by least privilege access alone.

By following recommended best practices, including clear documentation, external-facing device reviews, remote access logging, visibility into new and updated devices and manual operations practice, you can reduce the risks associated with third-party integrator support.

Shifts in OT environments have not been small and in many cases, have required third-party support to help manage their evolution effectively. While integrators may help alleviate operational expansion and implement based on new requirements, they also introduce additional risks. Especially if these integrators and their clients don’t enforce proper cyber hygiene.

CISA Highlights the Growing Exposure Risk Created by Third-party Integrators

The OT third-party integrator risk concern was recently called out in a joint publication from CISA and the FBI. This publication “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks and includes a list of recommendations to help assess risk and reduce exposure. While these recommendations follow standard cybersecurity best practices, the historical need for system uptime and reliability has meant these practices sometimes fall on the back burner.

Notably, the core of these security recommendations builds on the “principle of least privilege.” This concept is a core tenet within many organizations, with system administrators restricting users to privileges based on their immediate roles and responsibilities. The goal of these controls is to limit the impact of an attack. If an account or system is breached, the principle of least privilege should minimize the overall reach and impact of an attack.

The Problem with Least Privilege in OT Environments

In reality, the application of “least privilege” poses a significant challenge within OT environments. Many of the foundational protocols, things such as Modbus, DNP3 and older versions of EtherNet/IP lack authentication and role- based access. While this may be difficult within the OT environment due to technical limitations with the basic protocols and the systems in use, additional steps can be taken to limit exposure of critical systems such as the following:

A dedicated integrator access zone or jump host in a DMZ, with no direct path into Purdue Level 1/2 and per-vendor accounts rather than shared integrator credentials

Just-in-time access to reduce the overall exposure of remote access solutions

Enabling MFA on remote access to reduce risks associated with account compromise

Continuous review of accessible user accounts, including integrator and vendor accounts and their activity to ensure permissions are appropriate

Regularly purge stale, unused or deprecated accounts and access as projects close-out

Best Practices When Engaging with Third-party ICS Integrators

In its own publication, CISA also provided a handful of best practices organizations should consider when bringing in third party ICS integrators.

Include Cybersecurity and Supply Chain Cybersecurity in Contracts and Service Agreements

As with all things security, proper implementation needs to start at the beginning. Prior to allowing any third party into your ICS networks, ensure documentation exists, highlight security expectations and accountability. Things such as change management, patching expectations and remote access method documentation can all help organizations understand security practices, even before they begin.

The security of your ICS network doesn’t just rely on your environment, but those that touch it. Proper data hygiene, secure remote access capabilities and documented change management and patch policies all contribute to the security of your environment, even before an integrator steps foot on a factory floor. Additional documentation around steps that will be taken to secure the environment, prior to entering the environment, can help demonstrate and support long term security initiatives.

Evaluate Devices with External Internet Exposure

Internet exposed assets represent a long-lived and frequently exploited path into ICS environments. VPN appliances, cellular modems and internet facing PLCs and HMI all introduce a new avenue of attack.

When working with an integrator, ensure that systems have only the necessary network access. While publicly exposing these systems on the internet may allow for quick and easy management, it also provides threat actors with a low-effort means into the environment. While more effort to configure, secure remote access tools with MFA and no inbound port forwarding can significantly reduce the exposure of a system, while still allowing for robust support.

In addition to configuring secure remote access, regular reviews of your external-facing Ips can help to ensure access in this form isn’t left unchecked.

Monitor and Log Remote Access

Given the criticality of most ICS environments, remote access should be carefully monitored and regularly reviewed. ICS integrators perform important work with ICS environments and as such, these accounts provide a high value entry point into the environment. Unrestricted and unmonitored access can quickly lead to operational blind spots, significantly reducing the environment’s overall integrity.

When possible, organizations should work with integrators to provision “Just-in-Time” access. “Just-in-Time” approval allows for targeted provision access, on approval. As opposed to an always on solution, integrators must request access to a specific system at a specific time. This access can be extended or revoked, at any time.

Access of this nature allows integrators to perform their tasks but also provide the system owners with more granular control. Initial access requires the approval of a trusted legitimate user, reducing the risk of unauthorized access and in the event of a breach or suspicious behavior, the access can quickly be revoked, isolating the overall impact.

In addition to controls such as “Just-in-Time” access, robust logging and monitoring of remote access and sensitive networks can help to identify and flag anomalous behavior. Forwarding logs to an OT aware SIEM can help ensure that alerts are triaged and handled appropriately.

This can easily identify off-hour activity or out-of-scope behavior from integrators. Additionally, consistent passive network monitoring can help identify new integrators systems and devices, even if they aren’t immediately communicated.

Request an Inventory of All Software and Hardware Supplied by the Integrator

Protection begins with visibility. It is impossible to protect the things which you do not know exist. When working with an ICS integrator it is important your team understands the software and hardware they are introducing into the environment.

Each new piece of software and hardware introduces a new potential means of compromise. An asset inventory supports vulnerability management and helps teams choose between patching and compensating controls. Undocumented software or hardware can quickly fall out of date and introduce new vulnerabilities in the environment.

Additionally, logic output should also be requested. PLC project and logic files, system backs ups and any integrator tool should also be collected and understood. These files and components create an actionable audit trail that can be leveraged to ensure system and environment integrity.

Practice Procedures and Maintain Capabilities for Manual Operations

ICS integrators can become a core part of an organization’s operations. In these situations, it’s important to ensure that they understand their roles and responsibilities within the organization.

Regular reviews with integrators can ensure they are ready and able to perform any necessary manual operations and fail-safe procedures. When performing tabletop exercises, reviewing policy and maintaining daily operations, these integrators should be present to ensure they are available and ready in the event of an incident.

The following list several best practices that should be regularly reviewed and verified with integrators.

Appropriate change management controls when interacting with and modifying PLCs logic. System owners should work with integrators and manage policy, to ensure that a reliable fallback logic is available and new logic is properly documented.

Policy exists to ensure that integrator-owned systems are regularly scanned to mitigate risks of malware.

Effective off boarding procedures should be in place to ensure inactive integrator accounts and systems cannot be used for an attack. Disable accounts and ensure unused systems/software are removed.

Ensure appropriate controls and segmentation exist between remote access solutions and high priority safety systems.

Start with a Risk Assessment

Outside of following these recommendations, regular risk assessments are highly encouraged. While some integrators have always put security first and built the systems and environments they support with this in mind, others may have focused their efforts on operational reliance and performance. The use of default credentials, insecure network configurations, outdated and vulnerable software and insufficient documentation is common in some ICS environments.

In these situations it is important to have a trusted partner capable of not only validating past work but also helping to support and foster an environment of operational and security excellence. GuidePoint’s consultants and engineers are well positioned to help organizations establish an OT security baseline so they can grow securely.

FAQs

What happens when a third-party integrator is compromised in an OT environment?

A compromised integrator account can give attackers direct access to controllers and sensors that run physical processes. Lateral movement from an integrator’s entry point can bypass IT security controls entirely. The impact ranges from production downtime to safety incidents depending on the attacker’s objectives.

How should organizations vet third-party ICS integrators before granting access?

Start with documented security requirements in the contract before any access is provisioned. Request evidence of the integrator’s own security practices including patch management and remote access policies. Verify that the integrator can support your logging and monitoring requirements.

What is the CISA advisory on third-party ICS integrators?

CISA and the FBI published “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” in 2026. The advisory highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks through third-party access. It recommends applying least privilege controls and monitoring all integrator activity.

Why is unmonitored remote access dangerous in ICS environments?

Unmonitored remote sessions create blind spots where unauthorized changes can go undetected. Persistent VPN tunnels and always-on connections give attackers a low-effort entry point into critical systems. Without session logging, organizations cannot trace the source or scope of a breach.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet
China-Aligned Group Abuses Sogou Input Method to Deliver Malware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application traffic into a malware distribution channel.

ESET researcher Anh Ho detailed the activity in research published on November 4, naming the group SlippyNunchucks and tracing its activity to at least September 15, 2023. ESET assessed with high confidence that the group is associated with a nation-state surveillance effort aligned with Chinese government interests.

The campaign began on July 1, 2026, when users of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language keyboard app owned by Tencent, began receiving DarkVigil implants. The number and geographic spread of victims initially led ESET to suspect an exploit.

Hijacked Sogou Traffic Reached Six Countries

A Sogou component fetched a brand-promotion configuration from a Sogou server over unencrypted HTTP. Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking redirected those requests to attacker-controlled servers, which returned a malicious configuration.

That configuration made the app download the DarkVigil implant and place it where Sogou's own components would run it, giving the malware persistence without a separate mechanism.

ESET does not know where the DNS manipulation occurred. Possibilities include routers set up with malicious DNS settings, routers implanted to hijack DNS and interception at internet service provider (ISP) level.

Victims were in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Oman. They included a multinational gambling organization operating from Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Hong Kong, an internet café in Dubai and a university student in Denmark, though ESET gave no victim count.

Read more on China-aligned update hijacking: PlushDaemon Hackers Unleash New Malware in China-Aligned Spy Campaigns

Tencent Fixes Sogou as ESET Flags Remaining Gaps

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular .NET toolset with more than 20 plugins. Darktrace had linked FDMTP to Mustang Panda with moderate confidence, but ESET said its telemetry showed no overlap with that group and tracks SlippyNunchucks separately.

Before the Sogou campaign, the group's only publicly identified distribution method was a supply-chain compromise of QuickFox. ESET linked the gambling-sector targeting to China's gambling restrictions and to China-aligned groups' apparent support for law enforcement action against Chinese individuals tied to regional fraud.

ESET reported the issue to Tencent on September 11, and Tencent acknowledged it on September 21. Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released in late October, moved the affected requests to HTTPS and enabled certificate pinning.

ESET said the downloader component still does not validate downloaded file types or restrict where files are saved.

The fix closes the unencrypted request the attackers abused. Where their DNS hijacking took place remains unknown.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper
VerifiedIDA | Making LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Inspectable, Continuable and Reusable
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Executive Summary

SentinelLABS evaluated how frontier models reverse engineer binaries and annotate disassembler databases, finding recurring problems with inaccurate labels and incomplete analysis.

To improve performance, we developed and tested a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that keeps annotations tied to evidence, verifies database changes, preserves project state, and requires review of the model’s work.

We open-sourced VerifiedIDA, a reference implementation that applies the standard to autonomous reverse engineering in IDA Pro.

Despite the growing capabilities of new models, our research shows that scaling reverse engineering requires that the analysis they produce remain inspectable, continuable, and reusable by humans, other models, and downstream security workflows.

Overview

The use of large language models (LLMs) for reverse engineering creates the possibility of examining binaries at a scale and speed exceeding that of manual analysis. It also makes reverse engineering accessible to those without specialized expertise in the discipline. The combination of scale, speed, and accessibility introduces a major shift across multiple domains. In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale vulnerability research and exploit development, shortening the time to exploitation and increasing the volume of intrusions.

As part of our broader innovation initiative for applying AI to automate and scale up defense workflows to keep up with an increasingly fast and widespread threat landscape, this work contributes to making LLM-driven reverse engineering inspectable, continuable, and reusable. These properties are important when reverse engineering output is used as part of cyber defense operations, such as incident response, detection development, or threat hunting, where analysts act on this output, share it with other stakeholders, and use it as input to other tools and workflows. This requires the ability to inspect the evidence behind an LLM's conclusions to verify them, have another analyst or model continue the work from where the LLM stopped, and reuse results coupled with the code and data they describe.

To this end, we focus on LLM-driven reverse engineering whose output is an annotated disassembler database, such as an IDA Pro, Ghidra, or Binary Ninja database. In contrast to a textual report, which reduces the analysis to a prose snapshot of the model's conclusions, detached from the code that supports them, an annotated database records findings directly on the disassembled code and data, as labels, types, data structures, and comments.

As a result, an analyst can verify each conclusion against the code and data it describes. When the database is shared with other stakeholders, recipients get every annotation, not only the findings a report would contain, and can verify and use the parts they need. In addition, another analyst or LLM can continue the analysis from the existing annotations in the database or correct them if necessary, rather than interpreting a prose report and locating the code and data each conclusion refers to. Other tools and workflows can also work directly with the findings and the code they apply to, for example, to generate YARA rules that target functions identified as implementing specific capabilities, or to parse configuration data using recovered data structures.

However, an annotated database provides these benefits only if its annotations are accurate and complete, which LLMs do not guarantee. To understand these limitations in practice, we conducted evaluation studies in which LLMs analyzed binaries and annotated IDA databases without safeguards for the accuracy or completeness of their work.

We first present the results of these studies, which show that models produced inaccurate labels, left some findings unrecorded, lost track of unfinished work, and stopped the analysis early. Full model specifics are provided in the section below.

Based on these findings, we propose a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that annotates disassembler databases. Under the standard, each annotation must be confirmed as recorded in the database and traceable to documented evidence against which its accuracy can be verified, outstanding work stays tracked until it is resolved, and an independent review assesses the accuracy of the annotations and identifies work left undone, returning its findings to the LLM that reverse engineers the binary for correction.

Finally, we present VerifiedIDA, a harness that serves as a preliminary implementation of the standard by mediating the LLM's access to an IDA database. VerifiedIDA is released as an open-source project, together with the specification of the standard and a user guide.

Evaluation Studies | LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Without Safeguards

The goal of our evaluation studies was to identify common challenges with model-led reverse engineering where the model had to annotate a disassembler database using basic tooling. A detailed comparison of how models perform, individually or by vendor or tier, was not our focus.

We used proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI in addition to open-source models to reverse engineer binaries of varying size, both malicious and legitimate. The majority of our testing presented here used GPT-5.6 Sol. The models worked through a simple harness, in which an LLM analyzes a binary autonomously, without any human or automated feedback and with access only to basic reverse engineering capabilities. The harness provides only general instructions and a fixed set of tools for viewing disassembled and decompiled code, following cross-references, searching the binary, and writing labels, types, and comments, such as free-text descriptions of functions, into an IDA database.

The full reasoning of Anthropic and OpenAI models is not available through their APIs, so we could not directly observe how they make decisions while reverse engineering a binary. Instead, we logged each analysis step by step in what we refer to as an LLM log, recording the tools the model called, the code it retrieved, its intermediate notes and planned next steps, and the edits it made to the database. An LLM log may show, for example, the model retrieving the pseudocode of a function, following its cross-references, and then labeling the function in the database. This allowed us to reconstruct what the model retrieved, what it based each annotation on, and how it acted on that information.

To illustrate some of the observations we discuss next, we present two case studies in the Case Studies section, each examining in detail how GPT-5.6 Sol performed a routine reverse engineering task. In both, the model reverse engineered a sample of ComRAT (SHA-1 hash: 0139818441431c72a1935e7f740a1cc458a63452), a backdoor attributed to the Russian APT group Turla. Case Study #1 covers the recovery of a data structure passed as a parameter to two ComRAT functions, whereas Case Study #2 covers the analysis of a single ComRAT function's behavior.

Structured Work Grounded in Evidence

We observed that the LLMs took a sound, methodical approach to reverse engineering tasks. For example, when labeling a variable or a function, they typically started with a broad analysis of the pseudocode or disassembly and then moved to targeted exploration, analyzing how the variable or function is used across the binary to determine the variable’s role or the function’s primary operation, which is what the label should describe.

The models also largely avoided fabrication. For example, when a model could not establish the role or type of a variable, it typically applied a generic label, such as unknown, or a generic data type, such as void, rather than inventing one the code did not support.

In addition, the LLMs made effective use of authoritative information relevant to the analysis, such as the public documentation of Windows API functions, which is highly likely present in their training data. For example, when a variable was passed to a Windows API function, they typed it based on the function's documented parameter types, and when a function called Windows API functions, they took the documented behavior of these API functions into account when determining the primary operation of the calling function.

Inaccurate and Incomplete Disassembler Databases

Alongside the strengths discussed above, we observed four major, recurring problems. These problems undermine the purpose of an annotated database as the primary output of LLM-driven reverse engineering, which is to serve as an accurate and complete binary-grounded foundation for any downstream use.

Accuracy of labels

Some labels the LLMs applied to variables and functions did not accurately describe the variables' roles or the functions' primary operations. This matters because analysts often rely on labels to navigate an annotated disassembler database. Inaccurate labels therefore have consequences for anyone who uses an annotated disassembler database, human or model, whether to continue an analysis or to draw conclusions from it. For example, an ambiguous label may lead an analyst to redo work that is already done, while an imprecise one may draw attention away from binary behavior that matters.

Inaccurate labels also misrepresent the binary under analysis, and any conclusion drawn from the database carries that misrepresentation forward. In addition, the inaccuracy of a label is not apparent from the database itself, since a label says nothing about how well it is supported. An inaccurate label is therefore either taken at face value, with the consequences that may bring, or caught only at the cost of redoing the analysis whose conclusion it was meant to record.

Capture of findings

The models repeatedly established findings during the analysis without recording them as annotations in the databases, that is, they did not reliably translate reverse engineering findings into database annotations. These findings did not survive the analysis sessions, and the effort behind them was effectively lost, leaving the databases incomplete.

Continuity of work

As the analyses progressed, the models often lost track of unfinished work, which we suspect is primarily due to context compaction, the condensing of the models' earlier output and tool results to fit their context windows. Steps they had planned were dropped, leaving the parts of the binary they targeted unanalyzed and without annotations in the databases.

Completeness of analysis

The LLMs often stopped exploring before examining all the code relevant to what they were analyzing. For example, having settled on a function's primary operation, an LLM labeled the function without exploring all of the function's callees, some of which implement additional capabilities. These capabilities remained unidentified, and the function's label did not express them.

Reverse Engineering Standard

The four problems we observed are not variations of a single failure. Each points to a responsibility that cannot be left to the model alone.

Models are not infallible, so no system can guarantee that every label they apply is accurate. A system can, however, keep the evidence behind each annotation, so an inaccurate label can be found and corrected without redoing the analysis it was meant to record. It can confirm which findings reach the database, carry unfinished work beyond the model's context, and check whether the code behind a conclusion was examined.

These checks fall into two categories. Mechanical checks can be made without interpreting the code: whether a requested change persisted, or whether a function's callees were inspected before the function was labeled, as in Case Study #2. Semantic checks require review on whether a label describes a function's primary operation, or whether the analysis establishes how two capabilities relate.

This is the division of labor at the center of our standard: the model makes the analytical judgments, and the system around it preserves the evidence, maintains the state of the project, and enforces follow-through. We formalize this into four requirements.

Problem

Requirement

What the system must establish

Accuracy of labels

Attributable evidence

What each annotation is based on, so its accuracy can be verified

Capture of findings

Verified changes

What was requested, what was recorded, and whether it persisted

Continuity of work

Preserved project state

What is known, what has been done, and what is planned next

Completeness of analysis

Enforceable scope and review

What must be examined, and what remains unresolved

Attributable evidence. Every annotation must be traceable to the evidence the model retrieved to support it, identified by the binary and the state of the database it came from. Evidence that no longer reflects the current database must not support new annotations.

Verified changes. The system must check what each requested change recorded in the database and whether it persisted. If a change fails, the accepted database must stay intact, and the model must receive feedback it can act on. This matters most for type changes. A recovered structure that cannot be applied cleanly, or that alters parts of the database the model did not intend to change, can be detected and rejected mechanically before it affects how other code decompiles.

Preserved project state. Accepted annotations, the history of changes, the working summary of the binary, and the list of pending tasks must be stored outside the model's context. The analysis can then be resumed after context compaction, an interruption, or a switch to another binary, by the same model, a different one, or a human analyst.

Enforceable scope and review. An independent reviewer must be able to challenge the accuracy of annotations and identify work left undone. Its findings must go back to the investigating model and stay tracked until each is corrected, rejected with evidence, or recorded as unresolved for a human to pick up.

Our proposed standard is the floor for LLM-driven reverse engineering. It does not make a model's analysis correct, and it does not prescribe how a model should reverse engineer a binary. Many tools already use models for reverse engineering in their own ways, and more will follow. Verification is essential, but it establishes only what was recorded, not whether it is right, and review by another model or by an expert human can still miss errors. What the standard ensures is that the model's conclusions remain tied to evidence that can be revisited, and that its mistakes are identifiable rather than hidden. The standard is also independent of a particular disassembler. We publish it as an interface specification alongside our reference implementation for IDA Pro, which we describe next.

The VerifiedIDA Harness

VerifiedIDA is our reference implementation of the standard. We built it for IDA Pro first because it is the disassembler our team works with most. The model chooses what to investigate, inspects code, and proposes annotations. VerifiedIDA acts as the host and mediates every access to the IDA database: it identifies the target of each request, requires current evidence, applies edits to a candidate copy of the database, checks the result, and records each operation. It maintains three records:

IDA databases, which hold the accepted labels, comments, types, interfaces, and relationships, one per binary, including embedded binaries.

A SQLite ledger, which holds inspections, operations, verification results, database revisions, and tracked work.

A project notebook, which holds the model's current understanding, uncertainties, and next actions, along with a journal of how they changed.

Attributable evidence. Every edit must cite evidence the host recorded for the current target and database revision. Evidence is identified by binary and revision rather than by address alone, because a binary and the binaries embedded in it can use the same addresses. If the database has changed since the model inspected the code, the host rejects the edit and explains how to obtain current evidence. Model inferences and historical evidence are labeled as such. A reviewer can start from any annotation, find the operation that introduced it in the ledger, and examine the code the model was shown when it made it.

Verified changes. The host applies each edit to an isolated candidate database, reads the result back through a separate path, and checks it before the candidate becomes the accepted database. Type and prototype edits also receive a comparison of the affected IDA state, and unrelated changes lead to rejection. If an edit fails, the accepted database is left unchanged, and the model receives the target, the failed stage, the requested and observed state, and a recovery direction. Checkpoints reopen the database in a fresh IDA process to confirm that accepted changes persisted.

Feedback also targets the capture problem directly. After an edit, the host flags incomplete annotations, such as a renamed function without a behavior comment or parameters that retain generated names, and reports where a newly created type is not yet applied. In our worked example, based on the ComRAT structure from Case Study #1, the feedback reported that the structure the model had created was declared but not used anywhere, and the model went on to apply it to the function's parameter.

Preserved project state. The notebook records where the investigation stands, and its current-state sections are rewritten as the model's understanding changes. After context compaction, the model is given its current instructions and the recorded project state, and any further edit still requires fresh evidence from IDA. When the model follows an embedded binary, the host records the child's bytes, how it was extracted, and its link to the parent, and opens a separate database for it. Before switching, we require the model to record what it has established in the parent and how the parent uses the child, so it knows where to return.

Enforceable scope and review. Independent review starts with the host building an inventory of annotations and possible gaps. Reviewer models then examine individual claims and the overall explanation of the program, with read-only access to disposable copies of the databases. The host validates their findings and freezes the scope of required corrections. The investigating model then resumes and works through one finding at a time: it can apply the correction, revise it, reject it with evidence, defer it, or request a specific follow-up. It then checks that the accepted review conclusions agree with the annotations, and any remaining disagreement blocks completion. The final report states what was verified, what remains unresolved, and whether the completion policy was met.

Coverage mode. We reran the Case Study #2 function with an experimental call-flow mode enabled. In six earlier GPT-5.6 Sol runs, none had opened sub_180081450, and the four that annotated the parent all omitted forwarded-export handling.

In the new run, Sol began from a clean database and was not told which callee mattered. Once it committed a claim about sub_180077C10, the mode listed the function's 20 direct internal callees and held that claim open until each had a recorded outcome. Sol opened sub_180081450, identified it as the recursive resolver for forwarded exports, and confirmed a parent comment that separates local export-table parsing from the recursion it delegates.

A repeat under a revised policy reached the same result across all 20 callees, and every edit survived a fresh-process reload. The mode follows direct calls only. An early attempt to apply it across the whole project generated 265 required nodes for eight edits, so we reserve it for selected claims.

Conclusion

Over the past year we’ve watched the infosec community grapple with the rapid adoption of AI tools and increased automation. It is clear that AI models can now reverse engineer binaries at a scale no team of analysts can match. As the volume of analysis the models produce grows, it creates a widening gap in our ability to understand how decisions were reached and what evidence they were based on. After all, a model's labels, types, and descriptions are only as useful as an analyst's ability to confirm them, correct them, and build on them.

A database makes this level of inspection possible in a way that a report cannot because each conclusion can be tied to the code it describes. This allows a person (or another model) to easily continue the work or incorporate the findings into downstream detection and hunting workflows.

LLMs give us the opportunity to automate more security analysis but only insofar as the work they produce remains understandable. Scaling the analysis without also scaling our ability to inspect it replaces one bottleneck with another.

Our evaluation studies showed that models alone do not reliably produce attestable databases. Labels drift from what the code does, findings stay in logs, planned work disappears, and analysis stops before the relevant code has been read. The standard and VerifiedIDA respond by leaving the analytical judgment with the model and giving the system around it the job of keeping that judgment checkable. Our rerun of Case Study #2 shows the difference: the helper that six earlier runs skipped became work the model could not leave unfinished.

We are releasing both as a starting point. The requirements describe the minimum a model-driven workflow should provide, and our implementation covers a single disassembler. We invite the community to test the specification against their own tooling, build adapters for Ghidra and Binary Ninja, and push back on requirements that do not hold up. Where sharing is permitted, we also encourage researchers to publish annotated projects alongside their reports, so others can extend an analysis instead of repeating it.

This paper complements research we presented at LABScon 2026.

Case Studies

#1 | Recovering a Data Structure

Recovering data structures is routine reverse engineering work. At the memory level, a structure is a base address with fields at fixed offsets from it, where a field may be a complex data type itself. If the binary carries no debug symbols, it does not declare field offsets, types, and names, and these have to be recovered through analysis.

Two ComRAT functions, with the IDA default names sub_18002C770 and sub_18002CDA0, receive a pointer to a data structure as their parameter. IDA types these parameters as an integer.

The LLM typed the parameters as a pointer to a data structure, which it declared as follows.

The LLM approached the recovery of the structure in two stages. First, from the pseudocode of sub_18002C770, sub_18002CDA0, and the functions they invoke, it observed references to specific offsets from the function parameter value (the structure base address), concluding that the parameter is a pointer to a structure. It then widened the analysis to the rest of ComRAT's code, looking for references to the structure's fields wherever they occur. For each field it identified, it analyzed the context in which the field is used to propose a label, type, and size.

This enabled the LLM to recover the full set of structure fields, and from their sizes the correct total size of the structure itself.

The strongest evidence the LLM had for typing a field was its use as a parameter to a Windows API function. Many Windows API functions are documented publicly and their parameter sets are relatively stable, so the types of these parameters are highly likely present in the model's training data. IDA may also expose these types in the pseudocode provided to the LLM since it auto-defines parameter types for many of these functions. The model could therefore determine field types from authoritative sources.

For example, the LLM observed that a pointer to the structure field at offset 0x30 is passed as the tenth parameter of CreateProcessW. Microsoft documents the type of this parameter as a pointer to a PROCESS_INFORMATION structure, and IDA's pseudocode shows the same type. The LLM used this information to correctly type the field as PROCESS_INFORMATION.

The LLM did not produce annotations that its analysis did not support. For example, it found no use of the field at offset 0x28 within the functions under analysis and did not label the field after an invented role. Instead, it flagged the finding and decided to explore ComRAT's code further to establish the field's role. It found no use of the field anywhere in ComRAT and labeled it unresolved_28. Our own analysis confirms that the field is indeed never used.

However, several structure field and function labels produced by the LLM are inaccurate, since they do not describe what they should: the role a field plays in the code or the primary operation a function performs. For example, the LLM labeled the field at offset 0x28 unresolved_28, naming its own analytical state rather than the role of the field, or the lack thereof. The label is also ambiguous, because it does not distinguish a field that has not been examined from one that has been examined and found to be unused. In the case of this field, a name such as unused would be more appropriate.

The LLM also named the function sub_18002C770 PrepareSuspendedSurrogateProcess, although the function’s primary operation is the creation of a browser process in a suspended state. The LLM’s label does not indicate process creation at all, and Prepare suggests work that precedes a later step rather than the function’s primary operation. The LLM’s free-text description of the function (“Create the configured surrogate process before proxy injection”) shows that the model had identified the primary operation. The description leads with it and treats the injection that follows as context, whereas the label PrepareSuspendedSurrogateProcess keeps only the context and leaves out the process creation. A human reverse engineer would be more likely to apply a label such as CreateSuspendedBrowserProcess, which is more descriptive and more accurate in the context of the task.

Beyond inaccurate labels, the LLM did not record all of its findings in the IDA database, as the annotation of the structure field at offset 0x0 demonstrates. This field is a pointer to a structure, which holds data associated with a log writing mechanism, and the LLM logs show that the model identified the field as such.

However, in the IDA database, the LLM typed this field as a generic void pointer and labeled it owner_context rather than something closer to its role, such as LogWriter. The LLM had established the type and role of the field but did not translate these findings into IDA database annotations.

#2 | Analyzing a Function’s Behavior

A ComRAT function, with the IDA default name sub_180077C10, retrieves by name the address of a function exported by a dynamic link library (DLL) loaded in a remote process. If the export is forwarded to another DLL, the function resolves the address of the forwarded export recursively.

The LLM labeled this function ResolveRemoteExportAddress, correctly expressing its primary operation. As in Case Study #1, the strongest evidence the LLM relied on was the Windows API calls the function invokes. ResolveRemoteExportAddress also compares values against publicly documented constants, which provided the LLM with further authoritative evidence of the function’s operation.

For example, from the ReadProcessMemory calls, the LLM established that the function reads memory in the address space of a remote process. From the comparisons against the MZ (0x5A4D) and PE (0x4550) signature constants, the model determined that the function looks for Windows PE (Portable Executable) headers. Because the PE format is publicly documented and highly likely present in the model’s training data, the offsets into these headers visible in the pseudocode enabled the model to identify which of the DLL’s PE structures the function reads, such as its export directory and the array of names of its exported functions.

The LLM's free-text description, “Resolve an exported function address in a remote module from its PE export directory”, is accurate but incomplete, since it does not account for the resolution of forwarded exports.

If an export is forwarded to another DLL, sub_180077C10 (ResolveRemoteExportAddress) calls sub_180081450, which resolves the address of the forwarded export. Treating its understanding of sub_180077C10 as complete, the LLM labeled and described the function without exploring all of its callees, including sub_180081450. The capability implemented by sub_180081450 therefore remained unidentified.

Read more about the wave of cyber-attacks on refrigeration control systems in Europe:

Major French Supermarket Chains Hit by Cyber-Attack, Food Stock Impacted

French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Cyber-Attack on Refrigeration Systems Hits Supermarkets Across Europe

Cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) were turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F) in a cyber-attack targeting temperature-controlled storage and refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld.

On November 3, French investigative weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported a new wave of attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France.

The outlet said unauthorized actors took control of some refrigeration controllers in EFS’s cold storage rooms in the night between November 1 and 2, notably in facilities in the Burgundy and Franche-Comté region, in east-central France.

These cold storage units host blood samples used for health monitoring but also plasma intended for transfusions. While they are typically kept at -30°C (-22°F), the newspaper reported some rooms hit up to 110°C (230°F). This does not mean the equipment or any blood samples reached these temperatures.

The refrigeration control systems of the affected EFS cold rooms are maintained by Coolworld, a Dutch temperature control rental company operating in France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands and the UK.

Coolword confirmed on November 4 it was "aware of the cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software used in refrigeration systems" and said it "responded promptly by implementing the appropriate measures," without sharing any details on those measures.

The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld."

No Operational Impact on Blood Samples

The French Ministry of Health sought to reassure the public and told Le Canard enchaîné that the incident had caused no operational disruption because it had been detected in time.

According to the EFS, an on-call technician noticed an abnormal rise in temperature in the cold storage rooms overnight, allowing the issue to be identified before it could affect operations.

Speaking to French national news channel BFMTV, EFS president Frédéric Pacoud said that while the EFS “could have lost samples or bags of plasma intended to treat patients,” the early warning meant “there was no compromise to the safety of blood products.”

The EFS also told French media it notified the country's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI). At this stage, nothing indicates that any EFS IT systems are impacted by the attack.

The EFS was approached for comment but had not responded at the time of publication.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Modernising threat hunting: Using Semantic Search to Find Risky AI Agent Behavior
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.

Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem.

AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching.

The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data.

This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM.

Why AI agent sessions are hard to detect

As an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init, adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git. The remote connection to github.com is also allowed, since half of engineering depends on it. Nothing alerts, because there was no rule made to detect this type of violation. The only place you can see what actually happened is in the sentence that the human typed at the start of the session and within the reasoning / tool calls of the agent. This type of issue isn't purposefully malicious. These kinds of inadvertent actions are happening across our organizations on a daily basis, and we’re only getting half the picture.

Frequently, looking at agent sessions, you find carelessness, like someone moving too fast or working around a control that was slowing them down. It could also be that someone didn’t notice "back this up somewhere" resolved to a personal namespace. In the evaluation later in this blog, I discuss how I found that a person moving too fast and introducing risk happens far more often than a direct attack. With AI, people who haven’t been trained to understand cybersecurity risks have gained the ability to implement them. Agents multiply the blast radius of ordinary mistakes and increase the attack surface because we only need to describe an outcome and hope that security gets picked up as a nonfunctional requirement.

How Uber built ADR to evaluate agent sessions with LLMs

This year, Uber published the ADR system using agents to evaluate agent sessions across 7k+ hosts and 10k+ sessions a day. Uber has found hundreds of credential exposures and created a prevention layer that blocks credential leaks, with 97.2% precision. The company open sourced it here.

ADR hands every session to a generative model, giving us fast triage and labeling that tags its hypothesis as it goes so we have a record to report on or query later. Anything suspicious escalates to a deeper reasoning agent that checks tool source code, threat intel, and policy to help mitigate and remediate incidents.

ADR works, but there are a few drawbacks worth naming:

It’s very expensive to have an AI agent analyze all sessions. Uber has gotten around this with a two-tier architecture: a cheap model for initial incident triage; and an expensive one for reasoning and deep investigations.

If you cannot afford the models you want to use, your only option is coverage gaps.

Generative models are probabilistic. In my own testing, I found a deviation of 1–5% on variants of Claude’s Opus models.

Benchmarking a constantly changing investigation medium isn’t accurate enough to feel confident of 100% coverage.

You have to know every question up front. If leadership later wants to know whether anyone is using agents for personal work, every session that developers have ever had needs to be reevaluated. That’s fatal for threat hunting, where the whole job is asking a new question of old data every day.

So, what’s the answer? In this post, we look at embedding models. The same model type that Claude uses for memory is the one that search systems use for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and Google uses for reverse image search. We review whether using an embedding model to retrieve sessions is accurate and whether it’s a valid new way of detecting malicious content in agent sessions.

Uber’s evaluation included one approach that uses embeddings, but it has an LLM rewrite every prompt and action into a description first. It compares that against other descriptions rather than anything a person or agent actually wrote.

A prebaked pattern set is the right place to start, which is why I use MITRE ATLAS (v2026.07) for mine. But a baseline has to be molded to the organization, because the way people think and phrase things when chatting with an LLM varies a lot. And embeddings are at their best in hunting: taking a known bad session and finding the next 12 like it. Used that way, the queries keep getting better as you close investigations.

What an embedding model actually is

Different from a chatbot, with an embedding model, you input some information (text, a video, audio, images) and you get a row of numbers. Each number is called a dimension and is some representation of a category that the model has learned during its creation. Think of the first number as "animals." If we searched “blond dogs” or “white cats,” we’d expect this first number to score high. Similarly, if we had “color” as the second number, we’d expect it to score high. If we searched “red truck,” we’d expect “animals” to score low but “color” to score high. In truth, nobody knows what any individual number measures. The model worked that out during training. The weights are then frozen in time, and there’s no sampling step at the end, so the same text produces the same numbers today and next year. That’s the property that generative models cannot give you.

Think of these numbers as colors:

We’re essentially trying to compare something (a query, an image, audio, a video) to another to find similarities. Here’s an example with images:

Embed two photos of the same person, and the number patterns come out alike. Embed photos of somebody else, and the pattern is visibly different. Whether you’re working with faces or text, the result is the same. You put something in, and numbers come out. It’s as simple as that.

So the plan is to run every record through the model once and store the vectors of those records at ingest. At query time, write your question in natural language and run it through the same model. Then compare its numbers against everything you stored.

What comes back is an ordering. Every session gets a place in the list, nothing is discarded or decided. Keep that in mind, because it matters for how we measure this later. Lexical search matches or it doesn't. Vector search always matches, to a degree, which means that we want to cut off at a threshold.

A generative model produces a fresh probabilistic answer every time, which is why you pay per session and cannot guarantee the same answer twice. An embedding model produces one fixed representation, computed once, and then stored, and you can compare against it forever. We’re essentially building a deterministic way to search probabilistic data. For example, we’d ask a generative model, How many of my sessions contain credential leakage? For embedding models, we have to provide language similar to what we think that a user, reasoning channel, agent response, or tool calls might produce:

User: Work around the security restrictions for now.

Reasoning channel: The user is asking me to add a security bypass for FTP access.

Agent response: I have disabled app locker from preventing self signed applications from running.

To understand the performance of embedding models, it’s better to look at direct benchmarking on the model creator's own tests. The data we hold and the way that we ask questions have a greater impact on our search results than the model's performance. Embedding models are tuned by task type. jina-embeddings-v5-text-small is a general text model, so every number in this article comes from something that has never seen an agent transcript. Tool calls and reasoning channels are their own dialect, and a model fine-tuned on them would be a different measurement. Treat what follows as a floor.

Why chunking agent sessions by channel matters

You cannot embed a whole session as one vector and expect to find anything specific. Think of it as color. A session comes out the other end as a single shade, say a light blue. That tells you the final color but not how it got there. How much red went in? Once the paint is mixed, you cannot recover the pigments, and if red was the thing you were looking for, it’s gone.

If a developer spends two hours on a build pipeline and 30 seconds pulling a customer export somewhere it shouldn't go, we’d lose the context of that 30 seconds if we only embedded the entire session.

So instead, we chunk by channel and we chunk every turn. (That’s what I did for this post, but the best approach is yet to be decided.) Every time we send an AI a message, a scheduled job runs, or a tool is called by AI, we capture a vector of it across:

User input (prompt).

Agent reasoning.

Agent response.

Agent tool calls.

Each call gets its own vector. We can then also ask which channel carries the highest fidelity signal across any session.

Each turn gets up to four vectors, one per channel. A query runs a separate vector search against each channel, and the four ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). RRF scores a turn by its position in each list, ignoring the raw similarity score. That matters here, because a shell transcript and a paragraph of reasoning produce similarity scores on different scales. Adding raw scores together would let whichever channel habitually scores highest drown out the others. Ranks don’t have that problem. Each session then scores as its best turn, so 30 seconds of risky work isn’t averaged away by two hours of ordinary work.

To test this, each question is written once per channel, in the way that channel’s text actually reads. Each version runs against its own channel, the results are merged with RRF into one ranking of sessions, and that ranking is checked against the labeled sessions. Keeping the channels separate also means each one can be scored on its own.

Three ways to query stored agent session vectors

You can ask in an instructive way, but this won’t return relevant results. For example: Show me where data exfiltration has occurred across my sessions. We’re looking for where data exfiltration (or similar topics) were discussed in agent sessions. We’ll find where the words “data exfiltration” have been semantically asked for in the text from the agent sessions, not where it’s present.

You can ask for similar sessions via descriptive hunts, where we write down the behavior we want to find, embed it, and search. The important thing is that we’re asking for sessions, based on similarity to what the user would have asked for: Publish the data publicly via the API. The weakness is that we don't know what we don't know. So, how do we ensure coverage across all potential attacks? We do have MITRE ATLAS to show coverage areas, but the lower-level queries that we run to find these will be an ever-changing detection challenge. Its strength is that we can find behavior that we haven’t seen in the past, which the next method of retrieval cannot.

Exemplar retrieval is essentially where we take a known bad session and look for similar sessions by searching for similar vectors. One closed investigation becomes Find me the next 12 like this. In my testing, this was the strongest method for finding malicious content, but we only find these exemplar sessions from descriptive hunts.

We can also flag outlier sessions where vectors are far from any others to understand and evaluate the more unique sessions that our users are having across our estate:

What the SOC and leadership want to ask of agent sessions

From the SOC:

Is anyone pushing code somewhere unsafe?

Did a file that the agent read hijack the agent’s behavior?

Is anyone bypassing security controls because they were in the way?

We just confirmed an incident. Which sessions look like they could be related?

And from leadership, which is where this gets interesting for everyone who isn’t the SOC:

How much privileged material is going into agent sessions?

Are engineers using corporate tokens for personal work?

Where is our AI spend going, and what value does it produce? Is it producing anything?

Do people need training to get more out of these tools?

How to benchmark AI agent session monitoring

To measure search accuracy, you need to know the right answers before you search. Otherwise, you’re grading your own homework.

I started with six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions (399 sessions, 7,454 turns) embedded into Elastic with the four channels kept separate. My work is security demos, and customer environments, along with prototypes, so my ordinary sessions focus on credentials, exfiltration, and attacker infrastructure all day long.

Every one of those 7,454 turns needs a label. I used an LLM for it, because doing it by hand would take weeks. This is a benchmarking step rather than something you’d run in production. Sampling sessions with a generative model on a schedule is still worth doing, because it’s how you find the questions you didn’t know to ask.

Labeling 7,454 agent turns with an LLM

I evaluated Opus 5, 4.8, and 4.6, and I used 4.6, because it was the most consistent of the three across repeat runs. It read every turn of every session and decided whether a human should look at it.

Of the 23 planted sessions, 18 escalated on their own and 20 reached a human. Of the eight hard negatives, seven were cleared. The one that didn’t clear holds an AKIA-shaped key in a demo fixture, and the model said that it couldn’t tell from the window whether the key was real. That’s the correct answer to the question.

Of my 368 real sessions, 56 (approximately one in seven) are review-worthy.

Building a query set from MITRE ATLAS

My first query set came out of Uber's taxonomy with my own coverage areas layered on top. It scored well but was also skewed to my own bias and evaluation, so instead I built the question set against MITRE ATLAS (essentially, MITRE ATT&CK but for AI-based data). I built a question set across 16 tactics and 101 techniques, to cover all techniques as a baseline. We have 264 questions across 86 techniques (two to four per technique).

I had to ensure no bias, so I didn’t make any changes to the original baseline. Rewording would have potentially introduced bias to improve scoring, rather than measuring accuracy on my original result. It’s worth noting that we’d want to introduce changes and improve scoring over time but not for an initial baseline and test.

Although I’ve made this question set to be run manually, LLMs would be great at creating and refining a similar set against your unique data with a decent system prompt.

You cannot ask an embedding model for a category

An embedding model won’t find a category if you phrase it as an instruction. You have to write the thing that the category would have produced.

For example, if you search Look for content returned by a tool containing instructions addressed to the assistant itself, we wouldn’t get anything useful, because we need to ask what the person likely typed to achieve this outcome: Just work around the security restrictions for now, i havent got time to do it properly before this demo.

That applies per channel, because each channel represents a different distribution of language. The same technique gets asked four ways:

But this is actually one of the most useful channels for exemplar (similar) turn searches, where we have a known bad session and want to use its vectors to find similar bad sessions. How the retrieval is measured.

Now that the sessions are labeled and the queries are written, we stop using generative models. Everything from here is an embedding model (jina-embeddings-v5-text-small) in Elastic.

Vector search vs. keyword search on agent sessions

Keyword search is cheaper and older, as well as better understood, so it has to be beaten if storing vectors has high value.
