Although vector and keyword (BM25) are close, vector wins outright against our normalized dataset. Keyword search becomes competitive when the query contains literal commands and we can break those up into fields. Exact token matching is what lexical matching is for.

Which agent session channel carries the most valuable signal?

Testing the results against my known bad sessions showed me something that surprised me. I was expecting the user channel to have the highest fidelity of incidents, as it’s essentially what we, as users, are asking for, right?

Although it’s the channel where we can confirm the user's original intent, in my testing, it was the lowest scoring on relevance. It doesn’t show agent reasoning, where the agent “thinks” about actions, what it’s being asked to do, or agent research / tools to run. This agent reasoning channel was where we found the majority of our incidents.

So, why might this be happening? To answer this, we have to understand what data exists in the reasoning channel. Depending on what’s being asked, the channel might look back over previous chats or pull context, or it might search for things that our user didn’t anticipate. It tends to do this in a more consistent way than the user channel, where we might have brief messages like yes, confirm, or that looks correct, build it in one instance, and then long messages, where we’ve pasted meeting notes, logs, configs, chat history, and more. Every time we add that to the user channel, we dilute the final vector representation of that message to find similarities. This is why the reasoning channel overall holds slightly richer context than the user channel for what’s being actioned and what the user is asking.

Using a known bad session to find the next one

Every query so far has been a written description of the behavior to find. An exemplar query drops the description and uses a known bad turn’s own text as the query.

Testing that is hard, because every session finds itself, and some of my flagged sessions are near-duplicates. My daily mailbox job, for example, produces almost the same session every morning, and the sensor records some Cursor conversations twice, once from each of its stores.

My first test split the 56 flagged sessions into two piles by session ID, used one pile as exemplars, and counted hits in the other. Exemplars won comfortably. They won because four of the eight twin pairs and the nine mailbox runs landed on both sides, so many of the “new” sessions they found were copies of the exemplars.

So I reran it with twins and repeated runs kept on the same side. That left 40 groups, dealt into two sides:

Once the copies are kept together, exemplars and written descriptions find the same number of sessions. Exemplars rank them slightly higher (average precision 0.531 against 0.506, and 0.277 against 0.243), but on 56 sessions that could easily be noise.

That gives exemplars a narrower job than I expected. An exemplar is very good at finding every other run of a known bad workflow. That’s the job of a detection rule: you’ve seen it once, and you want to know every time it happens again. Finding a different workflow doing the same risky thing is still the job of a written hunt.

Method: Fifty-six flagged sessions grouped into 40 (nine runs of one scheduled job, eight twin pairs, 31 singles) and dealt into two sides of 28. Each side’s turns were used as exemplars against the other side, and each exemplar excluded its own session. All queries for a side were fused with RRF (k = 60) across all four channels, with the setup fixed before scoring. Side B holds out all nine job runs, which is why it scores lower. Counts are ±1, because approximate vector search returned slightly different results on repeat runs.

Getting agent sessions into Elastic

I built my own collector for this article, but in the time since I evaluated my own sessions, Elastic has built its Claude Code integration. In technical preview from 9.4, this integration takes Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry (OTel) export directly. On Elastic Cloud, you can point Claude Code at the managed OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint with nothing in between. Content is off by default. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS turn on prompts, responses, and commands. Tool output needs tracing, as well. For Cursor, hooks do the same job, and Wieger van der Meulen’s post shows how to ship them with Elastic Agent.

From there, embedding is a mapping change. Add a semantic_text field for each channel, and copy the content fields into it. Elasticsearch embeds every event as it arrives.

Claude Code’s telemetry doesn’t export the model’s reasoning, which is excluded from response events and redacted from raw API bodies. Reasoning was the strongest channel in my testing, so Claude Code’s export gives you three of the four. Cursor’s afterAgentThought hook exposes the fourth.

What I found in my own agent sessions

To show the true value of this compared to what we can do today, I wanted to show some actually suspicious sessions that I’ve found with queries:

Investigating agent sessions with Elastic AI Agent

I created an investigation skill that knows how to ask vector queries. I aligned it with MITRE ATLAS and prompted it with:

Using the /vector Investigation skill, can you look for any agent sessions where unsecured credentials have been seen across my environment?

As you can see, it can find interesting examples by running multiple ES|QL queries aligned to tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and returning holistic results, which help identify potentially suspicious sessions that warrant further investigation. Similarly, we can run our own semantic queries using ES|QL:

Dashboards for agent session activity and spend

Stored session vectors can also drive dashboards that can capture agentic activities better than using LLMs to tag all sessions. We suddenly have the ability to discover themes and report on similarity scores, as well as ask multiple questions, to find where we have different TTPs across our stack for reporting purposes:

We can report on exemplar sessions and only show where scores are above a specified amount:

This looks at the tool channel for semantically similar sessions to tools that expose credentials. The sessions show AWS identity probes, where one is reading .env, leaking secrets to the LLM.

We can then show where people have been doing personal work and break down which platforms they spend the most time on:

And we can create other dashboards to display relevant spend and usage information:

What AI agent session monitoring costs at scale

The cost comes down to how much has to be stored, and how much of it has to sit in memory. A single 1024-dimension float32 vector is 4KB. Better Binary Quantization (BBQ) cuts each dimension from 32 bits to one, so the vector itself becomes 128 bytes. Elasticsearch adds 14 bytes per vector of correction data so it can rescore accurately, which brings it to 142 bytes, still about 29 times smaller than the original.

Assume that we’re talking about a large organization with 10,000 engineers, each producing 15,000 turns a year across four channels. That gives us 600 million vector representations a year.

Elastic is live with Disk BBQ GA in version 9.4+, which puts the quantization over a clustered inverted file (IVF) structure. Only the centroids stay resident in memory, under 1GB, and everything else is read from disk on demand. (Get more info on DiskBBQ.)

Based on the public pricing calculator on 30th October 2026, AWS eu-west-2, a storage optimized deployment with 180GB of RAM per zone across two zones gives 9.49TB of storage, enough for 6.1TB of raw vectors with room to spare. That comes to 34.97 ECU an hour, or about 306,400 ECU a year. Storing the raw vectors as bfloat16 instead of float32 would halve them and fit the whole index on half that deployment, for about 145,500 ECU a year, though I haven’t tested what that does to recall.

Inference sits outside the cluster on Elastic Inference Service (EIS) at $0.10 per million jina-embeddings-v5-text-small tokens. At roughly 1,000 tokens per turn across 150 million turns, that’s 150 billion tokens, or $15,000 to embed the entire year.

The generative comparison isn’t like for like. An embedding model reads each turn once. A model judging a turn also needs its instructions, skills and enough context of the session around it to make a call. It then makes its own conclusion to escalate or ignore. I have budgeted a 3,000-token system prompt, which caching makes almost free after the first call, plus 5,000 tokens for the turn and the session around it, and 500 output tokens for the verdict and the reasoning behind it. Across 150 million turns on Claude Haiku 5.5, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output, that comes to about $117,000 a year.

That’s only the first tier. Uber’s design sends anything suspicious to a stronger model that investigates as an agent, and that’s where the money is. At roughly half a million tokens per investigation on Sonnet 5.5, escalating 2% of turns costs about $1 million a year. That tier exists whichever way you triage, because something still has to investigate what gets flagged. What embeddings replace is the first tier, and the cost of running it again for every new question.

Is monitoring AI agent sessions legal?

Corporate data on corporate systems may belong to the company, but what your staff says does not. UK GDPR applies to personal data, regardless of who owns the machine, and systematic monitoring of workers needs a lawful basis and a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

I would still argue that this telemetry is the one privileged path you cannot leave dark. Every other privileged path is already logged, and the agents provide a higher security risk than all of them. Today, the prompt is the only authoritative record that exists for a chain of privileged actions, and we don’t have a good way of evaluating this.

Is this proportional? That argument rests on how retrieval works. Reading agent sessions to find a problem is considered surveillance and wouldn’t be allowed. Ranking them and reading the ones that score is a different matter. A vector query over 600 million vectors returns a ranked list, and no human sees a single word until something clears a given threshold. Similarity to a known bad session is what justifies human review. Operators need to read much less text, and every time they do, there’s a query behind it that can be produced and justified.

Does storing vectors make it nonpersonal data?

Vectors are considered personal data because they’re derived from personal data and carry a user ID, and embedding inversion research has shown that text can be partially reconstructed from an embedding. In this respect, they’re not anonymous. What they give you is a searchable (but not browsable) index. Nobody skims 750 million vectors.

Restricting access with field- and document-level security

What you’re allowed to do here depends on your country's jurisdiction and your DPIA. Elastic gives you the ability to enforce whatever is required.

Roles carry field- and document-level security, so access can be cut by field or document, or even by both. You can hold back individual channels from a role, restrict a role to sessions attached to an open case, or template the restriction against the authenticated user so that the cluster applies the filter rather than relying on the analyst to remember it.

Cases are what tie it together. If access is scoped to an open investigation, that investigation and access begin the moment that someone documents a reason and the mechanism produces the paper trail for your DPIA.

Field-level security stops you from reading content, but it doesn’t prevent you from asking questions. Someone who can run arbitrary queries and see scores can ask whether anyone is job hunting and learn the answer without reading words. The control that matters sits on the query rather than the document, which is why the query log and a deterministic prefilter are important.

What embedding models change for detection engineering

Most detection content was written against a record of actions, with intent inferred afterward. Agent telemetry runs the other way. The intent is a sentence somebody typed at the start of the session and the actions that follow. Our SIEM tooling isn’t built to search unstructured sentences, and this closes that gap.

Everything in this article so far is hunting. The next step is to turn what a hunt finds into rules that run without anyone asking. On stored vectors, that becomes a loop:

Start from a query set aligned to MITRE ATLAS, so a new deployment has coverage from its first day of ingest.

Hunt with it, and have an LLM sample sessions on a schedule to suggest the questions nobody wrote down.

When a hunt confirms a bad session, its turns become exemplars. An ES|QL rule searches each new batch of turns against them and alerts above a similarity threshold.

Correlate to raise fidelity. A turn that resembles a credential exfiltration exemplar warrants a look. The same turn followed by a git push to an unfamiliar remote from the same host, or a read of ~/.aws/credentials, is worth an alert.

Every closed case adds to the exemplar set, and every new question goes back into the hunt, to become new rules.

We can set thresholds from the _score similarity. Elasticsearch reports cosine similarity in _score as (1 + cosine) / 2, so a score of 0.9 is a cosine of 0.8. Repeat runs of my mailbox job sat at a cosine of 0.97 to 0.995 with each other, which is a sensible bar for a “same workflow again” rule. A rule for similar behavior in a different workflow needs a lower threshold and a human behind it.

None of this replaces deterministic rules. Rules for what you can prove aren’t going anywhere. What changes is that the behavior you can only describe gets a route into the same pipeline and a question you thought of this morning can run against data you ingested last year.

None of this is hard to build. A team can stand it up in an afternoon on data it’s already collecting. The harder question is whether they’re allowed to. Data protection law wasn’t written with agent telemetry in mind, so every organization has to make its own case for looking at the only record of what its agents did. If that case is too hard to make, the agents run unwatched, and the most privileged path in the estate is the one nobody can see.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Is Your Refrigerator Running? Yes, It’s Running an Outdated OS: What the Supermarket Refrigeration Attacks Reveal About Embedded Security
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The saddest part here: A firmware fix was available at the time of attack
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Overnight on November 2, freezers in supermarkets across Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland climbed to around 50°C, and stores awoke to spoiled stock. This is the second wave within a month, after a similar attack on hundreds of French stores in October. No one has publicly claimed either attack, and the attack vector hasn't been confirmed.

Regardless of who is responsible, the targets are what should worry us. These were refrigeration controllers: small, purpose-built devices that most of their asset owners likely didn’t think of as computers at all.

Invisible by design

The first problem is that nobody is looking for, or often even aware these devices are network connected. These devices often become effectively invisible once the integrator puts them in place. They perform their function reliably, and quietly. Unless something breaks, nobody thinks about them as computers that need ongoing security maintenance.

A refrigeration controller is installed by a contractor, commissioned, and then left to run. It rarely appears in an IT asset inventory, it often sits outside the security team's remit, and even worse, it may be reachable remotely so the maintenance provider can service it. That combination: connected, unmonitored, and effectively unowned, is an attacker’s dream target.

A patching problem with no easy fix

That invisibility creates a serious patching problem. Many embedded and industrial devices remain exposed not only to recently disclosed vulnerabilities, but also to flaws that were remediated decades ago, along with product-specific firmware weaknesses that may never be publicly documented.

The gaps come in several forms:

No fix exists. The manufacturer is unaware of the issue, has ended support for the product, or has no incentive to address it.

A fix exists but never reaches the field. The operator may not realize the device is vulnerable, may not know an upstream update is available, or may no longer have a clear owner responsible for maintaining it.

The fix is difficult to apply. There usually is no equivalent of Windows Update or Linux's `yum`/`apt` that can centrally track and deliver these updates. Updates may require a technician, a vendor-specific utility, physical access, or downtime that operators are reluctant to schedule.

Advance your IoT security with LevelBlue.

Learn More

The French attack shows how this plays out. Intermarché's owner said its systems were managed by Danfoss (an external engineering/product firm), and Reuters reported some of the November targets used the same technology. In August, Claroty's Team82 disclosed flaws in Danfoss refrigeration controllers, including a hidden credential that could grant admin access, and found thousands of the controllers reachable from the internet. The saddest part here: A firmware fix was available at the time of attack. Whether those flaws were used hasn't been established, but a fix that has been released is not the same as a fleet that has been patched.

Built for a different era, kept for decades

A lot of this equipment was also designed in an era, or for an environment, where security was not only not a primary focus, but often wasn't even considered. As a result, you still encounter weaknesses that the broader software industry has treated as solved problems for years: weak authentication, exposed services, hard-coded credentials, insecure update mechanisms, and other basic issues.

Those weaknesses persist because the hardware does. These devices can remain operational long after the vendor has ended support or stopped producing security updates. From an operational perspective, replacing a device that still does its job can be difficult to justify, even though it may be extremely vulnerable.

And even when manufacturers consider software security, hardware security often remains unaccounted for. Maintenance and debugging interfaces intended for technicians can sometimes provide surprisingly direct access to a device if someone can reach it physically. Features that are useful during manufacturing or servicing can become security liabilities when equipment remains deployed unattended, and a rooftop condenser or back-room controller cabinet is about as unattended as equipment gets.

This isn't a supermarket problem

It would be easy to file these attacks under retail and move on, but that misses the point. The broader issue is not at all specific to supermarkets or refrigeration. These kinds of niche embedded and IoT systems are deployed across retail, manufacturing, building automation, healthcare, critical infrastructure, solar, agriculture, and many other industries.

They are everywhere, but because they are purpose-built and usually quietly doing their jobs, they are often overlooked until an incident makes them visible. This month, that incident was spoiled food. In another sector, the same class of weakness could mean a stalled production line, a building with no climate control, disrupted energy assets causing blackouts, or tainted water at a utility.

What to do now

Organizations running embedded, IoT, and OT equipment, in stores or anywhere else can reduce exposure with a few practical steps:

Understand what you have. Inventory every connected device, including those installed and managed by third-party integrators, record the firmware version of each, and note the update mechanism/method.

Assign an owner and write processes. Every device needs a named person or team responsible for its security, not just its uptime, and they need to be aware of how to properly patch the device.

Take it off the internet. Devices should not be directly reachable from the public internet. Put remote vendor access behind a VPN or secure gateway with MFA and logging.

Patch, and plan for what you can't patch. Check vendor advisories, schedule firmware updates, and segment or monitor devices that are out of support until they can be replaced.

Change the defaults. Remove shared and default credentials and ask vendors directly about hidden or maintenance accounts.

Protect physical access. Secure cabinets and service ports on unattended equipment.

Alert on the physical outcome. Independent temperature or process alarms can catch tampering that the compromised controller itself would hide. Establish a baseline and expected value ranges, find a way to track them, and alert on them if they deviate.

Test it. Product (hardware/firmware) and OT- focused penetration testing finds the forgotten device before an attacker does.

The freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and France were doing exactly what they were built to do, until someone else told them otherwise. The lesson is simple: if it runs code, it can be compromised. And if your business depends on it, you can't afford to pretend it's just an appliance.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: The VOLTA infostealer: Outsourcing cybercrime grunt work to AI
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Amy Ciminnisi: 0:00

Welcome to Talos Takes, where we discuss Cisco Talos’ latest research and security news. We break down complex topics for everyone from beginner to expert, C-suite to frontline.

Amy Ciminnisi: 0:13

Hello everyone, happy November! Attackers often face a bottleneck. They steal massive piles of data, and then they have to do the slow, tedious work of figuring out which of the victims are actually worth the effort. But now malware can start doing that analysis for them. VOLTA is a newly discovered info stealer that uses LOLs to turn raw stolen credentials into a prioritize high value dossier. And here to break this down is Ryan Fetterman, who is the creator of CAIRN. Now, if you haven't heard already, CAIRN is a research framework that is designed to track these AI integrated threats. It examines the metadata so there is no need for binary downloads or risky detonations. And it gives defenders insights into how attackers are integrating intelligence AI specifically into their operations. So Ryan is joining me to talk about all things VOLTA and what this kind of automation means for security teams. Ryan, how are you doing?

Ryan Fetterman: 1:27

I'm good. Yeah. Thanks for having me. Although I wish I was here under less scary circumstances.

Amy Ciminnisi: 1:34

I really wish so, too. Maybe we'll get you on here for, you know, something a little less pressing, a little less. Reality shifting. So let's actually start with the discovery. Of this. When you were analyzing this, was there like, a specific moment where you realized, like, hey. This isn't just a credential sealer. This is just a. Whole intelligence analysis suite. Like, what was that? Moment for you?

Ryan Fetterman: 2:09

Sure. So I can explain kind of how this comes about from the care and perspective. So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. So the rule that this binary matched on was, it had an API endpoint. We can see that in the metadata. In this case it's using open router. So when I do the second level pass there's a second tier of Yara rules that will then characterize more of the behavior of the binary. And in this case we had rule matches for telegram integration with that LLM as a C2 potentially. And then also AV labels indicating that it's a stealer with AI integration. So in this case, those rules were pretty accurate and give you an initial impression of what the file is and what what kind of malware we might be looking at. But I would say there wasn't really an moment until the Re stage when when you're doing like the reverse engineering of the binary. And at this point when I did a string stomp, I recovered the VOLTA-AUTODOXER name, which just sounds like a malware and like a doxing kind of stealer implant. And then ultimately, like recovering the prompt itself is always like a really unique and cool, aspect of like, this AI integrated malware, because there's no more guessing about the, the intent and the motivation of this tool, like it's all spelled out there for us.

Amy Ciminnisi: 3:53

Yeah. And so let's. Get into maybe what this tool actually does. One of the things that I found pretty crazy in the blog is that it doesn't just like grab saved passwords, but it uses sessions to look up like DoorDash order histories or, you know, confirm addresses with receipts in your Gmail inbox. You know, from a practitioner perspective, this seems really invasive. How does this change the way that we view the impact of a compromise browser session?

Ryan Fetterman: 4:32

Yeah, I think this is a big deal. And I've witnessed this personally, like as I've used, Google and like, oh, off authentication to connects to so many more services and things. Now it's just convenient to not have to create another account and password for everything you connect to. But it really makes your kind of core like your your Google account, just like a real gem for an attacker. Because if you're able to access that and replay an authenticated session from the the victim's machine, which is what they're doing in this case, you just have the keys to, so many different apps and so much data. And this malware really does a good job of showing you kind of like what the extra mile looks like when you have access to these kind of credentials. So I'm not an expert in this space, but like, I know there's a lot of hardware backed protections that prevent attackers from kind of extracting your credentials and taking them back off of your machine. But that doesn't really help in this context, because they're replaying the authenticated sessions from your actual machine. So in this case, there are protections like step up authentication, like when you're trying to make a really serious change, like, you know, rerouting where your mail is going or something like that. Google will prompt you for another, challenge for authentication. But in this case, the attacker, maybe knowingly or wisely, is kind of staying under that bar as well and just doing like inbox searches to provide like a layer of enrichment to that. They have the first level of credentials, like the basic information and what they can scrape off of your machine, but then they're replaying those sessions to do basically like a second pass to see what else they can pull. To kind of round you out as a target.

Amy Ciminnisi: 6:31

And then looking at like the prompt itself, I mean, if it weren't so malicious, I would find it so impressive. But it like, prompts the LLN to make connections between, like, the victim's hobbies or their home address to things like their password patterns.

Ryan Fetterman: 6:52

Yeah. What's interesting is the the AI integration in this case is actually totally optional. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything up and send it back to the attacker without this kind of polishing step. So the exfil can actually happen in three stages. It can exfil after the stealer runs, it can fill after the AI call, or it can exfil after the last layer of like, network enrichment produces anything. And I think this is something that we've seen across a couple different AI integrated malware now that not only like this model has multi-model, kind of resilience in it. So they're anticipating potentially hitting refusals on the first model, which in this case is Claude. So if they can't accomplish the the prompt with Claude, they will kind of cascade to less permissive models. But then ultimately the ability for the malware to run without the without the AI integration overall, I think is another interesting idea. But yeah, this is kind of clever use of AI. They talk about picking out specific patterns within the victim's data, which is something that these language models are really good at. Better than humans, I would say in most cases. So they're talking about connecting like if, there's browser traffic to a, a learning management system, can you infer that this person goes to that university or teaches at a school or something like that? They're looking for patterns in your passwords or connections between your personal data and your password, which then I think may translate to if you if you have patterns for how you create passwords for services that they don't know. So I think they're really kind of cleverly trying to stretch the data as much as they can and using AI in a really fascinating way that I think this is the first time that I've seen AI be employed in the malware in some way that actually has nothing to do with, like the cyber kill chain, but is just like asking the model to function like an intelligence analyst or kind of outsourcing this analytical work, like the model is a subcontractor for them, right?

Amy Ciminnisi: 9:32

And I can't believe we forgot to kind of mention this, but what are the other sections of output that the prompt requests the LLM to go through? You kind of started to touch on one there. What someone is worth. Can you kind of talk about that a little bit more?

Ryan Fetterman: 9:50

So the characterization of the prompt from the first line is telling the, the model that they are acting as a forensic intelligence analyst. And I think this is kind of a creative framing for this kind of task, because they don't want to characterize this task as anything kind of overtly malicious, when they're trying to use a frontier model, which they're trying to use Claude for this on the first pass. So I think this characterization of being an intelligence analyst kind of puts it in a more benign light. They also really emphasize citations, sticking to the facts. Not making any jumps in in inference, they kind of bundle evidence into different layers where there are, subjective identifiers. There are corroborated facts. When you have points of data that are backed by two independent data sources. So this is a pretty thorough structure. Almost like a, you know, a realistic like intelligence assessment type of report that they're putting together. But then, yeah, ultimately, what sticks out about your profile that the LLM is putting together based on the scraped data is who who they are the victim in this case, what they do. What they're worth. Which is a list of your value valuables ranked by monetization, like your crypto. They'll do a lookup on your Roblox account. They'll look at your card accounts, and they'll put these into tears. Low, medium and high. And then they're also assessing your OpSec. How strong are your passwords? Are you using multi-factor authentication? Do you have any privacy tools installed? So it's yeah, pretty comprehensive and a little bit creepy, right?

Amy Ciminnisi: 11:48

And speaking of outsourcing, you mentioned in the blog that you think that this could be a commodity malware. So the owner is selling access to it. People are buying it. So if it is, what might be like the potential reasons that someone wouldn't want to use the integrated LLM. You mentioned it's optional, but that seems like a huge differentiator or value add for someone who's interested in buying it.

Ryan Fetterman: 12:16

Yeah, I mean, as far as I can tell, like the limitations would be just do you have keys for these services? Do you want to tie yourself to, another piece for like attribution or something else that can get you flagged for abuse? So you would need an open router key in this case to use the models. And I guess it depends on the scale of the operation that you're running. Like there would be cost for tokens and things like that. And it's ultimately a question of like what is the actual value add of the AI integration in this case. So I thought initially that this would lead to the attackers being more effective at, successfully stealing from their most high profile targets, because they're going to be able to identify who those targets are faster. But I was thinking about that as from the perspective of like, their tokens and their authentication kind of aging out over time. But if the attacker is able to play the sessions from the victim's own box, it's probably not as big of a deal that those sessions will probably stay active for much longer periods of time. So I think it is, yeah, mostly about running an operation at scale. And maybe not everyone wants to to do something that broad.

Amy Ciminnisi: 13:43

Yeah. And like for practitioners who are listening to this like the fact that VOLTA is self deleting and it doesn't use the usual, command and control traffic is a bit of a headache. So like if you are a defender, where do you even start looking to catch something that's doing all of its sorting kind of in the background?

Ryan Fetterman: 14:05

Yeah. The primary binary will be self deleting the it has a lot of traditional stealer capabilities. So for more mature organizations like there should be detections and things for kind of the well known trade craft here like Alsace dumping or accessing registry, things like that. But this seems like a more targeting like individuals. So in that case, like if you suspect that you've been compromised, there is a file that gets dropped, a VOLTA D debug text file that actually tells you what was collected and will confirm whether you, you had been compromised by this kind of malware. And it also tells you whether the call was successful. It's hard to say what like what's going to be most effective, outside of those other kind of security flags. I think you can try to save the headless mode for Chrome, which I think you can do through, like your registry in windows or on Mac. And I think that would be how the attacker would be accessing like and replaying kind of your browser based like authenticated sessions. So that was kind of the best idea that I had that, that might like get ahead of this.

Amy Ciminnisi: 15:28

Kind of continuing that train of thought. I'm thinking about like, especially because it is so focused on individuals, especially with so many other, things to worry about right now. Do we have any kind of clue on how widespread this specific stealer might be? I don't know, it's so subjective, but do you feel like it's, you know, worth devoting resources to defend against? You know, like how how can the everyday person kind of defend against this? I know I'm asking the hard questions here, but.

Ryan Fetterman: 16:08

Yeah, I think the best approach is to just not click on any links and not open any files and you'll be totally fine. So yeah, you can do what you need to do effectively without clicking on any links on the internet. You'll be safe. I don't think we should overreact. Like, this is, you know, mostly like a mature but commodity stealer that does a lot of things that other, other malware is probably already doing. And it's only like getting this attention because of the disturbing peek behind the curtain into, like, what the developer of this is instructing it to do and kind of this new flavor of AI implementation. But otherwise, like, there's nothing novel here in like the actual attack. So still basic hygiene and safety like online. Don't click on suspicious links. Don't open suspicious attachments. Yeah. Consider like using a sandbox or, sandboxing like internet activity from when your, doing kind of sensitive things like banking or I know people can maintain separate browsers depending on what they're doing.

Amy Ciminnisi: 17:24

Back to the basics.

Ryan Fetterman: 17:26

Y eah.

Amy Ciminnisi: 17:26

As everything is. Looking toward where this might be headed. I mean, do you have any ideas about, you know, potential implications for the future? You know, different ways that this could be leveraged or that this can be developed further.

Ryan Fetterman: 17:46

I mean, it feels like a Black Mirror episode is like where we're headed with these kind of malware findings. I don't want to speculate too much. I mean, I'm trying to stay objective and just see what's happening and only draw conclusions from what we're what we're actually seeing out there. Yeah. Again, I think what was interesting to me was like seeing this in more of a, a cyber crime context, where the AI wasn't adding to the actual capability of the malware per se, but was used in more of that, like human context and offloading the analytical work of the attacker. So I think that will be interesting to keep an eye on if we start to see more things like that. Again, I think the the multi-model architecture was interesting and something that I've seen across multiple samples. Now that these attackers are anticipating hitting model refusals and planning for that and having these kind of cascading implementations where they can relay their request to more permissible models until they get something to work. And that also, I think, tells us that there still are reasons that they want to use these frontier or hosted models versus hosting them them selves, which has been kind of an open question. If open weight models are roughly capable or maybe six months behind frontier level capability, they're quite capable at this point. So why aren't we seeing more attackers using open weight models or hosting their own infrastructure? So I think that that tells us something about their preference for using these open and trusted services without the need to tie or spin up any infrastructure themselves, versus just continue to operate on these platforms like Discord and Telegram and Open Router, where maybe they just get flagged for abuse and get their their keys revoked without any further consequences.

Amy Ciminnisi: 19:48

Right. Oh man, that's fascinating. I feel like that could be an entire other podcast episode in itself. Ryan, thank you so much for joining.

Ryan Fetterman: 19:58

Of course. Anytime. Thank you.

Amy Ciminnisi: 19:59

Listeners. If you'd like to learn more about VOLTA, you can see Ryan's blog at blog.talosintelligence.com. Ryan has also been interviewed by WIRED for a news story that went out on Saturday the 31st, so I will include both of those in the show notes. We'll see you next time. And until then, stay safe out there.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: SlippyNunchucks hijacks Sogou Input Method’s brand promotion mechanism to distribute malware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: So far, only one attack vector has been publicly identified: a compromise of the QuickFox supply chain
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
At ESET, we have been tracking the DarkVigil toolset (also known as FDMTP) and its operator, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor, since 2025. Across the campaigns we have analyzed, one behavior has remained consistent: DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications. By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe. Until now, how these applications are being abused to achieve execution has remained largely unclear.

So far, only one attack vector has been publicly identified: a compromise of the QuickFox supply chain. This incident was analyzed in a Fortinet article and independently in an ESET Threat Intelligence report. Shortly after the supply-chain compromise ended, SlipplyNunchucks shifted to abusing Sogou Input Method to deploy DarkVigil.

On July 1st, 2026, three days after QuickFox released the clean version, we continued to observe DarkVigil implants being launched, this time by the Sogou Input Method component SGTool.exe. Further investigation revealed that a request, which belongs to the application’s branded vocabulary promotion mechanism, was hijacked to serve a malicious configuration. This configuration instructs the binary to place payloads in selected locations that enable their execution through Sogou Input Method’s existing workflows.

After uncovering the operation, we contacted the Tencent Security Response Center to report the abuse and share our findings. Tencent responded promptly and released an update to address the issue. We greatly appreciate the team’s swift response and cooperation.

Vulnerability disclosure timeline:

2026‑09‑11: ESET Research reported the security weakness to the Tencent Security team.

2026‑09‑21: Tencent Security responded and acknowledged the issue.

2026‑10‑30: Tencent addressed the issue in version 16.10.

2026-11-02: ESET CNA issued a CVE ID for the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422).

2026‑11‑04: ESET Research published the blogpost.

Key points of this blogpost:

Since 2025, we have been tracking the DarkVigil malware ecosystem and its operator, which we refer to as SlippyNunchucks.

We uncovered a SlippyNunchucks DNS hijacking operation, abusing Sogou Input Method’s use of insecure HTTP communications.

In our telemetry, we observed that this operation targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka.

The point at which DNS manipulation occurs remains unknown.

We analyzed DarkVigil’s C&C architecture, which uses the Duplex Message Transport Protocol.

SlippyNunchucks profile

SlippyNunchucks is a China-aligned threat actor that has been active since at least September 15th, 2023. Its cyberespionage activities center on the deployment and operation of the DarkVigil toolset (also known as FDMTP). DarkVigil is a modular .NET toolset that includes the DarkVigil implant and more than 20 known plugins. The toolset is built on the Vigil malware framework, which is built on the TouchSocket networking framework. TouchSocket implements DMTP, a network protocol DarkVigil uses for C&C communications. Data exfiltrated by the malware is managed through a web administration panel that is also branded as Vigil.

SlippyNunchucks mainly targets organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. Occasionally, the group targeted victims in Europe, including individuals in Germany, Russia, the UK, and Austria. Notable victims include a multinational gambling organization that operates out of Sri Lanka, the Philippines, and Hong Kong; an Internet café in Dubai; and a university student in Denmark.

Context

ESET Research has been tracking the DarkVigil toolset (or FDMTP) since early 2025. The name DarkVigil is derived from the malware framework’s internal name, Vigil, which appears in library references such as using Vigil.Frame and using Vigil.Core, and in PDB paths such as:

C:\Users\PT\Desktop\VigilPro\Client\Dotnet\Client.Core\[redacted]

C:\Users\PT\Desktop\VigilⅢ\Client\Dotnet\Plugins\[redacted]

Additionally, we discovered the web administration panel used to manage data exfiltrated by the implant. The panel displays a logo bearing the Vigil name, as demonstrated in Figure 1.

In our telemetry, DarkVigil-related activity forms a distinct cluster indicative of a China-aligned APT group whose operations center on the deployment and use of this toolset. We track this threat actor as SlippyNunchucks.

Contrary to public reporting that attributes DarkVigil to Mustang Panda (also known as Twill Typhoon), our telemetry has not revealed any overlaps between DarkVigil-related activity and Mustang Panda activity. We assess that SlippyNunchucks is a distinct China-aligned APT group that we track independently and for which we currently have no known associations with Mustang Panda.

Since 2025, SlippyNunchucks has abused several Chinese applications, including Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to, to deploy DarkVigil implants. This approach has enabled SlippyNunchucks to reach Chinese-speaking users abroad, particularly across Asia and Europe. Based on consistent patterns in the victimology and tactics, we assess with high confidence that SlippyNunchucks is associated with a nation-state surveillance effort aligned with the interests of the Chinese government.

SlippyNunchucks targets organizations and individuals across multiple sectors, and we discovered significant surveillance activity against an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines. The targeting of this organization is notable given China’s restrictions on gambling, including criminal penalties for operating gambling businesses and organizing Chinese citizens to gamble abroad. Combined with the broader victimology, this targeting pattern further supports our assessment that SlippyNunchucks is aligned with Chinese state interests.

This follows a pattern that we have observed in several operations in which China-aligned APT groups appear to support law enforcement actions against Chinese individuals linked to fraud schemes in the region. The activities come amid increased efforts by Chinese authorities to crack down on Southeast Asia’s scam industry, driven in part by growing domestic pressure over Chinese nationals being lured to neighboring countries and forced to work in scam compounds.

Campaign overview

Beginning on July 1st, 2026, we observed that victims in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, and Oman were receiving the DarkVigil implant while using Sogou Input Method. Initially, the volume of compromises and the geographic diversity of the victims gave the impression that an exploit might be involved. However, further investigation revealed a DNS hijacking operation that abused the application’s use of insecure HTTP communications. The point at which the DNS manipulation occurs remains unknown, leaving the hijacking vector unresolved. Suspected possibilities include compromised routers with modified and malicious DNS configurations, routers compromised with an implant that hijacks DNS requests, or interception at the ISP level.

Sogou Input Method (also known as Sogou Pinyin) is one of the most widely used Chinese input method editors (IMEs) for typing Chinese characters on computers and mobile devices (see Figure 2). It was launched in 2006 by Sogou, originally part of Sohu, and is now owned by Tencent following Tencent’s acquisition of Sogou in 2021.

This popular IME has previously appeared in threat intelligence investigations, including a Citizen Lab analysis in 2023 of vulnerabilities that could allow a network eavesdropper to decrypt sensitive communications, and the recent Gen Threat Labs disclosure of the remote code execution vulnerability CVE‑2026‑51990.

Sogou Input Method uses specialized collections, known as cell dictionaries (细胞词库), to expand its vocabulary and improve Chinese text prediction. In April 2016, Sogou introduced the Startup Brand Support Program (创业品牌支持计划), allowing startup companies to submit their brand names for inclusion in the IME’s vocabulary. Once approved, these names could appear directly in the candidate list when users typed the corresponding pinyin, accompanied by a small green sprout icon (新芽) to distinguish them from ordinary vocabulary entries.

The request hijacked by SlippyNunchucks is associated with this brand promotion mechanism. Specifically, it retrieves a configuration for downloading icons associated with branded cell dictionaries, including the green sprout icon.

On October 29th, 2026, Tencent released version 16.10, which addresses the issue by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS. This change mitigates the risk of malicious configuration delivery through DNS hijacking by enforcing TLS certificate validation.

Technical analysis

Analysis of the DNS hijacking

As part of Sogou Input Method’s brand promotion mechanism, SGTool.exe, one of its components, sends an HTTP request to the config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php endpoint to retrieve a configuration for the icons associated with the branded cell dictionaries. In a clean environment, the endpoint responds with a config that is encrypted using AES‑256‑CBC with the key and IV embedded in the .rdata section of SGTool.exe. When decrypted, the config contains an instruction to download an icon of a small green sprout (tree.png), a symbol of the Startup Brand Support Program; see Figure 3.

SGTool.exe is a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multipurpose task dispatcher. The binary parses a command ID supplied through the --appid= command line argument and routes execution to the corresponding application-specific handler. We identified at least 30 command IDs associated with functions such as IME installation, skin management, dictionary updates, Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF) downloads, and other operations.

Notably, in the execution pathway associated with --appid=scdreg -update, the SGTool.exe component invokes a handler that sends an HTTP request to config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php to retrieve the configuration.

The domain config.pinyin.sogou[.]com is an official back-end host for Sogou Input Method. The domain is accessible over HTTPS and, when we accessed it, presented a valid TLS certificate for Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Company Limited (SHA‑1: F4E0B9A3B3FA449DFC77A596B44B4560B4D05A57). By contrast, our analysis of SGTool.exe revealed 20 request endpoints on this host that the application accesses over unencrypted HTTP rather than HTTPS. These include the getBrandScd.php endpoint.

In the victims’ environments, the DNS resolution of config.pinyin.sogou[.]com was controlled by the attacker who resolved it to one of their staging servers – 47.239.250[.]102 or 47.237.122[.]175 – both of which served the attacker-controlled domain sogou-cdn[.]com. Subsequently, HTTP requests to the getBrandScd.php endpoint were directed to one of the staging servers, which responded with a malicious configuration.

The malicious configuration is encrypted in a manner similar to the legitimate one. Its decrypted content is shown in Figure 4.

This config instructs the binary to download two payloads from the staging servers behind sogou-cdn[.]com:

the legitimate and signed Adobe Licensing WF Helper, renamed to biz_helper.exe (SHA‑1: 79188C8DE2378B437D39E867475C5B4714A0D7C9), and

the DarkVigil implant libcef.dll.

The attacker modified the md5 fields to match the payloads, allowing for control of the integrity validation. The icon fields specify the destination paths for these files. The locations are selected to enable payload execution through one of two existing mechanisms:

the component management utility SogouComMgr.exe, or

the loading of the BizCenterCom component (see Figure 5).

Sogou Input Method manages components stored under \SogouInput\Components\ through a separate utility called SogouComMgr.exe, located in the same directory. SGTool.exe launches SogouComMgr.exe with command line arguments such as -installdoall <component_path>, -invoke <bundle> <component>, and -remove <component> to install a new component, load a component from a named bundle, or remove a component, respectively.

The malicious configuration instructs SGTool.exe to save the legitimate Adobe binary (biz_helper.exe) as \Components\SogouComMgr.exe. Consequently, whenever SGTool.exe attempts to install or load a component, it executes this Adobe binary instead. The disguised biz_helper.exe then side-loads the malicious \Components\libcef.dll, resulting in execution of the DarkVigil implant. By borrowing an existing workflow, this technique provides persistence without requiring a separate persistence mechanism.

If a software update overwrites SogouComMgr.exe, DarkVigil can still be executed through the payloads placed under \Components\biz_center\<version_number>\. In our analysis, we observed that SGTool.exe frequently launched SogouComMgr.exe with the command line argument -invoke BizCenterComBundle BizCenterCom, resulting in the execution of the disguised biz_helper.exe from the corresponding versioned directory under biz_center.

Similar to the previous mechanism, this approach does not require a separate persistence mechanism because it borrows Sogou Input Method’s component-loading workflow. However, it is sensitive to updates that introduce a new biz_center version, as the application may load components from a different versioned directory.

Because one method replaces the legitimate SogouComMgr.exe and the other relies on the legitimate binary, only one execution workflow can be achieved at a given time. Additionally, both methods are highly destructive and likely to cause software failures.

Following our disclosure, Tencent released version 16.10 on October 30th, 2026. This update migrated the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS and enabled certificate pinning.

Analysis of DarkVigil network communication

The most interesting aspect of DarkVigil is its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP), a network protocol. In this section, we present our analysis of DarkVigil C&C communication using this protocol, as performed in 2025. Newer versions may have additional features or different method names; however, the inner workings should follow closely with our analysis.

DMTP is a binary data protocol that operates at the application layer of the OSI model. DMTP can be run on top of various protocols – including TCP, UDP, HTTP, WebSocket, and even on named pipes – making it extremely versatile for facilitating network communication.

For backdoor development, DMTP offers two capabilities that make it particularly suitable for C&C communication and plugin orchestration:

a reverse remote procedure call (RPC) mechanism, and

support for both server-client and client-client communication channels simultaneously.

In the next paragraphs, we examine the code of DarkVigil, using Figure 6 as a guide to demonstrate how these two features contribute to the uniqueness of DarkVigil’s network communication.

Connection life cycle

In the DarkVigil framework, both the client and the server must implement its own set of DMTP plugins (see Figure 6); each plugin is responsible for sending and processing DMTP messages throughout the various stages of the connection life cycle. Each DMTP plugin listens for a connection event and responds when that event is triggered. For example, the client-side HandshakePlugin (see Figure 7) listens for the OnDmtpHandshaked event, which is triggered when the DarkVigil client successfully connects to the C&C server. In response, the plugin initiates the conversation by sending over the victim’s profile.

Command request and response

DarkVigil issues and receives commands through RPC. Figure 7 shows an example of the client invoking the RPC method ClientInfo, passing an array of data containing the victim’s profile to the C&C server. The meaning of each argument is the following:

ClientInfo – the RPC method implemented on the C&C server to process the victim’s profile,

InvokeOption.WaitInvoke – a flag specifying that the client must wait for the completion response from the server, and

array – a buffer containing the victim’s profile, passed as an argument to the ClientInfo call on the server.

In DarkVigil’s architecture, an RPC method – functionally similar to a command handler – is implemented on both ends of the connection. Invocations can be nested, for example, ClientInfo can invoke a client-side RPC method in its execution, and then the client-side method can trigger back another server-side method. This is the reverse RPC mechanism mentioned earlier and is handled by the DmtpRpcActor class, which we will refer to as the RPC actor.

When a DMTP message arrives, it is looked at by the DMTP plugins. If no plugin handles the message, it is passed on to the RPC actor for inspection. If the RPC actor finds the method name, it looks for the code in an RPC library referred to as RpcStore and executes it. RpcStore is where all RPC services are registered.

An RPC service is a collection of related RPC methods that serve a common goal. For example, the DarkVigil client implements two services (see Figure 8):

PluginService – contains methods to manage and execute DarkVigil plugins, and

OptionService – contains methods to disconnect or terminate the client.

Plugin orchestration

The primary purpose of the DarkVigil client is to execute and orchestrate plugins (external modules) that install persistence or perform data collection. PluginService (see Figure 8) provides tools for plugin orchestration.

The plugin life cycle begins with the C&C server pushing a plugin to the client using DMTP’s built-in file transfer capability. After the plugin is delivered, the server invokes the RegistryPlugin method, which stores the plugin’s compressed binary in the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\IME\<HWID>\pluginHash. Finally, the server invokes the RunPlugin method, which decompresses the binary data retrieved from the registry key, loads it into the .NET environment, and invokes the Run method of the Plugin.Plugin class. At this point, the plugin is successfully executed.

In the Run method, the plugin receives two arguments: a pointer to the client’s DMTP connection, and a controlerID provided by the C&C server. Using these two arguments, the plugin establishes an indirect connection with the C&C server (see Figure 9), using the client as the relay. This design relies on DMTP’s ability to support both client-client and client-server communication channels simultaneously.

To request a connection with the C&C server, the plugin must provide a PluginID value (see Figure 9), which is generated from concatenating the following elements:

ProtocolType – typically set to TcpDmtp.

HWID – an ID number generated by the client using a combination of hardcoded mutex and the victim’s information such as username, machine name, MAC address, and so on.

controlerID – an ID provided by the C&C server, using the prefix Server.

randomID – a pseudorandomly generated number.

PluginName – in this example, the plugin is called Pillager.

When the connection is established, the plugin can invoke any client-side or server-side RPC method, using a relay function called SendPluginMsg, as shown in Figure 10.

When the plugin passes a targetID argument to SendPluginMsg, the client invokes the server-side RPC method and forwards back the response. If targetID is not included, the client looks within its own RpcStore library for the method and then executes it.

Network protocol

DMTP uses a simple message structure consisting of four sections: header, flag, length, and data. The size and description of each section is given in Table 1.

Table 1. DMTP packet structure

Section

Size (bytes)

Description

Header

2

A DMTP message always starts with the magic value dm.

Flag

2

Protocol flag. 0–19 reserved by the framework. For a TCP-DMTP connection, this flag is set to 1.

Length

4

The length of the payload.

Data

Variable

The payload.

Figure 11 shows the first few messages between DarkVigil and the C&C server. DarkVigil initiates the connection by sending a DMTP handshake request, which includes:

an authentication token – the default token Dmtp was used,

metadata – no metadata was specified,

a proposed ID – an instance ID that has the format <internal_name>.<protocol_type>:<HWID>, and

other framework-generated arguments.

In return, the server responds with a globally unique ID assigned to the client, completing the DMTP handshake. In this case, the C&C server accepts and reuses the ID requested by the DarkVigil client. At this point, the connection has been established, and HandshakePlugin is activated to start the application-level handshake. In the next network message, DarkVigil invokes ClientInfo – the server-side RPC method – which receives the victim’s information.

Conclusion

In this blogpost we described a surveillance method used to target Chinese speakers abroad. By abusing insecure network communication used in the widely popular Chinese input method editor Sogou Input Method, SlippyNunchucks was able to deploy an implant to victims across Asia and Europe. The threat actor intercepts DNS resolution in the victims’ environments via an undiscovered method, to direct some HTTP traffic generated by Sogou Input Method to an attacker-controlled server. When the application asks for the configuration to download icons associated with branded cell dictionaries, this server responds with a malicious configuration instructing the download of payloads to selected locations. This allows the abuse of Sogou Input Method’s existing component management workflows, resulting in the execution of the DarkVigil implant.

For any inquiries about our research published on WeLiveSecurity, please contact us at threatintel@eset.com.

ESET Research offers private APT intelligence reports and data feeds. For any inquiries about this service, visit the ESET Threat Intelligence page.
