Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update. Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Background On October 16, Huntress first reported the abuse of a ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to access Microsoft 365 tenants, and since then we have been continuing to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Eric Stride and Andrea Hatcher for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

On October 16, Huntress first reported the abuse of a ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to access Microsoft 365 tenants, and since then we have been continuing to investigate threat actor behavior related to this incident.

Now, we're pulling on a different thread: who, or what, was doing the typing during the unauthorized activity we observed. Microsoft has published its own findings, attributing the activity to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, to abuse the compromised ConnectWise application credentials and sign in to downstream Microsoft 365 tenants at machine speed. Our telemetry aligns with Microsoft's findings, but does not independently confirm them.

In the activity on the tenants we examined, we observed the tooling change in under a minute between runs and a retry loop appear in the run after a failure. Some actions were tested in one tenant before being run in batches, a pattern we saw three times across two tools.

Taken together, these observations form our working hypothesis: scripted tooling did most of the heavy lifting in this incident, while something adapted the tooling between runs, quickly. That something may very well be an agent. Below, we're providing details about what we saw, and leaving it to the audience to draw their own conclusions.

What we can and cannot see

Our view comes from Entra Sign-in logs and directory audit logs in the Microsoft 365 tenants we monitor, plus the fleet-wide sweeps we ran during the incident window. That gives us the timing, order, and shape of what the actor caused Entra to record. However, it leaves some large gaps:

Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in the Entra audit log, and no victim we know of had Graph activity logging enabled, so the scope and method of any Graph access cannot be seen in the logs available to us.

Application-only audit events carry no source IP address, so we cannot tie some of the activity, such as the credential changes, to a specific IP.

We have no visibility into the actor's own systems, so we cannot see the tooling itself, or whether any model provider sat behind it.

Lastly, we cannot say whether AI was used to plan the operation, develop target lists, or write the tooling.

One day, three modes of operation

Most of what we can see happened on October 15, in a little under 14 hours. Laid out in a single timeline, the activity falls into three distinct behaviors:

Scripted loops

Hands-on operator work (an "operator" being whoever steered the tooling, whether that's a person, automation, or an AI agent)

A stretch where the tooling kept running after the thing it was targeting was already gone

Figure 1: Activity on October 15 in Huntress-monitored tenants, grouped by behavior. Operator-driven means a person, or a model acting for one, was steering the tooling between runs.

How scripts, people, and AI agents look different in logs

The logs Huntress analyzes record behavior and help us figure out what occurred: how fast things happen, what happens after something fails, and how much the requests vary. The logs may show different types of fingerprints depending on if the behavior comes from a script, a person, or an LLM agent. Below is a table of possible behavioral signals between the three, though these are general characteristics and may have substantial overlap.

Signal

Scripted automation

Human operator

LLM agent in the loop

Pacing

Machine-regular, sub-second or fixed intervals

Uneven, with pauses that look like reading output

Steady, gated by model inference

Response to errors

None unless coded, repeats the same failure

Reads the error, adjusts, or gives up

Reads the error and changes approach

Variety of requests

Identical request shape, repeated

Efficient, goes to what it wants

Exploratory, retries with variations

User agent

One fixed string per tool

Varies with the tools the person picks up

Often SDK defaults (python-requests, httpx)

These categories are Huntress analyst heuristics for telling the three apart, not an industry standard. A tricky nuance here is that this isn't a black-or-white determination: no single row completely settles what's primarily behind the attack. For instance, a script can carry a sleep timer and a list of user agents, which could make its behaviors in the logs look more human than it is. One password spray against a single tenant may at first read like a person, but a fixed beat in the timing and a rotating list of user agents would indicate otherwise. When investigating these signals, part of what matters is the mix and whether the behavior changes in response to what just happened. A script repeats itself; a person or an agent adjusts.

Two limits apply to everything in our analysis below:

A person pasting commands from a chatbot into a terminal looks like a person in these logs, because the model never touches the API.

Logs show who ran the tooling, not who wrote it; a model can write a fixed script that looks like any other script.

What we saw

The loops: scripts at scale

The logs showed us that on October 15, between roughly 06:13 and 08:46 UTC, the credential was used against almost 1,000 tenants, one after another, in ascending tenant ID order. That is a loop over a sorted list: one token request per tenant, one to six minutes apart, with the same user agent (Python-urllib/3.12) every time. When the loop stopped partway through the list, it looked like an exhausted list or an interrupted process (as opposed to a concerted decision to stop).

The logs also showed that nine minutes earlier, around 06:04 UTC, about 100 failed token requests had landed within 10 seconds against the first 100 tenants of that same list of 1,000 tenants. Every request failed the same way, and nothing changed between attempts. This is a signature of a thread pool: a fixed set of worker threads pulling tenants off a shared list and firing requests in parallel, each blind to what the others get back. Nothing in the loop reads a response before the next request goes out.

The same thread-pool tool then ran a second time against 100 tenants, using a different application's key, at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and failed the same way. Both runs used application secrets that belong to a single tenant, which cannot authenticate anywhere else, and the tool kept firing regardless. Whoever built it, or at least launched it, did not account for that difference.

Here is what that does and does not tell us: 10 requests a second is faster than anything that reads each response before deciding its next move, whether that is a person or a model working step by step. So this was most likely one script, run at least twice. It does not tell us who or what wrote the script. A model can write a thread pool as easily as a person can, so while this rules out a model making each call, it does not rule out a model writing the tool.

Trial and error

On October 15 between 03:42 and 03:57 UTC, the logs indicated a pattern of trial and error in the unauthorized activity, with the tooling changing in less than a minute between runs. The activity outlined in the logs looked like an attempt to establish persistent access by adding credentials:

A secret was added, removed, and added again.

A certificate was uploaded, but it failed because the thumbprint did not match.

The operator fell back to a secret again before granting, then removing, the Global Administrator role twice.

The same sequence ran in a second tenant 47 seconds later, with both keys added in a single run.

During that window the tooling changed in response to results at least three times. The run after the failed certificate upload added a retry loop, the sequence repeated in a second tenant with both keys in a single run, and when that tenant refused a Global Administrator removal, the actor granted a different role to a sibling principal, and the original service principal was then deleted.

Based on this activity, it's possible that the credential planting and the targeted probe were steered by an operator adapting between runs. However, we can't determine whether that operator was a person, automation, or an LLM model.

The hand-picked targets: pilot, then batch

Between roughly 09:25 and 12:35 UTC on October 15, one sweep touched 17 tenants, with one Graph token request each in a hand-ordered sequence with irregular spacing over three hours. A second sweep at 13:54 UTC ran a fixed probe of six resources per tenant, in sorted order, with four seconds per tenant. Someone appears to have chosen the targets, checked them one at a time, and then handed the list to a script.

Where it started to look like an agent

No single observation here proves anything, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. But several of them pointed in the same direction, and the longer we looked, the harder it became to explain them away as a person at a keyboard or a script left to run.

First, there's the 55-second gap between retries that we described above. The certificate upload that failed on a thumbprint mismatch at 03:48:24 UTC ended that run with no retry. The next run, 55 seconds later, did retry the same error, at 3.5 seconds and then 7.1 seconds, until it worked, and it carried the same retry into the second tenant.

Figure 2: How the tooling changed

So what does this actually tell us about what was going on behind the scenes? Either someone edited the code in under a minute, or a prepared tool had a retry option nobody had used yet. A script left alone does not rewrite itself between runs. A person, a person relaying to a model, or an agent was likely adapting it as an operator. The speed of the change is consistent with an agent loop: read the failure, rewrite the call, run it again.

The retry logic is particularly revealing. Doubling the wait between attempts is textbook defensive error handling. This is something that generated code tends to add unprompted, and in this incident showed up in a tool that had none just a minute earlier. The tooling was also more elaborate than the job required: the 100-tenant burst used a thread pool, where a simple loop over the list would have done the same work.

Another notable pattern that we outlined above: An operator tried an action against one tenant first, then ran it as a batch, again and again. We saw that three times across two sets of tooling. That points to the habits of an operator, not a quirk of one script. Microsoft describes ARTEX as building a graph of the assets it discovers and running parallel breach paths, which has the same shape: probe, learn, and then fan out.

Finally, there is the speed. Our first enumeration activity started around 01:05 UTC, and the credential changes in the first tenant were complete by 03:50 UTC, in line with Microsoft's report of under three hours from targeting to privileged access in multiple environments. Speed alone does not separate an agent from a well-prepared script, but it is the kind of compression Microsoft describes agent frameworks delivering. Some of the user agent strings also look hand-set rather than library defaults. One tool identified itself as python-requests/2.31, where the library sends python-requests/2.31.0 by default, and on October 13 a browser string was missing its standard "(KHTML, like Gecko)" segment. Both fit a model producing user agents from memory, and both fit a person copying them from documentation.

Put together, these factors make up our working hypothesis: scripted tooling is doing the heavy lifting in this incident, with something adapting it between runs, quickly. That something may well be an agent. The next section is about how sure we are, and where the evidence runs out.

What the telemetry can confirm

A working hypothesis is only worth sharing if its limits are clear. Here are ours.

The best evidence against a fully autonomous agent is what happened after 03:57 UTC. The Teams service principal was deleted, and for the next 22 minutes requests using it kept firing every four to eight seconds. These were rejected every time, and subsequent requests didn't change. An agent watching its own output would be expected to stop. A multi-agent framework could keep unattended fan-out tasks running while other agents carry on, which could explain this behavior. So too could a person who launched some background loops and walked away. However we don't know which one played out in this situation.

Another consideration: curl/7.88.1 is the version Debian 12 ships with, and the official python:3.12 container image is built on Debian 12. That points to how the tooling was possibly packaged, since the user agent doesn't align with the system's external fingerprints.

The biggest gap is the missing Graph request logs. They would show query variety, the clearest difference between a script and an agent, and nobody we know of collected them.

So, how sure are we? We are highly confident that an operator, whether a person or an LLM model, adapted the tooling between runs. On our own telemetry alone, we put our confidence that an LLM was involved in the escalation tooling at low to medium. Taking Microsoft's attribution into account, we put it at medium to high.

What would potentially help settle it is evidence we do not hold: the Graph activity logs from a victim that had them enabled, the tooling itself, or traffic from the actor's systems to a model provider's API.

What Microsoft says: Storm-0940 and ARTEX

In its October 21 report Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise credential abuse to Storm-0940, a threat actor they say has been active since 2021. Microsoft asserts that the actor targets organizations across industries for data theft, and has historically gotten in through password spraying and internet-facing applications, then kept access by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

What is new, according to Microsoft, is the tooling. They report that from at least September 2026 the actor used ARTEX, an open-source framework in which LLM-driven agents run a penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction, building a graph of the assets and weaknesses they discover as they go. ARTEX can use any AI model, and Microsoft says it has seen other actors using it in several regions.

How does Microsoft connect that to this incident? The reasoning they've shared points to infrastructure, attributing a large password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between October 10 and 14 to Storm-0940, and noting that the same IP, and the surrounding range, appear in the ConnectWise advisory. The report does not describe how Microsoft identified ARTEX, or what links the earlier spray to Storm-0940. We have not independently verified either. However, Microsoft may know how to identify this particular tooling, which is why they have mentioned its usage in this campaign.

How our findings line up with Microsoft's report

Our telemetry is consistent with Microsoft's account in several ways.

We saw the same infrastructure (144.172.64[.]128) and user agents (Python-urllib/3.12, curl/7.88.1), and the same sequence: compromised application credentials, then Graph follow-on with credential additions and privileged role changes, including the Teams application assigning itself Global Administrator.

Our telemetry also corroborates the password spray Microsoft attributes to 144.172.64[.]99.

Scale is where we differ, by design. Microsoft counts more than 2,250 tenants and we see only the tenants we protect, so our numbers are only a subset, not a contradiction. We saw python-requests/2.34.2 from 144.172.64[.]99 in the October 10 to 14 password spray, but not azure-toolkit/1.0, and we saw no identity or group changes in the two tenants where we hold directory audit logs.

Why this matters

Whoever, or whatever was behind it, this operation was not polished. Over the course of our investigation we saw:

Secrets added, removed, and added again.

A certificate that failed to upload.

Secrets for one tenant sprayed at a hundred others, where they would never work.

Yet, as we saw in the two tenants where we hold audit logs, it took under three hours from the first enumeration activity to privileged role changes, in line with Microsoft's report across multiple environments, because the stolen application credential did much of the work.

It's clumsy, but it worked. If an agent was in the loop here, it was an early one. It already ran things in parallel, never needed a break, and left defenders a few hours. Tools like this get better quickly: they stop making the mistakes we saw, and they are cheap to point at hundreds of tenants at once. Microsoft makes the same point: agents can work around the clock and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously.

Defenders' visibility is also in flux. In our view, the signals we relied on here (a retry that showed up 55 seconds after a failure, a fixed beat between requests, and user agent strings customized away from the library default) are the first things a better tool will smooth away. Cadence will not be a reliable signal for long. What will hold up is what the activity does, which is where the detections below point.

What defenders can do

Speed is the biggest concern here. This activity moves faster than a person can triage. This is useful detection guidance regardless of the actor:

Alert when a service principal assigns itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator, deletes itself, or when one vendor principal grants a role to a sibling.

Alert on credential additions to high-privilege applications from unexpected sources.

Baseline each vendor application's normal user agent (kiota-dotnet for the ConnectWise applications), source ranges, and cadence. The clearest early signal here was a vendor application behaving differently from its baseline.

Turn on Microsoft Graph activity logs where licensing allows, and keep raw user agent strings and sub-second timestamps. Cadence and retry timing were our most useful signals, and normalization destroys both.

Watch across tenants, not only within one. A trickle in any single tenant can be one campaign running at thousands of attempts per minute across the estate.

We will update this post as ConnectWise, Microsoft, and others share more.

144.172.64[.]60

After an initial failure to upload an authentication certificate, the actor adapted tooling within 55 seconds to incorporate retry logic, successfully establishing secondary credentials before replicating the technique across a second tenant 47 seconds later.

The threat actor leveraged Microsoft Graph API calls to execute privilege escalation, having the Teams application identity assign itself the Global Administrator role. To secure redundant administrative access across victim tenants, the actor also granted elevated roles to sibling service principals originating from the same operational infrastructure.

The threat actor enumerated cloud infrastructure through a pilot-then-batch progression, shifting from broad automated loops across nearly 1,000 tenants to targeted reconnaissance of specific cloud resources via Microsoft Graph token requests. Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560(( Oracle has released its October 2026...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 26th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Japanese cloud hosting provider Onamae Desktop Cloud has confirmed a cyberattack in which intruders compromised its infrastructure and installed malware on customer servers. More than 26,000 servers were potentially affected. The provider began shutting down customer environments on October 21 to contain the intrusion and prevent further unauthorized activity.

India’s state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online. The exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records, and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.

WordPress backup developer TeamUpdraft has suffered a cyberattack after intruders accessed its website and potentially exposed customer information and management-service connection keys. Attackers subsequently abused compromised UpdraftCentral keys to install backdoors on WordPress websites during an 18-hour campaign on October 18 and 19.

LiteLLM, a widely used open-source AI gateway, confirmed an October 21 supply-chain attack in which attackers used stolen developer tokens to publish malicious packages and Docker images. The compromised version 1.107.0 was designed to steal cloud credentials and AI service secrets, with attackers subsequently testing stolen AWS credentials.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research uncovered how AI-enabled antidetect browsers allow operators to manage thousands of deceptive accounts while evading platform safeguards. Tools including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin facilitate account takeovers, financial fraud, and automated distribution of AI-generated content, supporting large-scale influence operations across social media platforms.

Researchers observed affiliates of INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups using AI agents to conduct human-approved cyberattacks. The operation targeted 62 organizations by exploiting remote-access systems and compromised credentials. Victims were concentrated in the manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and pharmaceutical sectors, primarily in the United States.

Researchers analyzed a cybercriminal operation that used multiple AI assistants to plan and execute different types of malicious activity. The attacker relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports to develop attack capabilities. Exposed operational records revealed how AI tools supported campaign planning, technical execution, and adaptation across different targets.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Critical PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been used in widespread exploitation attempts that could enable remote code execution. Attack traffic reportedly increased from thousands to millions of attempts following disclosure. As of October 23, approximately 97.5% of publicly visible PHP instances did not indicate patched versions.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560((

Oracle has released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update, addressing 1,209 unique vulnerabilities through 1,295 security patches across 33 product families. The update includes 95 critical CVEs and affects widely deployed enterprise products, including Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, MySQL, and Java SE.

GitLab has fixed CVE-2026-110264, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 10.0 affecting Community and Enterprise Editions. The integer overflow flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on affected servers. The vulnerability affects versions before 18.11.13 and several 19.x releases.

A critical privilege-escalation vulnerability, CVE-2026-114625, affects on-premises Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.4 and allows authenticated users, including those with read-only access, to obtain operator-level permissions. Successful exploitation can expose restricted management functions, and the vulnerability has been exploited in attacks.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has profiled Aokigahara, a newly identified infostealer targeting credentials and session data associated with AI applications, developer tools, and cloud platforms. Targeted applications include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Stolen information may include authentication tokens, account credentials, and other sensitive application data.

Researchers revealed that U.S. federal investigators suspect an executive at a ransomware negotiation company assisted the ShinyHunters extortion group in operating its victim disclosure website. The site reportedly listed nearly 100 organizations between May and October 2026.

Researchers mapped Lazarus’s Operation FlashHole, a cyberespionage campaign targeting organizations in South Korea’s software, construction, and telecommunications equipment sectors. Attackers used tailored phishing messages and fraudulent portfolio websites to deliver malware. The campaign exploited trusted financial-security software to execute malicious components.

Researchers have uncovered a large-scale campaign by threat actor k0t targeting Fortinet FortiGate, FortiWeb, and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect devices. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities and weak credentials to establish persistent access and steal information. The operation exposed more than 70,000 credentials and showed possible connections to ransomware groups.

The post 26th October – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Gheist Attackers Stumble in Attempt to Abuse GitHub Tokens
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across repositories using stolen access tokens.

In research published October 25, Wiz said it had tracked the campaign, dubbed Gheist, since September 15 and recovered the branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The operation targeted every repository the stolen tokens could reach, from personal projects to private enterprise repositories.

Wiz identified infostealer logs and earlier supply chain compromises, such as the March compromise of the Trivy security scanner, as sources of the stolen tokens. Some of the accounts were also being used for malware distribution and cryptomining.

Workflow Trick Meets GitHub Approval Hold

The attackers used the tokens to create branches and commit a GitHub Actions workflow that printed repository secrets into its own log. They then downloaded the log through GitHub's application programming interface (API) and deleted the run seconds later, so the campaign needed no external command-and-control (C2) server.

The campaign's main obstacle has been a GitHub control introduced July 28 that places potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories on hold until a collaborator approves them. Wiz said every public Gheist run it examined, across all variants, remained in an action_required state, preventing the malicious workflows from executing.

The protection does not extend to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. In those environments, Wiz observed workflows completing on attacker-created branches before the runs were removed.

Read more on stolen supply chain secrets: TeamPCP Explores Ways to Exploit Stolen Supply Chain Secrets

Private Repositories Remain Exposed

In enterprise organizations, Wiz observed the attackers cycling through user and automation account tokens and cloning private repositories. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organizations were used to enumerate Amazon Web Services' Secrets Manager.

Two variants of the tool ran in parallel. One added support for deployment environments, exposing environment-scoped secrets that are often production credentials. It later gained a job that searched self-hosted runners for credentials and other sensitive files, though Wiz described the job as "buggy."

As of October 24, roughly two-thirds of implicated accounts were no longer available on GitHub, which Wiz said likely reflected response activity after it reported the campaign to GitHub. However, the researchers said Gheist remained ongoing and continued to evolve.

The campaign demonstrates how stolen GitHub tokens can turn legitimate automation features into a credential theft mechanism, while newer platform controls can disrupt some abuse without eliminating the underlying risk from compromised credentials.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Beyond the Inbox: How Threat Actors Abuse Microsoft Teams External Chat for Initial Access
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Summary

Arctic Wolf Labs has observed a recurring social engineering pattern in hundreds of cases where threat actors have used Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature for impersonation scams, or to deliver malicious files. A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same “IT Support (Internal)” display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains.

In this report, we’ll explore our findings, examine how attackers weaponize the external access / federation feature in Teams to reach employees, reveal the infrastructure identified through Arctic Wolf’s telemetry, and discuss the defensive measures organizations can take to disrupt this attack chain.

Key Findings

Arctic Wolf analyzed more than 400 incidents involving abuse of the Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for social engineering activity and initial access.

Threat actors repeatedly used highly consistent IT-support impersonation tactics, including IT-themed display names, friendly-sounding first names, and “(Internal)” labels designed to undermine external-user warnings in Teams.

We observed a measured infrastructure shift, from disposable .onmicrosoft[.]com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, with .top domains accounting for roughly half of observed paid-domain cases.

Arctic Wolf detects this activity at the ChatCreated stage, creating a window of opportunity to identify and disrupt attacks before a victim engages with the threat actor.

Context

Microsoft Teams ships with external access (federation) turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access. This is the feature attackers most frequently abuse. This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability.

How Threat Actors Establish Teams Identities

Threat actors commonly establish external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30 to 40 percent of the cases we analyzed involved default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains. This default domain requires no verification and can be provisioned within minutes, giving attackers a functioning Teams identity with minimal setup.

Arctic Wolf observed that, even when using this default domain, attackers engineer the tenant’s sender name to read as IT infrastructure. We have supplied a list of the default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant names observed in use across multiple customers in the Appendix at the end of this report [1].

Arctic Wolf assesses that threat actors typically select a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, or the words online, portal, or a random number, to obtain a free tenant name. In a smaller number of cases, Arctic Wolf observed threat actors using legitimate company names in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

How the Attack Unfolds

In a significant number of cases, customers reported that the malicious Teams contact was preceded or accompanied by “mail bombing”, the flooding of a victim’s inbox with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes. The email storm is intended to manufacture urgency and bury legitimate emails such as security alerts, with the Teams “IT support” message arriving moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

This reflects an abuse of trust: employees are generally trained to treat email with suspicion, but a message delivered from inside their Teams instance bypasses that learned caution.

Beyond email masquerading, Arctic Wolf identified a range of consistent naming techniques used by threat actors across customer alerts. The attacker’s Teams display name is central to the deception. Arctic Wolf observed the following impersonation display names most frequently, meaning the pattern occurs across multiple cases: [2]

Attackers append “(Internal)” to the display name so the recipient perceives the message as coming from an internal IT sender, even though Teams simultaneously labels the sender as External.

Reoccurring usage of friendly-sounding names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam , IT Support (Scott McGhee)”, or “IT Service Desk (Matthew)”. Here, adding a first name makes the Teams message appear to come from a real member of their organization’s Service Desk.

In several cases, attackers used region-specific naming conventions tailored to the target’s locale: for example, “Supporte TI,” the French/Spanish variant of “IT Support.”

We observed roughly 100+ emoji markers ( 🛡 shield, 🛠️/🔧 tools, ✅ check) used in attacker display names: e.g., “IT Support 🛡| Corporate IT Service 🛠 (Internal).” This may be evidence of the use of AI such as ChatGPT and AI-related automation to create content and identities in support of this campaign.

Most recently, we observed the attacker/external Teams user adding the target organization’s domain or company name in their own display name to make the message appear more legitimate.

We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation. Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br.

This aligns with Sophos’s reporting on the STAC4749 / Chaos ransomware campaign, which found that attackers have moved away from onmicrosoft[.]com throwaway tenants and toward IT-themed .top domains for payload staging and command-and-control (C2), as the low cost of .top registrations allows for convincing “update/ security/support” hostnames. Arctic Wolf also observed repeated use of other common TLDs, including .com.br and .com.vn in activity reported during July and August.

In a subset of these custom domains, attackers deliberately configured DNS records to redirect web requests to the legitimate Microsoft or victim organization site to appear authentic.

Attack Chain for Teams Chat Creation

Attackers target organizations where external access is enabled. Chat creation itself is only the entry point. Arctic Wolf assesses that, once trust is established, the attacker’s immediate goal in most cases is to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool.

We also frequently observed attackers using vishing (a direct voice call to the victim from within Teams) to secure RMM installation. In cases where attackers target multiple victims simultaneously, typically via automation, the initial contact begins with a Teams chat message instead of a call. The most commonly observed RMM tools used in relation to this scam were Quick Assist (QuickAssist.exe / msra.exe), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Of these, Quick Assist is the most frequently used. This may be because it is built into Windows, signed by Microsoft, requires no installation, and only requires the victim to read back a six-digit code. When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool (AnyDesk, Atera, ScreenConnect, or a second platform such as Level, installed via msiexec), which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant.

Arctic Wolf identified a consistent attack chain across successful exploitation cases and correlated it with chains previously documented by security vendors such as Microsoft and Zscaler:

Attackers commonly target multiple users within short windows of time (approximately five minutes) to increase the likelihood of success, most likely performed through automation. Once a victim engages, the attack chain reported by customers shows threat actors reaching payload execution in under 15 minutes. Arctic Wolf observed similar compression in its own data: several cases recorded concurrent credential-access detections (Kerberoasting, GoldenPAC-related) firing alongside the initial Teams alert, indicating the endpoint was already compromised by the time the chat alert was triaged.

In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft’s notes. Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.

How Teams Chat Abuse Works

Threat actors using external Teams chat as an initial-access vector is not new. The practice was first documented by Microsoft in the Black Basta (Storm-1811) campaign in mid-2024, which used the now-familiar chain of email bombing → external Teams “help desk” → Quick Assist → QakBot/DarkGate/Cobalt Strike → ransomware.

The technique was later observed in the Cactus campaign and in 3AM and Chaos. Earlier this year, Zscaler reported on the GoGRPC campaign, in which Teams vishing and Quick Assist were used to deploy the GoGRPC backdoor.

Example Attack Observed by Arctic Wolf

Arctic Wolf recently identified a potentially novel infection chain leveraging external Microsoft Teams chat messages, in which the threat actor posed as an IT helpdesk employee to initiate the attack. In the case we observed, the attacker instructed the user to run a PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file. The initial payload retrieval was performed via PowerShell, and both actions executed under the victim’s account with a parent process of explorer.exe, reminiscent of ClickFix, though not disguised as a CAPTCHA.

Next, the PowerShell command downloads an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, which bundles a PowerShell script and a ZIP archive (archive6.zip). Approximately 30 seconds after the MSI is launched by the user, the bundled PowerShell script (cleaner.ps1) is dropped into the users’ AppData folder (AppData\Local\PowershellCleaner\scripts) and executed. The script cleaner.ps1 contains a large array of hexadecimal characters, preceded by an IEX instruction to execute the joined and decoded array; the resulting plain code is a loader that reads a block of AES-encrypted data, decrypts it using hard-coded key/IV and computes its hash. If the hash matches a hard-coded value, the resulting PowerShell is executed via ScriptBlock.

Ultimately, this is an obfuscated decryption and execution stub to build and run an additional PowerShell payload. The purpose of this final payload is to extract the pythonw interpreter and implant (ss.py), both from the bundled archive6.zip. After sleeping for five seconds, the implant is executed via pythonw.exe.

The implant then starts another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects (filtering for both Category and Class) using the System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher PowerShell shortcut adsisearcher, formatting the attribute output as [sAMAccountName] – [description]. This information is then transmitted to C2 server endpoints that are randomly selected from a list of domains and URIs laid out in the implant’s code.

How Arctic Wolf Protects its Customers

From the newly created tenant, the attacker initiates a one-on-one chat, which avoids the visibility associated with group conversations. Microsoft records this first contact as a ChatCreated event, which Arctic Wolf assesses to be the primary detection opportunity for defenders. Our alerts most frequently fire exactly here, before the user has done anything.

Arctic Wolf combines multiple detection engines to identify suspicious external Teams chats. Drawing on observations from thousands of customer environments, Arctic Wolf maintains indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with these campaigns, including impersonation-focused display names such as IT Helpdesk and Helpdesk Support as well as attacker-controlled tenant and domain patterns.

Arctic Wolf’s behavioral engine also monitors Microsoft tenants that initiate conversations with multiple Arctic Wolf customers. When activity from a tenant, account, or domain appears anomalous, particularly when combined with other signals such as email bombing or suspicious follow-on activity, Arctic Wolf flags it for investigation.

Arctic Wolf also tracks top-level domains that threat actors commonly use to create tenants, host payloads, or support command-and-control infrastructure.

Beyond monitoring the initial Teams-based social engineering lure, Arctic Wolf maintains detections for the remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools that attackers frequently push during these engagements. Arctic Wolf alerts on the execution of RMM tools that are not sanctioned or expected within a given environment, since the unauthorized installation of legitimate remote access software is a common technique used to establish persistence once a victim has been convinced to grant access.

Arctic Wolf also correlates behavior over time, flagging cases where an RMM tool installation is followed by reconnaissance commands, such as enumerating users, groups, or network configuration, and prioritizing these for investigation.

Conclusion

External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability.

Arctic Wolf has been able to monitor and protect our customers from these attacks with proactive defenses. Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise.

The recurring patterns provide defenders with valuable opportunities to interrupt the attack chain. An unexpected chat from an external tenant, particularly one that follows an inbox flood or uses an IT-themed display name, should be treated as suspicious. Correlating ChatCreated events with endpoint, identity, email, domain, and remote-access telemetry can reveal the progression even when the initial interaction appears benign.

Defensive Countermeasures for Organizations

Most organizations have no legitimate need for open, any-tenant external chat. Per Microsoft’s guidance in Manage external meetings and chat with people and organizations using Microsoft identities, move from “allow all” to an allow-list of trusted organizations. Organizations can take the following proactive steps:

In Teams admin center → Users → External access, select “Allow only specific external domains” and add only the partner domains the organization actively collaborates with. Once an allow-list is configured, all other domains are blocked by default.

Block chat with unmanaged / Teams-consumer accounts, and disable the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users.

Block federation with trial-only tenants, as attackers commonly prefer free or trial tenants for their minimal setup requirements:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

Enable “Allow my security team to manage blocked domains” so the security team can push blocks (e.g., the .top indicators listed in this report) through the Microsoft Defender Tenant Allow/Block List → Teams domains tab.

Harden the remote-access path: block or restrict Quick Assist to authorized IT roles (or remove it where unused), and block or uninstall unsanctioned RMM tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Atera, Level, Splashtop) via Defender for Endpoint or application control. Alert on any RMM tool not deployed through the Arctic Wolf agent.

Because this attack vector relies on social engineering rather than technical exploitation, people and process controls are critical to closing the gap:

Out-of-band verification for all remote-access requests. Mandate a callback to the user’s registered number or an approval flow in a separate trusted app. An impersonator controlling the Teams channel can’t complete a verification that lives outside it.

Tell staff exactly how real IT reaches out (which channels, which domains, which named contacts), and that unsolicited external “IT support” is inherently suspicious (especially if it appears right after an inbox spam flood).

Train users to read the External tag and the real sender domain, and to never dismiss the Accept/Block, Safe Links, or first-contact warnings. Provide side-by-side examples of the organization’s real help desk communications versus an impersonator’s.

Conduct targeted training for personnel regarding the specific social engineering tactics used in this campaign. For those without the time to devote to creating security training resources from scratch, the Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Security Awareness and Training solution delivers easily digestible security lessons for employees, including regular phishing simulations and a “Report Phish” button.

Microsoft is also clearly taking this threat seriously too. They’ve now built end-user reporting for security directly into Teams, letting employees report a suspicious message or an external user with a couple of clicks.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief on Attacks Against Refrigeration Controllers
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Executive summary

CERT-FR’s October 13 update reports compromises of refrigeration controllers, naming Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC alongside Copeland/Dixell XWEB systems. The entry methods remain unconfirmed. CERT-FR warns that attacks are probably continuing and recommends removing public exposure, checking configurations, and securing remote access. Compromised operational technology (OT) can disrupt cooling, compromise stored products, and threaten cold-chain continuity.

Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. This work supported deployment of IPS signatures within 24 hours of the initial incident reports as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings across refrigeration vendors to assess the need for additional signatures.

Operational and business impact

Operational disruption. Unauthorized changes to setpoints, defrost schedules, or alarms can disrupt cooling across multiple units, spoil products, and delay detection.

Business and supply-chain impact. Inventory losses, interrupted sales, equipment damage, and emergency maintenance can cause financial and reputational harm. At scale, disruption could affect food availability and national resilience.

Security exposures to assess

Internet-exposed management interfaces. Publicly reachable controllers face greater risk of unauthorized access where authentication and access restrictions are inadequate.

Remote access without least privilege. Shared accounts, weak authentication, and excessive permissions increase the risk of unauthorized changes. Access across sites and weak segmentation can widen the impact.

Vulnerable or unsupported systems. Published research into Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWEB Pro controllers documented multiple vulnerabilities. Their exploitation in the reported attacks has not been confirmed.

Overlooked cellular connections. Supplied SIMs and vendor-managed 4G/5G routers may bypass network controls and escape inventories, monitoring, and risk assessments. Private APNs also need verified isolation between subscriber devices.

How Agentic AI Can Accelerate OT Attacks

Agentic AI could accelerate reconnaissance, analysis of disclosed vulnerabilities, and repeated exploitation attempts against reachable controllers. This may reduce the time and expertise needed to turn an exposed interface into operational disruption. At the time of writing, we have not identified public evidence of AI involvement in the refrigeration incidents.

Protection and recommendations

General recommendations

The following are general recommendations for reducing risk across connected refrigeration environments.

Reduce internet exposure. Remove unnecessary public access. Authenticate and authorize remote users before granting equipment access through a secure VPN or protected network, following CERT-FR guidance.

Secure maintenance access. Change default passwords. Use unique credentials, named accounts, MFA where supported, and least privilege, separating monitoring from configuration access where possible.

Maintain supported systems. Track firmware and support status, apply vendor updates, and replace unsupported equipment. Follow Danfoss security guidance and guidance for other deployed platforms.

Segment operational equipment. Allow only required traffic between refrigeration equipment, corporate IT, maintenance networks, and sites.

Monitor operating conditions. Alert on unexpected changes to temperatures, defrost schedules, alarms, and accounts. Consider independent temperature monitoring and verify safe operation after incidents.

Assess cellular access. Inventory SIMs and vendor-managed cellular links. Include them in risk assessments, verify access controls and logging, and validate private APN isolation and routing.

Cato protection

Our SASE platform supports authenticated remote access, least-privilege access policies, and network segmentation. SASE allows these controls and traffic inspection to be managed centrally across sites and remote maintenance connections routed through the platform. In a previous blog post, we discussed OT security recommendations and showed how the platform supports secure remote access, segmentation, and monitoring of device communications.

In another previous blog post, we discussed how Cato Autonomous Policies for FWaaS analyzes policy rules and their context to help identify misconfigurations and overly permissive access.

Our Researcher Agent helped us create a proof of concept for Danfoss controller vulnerabilities, supporting our mitigation work. This agent-assisted workflow helps accelerate vulnerability analysis and protection development while retaining researcher review.

IPS virtual patching provides network-based protection against applicable vulnerability exploitation. Coverage depends on the vulnerability, enabled controls, and traffic reaching the relevant inspection point.

In another blog post, we discussed how our Agentic Threat Prevention correlates suspicious host activity and applies inline controls to help interrupt attack progression, including lateral movement. This is relevant where a compromised system could provide a route toward operational equipment or other connected assets.

We have added IPS signatures for applicable, publicly disclosed Danfoss vulnerabilities as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings involving Danfoss and other refrigeration vendors. As new information becomes available, we will assess the need for additional IPS signatures and updates to our virtual patching coverage.
