What does the dark web look like?

The dark web often looks surprisingly ordinary—with familiar features like About Us sections, pricing pages, and even customer reviews. You’ll see, though, in the screenshots below, that a lot of sites are basic or outdated, often tricky to navigate.

Many of these sites still work like any other ecommerce website. Threat actors advertise, highlight their skills, and market themselves, their expertise, and their services just like any salesperson.

How does the dark web work?

Frankly, the dark web has earned a bad reputation—and unfairly so. At its core, the dark web isn’t inherently evil or mysterious. (Okay, it's a little mysterious.)

It’s simply a collection of websites that require a specific, anonymity-powered web browser to access. Usually, these sites use a .onion domain and are only accessed through the anonymous Tor Browser.

The dark web isn't all crime and chaos—detectives and journalists sometimes access the dark web to do research while maintaining their anonymity. You can play chess on the dark web. At one point in time, you could even navigate to a Tor website and watch a slideshow of cats and kittens submitted by other users.

The dark web isn't any one thing—it's shaped entirely by how people choose to use it.

How to safely access the dark web

Because there are so many different reasons that you might be interested in the dark web, it’s important to know how to access it safely. Here are some tips:

Use a dark web browser: Use the official Tor browser to access the dark web. This is the essential tool for "onion routing" that provides anonymity.

Use a VPN: While Tor provides encryption, using a high-quality virtual private network (VPN) before launching adds an extra layer of privacy by hiding the fact that you are even connecting to the Tor network from your internet service provider (ISP).

Never use personal information: Don’t log into any personal accounts—email, social media, or bank accounts—while using Tor because it immediately de-anonymizes you.

Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal your identity or install malware.

Know what’s legal: Accessing the dark web is completely legal in the US, but engaging in illegal activities (such as buying/selling drugs, weapons, or accessing child pornography) is a serious felony, regardless of anonymity.

Our journey into the dark web

We’re firm believers in the buddy system when it comes to doing scary things like journeying through the dark web. Don't worry, though— we’ve suited up, strapped on our protective gear, and done the risky part for you.

How did we suit up?

First, we booted up our virtual machine (VM) to add an extra layer of security while browsing. Then, we fired up our anonymous Tor Browser. Finally, we disabled JavaScript—a quick but important safeguard against websites that run malicious code.

With these precautions in place, we were ready to access the dark web. We began our journey by navigating to a few .onion directories to find some ~shady~ websites to peruse.

One of the first things we found? A Tor scam list, complete with "safe" browsing recommendations. How… thoughtful.

Who is using the dark web?

There are About Us pages to answer that question.

Chances are, you wouldn’t hire a plumber without doing some research. You’d want to make sure she’s got the experience and skills to leave your pipes in better shape than she found them. So why would anyone hire a hacker without seeing a well-written About Us page?

You might think this requirement would narrow the pool of hackers to choose from, because are hackers really spending their time writing About Us pages? Yes. Yes, they are.

You’ve got to hand it to them: These hackers did a great job at flexing their hacking skills while staying anonymous. It's not exactly LinkedIn, but the info they share gives these folks some credibility (in a strange way).

If you’ve never browsed the dark web before, you probably weren’t expecting to see several websites with About Us pages. It’s eye-opening to see these hackers flaunting their skills and competing with one another to earn new business.

One site was even gracious enough to list the team’s favorite well-known hackers:

It’s kind of sweet, in a weird sort of way.

The takeaway: Threat actors are just like any other entrepreneurs out to make a profit. The difference? They skip the red tape and regulations that everyone else has to follow. This leaves the door wide open for them to advertise whatever services they please—as long as they abide by the Hacker’s Code of Conduct. (More on that later.)

What’s on the dark web?

Product pages, packaged deals, and more.

Now that we know our threat actors, let’s investigate what they can do for us.

Like any good businessperson, hackers aren’t shy about broadcasting what they can do if the price is right. In fact, some are so business-savvy that they provide packages and tiered solutions:

Others simply prefer to put all their services out there for people to pick and choose from:

But then, we stumbled across two different websites that made us raise an eyebrow. Here’s the first site:

And here's the second site:

These two sites look eerily similar to each other except for one thing: on the latter site, the prices for each service are noticeably higher. That’s weird, wouldn’t you say?

The takeaway: Just like any other website where you can purchase products or services, threat actors also have tiered options, promotional packages, and detailed descriptions of their offerings.

One key difference that seems to be standard across dark web websites is that hackers request that their payments be made in cryptocurrencies. Why? Because it’s anonymous.

Our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, nicely sums up why cryptocurrencies are a hacker’s best friend:

"No other technology offers a bad actor the perfect crime: anonymous threats without borders, blackmail and extortion without a financial oversight or governing authority. [...] Unless the bad actors make any unintentional mistake, the inherent design of cryptocurrency makes for a perfect getaway car."

Dark web customer experience and reviews

Threat actors are actually quite concerned with creating a positive customer experience, with features like customer reviews and FAQ on many of the pages we visited.

The takeaway: Just like any other website selling goods and services, threat actors also want to show that they have happy customers and give potential customers all the info they need to make an informed purchase.

Bottom line: The dark web is a business

If a business owner feels she’s been wronged, there are courts for that. The same can be said for hackers. That’s right—threat actors have their very own court system, along with codes of conduct to follow to minimize the chances of landing there themselves.

What happens in “hacker’s court”? The same thing that happens in any other court: Plaintiffs and defendants get together to tell their respective stories in front of a jury before a ruling is made.

We can't stress this enough: Most bad actors today don’t just hack into websites and devices for the fun of it. These are professionals who become experts in their trade and master their skills to earn a paycheck.

They build websites to sell their services, cut their customers special deals, and ask for reviews from satisfied customers. If they’re wronged, they handle it in a civilized manner in hacker’s court. These are organized operations that function just like any other business.

Don’t be afraid of the dark (web)

We hope that this field trip to the dark web has been enlightening. It’s incredible to see just how many parallels exist between anyone with a “normal” day job and dark web threat actors. Many different careers, from marketing and sales to cybersecurity and infosec, have dark-mirror versions of themselves—hackers and scammers running the same playbooks in reverse—on the dark web.

If nothing else, we hope this blog will make you more vigilant against cyberattacks. Hackers are in it for the money. What could destroy your personal records or your business’s reputation is just another payday for a hacker. Think twice before clicking on an email from an unfamiliar sender. Keep your devices updated and install patches as soon as they become available.

Threats can seem overwhelming, but with our in-depth understanding of how threat actors think, we know what to look for. Huntress gives you fully managed endpoint detection and response (EDR), so you've got 24/7 support from security experts ready to respond to threats.

* Special thanks to our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, for his help with writing this blog.

FAQ

Is it legal to look at the dark web?

Yes, exploring the dark web is legal—as long as you aren’t breaking any laws. If you’re just browsing or doing legitimate research, accessing the dark web is fine. If you engage in any criminal act, you’ll be subject to prosecution.

What is the dark web actually used for?

The dark web is a mixed bag. Some people use it for both legitimate purposes, like preserving privacy and free speech, especially in restrictive countries, and, unfortunately, others for shady activities like selling stolen data or illegal goods.

How do I know if I’m on the dark web?

If you're using a specialized browser like Tor to access websites ending with .onion that aren't reachable through regular browsers or search engines, congrats (or maybe not)—you're on the dark web!

Can you be tracked on the dark web?

The dark web offers more anonymity, but it's not exactly an invisibility cloak. With sophisticated methods and one careless click, determined parties can still track your activities, so anonymity isn't guaranteed.

What is a crime on the dark web?

Crimes on the dark web include activities like selling illegal substances, hacking services, and trafficking stolen data. Basically, if it's illegal in the real world, it's illegal on the dark web too—no free passes.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Passkeys Raise the Bar. Here’s Where Attackers Can Still Get In.
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The goal is to steer them toward an authentication flow the attacker can exploit
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Passkeys are a major step forward in authentication, but protecting a credential is only part of protecting an account. Attackers can still target enrollment, recovery, compromised endpoints, alternative authentication flows, and social engineering.

Recent reporting highlights these gaps. This post examines them and shows how phishing-resistant authentication, identity protection, endpoint protection, security awareness training, and detection work together to close them. The goal is not to weaken the case for passkeys, but rather to show how organizations can make their protection count across the full account lifecycle.

What "passkey-themed phishing" actually means

Passkey-themed phishing is a social engineering attack that uses the passkey as bait, rather than defeating the passkey itself. Attackers impersonate a trusted source, typically IT staff, and urge employees to update or set up a passkey. The goal is to steer them toward an authentication flow the attacker can exploit.

Device code phishing shows how far this approach can reach. Huntress researchers tracked a campaign called EvilTokens that hit 344 organizations across five countries in about 16 days. Device code authentication is the same flow that lets you activate a streaming app on a smart TV by typing a code into your phone. Attackers start that process themselves, then send a convincing email that leads the victim to enter the code on a real Microsoft page. The victim completes MFA correctly, and the attacker walks away with a valid session. No password is stolen, no malware is required, and the attacker does not need to break passkey cryptography. The attacker abuses a legitimate device-code flow to obtain a valid session after the victim authorizes the attacker-controlled client. EvilTokens packaged the technique as a phishing-as-a-service kit with AI-generated lures tailored to each victim's role, which means the pattern can scale.

In another campaign, attackers impersonated IT staff and told employees to update their passkey or sign-in configuration. When Microsoft researchers dug into the incident, they found that the passkey served as the lure, while attackers pursued other authentication flows to get in. One documented attack sequence explicitly involved non-phishing-resistant MFA.

Both campaigns point to the same lesson: attackers look for any legitimate sign-in path that still works in their favor. The passkey may remain secure and untouched. A passkey-themed phishing attack does not mean attackers defeated passkey cryptography. Defenders need to identify the authentication method and policy that actually allowed access, because that is where the fix belongs.

That distinction is where identity threat detection and response (ITDR) becomes relevant. ITDR does not make the passkey itself stronger. It helps defenders identify and contain suspicious activity around a legitimate sign-in.

Enrollment and recovery are security boundaries

An attacker may not need to steal an existing passkey if they can register another credential or exploit a weaker recovery process. The original credential can remain protected while the attacker gets into the account through a separate door.

Closing that door starts with a clear answer to one question: what proof does your organization require before someone adds an authenticator, replaces a lost key, or resets MFA? Those actions deserve strong verification and monitoring.

A compromised endpoint can undermine authentication

SpecterOps' research demonstrates techniques that manipulate Windows WebAuthn interactions, including browser hooks that capture authentication responses or alter challenges. These attacks have specific prerequisites, including local execution or access to the authentication process. That makes them a different class of threat from an ordinary phishing website.

This is why endpoint protection remains necessary after a passkey rollout. Malicious software can target the environment handling authentication without extracting the private key. Protecting the endpoint that handles authentication starts with ensuring that every device signing in to company resources is managed and protected by an active and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent.

Employees can play a real part in endpoint defense too. This includes things like:

Install updates promptly when your computer or browser asks. Prompt updates close the doors attackers use to get a foothold.

Add browser extensions and software only from your company's approved list.

Lock your screen whenever you step away.

Tell IT when your browser behaves strangely, such as unexpected redirects, new toolbars, or sign-in pages that look slightly off.

Where the passkey lives matters

Passkeys come in two storage models, and each carries a different set of dependencies.

Synced passkeys live in a cloud-backed account, such as a platform keychain or a password manager, and follow the user across their devices. That convenience means the account that stores, synchronizes, and recovers the passkey becomes part of your security perimeter.

Device-bound passkeys live on a single piece of hardware, such as a security key, and stay there. They reduce the dependency on sync accounts, but they require more from your team in the form of key distribution, spare-key management, and replacement processes.

Whichever model you choose for a given group of users, evaluate it together with its enrollment process, recovery process, and endpoint protections. Those surrounding controls determine how much protection the passkey delivers in practice. A practical deployment may use device-bound keys for high-risk roles and synced passkeys for the broader workforce, with managed accounts and strong recovery behind them.

Security awareness training must keep pace

Passkey adoption works best when paired with safe credential handling, strong privilege hygiene, and training on current social engineering tactics. Employees need to be able to recognize fake help-desk calls, urgent enrollment requests, and messages asking them to authorize unfamiliar devices.

Effective training gives people concrete habits:

Use a trusted enrollment route. Open approved account settings directly instead of following unsolicited setup links.

Verify unexpected support requests. Contact IT through an established channel before changing authentication or recovery settings.

Know what you are approving. Stop when an unexpected prompt asks for a device code, biometric verification, or security-key touch.

Protect keys and recovery options. Keep hardware keys under your control, never disclose their PINs, and follow approved storage, spare-key, and recovery procedures.

Report fast, with no blame attached. Make it easy to report suspicious requests, mistaken approvals, and lost keys.

A good security awareness training solution pairs what attackers are doing right now with how people actually learn. That could include things like simulated phishing scenarios that build the instinct to pause in a safe setting before a real phishing email arrives.

Hardware keys remain among the strongest MFA options

Hardware security keys used in FIDO2/WebAuthn mode are among the strongest MFA options available. CISA identifies phishing-resistant MFA as the gold standard. The protocol matters: using a hardware token to generate a one-time code does not provide the same phishing resistance as FIDO authentication.

That distinction makes FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys an excellent choice, and should encourage adoption alongside secure handling, recovery controls, and endpoint protection.

Keep watching after authentication succeeds

Passkeys strengthen the authentication event, but they do not tell defenders whether the session, device, account changes, or follow-on activity are legitimate. ITDR extends protection beyond sign-in by connecting signals such as unusual access, newly registered authentication methods, suspicious cloud activity, and abnormal mailbox or file activity. When those signals indicate compromise, responders can revoke sessions, remove unauthorized authenticators, and investigate persistence.

A successful sign-in is one event in a longer story. An attack may look benign at each layer until defenders ask whether the sign-in makes sense for that person. Is this the device they normally use? Does this authentication flow fit their role and workflow? Defenders can connect those questions to newly registered authentication methods, cloud reconnaissance, and abnormal file or mailbox activity.

For confirmed compromise, effective containment includes revoking sessions and removing unauthorized authentication methods. After cleanup, search for persistence, including inbox rules, OAuth app grants, and forwarding addresses.

A practical passkey deployment checklist

Before rollout, teams need clear answers to these five questions:

How will users enroll a passkey through a trusted route?

What proof is required to recover an account or replace a lost key?

How are the endpoints that handle authentication managed and monitored?

How will employees recognize and report passkey-themed social engineering?

How will the team detect and contain suspicious activity after a successful sign-in?

The Lesson

Passkeys significantly improve account security, but they work best as one layer in a complete identity strategy. Attackers can abuse a legitimate authentication flow to obtain valid sessions while passwords and cryptography stay intact.

Phishing-resistant authentication works best alongside protected enrollment and recovery, identity security, endpoint security, security awareness training, and monitoring that can spot what happens after a successful sign-in. Deploy strong authentication, teach people how to use it safely, and maintain visibility into the activity around it. Protecting the full account lifecycle makes that improvement count.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC) Attacks: How to Stop Them
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Our survey of more than 500 US IT professionals found that 36% of organizations experienced a BEC attack in the past 12 months, making it the third-most-reported type of...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Business email compromise (BEC) is a phishing scam where threat actors impersonate a trusted source to convince others to give them sensitive information or take specific action.

Among the threats targeting businesses of all sizes today, business email compromise is a particularly growing concern, and for good reason.

Business email compromise (BEC) is a type of cybercrime where threat actors seek to manipulate or compromise email accounts within an organization to commit fraudulent activities like wire fraud and credential theft. In simple terms, a BEC attack uses email impersonation to commit fraud, usually to redirect a payment or steal login credentials.

These attacks result in some $55 billion in losses worldwide, and that number is expected to rise. Our survey of more than 500 US IT professionals found that 36% of organizations experienced a BEC attack in the past 12 months, making it the third-most-reported type of cybercrime (behind malware infections and phishing). The primary suspected motivation is financial gain, cited by 27% of respondents, which is exactly what BEC attacks are engineered to deliver.

Let’s dive into the world of business email compromise, explore what a BEC attack is, how it works, and learn practical tips for defending against BEC attacks.

Table of contents

How do business email compromise attacks work?

Warning signs of a BEC attack

Types of business email compromise scams

Real-world BEC attack examples

How to prevent business email compromise

How Huntress stops business email compromise

How do business email compromise attacks work?

BEC attacks work by impersonating a trusted source through email to trick employees or organizations into sending money or sensitive information.

Threat actors create these emails, often with help from generative AI tools that quickly and efficiently make the content look legitimate and mimic the tone and writing style of people you trust. This makes it hard for recipients to tell the difference between legitimate emails and scams.

The AI piece is only getting harder to ignore. Our Cybercrime Report found that 38% of IT professionals consider AI-powered social engineering the biggest unanticipated risk to their organization, and 42% believe AI-powered attacks will be the biggest game-changer in cybercrime over the next five years. BEC is a natural fit for AI-driven tactics, since the attacks rely on impersonation and manufactured trust.

BEC attacks typically follow a structured path, from reconnaissance to impersonation and fraud:

Research and reconnaissance: Attackers gather information about their targets, like names, roles, and relationships within the organization.

Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks: These attacks help attackers gather information about your organization, login credentials, and other sensitive data. Attackers place themselves between you and whatever you’re trying to access, like a web page or service, letting them monitor your activity before moving on to the next step.

Email compromise or account takeover: Attackers gain access and essentially take over an email account. They often do this through phishing email scams, social engineering, or exploiting software vulnerabilities.

Impersonation: The attacker impersonates a trusted person at the organization, like a CEO, CFO, or vendor, using a spoofed or compromised email account.

Deception: Threat actors send convincing emails to trick employees into transferring money, sharing sensitive information, or downloading malicious attachments.

BEC attacks rely heavily on social engineering techniques to identify potential targets, executives, or trusted contacts to mimic or hijack their communications. The attack emails often look legitimate at first glance, and without closely scanning the address, contact information, and other details, recipients may not recognize the emails as suspicious.

As a result, these attacks are difficult to detect or prevent with traditional security tools or spam filtering. The goal is to trick employees into giving sensitive information or transferring money freely without making them doubt the legitimacy of the request.

Looking to brush up on your security savvy? Explore the Huntress Cybersecurity Glossary for all things cyber safety.

Warning signs of a BEC attack

Preventing BEC attacks from hitting your inbox is possible, but even the most well-guarded business email system may see one or two BEC attacks slip through the cracks. You can avoid falling victim to these attacks by knowing what to watch for.

Here are the warning signs most BEC attacks have in common:

Rampant typos: If the email misspells company names and contacts or contains tons of errors that your clients, customers, and team members wouldn’t make, it’s likely a scam.

Suspicious requests: BEC attacks often make requests that aren’t common or sound suspicious, like asking you to communicate on a third-party app like WhatsApp, share your login credentials, or make gift card purchases.

Forced urgency: Threat actors often use phrases like “quick” or “urgent” to imply that the email is important and needs a response immediately.

Generic terms and names: BEC attacks often use generic terms or titles rather than specific names or terms unique to your business.

Fake personal email addresses: Scammers may also pretend to be a business executive or manager by using a fake personal email address that mimics a real address.

Review any unfamiliar or unexpected emails closely. If you see anything that looks suspicious or doesn’t feel legitimate, don’t reply.

“BEC attacks rely on humans to perform actions on behalf of attackers,” says Truman Kain, Offensive Security Researcher at Huntress. “Employees need to understand that even emails from legitimate internal addresses can be sent by attackers. Your inbox is not a safe place.”Instead of replying to the message, speak with the person the email supposedly came from directly by sending a new email through their company email address or talking to them in person or over the phone.

Types of business email compromise attacks

BEC attacks can take many forms, and as technology improves, new scams and types of attack vectors will become more popular. But some common tactics include:

Invoice scams: Attackers compromise a supplier's or vendor's email account and send altered invoices or payment instructions to customers. The altered details then send payments to the attacker's account—and the legit vendor is left empty-handed.

CEO fraud: Attackers impersonate a high-level executive and ask for urgent wire transfers or sensitive data from employees. Employees are tricked into making payments or even purchasing gift cards, believing it's a legitimate request from their boss.

Payroll diversion: There are two types of payroll diversion scams. In the first, attackers pose as HR personnel and request changes to an employee's direct deposit information. In the second, attackers pose as the actual employee requesting that their own direct deposit information be updated. As a result, the employee's salary is redirected to the attacker's account.

Voice cloning: Attackers use AI tools to mimic the sound and tone of a business leader’s voice on a phone call or in a virtual meeting to phish for information or get someone to take a specific action.

Email spoofing: Scammers create email addresses similar enough to legitimate addresses to appear real at a glance. They often use these addresses to request money or sensitive information.

Gift card scams: Attackers send emails or text messages to employees requesting that they buy digital gift cards and send them to the attacker-controlled email address or phone number.

Account compromise: Attackers send emails notifying employees that their accounts have been compromised and request that they do things like reset passwords through a phishing link to prevent further suspicious activity on the account.

Attorney impersonation: Attackers pretend to be a lawyer or attorney requesting information from an employee who may not know to question the legitimacy of the request.

Data theft: Attackers pose as new employees or vendors requesting access to sensitive information about executives in the company.

Any of these tactics can combine the use of AI tools to create deepfakes that make requests seem more legitimate. Encourage your team to use their best judgment and ask them to verify any questionable email or phone call by reaching out to the sender through company channels before sending any sensitive information.

Real-world BEC attack examples

BEC attacks might seem theoretical if you’ve never experienced one. But they’ve done a lot of damage in the past. These high-profile BEC attacks cost businesses millions in the last 10 years:

Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta: An attacker targeted the organization by pretending to be a construction company’s chief financial officer. The attack resulted in $3.6 million in damages.

Facebook and Google: Scammers impersonated a legitimate hardware provider and sent emails to Facebook and Google requesting payment for products. The scam cost Facebook and Google more than $100 million.

Toyota Boshoku Corporation: Attackers requested funds transfers without the organization realizing the requests were fake. It cost Toyota more than $37 million.

Grand Rapids Public Schools: Attackers impersonated the district’s health insurance provider and emailed the school administration requesting that they change wiring information for upcoming payments, sending the insurance payments into the scammers’ accounts. It cost the district $2.8 million.

For more cases and what each one teaches, see our full list of business email compromise examples. Even a single attack could end up costing businesses a lot of money—and it’s hard to get that money back once the scammers take possession of it.

How to prevent business email compromise

Because BEC attacks are generally human-centric, protection and prevention methods must also be human-centric. Check out these tips to help you keep your employees and your company’s information safe from bad actors:

Host security awareness training sessions: Conducting regular security awareness training can help educate employees about the dangers of BEC attacks, how to recognize them, and how to avoid becoming victims.

Use multi-factor authentication (MFA): Implementing MFA adds an extra layer of security to email accounts, making it more challenging for attackers to gain access.

Verify payment changes out of band: Confirm any new or changed banking details with a phone call to a known number, never a number listed in the email.

Implement managed identity threat detection and response (ITDR): ITDR solutions proactively monitor for and detect anomalies, including looking for behavioral indicators of BEC, like suspicious inbox rules or login attempts from unusual locations.

Invest in a secure payment system: Rather than sending invoices through email, upgrade your payment collections system to a dedicated service. Make sure the system can authenticate payments and only accept payments through that portal.

BEC attack tactics are constantly evolving, but by being proactive with BEC security awareness training sessions, businesses can better protect their sensitive information well into the future.

“Regular simulated phishing exercises maintain a higher security awareness baseline for employees versus those without exposure to the exercises,” says Kain. “Additionally, phishing simulations and educational episodes highlight the newest and most topical threats that employees are likely to face, for example fake CAPTCHA attacks or deepfakes.”

While the BEC threat is real, it's not insurmountable. By understanding attackers' tactics and implementing proactive measures, businesses can be better prepared to face today’s email and identity-based attacks.

How Huntress stops business email compromise

Business email compromise threats will only become more common as more attackers take advantage of weak points in companies’ data security efforts. By training your team and taking the necessary precautions, you can keep your data safe well into the future.

Huntress Managed ITDR detects the behaviors behind BEC, like suspicious inbox rules, logins from unusual locations, and session hijacking, and our 24/7 SOC responds before attackers can move money. Pair it with Huntress Security Awareness Training to help employees spot the lures that get through. See how Huntress stops BEC.

Don't face BEC threats alone. Huntress has your back.

FAQs on BEC

What is the difference between BEC and phishing?

Phishing is a broad tactic; fake messages sent to trick people into clicking a link, opening an attachment, or handing over credentials. BEC is a targeted type of phishing. Instead of casting a wide net, attackers research a specific organization, then impersonate or take over a trusted account, like a CEO, vendor, or HR contact, to request money or sensitive data. Many BEC emails contain no links or malware at all, which is why they slip past email filters built to catch traditional phishing.

How is AI changing business email compromise attacks?

AI makes BEC attacks faster to launch and harder to spot. Generative AI tools can write polished, error-free emails that copy the tone and writing style of the person being impersonated, so the typos that used to give scams away are disappearing. Attackers also use voice cloning and deepfakes to back up email requests with a phone call or video meeting. That’s why verifying requests through a separate, trusted channel matters more than ever.

Can MFA stop business email compromise?

MFA makes account takeover much harder, but it can’t stop BEC on its own. Attackers use adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits to steal session tokens after a user completes MFA, and many BEC scams don’t need account access at all because they rely on spoofed addresses. For stronger protection, combine phishing-resistant MFA (like passkeys or FIDO2 security keys) with ITDR and security awareness training.

What should you do after a BEC attack?

Treat it like a live intrusion, not just a bad email. The attacker may still be in the account, so contain first and investigate second.

Cut off access. Revoke all active sessions and refresh tokens, then reset the password. A password reset alone won’t remove an attacker who already holds a valid session token.

Remove what they left behind. Attackers rarely just read email. Look for the new inbox rules that hide, delete, or forward messages along with external forwarding addresses, MFA devices registered to someone unknown, and OAuth app grants nobody approved. Remove anything you can’t explain.

Find out how they got in. Review sign-in logs for unusual locations, VPN or hosting provider IPs, and logins that happened at “impossible travel” speeds. Look for a phishing email or AiTM sign-in page around the time of first access.

Figure out what they touched. Check sent items, deleted items, and mailbox audit logs for emails sent as the user, files accessed, and conversations they inserted themselves into, especially anything involving invoices or payment details.

Check whether they spread to other accounts. Compromised mailboxes are often used to phish coworkers and partners, so review accounts that got messages from the compromised user.

Escalate the money side right away. If any payment went out, call your bank immediately to request a recall, and file a report with the FBI’s IC3. Speed matters more here than anywhere else.

Warn anyone who might act on a fake request. Tell finance, vendors, and customers who were in contact with the account to verify any recent payment changes by phone.

Steps 1 and 2 matter most. If you skip them, the attacker can walk right back in while you’re still investigating.

Record non-GAAP operating margin, reflecting focused execution and operating efficiency

Broad-based high demand for Cisco technology with double-digit growth across all geographies and customer markets

Raised FY27 revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance

Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today reported first quarter results for the period ended October 24, 2026. Cisco reported first quarter revenue of $18.5 billion, net income on a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis of $4.6 billion or $1.14 per share, and non-GAAP net income of $5.6 billion or $1.40 per share.

"In Q1, we delivered the strongest revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share growth rates for Cisco in over 15 years," said Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era. We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle, and we're confident in our ability to continue capturing the multi-billion-dollar opportunity it represents for Cisco."

"Q1 FY27 was another record quarter for Cisco, with revenue, non-GAAP operating margin, and non-GAAP EPS all exceeding the high end of our guidance ranges. The strength of our Q1 performance gives us confidence to raise our revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance for FY27," said Mark Patterson, CFO of Cisco. "As our business continues to scale, we are unlocking significant operating leverage which is enabling us to grow earnings much faster than revenue. Looking ahead, we remain focused on delivering durable growth and driving continued capital returns."

Cisco Declares Quarterly Dividend

Cisco has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.42 per common share to be paid on January 20, 2027, to all stockholders of record as of the close of business on January 4, 2027. Future dividends will be subject to Board approval.

Financial Summary

All comparative percentages are on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted.

Q1 FY 2027 Highlights

Revenue -- Total revenue was $18.5 billion, up 24%, with product revenue up 32% and services revenue up 1%.

Revenue by geographic segment was: Americas up 28%, EMEA up 18%, and APJC up 21%. Product revenue performance reflected growth in Networking up 43%, Security up 7%, Collaboration up 8%, and Observability up 2%.

Gross Margin -- On a GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 63.7%, 61.8%, and 70.9%, respectively, as compared with 65.5%, 64.5%, and 68.4%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Total gross margins by geographic segment were: 64.1% for the Americas, 68.9% for EMEA and 66.5% for APJC.

On a non-GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 65.6%, 63.7%, and 72.9%, respectively, as compared with 68.1%, 67.2%, and 70.7%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Operating Expenses -- On a GAAP basis, operating expenses were $6.2 billion, down 3% year over year, and were 33.4% of revenue. Non-GAAP operating expenses were $5.1 billion, up 2%, and were 27.8% of revenue.

Operating Income -- GAAP operating income was $5.6 billion, up 66%, with GAAP operating margin of 30.2%. Non-GAAP operating income was $7.0 billion, up 37%, with non-GAAP operating margin at 37.8%.

Provision for Income Taxes -- The GAAP tax provision rate was 17.2%. The non-GAAP tax provision rate was 18.5%.

Net Income and EPS -- On a GAAP basis, net income was $4.6 billion, an increase of 59%, and EPS was $1.14, an increase of 58%. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $5.6 billion, an increase of 39%, and EPS was $1.40, an increase of 40%.

Cash Flow from Operating Activities -- $4.4 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, an increase of 36% compared with $3.2 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Balance Sheet and Other Financial Highlights

Cash and Cash Equivalents and Investments -- $15.8 billion at the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with $15.9 billion at the end of fiscal 2026.

Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) -- $46.2 billion, up 8% in total. Product RPO was up 7% and services RPO was up 9%.

Deferred Revenue -- $30.1 billion, up 7% in total, with deferred product revenue up 6% and deferred services revenue up 9%.

Capital Allocation -- In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, we returned $3.7 billion to stockholders through share buybacks and dividends. Business & Industry News.title: Silverfort Named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026
Business & Industry News.context: Our acquisition of Fabrix Security, which was announced in April 2026, adds an AI decisioning engine and an Identity Knowledge Graph that analyzes access activity,...
Business & Industry News.full_text:
Identity Security was built around the front door. Verify who is logging in, grant access, and trust policy to hold from there. That worked when only people logged in. It stops working once service accounts and AI agents authenticate alongside them.

We built Silverfort around that problem. We believe it is why we have been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment (doc# US54116526, November 2026).

What changed in Identity Security

An AI agent can use one identity or session to make hundreds of tool calls: pulling records, calling APIs, moving data. In the environments we work in, how many agents exist, and what each one is allowed to do, is often an open question.

The IDC MarketScape describes the shift in the report’s market definition:

“The breach does not occur when access is granted. It occurs when control fails to follow what happens next.”

What does the IDC MarketScape evaluate?

IDC MarketScape positions vendors into four categories: Participants, Contenders, Major Players, and Leaders. For this study, IDC analyst Emmanuel Figueroa evaluated 18 identity security vendors, including Silverfort.

The report defines the category, the five capability areas IDC assessed, and how each vendor was evaluated. The five areas are:

Identity Coverage

Continuous Risk Scoring

Automated Enforcement

Bidirectional Interoperability

Identity Observability and Delegation Governance

What does enforcement at every access request look like?

Silverfort’s Runtime Access Protection (RAP) operates from within the identity infrastructure, where it sees each authentication. When someone or something requests access, the identity system forwards the request to Silverfort. Silverfort assesses the risk, applies inline controls such as MFA or a block if needed, and returns a verdict. The identity system then grants or denies access. It covers workforce and privileged users, third parties, non-human identities, and it needs no proxies, app changes, or changes to user workflows.

In Active Directory, that means visibility into Kerberos, NTLM, and LDAP authentications in real time, without rewrites or architectural changes.

We also extended our runtime protection to include AI agents. Agents are protected not at the authentication layer, but in the tool call process—each tool call is checked against policy before it runs.

What does IDC MarketScape say about Silverfort?

On how Silverfort works, IDC MarketScape notes:

“Silverfort enforces at the authentication layer, so domain controllers and identity providers become policy points, and legacy protocols such as NTLM, Kerberos, LDAP, and RADIUS receive step-up MFA, access blocks, and service-account fencing without endpoint agents or application changes. In IDC’s view, that is a practical answer to a long-standing hole in the identity stack.”

IDC MarketScape also comments on enforcement:

“Silverfort names automated enforcement as its primary strength, and IDC agrees: it acts before access is granted, not after someone reads a log.”

The IDC MarketScape profile also covers when buyers should consider Silverfort. You can read that in the vendor excerpt.

Where we go from here

We started a few years ago by bringing MFA to systems that had always been out of reach. Since then, we’ve evolved into a complete Identity Security Platform that secures every identity across every environment. Our acquisition of Fabrix Security, which was announced in April 2026, adds an AI decisioning engine and an Identity Knowledge Graph that analyzes access activity, organizational context, and intent—laying the foundation for our autonomous Runtime Identity Security Platform.

Four questions we think are worth asking

These are our questions, not IDC’s. They reflect how we think about Identity Security.

Does it enforce, or only alert? Enforcement decides at the moment of access. An alert tells you what already happened.

Does it cover Active Directory and legacy protocols? These are where attackers look, and they are often the hardest systems to change.

Does it treat AI agents as identities? An AI agent can make hundreds of tool calls during a single session, all under the same identity. Each request—not just the initial sign-in—should be evaluated against policy.

Does it re-evaluate risk on every access request? Risk can change between one request and the next. The decision should change with it.

Thank you

Thank you to the customers, partners, and Silverfort team members who made this possible.

Next steps

Read the Silverfort vendor excerpt for the IDC MarketScape

See a real AI attack, then see it stopped. Book a session in our AI Attack Lab.

FAQ

What is an IDC MarketScape?

The IDC MarketScape is a vendor assessment model for a technology market. IDC’s own description of the methodology appears under the graphic at the top of this post.

What is augmented identity security?

It is the category name IDC uses in this IDC MarketScape. IDC’s definition is in the full report. In our view, it means Identity Security that keeps enforcing after the login, not only at it.

What is Runtime Access Protection?

Runtime Access Protection (RAP) is Silverfort’s patented technology. It operates from within the identity infrastructure, sees each authentication, and enforces a decision at the moment access is requested.

Which identities does Silverfort protect?

Workforce users, privileged users, third parties, non-human and machine identities, and AI agents, across on-premises, hybrid, and cloud environments.

What is the AI Attack Lab?

It is a session with a Silverfort Identity Security specialist, about 30 minutes, that shows a real AI attack and how inline identity controls can stop it.

TOKYO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Trend Micro Incorporated (TSE: 4704) today reported a 9% year-over-year increase in consolidated net sales for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. Enterprise investments begin to show results

Business & Industry News.full_text:
CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment.

Identity has become a critical attack surface. Adversaries exploit valid credentials to move laterally, escalate privileges, and operate undetected. Human, non-human, and AI agent identities continue to multiply across organizations, both expanding the attack surface and introducing new security challenges. AI agents in particular can autonomously access applications, invoke tools, and take action at machine speed, fundamentally changing how organizations must approach identity security.

Traditional identity security, built around static access decisions and periodic checks, can no longer keep pace. Organizations need continuous visibility into identity risk and the ability to enforce access decisions in real time.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader validates our approach to Continuous Identity, which brings together identity visibility, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. With innovations like the recent CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider, we're extending our approach to secure AI agents with verifiable identities and tightly scoped, just-in-time access.

Identity Security for the Modern Enterprise

CrowdStrike capabilities demonstrate the value of Continuous Identity, from unified visibility and real-time risk intelligence to dynamic enforcement across the enterprise:

Unified endpoint and identity visibility: Identity attacks do not stay in one domain, and neither does our view of them. The CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor sees local and bypass authentication, network telemetry decrypts NTLM and SMB exchanges, and the identity graph updates in real time. By correlating endpoint and identity signals, CrowdStrike helps security teams identify suspicious behavior across the attack path and respond with greater context.

Rapid deployment: The Falcon platform brings identity and endpoint security together through one console and one sensor, which establishes identity visibility and coverage in hours to days. Policy templates, simulation, and audit modes support staged rollouts, which helps organizations operationalize identity security while minimizing disruption.

Real-time identity risk intelligence: CrowdStrike’s unified risk score updates in under a minute, includes blast radius, and feeds every downstream enforcement control with reevaluation after authentication and midsession intervention. These capabilities help security teams understand identity risk in context, prioritize threats, and make enforcement decisions. By connecting identity signals with security context from across the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike helps turn visibility into action.

Enforcement that keeps up with the session: CrowdStrike enforces zero standing privileges with auto-approved just-in-time elevation, bidirectional enforcement, post-authentication risk reevaluation, and mid-session intervention. This is Continuous Identity in practice: Access is continuously evaluated as risk changes, and privileges are adjusted or revoked when conditions warrant.

Standards participation: CrowdStrike leads working groups on CAEP, Shared Signals, RISC, and AuthZEN. These initiatives support interoperability and the exchange of identity risk signals across systems, helping organizations extend continuous identity security throughout their environments.

Together, these capabilities bring Continuous Identity to life, connecting visibility, risk intelligence, and real-time enforcement to help organizations stop identity-driven attacks.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider

CrowdStrike's approach to Continuous Identity goes beyond point-in-time authentication. By unifying identity posture management, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the Falcon platform, organizations can continuously assess identity risk, reduce standing privileges, and dynamically adjust or revoke access as risk changes.

As AI agents operate autonomously across enterprise environments, this approach is even more critical. CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

The Future of Identity is Continuous

Identity security can no longer rely on point-in-time decisions. As human, non-human, and AI agent identities expand, organizations need continuous visibility into risk and the ability to enforce access in real time.

CrowdStrike is redefining identity security by moving beyond traditional approaches:

Static access becomes real-time control.

Fragmented tools become a unified platform.

Implicit trust becomes continuous, risk-based enforcement.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape reinforces our vision for Continuous Identity and our commitment to securing every identity and stopping identity-driven attacks.

Read the IDC MarketScape excerpt to explore the research.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Augmented Identity Security?

Augmented Identity Security is an operating model that shifts identity management from static, periodic authentication to continuous, real-time risk evaluation. By fusing endpoint, directory, cloud, and runtime telemetry, augmented identity platforms continuously inspect session behavior, identify anomalous privilege escalation, and dynamically adjust or revoke access across human, machine, and AI agent identities.

How does the Falcon sensor simplify identity security rollouts?

Unlike legacy tools requiring dedicated domain controllers or network proxy infrastructure, Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security delivers immediate identity visibility and threat prevention through the existing single Falcon agent, which establishes coverage in hours to days.

How does CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider protect AI agent identities?

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

Business & Industry News.full_text:
Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates

Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains.

The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it.

In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability.

Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see.

“Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund. “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking. “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.”

Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031,[1] Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it.

Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD., a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: “The depth of Finite State’s binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what’s in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable.”Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.”

Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category.

By continuously generating SBOMs, VEX, and signed compliance packages, Finite State enables connected device companies across industries such as medical devices and automotive to meet evolving regulations, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and deliver continuous compliance at speed.

Business & Industry News.context: The window between a vulnerability going public and being exploited has shrunk from years to weeks
Business & Industry News.full_text:
In October, two critical PHP vulnerabilities went public before a patch was ready. PHP runs beneath a large share of the web, often inside software that bundles it without saying so, so updating the applications on top of it changed nothing. Hundreds of thousands of internet-facing systems were exposed, and many had never been watched as risks.

This is the new normal. The window between a vulnerability going public and being exploited has shrunk from years to weeks. Detect, patch, and respond assumes you have time to react, but once an attacker is in, the damage is done. Protection has to be in place before the first attempt, across every reachable system, including the ones nobody treated as a risk. Security has to shift from stopping attacks to removing the opportunity for them.

That shift is what Forrester’s evaluation measures — and where Check Point was recognized as a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Enterprise Firewall Solutions, Q4 2026.

Why This Recognition Matters To Us

That placement rests on more than a strong product. Check Point tied for the highest score in the current-offering category among the vendors evaluated, and we also received above average customer feedback.

We are honored. But the recognition matters most for what we believe it reflects: network security that prevents, in any environment, with no gaps for attackers to find.

What That Looks Like in Practice

We stop attacks before they land. Live threat intelligence acts in runtime, against both human- and AI-driven attacks, so an attempt is blocked rather than investigated after the fact

Every environment is protected the same way. One set of policies covers your data center, cloud, branch, and edge, managed from a single console, with nothing left uncovered in between

Your team moves faster. Agents turn business intent into automation across workflows, usability, and policy management. Forrester cited our “solid innovation with its extensive use of AI for security”

Pricing stays flexible, transparent, and scalable. It grows as your needs do — our Firewall-as-a-Subscription offering delivers scalable protection without a large upfront investment

Our Customers Said it First

The part we are proudest of came from you. Customers told Forrester they appreciate the level of detail in our product logs and praise the support they receive for routine requests and during security incidents.

Forrester’s own take points the same way: organizations with advanced AI use cases or complex firewall management needs should consider Check Point.

If that is your environment, AI moving in, more places to protect than ever, this report was written for you.

AI is reshaping security. We are transforming with it, and keeping you protected through the shift. See how we earned our place, and what it means for the way you defend your network.

Business & Industry News.full_text:
ARMONK, N.Y. and REDMOND, Wash. – November 10, 2026 – IBM (NYSE: IBM) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) today announced Imagine Enterprise, an agentic platform designed to help enterprises build, run, and govern AI agents that help people execute industry-specific processes. IBM Consulting and Microsoft have combined their technologies and expertise with forward-deployed engineering support for qualifying engagements to help enterprises accelerate AI deployment.

Imagine Enterprise aims to help organizations—especially in regulated industries—combine human expertise with AI agents and connect them to unique enterprise data and daily processes. The platform is built to help organizations govern AI agents with controls, observability, and AI-compliance support designed to help secure industry-specific AI deployment.

IBM Consulting brings AI transformation expertise and a fleet of more than 6,000 AI agents and assets built on IBM Consulting Advantage, the company’s AI-powered delivery platform. Microsoft provides the AI, data, cloud, and security foundation that is designed to help the agents operate securely across the enterprise, while forward-deployed engineers from both companies can help customers move from experimentation to production.

Instead of organizations having to start from scratch, replace the platforms they already depend on, or spend months assembling the pieces themselves, Imagine Enterprise is designed around three simple advantages:

Instant Expertise: More than 6,000 AI agents and assets Starting with pre-built AI agents, assets, and deep industry expertise from day one. Organizations can begin with capabilities already built for their industry and adapt them to the unique needs of their business.

Fits the Enterprise: A platform that adapts Imagine Enterprise is designed to connect with an organization’s existing data, processes, systems, and technology environment. Enterprises can start where they are, build on what they already have, and scale over time, with enterprise security, identity, AI governance, and control built into the experience.

Intelligence Multiplier: Puts the knowledge of the business behind people and AI agents Imagine Enterprise brings IBM Consulting’s hands-on experience building and running more than 6,000 AI agents together with the Microsoft technologies to connect enterprise knowledge, data, and context across the organization. People and agents can operate with richer enterprise knowledge and context behind them, helping put what they already know to work across people and agents.

Supporting these advantages, Microsoft and GitHub technologies including Microsoft Foundry, GitHub Copilot, and Microsoft Copilot Studio help coordinate AI agents and enterprise systems, while Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft 365 infrastructure, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Defender, and Microsoft Azure provide the data, identity, AI governance, security, and cloud foundation. IBM Consulting Advantage’s Process Studio, Context Studio, and Advantage Core help organizations design, deploy, and govern tailored AI agents.

From Emerging Technology to Business Opportunity

SEI, a leading global provider of financial technology, operations, and asset management services within the financial services industry, is looking to advance its enterprise transformation by exploring emerging and agentic technologies with IBM Consulting, with the support of Microsoft, and is leveraging other technologies from IBM Consulting and Microsoft to help improve how the company operates and enhance the experiences it delivers to employees and clients, supporting SEI’s commitment to sustainable growth.

“AI is evolving quickly, and our focus at SEI is on applying it with intention in ways that strengthen trust, enhance human decision-making, and create meaningful value across our business,” said Sneha Shah, Chief AI Strategist and Head of SEI Next. “Our work with IBM Consulting and Microsoft is helping us explore how emerging capabilities could support critical processes and be responsibly scaled over time, with the goal to create better experiences for our employees and clients. By combining emerging technology with SEI’s deep industry and operational expertise, we can move faster, scale more effectively, and create new opportunities for growth.”

“Clients are no longer looking for AI that simply helps people do the same work a little faster. They want to build an agentic business,” said Mohamad Ali, Senior Vice President and Head of IBM Consulting. “Microsoft and IBM are helping organizations bring human expertise and digital labor together in a way that can scale across the enterprise, to turn AI from a productivity aid into a real competitive advantage.” “Enterprise AI will be won by organizations that can turn their data, industry expertise, and AI into action,” said Rodrigo Kede Lima, President, Microsoft Frontier Company. “Together, Microsoft and IBM Consulting are bringing the best of our technology and expertise, to help customers move from AI ambition to business impact faster and with confidence.”

Imagine Enterprise’s industry-specific frameworks initially include financial services, insurance, and retail, and are designed to establish a repeatable blueprint for potential additional industries such as manufacturing, energy, public sector, mobility and more in the future.

Imagine Enterprise is available to clients by engaging IBM Consulting to deploy and operate the platform on the client’s behalf or co-innovating with IBM Consulting on enterprise-scale implementations. Self-management options are also available.

To learn more, visit: https://www.ibm.com/consulting/imagine-enterprise, or read the blog here.

Thousands of governments and corporate entities in critical infrastructure areas such as financial services, telecommunications, and healthcare rely on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform and Red Hat OpenShift to affect their digital transformations quickly, efficiently, and securely. IBM’s breakthrough innovations in AI, quantum computing, industry-specific cloud solutions, and consulting deliver open and flexible options to clients. Microsoft enables digital transformation for the era of an intelligent cloud and an intelligent edge. Its mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. Business & Industry News.title: Snyk Named a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Agentic Development Security Tools, Q4 2026
Business & Industry News.context: AI makes it cheap to chain several of those minor issues into a critical exploit path, so the backlog now functions as an attack surface rather than deferred cleanup
Business & Industry News.full_text:
We're proud to share that Snyk has been named a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Agentic Development Security Tools, Q4 2026. Snyk received the highest score in the Strategy category, along with the highest scores possible in these criteria:

Strategy: Vision, Roadmap, and Partner Ecosystem

Current offering: AI dynamic testing, AI coding guardrails, autonomous proprietary code remediation, and developer experience

Software development changed who does the work

For two decades, software development moved at a human pace where developers wrote code, peers reviewed it, and security teams tested it on a schedule. AI coding assistants compressed that cycle, and coding agents are now changing who does the work. Forrester frames the shift: "AI coding agents are changing how software is built, moving from developer assistants to active participants in development workflows."

Adoption has moved well past the pilot stage. In the Stack Overflow 2026 Developer Survey, 66% of developers who use AI work in coding agents, and 73% of those using AI coding assistants or agents use them daily. As a result, the developer's role is shifting from writing every line to orchestrating the agents that write it.

Each of those agents brings its own supply chain; it installs packages, connects to MCP servers, loads skills, and invokes tools the security team may never have reviewed. Because it can also run commands, edit files, and access sensitive data, its actions need to be governed as much as its code needs to be tested. In our view, security models built to scan code after it is written were not designed to govern the systems creating it.

Attackers are moving at machine speed too

In 2025, Anthropic's threat intelligence team disrupted an espionage campaign in which AI carried out an estimated 80 to 90% of tactical operations, with humans in a supervisory role. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report puts average eCrime breakout time, from initial access to lateral movement, at 29 minutes, with the fastest observed case at 27 seconds.

Those timelines change how teams should think about their vulnerability backlog. Pull request queues, ticket triage, and quarterly pentests were designed around attackers who moved slower than the fix. Most backlogs consist of low- and medium-severity findings, deprioritized one at a time. AI makes it cheap to chain several of those minor issues into a critical exploit path, so the backlog now functions as an attack surface rather than deferred cleanup.

The pressure is also building inside the codebase; Snyk’s product data shows new critical and high-severity issues detected grew 10x in the past year, and roughly eight new issues are introduced for every one remediated. When risk is created faster than it is fixed, the answer is a different operating model: security agents that fix continuously, guardrails inside the agent workflow, and adversarial testing that proves controls hold

AI applications are reaching production faster than governance

Teams are shipping AI applications and agents into production faster than governance processes can keep pace with. Many security leaders are still working to answer basic questions about their AI estate:

Which models, agents, and MCP servers are running, and what data can they reach?

Which skills were pulled from public registries, and who approved them?

Could you audit what a given agent did last week?

This is shadow AI at enterprise scale. Its risks, such as prompt injection, excessive agency, and data leakage, are behavioral: they live in an agent’s decisions as well as its code, which is why code scanning alone can’t surface them. Model choice is part of that risk. In Snyk’s 2026 State of Agentic AI Adoption, Volume III, the lowest-capability models averaged 501 on decision override, a 0 to 1,000 score, while the most capable models averaged 45, a gap of more than 10x. Roughly a third of the scored model references in US environments fall in that lowest group. Governing them starts with a live inventory of the AI estate, including which models are in play, and policies that apply before an agent acts.

Why this evaluation matters

In our view, Forrester's evaluation reflects these shifts in operating model, and it assessed agentic development security across the full span of AI-driven development: the code agents produce, the agents and the components they pull in, and the AI applications teams build. Forrester asks buyers to weigh three considerations:

Visibility and governance of agentic development

Verification of AI-generated code and AI applications

AI risk reduction at agentic speed

Teams now need coverage across all three, on one platform that shares context between them, and that is the standard we have been building toward.

A decade of conviction, pointed at where software is created now

Snyk has operated on a core belief for more than a decade: security belongs where software is created. We believe agentic development moves that point of creation inside the agent workflow, and that is where the Snyk AI Security Platform is built to operate. Forrester’s report states that "Snyk articulates a farsighted vision to secure AI-written code, the agents that run it, and the applications they build, while advancing secure-at-inception development and governance."

On capabilities, the report states that "Snyk brings security into developer and AI coding agent workflows through autofix and coding guardrails that secure AI- and human-generated code and block risky agent actions." It also notes that Snyk's "strong AI dynamic testing uncovers business logic flaws and vulnerability chains and validates findings with working exploits."

How Evo by Snyk secures each layer of AI-driven development

Last year, Snyk expanded the Snyk AI Security Platform with Evo by Snyk, a suite of agent-native security solutions that secure, protect, and govern AI-driven development across three loops: the code artifact, the AI workforce, and the AI applications teams build. A validation layer tests all three.

Evo Agentic AppSec: Secure the code artifact. AI security agents that find, fix, and block vulnerabilities at the speed agents write code, with every result verified independently. This includes Snyk Secrets for blocking leaked credentials.

Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS): Protect the AI workforce. Governs what AI coding agents use, what they do, and what they generate, from the MCP servers and skills they pull in to the code they write. This includes Snyk Studio for real-time guidance in AI coding workflows.

Evo AI-SPM: Govern every AI app you build. Discovers and assesses risk of the models, agents, skills, and MCP servers in your software, generates a live AI-BOM, and turns AI policy into enforceable controls.

Evo Continuous Offensive Security (COS): Validate every loop. Continuously tests applications and AI agents, leveraging Agent Red Teaming, and returns validated proof of what an attacker could actually exploit, so no loop grades its own work.

As AI takes on more of the work of building software, we believe its output needs a separate, deterministic layer to verify it. That is why Snyk pairs frontier AI reasoning with our deterministic engines and ten years of security intelligence, so organizations can adopt AI at full speed and stay accountable for what they ship.

What this means for teams building with AI agents

Forrester's take: "Snyk is a good fit for enterprises that want to accelerate agentic development while embedding security directly into agent workflows." For teams evaluating this market, three questions help separate tools built for agentic development from tools adapted to it:

Governance: Can you see and control what your agents use, what they do, and what they generate before it ships?

Remediation: Is your fix rate keeping pace with your rate of new risk, across new code and the existing backlog?

Proof: What independent evidence shows your controls hold against a real attacker?

We are grateful to our customers, partners, and the developer community, whose feedback shapes the platform every day. We will keep investing inside the agent loop, where software is now created. Our mission remains the same: unleash AI innovators, securely.

Curious how Snyk secures code, agents, and AI applications in your environment? Talk to an expert to see the platform in action.

Secure AI adoption at scale with Evo

LevelBlue has been named Editor's Choice for Managed Detection and Response (MDR) in Cyber Defense Magazine's Top InfoSec Innovators awards for 2026. The award was announced on October 20, 2026, during CyberDefenseCon 2026 in Orlando, Florida.

It's a recognition we're especially proud of. MDR sits at the heart of what LevelBlue does every day: helping organizations detect threats faster, respond with confidence, and stay one step ahead of attackers.

Now in its 14th year, Cyber Defense Magazine's awards program honors the cybersecurity companies doing the most to get ahead of tomorrow's threats. Ackerman Jr. of DataTribe.
