Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures.

The advisory, issued by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the FBI and other federal agencies, said that US authorities “are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally.”

The warning follows a number of recent incidents in which hackers accessed internet-connected refrigeration systems and have attempted to tamper with temperatures.

Such attacks can have had huge real-world impacts, including ruining food and medical supplies.

On October 11, 2026, it was reported that several supermarket chains in France and other countries in Europe were forced to destroy food stock after hackers compromised systems administered by refrigeration systems provider Danfoss. The attackers reportedly programmed systems to reach temperatures as high as 50 °C (122°F).

A similar incident occurred on November 1, with supermarkets in at least nine European countries reportedly impacted.

Most recently, a cyber-attack targeting refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld saw cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F).

The US advisory, published on November 5, warned operators and owners of refrigeration systems in the US to be vigilant for similar attacks.

This is particularly in sectors such as healthcare, chemical, food and agriculture, and transportation, which widely use these systems for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management and energy optimization.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the authoring agencies wrote.

They noted that hackers can use techniques like authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection and weak configurations to gain remote access to these internet-exposed systems.

Urgent Action Required to Protect Refrigeration Systems

The authoring agencies set out a number of immediate actions security teams should take to mitigate risks to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, based on the recent threats observed. These include:

Ensure control system devices, particularly controller panels are not exposed to the internet

Should remote access be necessary, protect these systems using a firewall or edge device and update them to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities

Isolate operational technology devices from business networks

Change default passwords and implement strong authentication policies, including phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA)

Establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire and replace legacy devices that are end of life

Limit access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes

Maintain backup systems offsite and offline and regularly test them

CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity Chris Butera, commented: “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target. We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps.”

Refrigeration Systems Taken Offline Following Europe Incidents

Data published by Censys on November 5 revealed there has been a 53% reduction in internet-exposed refrigeration controllers across the Danfoss StoreView and Copeland/Dixell XWEB products that were compromised during the supermarket incidents on October 11 and November 2, respectively.

The big fall in exposure is consistent with provider action or owners disconnecting devices, Censys noted.

So far, the incidents have not been attributed to a particular threat actor.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks. News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool. “The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email. For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year. The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent. Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained. According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said. Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem. “Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while. “Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.” Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them. Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems. Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over. “Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed. The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time. In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company. Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials. Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials. In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work." These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page. Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5). Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords. "We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary. "We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely." Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30. "Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems." In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed. Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base. It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations. Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews. It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Residential Proxy Traffic Traced to White House Network
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network 236 times over a 30-day period, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses.

Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4. Residential proxies are services that sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from each device's network.

The addresses sit in AS2650, the block of internet addresses (autonomous system) registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Layer3 spotted the exits, recorded on 26 of the 30 days between October 5 and November 3, in its newly launched Residential Proxy Observatory.

Layer3 cross-checked the addresses against public lookup pages from proxy detection services Spur and Synthient, which independently identified them as residential proxy exits.

Evening Pattern Suggests a Single Device

Layer3 said anyone could route traffic out through the same addresses by signing up to a public residential proxy service and paying a few dollars. It found the activity by chance, while requesting ordinary global rotating access through these services.

About half of the activity fell between 5pm and midnight Eastern Time, with almost none in the early morning.

Layer3 said that pattern suggested a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device was infected with a proxy software development kit (SDK).

"Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them," the firm wrote.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk said: “The most recent activity was recorded in the evening of November 4; hopefully, it stops soon!”

Read more on residential proxy networks: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet

No Compromise Reported, but Proxy SDKs Carry Risk

Layer3 did not report any compromise of White House systems. It said it has backed up the raw logs of the activity and has shared their finfings with a US federal agency.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow access to internal networks and lateral movement, which is how past botnets have spread.

Layer3 cited Synthient research showing the Kimwolf botnet reached at least two million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed Android Debug Bridge (ADB) service, through residential proxy networks.

If an SDK on the White House network had the same kind of flaw, Layer3 said, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

Infosecurity has contacted the White House for comment.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023. Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began. The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters. Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia. Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors. According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information. Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government. Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023. The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials. On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000. "Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: The Race Against the 3-Day Clock: How Rapid7 Helps Meet BOD 26-04 Compliance
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Introduction to BOD 26-04

On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached.

The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers.

This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all.

What did CISA actually change?

BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context.

Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't.

The four variables to BOD 26-04

BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA):

Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network?

KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog?

Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation?

Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)?

Asset exposure is the highest-leverage variable. If you remove an asset from public reach, you flip the exposure variable from Yes to No, and the required timeline relaxes accordingly. Rapid7 Labs data underscores why exposure dominates: half of the vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild in Q1 2026 were zero-click, network-facing issues requiring no authentication, and by Q2 2026 nearly two-thirds required no user interaction at all. Attackers are going straight at exposed, unauthenticated surfaces.

CISA's new remediation tiers

The four variables combine into a graduated timeline (CISA BOD 26-04, Appendix A, Table 1). The tiers, simplified:

Tier

Timeline

Core criteria

1 (Critical)

3 days + forensic triage

On KEV and Total control

2 (High)

3 days (no triage)

Publicly exposed + Automatable + Total control, not yet on KEV

3 (Accelerated)

14 days

KEV-listed without Total control; or exposed + Partial control

4 (Standard)

60 days

Internal, automatable, Partial control

5 (Deferred)

Fix on next system upgrade

Internal + not KEV + not automatable + Partial control

Note that these timelines are dynamic. If a dormant vulnerability is added to the KEV, its clock can compress from 60 days to 3 overnight. Conversely, if you isolate an exposed asset, its clock relaxes. CISA explicitly counts isolation, mitigation, and uninstalling the vulnerable software as valid remediation; as such, a compensating control is a legitimate, compliant way to buy time for a safe patch.

The forensic triage mandate

This is the first of the requirements to have no precedent in earlier directives. For Tier 1 vulnerabilities (KEV + Total control), you must not only patch within three days, but run a concurrent forensic investigation to determine whether the asset is already compromised. Why? When an attacker exploits an exposed edge device, they establish persistence within hours; thus, patching three days later closes the door with the intruder already inside.

CISA's implementation guidance lays out a six-step, 72-hour protocol:

Phase

Window

What happens

1. Scoping

0–2 hrs

Identify in-scope devices; activate response team; open out-of-band comms

2. Preserve evidence

2–24 hrs

Capture volatile data (RAM, cache, registries) before any change

3. Patch & stabilize

2–24 hrs

Apply patches only after evidence is collected

4. Contain

6–24 hrs

Isolate infrastructure without tipping off the attacker

5. Triage analysis

24–48 hrs

Hunt IOCs; look for lateral movement and data staging

6. Escalation decision

48–72 hrs

Formal report; if compromised, report to CISA and pivot to full IR

Note the built-in tension between Step 2 and Step 3: patching reboots systems and overwrites the exact volatile memory that proves or disproves a compromise. You have to capture forensic evidence before you patch — at speed, across every affected endpoint. Doing that manually inside 72 hours is not always realistic.

Who CISA's BOD 26-04 applies to

BOD 26-04 is compulsory for all Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It excludes national security systems and DoD/Intelligence Community systems.

It reaches the private sector indirectly, but firmly. Agencies must review contracts and push compliance onto supply-chain partners. For FedRAMP and cloud offerings, agencies stay responsible for their hosted systems' compliance, which forces CSPs handling federal data to adopt the same 3-day triage standard. If you're a contractor or CSP touching federal data, treat this as your standard too.

Mapping Rapid7 to the directive

Meeting a 3-day clock with mandatory forensics is impossible through manual process. Here's how the Rapid7 Command Platform maps to each requirement.

Variable 1 (Exposure) → Surface Command

You can't calculate a timeline if you don't know what's exposed. Surface Command combines Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management (CAASM) with External Attack Surface Management (EASM), correlating continuous external scanning against an internal asset inventory ingested from your existing tools. The result is a single view of your true external attack surface — including the shadow IT attackers can see but your team can't. When it flags an exposed asset carrying a KEV-listed CVE, you can sever exposure to flip Variable 1 and de-escalate the timeline while you test the patch.

Variables 2 & 3 (KEV + Automation) → InsightVM and Active Risk

InsightVM tracks the KEV Catalog natively in its Threat Feed Dashboard, continuously updating which assets carry actively targeted vulnerabilities. Its Active Risk score — a 0–1,000 scale — moves beyond static CVSS by ingesting exploit intelligence from Metasploit, ExploitDB, the CISA KEV list, and Rapid7 Labs research. That mirrors the directive's own logic: a CVSS 7.5 bug with a weaponized Metasploit module will outrank a CVSS 9.8 bug with no known exploit — exactly the prioritization BOD 26-04 demands.

The NVD scoring gap → Exposure Command AI CVSS

The National Vulnerability Database can't keep pace with disclosure volume, leaving many CVEs unscored — a blind spot when a zero-day drops and you need a timeline immediately. Exposure Command fills it with an AI model trained on historical NVD data. On its own the model returns the correct severity classification 76% of the time; combined with Active Risk, that rises to 87%, with any miss never more than one classification off. Exposure Command also enriches every asset with business criticality and threat telemetry, and its Remediation Hub surfaces the fixes that cut the most risk.

The forensic mandate → Velociraptor

Velociraptor — the open-source DFIR project Rapid7 acquired in April 2021 — is built for exactly the scale and speed the triage mandate requires. It maps directly to the protocol: agents capture volatile memory and running-process data across thousands of endpoints simultaneously (Step 2), and analysts use Velociraptor Query Language to hunt CISA-provided IOCs enterprise-wide in real time, returning only relevant artifacts instead of pulling full disk images over the network (Step 5). That lets you satisfy the evidentiary requirement without delaying the Step 3 patch.

From severity to dollars

BOD 26-04 shares a core idea with modern risk management: technical severity isn't business impact. A high CVSS score doesn't answer the board's question of "how likely is this to cost us?"

The FAIR framework closes that gap by expressing risk as expected annual loss: Annualized Loss Expectancy = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude

BOD 26-04 is effectively a mechanism for pinning down Loss Event Frequency: by isolating vulnerabilities that are exploited (KEV), reachable (exposure), and scalable (automation), it identifies the ones statistically most likely to become a loss event. Feed Active Risk into the frequency side and FAIR into the cost side, and you can brief leadership in the language of capital, not CVE IDs.

Rapid7 case studies in the wild

Recent discoveries from Rapid7 Intelligence show the top tier in action:

Vulnerability

Impact

Why it's Tier 1

Rapid7 action

Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040 + CVE-2026-63520)

Chained, the two flaws yield unauthenticated RCE via JWT bypass, running commands as the SharePoint service account

Internet-facing + total control (via the chain) + added to KEV after in-the-wild exploitation

Authenticated checks shipped to InsightVM/Exposure Command customers; Active Risk escalated to trigger triage

Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0300)

Unauthenticated buffer overflow in the User-ID Auth Portal; arbitrary code execution as root (CVSSv4 9.3)

Firewalls are exposed by definition; total impact; added to KEV May 6, 2026

Threat Feed integrated KEV status instantly; Velociraptor captured volatile RAM ahead of the patch

N-able N-central (CVE-2026-18577 + CVE-2026-18556)

Authentication bypass enabling full takeover of remote-management endpoints

High-value management assets; total control; added to KEV August 2026

Checks shipped via content release; Velociraptor hunted endpoint artifacts to satisfy triage

What's next for federal agencies and contractors?

If you're an FCEB agency or a contractor or CSP handling federal data, the following three moves matter most:

Get exposure right. Everything downstream depends on knowing what's publicly reachable. Establish continuous external-plus-internal asset visibility now.

Wire KEV into prioritization, not a spreadsheet. The clock starts the moment CISA updates the catalog. Ingestion has to be automated and continuous.

Pre-stage forensics. Decide today how you'll capture volatile evidence across endpoints inside 72 hours. If that's a manual runbook, it will fail under a real Tier 1 event.

CISA BOD 26-04's bottom line

BOD 26-04 retires "patch everything" in favor of operational precision: remediate the actively exploited, exposed, high-impact vulnerabilities in 72 hours, prove whether you've already been breached, and defer the rest. Meeting it takes continuous asset discovery, live threat intelligence, context-aware prioritization, and forensics at scale — which is precisely the shape of the Rapid7 Platform. For federal agencies it's a mandate; for everyone else, it's the clearest blueprint yet for risk-based vulnerability management.

Sources: CISA BOD 26-04 and its implementation guidance; 2026 Verizon DBIR; Rapid7 2026 Global Threat Landscape Report and Q1/Q2 2026 threat data; Rapid7 product documentation for InsightVM, Active Risk, Surface Command, Exposure Command, and Velociraptor.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: FedRAMP Authorization Is the Easy Part: How to Stay Authorized with Qualys Policy Audit
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Key Takeaways

FedRAMP authorization isn’t the finish line. Providers are expected to keep monitoring their security posture and give federal agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions.

CISA’s BOD 26-04, issued on June 10, 2026, moves federal vulnerability management toward risk-based prioritization instead of a single fixed deadline for every finding.

FedRAMP has said the legacy monthly scan is no longer sufficient. Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026.

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey, 85% of executives said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years.

Qualys Policy Audit supports a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate, and report workflow. Audit Fix automates remediation, and control mapping lets one validated control count across multiple frameworks.

Ask anyone who has taken a cloud service through the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) what the process feels like, and you’ll hear roughly the same story. Months of control documentation, a System Security Plan running hundreds of pages, a Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment that turns up gaps nobody saw coming, and finally an Authority to Operate (ATO) letter. What that story usually leaves out is that the letter isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work starts.

Once a Cloud Service Offering is authorized, FedRAMP expects the provider to continue monitoring its security posture and keep feeding federal agencies the information they need to make ongoing, risk-based decisions. On June 10, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) raised that bar again with Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, and FedRAMP moved fast to bring its own rules with it.

The takeaway is fairly simple. Getting authorized was never the hard part. Proving, day after day, that your controls are still doing what they’re supposed to do is the hard part, and it’s the problem policy audit automation exists to solve.

Getting FedRAMP authorized is step one. Learn how to stay authorized.

Watch on Demand

Why Point-in-Time Compliance Stopped Working

FedRAMP used to run on a predictable cadence. Assess, authorize, submit monthly scans, repeat. That model has been cracking for a while now, and three things are driving it.

Vulnerability doesn’t just mean a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry anymore. Misconfigurations and control drift are squarely in scope now, so a clean scan can still be hiding a compliance failure.

Environments move faster than assessment cycles do. Cloud-native infrastructure can drift a dozen times a week, while monitoring reports still tend to go out monthly or quarterly.

Regulators have stopped accepting “we’ll catch it at the next audit.” Federal risk management is moving away from calendar-based reviews and toward real-time, exposure-based decisions.

CISA BOD 26-04, in Plain Terms

BOD 26-04, issued by CISA in June 2026, moved federal vulnerability expectations toward continuous, risk-based validation instead of a single fixed deadline applied to every finding. FedRAMP responded within days, confirming that the legacy monthly scan most Rev5 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) still lean on for their compliance evidence isn’t going to hold up anymore, and setting December 7, 2026, as the date its new Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules become mandatory for certification. For compliance and audit teams, the practical read is simple. The evidence you hand to an assessor has to reflect what’s true right now, not what was true at the last scan.

The Pain Points Teams Keep Naming

Talk to FedRAMP compliance teams, and the same challenges come up again and again:

Finding control gaps before an assessor does, instead of during the assessment window

Keeping configurations from drifting after they were compliant on day one

Prioritizing remediation when continuous assessment produces a continuous stream of findings

Providing continuous visibility instead of handing over a report generated the week before an audit

Producing audit-ready evidence on demand instead of assembling it after the fact

Cutting duplicate effort across overlapping frameworks, since most FedRAMP teams are also carrying National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and increasingly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) on the same infrastructure

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey of 1,802 executives across 63 territories, 85% said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years, and nearly 90% said the breadth of their compliance responsibilities has expanded over that same period. That pressure adds cost and strains the teams that have to prove compliance. Misconfigurations make it worse: Qualys analysis of more than 1 billion misconfiguration findings shows access control failures account for 38% of exposures, and organizations take an average of 14 months to fix these basic gaps.

None of this is a documentation problem. It’s an automation problem that’s been wearing a documentation costume.

How Policy Audit Solves the Problem

This is where a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate report workflow stops being a slide in a deck and starts being how the work actually gets done.

On the assessment side, instead of a monthly scan, Qualys Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline, mapping each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result across every system in scope. That’s the difference between documenting a control on paper and being able to prove it’s still operating the way it was the day you got your ATO.

Qualys lays this out as five practical steps rather than a single feature:

Connect findings to the control context. Connect raw findings to the control and framework context instead of handing teams a pile of technical output to interpret on their own.

Prioritize what impacts audit outcomes. This is where the volume problem gets solved. Research behind the approach found that fewer than 1% of vulnerabilities in a typical environment pose the highest risk or genuinely need immediate action to move audit outcomes, so results get filtered by control criticality, asset scope, internet-facing devices, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, and risk signals like MITRE ATT&CK mappings, not just counted.

Automate remediation. Remediation is where the old workflow falls apart. Flag a finding, file a ticket, wait, hope someone remembers to re-scan. That process was never fast, and BOD 26-04’s tighter windows make it untenable. Audit Fix closes the loop instead, automating the fix itself and applying it consistently across assets rather than leaving it to a ticket queue.

Map controls across frameworks. A control validated once, whether that’s for FedRAMP, System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2, ISO 27001, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or something else, counts toward every other framework it maps to as well, so teams stop re-proving the same control for every audit that comes around.

Shift to continuous audit readiness. Audit outcomes should reflect the current state of the environment, not a snapshot from whenever someone last pulled a report. That’s the same point CISA and FedRAMP are making. For a closer look at each step, read 5 Steps to Turn Compliance Checks into Audit Outcomes.

Qualys Policy Audit doesn’t replace governance, training, or personnel security. Those stay organizational, and a configuration scanner can’t assess them. On the technical side, it assesses your systems against NIST 800-53 controls in families such as:

Configuration management (CM): settings checked against baselines, with drift flagged

System and information integrity (SI): integrity protections and file changes

Audit and accountability (AU): logging and audit settings

Risk assessment (RA): gaps ranked by risk, not just counted

Assessment, authorization, and monitoring (CA): continuous monitoring of control status

That’s not a coincidence. It’s the reason this category of tooling exists in the first place.

The Takeaway

FedRAMP compliance isn’t a project with an end date anymore. It’s an ongoing discipline, and the rules keep tightening. Teams that still treat authorization as the finish line keep getting caught off guard at reassessment. The teams staying ahead of directives like BOD 26-04, rather than scrambling to react to them, are the ones who’ve built assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and reporting into how they run compliance day-to-day, not just how they prepare for an audit.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch our on-demand webinar, “FedRAMP Authorization and What It Now Takes to Keep It.” It features Kaleb Knobel, Senior Security Analyst and Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Anu Kapil, Director of Product Management. They share how Policy Audit helps organizations continuously assess, prioritize, remediate, and report on FedRAMP readiness, plus what FedRAMP Moderate and High teams should be doing right now.

See what FedRAMP Moderate and High teams should be doing right now.

Watch on Demand

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Why isn’t FedRAMP authorization the finish line?

After authorization, FedRAMP expects providers to keep monitoring their security posture and give agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions. Proving that controls still work, day after day, is the harder part.

What is CISA BOD 26-04?

It’s a Binding Operational Directive that CISA issued on June 10, 2026. It prioritizes vulnerability remediation by risk factors such as public exposure, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) status, automatability, and technical impact, instead of applying one fixed deadline to every finding.

How did FedRAMP respond to BOD 26-04?

Within days, FedRAMP said the legacy monthly scanning that most Rev5 services rely on is insufficient. It set December 7, 2026, as the date its new VDR and VER rules become mandatory for certification. Under these rules, providers must evaluate whether each vulnerability is reachable from the internet and likely to be exploited, fix KEVs within BOD 26-04 timelines, and keep responding to vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis.

How does Qualys Policy Audit support FedRAMP compliance?

Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline. It maps each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result so that teams can prioritize, remediate, and report on gaps between audits.

Does Policy Audit replace governance or training?

No. Governance, training, and personnel security remain organizational responsibilities. Policy Audit focuses on technical controls.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: AI Outside Your Pipelines: Orca Extends AI AppGen Security to Base44’s Compliance API
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
For years, software reached production through checkpoints security controlled: a ticket, a code review, a CI gate and a security sign-off.

AI app builders skip all of them. An HR coordinator describes an app in plain English and can publish it within the hour. 52% of organizations already build custom applications with AI. The opportunity is huge, and so is the need to secure it without slowing anyone down.

Base44 is where much of that building happens, no coding required. Base44 passed $100M in annual recurring revenue by early March 2026 and $200M ARR in August. JH Kelly builds department apps in about a week with a 4-person data team, and teams can go from an idea to a live app in a single day.

Every AI-generated app has the same parts: the builder, the site it runs on, the database, the login and, more and more often, an AI agent. Most stacks spread those parts across 4 or 5 vendors. Base44 puts all of them in one workspace. With its new Compliance API, it also gives enterprise admins one place to govern them: who can open an app, who can read its data and who its agents can talk to.

Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one. Today, Orca is extending AI AppGen Security to Base44. It joins Vercel and Claude in the same risk model and alert queue you already use for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

You can’t block your way out of AI outside your pipelines. You secure it through the platform’s control plane, then rank its risk against everything else you run.

Base44 built the controls. Orca keeps drift in check.

A single Base44 app now leaves a trail in three places: its settings live in Base44, its code can sync to GitHub, and the data it touches sits in your cloud. Each place has its own security view, and none of them shows the whole app. Security teams end up asking three tools one question: can this app put us at risk?

Base44’s enterprise controls are the foundation: SSO enforcement, SCIM, audit logs, IP allowlists, a Security Center that scans app code, and now a Compliance API that opens workspace settings to the rest of the security stack. The next question for security teams is whether those controls stay on as builders publish new apps.

Across AI app builders as a whole, drift is common for security controls. Escape’s passive scan of 5,600+ public vibe-coded apps found 2,000+ vulnerabilities, 400+ exposed secrets and 175 instances of exposed PII.

Take two apps from the same well-governed workspace:

App A is a sales deal-tracking dashboard. It’s restricted to the workspace, each rep sees only their own records, and every admin uses MFA.

App B is an HR onboarding portal published last week. Its builder switched it to public for a vendor demo and never switched it back, so its Employees table is now readable without login.

From the outside, both are just URLs. Only the workspace configuration, now readable through Base44’s Compliance API, shows that App B drifted from policy.

The question isn’t “is anything misconfigured?”

It’s “which of these apps can actually create risk?”

Introducing the Orca Base44 connector

Orca’s connector is built on Base44’s new Compliance API, which gives enterprise admins a read-only view of how a workspace is set up. There’s nothing to install, and nothing to add to the builder’s workflow. The Compliance API is available to Base44 Enterprise customers. A workspace admin creates an API key with the Compliance API permissions and adds it to Orca’s Base44 connector.

Discover. Orca inventories apps, data schemas, backend functions, secret names, API keys, integrations, custom domains and AI agents, plus members if the admin allows it. It ties each app to the person who built it.

Inventory of Base44 apps and assets in the Orca Platform.

Govern. Orca checks the workspace against more than 30 out-of-the-box posture rules:

Data exposure: Public apps without login, data entity permissions that don’t match app visibility, public apps holding secrets, and backend functions with no login wall.

Identity: Admins without MFA, SSO that is configured but not enforced, guest SSO exemptions, and risky or stale API keys.

AI agents: Superagent and embedded-agent access settings, checked against each app’s visibility.

Workspace guardrails: Public default visibility, non-admins who can publish to the internet, a disabled IP allowlist, unrestricted iframe embedding, and domains that point at deleted apps.

Findings map to SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, GDPR, PCI DSS and HIPAA, so GRC teams get evidence without chasing app owners.

Security alerts for a Base44 app in the Orca Platform.

Context that tells you which app to fix first

In Orca, Base44 findings join the same Unified Data Model as the rest of your environment.

Exposure, ranked. Orca adds every live, published Base44 app to its exposure graph as internet-reachable. It then precisely prioritizes apps that combine public access with open data, secrets, outside connectors or anonymous agents. App B rises to the top, and App A stays quiet.

One queue for every AI builder. Base44 findings sit next to Vercel and Claude findings, with the same workflow, ticketing and compliance reports, and a named business owner on every finding.

Code and workspace, side by side. Base44 builders usually never see a pull request, yet their apps still produce code, and with Base44’s GitHub sync (Builder plan and up) that code lands in your repos. Orca already scans the repos you connect to. Now it also sees the workspace that published them: who has access, what is exposed, and what agents and connectors can reach. Base44’s Security Center also checks code inside the builder.

Builders keep their platform and their speed. Security gets enough context to approve apps instead of blocking them. That’s how AI AppGen Security turns “no” into “go.”

Want to see how Orca keeps your Base44 workspace enterprise ready? Book a demo and we’ll walk through a live workspace.

About the Orca Platform

Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Trusted by hundreds of organizations, including SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, and Digital Turbine, Orca is backed by leading investors including Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, and Redpoint Ventures.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.

Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”

The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.

It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.

Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.

The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”

He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”

“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.

“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.

UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments

The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.

He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.

The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.

Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.

More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.

The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.

A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations

Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.

The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.

He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”

“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”

“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.

The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was endorsed in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number
