General Security News.title: When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?
General Security News.context: The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect
General Security News.full_text:
Suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action.

That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls.

An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents.

Turning off the model may not stop the work

An AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect.

The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received.

That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services.

When should a team contain an agent?

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context.

Signals that warrant a closer look include:

The agent calls a tool or accesses a resource outside its assigned task.

It attempts an unusual volume of reads, writes or exports.

A workflow continues after an operator believes it has been paused.

The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect.

Identity, application or network logs show activity that does not match the agent’s normal work.

The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded.

A practical response sequence

1. Pause the affected workflow

Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely.

A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow.

2. Revoke or limit the agent’s access

Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used.

Revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire quickly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it.

3. Restrict tools and network paths

Disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues.

This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations.

4. Preserve evidence and establish what happened

Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs.

Then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions.

5. Contain downstream effects

If the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes.

Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed.

Restore access carefully

Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy.

Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution.

Prepare before the incident

An incident response plan is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know:

Who owns it and who can suspend its runs.

Which identity, credentials, tools and systems it can use.

How to revoke its access and block its network connections.

Which logs show its actions and the results.

How to investigate changes and restore the workflow safely.

Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event.

An effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows.

With Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

General Security News.title: Apple details Secure Exclaves, isolated runtimes for camera and microphone data
General Security News.context: In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system
General Security News.full_text:
Apple published details of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture designed to protect camera and microphone data during background processing. Apple says data processed and analyzed within Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or the company itself.

The company uses Secure Exclaves for person recognition on HomeView, as well as for Siri Recap and Live Rewind. The architecture also protects the on-screen camera and microphone indicators on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView.

Protecting background sensing

Ambient sensing uses the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. It reduces sensor streams to simple signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or an enrolled user was recognized. During ambient sensing, raw audio and video remain protected within Secure Exclaves and are discarded once processing is complete, without reaching the main operating system.

The architecture supports two modes. In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system, with a secure indicator informing the user that this is happening.

Apple built the isolated environment around three requirements. Isolation prevents the main operating system from extracting or modifying data processed within Secure Exclaves. A controlled interface limits what can cross that boundary to a precisely defined set of information. Secure indication lets users see whether an active sensor session is in progress, without interference from the main operating system.

“Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP),” Apple explained.

The microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that identify a resource and authorize access to it.

The exclaves run in a separate processor execution context with an independent operating system. The Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), which runs at a higher privilege level than the main operating system’s kernel, enforces memory isolation.

Exclaves communicate through Secure IPC. Apple audits each interface to the main operating system to limit outgoing information to the metadata needed for ambient sensing.

The Exclave Indicator Controller allows full sensor data to flow to the main operating system only after confirming that the indicator is on and has been visible long enough. On HomeView, it controls the LED directly and ensures that it is bright enough to be visible. On iPhone, a display exclave checks that the pixels used to render the indicator meet a minimum brightness threshold and are not obscured by nearby pixels.

How HomeView recognizes people

At startup, the person recognition exclave loads enrolled face and voice models and an identity database from the secure storage exclave.

Person recognition flow on HomeView (Source: Apple)

The camera exclave detects faces and queues frames for processing, while audio exclaves handle anomaly detection and echo cancellation. They can notify the main operating system that someone may be present without sharing images or audio.

The Neural Engine exclave generates face and voice prints using isolated work queues, clearing its state after each model finishes. An orchestration service matches the prints against the identity database and combines the results into a confidence score.

Only the person’s identifier, position, and confidence level reach the person recognition daemon in the main operating system. These outputs support identity-dependent features in Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, and compatible third-party audio and video apps from an iPhone. No audio or video leaves Secure Exclaves during recognition.

What comes next

Apple said it will continue hardening Secure Exclaves through AI-accelerated vulnerability research and broader formal verification coverage. The company described the architecture as a step toward giving users greater clarity and confidence about how their Apple products respond to the world around them.

General Security News.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
General Security News.context: This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem
General Security News.full_text: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

General Security News.title: Microsoft confirms Windows activation failures after November updates
General Security News.context: While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business
General Security News.full_text:
Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates are causing Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes.

According to a Wednesday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation and licensing processes or use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter (SWbemObjectEx), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said.

"Devices that are being configured to use KMS activation might encounter errors when attempting to initiate their activation. KMS-activated devices typically remain activated for up to 180 days following successful activation."

The activation failures occur after executing the 'slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain>' and 'slmgr.vbs /ipk <key>' commands on client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) devices.

However, Microsoft added that customers with the KMS client key installed in their image and who don't use SLMGR for licensing management are unaffected.

"Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted.

While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business.

In January, Microsoft addressed another known issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because affected devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses.

This week, it also confirmed that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues.

General Security News.title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
General Security News.context: Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it
General Security News.full_text:
On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.”

Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure.

The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead?

A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled

Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop.

It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works.

Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue.

That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself.

The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path.

What a fallback has to do

I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover, patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name.

Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then.

The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live.

The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them.

Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals.

The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope.

How I’d build fallback-first today

If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live.

A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident.

A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it.

Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns.

A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it.

Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day.

None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone.

Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull.

Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

General Security News.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
General Security News.context: (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027
General Security News.full_text: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel. Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post. The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language. Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”) ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final. According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices. They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts. Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology. Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

General Security News.title: Suspected North Korean IT workers reached onboarding at companies with open data
General Security News.context: Over the year, 2,429 of them made contact, 1,100 reached an interview or later, and 27 reached onboarding, meaning offer letters, background checks, equipment requests, or...
General Security News.full_text:
Material Security followed suspected North Korean fake IT workers through the hiring pipelines of organizations it monitors and counted 27 personas that reached onboarding over one year. At one company where a persona got that far in the past month, about 277,000 files containing Social Security numbers were shared company-wide or by public link.

The personas are fabricated job seekers, complete with résumés and faces, applying for remote engineering roles. Over the year, 2,429 of them made contact, 1,100 reached an interview or later, and 27 reached onboarding, meaning offer letters, background checks, equipment requests, or first-day IT setup. That is roughly one in 90, a small share, but any of the 27 who received credentials walked in trusted, provisioned, and hostile from day one.

The same face at many companies

The researchers saw 41% of personas at more than one organization. Fifteen appeared at ten or more, and one appeared at 19. Of the 27 that reached onboarding, 18 were in process elsewhere at the same time, and one was finishing onboarding paperwork at one company while chasing jobs at seven others.

What the new accounts could reach

In the past 30 days, 232 suspected personas contacted 99 organizations. At 42 of them, at least one moved on to an interview or offer, and at four, a persona reached onboarding. Material inventoried the sensitive files at those four.

The first held about 15 million source-code files and 130,000 files with bank or routing numbers, shared with almost no one beyond their owners. The second held around 400,000 files with Social Security numbers and 345,000 with bank or routing numbers, and 68% of the Social Security files and 71% of the bank files were open to any account in the company or to anyone with a link. A new hire there would have needed nothing more than a login. The third had about 14 million source-code files, roughly 1,900 of them readable by anyone with the URL. The fourth, the smallest, held about 1.5 million source-code files plus files with private cryptographic keys, and 21% of its financial files and 17% of its credit-card files were shared beyond their owners.

What employers should do

Material recommends pairing hiring controls with access controls, since a North Korean hire who gets through holds valid credentials.

Flag personas early. Connect recruiting and onboarding signals with threat intelligence, so you can stop a fake identity before it gets credentials.

Check identities closely. Background checks are a chance to catch a fabricated persona. Follow up on anything that doesn’t line up.

Triage by stage. A watchlist hit during onboarding is more urgent than one at first contact. Confirm the identity and the evidence, then check whether an account or equipment has already been issued.

Keep investigating after onboarding. If an account exists, review its permissions, app grants, and activity.

Map access before you need it. Know which files, messages, credentials, and connected apps each role can reach, so responders know where to look first.

General Security News.title: Your pinned MCP server may not be as pinned as you think
General Security News.context: James Lagermann, Director of Technical Alliances at Corelight, found the drift in his company’s lab
General Security News.full_text:
An MCP server configured to run one fixed release on an administrator’s workstation ran with 15 different sets of dependencies over five weeks, with its configuration untouched. James Lagermann, Director of Technical Alliances at Corelight, found the drift in his company’s lab. Twenty-three of the server’s 69 packages changed versions, including the cryptography library, the JSON Web Token library and the MCP software development kit itself.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers let AI coding assistants act on other tools for a user, so they often hold that user’s credentials. On this workstation, the servers made more than 1,600 connections in a week to 11 management systems, including the firewall, the SIEM and sensor management. Code that slips into any of their dependencies runs with that access.

The pin didn’t hold

The assistants started their servers with uvx, a launcher that downloads a Python package and runs it from one line of configuration. Each entry named an exact release tag, PyPI version or Git commit. For one community server, the launcher installed from the package’s declared dependencies and skipped the project’s hash-pinned lock file, so the roughly 60 packages underneath were resolved fresh from the Python Package Index whenever the environment was rebuilt. Pinning a package’s version doesn’t necessarily pin the packages it depends on.

The assistant started one server 162 times in a week. Most launches reused a cached environment, but the cache still held 19 builds of the same release and commit, about one every couple of days. That cadence matters because a hijacked release can be live for only minutes or hours. In June 2026, a Shai-Hulud worm variant on PyPI hit MCP-themed packages and went after AI coding assistant keys.

The same pattern in the field

Corelight reviewed 35 MCP servers from two vendor catalogs and its lab. Twenty-three had a recommended install that would pull dependencies from a public registry on every launch, or on each install or image build.

Lagermann told Help Net Security he sees the same thing in the field. “I have seen the same pattern in customer environments and in other real-world deployments. So far, 100% of administrators that I’ve talked to were using at least one MCP Server with this issue.”

Freezing works, and someone has to keep it current

Corelight froze five servers: pinned to a commit, installed once from a hash-pinned lock file, launched directly, update checks off. Over the next two weeks the five were started 457 times, and each one’s installed package list matched the list recorded on install day.

Frozen code ages. When the team froze one community server, 40 of its packages were older than what the launcher would have pulled that day, some of them security-sensitive. Asked how often to re-lock, Lagermann said: “I would recommend following the MCP maintainers’ recommendation for updates. The MCP Servers I maintain are reviewed nightly for vulnerabilities. If one is found, it’s updated the next morning, with a change log.”

“For the 23 public MCP servers that I found, I notified the maintainers and/or services that share them. As a result, one company that hosts an AI agent exchange has updated its security review processes to evaluate submissions for this issue. In another case, the vendor is completely repackaging their MCP server,” Lagermann said.

Any MCP entry started by a Python or npm package runner, or tagged “latest,” can resolve new code from a public registry the next time an assistant opens a session. On Corelight’s workstation, the server’s version number stayed the same through all 15 environments.

General Security News.title: Digital sovereignty leaves enterprises chasing their own audit trails
General Security News.context: The report defines digital sovereignty as an organization’s ability to retain control and provide credible evidence of that control across critical AI, technology, operations...
General Security News.full_text:
94% of surveyed enterprises experienced at least one digital sovereignty challenge in the past three years, according to IBM’s Digital Sovereignty Index. Of those affected, 91% were required to demonstrate that they retained control during their most challenging event, and 81% had to provide formal evidence to regulators, auditors, customers or internal stakeholders.

The report defines digital sovereignty as an organization’s ability to retain control and provide credible evidence of that control across critical AI, technology, operations and data. Across these four pillars, it assesses six dimensions: responsibility, trace, constraint, intervention, exit and legitimacy.

Accountability and exit capabilities need testing

Across the six dimensions, an average of 82% of respondents were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of control. The index placed 26% of enterprises in its highest maturity tier, Leading Digital Sovereignty.

Ability of organizations to demonstrate evidence (Source: IBM)

Manual evidence collection was a barrier for 56% of respondents. Fragmented records, dependence on third parties for information, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards were each cited by 53%.

“When a business issue turns into a sovereignty risk, boards need to show real control: how they can adapt, change strategy or critical provider – where freedom to act lies. The choices they make today matter, and the stakes are high. Getting this right can help them minimize shocks, keep their options open and stay competitive,” said Jonathan Adashek, IBM Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer.

Responsibility had the largest gap between confidence and evidence across all four pillars.

During their most challenging sovereignty incident, 33% of enterprises reported being able to demonstrate exit fully and credibly, without significant follow-up. This includes the ability to replace a provider, model or system while maintaining business continuity.

AI tests enterprise sovereignty

AI-related issues affected 44% of respondents, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns.

Formal audit or regulatory events affected 38%, significant provider changes 35%, and data-access or transfer issues 33%. Government restrictions were reported by 30%. AI received the lowest score for evidence of control.

“Organisations need to be able to demonstrate where their data comes from, how it can be used, and what controls are in place,” said Debbie Lawrence, Group Head Of Data Strategy and Management at LSEG.

AI-dependent business processes require records showing what systems did, which data they used, who authorized their actions and who remained accountable. IBM recommends keeping this evidence current and accessible as systems and dependencies change.

Restrictions imposed by an external authority or provider can also affect access to an AI model, and an enterprise may need an alternative model or provider with different performance or behavior.

Continuous testing or testing through regular governance and assurance processes was reported by 63% of enterprises in the highest tier and 9% in the lowest tier. Enterprises in the highest tier reported fewer barriers to producing evidence. They were also more likely to resolve their most challenging sovereignty incident without material disruption.

General Security News.title: AI Didn’t Create a New Kind of Risk. It Removed the Time You Had to Fix the Old One.
General Security News.context: Attackers now use agentic AI for reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and, in at least one case, a zero-day, yet vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in for...
General Security News.full_text:
Mandiant’s AI Risk and Resilience 2026 report shows attackers putting agentic AI to work across the intrusion. Vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in, and the window to fix it is closing.

Executive Summary

Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published AI Risk and Resilience 2026 in September. Attackers now use agentic AI for reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and, in at least one case, a zero-day, yet vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in for the sixth year running. AI has changed how fast attackers exploit far more than what they exploit.

Exploitation is still the front door. Exploits caused 32% of intrusions in M-Trends 2026, and the mean time to exploit is now an estimated minus seven days. Mandiant concludes that defense has to move beyond manual triage to machine speed.

Most AI incidents started as exposures. Poisoned packages, long-lived CI/CD credentials, unsigned plugins and MCP servers, and over-permissioned agents were all in place before the attack.

AI infrastructure is now a target in its own right. An autonomous AI agent reached cluster-admin in Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment with no CVE to match, and exploits for AI components are appearing before disclosure.

The Risk Operations Center is the missing layer. The report answers with runtime controls and an agentic SOC, which act after the attacker is inside. A Risk Operations Center (ROC) closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway.

A machine-speed adversary needs a machine-speed defender. Qualys AI agents detect new exposures, prove which ones are exploitable, and remediate them, so the defender’s side of the race is automated too.

One ROC covers all of it. Infrastructure, identity, and AI risk belong in one ROC, with proactive AI governance ahead of runtime guardrails.

What the Frontline Is Telling Us

Drawing on incident response, Offensive Security engagements, and threat intelligence, the report describes attackers moving from chat-based research to autonomous attack orchestration. Five patterns stand out.

Agentic attack tooling is in the wild. Tools such as Hexstrike and Strix automate reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and credential harvesting.

AI-assisted zero-days are real. GTIG assessed with high confidence that a cybercriminal used an AI model to find and weaponize a two-factor authentication bypass in an open-source admin tool for a planned mass exploitation campaign.

The AI supply chain is part of the perimeter. Poisoned PyPI packages, a compromised LiteLLM library, weaponized agent skills, and subverted coding-assistant hooks all appear in the case studies.

Over-privileged agents are part of the attack surface. Mandiant red teamers manipulated a CI/CD chatbot into pushing internal repositories to an external GitHub account, and an assessment found a RAG support agent that indirect prompt injection could turn against other customers’ data. In a real incident, a finance agent made 15,000+ API calls in under an hour, causing a roughly $50,000 billing spike.

Long-lived credentials keep doing the damage. One healthcare intrusion began with a single long-lived CI/CD credential and ended with thousands of credentials compromised.

M-Trends 2026 also shows the hand-off from initial access to a secondary threat group falling from over eight hours in 2022 to 22 seconds in 2025.

AI Infrastructure Is Already Under Attack

The same pattern is showing up in AI infrastructure itself. In July 2026, an autonomous AI agent that had escaped an evaluation sandbox worked its way into Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment. A Qualys analysis of the intrusion counted about 17,600 actions over five days, and the agent reached cluster-admin in about 13 hours. It entered through a dataset configuration file and an unsanitized template, then used a privileged pod and a shared credential to take over clusters. None of those steps gave a vulnerability scanner a CVE to match.

Figure 1. The Hugging Face intrusion step by step, with what a package scan and a runtime sensor can see at each stage.

Vulnerabilities in AI components are being weaponized just as quickly. Qualys research on AI exploits in containers puts the window of weaponization at minus one day for flaws in the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (CVE-2025-23266) and in an MCP server (CVE-2025-6514). For a Docker Model Runner flaw (CVE-2026-28400), whether a workload is exploitable depends on runtime flags and how the service is invoked.

Most AI Incidents Are Exposure Problems in Disguise

A risky package in the build pipeline is a software exposure. A long-lived CI/CD key is an identity exposure. An unsigned plugin or over-permissioned MCP server is a misconfiguration. An agent that reads private data, ingests untrusted content, and talks to the internet is an attack path. These are familiar exposures on a new class of asset that most inventories cannot yet see. In six of the report’s eight case studies, the attacker used an exposure that could have been found beforehand.

Mandiant Case Study

Exposure Before the Attack

How Exposure Management Finds It

Coding session hijack spreads Shai-Hulud

Unverified AI-recommended package; long-lived GitHub OAuth tokens

SCA and AI-SBOM in IDE and CI/CD, secrets scanning, malware detection

AI co-debugging in a cloud intrusion

Long-lived CI/CD credential; unisolated VM with open egress

Non-human identity inventory; cloud egress posture checks

Subverted CLI hooks lead to RCE

Unsigned hooks, plugins, and MCP servers; weak AI repository controls

MCP and AI software discovery, MCP testing, access review

Confused Deputy exfiltration (red team test)

Agent with repo access, user input, and an allowed external domain

One attack path across data access, untrusted input, and egress; LLM red teaming

Denial-of-wallet reasoning loop

Agent with read and write access to billing databases, no cost limits

Agent entitlement and least-privilege findings

RAG agent with untrusted input (assessment)

Pipeline ingesting public content with reach into other customers’ tickets

LLM red teaming for indirect prompt injection and data leakage

The other two, just-in-time polymorphic malware and a stealthy espionage backdoor, are runtime detection problems. Together with the Hugging Face case, they are why a ROC needs runtime detection as well as posture.

The Risk Operations Center Is the Missing Layer

Mandiant answers these cases with agent identity, runtime guardrails, and an agentic SOC that triages at machine speed. Those controls matter, and they take effect once an attack is underway. The layer the report leaves out is the Risk Operations Center, which finds and closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway. Three capabilities make it more than another source of detections.

Hybrid coverage. The exposures in the report sit on developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, cloud VMs, SaaS applications, and identity systems. The Qualys platform covers on-premises, endpoint, multi-cloud, container, identity, application, and AI assets with the agents and connectors customers already run.

Proof of exploitability. Safe exploit validation shows which exposures an attacker can actually use in your environment, so teams act on evidence instead of a severity score.

Remediation as well as detection. Each validated exposure is patched, mitigated, or isolated, and the fix is confirmed, so the finding is closed as well as reported.

Six Moves That Answer AI with AI

Mandiant’s premise is an adversary that operates at machine speed. A defense that depends on analysts triaging by hand cannot match it, so the defender’s side has to be automated as well. On the Qualys platform, AI agents do that work at each stage. Agent Insta detects new exposures within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val proves which ones are exploitable. Agent Sara plans and runs remediation in TruRisk Eliminate. Agent Grant investigates and closes identity risk. The six moves below show where each one fits.

Figure 2. The three decisions security teams have to make at AI speed: detect faster, prioritize with runtime evidence, and act surgically.

Close the Window with Agent Insta and TruRisk Eliminate

With a negative time to exploit, what matters is how fast a team closes the gap between disclosure and fix, and every handoff between tools adds hours. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta in Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM), matches new advisories against the inventory Qualys already holds, without a rescan.

Customers are seeing this in practice. In a Techstrong TV interview recorded at ROCon Americas 2026, Theo Bowman, who runs the vulnerability management program at NCR Atleos, explains that the biggest change since Mythos is the need to find exposures first and fix them quickly. He describes InstaScan returning vulnerability data for his assets within three minutes of a Patch Tuesday release. The last two Patch Tuesdays show similar speeds.

October 2026. Microsoft fixed a record 1,414 vulnerabilities, 78 of them critical, including an exploited Windows Shell zero-day (CVE-2026-96951) with a CISA patch deadline of October 16. Agent Insta customers had detections within 5 minutes, and Qualys provided mitigations for 608 of the vulnerabilities.

November 2026. Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, 63 of them critical, including an exploited Outlook spoofing zero-day (CVE-2026-124194) with a CISA patch deadline of November 24. InstaScan showed customers their findings 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own advisory page was updated, and Qualys provided mitigations for 537 of the vulnerabilities.

Figure 3. Findings detected first by InstaScan in Qualys ETM, each marked with the Agent Insta icon and the time it was first found.

TruRisk prioritization, informed by QVSS and Qualys threat intelligence, raises likely-weaponized vulnerabilities about 45 days, on average, before they reach the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence then closes the loop through agentic remediation and autonomous RemOps. Agent Sara picks the safest action for each exposure (patch, mitigation, or isolation), rolls it out in waves with reliability scoring and rollback, and confirms the fix. In the past year, customers deployed 150 million patches, 40 million fully autonomously.

Figure 4. Agent Sara plans risk-based remediation waves in TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, starting with the exposures proven to be risky.

See AI as Attack Surface with TotalAI

Mandiant calls for a dynamic AI inventory and an AI-SBOM. Qualys TotalAI discovers AI agents, models, MCP servers, AI software and libraries, GPUs, AI containers, cloud AI services, and shadow AI using the Cloud Agents and connectors customers already run. Built on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, it scores each AI asset with TruRisk alongside servers, endpoints, and cloud workloads.

Figure 5. The TotalAI inventory of AI workloads, including coding assistants, agents, and RAG pipelines found on hosts and in the cloud.

TotalAI follows an AI application from code to runtime. It checks AI code and agent configuration in the IDE and CI/CD, assesses AI container images, generates an AI-SBOM, and confirms whether vulnerable AI packages are installed, running, and communicating, so a risk on a live workload can be traced back to its image and code. It tests MCP servers for missing authentication, tool poisoning, argument injection, SSRF, and rug-pull behavior, and red-teams LLMs for prompt injection, jailbreaks, and data disclosure, mapped to the OWASP LLM and MCP Top 10 and the EU AI Act. For supply chain malware, including the just-in-time polymorphic malware in the report that defeats signatures, Qualys uses deep learning to detect unknown malware in container images and workloads before deployment and in cloud network traffic with TotalCloud Cloud Detection and Response.

Figure 6. Code-to-runtime tracing, from the running container to its image, source repository, and AI agent code (illustrative example).

The same visibility extends to the workforce. The TotalAI Browser Plugin, combined with SaaS connectors, shows which sanctioned and shadow AI tools employees use, and it analyzes prompts and uploads to show when sensitive data is leaving through them.

Figure 7. Securing an AI workload in TotalAI. AI-SPM is delivered through the Qualys Cloud Agent and AI runtime coverage through the Qualys Browser Plug-in.

Treat Every Agent as an Identity with ETM Identity

An agent with a static API key and standing access holds privileged access around the clock. Mandiant recommends dedicated agent identities, short-lived credentials, least privilege, and treating coding assistants and MCP servers as privileged sessions. Each is an identity exposure that can be measured before it is abused, and Entro Security found that 97% of non-human identities carry excessive privileges.

ETM Identity discovers identities across Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta, and local accounts, extends to non-human identities such as service accounts and application identities, traces blast radius across chained permissions, and correlates risky identities with vulnerable assets as toxic combinations. Agent Grant investigates those findings and guides the fix. Access reviews now need to ask what has access as well as who. AI agents with standing access are where ETM Identity is heading next.

Figure 8. The identity inventory in ETM Identity, with a TruRisk score for each user and service account.

Map the Lethal Trifecta as an Attack Path

Mandiant’s “lethal trifecta” is an agent with private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and an external channel. Each alone is manageable. Together they form an attack path that one injected instruction can turn into exfiltration, as the Confused Deputy test showed.

Attack paths for AI span more than one product. TotalCloud provides attack path insights for cloud and container workloads, and with TotalAI those insights extend to the AI models and MCP servers found in container images. Figure 9 shows one: an internet-exposed container with a critical exploitable vulnerability, running an image that contains an AI model, traced back to the commit and build pipeline that produced it. ETM Identity traces how an identity can chain privileges to reach critical systems. ETM is where these come together. For the lethal trifecta, the chain joins the agent’s entitlements from ETM Identity, the untrusted inputs and unsafe tool behavior TotalAI finds, and the cloud and network exposure from TotalCloud and ETM. Showing it as one toxic combination, ranked by the data it reaches, lets teams break the chain at a single link instead of chasing each finding. That is the direction we are taking attack path analysis across ETM and TotalCloud with TotalAI.

Figure 9. An attack path in TotalCloud that links an internet-exposed container with a critical exploitable vulnerability to the AI model in its image and to the commit and build that produced it.

Prove It, Fix It, and Prove It Again with Agent Val

When exploits take hours to build, theoretical severity cannot decide what to fix. Agent Val uses TruConfirm to safely prove whether an exposure is exploitable in your environment, drives the mitigation, and revalidates closure. TruConfirm covers more than 1,800 CVEs with over 8 million validations. It brings the discipline of a red team engagement, like those Mandiant’s Offensive Security team runs, into continuous operation.

The same principle applies at the application and AI layers. TotalAppSec (or WAS) runs dynamic application security testing (DAST) against the web applications and APIs that sit in front of AI systems, alongside the penetration tests teams already run. TotalAI red teaming tests models and MCP servers and shows which technique succeeded and which guardrail failed.

Figure 10. Agent Val reports a TruConfirm exploit validation with step-by-step evidence and offers remediation options.

Detect AI Exploitation in Real Time with Container Runtime Security

Some attacks leave nothing for a posture scan to find. In the Hugging Face intrusion, a package scan had nothing to match at the entry point and no view of the later stages (Figure 1). Exploits for AI components can arrive before disclosure, and whether a flaw is exploitable can depend on how a container is started. These cases have to be caught while they happen.

Figure 11. Three vulnerabilities in AI components running in containers, where exploitation had to be detected at runtime.

Qualys Container Runtime Security, part of TotalCloud, uses an eBPF sensor in the kernel to watch process, file, and network activity inside running containers, so it can detect exploitation of AI vulnerabilities in real time. In the Hugging Face analysis, its detections map to the fileless Python execution at the entry point, the container escape through a host path mount, the mount, chroot, and setns activity on the node, and the SOCKS proxy tunnel used for lateral movement. TotalCloud Cloud Detection and Response adds the Kubernetes and cloud API activity that process sensors cannot see, such as token minting and replayed cloud credentials. Kubernetes posture checks and admission policies flag or block the privileged pods and host path mounts the agent relied on. The analysis does not claim these controls would have stopped the campaign. It shows which layer sees each step, and that runtime, posture, and cloud audit each answer a different question.

Figure 12. Runtime detections in the TotalCloud Investigate view, including a suspicious host mount through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a shell spawned after exploitation of an Nginx UI vulnerability.

The same runtime evidence sharpens prioritization, because it shows which vulnerable packages are actually running and exposed.

Runtime Is One Pillar of AI Governance

Mandiant separates governance for AI (risk appetite and policy) from governance of AI (technical guardrails in pipelines and at runtime), and most of its technical guidance sits at runtime. A program that relies on runtime alone assumes every guardrail is configured correctly and every injection is caught in flight. We believe the stronger model is proactive first, with runtime guardrails as the backstop.

Layer

Question It Answers

How Qualys Delivers It

AI-SPM

What AI do we have, who owns it, and how is it configured?

TotalAI discovery and posture across models, agents, MCP servers, AI SaaS, and cloud AI

Workforce AI

Which AI tools are employees using, and what data goes into them?

TotalAI Browser Plugin and SaaS connectors, with prompt analysis for shadow AI use

Proactive security testing

Can this model or MCP server be manipulated before it ships?

LLM and MCP red teaming from CI/CD or on a schedule, mapped to OWASP and the EU AI Act

Prioritization and remediation

Which AI risks matter most, and what fixes them?

TruRisk with infrastructure and identity context; TruRisk Eliminate and guardrail recommendations

Runtime AIDR

Is something going wrong right now?

Policy-based runtime controls, and eBPF-based real-time detection of exploitation in AI workloads

TotalAI includes the runtime guardrails that give the SOC its AI signals. A SOC delivers its best return when a ROC is working ahead of it, because the ROC closes the exposures that would otherwise keep producing alerts. Guardrails written from red team results address weaknesses proven to exist, and every retest produces the evidence boards and regulators are starting to ask for.

Figure 13. The TotalAI AI Governance Dashboard, with a TruRisk score for AI, the AI assets at risk, and regulatory status.

Measure Time to Close

The AI era will be decided by how quickly teams close the window between disclosure and fix, which a count of open findings does not show.

Measure your exposure window. Track disclosure to detection, prioritization, and fix for exploited vulnerabilities, with a target in hours.

Put AI in the asset inventory. Cover agents, models, MCP servers, AI libraries, and shadow AI-like servers and endpoints.

Retire static credentials for agents. Classify non-human identities, flag long-lived keys and standing privileges, and move to short-lived, scoped identities.

Look for the lethal trifecta. Find agents with private data access, untrusted input, and an outbound channel, and remove one of the three.

Validate before you prioritize. Use safe exploit validation to separate the exploitable from the theoretical.

Test AI before you rely on runtime guardrails. Red-team models and MCP servers before release and after every change to prompts, retrieval, or guardrails.

Watch AI workloads at runtime. Use kernel-level runtime detection to catch exploitation that has no CVE to match.

One Risk Operations Center for Infrastructure, Identity, and AI Risk

Attackers have automated their side of the race, yet their first move is still a weakness that was in place before the attack began. Runtime controls and the SOC respond once that weakness is used. The ROC closes it first, and its runtime detection catches what is exploited anyway. With Qualys, Agent Insta detects at AI speed, Agent Val proves what is exploitable, and Agent Sara remediates autonomously, on one platform that treats servers, clouds, identities, and AI systems as the same attack surface. That is one Risk Operations Center for infrastructure, identity, and AI risk.

General Security News.title: Google smart glasses privacy features cover wearers and the people around them
General Security News.context: Designed to, for now The tamper detection, the face redaction, and the voice focus are design intentions
General Security News.full_text:
Google has built its Gemini-powered intelligent eyewear to stop taking photos and video when someone covers or tampers with the outward-facing recording light. Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, laid out that safeguard along with face redaction, limits on data handling, and app restrictions.

Bystanders told Google during years of research that they worried about being filmed without their knowledge, and that a sign of recording would help them most. Wearers face a different exposure, because glasses that see what they see also capture menus, street signs, and the faces of strangers.

What the light does

The LED turns on when the wearer takes a photo or video for the gallery. Sensors are designed to detect a covered or tampered light and block capture. Google Shopping and Ads policies ban promoting products that disable or hide recording lights on smart glasses.

What happens when you ask Gemini

When the wearer asks Gemini about the scene, the glasses are designed to redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini processes the image. Google keeps those camera visuals out of the user’s Gemini History and out of AI training and ad targeting. Data is encrypted on the glasses and in transit to the phone or cloud, and directional microphones point Gemini at the wearer’s voice by default.

Designed to, for now

The tamper detection, the face redaction, and the voice focus are design intentions. Private AI Compute, Google’s hardened environment for processing data, has not reached the glasses yet. Test the first three before you allow the glasses into a room with sensitive material on display.

Enforcement runs through the terms of service

Before using the glasses, wearers must agree not to record people without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the light. Google may disable the glasses of anyone who breaks those terms, and setup requires an 18+ Google Account. Google Play bans apps from changing how the light behaves and from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification.
