A patchwork of problems.
General Security News.context: Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook. Most notably, CVE-2026-124194 is an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw that leaks a user's NTLMv2 authentication hash if they open a malicious message file,...
General Security News.full_text:
Patch Tuesday. Maersk investigates a legacy system breach. A chip-smuggling probe stalls after Nvidia reaches out to Commerce. A US Army officer is arrested in the UK for alleged Russian espionage. Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents across Central Asia. Opsec blunders unmask an alleged Qilin ransomware boss. Researchers hijack connected cars via Android apps. Our guest is Tim Starks from CyberScoop to discuss what Democratic control of Congress means for cybersecurity. A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Today is Thursday November 12th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Patch Tuesday.

In honor of the Veterans Day holiday here in the U.S. we did not publish yesterday, which means we are playing a bit of catch up for this month’s patch Tuesday.

Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook.

According to SecurityWeek, Redmond addressed one thousand ninety-four vulnerabilities this month. Most notably, CVE-2026-124194 is an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw that leaks a user's NTLMv2 authentication hash if they open a malicious message file, allowing attackers to impersonate them. Windows accounted for seven hundred twenty-six of Microsoft's patches, alongside one hundred seventy-four for Office.

Meanwhile, Fortinet published eighty-nine advisories resolving nearly one hundred flaws, including roughly seventeen critical issues across products like FortiMail, FortiOS, and FortiClient, which researchers note were discovered with the help of frontier artificial intelligence models. Ivanti and Citrix patched nineteen vulnerabilities combined; Ivanti's fixes address critical unauthenticated remote code execution and authentication bypass defects in Endpoint Manager and Cloud Services Application, while Citrix resolved six XenServer flaws and mitigated AMD processor issues. Finally, Zoom patched two unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, and Asus addressed four router firmware bugs.

Attackers rapidly weaponize edge devices and collaboration tools, requiring security teams to prioritize patching Outlook and internet-facing enterprise infrastructure immediately, even where active exploitation has not yet been reported, according to vendor advisories.

Maersk investigates isolated security incident on legacy system.

Shipping giant A.P. Moller-Maersk is investigating a security incident involving potential data theft from an isolated legacy system.

In a Wednesday statement, the Denmark-based logistics firm confirmed it secured the affected platform, a local system from a previous acquisition. Maersk said initial findings strongly suggest no sensitive information was disclosed, and there is no evidence of impact on core operations or customer integrations like APIs and electronic data interchange.

Any cyber incident at Maersk recalls the devastating two thousand seventeen NotPetya attack, attributed to Russia's Sandworm group, which cost the firm roughly three hundred million dollars. While this localized intrusion appears far less severe, it highlights persistent cybersecurity risks within inherited acquisition infrastructure, according to Maersk and reporting from The Register.

The Commerce Department halted a chip-smuggling probe after Nvidia outreach.

Federal investigators at the Commerce Department abruptly paused a monthslong probe into suspected artificial intelligence chip smuggling to China late last year after receiving unusual outreach from Nvidia.

According to The New York Times, the inquiry focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed, led by Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials now believe spied for Beijing and who had an acknowledged intimate relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The case was hastily transferred to the Justice Department after Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter emailed investigators, claiming Commerce official Jeff Kessler authorized the company to inquire about the probe.

The episode highlights growing tension between national security enforcement and corporate influence over semiconductor export controls, raising concerns among officials that executive intervention could compromise federal investigations into illicit technology transfers.

Nvidia shares fell ten percent after CEO Jensen Huang resigned today, naming CFO Colette Kress interim chief executive.

The Wall Street Journal reports the board met following a New York Times report alleging a second affair with executive Kimberly Powell.

A US Army officer is arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia.

British police have arrested a forty-one-year-old US Army lieutenant colonel on suspicion of attempting to steal secret information from a NATO installation for Russia.

According to The Washington Post, the unnamed officer was stationed at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire, England, which houses NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. A joint counterintelligence operation involving Britain's MI5, Metropolitan Police, and the FBI detained the officer before any sensitive files were transferred to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any Russian link to the incident.

US Army Counterintelligence Command noted the arrest is a sobering reminder of persistent insider threats within allied defense infrastructure, as Western nations navigate heightened Russian hybrid operations across Europe alongside ongoing Ukraine peace negotiations.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents in Central Asian espionage.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an autonomous artificial intelligence agent to conduct cyberespionage against Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure, according to Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK.

Researchers uncovered the operation on an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, also tracked as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper. The operator configured an open-source AI agent named Hermes, powered primarily by DeepSeek models, to act as an offensive security specialist. Controlled remotely via a Telegram bot in Russian, the agent automated reconnaissance, data theft, and log erasure.

Using compromised railway credentials, the attackers breached Tajikistan's national electronic document platform, stealing thousands of files linked to the Defense Ministry and security agencies. They also compromised a server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and prepared phishing lures targeting Turkmenistan.

The discovery underscores how threat actors are operationalizing agentic AI to automate complex intrusions, lowering the operational friction required to pillage government networks.

Operational security missteps expose an alleged Qilin ransomware administrator.

Operational security mistakes over the past decade have exposed the alleged real-world identity of the administrator behind Qilin, currently the world's most active ransomware affiliate program.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, Qilin, which claimed at least three hundred sixty-five victims in the past three months, is led by a threat actor using the handle "Haise." Threat intelligence firms IntelHawk, Intel 471, and Flashpoint traced Haise back to older cybercrime forum monikers, including "Rjun," and a Telegram account tied to an email address exposed in a late two thousand twenty-five breach of Russia's state services portal, Gosuslugi. Those records, alongside leaked travel and education data, point to thirty-six-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev of St. Petersburg.

The attribution demonstrates how even sophisticated ransomware operators leave persistent digital breadcrumbs across seized forums and breached databases, aiding defenders and law enforcement in piercing criminal anonymity.

Security researchers exploit Android apps to remotely control connected cars.

Security researchers uncovered critical flaws in Android applications from two major automakers that enabled remote access to connected vehicles in the United States and Australia.

According to research published by Assetnote co-founder Shubham Shah and Sam Curry, the exploit chains targeted weaknesses in the manufacturers' ForgeRock identity platforms. In Australia, hardcoded staging credentials and path traversal flaws allowed account takeovers using just a license plate lookup. In the US, path confusion and factory default credentials on an Apache Felix console yielded shell access to identity servers, letting the pair start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. The unnamed automakers, widely speculated by observers to be Toyota and Lexus, patched the vulnerabilities within two hours of disclosure earlier this year.

The findings underscore how backend identity misconfigurations and hardcoded credentials in connected vehicle ecosystems can turn everyday mobile apps into remote-control attack vectors.

A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Officials in Cranbury, New Jersey, intended to buy land for affordable housing, though they inadvertently subsidized some ambitious cybercriminals instead, wiring twenty-six million dollars straight into fraudsters' hands.

According to The Wall Street Journal, police expect to recover seventeen point three million dollars, leaving roughly nine million missing, an amount comfortably exceeding the township's five-million-dollar insurance policy. Adding salt to the fiscal wound, officials waited until the Friday afternoon after Election Day to announce the heist. While the police chief took responsibility, explaining a gag order prevented thieves from liquidating the stolen funds, residents packed a town meeting expressing skepticism over the timing and marveling that an eight-figure transfer proved easier than logging into an iCloud account.

The episode offers a sobering reminder that business email compromise doesn't spare small municipalities, and that delayed breach disclosures rarely play well with voters, even when investigators have sound operational reasons.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox
Still in the Meeting: BlueNoroff Six Months On
General Security News.context: We have leveraged threat intelligence around this threat activity to enhance detections in the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora® Endpoint Security, subject to...
General Security News.full_text:
In April, Arctic Wolf Labs documented how BlueNoroff used fake Zoom and Microsoft Teams meetings, ClickFix prompts, and AI-generated participants to compromise leaders in the Web3 and cryptocurrency sector. We expected the threat actor to adapt after we published that report. Instead, BlueNoroff spent the next six months meticulously changing almost every red-flag “tell” a target can see, but changed almost nothing about how the intrusion itself works.

Now, the fake meeting is no longer the lure. Through access to the threat actor’s own infrastructure, Arctic Wolf tracked BlueNoroff expanding its operation into the everyday workflows of crypto and venture-capital professionals. New lures have been set up to target high-ranking targets such as founders, CEOs and senior executives, in the form of shared financial documents, PDF viewer updates, fake media players, identity verification prompts, hardware-wallet access, and security audit workflows.

This blog offers a brief overview of our findings. Full details of our investigations into BlueNoroff’s latest campaign tactics can be found in our new white paper on the topic.

What’s Inside the Full Report

A tour of BlueNoroff’s lure factory. New lure themes we uncovered appeared as custom artwork, operator guides, and test scripts in the actor’s media library before going live. We walk you through one end to end: a fabricated media player named NovaStream that progressed from AI-generated artwork to a fully operational malicious delivery kit.

Same trick, new pretext. Every lure still follows the same pattern. The threat actor establishes professional trust with the intended target, manufactures a technical problem, and persuades the target to run a “fix” that retrieves the next stage of the attack.

A wider net, with leadership the primary target. The number of individuals we identified in BlueNoroff’s media library grew from roughly 400 (of which we independently verified 100 in our April report), to 677 individuals across 58 countries. Founders and C-suite executives make up 84% of that total. These counts describe who the threat actor prepared material against, not confirmed compromises.

Custom guides help targets compromise themselves. BlueNoroff crafts “helpful” instruction videos that walk targets past browser warnings and through unfamiliar macOS and Windows workflows.

AI as a production multiplier. Generative AI now supplies attackers with platform artwork, avatars, and realistic synthetic participant video at a much higher volume and degree of realism. We show how we identified deepfakes using provenance evidence rather than visual inspection, and why AI sped up the operation.

New infrastructure with familiar habits. The BlueNoroff campaign moved to a coordinated cluster of servers, but its naming conventions, delivery commands, and certificate habits tie it directly back to the April activity. We document 98 high-confidence domains, 73 of which had not been previously reported.

How to protect yourself and your organization. We provide a robust Appendix of tips for defenders, including detection opportunities, MITRE ATT&CK® information, YARA rules, and a full list of Indicators of Compromise (IOCs).

Meet BlueNoroff

Back in April, our Adversary Operations team identified and tracked BlueNoroff activity as part of our ongoing threat research investigations. During that process, we uncovered infrastructure, targeting patterns, and operational tactics associated with the group’s campaigns, and realized we had something larger on our hands.

BlueNoroff is a financially motivated subgroup of North Korea’s Lazarus Group, publicly attributed to the DPRK’s Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB). The group has been active since at least 2014 and is highly focused on revenue generation through theft of cryptocurrency and financial assets. BlueNoroff primarily targets individuals with access to, or influence over digital assets, particularly those who have authority and trust, and uses social engineering techniques to gain access to systems, credentials, and digital assets.

In more recent years, the group’s activity has been heavily focused on the Web3 and digital asset ecosystem, and the latest campaign Arctic Wolf observed tells its own story along well-worn lines.

How BlueNoroff Helps Targets Compromise Themselves

We’ve all been there: we’re about to hop on a long-awaited Zoom call with a peer or a prospect when the audio breaks, or the video connection fails. Our blood pressure and stress levels rise as we search for a “quick fix.” That very human response is what BlueNoroff counts on, so they can covertly hand targets the means to infect themselves: a popup that we might expect to see appear while having technical troubles, with helpful instructions that guide the target through running commands or clicking buttons they might ordinarily think twice about interacting with.

The BlueNoroff Cycle of Compromise

In our April report, we showed how BlueNoroff secretly recorded the live webcams of targeted individuals as they tried to fix a fake Teams or Zoom call with no audio. What the targets didn’t know was that all the other “participants” on the call were either deepfakes, static profile pictures scraped from the internet, or pre-recorded stolen footage from other people they knew. As they tried unsuccessfully to fix the call’s audio, their own accounts were covertly compromised and plundered for contacts.

Each newly compromised target yielded real video material to populate future fake meetings, plus contacts for BlueNoroff to reach out to others in the target’s professional circle.

BlueNoroff’s foundational social engineering cycle.

What’s New in This Campaign

Over the last six months or so, Arctic Wolf Labs observed a significant evolution in both the scale and the complexity of this operation. Back in April, through access to the threat actor’s media library, we identified 400+ targets (100 of whom we independently verified) spread over 20 countries. In more recent months, we’ve identified 677 targets across 58 countries, and observed through continuing access to that same media library that BlueNoroff’s social engineering pipeline has changed at both ends.

Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate. Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims’ webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person’s likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves.

BlueNoroff’s updated attack flow (Click to enlarge).

Manipulated Media

Downstream, the “recycling” loop that turns compromised victims into material for the next scam has sped up and improved. By November 2026, production had moved from one editor on one laptop using Adobe Premiere to create basic deepfakes (which we documented back in April), to a full chain of generative AI-based services. BlueNoroff is now using and combining legitimate tools including Google Generative AI, Grok Imagine, Wondershare AIGC and GPT-4o to create a more mature editing workflow, and the videos they produce can no longer be distinguished from genuine webcam footage by visual inspection alone.

As a result, we based all deepfake determinations on provenance evidence rather than appearance. Arctic Wolf uses the U.S. Government Accountability Office definition of a deepfake: video, audio, or imagery generated or manipulated with AI to create, replace, or alter a person’s likeness or synthesize speech. Media edited exclusively with legitimate production tools such as Adobe Premiere Pro, Microsoft Clipchamp, or Wondershare without an observed generative AI step was classified as manually manipulated content rather than a deepfake.

Our forensic analysis of 349 videos in BlueNoroff’s media library flagged as “likely modified” as of November 6. A video with several signatures appears in several ribbons (Click to enlarge).

New Lure Themes

Instead of relying on their previous “fake meeting” ruse, BlueNoroff now leverages multiple lure themes to socially engineer targets and deliver payloads through platform-specific workflows. Although the branding, content, and delivery mechanisms varied, each lure followed the same underlying pattern. The document-themed lures we observed used several related pretexts: a protected file could not be decrypted, a shared document required verification, or the browser’s PDF viewer needed an update.

One of the platform-specific lures we observed used a fake Chrome PDF Viewer that claimed that Chrome’s built-in PDF component could not display a document without an update. Selecting “Update Now” initiated an AppleScript download in the recovered macOS flow. Windows and Linux users were instructed to execute commands that retrieved a payload from a fake Chrome update site set up by the threat actor.

After execution, the page displayed a Chrome-branded “Update Complete” dialog, reproducing the false-success mechanism observed in the earlier fake-meeting intrusions.

Fake Chrome update popup lure created by BlueNoroff. Clicking “Update now” initiates an AppleScript download.

Conclusion

BlueNoroff’s new lures and intrusion scenarios (painted in more detail in our full report) align closely with common workflows in venture fundraising and digital-asset investment, where pitch decks, investment agreements, and restricted documents move between founders, investors, and advisers. By aligning lures with fundraising, investment, scheduling, media, wallet, and security workflows, BlueNoroff places malicious execution inside activities that targets routinely perform.

Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff’s efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships.

While AI is now being used as production multiplier that helps BlueNoroff scale and diversify, it has not fundamentally changed the intrusion mechanism. The campaign still remains dependent on target research, operator engagement, tailored infrastructure, and manual user execution.

Why it Matters

Individual brands, domains, and visuals used as lures by attackers will keep changing. The step they all depend on remains the same: a trusted-looking page asks the target to run something locally, which most often involves a manual step like clicking a button on a popup. That behavior is the most reliable place to disrupt this campaign, and our report includes the detection logic, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, YARA rules, and indicators of compromise to help defenders protect their organizations against these types of social engineering attacks.

The TL;DR takeaway: treat any request to run a command, script, shortcut, or workflow as a red flag, however polished the interaction looks, and confirm unusual requests through a separate, out-of-band known-good channel.

Get the full analysis, detections, and indicators. Download the full report (PDF).

How Arctic Wolf Protects Its Customers

Arctic Wolf is committed to ending cyber risk, and when active campaigns are identified, we move quickly to protect our customers. We have leveraged threat intelligence around this threat activity to enhance detections in the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora® Endpoint Security, subject to customer environment and available telemetry. Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Detection and Response (MDR) provides detection for the PowerShell, curl-piped and osascript execution patterns plus the process-injection and persistence techniques documented in our April report, and the network indicators in our November report.

As this campaign develops, Arctic Wolf may refine detections for additional indicators of compromise and techniques leveraged by this threat.

Recommended Mitigations

While no organization is immune from social engineering attacks, there are steps that can be taken to minimize the likelihood of an intruder succeeding in gaining a foothold. While BlueNoroff’s campaign may seem sophisticated, their attack chain goes nowhere when their intended victim exercises basic security hygiene.

We recommend the following additional mitigations:

Verify unexpected requests. Organizations should focus on teaching employees at every level of the company to exercise caution around unexpected requests of all types, which strengthens internal defenses against social engineering. Train employees to independently verify meeting invitations and identity verification requests through a separate trusted channel.

Beware of third parties bearing gifts. Be wary of “helpful” materials sent by an external contact, particularly PDFs and links to videos and other recordings, even those that seem legitimate or contain known/trusted company and brand names.

Beware of scams that involve fake “fixes.” Be particularly cautious of requests to install software, run scripts, or execute commands, especially during meetings, videos, phone calls, and other seemingly personal interactions that create a sense of urgency.

Provide deepfake training. Train employees to recognize modern social engineering techniques, including the use of AI-generated content and deepfakes by those seeking access to company credentials. For those without the time or resources to create their own training program, the Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness® training solution includes content on fake-meeting and ClickFix social engineering, including a “Report Phish” button.

Recognize leadership as the primary target set. C-suite executives and founders account for 84% of identified targets in the BlueNoroff campaign we observed. Implement strong authentication and access controls for high-risk users, including executives and employees with access to company finances or digital assets.

About Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence enables organizations to leverage the same intelligence that powers the Arctic Wolf Security Operations Center (SOC), delivering real-time data on emerging threats. With curated reporting and real-time threat campaign notifications, businesses stay informed and increase prevention without needing to sift through vast amounts of information.

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence leverages over 8 trillion weekly security observations across 10,000+ customers, spanning industries and geographies, and provides actionable insights in an easy-to-digest format even outside Arctic Wolf. With IoC QuickLinks into Data Explorer, customers can rapidly check their environments for active threats, and take swift action to mitigate risks.

The insights generated can be automatically operationalized across Security Operations technologies, including EDR, SIEM, and network security controls, leveraging industry-standard integrations such as STIX/TAXII and dynamic blocklist APIs to accelerate detection and response. Arctic Wolf’s Threat Intelligence solution is available as an MDR add-on or a standalone deliverable.

General Security News.title: Microsoft Cloud Outage Hits Outlook, Teams, Copilot and AI Services
General Security News.context: However, it later found that increased traffic was not the cause
General Security News.full_text:
A Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot, also breaking OpenAI and Anthropic connectors to Microsoft 365 accounts.

Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams went down for thousands of US users on Thursday, November 12. Reuters reported that the disruption also hit the connectors OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services use to reach Microsoft accounts.

“Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams were down for thousands of US users on Thursday, ​according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com, with the disruption ‌also hitting connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.” Reuters states

Downdetector, which collates status reports from several sources, logged more than 97,000 Outlook incidents at 2:07 p.m. ET. It also recorded more than 38,000 reports of Microsoft 365 problems and about 4,500 for Teams. Reuters notes the number of affected users may vary. Expers observed complaints surge that afternoon across Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive and the Microsoft Store.

In a Microsoft 365 admin center notice (MO1550821), Microsoft warned that users might have trouble accessing several services, including Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR.

Microsoft said the outage started at 1:26 p.m. ET. However, it had already been investigating problems connecting to Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas earlier that day. The company later confirmed that users worldwide could be affected.

Microsoft initially blamed heavy workloads across several regions. However, it later found that increased traffic was not the cause. In an update on X, the company said it was working to safely bring several unavailable servers back online. Their loss was putting extra pressure on the remaining infrastructure.

Its response so far has been to pause all deployments, redistribute connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure and move additional traffic away from affected systems. It’s also restarting the affected servers to restore capacity. In a statement to Reuters, Microsoft said it was aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.

“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” ​states Microsoft.

“We determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We’re working to safely return them to service,” Microsoft wrote on X.

Microsoft first blamed the disruption on high infrastructure demand across several regions. However, it later found that the issue was caused by servers unexpectedly going offline.

Microsoft also reported a separate Teams outage (TM1550488) that affected users in North and South America from 9:45 to 10:53 a.m. ET. Users experienced delays or failures when sending messages, creating or updating conversations, and retrieving chat messages. Microsoft traced the problem to resource contention within its infrastructure, which increased resource usage and prevented Teams from processing messages properly. The company confirmed that the issue has been resolved.

We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365…

— Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026

At this time the massive outage has yet to be resolved. Reuters says Microsoft later told customers the issue may also affect Microsoft 365 connectivity for users in other regions.

The impact also extended to AI services. OpenAI reported problems with its Microsoft connectors, saying new connections might fail and tools might not work properly. Anthropic also reported an issue with its Microsoft 365 connector caused by a problem at an upstream provider. As a result, Copilot and competing AI services were unable to access users’ inboxes because the underlying Microsoft services were unavailable.

IT teams should check the Microsoft 365 admin center for updates rather than make assumptions about the cause. They should also expect emails and messages to be delayed until services fully recover.

General Security News.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
General Security News.context: " The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack
General Security News.full_text: Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ®

General Security News.title: Major Microsoft Outlook Outage Leaves People With Email Jobs Unable to Email
General Security News.context: In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it’s...
General Security News.full_text:
It’s not just you. Microsoft’s 365 business and enterprise services suffered a major outage on Thursday, preventing users of its popular cloud suite from accessing their accounts.

Around 10:40 am ET on Thursday morning, Microsoft posted on its 365 status page on X that it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America.” By just before 1pm ET, it said it was aware of “issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.”

Microsoft later said that its network was also “experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” but that the issue was related to servers going offline, not due to increased traffic.

Around an hour later, Microsoft said it had “begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load” and was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.”

“We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service,” Microsoft wrote.

In an update on its status page, Microsoft said impacted services may include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, and Microsoft Defender XDR.

“We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement. “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."

Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon.

It is currently unclear when the outage may be over or what its cause may be. In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it’s attempting to reboot its systems to hopefully bring them back online.

Outages in cloud services occur frequently, and their causes can vary. Configuration errors, resolution issues with the Domain Name System, and cyberattacks can all cause connection errors. There is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused the current Microsoft outage.

While major Microsoft outages are relatively rare, they are far from unprecedented. In July 2024, a corrupted update from the security firm Crowdstrike knocked out Microsoft Azure services for hours, causing untold millions of dollars in lost revenue due to companies’ inability to function as normal.

Updated 11/12/2026 at 3:05 pm ET: Added comment from Microsoft.

Additional reporting by Matt Burgess.

General Security News.title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 3: Fixing Risk at the Speed of Code
General Security News.context: True AI threat readiness requires an active ASPM strategy that bridges static code with live cloud context to elevate real, exploitable attack paths over theoretical noise
General Security News.full_text:
In parts one and two of this series, we covered how to centralize your AppSec tools and use the Wiz Security Graph to isolate critical attack paths. The natural next step to securing your environment is remediating those risks, but for most AppSec teams, fixing vulnerabilities at scale remains a challenge.

Teams invest heavily in SAST, SCA, Secrets, and DAST scanners, only to generate backlogs that stall after triage. According to the Verizon DBIR, unpatched vulnerabilities remain a top attack vector, with organizations taking a median of 47 days to apply a patch, up from 32 days. Those legacy timelines are no longer viable when AI models are compressing the window from vulnerability discovery to active exploitation.

It’s clear the primary bottleneck in AppSec is not finding the risk, but fixing it fast in the code. Driving rapid remediation requires solving three challenges: knowing exactly which developer owns the fix regardless of the scanner, providing them with the precise context needed to execute the fix, and automating that entire workflow at scale.

In this final instalment, we will explore how Wiz Code accelerates remediation and reduces friction for engineering teams:

Simplified ownership mapping: Identifying the right developer to assign remediation tasks to

Deliver agentic, tailored remediation: Generating step-by-step remediation plans and direct pull requests and coding agent handoffs with the Green Agent.

Automate your response: Orchestrating ticketing, developer alerts, and SLA-driven security campaigns via Wiz Workflows.

Remediation Starts with Ownership Mapping

The first major hurdle in remediation is simply knowing who should do the work. In complex enterprise environments, security teams often struggle to map a running cloud vulnerability back to the developer who wrote the original code. Traditional code scanners only see a repository name, branch, or container digest without understanding organizational structure. Teams often manually maintain mappings of Applications to owners, so optimizing this step can significantly deter mean-time-to-remediation (MTTR).

Because of our agentless connection to your Version Control System (VCS), Wiz traces the cloud asset directly back to the specific repository and commit author.

To ensure accuracy, Wiz resolves ownership by correlating multiple data points across your infrastructure. By analyzing resource tags, cloud logs, CMDB data, code commit history, Service Catalog mappings, and Project ownership, the platform routes Issues to the exact person equipped to act on them.

This is the critical first step for the Wiz Green Agent investigation. Before generating a fix, the agent automatically identifies and suggests the most relevant code owner based on your tiered ownership policies.

Tailored Fixes Grounded in Code to Infrastructure Context

Once the right developer is assigned, the next hurdle is actionable guidance. Developers are focused on shipping features, not researching security findings, but in a DevSecOps model, they’re tasked with remediation. Standard fixes from standalone scanners evaluate isolated files and often recommend generic version bumps. The Wiz Green Agent goes beyond generic LLM guidance by providing multi-step remediation plans tailored to your exact environment based on access to the Security Graph.

This includes fixes for Application Security findings surfaced from third party scanners like Snyk, Checkmarx, Semgrep, and more.

Because the agent understands the full code-to-cloud context, it generates a comprehensive plan to eliminate the root cause. For fixes in code, Developers receive two actionable options:

Create a Pull Request: Wiz generates the exact code fix and opens a Pull Request (PR) directly in your repository for the developer to review and merge.

Send to a Coding Agent: Wiz can share the Green Agent’s remediation guidance with an organization's coding agent like a Claude Code to create a PR for a developer to review.

Automate Remediation Playbooks Where Developers Work

Generating a tailored fix is only helpful if the right developer actually sees it. Developers rarely want to log into a dedicated security platform to understand their task backlog, and nothing erodes trust faster than receiving separate tickets for the same finding from different tools. To accelerate remediation, AppSec teams must meet developers in the tools they already use.

This is where Wiz Workflows serves as your automation engine.

Once anIssue is identified and an owner is mapped, Wiz Workflows can automatically route a ticket directly to Jira, ServiceNow, or your supported ITSM platform of choice. You can also configure workflows to send real-time alerts to specific code owners via Slack or Microsoft Teams. Workflows are a powerful system to allow you to coordinate actions across systems (Wiz or external), within customizable, multi-step workflows.

Crucially, these automated tickets include all the original context from your connected third-party scanners alongside the Green Agent's remediation plan. The assigned developer receives the repository details, component versions, vulnerability data, and cloud/runtime context they need. By delivering complete context directly into their native workspace, you eliminate the need for developers to switch between tools to execute a fix.

Moving from Visibility to AI Threat Readiness

In an era where AI accelerates both code generation and exploit velocity, traditional ASPM tools that simply aggregate alerts leave security teams stranded in triage. True AI threat readiness requires an active ASPM strategy that bridges static code with live cloud context to elevate real, exploitable attack paths over theoretical noise.

Wiz Code delivers this complete operational framework by uniting proprietary and third party scanners, Security Graph risk analysis, and agentic remediation into a single platform. By automating the journey from code ownership to verified pull requests, Wiz Code empowers security teams to fix risk at machine speed and stay ahead of modern threats.

General Security News.title: Webinar: See How Identity Blind Spots Put Your SOC at Risk and How to Close Them
General Security News.context: Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation
General Security News.full_text:
Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access?

A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently.

Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story.

And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem.

Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence.

The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations

Here's the problem.

Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats.

But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities.

When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means.

Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain:

What applications and systems can this account access?

Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network?

How much damage could it cause?

Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process?

These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move.

And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated.

More Identities, More Access, More Risk

Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity.

Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement.

These identities often have access to important systems and data.

If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact.

That's where identity context changes the investigation.

Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations.

📅 Save Your Spot: See how identity context can improve your SOC response in this free webinar.

What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like?

The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts.

It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding.

That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can:

Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved.

See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement.

Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation.

Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals.

The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable.

Learn How to Close the Gap

In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together.

Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems.

It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks.

Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act.

General Security News.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
General Security News.context: First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess
General Security News.full_text: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month, eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort. eMudhra has since left the CA racket, saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue. What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of. eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing. By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task. “Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.” The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers. As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work. “It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo. It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads. “The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.” As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself. “I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained. We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

General Security News.title: The Token Cost of Shell Commands
General Security News.context: Even if an agent later summarizes its history, the initial ingestion of these massive, unfiltered outputs causes severe token spikes
General Security News.full_text:
You asked your AI coding agent to debug a simple test failure, and it somehow ended up recursively reading your entire .git/objects history. If your API bills are climbing while your agent seemingly just browses your codebase, you aren’t alone.

Developers often blame the LLM model choice or a poorly written system prompt. But the real budget killer is input context. Your agent isn’t paying to think, it’s paying to re-read a 4,000-line grep output it already understood six turns ago. The biggest culprits are everyday shell commands developers have used for decades without a second thought.

Why Do Shell Commands Break AI Agent Budgets?

Shell commands like ls, find, and grep were built for humans, and human brains filter out terminal noise automatically to find the one line that matters. AI coding agents don’t have that filter. They process raw terminal output as billable context. Even if an agent later summarizes its history, the initial ingestion of these massive, unfiltered outputs causes severe token spikes.

As autonomous coding agents move from simple autocomplete into planning and executing multi-step workflows over a terminal, they call these commands again and again. Each call adds tokens that build up rapidly until the session ends or the agent compacts its history. The gap between a human skimming an output and an agent absorbing every character of it is where your budget gets burned.

The three everyday culprits

Alongside verbose test logs, these three ordinary shell commands are frequent sources of the runaway costs that agentic workflows can rack up. Recognizing them is the first step toward controlling them.

ls, the directory dump: An agent asks what’s in a directory and runs ls -la. In a small folder, that’s harmless. In the root of a monorepo, that single command can dump tens of thousands of tokens of permissions, timestamps, file sizes, and hidden files nobody asked for.

find, the infinite tree: Asked “where is the database configuration?”, an agent runs find . -name "*.yaml". Without depth limits, find recursively walks every hidden folder, cache directory, and build artifact path it can reach.

grep, the context killer: An agent hunting for a function call runs grep -r "processPayment". Left unconstrained, it can return minified JavaScript, binary garbage, and endless test-mock data. Worse, if it matches a 10,000-character line in a generated JSON file, that entire line lands in the prompt.

Each of these commands is safe in isolation and expensive at scale, which is exactly why they slip past code review unnoticed.

Why Doesn’t Blind Truncation Fix the Problem?

Blindly truncating shell output (i.e. just capping every command at 1,000 tokens) sounds like a quick fix, but it quietly breaks the agent’s ability to reason about what it’s looking at.

If you silently truncate a grep output, the agent may not know it received partial results. It may assumes the results don’t exist. From there, it can guess, hallucinate, or spiral. In our internal testing, agents re-ran the same ls command up to six times trying to re-establish where they were in the filesystem.

An optimizer the agent can’t detect is an optimizer you can’t debug. Any compression layer you build has to tell the agent what it’s not seeing, or you’ve traded a cost problem for a correctness problem. This is the exact failure mode a token-compression tool like JFrog Boost is built to avoid. It compresses output and tells the agent when it has done so, so the agent can request the full output.

The Snowball Effect: How One Bad Command Multiplies

This is the most easily missed cost in agentic workflows: a bad command isn’t paid for once. Because of how multi-turn LLM conversations typically work, prior turns’ tokens are resent with each new message until the session ends, the agent compacts its history, or the session hits its context limit.

That resend behavior turns small waste into compounding waste. The value of trimming a command’s output isn’t just the tokens you cut, it’s those tokens multiplied by the number of turns they would otherwise have sat in context. For instance, a 3,000-token log removed at turn four of a 40-turn session isn’t a 3,000-token saving.Before prompt caching or history compaction, it’s more than 100,000 input tokens avoided over the life of that session.

Scenario

Illustrative calculation. Assumes no prompt caching or history compaction.

The earlier a command’s output gets optimized, the more that optimization is worth because it avoids being re-processed on every subsequent turn, not just the current one. Note: Prompt caching can reduce some re-processing costs, but cache lifetimes and discounts vary by provider and model, and cached tokens are still billed. In our view, caching complements output optimization rather than replacing it.

At list prices as of October 2026, 100,000 input tokens cost roughly $0.15 to $0.30 on models such as GPT-5 or Claude Sonnet 5, before caching or batch discounts. That sounds cheap until it repeats. If each of 50 daily debugging sessions wastes about 100,000 input tokens on noise, that adds up to roughly $200 to $300 a month at those rates. Suddenly, a team is burning hundreds of dollars a month letting an AI agent stare at hidden cache directories.

Key insight: Saving 2,000 tokens on an early grep command can save far more than the same cut late in the session, because those 2,000 tokens would otherwise be re-processed on every later turn.

How Can You Stop Shell Commands from Draining Your Token Budget?

If you’re building agentic workflows, MCP servers, or custom developer tools, you need an optimization layer that trims noise without blinding the LLM to what it’s missing. JFrog Boost, a free CLI wrapper currently in public preview, is built around four rules for optimization that any team can adopt even without the tool itself.

Force constraints by default. Where your agent setup allows it, route shell commands through wrapped versions instead of raw commands. Expose wrapped versions or aliases that enforce limits automatically — a safe ls that forces ls -1 (names only) instead of ls -la, and a safe find that enforces depth limits, such as find . -maxdepth 2 -name "*.ts".

Tell the agent what you filtered. If a 10,000-line log has to be truncated, don’t do it silently. Append a system message to the output so the agent knows a summary, not the full picture, is in front of it.

Provide a recovery hatch. Give the agent a specific tool, such as cat_full_file <path>, so it can explicitly request the dropped data instead of hallucinating an answer.

Instrument the recovery path. Track how often the agent actually uses that recovery hatch. In our view, your retrieve rate is a better measure of a tool’s usability than your compression ratio alone.

Applying these rules consistently helps keep an agent’s context lean without leaving it guessing about what it can’t see.

Building a Safer Tool Wrapper That Reduces Injection Risk

To make this concrete, let’s look at how to implement Rule 1 (forcing safe constraints). Instead of letting the AI agent execute grep directly on your operating system, we create a Python function that acts as a “wrapper” around the command.

This wrapper intercepts the agent’s request, makes the command safe, runs it, and then filters the output before sending it back to the LLM. Here’s how JFrog Boost and similar tools build these baseline patterns, broken down step-by-step:

Step 1: Pass the Command Arguments as a List. First, we construct the command. Instead of passing a single string to the shell (which can expose you to command injection), we pass a list of separate arguments. We also force grep to ignore notorious token-wasting directories like .git and node_modules.

import subprocess def safe_grep(search_term: str, directory: str = "."): """"Illustrative agent tool for searching a codebase with output limits.""" # 1. Passing arguments as a list (no shell) reduces command-injection risk cmd = [ "grep", "-r", "-n", "-I", "--exclude-dir=.git", "--exclude-dir=node_modules", "--exclude-dir=dist", "-e", search_term, "--", directory, ]

Step 2: Execute Safely and Capture Output. Next, we run the command. We explicitly set check=False so that if grep finds nothing (which returns a non-zero exit code), it simply returns an empty string rather than crashing our entire agent loop.

try: # 2. Execute without shell=True result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False) output = result.stdout

Step 3: Enforce Limits and Add the Recovery Hatch. Finally, we check the length of the output. If it exceeds our token limit (roughly 8,000 characters), we truncate it. Crucially, we append a [System] note directly to the output. This tells the LLM exactly what happened and gives it the exact tool command (cat_file) it needs to use if it genuinely needs to read the rest of the file.

# 3. Token limit safeguard (~2000 tokens) char_limit = 8000 if len(output) > char_limit: truncated_output = output[:char_limit] # 4. Tell the agent what happened and provide the recovery hatch return ( f"{truncated_output}\n\n" "[System: Output truncated. Use `cat_file` for specific files.]" ) return output except Exception as e: return f"[System Error: {str(e)}]"

This wrapper passes arguments as a list instead of a shell string, which reduces shell command-injection risk, and it pairs each truncation with an explicit note the agent can act on. Production versions should also limit which paths the agent can search and run with the least privileges needed. An agent’s outputs are only as trustworthy and cost-effective as what it’s allowed to consume; don’t let a stray shell command break that trust.

How JFrog Boost Helps: Build and Scale Agents with Confidence

Manually wrapping every shell command is a reasonable starting point, but it doesn’t scale across a team running dozens of agentic workflows a day. JFrog Boost, currently in public preview, is designed to apply these rules automatically: it’s a free CLI wrapper that compresses noisy command output before it reaches agents like Cursor, Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot. JFrog Boost is designed to strip irrelevant noise from test runs and searches while preserving failures, summaries, and other signal agents typically need.

This is why JFrog Boost targets compression at the command level, right where the output first enters context, instead of trying to clean up the conversation after the damage compounds.

Paired with that kind of compression layer, the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform gives teams a single system of record for the artifacts, packages, and binaries their agents touch.

General Security News.title: From AI ambition to business impact
General Security News.context: They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning
General Security News.full_text:
Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs?

That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries.

Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams.

More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning.

The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together.

What this looks like in practice

Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations.

3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations.

Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees.

Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing. Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service.

KT, one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions.

Saint-Gobain, the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab.

Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same:

Begin with the value, not the technology.

Redesign the process, not just the task.

Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams.

Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one, so scaling doesn’t stall.

This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time.

New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact.

We’re holding ourselves to the same standard

If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to.

The real measure of success

The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build.

Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours.

Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company.

Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world.
