General Security News.title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
General Security News.context: “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information...
General Security News.full_text:
Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC, commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain.

In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale.

What the research found

Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters.

Measurement is the next test. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms.

Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks.

Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy.

“Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC.

AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings

Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses.

Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability.

Where scale stalls

66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them.

The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design.

Inside the Frontier Firm

IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause.

What they do differently comes down to five behaviors:

They invest ahead of plan. 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend.

They deploy AI broadly, across most of the business, not just a few teams.

They put agents to work. 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows.

They govern so they can scale. 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters.

They build skills everywhere. 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters.

At Bristol Myers Squibb, the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time.

Four disciplines for scaling AI value

The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off.

I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER. “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.”

Unlock model choice

Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data.

Redesign workflows around agents

Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters.

Govern decisions and actions

Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do.

Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.”

Measure and optimize value

Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest.

Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start.

Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch.

Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite

IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall.

What this means for business

The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation.

First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day.

Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business.

Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI.

The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next.

Get the full picture

Download the global infographic, The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe, Asia Pacific and the Americas. The full InfoBrief will follow.

Alysa Taylor is the Chief Marketing Officer for Commercial Cloud and AI at Microsoft, leading teams that enable digital and AI transformation for organizations of all sizes across the globe.

General Security News.title: Your Endpoint Management Platform Could Be Your Biggest Security Risk
General Security News.context: An attacker exploiting a vulnerability in the underlying system, compromising a privileged service, or hijacking an authenticated administrative session may be granted the...
General Security News.full_text:
Author: Gene Moody, Field CTO at Action1

Endpoint management platforms have become essential in modern IT operations and enterprise security. They allow administrators to deploy patches, install software, execute scripts, enforce configurations, and remotely manage thousands of devices from a centralized system.

Without these types of systems, maintaining consistent security across large environments would be extremely difficult and labor-intensive.

However, the administrative authority that makes these platforms valuable also makes them very attractive targets for attackers. An endpoint management platform already has established and approved communication channels, elevated permissions, and trusted relationships with the devices it manages.

Any attacker who gains control of that infrastructure will be able to use those existing capabilities to distribute malware, execute malicious commands, disable security controls, or disrupt operations across an entire organization. All with the same level of authority as the real admin.

The same capabilities that allow an administrator to secure thousands of endpoints can allow an attacker to compromise them.

When trusted management infrastructure is compromised

Recent incidents demonstrate how compromised remote management infrastructure can extend attacks across compromised environments.

In 2026, Huntress documented attackers abusing compromised BeyondTrust Bomgar remote support infrastructure to deploy ransomware and access downstream organizations. In 2025, ransomware operators compromised an MSP's SimpleHelp platform, using its existing management capabilities to access protected systems, steal information, and deploy ransomware.

Similarly, in 2024, attackers exploited ConnectWise ScreenConnect vulnerabilities, with investigators documenting Play ransomware deployment through a compromised MSP instance. And who will forget the 2024 incident abusing Microsoft Intune to remotely wipe hundreds of thousands of corporate devices at Stryker!

In each of these cases, attackers exploited the administrative reach of infrastructure already trusted by the organization. The incidents warn us why protecting systems against the management platforms’ misuse is essential, and why independently verifying sensitive endpoint operations can help limit the consequences of a successful compromise.

These attacks against centralized management and software distribution systems often lead to compromise well beyond the initially compromised infrastructure.

For cloud-hosted platforms, the security of the provider's hosting environment, management services, and software delivery mechanisms becomes particularly important. A compromise there may affect multiple environments simultaneously.

Why traditional security controls have limitations

Multi-factor authentication, role-based access controls, privileged access management, and activity monitoring are bare minimum safeguards. They help restrict administrative access, limit permissions, and identify suspicious behavior.

However, these protections primarily operate within the management platform's security boundaries.

An attacker exploiting a vulnerability in the underlying system, compromising a privileged service, or hijacking an authenticated administrative session may be granted the ability to issue commands that endpoints recognize as legitimate. Because they are impersonating a user, and the restriction is BY user.

Even with strong authentication and carefully configured permissions, the endpoint may have no independent way to determine whether a sensitive instruction was explicitly approved by a legitimate administrator.

This security implication is: high-risk endpoint operations should have authorization that remains verifiable independently of the management platform delivering them!

Adding owner-controlled authorization

Cryptographically verified authorization, independent of anything the platform stores or directly handles, provides the platform a way to establish that independent security boundary.

Under this approach, sensitive endpoint operations require authorization signed using a private cryptographic key controlled only by the legitimate admin. The endpoint independently verifies the signature before executing the protected instruction. The management platform can continue coordinating and delivering administrative operations, while the authority to approve protected actions remains separately controlled.

An attacker who compromises the management infrastructure cannot simply create valid authorizations without obtaining the owner’s signing key or compromising the verification process.

Action1 implements this approach through Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP).

ETP uses customer-controlled cryptographic authorization to protect high-risk operations, including script execution, software deployment, automations, and remote sessions.

Because the private authorization key is maintained independently of Action1's cloud infrastructure, a compromise of the management platform alone does not provide the ability to authorize these protected actions.

Keep Attackers from Taking Over Your Endpoints

Action1's Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP) protects high-risk endpoint actions with customer-controlled cryptographic authorization, even if the management platform is compromised.

Take control of endpoint security with Action1. Your first 200 endpoints are free forever.

Start Now

Of course, the effectiveness of this protection depends on secure key management, endpoint integrity, and appropriate configuration of protected operations, but that becomes customer responsibility by becoming customer privilege. It is protected by a key they, and only they control.

Securing an essential part of enterprise IT

Endpoint management platforms will continue to be essential parts of modern infrastructure by maintaining secure and operationally manageable environments. But they now demand particularly strong safeguards against compromise and abuse. We have new threat metrics, we need new defense metrics,

Organizations should re-evaluate how these platforms are secured, how suspicious activity is monitored, and which protections remain effective if management infrastructure is compromised. Practice failure, so when it happens you can understand it, and contain it more effectively.

Customer-controlled cryptographic authorization adds a crucial layer by ensuring that sensitive endpoint operations require independently verifiable approval.

Protect your endpoints from management platform compromise with Action1 Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP). Keep sensitive operations under your control with customer-owned cryptographic authorization, even if the management platform is compromised.

The goal is to preserve the administrative power organizations depend on while keeping the authority to approve its most sensitive uses under the owner’s control.

General Security News.title: Apple’s HomeView Tries Face Authentication Without FaceID
General Security News.context: “This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post
General Security News.full_text:
Apple's HomeView, which debuts on Friday, is a smart home device—think of it as a an iPhone-Apple Watch hybrid sitting on your counter—that can be personalized for up to six people and connected to each of their iCloud accounts. Using ambient face and voice data, it is designed to seamlessly switch between users while maintaining each of their privacy. You can ask HomeView about your schedule for the day and what movie your friend recommended in a text, but you'll be stopped from asking about your roommate's travel plans or her texts from last night. The feature doesn't rely on one of Apple's battle-tested biometric locks, like FaceID or TouchID, though. Instead, it uses new “person recognition” technology built off of an Apple architecture for securing sensor data.

This is a key departure for Apple. On the one hand, the company has still been very careful to think about security and privacy comprehensively. Not only does HomeView check for your face and voice before accessing your data from iCloud, it is also designed like an Apple Watch to check that your iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView and has been recently unlocked (with FaceID or a PIN). On the other hand, expanding the architecture used to process biometric data and authenticate users creates more opportunities for mistakes and potential vulnerabilities. And when it comes to attempting to access users' Apple data, both law enforcement and exploit brokers consistently go to great lengths to attempt to break the company's on-device defenses.

FaceID is built for the use case where a person is staring at their device head-on from less than an arm's length away. It provides reliable security that’s difficult to defeat because it stores your biometric data on a special, physically isolated chip known as the Secure Enclave—first introduced in 2013 for the iPhone 5s. The architecture is so robust that Apple also relies on the Secure Enclave as the foundation of a device's entire encryption scheme. But Apple concluded that FaceID wasn't the best fit for the HomeView, because it needs to bounce quickly between users and relies on AI processing, which can't all be squeezed into the Secure Enclave.

As a result, HomeView uses Apple's recently announced Secure Exclave (note the “x”) to handle the video and audio data the device uses to evaluate who is in a room at a given time. Apple says it has actually been laying the groundwork for the Secure Exclave for a long time—early versions of the architecture were already in place for the iPhone 16 and 17 and MacBook Neo. Instead of being an entirely separately chip, the Secure Exclave is a dedicated, memory-protected space in recent Apple processors. It is in Apple's latest S11 chip for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, as well as the A20 Pro chip for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

Even though the Secure Exclave isn't based on the tried and true Secure Enclave technology, Apple argues that it is robust and expands the company's ability to secure a range of features, including improving the security of existing mechanisms. In a blog post on Thursday, the company even goes into some detail about how it used the mathematical technique known as formal verification to vet the “microkernel” designed for the Secure Exclave.

“This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks.”

HomeView and the MacBook Neo also use the Secure Exclave to govern the indicator light that tells users when their camera or microphone is active. The goal is to isolate this process and the chain of command governing it to make it even more difficult for attackers to try to disable an indicator light when it should be on or stop it from coming on in the first place.

The HomeView's “person recognition” technology is simply not as comprehensive as FaceID, though, and it is possible that the technology is more susceptible to reconstructed 3D depth map attacks—and potentially voiceprint attacks—than FaceID.

Of course, you don't have to have a HomeView in your house. Or if you do, you can use it on guest mode or a less involved “personalized” mode that only incorporates things like your playlists for other users to access as well and doesn't access calendar or Messages data. But as Apple forges deeper into AI integration, HomeView's departure from FaceID provides insight into the scale of the changes Apple is planning.

General Security News.title: Lego Takes BrickLink Marketplace Offline After Detecting Unusual Activity
General Security News.context: In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to...
General Security News.full_text:
Lego Group has taken its BrickLink Marketplace offline after identifying “unusual activity” on the platform.

An update was posted on November 11 by the Danish toy firm which said, “Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.”

The company is currently investigating the activity and said it needs to “fully understand” what has happened before bringing the site back online.

“That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.”

It is not yet known how long the downtime is expected to last and when the service will be reinstated.

BrickLink is an online marketplace owned by Lego Group where independent third-party sellers can buy and sell individual Lego parts – like eBay for Lego. Lego Group acquired the online marketplace in 2019.

The Lego marketplace has previously found itself at the center of security issues. In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to internal production data. Lego resolved the issues after Salt Labs disclosed the issues to the toy firm.

In November 2023 BrickLink was taken offline for a number of days due to a suspected cybersecurity incident.

Professional Lego reviewer Jay Ong, who runs Jay’s Bricks Blog, covered the downtime and noted that users were prompted to update their passwords. However, in an email he received at the time of the incident, he was reassured that his BrickLink account had not been compromised.

General Security News.title: EY Cyprus recognized as the winner of 2026 Microsoft Partner of the Year
A Single Branch No Longer Operates in A Single Place
General Security News.context: Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools
General Security News.full_text:
Branch Traffic Has Changed. Security Has to Follow.

A traditional branch was simple in nature: a location that connects back to headquarters where applications, data, and security controls were housed. Today the landscape is wildly different. A branch may connect directly to SaaS apps, clouds, data centers, the open internet, and other locations within the enterprise. And while all those connections are being made, often many at one time, employees expect video calls and cloud applications to perform just as well in the office as they do at home.

The branch itself has become more complex, too. Connected devices can range from printers and ‘smart building’ systems to specialized IoT equipment. Employees may also access AI applications and services directly from the network. And many branch locations are expected to manage all of this without dedicated security personnel on site.

Routing all that activity back through headquarters can introduce unnecessary latency and cost. However, without the right controls you’re opening yourself up to new exposure. The modern branch needs connectivity, protection, and resilience to work together.

Now is the Time for Connectivity to Adapt to the Application

Not every application needs the same network path.

Video calls? Highly sensitive to latency and packet loss. Large backup transfers? Often prioritize cost over speed. Internal business applications? Might need an encrypted route back to a data center.

Software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN) gives organizations more control over those decisions because, rather than relying on one fixed route, SD-WAN can evaluate available connections and steer traffic based on the application, business policy, and real-time network conditions.

Multiple links can add another layer of resilience. If one connection degrades or fails, traffic can move to a healthier path automatically. But branch continuity depends on more than WAN alone. Firewall clustering and hardware redundancy can help keep both connectivity and protection available when individual components fail.

For businesses that depend on real-time transactions, voice and video, cloud apps, or always-on access to corporate resources, that resilience helps keep a local issue from becoming a larger business interruption.

The Branch Has Become A Bigger Security Surface

Direct internet access improves performance, but it also changes where traffic needs to be inspected and protected. Branch firewalls increasingly need to secure traffic locally while supporting the same high-bandwidth applications they are helping accelerate.

And the risk now extends well beyond internet traffic: printers, cameras, building systems, medical devices, and industrial equipment can all expand the internal attack surface. Many of those devices were never designed with modern cybersecurity in mind, making visibility, segmentation, and threat prevention increasingly important inside the branch as well as at its perimeter.

And of course AI adds another consideration entirely. Employees may use third-party AI applications, agents, or connected tools directly from the branch. Security teams need visibility into that activity and the ability to apply policy, including controls that help prevent sensitive data from being shared through prompts. Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools. Branch security therefore needs strong prevention at the point where traffic is already being inspected, rather than relying on another, additional layer.

Every Branch Should Be Easier to Operate

A distributed enterprise may have dozens, hundreds, or thousands of locations. Managing each branch as its own network creates complexity that grows exponentially with every new site that needs to fit within the existing architecture.

Centralized policy, zero-touch provisioning, network-health monitoring, and unified visibility can make branches easier to deploy and manage while keeping protection more consistent across locations.

That matters especially when there is no security specialist sitting at every branch. Centralized management allows teams to deploy and maintain protection across large numbers of sites without turning every new location, policy change, or connectivity issue into an on-site project.

Bring Connectivity and Security Together at the Branch

Hybrid Mesh Network Security connects the branch with the security architecture protecting data centers, clouds, applications, and users across the enterprise.

Check Point Firewall combines advanced threat prevention with Check Point SD-WAN to help organizations protect branch traffic while optimizing how applications connect. AI security at the firewall adds visibility and policy controls for employee AI usage, while centralized management and zero-touch deployment help maintain consistent protection across distributed locations.

Integration with Check Point SASE extends that approach beyond the branch, helping connect users and locations to the applications and resources they need while keeping branch security part of the broader enterprise architecture.

Organizations who prefer a hybrid security approach can benefit from a hybrid SASE deployment. This way, they can cater to remote users with cloud-based security (SSE) connected to on-prem SD WAN, and also protect office users through network firewalls embedded with SD WAN for optimized branch connectivity.

General Security News.title: When Coding Agents Inherit Your Pipeline’s Permissions
General Security News.context: Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds
General Security News.full_text:
What you will learn

How coding agents borrow the permissions of your CI/CD pipeline, why enforcement is thinnest in those environments and how to scope agents to the task, treat pipelines as privileged identities and check each action at runtime.

A coding agent working in PocketOS’s staging environment hit a credential error, found an unrelated API token and used it to delete the production database and the backups stored alongside it.

Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds.

Most of the conversation about coding agents is about the code they write, but engineering and security leaders need to be able to say what an agent can set in motion, and whose authority it uses when it does.

Enforcement is thinnest where AI agents do their work

In Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition, 2,254 IT and security leaders told us where AI access is checked at the moment of action, before the action runs. CI/CD pipelines came in at 35% and Kubernetes at 28%, the lowest of the six environments we asked about. And 47% of organizations lack enforcement at the moment of action across at least two of the six.

Those are the environments developers hand off to agents first, and they're where deploy roles, cluster permissions, and production credentials live.

The agent doesn’t need the prod credential

Say you ask an agent to bump a service in staging. It updates the deploy workflow and opens a pull request. On GitHub, a pull request from a branch in the same repo runs the workflow as modified in that PR. If the workflow can pick up the pipeline’s cloud role, and that role reaches prod as well as staging, the agent’s edit now has production authority behind it.

The agent never touched a prod credential. It borrowed the pipeline’s.

Over-scoped CI roles were a problem long before agents showed up. Workflows branch too, but someone wrote and reviewed every branch. An agent can write a new one and trigger it in the same session.

Permissions that were safe for a predictable job become much broader once the identity using them can improvise

Identity has to follow the action

Security teams already know how to limit privileged access. Agents need those same controls applied to each action because they decide what to do next on their own.

Scope the agent to the task, not the person who launched it. You might be allowed to query the production database, but your agent shouldn’t inherit that because you started it. A policy that can tell the two apart lets your query through and stops the same query when the agent sends it.

Treat the pipeline as a privileged identity. The deploy role is what actually touches prod, so it deserves the scrutiny you’d give an admin account: one role per environment, and a human review before anything reaches production.

Keep enforcing policy after access is granted. Authentication only checks who's connecting, so a command an agent runs 40 minutes into the session goes through unchecked. Access should exist only while the task needs it, and each consequential action should be checked against policy before it runs.

Where Delinea fits

Delinea extends Privileged Access Management from the point of access to the moment of action. For the connections it brokers, including databases, servers, Kubernetes and MCP tools, access is granted just-in-time for the task, and in a brokered session the credential is injected at the proxy so it never reaches the agent. Each query, command and tool call is checked at runtime, and one that’s out of scope doesn’t run.

Start with one agent-assisted workflow

Pick one agent-assisted workflow and trace it to production. List each identity it touches, from the agent to the runner to the deploy role to the cluster, and what each one is allowed to do. Then find the point where a production action from a staging task would be stopped. If the answer is “we’d catch it in the logs,” you’ve found your gap.

Microsoft: Recent Windows updates cause SQL Server performance issues
General Security News.context: Microsoft has confirmed that Windows updates released since the October 2026 Patch Tuesday are causing SQL Server performance and stability issues
General Security News.full_text:
Microsoft has confirmed that Windows updates released since the October 2026 Patch Tuesday are causing SQL Server performance and stability issues.

As detailed in a Windows release health dashboard update on Wednesday, this is caused by server queries that leave connections open after the queries complete. These connections accumulate instead of closing, degrading server performance over time.

"This issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. Oracle and PostgreSQL connections are among those known to be affected," Microsoft explained.

"In affected environments, administrators might observe an increasing number of open connections to external databases, even when the associated SQL Server linked server queries are no longer running."

It also added that admins may be able to manually close connections left open due to this bug or restart the SQL service to temporarily address stability and performance issues, but this can also kill active queries and may not fully address the issue, as it will resurface again after some time.

Microsoft says the issues impact both client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) and server (Windows Server 2012 and later) systems and will be fixed with an out-of-band Windows update to be released over the next few days.

While it works to resolve the bug, Microsoft said IT administrators can reach out to Microsoft Support for Business for a mitigation that can address the issue until a fix is available.

In September, Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for SQL Server crashes on some Windows Server 2025 due to recent memory management changes.

The bug affects SQL Server when the Lock Pages in Memory (LPIM) Windows policy is enabled and may cause SQL Server crash dumps, SQL Server services to stop or restart unexpectedly, failures during database maintenance operations, memory corruption errors, and access violation exceptions (with 0xC0000005 error codes).

Yesterday, the company also confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to deploy on Windows 11 systems where the October preview update has been installed, with affected users seeing 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993 error codes.

General Security News.full_text:
Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones

Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police.

The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg.

General Security News.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
General Security News.context: NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to...
General Security News.full_text: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic. ®

General Security News.title: Beyond Storage: Your Repository as Software Inventory
General Security News.context: But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job
General Security News.full_text:
Repositories give teams a managed source for build inputs. They proxy public registries, host internal components, and cache packages.

That work remains essential. But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job.

A typical build may pull in open source packages, container images, internal libraries, build tools, and models. Those inputs can enter in several ways:

A developer selects a package or library.

A pipeline retrieves a component.

An AI agent adds a dependency while changing code.

A package manager resolves additional components required by another library.

Because many requests happen automatically, teams need to understand what is available through the repository path and manage the inputs that pass through it. A repository used as a common source can provide that operational inventory.

From Artifact Storage to Software Inventory

A repository inventory describes the artifacts available through a managed source: the formats and versions present, and the assets associated with them.

Sonatype Nexus Repository gives teams a shared view of components available through managed repositories.

That view can help answer questions such as:

Which packages, containers, models, and build artifacts are available through managed repositories?

Which versions are hosted or cached?

Do developers, pipelines, and agents have a common route to obtain software?

Can teams apply consistent policies and block known malicious packages before they are served?

Consider a routine library update. An engineer needs to know which versions are available through the team's standard source. When groups rely on separate proxies or caches, that information may be scattered. A shared repository gives teams a common place to check.

Know What the Repository Inventory Covers

A component appearing in Nexus Repository does not necessarily mean it is included in a deployed application. It means the component is managed or available through the repository. Build records or software bills of materials (SBOMs) identify what went into a specific application or release.

These views answer different but related questions. The repository inventory helps teams manage the shared supply path, and build records help them understand a particular application's inputs.

That distinction also gives teams a place to start an investigation. If a package is flagged, they can check whether it is managed or available through Nexus Repository, then consult build records to determine if a specific application included it.

Software Delivery Starts With What Teams Pull

Most applications depend on components their teams did not write. A developer might add a framework, then a package manager resolves its dependencies.

Each component can affect the application in different ways:

Compatibility: Dependencies may conflict or require specific versions.

Maintenance: Older or unsupported components create upgrade work.

Security: A malicious component requires investigation and response after it enters development.

When these issues surface after development begins, replacing a component can mean code changes, retesting, and release delays.

AI tools can add or update dependencies while changing code, increasing the pace of these choices. A faster request does not tell a team whether or not a component is compatible, maintained, or appropriate for the application. Teams need enough context to assess those choices before they create work downstream.

Make Centralized Access the Trusted Default

A shared repository gives teams a consistent place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs their workflows need. Developers and pipelines can use a managed route that supports their existing package managers and build tools, instead of relying on separate collections of external sources.

In day-to-day work, that shared route gives teams a common way to:

Retrieve components and resolve dependencies through the organization's configured source.

Manage the software supply chain used by multiple groups, rather than having each team create its own process.

Route AI agent dependency requests through the same access and intake controls used for other development activity.

Configure supported formats in a shared repository, giving new projects a starting point instead of another one-off source.

Centralizing access does not automatically cover packages downloaded directly from a public registry or through an unconfigured source. Teams need to route the requests they want managed through Nexus Repository. Then it can serve as a common point for understanding the inputs it handles and applying controls to them.

Block Known Malicious Packages Before They Reach the Build

Nexus Repository sits between upstream sources and the developers, pipelines, and agents requesting software. In the Pro+ and Enterprise editions, malicious package protection and configurable policies can block known malicious packages when requests pass through a protected repository path, before Nexus serves them downstream.

If a malicious package reaches a development environment, teams may need to remove it from the repository if it is still available, then:

Identify which developers, pipelines, or agents retrieved and used the package, and assess what systems or data may be affected.

Assess which systems or credentials it could access.

Determine whether builds or releases incorporated it, and assess downstream exposure.

Blocking the package at the repository can prevent that specific input from becoming part of a downstream investigation. Developers also do not have to identify every suspicious package name or track each campaign themselves. Protection applies where component requests already flow.

Repository protection does not address every dependency or application risk. A component can cause compatibility problems without being malicious, so teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. For dependency decisions and remediation, Sonatype Guide brings intelligence into developer and AI coding workflows to inform component choices and help automate dependency upgrades.

Within the broader Nexus One platform, Guide complements repository protection: developers and agents get support for choosing and updating dependencies, while Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can block known malicious packages and packages flagged as suspicious, even before they are confirmed as malicious at the repository request point.

Make the Repository Part of Delivery Infrastructure

A reliable software supply chain depends on more than where artifacts are stored. Teams need a consistent way to find the components their workflows can use, manage the route those components take, and keep known malicious packages out.

Nexus Repository provides a shared source for the software inputs it manages. Its Pro+ and Enterprise editions add protection that can block known malicious packages at the point where components enter the managed path. Together, these capabilities give teams both a clearer view of available inputs and a way to stop a known threat before it reaches a build.

As developers and AI agents make more requests, that combination becomes more useful. Teams can make software available through a common route, apply consistent controls to incoming requests, and understand the limits of what the repository inventory shows.

Know what your teams can get through the repository. Make trusted access the default. Block known malicious packages before they become part of the work.

General Security News.full_text:
Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027: Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline

November 12, 2026

Kyle Koppe

BLOG

5 min.

Have you been wondering what the prevailing cloud security best practices for 2027 might be? Unlike years past, 2027 is set to center around the data-to-AI pipeline. Data platforms, AI services and autonomous agents now run side by side across multiple clouds and the data moving between them carries the most business value and the biggest security risk. Organizations planning their 2027 security programs need practices that protect that entire movement, not just the environments on either end.

TL;DR – A critical cloud security best practice for 2027 is going to center around securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system, with protection and access policies following data from collection through model training, deployment and agentic AI use.

Key takeaways:

Own the configuration. Under the shared responsibility model, organizations are responsible for securing the AI and data services they use and default settings need tuning to each environment.

Enforce through architecture. Policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code and automated guardrails turn security strategy into controls that hold up at scale.

Start with a baseline and build from there. Assess, plan and engineer pipeline security as a holistic motion, starting from wherever you are and building toward a scalable architecture that’s ready for what comes next.

Six Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027

Data teams and AI teams often work on different platforms with different priorities. Similarly, security programs have traditionally treated data security and AI security as separate disciplines. Moving into the coming year, organizations that secure the pipeline end-to-end will allow protection and access policies to carry forward as information moves between environments. This strategy allows them to enable new AI workloads to come online quickly without sacrificing security.

By following six interconnected practices, organizations can strengthen each individual layer of the cloud environment and then connect them into a cohesive, policy-driven foundation.

1. Treat Shared Responsibility as an AI Practice

Under the cloud shared responsibility model, the customer owns the security configuration of services such as Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker and Google Gemini Enterprise (Vertex AI). These services ship with default settings designed for broad use. Organizations should review and tune access controls, content filtering and model permissions to match their own data, risk tolerance and compliance obligations.

2. Classify Data Before AI Consumes It

Sensitive data discovery and classification work best when they happen early. Data security posture management (DSPM) gives teams visibility into where sensitive information lives, who can reach it and how it moves, so they can apply protection before data reaches a model or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application.

3. Enforce Policy as Code

Documented policies only reduce risk when they are enforced. Policy-as-code and infrastructure-as-code let teams define security requirements once and apply them consistently across every environment, pipeline and deployment, which keeps controls aligned as cloud footprints grow.

4. Govern Every Identity, Human and Non-Human

AI workloads and agents act as identities in the cloud and they can accumulate permissions quickly. Mapping entitlements, enforcing least privilege and reviewing privileged access for data and AI administrators help limit the reach of any single account or agent.

5. Build Compliance Into the Architecture

AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and the CSA AI Controls Matrix sit alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS. Aligning architecture to these frameworks from the start creates audit-ready governance and reduces rework as new regulations take effect.

6. Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline as One System

This is the practice the others point toward. Before data reaches a model or agent, teams copy, combine and transform it across databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines. At each stage, organizations need to preserve data integrity, understand sensitivity and origin and limit access to sensitive information.

GuidePoint cloud experts translate governance requirements into enforceable controls such as encryption, access policies, content filtering and model access restrictions.

AI Services: Strengthen AI platform configuration, machine learning operations (MLOps) pipeline integrity and policy enforcement across native AI solution and third-party AI SaaS platforms.

Every engagement scales to the organization’s maturity, risk posture and AI roadmap:

Health Check: Baseline security posture across platform configurations, data exposure and AI operational readiness so remediation starts with what matters most.

Advisory: Align security investments with regulatory and business requirements through data protection strategies, governance frameworks and roadmaps.

Engineering: Turn strategy into production infrastructure with secure databases, automated pipelines, policy-as-code enforcement and infrastructure-as-code foundations designed to scale with continued AI innovation.

GuidePoint Security brings vendor-objective, hands-on experience across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and major SaaS ecosystems, including native tools such as Microsoft Purview, Amazon Macie, Google Cloud DLP and Oracle Data Safe. Engagements also connect with complementary GuidePoint services, including Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), Application Security, Identity and Access Management and threat simulation.

Get Started

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top cloud security best practices for 2027?

Key cloud security best practices for 2027 include owning the security configuration of cloud AI services, classifying data before AI consumes it, enforcing policy as code, governing human and non-human identities, building compliance into the architecture and securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system.

What is the data-to-AI pipeline?

The data-to-AI pipeline is the path data takes from collection and preparation through storage, transformation, model training, deployment and use by generative and agentic AI applications. It typically spans databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines across multiple clouds.

Why is securing the data-to-AI pipeline a cloud security best practice?

AI models and agents are only as trustworthy as the data they rely on. Securing the pipeline end to end preserves data integrity, tracks sensitivity and origin and keeps access policies in place as data moves between environments and new AI workloads are introduced.

Who is responsible for securing cloud AI services like Copilot, Bedrock and Vertex AI?

The customer is. Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure, but the customer owns configuration, access controls, content filtering and model permissions for AI services. Default settings are designed for broad use, not your risk profile.

What is policy-as-code?

Policy-as-code is the practice of writing security rules as machine-readable code that deploys automatically with infrastructure. It eliminates manual configuration and ensures every environment gets the same controls from day one.

What is DSPM and how does it support AI security?

DSPM continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud environments. For AI security, it identifies which data AI models can access, flags overexposed training sets and tracks data lineage from source to model.

Which AI regulations and frameworks should cloud security programs plan for in 2027?

Organizations should plan for AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and state AI legislation, alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS.

What are GuidePoint Security's Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI?

Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI are GuidePoint Security services that combine health checks, advisory and engineering to secure the full data-to-AI pipeline across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and major SaaS platforms.

Where should an organization start with Secure Cloud Platform Services?
