The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt.

Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.

Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent

Review every identity that each individual agent has access to

Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls

Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.

Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

General Security News.title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
General Security News.context: Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings
General Security News.full_text:
A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals.

Command approvals turn into credential storage

Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file.

The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it.

For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file.

Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked.

Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens.

It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for.

Leaked credentials on Docker Hub

GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected.

The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image.

Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore.

One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets.

GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.

General Security News.title: Accenture Federal Services Names Edward Wood CTO
What 70 European CISOs told us about securing the AI era
General Security News.context: Prevention has become more urgent AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited
General Security News.full_text:
Last week I spent three days in Bavaria with more than 70 CISOs from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Leaders Point EMEA. Led by our CEO Nadav Zafrir and hosted with Team8’s CISO Village, it was our second Leaders Point and the first in Europe. We kept it invitation-only so people could speak openly.

The timing was hard to miss. Over the past month, attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have spoiled food and emptied shelves in stores across France and several other European countries. Nobody has yet been shown to be behind them. For anyone who still sees cyber risk as an IT problem, it was a sharp reminder of how physical it has become.

As Nadav told the room, our industry is going through its most dramatic shift in 30 years. CISOs now have three jobs at once: protect their organizations from AI-driven threats, secure the AI their own teams use, and apply AI in their own defense. They are doing all of this while the rules are still being written.

We host Leaders Point to listen, because Check Point’s strategy depends on seeing these challenges from our customers’ point of view. We covered a lot of ground, from a CISO panel on “Whose AI Can Europe Trust?” to national cyber leadership in the AI era and a look inside the frontier AI labs. Four themes kept coming back.

Prevention has become more urgent

AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited. Attackers can use AI to find weaknesses and turn them into working attacks far faster than before. Patching faster on its own can no longer keep up.

The CISOs I spoke to are rethinking what prevention means. They want to harden their environments and remove whole classes of risk before an attack arrives, so that each new vulnerability matters less. Prevention has been at the heart of Check Point’s approach for a long time, and it was powerful to hear the same conclusion from the people running security every day.

The supermarket attacks show why. Reporting on them points to refrigeration controllers that could be reached from the open internet, many on software their maker no longer updated. No patch was ever coming for those systems. The only real defense was to close those doors before anyone went looking.

AI agents need controls built around their purpose

AI agents now act with legitimate credentials across email, endpoints, networks and the cloud. That makes them hard to police with traditional tools. To most systems, an agent doing something harmful looks the same as an agent doing its job.

The room kept coming back to purpose. To secure an agent, you need to know what it is supposed to do and check every action it takes against that, in real time. An agent built to summarize contracts has no reason to change firewall rules, and security teams need to be able to see and stop that the moment it happens.

There has been plenty of talk lately about kill switches for AI agents. You should have one: if an agent is hijacked, you pull the plug. But most risky agents aren’t malicious. They’re just determined, and take a dangerous shortcut to finish the job. Switch that agent off and you lose the work too. The kill switch is the last resort. Steering is the first move: catch the agent drifting toward danger, stop the risky step and keep the work going. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

Every AI use case needs a human owner

As AI makes more decisions and takes more actions, it becomes easy for the outcomes to end up as nobody’s responsibility. The CISOs were clear that this can’t be allowed to happen.

Every AI use case needs a named owner who signs off on its risk, the same way they would for any other business risk. Clear ownership is what lets organizations move quickly with AI and still know who answers when something goes wrong.

European organizations want control over their AI choices

Many conversations, including our panel on whose AI Europe can trust, came back to control. European organizations want the freedom to switch AI models and suppliers as the market changes, and to build independent capability where it matters most.

For CISOs this is a practical question of resilience. Relying on a single model or provider is a concentration risk like any other. Our job is to secure AI whichever models and suppliers our customers choose.

The decisions that matter will be made this year

By this time next year, many of the decisions that define how organizations secure AI will have been made. The leaders in that room in Bavaria will make a lot of them.

I’m grateful to every CISO who gave us three days of their time and their candor, and to Team8’s CISO Village for building Leaders Point with us. What we heard will shape what Check Point builds next, and we’ll keep listening.

General Security News.title: Why does old access outlive the job?
General Security News.context: Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone
General Security News.full_text:
Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them.

Why is granting access easy but removing it hard?

Granting has an owner and a deadline. A manager submits a request, an approver clicks yes and the process is completed in just a few hours since someone is involved in it. Removal does not have any of the two. Nobody opens a ticket when permission becomes unnecessary, as the only person who notices will not submit the ticket for lack of reason to do it. The cost of maintaining the permission is high, but it is not visible and it comes in the future. The incentives work the same way. Nobody evaluates how low an access level their team maintains, while a permission that was mistakenly removed and became necessary results in an irate support ticket submitted the same day.

And this is something that has to be done via reviews, but, in my opinion, is not done like this. And, at least in all attestation and recertification activities I was involved in, there is simply a basic question for the reviewer: is access still valid? Saying “yes” is not really difficult — access was granted, there were no actions following and reviewing several hundred takes less time than investigating one particular access. This is not what will appear on your screen. When reviewing account names, you do not know whether they were used last week or last year.

Role-based access control helps here, but the problem is that, when a user changes his role, his role gets updated, but not the direct access, groups and folders he acquired during the time.

What does leftover access actually cost?

I have to be quite careful here, as this metric does not reflect the access that remains. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report demonstrated that exploitation of vulnerabilities was the most frequently used method of the breach, making up 31% of all breaches, while the previous leader — abuse of credentials — was reduced to 13%. However, I want to emphasize that this particular report is unrelated to the issue of obsolete permissions. Yet, what the intruder could do after penetrating the system depends on the permissions of the breached account, which in turn depends on the number of permissions acquired. In practice, it looks like findings of audit and investigation, which go on forever, because nobody knows whom exactly to permit to access the corporate data.

However, there is information proving the case of the leavers, although quite meager. Thus, according to the PasswordManager.com survey carried out in March 2023, among 1,000 American workers, 58% of the workers who responded that they had used the passwords of their previous employers admitted that they had never updated their passwords after leaving the company. It is an opinion survey carried out online, and that is why it is an indicator. Indeed, I noticed this too: The departures have to go through the HR offboarding checklists, but not the permissions and certificates created by hundreds of people over many years.

Transfers are even more of an issue and there are fewer studies regarding them. In the case of a leaver, at least something happens — the offboarding process is triggered. Nothing triggers in case of a transfer. And thus I think that transfers should be equally important as terminations, because the standards require exactly that. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — security and privacy control catalog used throughout organizations — contains AC-2 and AC-6 account management and least privilege controls requiring review of accounts, processing of transfers and terminations, and granting only privileges required by the role of the individual.

3 fixes that make leftover access hard to ignore

And here is how I will make sure that the changes will be adopted. There is no need for any new technology to be implemented. Just the decision regarding the ownership of the deletion process.

1. Every change in position will be regarded as an event of deletion

Start from the HR record of the system. After the change takes place, generate a task for the outgoing and incoming manager where there will be only one question for the manager to answer — what will the individual no longer need? Provide them with the access list and 10 minutes to answer the question. All the access the individual had created during this period needs to have an owner. If you only do one of these three, do this one.

2. Each permission must have its own unique owner and expiration date

Permissions or access to the project folders, special permissions or access to the production system must expire on a particular date, which could be either the date the project expires or, by default, three months after its issuance, unless renewed by the owner, who must be a named person, not an e-mail address. I think of the account, the owner and the applications it accesses as a graph, because if there is any change in accounts, then with one query, it can determine what he/she owns and his/her dependencies. Renewal must be a one-click option, but in the event of that person’s no longer being available, it should be done through his/her manager so that it does not get lost in the cracks. It is a default setting. In the current scenario, if you do nothing, it is your permission; hence, laziness is the dangerous path. Do not make the default action renewing the permission.

3. Present last-used information on all reviews, and allow people to act on it

Pull last login and last activity timestamps from your identity provider and application logs and present them along with each entitlement. Order the list such that the least used access appears at the top, select it for removal and ask the reviewer to explain why they need to keep it. From experience, I have found that people are happy to confirm when “this entitlement hasn’t been used in seven months” shows up on the screen. Then allow them to take action based on what they think is best. If attestation takes place using one tool and rotation/vaulting takes place using another tool, then you would find people confirming the question and skipping the action. That’s why I’ve started to keep attestation, rotation, vaulting and retirement of access in one process. Remember, however, there are limitations to this approach. Not all applications maintain usage logs, and sometimes there is legitimate access that is rarely used. Take the case of quarterly close accounts and break glass accounts, for example. They should be assigned an owner and a note.

While employees will be able to identify what they don’t need anymore, this is effective only when there is a system in place which allows them to do so safely and easily, and this is yet another reason why we need to implement the three above fixes.

In this quarter, start with a single system where sensitive data is stored and run a last-used report on that system. Begin with the users who have been moved to a different role within the past year, since no one has reviewed their access rights since then. Send a list of all those users who haven’t used that system in the past six months to the system owner, and ask them one simple question — Do they still require this? The findings will be enough to make the case for the rest stronger than any framework.

General Security News.title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
General Security News.context: ” Autonomous patching may only be transitional Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove...
General Security News.full_text:
Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea.

The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.”

Not your father’s vulnerability management program

The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.”

Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities.

They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices.

“The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.”

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices.

“It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO.

“Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline.

Is human-in-the-loop dead?

Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed.

“The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains.

“And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.”

That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop.

CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says.

Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’”

“Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.”

Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.”

On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.”

Autonomous patching may only be transitional

Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.”

Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential.

He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines.

The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime. Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference, Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says.

The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.”

Steps CISOs should be taking now

According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment.

For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds.

And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.”

Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate.

“If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.”

Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.”

He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”

General Security News.title: AI now Ireland’s top cyber concern
CyberWire Daily at 10: Developments in AI and machine learning over the past decade. [Special Edition]
General Security News.context: I want to say it was 2016 or so was the year at the RSA conference was the first year that everything was AI. So, one of the first widely available AI toys was called Eliza, and -- Maria Varmazis: Oh.
General Security News.full_text:
Maria Varmazis: Hello, I'm Maria Varmazis, and you're listening to a special edition of the CyberWire. In this episode, I'm speaking with the host of the "CyberWire Daily," Dave Bittner, about the last ten years of AI in cybersecurity, as we take a look back at ten years of the "CyberWire Daily." Here's our chat. [ Music ] All right, it is my distinct pleasure once again to welcome back the host of the "CyberWire Daily," Dave Bittner. Hi, Dave.

Dave Bittner: Hello, good to be back.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, thanks for joining me yet again. And we are as we have been all year talking about the ten-year anniversary of the "CyberWire Daily." Again, congratulations, Dave. That is a wonderful milestone.

Dave Bittner: Thank you.

Maria Varmazis: And we've been in these conversations eventually getting to a topic and ringing the bell of oh, we have to talk about AI. It just feels inevitable when we talk about cybersecurity nowadays.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: We're getting that out of the way real early in this conversation today because we're going to be talking about AI and cybersecurity as our topic for today. So --

Dave Bittner: Right, right.

Maria Varmazis: -- ding a ding a ding. Here we are. We're talking about it the entire time today.

Dave Bittner: Yes, it's a funny thing because I feel like in my interviews, you know, as a interviewer you always have go-to questions, right? I refer to it as a bag of tricks. You know, there are things that if you find yourself out of things to ask or for some reason distracted or flummoxed, you can reach into your bag of tricks and buy yourself some time in these days.

Maria Varmazis: You're giving away our secrets to people.

Dave Bittner: Oh, sorry. But these days --

Maria Varmazis: No, no, we're brilliant. We always think on our feet.

Dave Bittner: That's right.

Maria Varmazis: We don't have shortcuts. Yes, it's great.

Dave Bittner: Exactly. Spontaneous. Yes, but these days you can always say, "Well, how does AI affect this?" And off you go, right?

Maria Varmazis: Off you go. Yes, there's always a great answer to that one because inevitably it's doing something. So, when I was preparing for this chat, I think I'm having the same whiplash every human being is having with how much AI as a concept, as a broad umbrella of technology, has quickly progressed in just the past months, if not years. So, trying to go back ten years thinking about this, I'm not sure how much of my own recollection I can honestly trust. Just putting that out there.

Dave Bittner: Yes.

Maria Varmazis: But if -- I'm trusting you a lot more than I'm trusting myself, Dave, if you can go back ten years and remembering, we were talking about AI back then, but it to me seems like it was one day far off or very vague. We're not there yet tech. Maybe your recollection is different. What do you remember?

Dave Bittner: I think you're right. I was -- I think back then it was more the promise of AI versus the reality and much of the AI that was happening was happening under the hood and it wasn't anything that a regular user could really get their hands on. It was just this thing that the folks with technical expertise had included in whatever platform or package you had purchased and it was somehow going to help you do your work more quickly, more efficiently, more securely, all those good things. I want to say it was 2016 or so was the year at the RSA conference was the first year that everything was AI.

Maria Varmazis: Oh.

Dave Bittner: And it was that kind of AI. It wasn't large language models. It wasn't chatbots. It was just everybody. If you were selling a product, you had to say somewhere under the hood, there was AI. And --

Maria Varmazis: That hasn't changed in ten years. Yes.

Dave Bittner: It has -- no, it hasn't changed. But there was a lot of eye rolling back then because I think the notion of what it is and what it could do and like there are still people who get bent out of shape when you say AI versus machine learning and is it this, is it really that or you know, and you have those debates and conversations till the cows come home. But I guess the challenge back then was how much of this is real and how much of it is marketing, particularly when it's all under the hood and you really can't see it yourself?

Maria Varmazis: Were you seeing it in specific contexts at that time? I mean, I know it was sort of being spammed everywhere as the you know, marketing team has been given their directive. You have to include it. But were there certain defense or attack areas that were seeing you know more successful deployment? And if you remember any of this, what was the (inaudible)?

Dave Bittner: Yes, I mean I guess the promise was that these AI systems could recognize attacks that had never been seen before. Right? So, we were coming from the days of indicators of compromise and malware signatures. So, it was really built off of the fact that somebody saw something, documented it, reported it, and your antivirus software would then start scanning for that. And the idea was that these AI systems didn't need that, that they could just look for anomalies or they could even look at behavioral things and that -- what black magic was that? And so, raise alerts that your normal virus searching software would miss.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, I want to say there's also a confluence of you know, we were coming off of sims being a big thing that -- not that new at that time, but there was just -- we were well into that world of sims and the flood of alerts and that just became a huge problem also that I think AI was being promised as a potential solution for, but again, I don't remember as well as I'd like.

Dave Bittner: I think also, like just a fun thing to remember is like it was back in 2011, I believe, that IBM's Watson competed on Jeopardy and won.

Maria Varmazis: What? What?

Alex Trebek: And now the newcomer, developed and programmed especially for this moment, making its first appearance on our national television program, ladies and gentlemen, this is Watson.

Dave Bittner: Pretty sure that was 2011, and Watson you know, kicked Ken Jennings' butt on Jeopardy. Ken Jennings now the host of Jeopardy.

Maria Varmazis: I was going to say I think somebody might -- well, I mean who really won? Yes.

Dave Bittner: Yes, right, exactly. In the end, Ken got the last laugh. But what was so interesting about that, and I think what captured people's imagination was like we've been used to computers being able to play chess.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Which is very deterministic. You know, you could -- most people who know how to play chess can understand how computing power could be thrown at the problem of chess, because of the limited amount of things that chess pieces can do and all those kinds of things.

Maria Varmazis: It's basically an extremely complicated algorithm that the more you study it, you understand certain outcomes. I don't play chess, but this is also my understanding. Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right. And so, you could see that how you could throw computing problem at that and get good results. And so, computers had been competing for chess championships for long periods of time up to this point. You know, there -- you could go to your local radio shack, which still existed, and buy a computer chess set that would play against you. And depending on how good you were, well, if you were at my level, it would beat you every time. Right.

Maria Varmazis: Same. Yes, same.

Dave Bittner: By the way, I should add in preparing for today's episode, I went -- I found a clip of me at the 2016 RSA conference. I was being interviewed by Matt Stephenson, who was working at Cylance at the time. And so, we caught up at the Cylance booth, and we actually discussed this very topic about AI and playing chess. So, here's a clip from that interview.

Matt Stephenson: Any other kind of fringe technologies, maybe you personally, that are grabbing your attention? Obviously, AI and machine learning, big deals as that is maturing in the security market. But is there any kind of outlier that's worth keeping your eye on for the next year or two?

Dave Bittner: Oh boy, that's a good question. I mean, I think a lot of it is -- I think we have this huge problem with workforce issues. So, I will tell you, I heard an interesting interview last week with Garry Kasparov, the famous chess player, and he said that we are at the point where any computer, the best chess playing computers can beat any human. However, if he teams up with a chess playing computer, they can beat any machine. So, I'm really intrigued by that notion of not just the AI, but if you team up AI with a really smart human, how does that change the game? I think that's going to be something looking forward to really pay attention to. Do I sound ten years younger, Maria?

Maria Varmazis: Honestly, I didn't want to say it, but you --

Dave Bittner: Butter me up, flatter me. Tell me what I want to hear.

Maria Varmazis: The optimism and brightness in your voice and kind of how like "Isn't this going to be cool?" you know?

Dave Bittner: Right, right. No, the weight of the world had not yet crushed my spirit.

Maria Varmazis: I know.

Dave Bittner: So.

Maria Varmazis: But also, the tenor of which you speak about AI as a great potential thing as opposed to I think the existential dread most of us can't help --

Dave Bittner: Sure. Yes.

Maria Varmazis: -- but inject now.

Dave Bittner: Yes, the cynicism had not completely set in yet.

Maria Varmazis: No. It's a little wild, but it was also kind of sweet. I --

Dave Bittner: Yes. No --

Maria Varmazis: -- no but, how much things have changed in a decade though? I mean, truly.

Dave Bittner: Yes, and you know, of course, Matt was a great host and Matt passed away recently, so we miss him very much. But getting back to Watson playing Jeopardy, I think the thing that was so remarkable about that was that that was a natural language engine, and that I think was something that most of us hadn't really experienced before. At the time, that took the big compute that IBM's, was it Big Blue or whatever their Watson engine had that was able to do that to be able to just understand spoken word, interpret it and come back with a meaningful answer, that seemed magical at the time. But, now it's part of everyone's everyday thanks to the large language models we have. But it -- back then, it was magical.

Maria Varmazis: In that vein, that kind of capability and extrapolating out to going a bit back to what you talked about you know, signatures for example. On the defensive side, you could see how these kinds of capabilities would make a lot of sense as an you know, something that can help the defenders aggregate you know, things that are trending or you know, all the unbelievable amount of things that the defenders have to just comb through, but eventually I mean the attackers started figuring out how they could use these kinds of tools to their advantage, and not to sound too dramatic, but that's when everything changed. Okay, that was too dramatic. But I mean, eventually we did start seeing attackers using AI to their advantage, and I do feel like that was a bit of a shift. You could feel the cold winds blowing when we started seeing more of that happening. Can you paint a picture for us about what you remember from when these started appearing more and more, I guess, across your desk at the CyberWire?

Dave Bittner: Yes, I mean, there was the rise of adversarial machine learning. And as you say, sort of a way for the bad guys to parry against malware detection, you know, spam filtering, all those kinds of things, to be able to use this technology to morph your code so that it wouldn't trigger recognition from you know, something that was checking for viruses, just what -- things that are considered simple and maybe quaint by today's standards, but back then were pretty advanced things. You know, DARPA had their Cyber Grand Challenge back in 2016, I believe, which was -- they were looking to see how autonomous systems could work with all this for both discovery, exploitation, and patching of software vulnerabilities. So, they were kind of on the early edge of that. And then I guess around 2018, 2019, we saw SOAR platforms became the new hotness, right? Their Security Orchestration Automation and Response, and that was supposed to make life easier for the SOCs.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: And I think in many ways it did, but that was again looking to automate things to get rid of those repetitive security tasks, to take away the drudgery from the people running the SOCs to, you know, the phrase is always to "allow them to focus on more important things." Right?

Maria Varmazis: This is true. Although I do wonder, I mean that kind of work also, not that this is something you control, just that's also a lot of work for junior analysts and it's a shame for that to go away. But I understand it is the volume that we're talking about. It's just human beings can't keep up with it at a certain point.

Dave Bittner: Yes, and I mean it's an interesting point you bring up because one of the things that I've heard from many folks in security leadership is how do we take junior analysts and turn them into senior analysts when they're not doing the work anymore?

Maria Varmazis: Yes. Ten years ago, you were talking about workforce concerns. Here we are ten years later, I don't think those concerns have gotten any better. In fact, they've gotten a lot worse in many ways, but that is a totally different conversation, but --

Dave Bittner: No, it's weird. I mean, you're right. It's weird. I mean, on the one hand, back then there were all these, oh -- there's so much talk about how are we ever going to fill all these empty positions in cybersecurity? How are we going to ever find enough qualified people? And now, we're talking about Microsoft looking for voluntary layoffs or voluntary separations with 25% of their workforce. So, things have changed. I think there's still demand for folks who know a lot, but sort of to what we were just talking about, it -- it's really tough out there for those folks who are looking for entry-level positions.

Maria Varmazis: It is, yes, and you know what? Every conversation we've had this year, AI has been part of that conversation, so I say it's only fair that workforce comes part of the AI conversation. The tables have turned a little bit. It's only fair. Yes, so all right. So, you were in 2018, 2019. And then COVID hit and we were all stuck at home looking at really funny videos coming across our devices that were in some cases AI powered, and they were a bit of a novelty, but there was of course a security implication of these things as well. And I'm remembering Will Smith eating spaghetti as --

Dave Bittner: Right, right, right, and of course --

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: -- we're talking about deepfakes.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes, what deep fake -- I'm -- there have got to be deep fake stories from back then that you remember that made you go "uh-oh." There've got to be.

Dave Bittner: I guess so. I mean, I think a lot of the conversation was about the uncanny valley, and I remember as a huge Star Wars fan, I remember Rogue One coming out, and of course at the end of that film they have the AI-generated version of Carrie Fisher playing Princess Leia, and it was okay. It wasn't great. You know, it was one of those things where you could see, all right, where's this going? How interesting that the -- and clearly this is the future. But what I remember specifically about that is, not long after the movie came out, people were homebrewing versions that were way better.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right?

Maria Varmazis: I was wondering if you were going to mention that because that was my recollection, too. That was my oblique moment was the homebrew versions are way better. I mean, not a surprise. Nerds, we're awesome like that. But at the same time that home capabilities were able to beat Lucasfilm.

Dave Bittner: Yes, exactly.

Maria Varmazis: I mean --

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: -- this just was a sign of this is -- it's going to pop off real fast and boy, did it ever.

Dave Bittner: Right, and how quickly it was changing to go from the probably, you know, the most well-known special effects company in the world, ILM, doing a fine job, but only you know, let's say a year later, people being able to do a better job just at home.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right? And so, again, you sort of recalibrate what your expectations are and what does this mean for the future if we can no longer trust our eyes, what we see, that's a big deal.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, I remember on a personal note around that time just the biometrics and identity verification procedures for so many things having to evolve extremely rapidly to keep up with just how well deepfakes were evolving and how effective they were becoming. And I was seeing that as you know a consumer in my day to day, and I remember thinking and wondering, what is this like for people who are actually, you know, are defending against something like this? This has got to be crazy. This fire hose. And truly around that same time, not that long ago, I mean four, five, six years ago, instead of AI being sort of this magical under the hood, magical, but under the hood thing for people who really knew what they were doing, it became a thing that a lot of us could homebrew and start using at home and then I mean, I think that's really when, I mean, not to use that again cliche phrase, but a lot of things changed when we started being able to play with it ourselves.

Dave Bittner: Right. ChatGPT comes out 2022 or so, '22, '23, around that time. Yes, it was late '22 was when it came out, and suddenly the world had a new toy, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes.

Dave Bittner: And you -- are you -- I'm sure you remember, and I'm sure our listeners are vigorously nodding their heads at the avalanche of articles and podcasts and everything that at the end of it they said, "In fact, this article was written by ChatGPT. Ha ha ha ha."

Maria Varmazis: Got you, humans.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: That em-dash didn't give it away? No.

Dave Bittner: Yes. Yes.

Maria Varmazis: And in a security context, also, it couldn't not -- it couldn't not change things. All the double negatives, triple negatives going on there. Things like intellectual property, you know, code bases, all sorts of stuff leaking out through ChatGPT. People putting things into these public tools that they really shouldn't. But also, how do you use these kinds of things in a secure way at work? And then all of our advice, I'm thinking you know on "Hacking Humans," a lot of our advice for people on how to detect phishing campaigns, for example, almost overnight became ineffective. You know, the old tells gone.

Dave Bittner: Just supercharged it, right? No longer do you look for clunky English that was oddly translated from whatever the mother tongue was, but no, there -- all of a sudden, you can take anything, run it through one of these large language models. Say "Clean up my English, make it flawless," and it was so.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, it's almost quaint now when I get something that has broken English in it. It's like, "Oh, oh, don't you know about AI, my friend?" Yes, but in terms of, you know, the really heavy-duty lifting of you know, the work that defenders are doing every day in their organizations, I mean, people are using AI in their workflows now in all sorts of creative ways, but also, it's -- you can't ignore its capabilities now, too. So, what have you seen in the last few years as you know trends in that direction?

Dave Bittner: Well, I think similar to what we were talking about from back in the early days of 2016 when it was under the hood but still part of everyone's marketing pitch. Here we are again, right? History may not repeat itself, but it sure does rhyme. And are there any cybersecurity companies out there who do not have AI as part of their marketing pitch? You have to. It's required. And I think it's easy to be cynical and poo-poo that. But on the other hand, it may be required. It may -- like to keep up with because the adversaries are using it, so why not? It's part of the toolbox now, and it's expected. I think it's just a matter of what are you using it for? Who's using it? How much does it include the human in the loop? You know, getting back to the clip of where -- from the old clip of me talking about chess, how the human plus the computer was the real chess champion. And I think a lot of folks are settling into that that you want the AI to handle the stuff that requires high speed analysis, but at the end of the day, you still need a human to sign off on it. The analogy I use all the time is that AI is like a tireless intern, which is great, but you're not going to bet the company on the output of an intern.

Maria Varmazis: And on the attacker side, to me, AI has been like pouring gasoline on a fire in terms of just what -- the volume that attackers have been able to you know, pump out what they do essentially, and the effectiveness and the way that they can iterate and the speed at which they can iterate. And we haven't even touched on things like prompt injection attacks. That's like a whole other world. But in terms of you know, what defenders are seeing coming across their worlds from the attacker side, AI has been an incredible tool in the arsenal for attackers and it also has, I mean to me, I don't know about you, but I'm sure in the conversations you've had, it has significantly lowered the bar for how technically sophisticated an attacker needs to be. You know, you don't even have to be a script kitty.

Dave Bittner: No.

Maria Varmazis: And that's alarming.

Dave Bittner: No, and to anyone who's experienced the joy and delight of vibe coding, you know, which I personally held off on for a long time because I just -- I don't know, it didn't -- didn't really see how it applied to me. It's not really part of what I do, but a friend of mine, I was asking a friend of mine who knows a lot about developing websites. I said, "I want to make some updates, but I feel like I'm you know, out of my realm here," and he said, "Well, just vibe code it." And I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "Just tell -- ask one of the language models what you need to do, and it'll do it for you." And sure enough, I tried and it did.

Maria Varmazis: Yes. Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right? My point being that, as you say, the bar is on the floor now for being able to create technically sophisticated things quickly, without having that technical expertise. And I think that's another big part of the story here is how much AI is a velocity engine, how it allows you to iterate quickly and just hammer away at things, set the system out on a task, and all the AI engines want to do is please you. And as we've seen story after story, they will do whatever it takes to please you, even if that means escaping their sandboxes.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, and we've -- that's been really the story of the last year, is exactly what you just said, and that has felt extraordinarily consequential, I'm sure, for everybody listening. And not that you have a crystal ball, Dave, but you know, given again the conversations you've had over the years and the trends that you've been following, where could you imagine this going?

Dave Bittner: Boy, that is the big -- that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? But it -- to be fair, it's a question I get to ask people all the time, as do you.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: And it's been very interesting to me to hear the question -- the reactions that people have, the responses that people have to that question. I was asking someone recently, I was at a conference and had the opportunity to speak off the record with someone who was a very, very high -- high level person when it comes to all of these things. This is someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity and has been at leadership positions at the highest levels. And I said, "What do you think? What's the future hold?" And this person said, "I think like sort of like California wildfires, it has to burn down before it can be rebuilt." In other words, there's so much deadwood, there's so much brush, inflammable material at the ground level, and by that I think they meant just pre-existing bugs and vulnerabilities, all of these things that we're seeing being discovered at machine speed, and that all has to be cleared out before we can build the next thing. So, I think it's a interesting possibility that the next few years are going to be those wildfires making their way through the ecosystem, burning out all the dead wood, but then after that there won't be as many fires because all that kindling, all that tinder is gone. And then hopefully, it'll put the defenders in the better position of being able to spend their time on new novel things rather than having to clean up all the messes that were left behind.

Maria Varmazis: That is an oddly optimistic and I mean that it's a really optimistic take actually. It -- more optimistic than I would have guessed.

Dave Bittner: I'm hopeful. I'm buoyed by how many people I've talked to, people who I respect who believe that ultimately the defenders are going to have the advantage. It may take us a while to get there, but it seems like there are plenty of people who think that that's how it's going to play out. And here's hoping, my friend, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes. I mean, this is one of those things like I trust people with much greater technical expertise than I certainly have. If you had asked me to guess how people would feel, it would not have been that. Which -- so that does -- that honestly gives me a lot of hope as well. Dave, in your capacity as host of the "CyberWire Daily," doing a daily cybersecurity news show, talking to so many people and just watching these trends, especially with AI, when did it crystallize for you that AI was going to be basically a required component of any major cybersecurity news story? Was there an incident or a year, a date, anything like that where you went, "Yes, this is real, this is permanent."

Dave Bittner: I think it was the release of the large language models when those became publicly available, I'd say the year after that, when anybody who was paying attention could project out where this was going, right? Because the models were only going to get better and they have. The GPUs have only gotten fast -- or were only going to get faster and they have. People learning how to apply these things effectively gotten better, right? These tools have gotten more powerful. If you just look at the answers that you get back from these systems compared to what we did four years ago, they're so much more capable than they were. And the -- again, the folks I talk to who are working on the cutting-edge versions are saying, "You ain't seen nothing yet," right? Like they're -- it's just -- we've got a long way to run out. Like Moore's law isn't going to run out for AI for a little while. Like don't -- we don't seem to be up against that wall. Obviously, there are concerns about the toll that may play on our economy, our -- the environment, you know, all of those things which I think are legitimate concerns of -- as a civilization balancing out our needs and the advantages versus the resources that they demand. So, that's a whole other conversation for another day, but they're here to stay. I do believe that the release of the large language models was an inflection point in history. There was before and there is after, and now we're in the aftertimes. And so, we'll see how it plays out. I try to stay optimistic. I try not to get overly cynical about it. Some days it's easier than others. Some days it's harder than others. I think we're all fighting that fight and particularly folks who have an inside view of this, it's hard to know what ground truth is sometimes from day to day. It's hard to know what to believe, who to believe, and so hopefully, you know, something that we're really focused on is trying to provide that ground truth and you know, pre-filter things so that our listeners don't have to. But hasn't gotten any easier. I'll tell you that.

Maria Varmazis: Well, Dave, it's been an honor and a joy speaking with you, as always, and I want to make sure that if there's anything you want to leave the audience with before we conclude, that we -- I give you that chance.

Dave Bittner: So, just for fun --

Maria Varmazis: Okay.

Dave Bittner: -- if you have not done so, and I suspect a lot of people out there who are younger than me, and that would include you, Maria, go online. There are a million different versions of this online and search for Eliza. Maria, have you ever played with Eliza?

Maria Varmazis: As in like Eliza Doolittle, Eliza?

Dave Bittner: Just it it's -- yes. So, one of the first widely available AI toys was called Eliza, and --

Dave Bittner: And it's very clever, but I first came across it in the 70s, I think. It was running on like on a TRS-80 or an Apple II, but it's interesting to look back at something like Eliza, which is from a different time, but how Eliza can capture your imagination, how Eliza can make you feel like you're interacting with someone and not something. General Security News.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
General Security News.context: The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a...
General Security News.full_text: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post. The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

General Security News.title: Your training data is boring: Anomaly detection with LLMs
General Security News.context: The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly...
General Security News.full_text:
Following on from research presented at Black Hat USA 2025, Sophos data scientists Ben Gelman, Tamas Nyiri, and Tibor Kristóf Lányi recently showcased new work on anomaly detection at BSides Las Vegas 2026. As promised, we’re sharing more details of that research (the recording of the talk is also available here).

Supervised classifiers in cybersecurity are often trained on data that doesn't capture the most unusual examples. Benign training sets are dominated by simple, common patterns, while malicious sets reflect known attacks from past investigations. The long tail of unusual files on both sides goes unlabeled.

When these files appear in production, classifiers are more likely to misclassify them, generating false positives that overwhelm SOCs, and false negatives that let threats through.

Traditional approaches to labeling difficult examples rarely scale. Doing it manually is expensive, rule-based collection is too narrow, and anomaly detection alone has historically produced unacceptable false positive rates. But anomaly detection combined with LLMs is excellent at something else: finding and labeling the unusual data that is missing from cybersecurity training sets.

The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly detection methods, viable across feature representations, to surface distinctly unusual data. Then, an LLM classified each anomaly with format-specific prompts calibrated per data type.

Critically, Ben and his colleagues used separate prompts that err toward malicious and benign respectively, achieving high precision on both label types. More specifically, one prompt instructed the LLM to only evaluate the input as benign when it was confident that it was benign; the other prompt instructed the same but with the malicious label. This way, they only accepted the labels when the two LLMs with the two different instructions agreed, otherwise they threw that example away and didn’t use it for training. In practice, this method produced labels with better precision (tested on labeled data). The labeled anomalies augment the training data for cybersecurity classifiers.

The Sophos AI team evaluated their method across three structurally different data types with monthly ingestion scales spanning four orders of magnitude: command lines, HTML, and RTF.

The problem

Every detection team is familiar with the core issue: supervised classifiers are only as good as their training data, and that data is systematically biased. Benign training data comes from sources chosen for labeling confidence.

Known-clean networks, corporate environments without incidents and regex-capturable patterns are obvious choices, but they inherently exclude the long tail of unusual but legitimate data.

Malicious training data is similarly constrained to known attack types from incident investigations. The events that classifiers get wrong in production are precisely the unusual events missing from both sides of the training set.

Using command lines as an example: prior work on anomaly detection for command-line classification has attempted to address labeling oversights by surfacing anomalies as direct alerts. SCADE uses isolation forests and engineered features to flag potentially malicious command lines at scale, but reports false positive rates around 2%. Filar and French discover anomalous parent-child process relationships using tree-based models, reporting similar ~3% false positive rates. Nisslmueller combines explicit command-line featurization with parent-child context for unsupervised LOLBin detection, also landing under 2% FP.

Although these rates sound low, at tens of millions of daily events they still produce overwhelming alert volumes. All three share the fundamental limitation of treating anomaly detection as an end-to-end alerting mechanism.

Ben and team’s approach sidesteps this limitation entirely: anomaly detection surfaces candidates, an LLM labels them, and the labels improve a downstream supervised classifier.

A key takeaway from the team’s work is the prompt strategy for achieving high precision on both malicious and benign labels. A single prompt struggles to simultaneously maintain high precision on both labels. Instead, the team used two separate prompts per file type: one that errs on the side of calling files malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), and another that errs on the side of calling files benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). This allows both label types from anomaly detection to be usable as training data, which was not achievable in prior work that relied on a single labeling pass.

Stand back, we’re doing science

The pipeline for Ben and team’s research was as follows:

Raw production telemetry

Feature extraction

Multi-method anomaly detection

LLM classification

Newly labeled training data from the long tail

Supervised classifier improvement

A key architectural decision was to treat anomaly detection not as the detection system itself, but as a prefilter that surfaces candidates for LLM labeling, which in turn produces training data for a supervised classifier whose precision can be controlled empirically.

Because each anomaly detection method has blind spots – it catches certain types of unusual data and misses others – Sophos AI used three methods (isolation forest, k-means anomaly, and PCA reconstruction error) on different feature representations, producing broader coverage with low overlap between methods.

The team employed several different feature sets, which contributed to data diversity:

Hand-crafted features: Catching structural anomalies, such as files with extreme length, abnormal Shannon entropy, rare character distributions. Hand-crafted features included character-level statistics, operator/case proportions, and file-type-specific markers.

TF-IDF vectors: To catch content-level outliers, e.g., files whose token distribution didn't match any typical cluster.

Binary vocabulary vectors: For the unusual feature correlations, e.g., files with atypical token co-occurrence patterns.

Prompt needed

A single LLM prompt can’t always achieve high precision on both malicious and benign labels simultaneously, especially in cases where the problem itself is inherently ambiguous, such as dual use scripts . For example, if the prompt says, ‘when uncertain, lean toward malicious,’ benign precision is high, but malicious precision suffers and vice versa.

Sophos AI’s solution was to run two separate prompts per file type. One erred towards malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), the other toward benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). Each prompt was calibrated to the file type's specific attack surface.

For example, with HTML, the malicious-leaning prompt defined what normal HTML looks like (JavaScript, forms, analytics) so it didn’t over-flag standard web features. The benign-leaning prompt defined specific malicious indicators (obfuscated payloads, credential phishing, exploit kit structures), so it didn’t under-flag real threats.

Putting it to the test

Ben and colleagues evaluated this method across three structurally different data types:

Command lines: ~10,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: LOLBin abuse, obfuscated PowerShell, encoded payloads.

HTML files: ~1,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: exploit kits, credential phishing, obfuscated JavaScript.

RTF documents: ~10,000 monthly ingest (testing under data scarcity). Attack surface: Equation Editor exploits, DDE attacks, malicious OLE.

The results on LOLBins can be found in the previous research. But expanding the work to HTML and RTF files elucidated more generalizable trends, and suggests that the method can work with a variety of data types.

Like LOLBins, RTF performed best with isolation forest, showing a 2.41% increase over the existing model, which is an encouraging jump at such a high ROC AUC.

With HTML, we see a different result. The baseline performance of the model is higher, so the increase is more modest, but the team found that K-means was the most effective with a 0.68% increase over baseline. They also noted that PCA decreased the score, which highlights exactly why they used three different anomaly detection methods: they didn’t know in advance which method would capture the most valuable anomalies in a particular dataset. And since running these algorithms is relatively cheap, the small extra cost only comes from running the evaluations on the extra anomalies with the LLM.

Try it yourself

Here’s something our data science-minded readers can try out for themselves:

Pick a file type where your classifier has a false positive or false negative problem

Pull a sample of unlabeled production data, featurize it, and run Isolation Forest (it's 10 lines of sklearn)

Send the top anomalies to an LLM with a format-specific prompt. Use two prompts: one that errs malicious, one that errs benign

(Optional) Check the quality of the LLM output on a sample either by running it on a set of your labeled data or even better, have an analyst verify the unlabeled ones

Add the high-precision labels to your next training run and measure the difference

Wrap it in a YAML config and schedule it. All being well, you now have a self-improving data pipeline

Top takeaways

Classifiers’ failure cases are a training data diversity problem; anomaly detection finds the unusual files that rules and manual labeling miss

Multi-method anomaly detection (IF + KMeans + PCA) on different feature representations catches more than any single method

Dual-prompt LLM labeling achieves high precision on both malicious and benign labels, making both usable as training data

The pipeline is filetype-agnostic (as long as an LLM can produce high precision labels for them – test this empirically first) and runs on a single machine. A new data type therefore requires a config file, rather than having to become an onerous engineering project

Although research on traditional ML models has slowed in recent times, this research shows that LLMs can help revitalize the field by infusing them into the process for significant performance gains
