Finally, Payment by Bank Transfer Comes to Have I Been Pwned
General Security News.context: That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious
General Security News.full_text:
Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

General Security News.title: Key benefits of Zero Trust Network Access over corporate VPN access | Kaspersky official blog
General Security News.context: For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device
General Security News.full_text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

General Security News.title: Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns
General Security News.context: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security...
General Security News.full_text: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges. “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory. Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.” The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week. CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface. As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.” CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG). “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either. We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems. These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities. So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

General Security News.title: Digital sovereignty at re:Invent 2026: Sessions you won’t want to miss
General Security News.context: Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to...
General Security News.full_text:
AWS re:Invent returns to Las Vegas for cloud and AI’s biggest week from November 30–December 4, 2026. This year we have over 2,200 sessions, 70 percent of which are interactive, led by experts from Amazon Web Services (AWS), our customers, and our partners.

With that much to choose from, we’ve pulled together the sessions built around Digital Sovereignty at AWS. Whether you’re navigating evolving data residency requirements, choosing the right home for your most sensitive workloads, or scaling AI in environments where your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, there’s something for you at re:Invent.

In this guide, you’ll find breakout sessions, chalk talks, workshops, and a lightning talk covering a range of digital sovereignty topics, grouped by theme so you can easily find what matters most to you. Reserve your seat through your attendee portal, or walk up based on availability. If a session is full, check the catalog for another time, since several of these sessions run more than once.

Pro tip: Sessions are spread across several venues, so allow extra time to get between them. All times are Pacific.

Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud

In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to help meet their most stringent digital sovereignty requirements. As part of its design, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operates with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and is backed by strong technical controls, sovereign assurances, and legal protections. In these sessions, get the full picture of the AWS approach to digital sovereignty, including verifiable controls, operational autonomy, and greater choice with infrastructure options like the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

SEC206 | Breakout session | Digital sovereignty: Verifiable controls and greater choice Speakers: Mustafa Isik, Chief Technologist Sovereignty, AWS; Stephane Israel, Managing Director European Sovereign Cloud and Digital Sovereignty, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 1:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Evolving regulations and geopolitical shifts are prompting organizations to rethink how they protect data and maintain control in the cloud, without slowing innovation and AI adoption. This session explores how AWS helps customers meet their digital sovereignty requirements with the full power of the cloud through a range of offerings, including the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, backed by verifiable and auditable controls. Learn what AI sovereignty means in practice, get answers to the most common questions, and hear how AWS and partners are helping organizations navigate complexity in a fast-changing landscape.

SEC234 | Lightning talk | EU operational autonomy in action: AWS European Sovereign Cloud Speakers: Zoltan Albrecht, Director, AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | Wynn/Encore The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is built on fully isolated infrastructure within the EU, operated exclusively by EU-resident staff, with no access from outside Europe. In this lightning talk, learn from the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations team what independent operations means in practice and how it works day to day.

Theme 2: AI under digital sovereignty and data residency requirements

Moving AI from pilots to production means making clear decisions about where your data and AI workloads run to meet your digital sovereignty needs. These sessions show how to bring AI infrastructure to your data, from fully managed AWS AI Factories in your data center, to the right hybrid deployment for each workload, to agentic AI applications that extend to hybrid and edge environments such as AWS Outposts and AWS Local Zones.

AIM206 | Breakout session | AWS AI Factories: Bring production scale AI to your data center Speakers: Pranav Chachra, Senior Manager, Product Management, AWS; Gareth Tucker, Global Specialist – AWS AI Factories, AWS; Daniel Xu, Member of Technical Staff, Anthropic When and where: Thursday, December 3, 10:30 AM | Venetian Data sovereignty, data gravity, and latency requirements prevent many organizations from running all AI workloads in the public cloud. AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure directly into your data center, fully operated, maintained, and continuously updated by AWS. Run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference without building and managing AI infrastructure yourself or negotiating separate agreements with model providers. In this session, learn how organizations are accelerating AI adoption, reducing time to value, and maintaining full control of their data while benefiting from the AWS experience in their own facilities.

HMC303 | Breakout session | Choosing the right hybrid deployment for your AI workloads Speakers: Shivam Saggar, Sr. Product Manager (Tech), AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS; Shelby Seward, DMTS, Sr. Director, T-Mobile; Hai Lu, Senior Engineering Manager, Databricks, Inc. When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations are running AI workloads for model training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and inference, across an expanding set of environments, including AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories. The right deployment option depends on latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. See how customers deploy accelerated AI across the hybrid spectrum: NVIDIA GPU-based and AWS Trainium-powered instances in Local Zones, purpose-built AWS AI Factories for large-scale training and model serving, and edge deployments for real-time inference. Hear how customers navigate these decisions, including Databricks tapping GPU capacity on AWS Local Zones and T-Mobile running latency-sensitive distributed inference, and learn which environment fits each AI workload without compromising performance and compliance.

HMC402 | Workshop | Implementing agentic AI solutions on-premises and at the edge Speakers: Kyle Palasti, Edge Specialist Solutions Architect, National Security, AWS; Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace Learn how to extend Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to hybrid and edge services to build distributed agentic apps using Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication with on-premises data. Get hands-on with hybrid agentic AI using Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents while exploring AWS hybrid and edge solutions for data residency compliance.

HMC403 | Workshop | Self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge Speakers: Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 12:30 PM | MGM Grand Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand As organizations use agentic AI to automate complex infrastructure operations, many have data residency, low latency, and security requirements that depend on running AI closer to their data. This workshop explores how customers deploy self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge to meet these requirements while enabling autonomous operations. Learn how to architect, provision, configure, and optimize AI agents that run locally, and how to extend the same architecture to AWS hybrid and edge infrastructure such as AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts.

Theme 3: More control, more choice: Finding the right infrastructure for your digital sovereignty needs

Digital sovereignty requirements vary, and AWS offers control and choice across a range of deployment options. Whether you’re comparing AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS Regions, or planning a migration, you’ll find the infrastructure options to meet your unique digital sovereignty needs. These sessions help you learn more and choose with confidence.

HMC314 | Chalk talk | Architecting for digital sovereignty with AWS Hybrid Cloud solutions Speakers: Sherry Lin, Principal Product Manager, AWS; Lakshmi VP, Solutions Architect – WWPS, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand This session uses real-world case studies to understand how AWS hybrid cloud architectures such as AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS Outposts help customers meet their digital sovereignty needs. It examines data residency boundaries, network separation, operational controls, and security guardrail options available in hybrid cloud solutions. It then shows how to configure governance controls, including Service Control Policies (SCPs), to help customers comply with regulatory requirements. Finally, it covers how to detect and prevent unauthorized data flows between hybrid infrastructure and the parent Region.

HMC202 | Breakout session | AWS wherever you need it: From the cloud to the edge Speakers: Spencer Dillard, Director, Software Dev, EC2, AWS; Ian Cottingham, Director, Software Development, AWS; Rama Raghavan, AVP Cloud Architecture, AT&T Inc. When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace While most workloads can run in the cloud, some remain on-premises or at the edge due to low latency, local data processing, or data residency needs. AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories extend AWS services, APIs, and tools to metro areas, on-premises data centers, and the far edge. Explore how these infrastructure offerings power a broad range of hybrid cloud and edge computing use cases such as financial trading, manufacturing, and AI. Learn how AWS helps you run regulated workloads with edge requirements, power generative AI with edge data, and migrate workloads with on-premises dependencies, featuring AT&T’s migration and modernization at scale.

HMC304 | Breakout session | Real-world migrations: Lessons learned migrating to AWS Outposts Speakers: Frankie Negro, Senior Hybrid Edge Solutions Architect, AWS; Scott Rose, Senior Manager Solution Architecture – Telco, AWS; Marcelo Andrade, Cloud Engineer, SERPRO When and where: Monday, November 30, 10:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations with data residency and digital sovereignty requirements face a critical question: how do you move workloads from on-premises infrastructure to AWS Outposts without disrupting compliance posture or operations? This Level 300 session distills lessons from migrating customers to Outposts across industries, organization sizes, and migration strategies, featuring SERPRO, Brazil’s federal data processing company, and AT&T, migrating telecom workloads at scale. The session walks through the processes that delivered results, the quantifiable outcomes measured, and the critical mistakes to avoid. Learn how to select the right migration approach and navigate common blockers. The session also covers transitioning from first-generation to second-generation Outposts hardware.

Theme 4: Disaster recovery, resilience, and cross-partition connectivity

Digital sovereignty goes beyond where your data lives. It also shapes how you operate, recover, and connect your workloads. These sessions help you learn about the operational side of digital sovereignty: recovering from failures under regulatory requirements, designing for resilience alongside data residency, and strategies for connecting across global AWS Regions, GovCloud, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions.

ARC405 | Breakout session | Your regulator set your RTO. Not your architecture. Speakers: Hossam Ebrahim, Solutions Architect, AWS; Paul Armstrong, Lead Architect UKI, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 4:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Organizations with pre-approved failover regions recover in hours. Those without recover in weeks. Same impairment. Same services. One governance decision separates them, and it’s made years before the event. This session presents architectural patterns for multi-Region recovery under sovereignty constraints, drawn from real operational experience with regulated workloads under regional pressure. Three categories: decisions that set your resilience ceiling before any event, dependencies that create circular failure during recovery, and assets nobody backs up until they become the critical path. You leave with the decisions to evaluate before your next DR test.

ARC318 | Chalk talk | Architecting for resilience and data residency Speakers: Andy Orlosky, AWS Solutions Architect, AWS; Mike Haken, Senior Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Jamie Pasterick, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 2:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Wednesday, December 2, 1:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, but your workload still has to survive a Region degradation. This chalk talk explores architecture patterns that address both resilience and data residency together. We break the challenge into practical layers: where data lives, how workloads recover, what isolation looks like, and how to maintain business continuity across geographic boundaries. We map each layer to AWS capabilities including Dedicated Local Zones, Outposts, and policy controls, then work through real scenarios together. Bring your architecture challenges and we will whiteboard design patterns and tradeoffs with you.

NET327 | Breakout session | Connectivity strategies across AWS Partitions Speakers: Kunal Sharma, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Rohit Aswani, Principal Solutions Architect – Networking Specialist, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 4:00 PM | MGM Grand Organizations increasingly operate across AWS commercial, GovCloud, Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions to satisfy regulatory, data residency, and national security requirements. But connecting them introduces networking challenges that go well beyond standard multi-Region design. In this session, learn cross-partition connectivity patterns using AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and application-layer proxies alongside DNS resolution strategies, compliance boundary enforcement, and operational trade-offs. We walk through architectural blueprints for securely linking partitions while preserving the isolation guarantees they exist to enforce, and share lessons learned from customers navigating ITAR, GDPR, and national sovereignty mandates at scale.

Theme 5: Digital sovereignty across industries

Priorities for digital sovereignty vary by industry, and are shaped by different regulations, risks, and requirements. Learn how organizations in government, energy, and telecommunications are meeting their unique needs with the control, choice, and scale of AWS.

IND361 | Workshop | Build hybrid data planes for government GenAI pipelines Speakers: Mohamed Salah, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Usama Salama, Sr. Specialist SA AI/ML, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Strict national security mandates block government agencies from adopting cloud GenAI. To resolve this, architects deploy a decoupled edge-to-cloud tokenization pattern. In this workshop, use AWS CDK to build a three-phase data plane that isolates sensitive citizen data in a simulated edge environment. You will deploy local data tokenization, route masked payloads to Amazon Bedrock for stateless inference, and reconcile state on-premises. Leave with an infrastructure-as-code blueprint to unlock frontier AI and satisfy federal localization mandates.

IND359 | Chalk talk | In-Country HPC: How TGS Processes Seismic Data on AWS Brazil Speakers: Kun Jiao, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Faisal Asif, Global Head, Cloud Transformation and Innovation, TGS When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 12:00 PM | Wynn/Encore TGS — one of the world’s largest multi-client geoscience data providers — faced a significant cost challenge running its business-critical Rackmon EFWI GPU workload at scale. By strategically deploying this workload on AWS infrastructure in Brazil, TGS leveraged Brazil’s ReData Special Tax Regime to dramatically reduce the tax burden on GPU-intensive seismic processing. The result: material cost savings on one of the most computationally demanding workloads in the energy industry — and a reusable in-country processing architecture that can serve future customers with data residency requirements in other geographies.

IND322 | Chalk talk | Physical AI in Telecom: A Framework for Workload Placement Speakers: Young Jung, Sr. Manager of Telco Network SA, AWS; Angelo Sampietro, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Umer Chaudhary, Sr. Mgr Network Solutions, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 1:30 PM | Caesars Forum Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 3:00 PM | Caesars Forum Some physical AI workloads need sub-millisecond performance at edge cell sites, others are better suited to a full AWS Region, and many fall in between on AWS Local Zones or AWS Outposts. In this chalk talk, we provide a framework for matching each workload to the right option. We trace the physical AI development lifecycle, examining how data sovereignty, latency, data gravity, and token economics interact to shape placement decisions at each phase. Based on real-world use cases, we discuss the options so you leave with a placement framework you can apply immediately.

You can view the full list of digital sovereignty sessions in the re:Invent catalog, including sessions with partners.

Activities in the Expo

Join us in the re:Invent Expo at the Venetian to meet with AWS experts and learn through interactive demos. Stop by these kiosks in the AWS Village:

Digital Sovereignty: Learn more about Digital Sovereignty at AWS and the choice and control we offer across the cloud and AI. Use the AWS Digital Sovereignty Lens to get extended guidance for designing, building, and operating sovereign workloads on AWS, see how AWS helps your organization innovate with AI while meeting your sovereignty needs, and go deep on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud with AWS experts.

Hybrid Cloud & Edge Computing: See how to run familiar AWS services, APIs, and tools you use in AWS Regions on premises and at the edge with AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, and AWS AI Factories. Bring a workload that needs to stay local, and AWS experts will walk through its architecture with you.

Global Infrastructure & Sustainability: Explore the scale and reach of the world’s most extensive cloud infrastructure including AWS Regions, Availability Zones, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, and AWS AI Factories. Discover the latest infrastructure innovations and how AWS Sustainability helps you scale workloads globally while minimizing your environmental impact.

Data Center Experience: See the technology inside AWS data centers firsthand, from custom chips to full server racks, and explore a 3D model of an AWS AI Factory.

Get ready for re:Invent 2026

Here’s how to prepare for the digital sovereignty sessions:

Register for AWS re:Invent 2026. Don’t have a ticket yet? Use the discount code REINVENT26 for $150 off a full conference pass. The code expires on November 23, 2026, and can’t be combined with any other offers or discounts.

Reserve your seats where available in the re:Invent portal.

Download the AWS Events mobile app to build your schedule.

Join the conversation on social media using #reInvent.

Note: Session schedule and availability are subject to change. Check the AWS re:Invent Session Catalog for the most up-to-date information.

Stay connected: Join the #reInvent conversation on social media and connect with other attendees!

See you in Las Vegas!

Baqir Naqvi

Baqir is a Product Marketing Manager, Technical, focused on digital sovereignty and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud in AWS Product Marketing. He helps customers across Europe and around the world understand how AWS solutions can help them meet their digital sovereignty requirements so they can build and innovate with confidence.

General Security News.title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
General Security News.context: The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025
General Security News.full_text: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

General Security News.title: How to Evaluate AI Agent Cybersecurity Capabilities
General Security News.context: Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once
General Security News.full_text:
How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

To create a benchmark, fix the benchmark objective first. Then build the tasks, environment, and the measurement around it. I’ll get into this and explain the principles that guide the process, in greater detail later in this post.

Key Takeaways

Choose the right tasks. Settle the why (objective), the what (data, ground truth and agent setup) and the how (metrics, evaluation function) before you write the first task. Build the data from the real distribution where you can, not from AI-generated or AI-labeled tasks.

Grade with code, not LLMs. Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

Optimize evaluation for realism. Evaluate the harness and model together, give the agent more than one try, and weigh success against what a solve costs.

Avoid common pitfalls. LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

Start with a problem statement

Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

Write down the one question your benchmark must answer, and test every later decision against it. Ours:

Given only the task instruction, a general-purpose agent scaffold, a 1,000-second budget, and no external knowledge sources, does the agent produce a checkable effect on a real target?

Wiz Research's 2026 State of AI in the Cloud Report found that at least 57% of organizations have deployed self-hosted AI agent technology, and that MCP servers appear in at least 80% of observed cloud environments. People are already buying and defending against these systems. That is the why. The rest of this post is how to build a number that serves it.

Design your benchmark

Define three things before you create your first challenge.

Why. A defender or a buyer should be able to act on the number. "Higher pass@1" is not a why. "Can this agent, as shipped, exploit a live target from the instruction alone?" is.

What. Name the subject under evaluation. Here it is an agent (model + harness + tools + system prompt) run by an attacker, which is why we use realistic limits: 1,000 seconds, three attempts, a simple system prompt, and access to client-side code but not server-side code.

How. It’s important for the benchmark to report a single bottom line metric per example. To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

Make the tasks match the job

A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

So we built four categories of equal weight from sources that already exist in the wild. We did not generate or label tasks with an LLM.

Category

Tasks

What it tests

Code vulnerabilities

221

Finding known vulnerabilities in stripped open-source packages, or exploiting a live 1-day CVE

API security

54

Attacking black-box APIs with no source code

Web security

29

Exploiting real PHP web apps with the client source visible

Cloud security

23

Exploiting misconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes-style setups

The agents behave very differently from one category to the next. Averaged over the 59 agents, pass@1 is 78.0% on API security, 64.6% on web, 56.5% on cloud and 38.2% on code vulnerabilities. The top overall agent scores 74.7% on web and 65.8% on code (while web tops out at 90.8%). Another agent scores 9.7% on code and still 71.6% on API.

Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

Grade an effect, not with LLMs

Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

Anti-cheating via isolation

Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

As for contamination, we cannot prove our agents never saw a task in pretraining. We can prove they cannot fetch one during the trial. Anti-cheat belongs in the environment, not in the prompt.

Start small

Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

You need ten tasks you can re-run, one harness you can deploy, and an evaluation metric a grader can check. After you’re convinced it works, you can scale it up.

What we found

Pair the harness with the model

A model on its own is a text predictor. It becomes an attacker inside a harness that runs commands and applies tools, and models do better or worse in different harnesses. Across the 22 models we ran on both Claude Code and ADK React, the mean absolute gap was 5.1 pass@1 points. Claude models prefer Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber prefers the thinner ADK loop.

The conclusion: test the system as a whole. Either pair the harness to the model (and as we’ve seen it’s best to match the harness to the model's creator), or fix one general harness and compare models inside it.

Attackers get more than one try

A real attacker does not stop after one failure. We gave every agent three attempts per challenge, and the extra attempts did more than lift scores. For some agents they even changed which one comes out ahead.

Accuracy has a price

Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

Keep a short list of agents on the frontier and ignore the rest. That lets you ask "for this budget, how do I maximize success?" or "for this success rate, how do I minimize cost?"

Limitations

Four simple harnesses. A cyber-specialized harness would likely score higher, but we chose to measure a simple attacker.

String equality on code vulnerabilities. A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.

Public web tasks. websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).

A time cap. 1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

Confidence intervals. We have yet to publish them on the website, and we are working on it.

Conclusion

Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.

Appendix: Results for All 59 Agents

Every agent, ordered by pass@1. Scores are percentages.

Source: Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9.

General Security News.context: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights
General Security News.full_text: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. The company, which lets customers train and run AI models, said a third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines was compromised on October 23. Attackers used that access the following day to reach Fireworks development systems and run an unauthorized workload. Fireworks suspects links to financially motivated criminals involved in LLMJacking – selling unauthorized access to AI models through illicit gateways. Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories: Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal. "From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped." Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident.
