General Security News.title: UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash
General Security News.context: The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats
General Security News.full_text: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail. An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week. In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation. The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats. Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations. Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology. "Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law. Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties. "The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said. "The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened. "Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

General Security News.title: Half of Security Leaders Report Sensitive Data Exposure Through AI Tools
General Security News.context: Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found
General Security News.full_text:
Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found.

Of these incidents, 77% involved a company-approved AI tool.

The researchers said the findings demonstrate that many organizations lack visibility into the types of data being shared with AI tools, even those that are approved for use in the enterprise.

While 62% of respondents could identify users or departments sending data to AI tools, less than half (48%) said they could provide any record of the types of data that had left the organization through AI tools.

“This shows why security teams cannot stop at deciding which AI tools employees are allowed to use. Organizations also need to control what information is shared with them," commented Darren Williams, founder and CEO of BlackFog.

Almost all organizations (98%) reported having an AI usage policy in place. However, the ability to enforce such policies varied significantly.

Just over half (56%) support their broader AI usage policies with comprehensive technical controls. Around a third (35%) said that while their organization has a written policy specifying what information employees must not enter into AI prompts, there is no technical enforcement.

Meanwhile, 39% of security leaders admitted that AI adoption is moving faster than they can govern it. Of those respondents feeling outpaced, just 27% have comprehensive AI controls in place.

AI Agents Fall Outside of Organizations’ Governance Strategies

The BlackFog research, published on November 4, also highlighted a significant governance gap around AI agents operating in organizations’ environments.

Over half (56%) revealed that autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of employees fall outside their organization’s existing controls.

Read now: Unchecked AI Agents Cause Cybersecurity Incidents at Two Thirds of Firms

Technology and telecoms were the industries where this issue was most prevalent, with 70% of respondents stating that autonomous AI agents were outside of organizational controls.

In addition, only 54% of security leaders said they had the ability to block or restrict unsanctioned AI tools and around a third (32%) are able to detect shadow AI use but are unable to consistently stop it.

General Security News.title: UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk
General Security News.context: At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure
General Security News.full_text:
At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

The State of UK Critical Infrastructure

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

Andy Burnham's Government Makes Cyber Changes

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Specialized reporting requirements

Evidence preservation requirements

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Cybersecurity Experts Weigh in on CNI Defense

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

General Security News.title: Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his very personal use
General Security News.context: " After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's...
General Security News.full_text: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs. "One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call. The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware. Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week. The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies. Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened. And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived. Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action. Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work. The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job. "Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered. By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong. "What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job." After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes. Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place. "You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them." Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

General Security News.title: When cyber moves at AI speed, the model has to change
AI agents are a 'bane' for some website operators, says Cloudflare
General Security News.context: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince
General Security News.full_text: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince. “These vulnerabilities, like the PHP vulnerabilities that were disclosed the other day, had been in the wild for years,” Prince said on the company’s third quarter earnings call. “We're going back through our logs looking for any evidence that hackers or nation-state actors or others had been using them in the past. I know that we're going to find examples of that.” That was just one of the warnings he offered on the call, among them that some of Cloudflare’s customers believe AI agents are “a bane to their business and want to keep them away.” To explain why, Prince hypothesized that he could use an agent to find him a restaurant to eat at after he finishes his day of investor relations duties. “It might go and scour the internet and look at 1,000 different restaurants' websites, pull down 1,000 different menus, and then I might choose to only go to one of those,” he said. “The problem is that 999 of those restaurants have now had a cost that is just been applied to them, but they are not getting any benefit.” The CEO admitted that web searches have always driven some low-value traffic but feels the volume of agentic activity – which Cloudflare has previously predicted will be one thousand times greater than clicks from humans – means the problem is now at a different scale. Prince also had bad news for Kubernetes aficionados, because he thinks containers might become another casualty of the agentic age. The CEO allowed that containers are “a significant improvement over bare metal or even virtual machines,” and said they fueled the growth of hyperscale clouds and mobile applications. But he thinks containers are already cooked. “The container-based architecture of the hyperscalers and neoclouds just can't keep up in a cost-effective way with the new agentic paradigms of today,” he argued, again citing the 1000:1 ratio of bot:human traffic Cloudflare expects to see online any year now. That’s a Cloudflare-centric view, because Prince pitched the company’s serverless “Workers” service as an alternative to containers. The company also offers products that can either block agents, ameliorate the cost and traffic impacts of agentic activity, or allow organizations to monetize traffic generated by AI. Prince said demand for those products is growing fast, claiming that since July 1st, “approximately five percent” of the web opted in to Cloudflare’s content protection products. The CEO said Meta is already a customer, and said Zuck’s new “Muse” agents will benefit Cloudflare by creating more agentic traffic that third parties want to tame. He also pointed to year-on-year revenue growth of 39 percent, which saw quarterly revenue reach a record $782.5 million. And he thinks there are better days ahead, due to the terrible state of security. “It may seem like the sky is falling with the number of new security vulnerabilities that have been reported over the last few weeks,” Prince said. “I wish I could tell you we were through the worst, but we're not.” He thinks Cloudflare can profit from security misery because the extent of its activities and client base mean it is “among the first to receive quiet disclosure of new vulnerabilities” and remediates them before disclosure. Investors thought this all made sense, and in after-hours trading sent Cloudflare shares up by around 15 percent, meaning it recovered and then improved on losses that it incurred earlier after major US indices dropped around four percent as investors who worry tech stocks are overvalued. ®

General Security News.title: Beyond the Endpoint: Rethinking Security for the Modern Workspace
General Security News.context: Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack
General Security News.full_text:
The way we work has changed significantly, and now the way we secure that work is changing with it. Again.

For years, organizations have added security technologies to address new risk categories as they emerged. Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack.

But today's attacks rarely stay within one of those boundaries. This shift is driving a broader approach to protecting the modern digital worker: Workspace Security.

How Do You Define Workspace Security?

The workspace has become an interconnected attack surface, and workspace security looks beyond traditional boundaries to focus on the ways attackers now reach users and business data. Several shifts are accelerating this pivot toward workplace security.

1. Work is increasingly distributed. Endpoints, mobile devices, browsers, SaaS applications, and cloud services have extended work far beyond the corporate network.

2. Identity has become a critical security boundary. Attackers don't always need to break through traditional defenses if they can log in using compromised credentials, tokens, or sessions.

3. Applications and collaboration tools are part of the attack surface. Email, browsers, SaaS, and collaboration platforms connect users directly to business data and provide attackers with more opportunities to target them.

4. AI is adding another interaction layer. Generative AI and copilots are quickly becoming part of everyday workflows, creating new interactions between users, applications, and organizational data. It is also increasing the need for visibility and control into how AI is being used and what data it can access.

Rather than isolated changes, these shifts increasingly overlap within the same workflows and the same attacks.

What are the Risks of Operating Security in Silos?

Because users, identities, devices, applications, data, and AI are interconnected, protecting each in isolation leaves gaps between them.

Security architectures have traditionally been organized around individual control points. Endpoint tools protect devices. Identity tools protect accounts and access. Email security protects communications. Other technologies manage vulnerabilities, applications, and data.

Attackers see the environment differently.

A phishing email might lead to credential theft. Those credentials could provide access to a legitimate application. From there, an attacker may establish persistence, elevate privileges, move across systems, or access sensitive information.

One attack can therefore generate signals across the environment.

How Are Organizations Breaking Down Cybersecurity Silos?

According to Gartner®, "Cybersecurity teams with limited resources and a need to reduce silos require a simpler, more unified approach to securing digital work than traditional multivendor tool stacks. WCPs address this by preintegrating modules to lower costs, reduce errors, and improve cybersecurity posture."

Is Endpoint Security a Key Part of Workspace Security?

The endpoint remains central to the evolution toward workspace security, especially because unified endpoint security platforms have expanded beyond malware protection to include numerous capabilities: attack surface reduction, behavioral detection, and vulnerability and patch management, along with EDR, XDR, and identity threat protection.

At the same time, the risks surrounding the digital worker increasingly extend beyond the endpoint itself. Gartner notes, "WCPs have replaced Gartner’s coverage of the extended detection and response (XDR) market, which no longer exists in its original form. As vendors expanded native modules and improved integration, XDR became a feature within WCPs and other cybersecurity markets."

Workspace Security isn't about making endpoint protection less important. It is about extending its context and connecting protection around the digital worker. This is why the distinction between a collection of security products and an integrated platform is significant.

Integration makes the security controls surrounding the user work together more effectively.

What Does Effective Workspace Security Look Like?

Workspace Security is an evolving approach that brings the protections surrounding digital workers together more cohesively, connecting proactive risk reduction, prevention, detection, and response across the workspace. Organizations evaluating their approach should consider several key principles:

Broad visibility: Can security teams understand risk and activity across endpoints, identities, applications, data, and emerging technologies such as AI?

Proactive risk reduction and prevention: Can the platform identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identity risks, and other exposures, reduce the attack surface, and prevent threats before they become incidents?

Connected context: Can telemetry across devices, identities, applications, and data be correlated to help teams understand the broader attack rather than investigate individual signals in isolation?

Deep integration: Do capabilities genuinely share telemetry, policies, behavioral analysis, and workflows, or are they simply a collection of products from the same vendor?

Simplified operations: Can teams manage policies, prioritize alerts, investigate threats, and take action through centralized workflows with less context switching?

Openness and flexibility: Can the platform integrate with the wider security ecosystem when specialized capabilities or existing investments are still required?

The goal is to reduce exposure, prevent more threats before they occur, and provide the context needed to detect and respond effectively to attacks.

Securing How Work Happens

Workspace Security represents an important evolution in cybersecurity, but not because organizations suddenly need another security product category.

It reflects a more fundamental change: the way people work is increasingly interconnected, attacks cross traditional security boundaries, and the security protecting digital workers needs to become more connected as well.

For resource-constrained IT and security teams, in particular, the opportunity is significant: fewer silos, better context, stronger prevention, and simpler security operations.

Ready to take a more unified approach to workspace security? Explore the Bitdefender GravityZone Platform to learn how you can protect users, data, and applications across the modern workspace. The future of Workspace Security is about protecting how work happens.

General Security News.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
General Security News.context: The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data
General Security News.full_text:
In 1951, Cambridge University’s computer went out of action for six months. This was inconvenient for physiologist Andrew Huxley, who, alongside his colleague Alan Hodgkin, had just built a set of equations to describe how a particular squid nerve cell fired. The scientists wanted to understand the “action potential” of these nerve cells: the electrical pulses they use to communicate, which underlie everything brains do, from perception to intelligence. The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data.

Huxley had hoped to use the newfangled computer to solve the equations. Instead, he was forced to solve them using a hand-cranked mechanical calculator. It took him over three weeks.

The basic structure of their model was dictated by known facts about the cell. Hodgkin and Huxley modeled its membrane as an electrical circuit. One part of the model, however, was just an educated guess. In order to make the curve fit the data they had measured, they found that they had to raise one variable to the fourth power—that is, to multiply it by itself three times. At the time, they did not know why. They just knew that otherwise the model didn’t predict the observed data as well.

They did offer a hypothesis, however. They cautiously suggested that the variable in question, which governed how particular gates in the cell membrane opened, might require the fourth power because multiple charged particles in the membrane had to move into place before the gate would open.

Decades later, long after both Hodgkin and Huxley had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963, another team found the structure of a related potassium channel protein. And they discovered that, yes, it had four identical pieces arranged around a central pore. The model was fit to the data in 1951. Even then, it predicted how fast the impulse travels relatively accurately. More than that, it turned out to have helped predict the structure of potassium ion channels themselves, which it had never been fit to.

Today, an AI system could plausibly find an equation like Hodgkin and Huxley’s in an afternoon, and perhaps it would fit the experimental data even more closely. But the point of the story is that simply knowing the fourth power did the job was not enough; what mattered was knowing that a simpler version of the model did not work. An AI system that merely hands you the model might give you an answer, but it does not give you understanding. Reproducing the data with a model is insufficient, because any number of models could do the same. What matters is being able to make claims about the real-world system itself, and ideally about other, similar systems. To do so, you need to know which features the model shares with other models that work, and which set it apart from models that don’t. As the mathematician Richard Hamming wrote in 1962, “The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.”

A three-step program

More than 70 years on, the Hodgkin-Huxley model remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons. The same kinds of equations, with different constants, describe nerve cells across the animal kingdom, from squids to humans, even though our evolutionary lineages separated more than half a billion years ago.

Even more important than its longevity, however, is what the Hodgkin-Huxley model tells us about how models work. Hodgkin and Huxley’s approach can be broken down into three steps, and most scientific modeling involves some version of them.

The first is building the model. This means deciding what the model is made of and what shape its equations take. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s case, that meant the parts of the electrical circuit—the membrane and the gates—and the form of the equations, such as raising the underlying variable to the fourth power.

The second is constraining the model—tuning its adjustable parameters to fit real measurements. For Hodgkin and Huxley, that included settings like how often the gates open under different voltages.

The third is interpreting the model—asking what the model says about the real system, such as suggesting that the fourth power meant the gate had four moving parts.

In practice, scientists go through these steps repeatedly. If the numbers fail to fit the measurements, or if the interpretation makes no sense, they go back and revise.

All three steps were once done by people, but AI systems are increasingly involved in each of them. Machines have arguably made the most progress in constraining models, so we’ll start there.

Splitting the bill, or how to constrain models

When Hodgkin and Huxley constrained their model by eye and intuition, they ended up with a single set of numbers. This told them that the model could match the data. It didn’t tell them whether other numbers would have worked just as well or even better.

Imagine you know that a group dinner added up to $120, but not who ordered what. Many different combinations of orders could have added up to that amount—perhaps everyone ordered a mid-priced burger, or perhaps one person had steak and lobster while everyone else had soup. Models of nerve cells work on the same principle: different combinations of gate parameters can produce near-identical electrical activity. Simply showing one combination that fits well hides all the other plausible parameter settings, and other combinations might have led to different predictions. This is true of almost any phenomenon being modeled. Many different sets of parameters can explain the observed data equally well.

The solution is a statistical method called Bayesian inference. It gives you every set of numbers that works reasonably well, as a probability distribution that takes into account their fit to the data and your prior knowledge about the parameters. The distribution takes the shape of a curve, with the best fits at the peak and the weaker ones at the fringes.

But this method has usually been impractical for complex models, because it involves calculating how likely your measurements would be under every possible set of numbers. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s model, that would still be feasible, but for anything more complicated, it would be computationally impossible. For example, if each of the thousands of ion channels opens and closes at random, you would have to work out every combination. Returning to our restaurant bill analogy: it would be easy to answer, “If person A had the burger and person B had the steak, what would the bill come to?” but much harder to show which combinations could have led to the final bill, especially as the number of people and menu options grows.

A different approach called simulation-based inference (SBI) overcomes this reverse-engineering problem with sheer computation. You pick random parameters, run the model, and record the output. You do it again and again—perhaps 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley, and millions of times for larger, more complex ones. Then you train a neural network on the results so that, given an output, it can return the range of parameters that could have produced it.

All SBI requires is that you can run the model: put in a set of parameters and get back the kind of data you would expect to see. A model you can run like this—parameters in, data out—is called a simulator, hence the name “simulation-based inference.” You never need to use a formula to calculate how likely your measurements are, which is the step that makes standard Bayesian inference often impractical. These days a simulator is usually a computer program, but it doesn’t have to be: Huxley, cranking through the equations by hand, was running one. Many simulators are easy to run forward but impossible to reverse. Some can’t even be written out as a tidy equation—their assumptions are built into the rules they follow—but they are models nonetheless. For many complex phenomena, from networks of neurons to colliding galaxies, simulators are often the only kind of model we have. SBI lets us constrain those models with data.

Running all those simulations is expensive and can take weeks. But once it is done, a trained network can perform inference on new data in seconds, without requiring further simulations. That speed has changed what’s possible. When two neutron stars collide, SBI can work out roughly where in the sky the collision happened, fast enough to point telescopes at it while the signal is still detectable. The same approach has been successfully applied to problems in cosmology, structural biology, geophysics, and many other domains.

And SBI has been applied to nerve cell models, including the Hodgkin-Huxley model. Because it returns a distribution rather than a single fit, we can see which parameters are well constrained by the data, where more than one explanation is plausible, and where more data—and thus another experiment—is most needed.

The bill, one level up, or how to build models

Before you can constrain a model, you need a model to constrain. The equations of the Hodgkin-Huxley model were not derived from first principles. Instead, the fourth power of the underlying variable emerged empirically from the scientists’ biological insight, and from finding that simpler versions didn’t work as well.

For most of the history of science, this is how models have been built. Scientists used their expertise and assumptions to write down a candidate model. Then they tested it, revised it, and tried again. The problem is that the space of possible models is essentially infinite, and a scientist proposing a handful of models from experience will very likely miss models that could have explained the observational data equally well.

AI systems can now help with, or even take over, this step. Given some data and a natural-language description of a system, an LLM-based agent writes code for a candidate model or a set of candidate models. Then it runs the model, constrains its parameters, compares the output to real-world data, and revises it, perhaps by modifying the form of an equation. This loop repeats until the model replicates the data accurately enough. Several such systems have appeared in the past two years.1 The details vary, but all use an LLM to design the model itself. Until recently, this was thought to be something only humans could do.

But the fact that a model replicates data doesn’t mean that it provides insight. As with the restaurant bill, or the Hodgkin-Huxley parameters, many different combinations of parameters within a single model can provide the same output. The same is true one level up, for the model itself: many different models, with differently shaped equations, can explain the same data equally well. Run an agent twice on the same data, and it might return two different, and equally good, models. An agent that returns only one of them is hiding the rest, just as a single best-fit set of numbers does.

So it is better to treat building a model the same way we treat constraining one: you ask for the whole range of models that could plausibly explain the data.2 The AI system proposes many candidates. Each is then weighted by how much it is supported by the data, and the ones that need a lot of flexibility to fit are given less credit than those that fit naturally. The weak candidates drop out, and the AI system proposes new variations on the stronger ones.

AI agents can thus provide a distribution of plausible models, rather than a single best fit, and that distribution tells you things a single model can’t. If every surviving model shares a feature, the data likely favors it. If the survivors disagree, that shows where the evidence is thin, and points researchers in the direction of the next experiment.

We shouldn’t get too far ahead of ourselves. So far, these systems have mostly been tested on rediscovering models that scientists already know. Evidence that they work on problems with no known answer is sparse. Still, newer LLMs perform better at research tasks than older ones, and we expect these systems to keep improving.

Lost in translation, or how to interpret models

Once a model has been built and constrained, it still has to be interpreted. What does it tell us about the real system being studied? Hodgkin and Huxley’s four-particle hypothesis came about because equations involving the fourth power are what you would expect if four separate things all had to happen before a gate could open. So they suggested that this might be what was happening inside the membrane. As we saw above, they turned out to be largely right.

That interpretation only carried weight because of what they had ruled out. If a simpler model had worked just as well, there would have been no reason to think the gate had several moving parts. It was the failure of the alternatives that allowed them to make that claim. There was some uncertainty about the exact number: Hodgkin and Huxley noted that a third or fourth power was needed and settled on four. They wrote that higher powers might even have fit slightly better, but that the potential “improvement was not considered to be worth the additional complication.”

The equations also let Hodgkin and Huxley reason out several other implications. For instance, the equations explained why nerve cells have a voltage threshold below which they don’t fire and above which they do, and why nerve pulses all have the same shape. They also predicted that a current rising slowly enough would never make the cell fire. Philosophers of science call a theory “intelligible” if it lets you work out its consequences without having to run it. That test works for a model with a handful of variables, like Hodgkin-Huxley. For a larger model with perhaps thousands of variables, the equivalent might be whether we can boil it down to a few crucial mechanistic ideas that are enough to rebuild it. The larger the model, the harder that becomes.

Of the three steps, interpretation is the hardest to hand over to AI. The goal is harder to pin down: we can measure how well a model fits the data, but not whether it leads to a better understanding of the system, and it’s not clear how to tell an AI system to make “understanding” its objective. One proposal is to judge an AI system’s understanding by seeing how well it predicts what a system does when you disturb that system. Another is to sidestep the question altogether, and instead ask whether the agent’s outputs help human scientists better understand the problem. One example is an AI system for designing quantum experiments. Rather than providing a single setup, it was trained to write a short program that generates the setups for a whole family of related experiments. A physicist can then read the underlying design principle straight off the program instead of reverse-engineering it from one experimental setup.

In both approaches, having access to a full distribution of suitable models, rather than a single best-fitting one, is crucial for interpretation. A single model cannot tell us which of its parts are actually constrained by the data, so it’s easy to read meaning into parts that are not. In Hodgkin-Huxley, as we’ve seen, the hypothesis about four particles only makes sense if you know that lower powers don’t work as well. A range of models also makes predictions more robust. Say you ask your models what happens when you disturb a system—for instance, by blocking all, or only some, of the sodium gates on the cell membrane. If all the models that fit the data return the same answer, as you would expect when every gate is blocked, then you can be fairly confident in it. If they disagree, as they might when only some gates are blocked, that can provide ideas for the next experiment.

Cells and scales

Most famous models, including Hodgkin-Huxley, are compact. They consist of a handful of variables and equations, small enough for a human scientist to write down and reason about. That’s no coincidence: they needed to be compact, because people had to build, constrain, and interpret them. Their smallness is also what made them intelligible. But as AI takes over more of the work, the size limit will start to lift. We can begin to model systems that are far too complex to write down by hand, even if we can no longer understand them just by reading the equations.

Brains are an obvious use case. The Hodgkin-Huxley equations describe a single nerve cell. But a fruit fly’s brain contains more than 100,000, and a human brain tens of billions. And it is the interplay between those neurons that gives rise to behavior and thought. For the fruit fly, we now have something that was impossible for previous generations of scientists: a complete wiring diagram of its brain, showing every neuron and how it connects to the others.3 Researchers have started building large-scale models on top of it, including one that predicts the activity of neurons across the fly’s visual system. That opens up questions nobody could sensibly ask before. How does a whole brain turn its wiring into behavior? How much of an animal’s behavior can be predicted from its wiring alone? And which connections actually matter?

But at these scales it will not be possible to find a single correct model. Indeed, in most cases there is no such thing. As the statistician George Box wrote, “All models are wrong but some are useful.” The data will always be compatible with many models. The question will no longer be which model is the right one, but which properties all data-compatible models share, and which predictions can be derived from them. The most useful experiments will be those that rule out the greatest number of remaining models, even if they are not always the ones a human scientist finds the most interesting.

This isn’t unique to neuroscience. Climate scientists already work like this: they build many gigantic numerical simulations, each based on slightly different assumptions, and report their projections as the spread across all of them. Particle physicists at the Large Hadron Collider work in a similar spirit: when they look for a new particle, they don’t just declare whether a particular theory worked or not; they produce a map of which versions of the theory are ruled out by the data and which remain open.

The painstaking work Hodgkin and Huxley did—building the model, fitting each curve by eye, trying the powers that didn’t fit, and, in Huxley’s case, spending three weeks hand-cranking the mechanical calculator—is not something we want to go back to. But it was not wasted. Much of the insight that a model provides comes from the process of creating it; Hodgkin and Huxley understood what the model was telling them because they had built it themselves, and they knew what hadn’t worked. This understanding let them formulate their interpretation of gating variables—part of the discovery that ultimately earned them the Nobel Prize.

An AI system could now plausibly do much of the same work in an afternoon. But to offer understanding, it needs to deliver what the two scientists’ slow work produced: not just the model that fits, but an account of which parts are pinned down by the data, which are still open, which alternatives failed along the way, and what new puzzles were uncovered in the process. A scientific model may provide an answer, but it is the process of constructing it that provides the insight.
