General Security News.title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
General Security News.context: Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
General Security News.full_text:
Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

General Security News.title: Cloud Agent, now in a Container: Host Security for Nodes You Can’t Touch
General Security News.context: TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS
General Security News.full_text:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.

It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.

A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.

Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.

Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64

ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm

How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years:

Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift

Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS

Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine

Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances

Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance

The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. Here’s how coverage splits across the stack:

Capability

Covered by

Vulnerability Management

Host: Containerized Cloud Agent. Containers: TotalCloud KCS

Drift detection

TotalCloud KCS

Compliance (CIS Benchmarks)

Data plane: Qualys Policy Audit. Control plane: TotalCloud KCS (Kubernetes Security Posture Management, or KSPM)

Threat detection and response/runtime security

TotalCloud KCS, via eBPF runtime sensors

Findings from both Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit flow into the same Enterprise TruRisk Platform views, dashboards, and workflows your teams already use. A Kubernetes node is just another asset with a Qualys TruRisk score, sitting next to the VM, the laptop, and the cloud account, and prioritized the same way.

Getting Started

Pull the image from Docker Hub: Intel/x64 or ARM.

Download the deployment YAMLs or use the Qualys Helm chart.

Deploy as a DaemonSet to your cluster with your Agent Activation Key, following the Intel or ARM getting started guide.

Platform-specific guides are available for AWS Bottlerocket, Google COS, and Red Hat CoreOS.

Coming in Cloud Agent 2.9.0

Today, images are available on Docker Hub. With Cloud Agent release 2.9.0, you’ll be able to download the Containerized Cloud Agent package directly from the Qualys platform alongside every other Cloud Agent installer. The Common Container tiles will appear in the Download and Install Cloud Agent workflow, with your activation key, supported OS list, and installation steps right there.

Common Container installation instructions in the Qualys Cloud Platform (Cloud Agent 2.9.0).

The Host Is Half the Story: Securing the Whole Container Stack with TotalCloud

The Containerized Cloud Agent secures the layer beneath your workloads. It doesn’t look inside the containers running on top of it, and it isn’t meant to. That job belongs to Qualys TotalCloud, and the two are designed as complementary halves of a single answer to the question every platform team eventually has to answer: how exposed are our container workloads, end to end?

Container risk doesn’t live in one layer. It spans the cloud account the cluster runs in, the node operating systems, the Kubernetes control plane and its configuration, the images in your registries, the containers running in production, and the identities and network paths that connect all of it. Securing any one of those layers in isolation leaves you with a partial view and a false sense of coverage. TotalCloud is built to cover all of them on one platform, with one risk score.

Container Security: From Registry to Runtime

TotalCloud’s Container Security sensor picks up where the host agent leaves off. Deployed as a lightweight container alongside your workloads, it discovers and inventories every image, container, and cluster across your environment and assesses them at every stage of the lifecycle:

Build and registry: images are scanned for OS and application-layer vulnerabilities and embedded secrets as they land in registries or move through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, so a critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry in a base layer is caught before it’s ever deployed, and admission policies can block it from being scheduled at all.

Running containers: containers in production are continuously assessed against the same KnowledgeBase, with drift detection that flags containers that no longer match the image they were launched from.

Kubernetes posture: clusters, namespaces, workloads, and role-based access control (RBAC) are assessed against CIS Kubernetes Benchmarks and best practices to surface over-privileged pods, exposed dashboards, missing network policies, and other control-plane misconfigurations.

Runtime defense: behavioral monitoring of running containers detects and blocks malicious activity such as unexpected process execution, file tampering, and anomalous network connections, so an exploit that slips past the earlier stages is caught in the act.

TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS.

Want to see how TotalCloud secures containers from registry to runtime?

Start Free Trial

Cloud Posture, Identity, and Infrastructure-as-Code

Clusters don’t run in vacuums. TotalCloud’s cloud security posture management (CSPM) continuously assesses the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts your clusters live in, covering misconfigured storage, over-permissive identity and access management (IAM) roles, exposed services, and hundreds of other controls mapped to CIS and regulatory frameworks. Infrastructure-as-code scanning applies the same checks to Terraform, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes manifests in your repositories, so misconfigurations are fixed in the pull request rather than in production. Together, they close the loop around the cluster itself.

One Risk Picture, Scored with TruRisk

What makes this a platform rather than a collection of tools is that every finding, from the host agent, the container sensor, and the cloud posture assessment, is normalized, correlated, and scored with TruRisk in one place. That changes what you can see. A vulnerable kernel on a Bottlerocket node, a critical CVE in a base image, an over-privileged pod running on that node, and a public ingress in front of it are no longer four alerts in four consoles. They’re one attack path, with one risk score, and one clear answer to what to fix first. The same correlation lets you dismiss noise with confidence: a critical CVE in an image that never runs, on a node with no external exposure, is scored accordingly.

And because it’s all on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, container risk sits alongside the rest of your attack surface. The Kubernetes node, the VM it replaced, the developer laptop that pushed the image, and the cloud account that owns all of them are managed, prioritized, and reported on the same way, by the same teams, with the same workflows.

Close the Gap from Host to Cloud

A clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload. Pull the Containerized Cloud Agent from Docker Hub today and bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate. Then talk to your Qualys representative about TotalCloud to extend that coverage from the host to every image, container, cluster, and cloud account your workloads depend on.

Bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate.

Get the Containerized Cloud Agent

General Security News.title: LevelBlue and rrelentless: Bringing Proactive Cyber Resilience to Cyber Insurance Policyholders
General Security News.context: Why cyber insurance needs security expertise built in Threats evolve constantly, and a policy that only pays out after a breach leaves organizations to manage that risk on their...
General Security News.full_text:
Cyber insurance has traditionally done its most important work after something goes wrong. We think it can do much more before an incident ever happens.

That's why LevelBlue is partnering with rrelentless, a UK-based specialist Managing General Agent (MGA), to give its cyber insurance policyholders access to LevelBlue's cybersecurity expertise as part of their policy. Every rrelentless cyber policyholder can now tap into LevelBlue Security Colony, gaining practical tools and expert guidance to understand their exposure, prioritize improvements and build resilience day to day.

Why cyber insurance needs security expertise built in

Threats evolve constantly, and a policy that only pays out after a breach leaves organizations to manage that risk on their own the rest of the time. Many small and mid-sized businesses don't have the in-house security staff to know where their weaknesses are, let alone fix them.

rrelentless shares our view that insurance should play an active role in reducing risk, not just transferring it. By embedding LevelBlue's services directly into its cyber policies, rrelentless gives policyholders a clear path to find vulnerabilities, assess their readiness and act on them before a claim is ever needed. That's good for the businesses, and good for the long-term health of the cyber insurance market.

What rrelentless policyholders get with LevelBlue

Through LevelBlue Security Colony, rrelentless cyber policyholders can access a suite of proactive services, exclusive to rrelentless customers and included with every cyber policy:

Vulnerability scanning to identify technical weaknesses across their environment

Cyber maturity assessments to benchmark their security posture and prioritize what to improve first

Ransomware readiness assessments to understand how prepared they are for one of today's most damaging threats

Vendor risk assessments to evaluate the security of the third parties they rely on

Unlock exclusive rrelentless access to Security Colony.

Learn More

Breach monitoring to spot potential exposure of their data early

Ask the Expert forum access, connecting them directly with LevelBlue security specialists

Together, these services turn a cyber policy into an ongoing resource for improving security, not just a safety net.

Resilience starts with understanding risk

"Cyber resilience begins with understanding where risk exists and having clear, practical guidance to address it," said Grant Duncan, SVP at LevelBlue. "Through this partnership, rrelentless policyholders will gain access to LevelBlue's Security Colony, connecting them with expert insights and practical resources to better understand their cyber exposure, prioritize areas for improvement, and strengthen their internal security capabilities."

"By combining LevelBlue's cybersecurity expertise with rrelentless' proactive approach to risk management, we can help more policyholders take meaningful action before an incident occurs, reduce risk, and build lasting resilience."

Gary Gallen, Chief Executive of rrelentless and its parent, the rradar group of companies, sees the partnership the same way: "Cyber risk does not stand still, so neither can cyber insurance. Partnering with global cyber specialists LevelBlue and Pistachio and leveraging the power of their expertise will bring significant value to our customers."

Part of a 360-degree view of cyber risk

LevelBlue's technical services sit alongside two other layers of support in the rrelentless cyber proposition. Legal firm rradar provides specialist cyber legal, regulatory and risk management guidance. Security awareness training provider Pistachio, which joins as a partner at the same time, offers personalized training, simulated phishing campaigns and behavioral insights to strengthen the human side of security.

The result is legal, technical and people-focused support before, during and after a cyber incident, with LevelBlue providing the technical insight that helps policyholders see and close their gaps.

Bringing LevelBlue expertise to more organizations

As the world's largest and most analyst-recognized pure-play managed security service provider, LevelBlue supports thousands of organizations across 96 countries with managed security services, threat intelligence and risk consulting. Partnerships like this one with rrelentless let us extend that expertise to businesses that might otherwise never have access to it, through a channel they already trust.

We're proud to help rrelentless policyholders take meaningful action before an incident occurs. To learn more about LevelBlue Security Colony and our partnerships with insurers and MGAs, visit LevelBlue.com. Businesses interested in rrelentless cyber insurance should speak to their insurance broker, and brokers can contact brokerenquiry@rrelentless.com.

General Security News.title: See the agents, set the terms: New visibility and control for personal agents
General Security News.context: Agent identity is only part of the story The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access
General Security News.full_text:
Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site.

Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business.

See how agents access your site

Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time.

In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use.

For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.

Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it.

Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block.

Set access policies that reflect your preferences

We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads, then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are.

You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings.

The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business.

Agent identity is only part of the story

The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply.

Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users.

Make the choice for your site

That person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

PHP2Shell on Windows and macOS: Automating the PHP Upgrade, With or Without an Agent
General Security News.context: PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated...
General Security News.full_text:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) allows unauthenticated remote code execution on exposed PHP servers. PHP has released fixed versions. On Linux, distribution packages carry the fix. On Windows and macOS, they don’t: Microsoft and Apple don’t ship PHP, so the fix is an in-place PHP upgrade that has traditionally been done by hand, one server at a time. Qualys TruRisk Eliminate’s Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability runs Qualys TRU-published scripts that upgrade each PHP installation to the latest patch release of its current minor series. On Windows, the script verifies the official build by SHA256 and rolls back on failure. On macOS, it upgrades through Homebrew. If a host is on an end-of-life series, the script stops, reports it, and then you apply the PHP2Shell mitigation script instead. The same script runs through the Cloud Agent or, on hosts without one, through an authenticated Qualys scanner. Agentless runs need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries. Plan a maintenance window for both because IIS, Apache, or php-fpm restarts during the upgrade.

PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated remote code execution against exposed PHP servers.

On Linux, patching is straightforward: distribution vendors ship updated packages, and Qualys TruRisk Eliminate deploys them.

Windows and macOS are a different story. There is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, so the fix must be a PHP upgrade, which has traditionally required someone to log in to each server and apply it manually. This blog explains how the Qualys Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability in Qualys TruRisk Eliminate closes the gap for both deployment models: agent-based and agentless (scanner-based).

Why Patch Management Can’t Deliver the Fix on Windows and macOS

Patching works by deploying the fix that an operating system or software vendor publishes. For PHP on Windows and macOS, that fix does not exist in a deployable form.

Windows: no official installer or updater. Microsoft does not ship PHP, and PHP does not ship an installer or an in-place updater for Windows. The official builds on downloads.php.net are plain ZIP archives published in multiple flavors (Thread Safe / Non-Thread Safe, x64 / x86, and per Visual Studio compiler). Upgrading means picking the right build, stopping IIS or Apache, replacing the binaries in place while preserving php.ini and custom extensions, and restarting services. Third-party stacks such as XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, Chocolatey and Scoop each add their own layout on top of that.

macOS: Apple no longer ships PHP. PHP was removed from macOS in Monterey (12.0), and Apple software updates do not touch it. php.net publishes only source code, so on modern Macs, PHP most commonly comes from Homebrew (the php formula or a versioned php@8.x formula).

The result is that a PHP server on Windows or macOS will appear vulnerable, with no corresponding patch in the TruRisk Eliminate patch catalog. The vulnerability is real; the remediation path is not a patch.

Custom Assessment and Remediation Closes the Gap with TruRisk Eliminate

TruRisk Eliminate covers four remediation paths: patch, mitigate, isolate, or run a custom script. PHP on Windows and macOS needs the fourth. The CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate lets you run controlled remediation scripts on your assets from the same platform that detected the exposure. The Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU) has published PHP upgrade scripts for Windows and macOS in the CAR library so that every host is upgraded the same way. Search the library for “PHP Update to Latest Patch Version” under the PHP2Shell category and import the script for each platform.

Figure 1: PHP2Shell category in the CAR script library. Figure 2: The PHP Update to Latest Patch Version script in the CAR script library (PHP2Shell category).

Both scripts are built around the same principles:

Upgrade within the installed minor series only. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x, 8.4.27 to the latest 8.4.x. The scripts never jump a major or minor version, so applications keep running on the branch they were tested against.

Mitigate what can’t be upgraded. If the installed series is end-of-life and no longer published, the script stops and reports it instead of guessing. For those hosts, deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script from the CAR library. It applies configuration changes that block the attack path and restarts the affected services. Mitigation reduces the risk until you can move to a supported branch; it doesn’t replace the upgrade.

Windows: Official Builds, Verified and Rolled Back on Failure

Discovers every PHP installation on the host, not just the one on PATH: machine and per-user PATH entries, common folders (C:\php*, XAMPP, WAMP, Laragon, Program Files, Scoop), IIS FastCGI handlers in applicationHost.config, and any Windows service that launches a PHP binary.

Detects each installation’s exact build flavor (TS/NTS, x64/x86, VC15/VS16/VS17) by querying php.exe itself, then selects the matching official build from downloads.php.net/releases.json.

Honours the machine WinHTTP proxy automatically, since the SYSTEM account has no user proxy settings.

Downloads the archive and verifies its SHA256 against the published hash before anything is touched.

Stops IIS (W3SVC/WAS), Apache and any php/php-cgi processes using that directory, takes a full backup of the PHP folder, copies the new binaries over the top (php.ini and extra extensions are preserved), and confirms the new version by running php.exe.

Rolls back from the backup and restarts services automatically if the post-upgrade version check fails.

macOS: Homebrew Upgrades Within the Same PHP Series

The macOS script handles the realities of Homebrew, as follows:

Confirms PHP is present and resolves the real binary through symlinks into the Homebrew Cellar to determine which formula owns it (php or php@8.x). PHP from MacPorts, MAMP or a manual build is reported and left alone.

Runs brew as the user who owns the Homebrew installation, because Homebrew refuses to run as root even though CAR executes as root. It also repairs any Homebrew files left owned by root from earlier runs so brew can write to them.

Refreshes Homebrew with retry handling for the common “another brew update is already running” case, and falls back to cached formula data if the refresh fails.

Stays on the installed series. If the default PHP formula has moved to a newer series (for example, the host is on 8.2.x but PHP now tracks 8.4), the script installs or upgrades PHP 8.2 and relinks the PHP command to it rather than forcing a major upgrade.

Restarts the php-fpm service via brew services if it was running before the upgrade and prints the final php -v so the result is visible in the job output.

Agent or Agentless: The Same Script Reaches Every Host

When you create a script in CAR, you choose how it reaches the host. Agent Devices run the script locally through the installed Cloud Agent. Perimeter Devices require no Cloud Agent. The script is delivered and executed through an authenticated Qualys scanner. The script content is identical in both cases; only the delivery changes. Select Windows or Mac as the platform to match the script.

Figure 3: Creating the script in CAR. Choose Agent Devices or Perimeter Devices (agentless), then select Windows or Mac as the platform.

Agent-Based Remediation

In ETM, identify Windows and macOS hosts flagged for the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and tag them by platform.

In CAR, create or import the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts with Agent Devices selected and run each against its platform tag.

Schedule the install run in a maintenance window, since IIS, Apache, or php-fpm will be restarted.

Review job results and rescan to confirm the QID closes.

Agentless Remediation

Many exposed PHP servers sit on appliances, DMZ servers, legacy hosts, and systems owned by other teams: a Windows Server in the DMZ running a vendor web application on IIS and PHP, or Mac minis in a build lab owned by engineering. Many can’t run, or aren’t allowed to run, a Cloud Agent.

A network scan can show that these systems are exposed, but remediating them has usually required someone to log in and make changes by hand, one server at a time. With unauthenticated remote code execution on the table, that pace leaves your perimeter open.

With the CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate, the same Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts run directly on scanner-based hosts through the Perimeter Devices option.

Find your scanner-only hosts. In ETM, identify exposed PHP servers using the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

Create the scripts for Perimeter Devices. In the CAR module of TruRisk Eliminate, select the PHP upgrade script for the host’s platform from the library, choose Perimeter Devices and Windows or Mac, and point it at the scanner appliance that can reach those hosts with the appropriate authentication records (Windows or SSH).

Run the job. Launch the job against your scanner-based hosts. The scripts behave identically whether launched from an agent or a scanner.

Confirm the remediation. Review the job output for the recorded before/after version on each host, then rerun the scan and confirm the QID no longer reports.

What the Job Output Looks Like

Each host returns a short, readable log entry with the execution status and the before/after PHP versions. Below, a scanner-based macOS host is upgraded from PHP 8.2.33 to 8.2.35 within the 8.2 series, with the php@8.2 formula relinked as the active PHP.

Figure 4: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based macOS host.

On Windows, the log additionally lists every PHP installation discovered on the host, the detected build flavor, SHA256 verification, the services stopped and restarted, and the backup folder location.

Figure 5: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based Windows host.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is a reminder that remediation goes beyond patching. When there is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, you still need a safe, fast way to close the exposure. With TruRisk Eliminate, you can discover every PHP installation, upgrade it to the latest release of its current series with integrity verification, automatic rollback, and service restart, and do it from the same console that detected the exposure, agentless on scanner-only hosts and through the Cloud Agent where it is installed.

Qualys customers can find the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts, along with the PHP2Shell mitigation script, in the CAR script library. Review the CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in ETM and begin with your internet-facing perimeter.

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Will the script jump me from PHP 8.2 to 8.4?

No. It upgrades only within the installed minor series. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x. Applications stay on the branch they were tested against.

What happens on an end-of-life series?

The script stops and reports it. Deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script until you can move to a supported branch.

Does this work without a Cloud Agent?

Yes. Choose Perimeter Devices and run the same script through an authenticated Qualys scanner. You need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries.

What does the Windows script verify?

It detects the build flavor, downloads the matching official build from downloads.php.net, verifies SHA256 before anything is touched, and rolls back from a full backup if the post-upgrade version check fails.

General Security News.title: CrowdStrike Brings Enterprise Browser Security to the Falcon Platform
General Security News.context: The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface
General Security News.full_text:
The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface. Employees rely on the browser to access business applications, interact with AI tools, and handle sensitive data. Knowing this, attackers seek to exploit browser sessions for credential theft and data exfiltration.

Today, CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser is natively available on the CrowdStrike Falcon platform, extending protection into the browser. Security teams can manage browser security alongside existing Falcon capabilities through a unified platform experience. This provides a simpler way to protect browser activity across managed and unmanaged devices, without requiring employees to adopt a dedicated enterprise browser or reroute traffic.

The availability of Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser on the Falcon platform delivers three key advantages:

Less to manage: Browser security, secure remote access, and BYOD/contractor access are managed directly within the organization’s Falcon platform environment.

Faster to deploy: Protection works in the browsers teams already use; there is no need to deploy a dedicated browser or reroute traffic.

Coverage where the sensor can't go: Protection extends to unmanaged, BYOD, and contractor devices without mobile device management (MDM) enrollment.

Stop Browser-Based Threats, Protect Data, and Secure Access

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser provides real-time security controls inside browser sessions, where users access applications, handle sensitive data, and interact with AI tools. Its browser-layer capabilities address five important use cases:

Blocking browser-based attacks: Runtime inspection helps detect and disrupt malicious browser activity, including phishing, ClickFix, malicious scripts, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

Identity and session protection: Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser extends protection beyond authentication to help stop session token theft and session hijacking within active browser sessions.

Data and AI controls at the point of use: Teams can enforce policies on browser actions such as copy, paste, upload, and download; this helps prevent sensitive data from reaching unsanctioned web applications and generative AI tools.

Browser extension management: Security teams can inventory browser extensions, evaluate their risk, and enforce policies that allow or block risky extensions across supported browsers.

Secure access to private applications: Policy-controlled access to internal web applications and resources is provided for employees and contractors, including on unmanaged devices, without relying on traditional VPN or VDI for supported workflows.

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser complements the broader security context of the Falcon platform. With browser telemetry available in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, analysts can search, investigate, and correlate browser activity with endpoint, identity, and third-party data to accelerate triage and response. With richer context and more places to act, security teams can follow the adversary rather than the boundaries between products.

Built for How Teams Work

As enterprise work increasingly happens in browsers, SaaS applications, and AI tools, browser security can no longer operate in isolation. By bringing Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser into the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike extends protection into the browser while unifying security operations across more of the enterprise attack surface. This helps organizations stop threats, protect sensitive data, and reduce operational complexity.

General Security News.title: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On
General Security News.context: New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection
General Security News.full_text:
AI is accelerating both sides of cloud security. Developers and coding agents are writing more code, pulling in more open source packages, and launching more cloud and AI workloads than security teams can review by hand. Adversaries use AI to move faster, and they are targeting everything organizations build and run, from the packages in automated pipelines, to the identities that control cloud resources, to the infrastructure powering AI applications.

Security teams must keep pace on both fronts to defend against this acceleration and secure the cloud their AI runs on. CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security is built for this. It is powered by adversary intelligence tracking 290+ adversaries, so detections and risk prioritization reflect how attackers operate in the cloud. It runs on the same CrowdStrike Falcon platform that connects endpoint and identity protection with SOC operations, extending protection from developer endpoints and software supply chains to cloud workloads. Because proactive security and real-time cloud detection and response (CDR) share one platform, the exposure and attack path context teams build before an attack becomes the context analysts use to stop one.

The latest Falcon Cloud Security innovations, all now generally available, put this advantage to work from build to runtime. They help organizations stop compromised software before production, protect AI workloads and the infrastructure supporting them, and detect cloud attacks in seconds. Proactive security informs runtime defense by giving teams the context to understand risks and when to act on them. This connected defense spans business and mission-critical environments, including some of the hardest to secure.

Reduce Risk and Stop Threats Before Production

Securing the cloud that AI runs on starts with understanding where organizations are exposed and whether software entering production can be trusted. Falcon Cloud Security connects cloud risk, application context, and adversary intelligence to help teams close exposures before software is deployed.

Stop Supply Chain Threats

AI coding agents are pulling open source packages into automated builds faster than teams can review them. Adversaries can exploit that trust by compromising otherwise legitimate software. CrowdStrike observed ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day.1 A compromised dependency does not need a CVE to be dangerous, which means vulnerability scanning alone can miss the threat.

Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends the adversary intelligence CrowdStrike uses to detect and quarantine malicious packages on endpoints into container images. Falcon Cloud Security identifies compromised npm and PyPI packages during CI/CD and registry scanning, automatically reassesses previously scanned images as new threats are confirmed, and identifies affected running containers.

At deployment, the Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller uses image assessment policies to alert on or block compromised images before they reach production. Together, endpoint and cloud protection connect the defense from package download through deployment to help teams stop compromised software.

Expand Cloud Risk and Asset Visibility

Security teams need to understand how exposures combine into opportunities for an adversary. Cloud Risks coverage in Falcon Cloud Security now extends to Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, where it connects exposure, effective permissions, vulnerabilities, and sensitive data context to identify high-risk combinations that isolated assessments can miss.

Supporting coverage expansions help teams assess more of their environment. Agentless Vulnerability Scanning for Google Cloud adds vulnerability and malware discovery for Linux-based Google Compute Engine instances without requiring additional sensor deployment. Expanded OCI inventory brings additional infrastructure, identities, and secrets into view. Together, these updates help teams account for more cloud assets and assess workloads where they cannot install an additional sensor.

Understand Applications and What Exposes Them

Cloud risk becomes more actionable when teams can connect it to the applications their business depends on. Expanded Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) brings containerized applications into Application Explorer with workload and cloud context, allowing Cloud Risks to evaluate them alongside other resources. Teams can identify combinations such as an internet-exposed Kubernetes workload running code with a remote code execution vulnerability.

New package exports map vulnerable dependencies to their associated applications, which helps teams assess blast radius and plan remediation across the application fleet. Enhanced third-party API integration findings identify external payment-service integrations and the operations applications invoke, helping teams assess exposure when a provider is compromised and uncover unauthorized integrations. The result is a clearer picture of which applications are affected and where remediation is needed.

Stop Cloud Attacks and Protect AI Workloads at Runtime

When an adversary gains access, security teams need to recognize malicious behavior, understand what is at risk, and respond while the attack is in progress. Falcon Cloud Security connects real-time detection with workload, identity, and exposure context to help defenders interrupt attacks across cloud environments.

Connect Cloud Exposure with Real-Time Detection and Response

CrowdStrike is extending Real-Time CDR to Microsoft Azure and Kubernetes, building on existing coverage for AWS and Google Cloud. Falcon Cloud Security continuously analyzes cloud audit activity as it streams, applies adversary-informed detection logic, and surfaces high-fidelity detections in seconds. Identity, asset, workload, endpoint, and adversary context helps analysts investigate and act while the attack is still in progress. All within the Falcon console, they can deny credentials or shut down compromised instances, or automate those actions with CrowdStrike® Charlotte Agentic SOAR to contain the intrusion before it spreads.

New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection. Suspicious behavior is evaluated alongside conditions such as dormant identities, elevated privileges, public exposure, and sensitive data so analysts can understand its potential consequences and prioritize response. A privileged action from a long-inactive identity, for example, takes on different significance when viewed alongside the conditions that could make it dangerous.

AI-based Anomaly Detection strengthens this defense by identifying suspicious behavior that predefined rules may miss. A dedicated machine learning model learns each customer’s baseline and evaluates deviations involving identities, APIs, and resources across multiple events to help uncover threats such as account takeover and API misuse. It is now available for AWS CloudTrail.

Together, these innovations connect attack behavior with exposure to help teams identify affected identities and workloads, assess potential impact, and focus response.

Protect AI Workloads and the Cloud They Run On

Securing AI requires protection for both AI interactions and the environments supporting them. Falcon Container Sensor and Falcon Guardian support for Anthropic APIs extends runtime detection to the prompt layer for supported AI workloads to help teams identify threats in AI interactions while maintaining a unified view of their environment.

Workload protection for Google Cloud Workstations brings cloud development environments into Falcon Cloud Security visibility, detection, and response workflows. Expanded AWS Bedrock AgentCore inventory complements that protection with visibility into the managed infrastructure supporting AI applications. These capabilities address distinct needs: detecting threats in supported AI interactions, protecting development workloads, and accounting for the resources behind AI applications.

Extend Protection to Regulated and Specialized Environments

Government agencies and regulated enterprises need cloud protection that reaches the environments their missions depend on. Expanded Falcon Cloud Security capabilities in US-GOV-1 and US-GOV-2 bring cloud detections, detection-rule management, and CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM workflows to GovCloud, including Kubernetes audit-log detections across Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google GKE. Amazon S3 scanning in Merlin also extends sensitive-data discovery to customers in that environment.

DaemonSet support for Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Z and IBM LinuxONE, along with DaemonSet sensor support for Ubuntu Kairos, extends workload protection to specialized infrastructure. Teams can bring more of their environment into Falcon platform protection workflows without introducing separate tools, consoles, and investigation processes for each workload type. This helps close coverage gaps while reducing operational overhead.

Cloud Defense Built Around How Attacks Unfold

Securing the cloud AI runs on means understanding the software entering a build, the identities accessing cloud services, the data applications handle, and the behavior of workloads in production. Adversaries do not separate the software supply chain from the cloud identities, workloads, and data they want to reach, and defenders cannot either.

Falcon Cloud Security is built for this reality, combining CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence with endpoint, identity, and cloud context to unite proactive security and real-time detection and response on one platform. That connection matters at every critical decision: whether to allow software into production, which exposures to fix first, and how to contain an attack already underway. Proactive context makes every real-time detection more precise and every response faster.

Expanded protection for government clouds and specialized infrastructure brings more of that connected defense to government agencies and regulated enterprises, helping protect the environments their businesses and missions depend on.

AI will keep accelerating the cloud. Falcon Cloud Security makes sure defenders accelerate with it.

General Security News.title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
General Security News.context: We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells
General Security News.full_text:
We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is in our preprint, which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live.

Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, the existence of some crucial components, let alone their function, was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium E. coli, remain poorly understood. Another such enigma is the vault particle.

A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. It was discovered in 1986 by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle.

Vaults are found across most of the eukaryotic tree, from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm, protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs, and supporting innate immunity, but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that mice lacking vaults still survive, which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function?

Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had already been found in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults.

A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of cGAS–STING signaling, gasdermins, and viperins revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it.

Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for biotechnology—for example, as nanocapsules for delivering enzymes.

This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks.

Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said:

Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride.

Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods in our preprint, and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon.

A vault-like structure in prokaryotes

We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 megadaltons. By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes.

One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap.

Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell.

We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%. These experiments demonstrate how vaults could have changed size over their evolutionary history by duplicating pieces of their own wall without disrupting how they assemble.

Finding, isolating, and mapping a new vault with Claude

Part of the reason vaults have remained unexplained for 40 years is that they are missing from the organisms biologists rely on most for genetic experiments, including baker’s yeast, fruit flies, and nematode worms. In mice, which do have vaults, animals that are bred without a vault partner protein or the vault RNA develop normally, leaving no obvious defect to follow up. In recent years, bioinformaticians identified distant relatives of the vault protein in prokaryotes, but it wasn’t clear whether these proteins formed vaults.

Our team set out to answer that question. The research required several steps: surveying genetic sequences to find where vault proteins occur across the tree of life, producing and isolating the most promising candidates to test whether they actually assemble into vault-like particles, and determining the structure of one of the particles to see how its chains fit together.

We began by using Claude Science to search for the vault protein’s relatives across a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins. They turned out to be rare but widely distributed, present in 29 major groups (phyla) of bacteria and four of archaea (the other main group of prokaryotes) but in less than 1% of species with a sequenced genome. We then chose 44 of these proteins and tested each in a cell-free system to see which genes yielded full-length protein and how much. We chose the proteins, and Claude turned each protein sequence into DNA tailored to the host cell, added the control sequences that switch a gene on, and prepared the designs for ordering. We moved the best performers into living E. coli bacteria, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein.

Next, we needed to isolate the particles. The conventional method, developed for eukaryotic vaults, spins the sample through a tube of increasingly dense sugar and takes approximately three days. To speed this up, we decided to try size-exclusion chromatography. In this process, the sample flows through a column of porous beads. In a process called fractionation, small molecules get stuck in the pores, while the vaults, which are too big to enter, come out first, in what’s known as the void volume.

Claude first argued against taking the chromatography approach, because clumps of misfolded protein come out in that same void volume. We went ahead anyway, and Claude helped make it work by recommending a specific column as well as methods to track the vault protein and check whether particles had formed. Claude then proposed loading the contents of ruptured cells straight onto the column with no purification beforehand. We were reluctant at first because these columns are expensive, and the raw contents of ruptured E. coli cells can clog them or cause contamination. But we were willing to test an unconventional idea, and it worked.

We are not the first group to isolate vaults on sizing columns, but our optimized method takes about 90 minutes from cells to microscopy grid instead of days. Under an electron microscope, seven of the 15 proteins had assembled into vault-like particles.

Cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four of those seven, two from phages and two from bacteria. We chose one of the phage proteins, L05, for the detailed structure described above because it was among the best at forming complete, closed particles. Determining a biomolecular structure often takes weeks or months of manual work with specialized software. We directed Claude through the whole process. Working in an internal multi-agent harness with access to internal compute resources, Claude set up an open-source processing software (RELION) and ran each step, while we advised on the analysis decisions. A first full model was ready in 34 hours, and the final maps were ready about a week after processing began.

Claude also pointed out a feature of the structure we can’t yet explain. A pocket partway up each of the 96 protein copies holds a small molecule that shows up clearly in the map but that we haven’t been able to identify. Claude found that its shape resembles coenzyme A, a common helper molecule that cells use to shuttle chemical groups around. If it is coenzyme A, or something similar, it would be an early hint at a possible function.

A new way of doing science

For us, this was a dramatically different way of doing science. None of us had worked with a protein assembly this large, and we had limited experience in structural biology. We took the project on anyway, because Claude could make up for what we didn’t know and rapidly perform analyses that would otherwise have taken us much longer.

In under four months, we screened dozens of candidate vaults, prepared samples for the microscope, and solved the first vault structure found in prokaryotes. Most of this work could be achieved by a typical lab with access to existing Claude products. Only the cryo-EM analysis, which used hundreds of GPUs in parallel to save time, required more computing resources than might be available to an academic institution.

Working this way also showed us where Claude needed improvement. A protocol it wrote called for a growth medium containing an additive that interferes with getting DNA into cells, which set the project back by two weeks. Early in the cryo-EM processing, it skipped a standard step and produced a flawed map blended with its mirror image, and we told it to stop improvising (“Please let’s do normal things unless they don’t work”).

We have used what we’ve learned to inform Claude’s development. We shared our lab notes with the ML researchers who train Claude, so they could see where the model went wrong. This has informed the kind of data Claude learns from. Over the course of the project, Claude got much better at these tasks as new models arrived, making seemingly fewer errors in DNA construct design and better identifying potential pitfalls in experiments. In areas we knew well, we caught mistakes quickly, but they cost us time in areas we didn’t. Overall, we found that the benefits of working this way far outweighed the drawbacks, and Claude has become integral to our work.

So far, we have made these vaults only in E. coli, and have yet to test whether they form in the bacteria and phages where they’re naturally found. More work is needed to determine the function of these particles, and our work only deepens the mystery. As Dr. Rome put it:

Will we find out that they are all doing the same thing? Or will we see an evolutionary development of vault function? Maybe they are doing the same thing as human vaults, and that is also very interesting.

We will continue our research into the function of vaults, and will share more as this work progresses.

Work with us

We are releasing the details of our work in our preprint. If you have an idea for what these vaults might be doing, or a system in which to test it, we would like to hear from you: mdurrant[at]anthropic.com, nicholasp[at]anthropic.com.
