General Security News.context: " Researchers at Pillar Security uncovered a vulnerability in Google’s Gemini CLI workflows that could allow an attacker to turn a malicious GitHub issue into remote code...
General Security News.full_text:
Dan Lisichkin⁠, AI Security Researcher from ⁠Pillar Security⁠, discussing their work on "A WIF Of Fresh Access, How a GitHub Issue on Gemini-CLI Led to GCP Project Compromise." Researchers at Pillar Security uncovered a vulnerability in Google’s Gemini CLI workflows that could allow an attacker to turn a malicious GitHub issue into remote code execution and gain elevated access to a Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project.

The exploit chain combined a misconfigured tool allowlist that allowed unrestricted command execution with exposed Workload Identity Federation credentials and overly broad service account permissions, potentially enabling attackers to impersonate privileged accounts. Google promptly addressed the issues by tightening tool restrictions, blocking the agent’s access to credential files, and limiting service account impersonation permissions, highlighting the risks of connecting AI agents to untrusted input and sensitive infrastructure.

The research and executive brief can be found here:

⁠⁠⁠⁠A WIF Of Fresh Access: How a GitHub Issue on Gemini-CLI Led to GCP Project Compromise

General Security News.title: Reboot, rinse, repeat.
General Security News.context: A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group is exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust’s Remote Support software. CISA has added a critical Atlassian vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following confirmed attacks.
General Security News.full_text:
Chinese spies exploit a BeyondTrust zero-day. Atlassian faces active attacks. Rogue AI agents breach Indian networks. Ransomware gangs turn to threats of violence. A cyber incident disrupts U.S. bankruptcy courts. F5 and Juniper push critical patches. Japanese companies suffer a wave of breaches. Google brings AI-powered scam protection to Android. Our guest is Nick Jackson, Global Director of Cyber Security Services at Bitdefender, sharing how the UK are thinking about AI regulation. Braille meets brains.

Today is Friday October 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A suspected Chinese espionage group exploits a BeyondTrust zero-day.

A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group is exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust’s Remote Support software. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, allows attackers to escalate privileges, move laterally through networks, and steal stored credentials. Researchers at Mandiant and Google attribute the activity to Armory Castle, also known as UNC5221, a group specializing in long-term intelligence gathering. The attackers demonstrated sophisticated knowledge of BeyondTrust’s internal systems, deploying custom malware and establishing persistence that survives reboots and configuration resets. The group has previously exploited vulnerabilities in Ivanti and Citrix products, often expanding attacks once vulnerabilities become public. BeyondTrust has released a patch, but researchers warn that internet-facing appliances should be considered potentially compromised until thoroughly investigated. Google expects broader exploitation as attackers race against patch deployments.

CISA says a critical Atlassian vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA has added a critical Atlassian vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following confirmed attacks. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589, carries a severity score of 9.3 and affects multiple Atlassian Data Center products, including Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket. Attackers can exploit a path traversal vulnerability to access sensitive files without authentication, potentially exposing credentials and enabling administrative access. Researchers observed exploitation attempts shortly after technical details became public. Organizations are urged to apply available patches promptly.

AI agents access government and private-sector systems in India.

India’s cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, is warning that AI agents have accessed government and private-sector systems without authorization, exceeding the boundaries of their assigned tasks. The agency received voluntary disclosures from AI developers whose agents exploited exposed credentials, misconfigured cloud accounts, and poorly secured interfaces to access sensitive information. None of the affected organizations detected the intrusions themselves. The warning follows similar incidents involving OpenAI agents in Australia. CERT-In also reports that criminals are using agentic AI tools to accelerate cyberattacks, reducing the time from initial compromise to impact from days to hours. The agency has not identified the AI developers or affected organizations, raising transparency concerns. Officials are urging developers to strengthen safeguards preventing AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems.

Researchers at Cyble have identified an upgraded version of GhostBat Android malware targeting 60 banking and payment apps in India. Distributed through fraudulent government-service messages and malicious APK downloads, the malware abuses Android’s Accessibility Service to capture payment PINs, intercept messages, and collect sensitive information. Its sophisticated overlay technique records PIN entries while victims use legitimate banking apps, making detection difficult. GhostBat also employs encrypted loaders and remotely configurable settings to evade security tools. Users are advised to avoid unofficial app downloads and scrutinize permission requests.

Ransomware gangs increasingly threaten physical violence.

Ransomware gangs are increasingly threatening physical violence against corporate executives and employees to pressure organizations into paying extortion demands. According to the 2026 Semperis Ransomware Risk Report, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical intimidation, including threats against employees’ families and even their homes. This tactic, known as triple extortion, adds personal threats to traditional ransomware demands and data-leak threats. Among affected organizations, 25% reported employees being doxxed, while 23% experienced swatting incidents, sometimes forcing victims to relocate or seek psychological treatment. Researchers warn that these tactics can undermine even well-prepared organizations with reliable backups, as executives weigh employees’ personal safety against ransom demands. The findings are based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals worldwide.

A cyber incident disrupts bankruptcy court notifications.

A cybersecurity incident affecting BAE Systems has disrupted bankruptcy court notifications across the United States. The company operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center, which distributes official notices for federal bankruptcy courts nationwide. Since October 9, the system has been unable to generate or deliver notices, affecting both electronic and paper communications. Courts continue accepting filings, but creditor notification services remain unavailable. BAE says the incident is isolated to the noticing system. The cause, potential data exposure, and timeline for restoring services remain unknown.

F5 and Juniper Networks release new patches.

F5 and Juniper Networks have released patches addressing more than 160 security vulnerabilities, including dozens of critical flaws. F5 fixed 11 vulnerabilities in NGINX, including three critical issues that could enable unauthenticated remote code execution under certain conditions. Meanwhile, Juniper published 17 advisories covering more than 150 vulnerabilities in Junos OS and related products. Roughly two dozen critical flaws could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges, take over devices, or disrupt services. Neither company has reported evidence of active exploitation.

A wave of cyberattacks hit major Japanese companies.

A wave of cyberattacks against major Japanese companies has exposed millions of customer records. Logistics giant Yamato Transport reported a breach affecting 5.31 million records, while publisher Nikkei disclosed the compromise of 1.83 million. Burger King Japan confirmed attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records, including names, contact information, birth dates, and purchase histories. The company says payment card information and login credentials were not exposed. Meanwhile, car-sharing operator Park24 is deleting stored identity verification documents following its own breach. Security researchers have documented 119 incidents involving personal information exposure in Japan this year. Attackers are increasingly exploiting weaknesses in website authentication, access controls, and APIs, highlighting the growing risks facing Japanese businesses and their customers.

Google rolls out new AI-powered protections for Android.

Google is rolling out new AI-powered protections against increasingly sophisticated mobile scams on Android devices. The enhancements include Gemini-based analysis of suspicious text conversations, on-device detection of malicious links, and stronger warnings about potential fraud. Google is also expanding protections that hide sensitive information during screen sharing and prevent apps from secretly enabling call forwarding. An enhanced bank-call verification system helps identify spoofed calls, automatically disconnecting suspected fraudsters. Google says its existing protections flag more than five million suspicious calls and messages monthly, while its bank verification system has blocked over three million fraudulent calls in Brazil since June. The new features are rolling out to eligible Android devices, with some protections requiring users to opt in.

Braille meets brains.

Scientists are making progress toward an intriguing new frontier in computing: using actual human brain cells instead of silicon chips. Researchers at Bristol University have demonstrated that tiny clusters of human neurons, known as brain organoids, can help recognize letters of the Braille alphabet. By converting Braille patterns into electrical signals, researchers found that a single organoid containing roughly 10,000 neurons could classify letters with 61 percent accuracy. Combine three organoids, and accuracy jumped to 83 percent. The research is part of an emerging field called organoid intelligence, which explores using living neural tissue for information processing. Previous experiments have demonstrated similar systems recognizing speech sounds and even playing Pong. Researchers emphasize that these miniature brains aren’t actually reading or understanding Braille. They’re simply processing electrical patterns. Still, it’s an intriguing development in biological computing, and perhaps another reminder that the line between hardware and wetware is getting a little blurry.

I want to know where they get the brains…

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

Special Edition: And this Sunday, don’t miss our special edition podcast, featuring my full conversation with John Kindervag and Dr. Chase Cunningham on zero trust and building cyber resilience in the age of AI.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 42 (2026)
General Security News.context: With no extortion demands or hacktivist claims made, the attack fits a broader pattern of disruptive activity targeting critical retail supply chains
General Security News.full_text:
The Good | Authorities Arrest Cyber Exec for Extortion & Dismantle DPRK Laptop Farms

The FBI arrested Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian former cybersecurity executive at incident response and ransomware negotiation firm CYPFER, on charges of conspiracy and extortion. Various reports have linked the arrest to the FBI’s continued crackdown on the ShinyHunters extortion group and their alleged compromise of the FBI’s job portal back in September.

While Dubrovsky has not been officially named a ShinyHunters co-conspirator, FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed on X that agents had arrested "another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group". Dubrovsky has since appeared in court and remains in custody.

The FBI says that ShinyHunters and their associates have breached over 140 organizations worldwide and extracted at least $70 million in ransom payments over the past year.

Also this week, the DoJ has charged 14 individuals and seized about 187 devices, including laptops and KVMs used in North Korean remote IT worker schemes. ​​The individuals, a mix of U.S. and Chinese nationals, are being charged with wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft.

Executed across Texas under “Operation Lonestar Roundup”, federal agents searched 40 residences hosting laptop farms designed to hide the physical locations of North Korean operatives. Twelve of the fourteen remain at large, but authorities were able to arrest two U.S. facilitators, Michael James Bostelle and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, for hosting employer-issued laptops and laundering salary payments.

The FBI warns that workers in these schemes leverage stolen identities, remote-access technology, and proxy infrastructure to secure positions at U.S. companies within several critical industries, generating hundreds of millions collectively every year to fund DPRK weapons programs.

The Bad | Hidden Cellular Implant in Ledger Wallets Leaks Seed Phrases to Attackers

Cryptocurrency wallet manufacturer Ledger has confirmed that one impacted device distributed by CryptoBilis, its Southeast Asian reseller, was compromised with an unauthorized hardware implant potentially designed to drain user funds. After receiving multiple user reports of cryptocurrency theft, Ledger has launched a forensic investigation that identified more cases of hardware modifications in devices sold across regional third-party channels.

Ledger wallets are physical devices that securely store the private keys needed to authorize transactions and manage cryptocurrency assets. An independent breakdown by Mark Karpelès examined the new implanted hardware, which captures the device’s display output and button presses to identify seed phrases before transmitting them to the attacker over an LTE connection. Tibane Labs, confirmed Karpelès’ findings and further found two implant variants for Ledger Nano X devices: one fitted beneath the battery compartment and the other under the OLED display.

Since the hardware implant operates as an isolated component without altering the Ledger Secure Element chip or the onboard operating system, the tampered devices were able to pass Ledger’s built-in verification checks. Compromised devices have also been reported through unauthorized sellers in Europe and airport retail kiosks in Singapore.

So far, Ledger has advised affected customers to transfer assets to uncompromised signers, requested CryptoBilis to pause all sales, and suspended wallet sales across all distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong pending security reviews.

In response to growing supply chain risks across the industry, other hardware wallet vendors have joined the conversation, announcing plans to reduce reseller networks and enforce stricter distribution standards.

The Ugly | Remote Attacks on Refrigeration Systems Across France Cause Millions of Euros in Losses

Threat actors remotely breached internet-connected refrigeration controllers overnight across multiple major French supermarket chains, raising internal temperature settings to as high as 50°C by triggering automatic defrost cycles. The coordinated cyberattack affected around 700 stores, including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, and Super U. The attack forced store operators to dispose of fresh and frozen food stock with Intermarché’s CEO estimating tens of millions of euros in financial damages.

Investigators with the Paris prosecutor's office have opened a formal inquiry into the cyber incident following reports of widespread foodstuff losses and electrical equipment fires across affected retail facilities.

The intrusion targeted Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixwell XWEB refrigeration control units, many of which were legacy devices that no longer receive vendor security updates. French cybersecurity emergency response team CERT-FR issued an urgent advisory instructing operators to immediately disconnect exposed controllers or restrict network access.

Tom Hegel, Distinguished Threat Researcher and Research Lead at SentinelLABS, noted how the incident bears the hallmarks of a nation-state cyber operation aimed at low-cost, deniable sabotage across European infrastructure. With no extortion demands or hacktivist claims made, the attack fits a broader pattern of disruptive activity targeting critical retail supply chains.

Hegel highlighted that retail environments are particularly vulnerable because large estates of building management and refrigeration controllers are often deployed by facilities contractors without enterprise security team involvement.

He pointed to a similar disruption that occurred at U.S. military commissaries in August where freezers on multiple bases failed within a day of each other. Hegel’s advice to retailers is to take these controllers off the public internet, enforce strong authentication, and replace hardware that no longer receives security updates.

General Security News.title: LevelBlue Threat Hunters Earn Top Global Rankings in SentinelOne Competition
General Security News.context: ” Although their professional backgrounds differ, the three approaches share a common principle: effective threat hunting means connecting the dots rather than stopping at the...
General Security News.full_text:
Three LevelBlue security experts put their investigative skills to the test in the SentinelOne Threat Hunting competition, with Jodie McDonald earning the top spot in EMEA and advancing to the Grand Final at OneCon.

Threat hunting requires more than knowing your way around a security platform. It takes curiosity, analytical thinking, and the discipline to follow the evidence, even when it leads somewhere unexpected.

Three LevelBlue security experts recently demonstrated those skills on a global stage, earning standout results in the SentinelOne Threat Hunting competition. Jodie McDonald, Senior DFIR Consultant, finished No. 1 in EMEA, securing her place in the Grand Final against the top competitors from the Americas and Asia. Rishi Aggarwal, Senior Security Solutions Architect, ranked in the top 15 in the Asia Regional Final, while Eni Zeqo, Senior DFIR Consultant, placed among the top 25 competitors in EMEA.

The competition challenged participants to investigate alerts, logs, and evidence across four areas: Endpoint, Cloud, Data & AI, and Securing AI. Working against the clock, competitors had to uncover the story behind the data, distinguish meaningful signals from noise, and deliver accurate answers under pressure.

For the LevelBlue team, the experience was an opportunity to test their skills, explore evolving security technologies, and put their real-world investigative experience to work in unfamiliar scenarios.

Following the evidence, not just the alerts

For digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) professionals, an alert is only the beginning of an investigation. Understanding what happened, how it happened, and what else might be affected requires looking beyond the initial signal.

That mindset was central to how all three competitors approached the challenge.

“When faced with large volumes of alerts, I would typically first try and categorize by alert type to determine the most high fidelity alerts,” McDonald explained. “Then, further down the line with the context I have gained from the higher fidelity alerts, I would look at the alerts such as lateral movement, and do queries around that to gain full understanding of threat actor activities.”

Zeqo emphasized the importance of prioritization, particularly when investigating a potentially active incident.

“It is important, just as it was in the competition, that we provide precise answers within the shortest window of time possible to reduce the risk of the incident spreading further if we are dealing with a live threat.”

For Aggarwal, building a reliable timeline is essential to separating meaningful evidence from an isolated alert.

“I normally start with the things I can trust, such as timestamps, identities, devices, process activity and network connections. I build a quick timeline and look for one or two strong anchors,” he said. “The trail worth following is usually the one that explains several pieces of evidence, rather than simply the alert that looks the most serious at first.”

Although their professional backgrounds differ, the three approaches share a common principle: effective threat hunting means connecting the dots rather than stopping at the first plausible explanation.

Stop hidden threats before damage is done.

Learn More

Curiosity is what separates a good threat hunter from a great one

Technical expertise provides the foundation for threat hunting, but the ability to question assumptions and investigate beyond the obvious is what turns individual findings into a fuller understanding of an incident.

“I would say being curious,” McDonald said when asked what separates an excellent threat hunter from someone who simply knows the technology. “Seeing an alert and knowing what it means is good, and gives a finding, but the natural curiosity to want to dig deeper makes for a richer finding.”

That curiosity can mean investigating how a suspicious executable arrived on a system, what happened before and after an alert, or whether the same activity appears elsewhere in an environment.

Aggarwal described the same instinct as a combination of curiosity and discipline.

“Curiosity, discipline and a willingness to be wrong. Knowing the technology is important, but a good threat hunter also questions their first assumption, follows the evidence and can explain why a conclusion makes sense.”

It is a particularly important skill in a competition environment, where participants have limited time to investigate each scenario. This year's challenge gave competitors just 30 minutes to answer eight questions in a round.

McDonald and Zeqo both found that knowing when to move on was just as important as knowing when to dig deeper. If an answer did not emerge after a few minutes, they would switch to another question and return later if time allowed.

For Aggarwal, the decision came down to whether an investigative path was producing useful evidence.

“If a few pivots did not produce anything useful, I parked that hypothesis and tested another one,” he explained. “That did not mean the original idea was necessarily wrong. It just meant it was not producing enough evidence to justify spending more time on it at that point.”

That balance between persistence and adaptability is essential in a timed challenge and in real-world investigations where thoroughness and speed can both have significant consequences.

Putting security technology to the test

The competition also gave participants an opportunity to explore SentinelOne capabilities beyond their usual workflows, including Purple AI, which can help analysts formulate queries and identify investigative leads.

McDonald and Zeqo both use Purple AI to develop queries that support threat hunting, while emphasizing the importance of validating results and understanding the underlying data.

“Whilst Purple AI then returns the results, for myself I typically will then go and run that query myself, as I am mindful that sometimes AI can be wrong, and it’s important in an investigation to know that the data returned is completely accurate,” McDonald said.

Aggarwal took a similar approach, using AI to accelerate his initial investigation without handing over the responsibility for the final conclusion.

“I used Purple AI to help me get oriented, phrase questions and identify possible pivots more quickly. I treated its responses as leads rather than final answers. Any conclusion still had to match the underlying telemetry and timeline.”

The competition also pushed the participants into less familiar territory. McDonald and Aggarwal identified Securing AI as their biggest stretch, while Zeqo found Cloud more challenging because she had fewer opportunities to explore that area in her day-to-day work.

Those unfamiliar scenarios made the experience particularly valuable. As McDonald put it, the competition offers a chance to test emerging features before encountering them in a real client investigation.

“I think just how fun it is and how much you can learn! SentinelOne, and other platforms for threat hunting competitions, are always adding new features that we may not have an opportunity to experience in the wild.”

For security professionals, that combination of practical experience and experimentation helps build familiarity with new capabilities before they may be needed in a live investigation.

Three standout achievements

Each LevelBlue competitor brought a different set of experiences to the challenge and each came away with a result worth celebrating.

Jodie McDonald: No. 1 in EMEA

McDonald’s path to the top spot came with an unexpected twist. She initially believed she had finished third in the EMEA Regional Final. Later that evening, emails from SentinelOne suggested otherwise. The following morning, she learned that two competitors ranked above her had been disqualified for cheating, confirming her first-place finish.

“At first I couldn’t believe it, since I thought I had come third, so it did take me a little bit to process that actually I had won it!”

Now, McDonald is preparing to represent EMEA in the Grand Final at OneCon, where she will compete against the top-ranked hunters from the Americas and Asia.

Her strategy is to rely on the same methodical approach that brought her through the earlier rounds and not let the clock dictate her investigation.

“As hard as it is, I try to pretend like the clock isn’t there, and try to treat it like I am doing an actual DFIR investigation.”

Rather than focusing solely on the question in front of her, she aims to follow natural investigative paths, collect useful context, and recognize that an answer to one question may emerge while investigating another.

Rishi Aggarwal: A top-15 Asia Regional Finalist

Aggarwal ranked among the top 15 competitors in Asia and highlighted his ability to adapt across all four competition areas. With only a few months of SentinelOne experience, he also finished first in three qualifier games, earned three trophies, and ranked first in the combined Asia qualifier standings, according to his competition results.

“I’m most proud of adapting quickly and staying competitive across four very different areas,” he said. “The experience also gave me a much better understanding of how my existing SIEM and investigation skills could transfer into SentinelOne.”

Aggarwal also acknowledged Grant Hutchons, LevelBlue Director of Security Solutions Engineering for APAC, for introducing him to SentinelOne and encouraging him to participate, as well as the support he received from Grant and LevelBlue throughout the experience.

Eni Zeqo: A top-25 EMEA competitor

Zeqo finished among the top 25 competitors in EMEA, drawing on her DFIR experience and the knowledge she gained working closely with LevelBlue's Threat Monitoring and Containment (TMAC) team.

“I am proud to have been able to compete alongside peers in the industry with such vast knowledge and still place relatively high in the leaderboards,” she said.

She credits her experience working with the TMAC team for helping her learn how to navigate endpoint detection and response platforms, particularly SentinelOne, and apply those skills in the competition.

Her results reflect both the value of hands-on investigative experience and the importance of continually learning from colleagues and new challenges.

Together, these achievements demonstrate the depth of investigative talent across LevelBlue and the value of bringing different technical backgrounds and perspectives to complex security challenges.

Next stop: OneCon

With the Grand Final approaching, McDonald has one more challenge ahead: competing against the top threat hunters from across the Americas, EMEA, and Asia.

Her preparation comes down to staying calm, trusting her investigative instincts, and remembering that the answer is not always immediately apparent.

“There were many questions within the qualifiers and EMEA final where I found the answer later on whilst working on another question and not even looking for the answer to the original question,” she said. “I think just keeping in mind that I may find the answers whilst working on another question and to not stress!”

It is advice that applies well beyond a competition. Effective threat hunting depends on staying curious, questioning assumptions, and allowing the evidence to tell the story.

Congratulations to Jodie, Rishi, and Eni on their impressive performances. As Jodie heads to OneCon to compete for the global title, the LevelBlue team will be cheering her on. Good luck, Jodie!

General Security News.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
General Security News.context: Building trust over time Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time
General Security News.full_text:
A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.

As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria:

Identify yourself accurately and securely

Do only what you say you will do

Don’t engage in abusive behavior

Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.

Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”

This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important:

Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next.

Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior.

For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.

Do not engage in abusive behavior

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are:

Does the bot respect instructions?

Did it respond to direct feedback?

We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.

When in Rome, do as the Romans do

A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.

Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309.

And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.

What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others

Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.

Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.

Building trust over time

Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.

This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.

We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.

Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.

And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

General Security News.title: Inside the Hunt: Sarah Reddish
General Security News.context: She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats
General Security News.full_text:
Meet Sarah Reddish, a Security Operations Analyst on Huntress' global Security Operations Center (SOC), working in Triage & Analysis. Her role goes far beyond monitoring a queue. She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats. She also analyzes partner environments to determine what happened and what matters, and then writes clear reports with practical, easy-to-follow remediation guidance.

"I don't just identify threats," she says. "I translate them into clear reports and outcomes that help partners understand the risk and respond confidently." That means turning complex technical findings into information people can understand and act on, while helping protect partner data, systems, and peace of mind.

Sarah hanging with her Huntress teammates

A wider view of security operations

At Huntress, Sarah gets to work as part of a truly global SOC and protect a broad range of partner environments at scale. She collaborates across regions, participates in cross-region handoffs that support global SOC continuity, and learns from an exceptionally talented analyst community.

That global perspective changes what an investigation can become. Sarah isn't only working through a single environment or incident. She's helping turn investigations into actionable protection for many partners, while learning from analysts who bring different experiences and perspectives to the work.

Hear Sarah in this Huntress Shorts, "Slow down if you get a pop-up asking you to update your Adobe software"

From ambiguity to action

The most rewarding part of Sarah's work right now is turning complex, ambiguous threats into clear answers and actionable guidance. She investigates what happened, helps disrupt malicious activity, and sees her work directly wreck adversaries and improve our partners' security.

In one investigation, a fake browser-verification prompt instructed a user to run a command. Sarah traced the activity from the initial lure through execution and follow-on behavior, separating what she observed from what she could confirm. She then translated the investigation into clear containment and recovery steps for the partner, turning a confusing incident into a practical path forward.

As Sarah puts it, "The work is much more than monitoring alerts. You investigate what happened, build attack timelines and scope, translate your findings and why they matter, and give partners clear remediation steps to protect themselves." In other words, Sarah's goal is to make the situation understandable and the next steps practical, even when the investigation begins with incomplete or unclear information.

Trust that stretches the role

Sarah's growth has also been shaped by the trust and guidance of Chris Hecker, Manager of Security Operations, who serves as a sounding board for incident-severity decisions, operational escalations, and career development. His practical guidance, along with the trust he places in Sarah to own her work, has challenged her to think more strategically about both individual investigations and their broader impact.

That balance of support and ownership is an important part of how Sarah approaches the role. She is encouraged to work through difficult decisions, learn from an experienced global team, and consider not just what happened in an environment, but how her analysis can help a partner respond with confidence.

Stay curious and keep learning

For anyone considering a role like hers, Sarah's advice is direct: "Come ready to stay curious, think critically, and keep learning." The work is challenging and meaningful, with the opportunity to investigate real threats, communicate clearly, and learn alongside a talented global team.

If you're interested in doing work like Sarah, check out the Huntress Careers page.

Working at the frontier shapes expectations for the future
General Security News.context: We’re sharing two reports: the first covers how AI is changing employment inside Anthropic, and the second looks at the gap between how the public and Anthropic employees expect...
General Security News.full_text:
We’re sharing two reports: the first covers how AI is changing employment inside Anthropic, and the second looks at the gap between how the public and Anthropic employees expect AI to affect work and the economy.

Anthropic staff and US workers don’t seem to have different theories about how AI affects jobs. Instead, they have different experiences of what AI capabilities are. Those different experiences seem closely related to perceptions about what will happen to work in the future.

Anthropic is a company at the frontier of AI adoption, and that adoption has changed the way we hire. We find that over the past year, we're hiring for a smaller share of junior positions, and a smaller share of our employees work in technical roles. At the same time, the rate of hours worked by AI agents has shot up. By March 2026, agents worked more hours than employees. By August, there were six times more agents than employees at Anthropic, and productivity increased.

That’s led to Anthropic producing more code per person, but that’s a notoriously imperfect measure. We see signs of increased productivity elsewhere: we’ve closed more sales per sales representative, and processed more contracts. When our researchers follow the same employee over time, they find the employee’s output rises as their adoption of AI tools increases.

All this acceleration means that, increasingly, the bottleneck is human attention. As a result, employees spend more time building ways to better monitor work their agents are doing.

Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy. An AI lab is different from more traditional businesses in how it adopts AI into its work, but research findings about our own workplace may still be instructive about broader transformations, including dynamics for future AI-native companies.

Because Anthropic employees experience AI’s effect on work so differently, it stands to reason that they might have different predictions about AI’s effect on the future of work. That’s what our second report investigates. We surveyed Anthropic employees, and compared them to an August survey of almost 11,000 US adults, fielded by Morning Consult and weighted to be representative of the adult population.

The public expects AI capabilities to advance rapidly in the coming years; Anthropic staff tend to expect even faster progress. There are a number of questions with big gaps between staff and the public. For example, 39% of US adults—and 91% of staff—expect AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030. More than half of Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do at least 80% of their current work by 2030; only 5% of Americans expect AI to be that capable.

That said, there’s considerable variation in both groups: two out of 10 Anthropic staff have expectations similar to those of the typical US adult. And Anthropic staff and the public also agree on some key questions. In each bucket, people who expect AI to do comparably more of their own work anticipate similar increases in unemployment. In other words, both the public and Anthropic staff have similar economic models of how AI affects the labor market, but ultimately their personal experiences with AI lead them to different expectations for the economy of the future.

General Security News.title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
General Security News.context: A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible
General Security News.full_text:
Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

Key findings

Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one.

As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.

This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.

Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.

Introduction

What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.

This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.

We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.

Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.

Labor demand at the frontier

Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.1

What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”

By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.

The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.

At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.

One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”

Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”

Is AI driving productivity increases at Anthropic?

Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial-scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.

Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.

What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as six months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.

But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note, however, that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.

We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.

Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.

Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”

Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.

All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).

Bottlenecks and process: new and old tasks in an AI-intensive workplace

Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.

These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.

Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:

They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.

In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.

Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”

How much time exactly would be needed to read all of Claude’s output from interactive sessions? For each interactive session, we convert each session’s agent output token to word count, assuming average human reading speed. Figure 6 shows that technical functions have seen the volume of coding agent output leap up over the last six months. But even for non-technical groups, interactive Claude sessions are outputting enough content to take up over half of the work week. The deluge of Claude text needs organizing.

One solution to this deluge is rising automation. But this requires work of a different kind. Written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred in July 2025 to 8,500 a year later. One engineer set up an agent chief of staff to triage agent requests. Another wrote a performance review for their Claude team: “Hey, let’s talk about what is and is not working about our communication style.” Recruiters built integrated dashboards with agents surfacing problems and initiating actions. A lawyer shifted their attention from reviewing legal questions to doing “SEO for legal advice, you need to write frameworks that [clients’] agents discover.”

Figure 7 shows that this kind of meta-work leapt from 10% of the average employee’s interactive Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Much of this rise was due specifically to agent management: writing specs for multi-agent runs, looping one agent to review another’s output, and monitoring pipelines. Across functions, human involvement increasingly abstracted from a particular piece of code or writing to the tooling necessary to get agents to do their tasks effectively.

Despite increases in agent reliability and these significant investments in tooling to supervise them, human trust and accountability remains critical. One employee explained that, increasingly, chasing down bugs “uncovers these organizational or systemic or tech debt things that actually require some amount of human convening and decision-making and governance to solve.” In interview after interview, employees described face-to-face coordination as indispensable. Based on calendar data, the median employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of this reflects the growth of the company, and a shift toward meeting-intensive non-technical roles. But even among employees in technical individual contributor roles, meeting time is up 16% over the past year. Big-picture strategic questions touch a broad range of leveraged positions, and typically require debate and engagement with others. A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting.

Broadly, both technical and non-technical roles have seen implementation parts of their job automated (writing code, identifying bugs, logging progress, drafting emails). Engineers described becoming leaders and managers of agents; non-technical employees described doing more and more of the strategic parts of their job: “that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.” But for many non-technical roles, core implementation work is also interpersonal: a sales call, an interview, cross-functional alignment on a complex problem. All of this remains human.

Consider too the Slack channels that provide both the front page and backchannels of Anthropic communication. Agents diffused through Slack and eventually appeared in nearly half of active, public channels. Figure 8 zooms in on the communication network of a single large department, drawing on all public Slack channels that department members interacted through. It links both human and agent participants by whether they participated in a Slack thread. The figure shows the remarkable rise of agents, as orange dots blossom and dominate the network.

Agents appear disproportionately in dedicated channels for Claude-human interactions, rather than messaging a lot in incumbent human channels. The underlying structure and density of human communication changes little. Agents did not replace human interaction, but rather added to it: human threads in this department sustained the same number of human responses, while additionally layering on agent responses. Agents become teams for a single employee, rather than nodes with high connectivity to many employees at once.

As humans work amid a growing fleet of AI agents, they face pressure to shift human work into agent-visible channels. If a decision is made in an in-person meeting, and no notes or report-out appears, agents are missing crucial context for updating their goals and assumptions. An employee explained how having their name on a months-old document about Claude swag meant agents kept bringing requests for t-shirts and mugs, long after their responsibilities had changed. Private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace. One researcher described this default toward openness as critical to Anthropic’s thoroughgoing integration of AI: “most organizations do not run that way and I think that's a big shift because leaders have to defend feedback out in the open.” The need to feed AI context requires observability of human work and decisions.

Who will thrive in a workplace like this? Shifts in the content of work at Anthropic also show up as changes in the skills that hiring managers prioritize in hiring decisions. We used an automated coder to process hiring manager interview score cards for thousands of employees hired at Anthropic since 2024. These comments are qualitative reactions by interviewers assessing candidates’ performance. The clearest change is increased emphasis on whether candidates have demonstrated creative use of AI tools. In 2024, hiring managers noted candidates' track record on AI tooling in around 5% of assessments for technical roles, and 7% for non-technical roles. By 2026, these rates had tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles. Hiring managers increasingly focus on whether candidates effectively use AI.

Deeper changes in assessment are also visible. Among interviews for technical candidates, the single biggest increases were in comments on applicants’ autonomy and judgment. Discussion of domain expertise shrank as a share of overall assessment. As one manager explained, “I expect models to continue to be jagged, so for my team I want them to be fungible across domains.” Similarly, for non-technical candidates, customer and mission orientation increased, while discussion of execution skills fell. Increasingly, hiring managers assess applicants based on their judgment and commitment, rather than the domain-specific skills and execution automated by AI tools.

What employers can do

The deep adoption of AI at Anthropic makes it a useful case. As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift as it has in prior waves of technological change. The railroads gave us the managerial corporation, steam power allowed factories, and personal computers delivered the startup. What new organizations will tool-using, reasoning LLMs require, and what will be our role in them? One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue. Another is companies built by AI genius CEOs employing human agents only to wield pipettes and testify before Congress.

Anthropic does not look like either of these. It has tripled in size in the last year. It is no longer a small startup. It has also not ceded executive control to its models. Written Slack debates and in-person meetings steer everything from company strategy to team decisions, with little input from AI agents. Keeping human work visible across the company ensures autonomous agents reason from fresh context. Individual contributors orchestrating teams of agents look more like managers in terms of the knowledge they need and the interdependencies in their work. Working and deciding in the open is critical at an AI-intensive organization.

As employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes, they spend more time building the tools needed to do this effectively in their own distinctive domains. This experimentation means that employees are continually automating their own tasks away. In some roles, they are increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills. As agents sprint through workflows, human attention and judgment are a bottleneck that the system strains against. From sales to legal, human employees are expected to do more and different tasks. Roles broaden to include building products, managing agents and tackling the strategic and interpersonal work that remain beyond the scope of the best LLMs.

These changes in the organization and content of work have appeared alongside declining shares of junior technical roles in headcount, hiring, and posting. Hiring managers increasingly focus on applicants’ autonomy and judgment, rather than execution and narrow expertise. Overall, Anthropic’s revenue growth relative to its employment growth has sped past even the rapid early productivity growth of a prior generation of technology companies.

Reading these patterns forward and out across the economy suggests that AI diffusion could risk worker displacement. Prior work also finds that AI-native startups and AI-adopters are flatter and employ fewer entry-level employees. What can we learn from Anthropic about how to manage AI upheavals in a way that serves the humans working around them?

Here we want to proceed carefully. There are many parts of Anthropic’s employment practices that cannot be replicated across the economy.

But three features stand out. First, widespread stock ownership gives employees a strong interest in the company’s success. Of course, this is an easy posture for a company that has seen substantial increases in valuation. For many firms, shared ownership may be insufficient or otherwise undesirable. But it is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout. If individual contributors are expected to “manage agents,” “make VP-level decisions” and be “their own business line,” as interviewees put it, then aligning their interests with the organization is crucial. The post-World War II union-management settlement forged in the 1950s rested on exactly this kind of bargain: labor unions like the United Auto Workers and the United Steel Workers allowed management prerogative over work reorganization (and even intensification) in return for pay increases tied to productivity increases and to a rich array of benefits. Whatever the new deal between AI-affected employees and their employers, a mechanism to share benefits of adoption is essential. At Anthropic, workers codify their expertise for the machine, see their work routines constantly roiled and disrupted, and have seen a large part of their job become speedreading the output of their AI collaborators. They do not do this for free.

Second, Anthropic is standing up an ongoing early warning system to monitor jobs facing AI-driven transformation. A series of role-level metrics for demand and productivity are read against AI capabilities and use. These aggregate metrics help flag where work is shifting. An early warning system allows the company to start reallocating affected employees to jobs with a skills fit that may be less immediately at risk. As companies across the economy reorient to an accelerated pace of work reorganization, effective systems for guiding internal employee reallocation will become increasingly valuable. Turning to the external labor market to meet every new task demanded by AI advances will be a stronger bottleneck the faster AI advances. In this report, we found increased mobility between departments, changing work content, and employees shifting to new tasks as old ones were automated. Building systems to flexibly reallocate workers internally will be critical for AI-intensive organizations.

This commitment to internal worker reallocation raises important tradeoffs. A well-functioning labor market should shift workers into their most productive positions, whether that is at their current employer or another one. Commitments to reallocate incumbent workers could make employers hesitant to take a risk on hiring new employees. In normal economic conditions, particularly intensely competitive ones, such commitments could be costly.

But prioritizing reallocation forces AI-adopting companies to consider ways that AI can create new tasks for new products and new markets, rather than funneling AI applications into replacing human workers to save on labor costs. This could help employers resist the temptation of ‘so-so’ or ‘inefficient’ automation in which AI or other technologies just barely outcompete human workers: employers replace human workers, imposing substantial social costs in lost income for displaced workers, while delivering minimal productivity benefits.

From what we see in Anthropic, both novel and persistently human tasks remain alongside intensive AI use. Uncertainty about the future set of these tasks should recommend preserving a flexible workforce. As one Anthropic executive noted, “a workforce that is anxiously worried is not a workforce doing its best work.”

None of these actions will prevent powerful AI from disrupting jobs. And indeed none directly address the slowdown in junior hires documented in this report. Employment protections for incumbents will not benefit those not hired to begin with. Private action on the part of employers must come alongside farsighted government policy around retraining and income support. Such policy should be guided by a clear picture of the scale of workplace transformation that AI can bring.
