General Security News.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
General Security News.context: The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally
General Security News.full_text:
LAYER BY LAYER

Layers, not one gate

Six layers of checks, with rollback under them

1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.

REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.

4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

Risk

Examples

Human approvals

Low

Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag

None required once automated review and security checks are green

Medium

Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts

One person

High

The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people

Two people

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.

7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

General Security News.title: How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Managed Agents
General Security News.context: The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job
General Security News.full_text:
As a business development representative on Anthropic's Japan team, my job is to show Japanese companies how Claude can simplify and automate their workflows, but until earlier this year, most of mine were still manual. I was spending a couple of hours each morning routing and qualifying leads, then writing emails in Japanese or English. In the time I had left, I was updating our CRM, often a day or more behind. Now my agents prepare most of that before my day starts, and I review it.

The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job. I'd hand Claude one piece of my work at a time, correct what it got wrong, and save those corrections. Over time, that grew into a handful of agents, each covering a different routine.

Word got around quickly, and teammates started asking for my prompts and skills so they could build their own. All I could send them was a zip file with my skills and a few Markdown files from the knowledge base, which they had to upload to Claude and then answer a round of setup questions before anything worked. My own setup was getting harder to keep track of, too. Each agent was a skill, a scheduled task and a shared folder, and I changed them by asking Claude in whatever chat I had open, so the same skill was being edited from lots of different conversations.

I wanted to define each agent once, in one place, and be able to see every change I'd made to it. So I decided to try Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) (beta), our managed agent infrastructure on the Claude Platform.

I was hesitant to try it at first. The docs talk about schedules, tools, and credential vaults, and I'm a sales rep, so I assumed Managed Agents was for developers who can build and maintain the necessary infrastructure. I tried it anyway because my agents already existed, and I only had to move them over.

It turned out I didn't need to be a developer. I described each agent's job in plain language, Claude wrote a few short setup scripts, and I ran them from the terminal on my laptop. (If you're starting from scratch, the Console also has a quickstart with ready-made agent templates.) Since then, there has been no infrastructure for me to look after.

In this post, I'll walk through how I designed and prototyped the fleet, why I moved it to Managed Agents, how Claude Tag picks up anything that falls outside the routine, how it all changed my week, and what I'd tell sellers who want to build their own agents to automate manual, repetitive workflows.

Designing my fleet of agents

I divided up my workflow across several agents and gave every agent one clear job. A single responsibility keeps each one easy to reason about and easy to track, especially when something is off. I also gave every agent a Japanese name, because they mostly work in Japanese. Together they're called the Nakama, "the crew," or more literally, the companions you work with:

Furiwake ("sorting") kicks off first: it reads the daily inbound queue and routes each lead to the right rep on the team, balancing the number of leads and the priority of each one and checking who's in that day, so every lead has an owner before any of us start our day. At the end of each run it posts a report to a dedicated Slack channel (every lead in, every lead assigned) so I can track the handoff.

Sabaki ("handling") triages the leads that are assigned to me: it qualifies each lead, categorizes it against pre-set criteria, takes the defined next step for that category (draft a reply pointing them to to self-serve, craft a customized first email), updates the lead record in Salesforce, and drafts the first-touch email. It sources the draft's contents from the Nakama's shared knowledge base, a memory store (opens in new tab) every agent reads and writes (more on this below).

Henji ("reply") scans my inbox hourly for customer emails that need a response and prepares a draft reply in Japanese or English, depending on the thread, drawing on the same knowledge base as Sabaki. I can review, edit, and send the draft.

Shoudan ("opportunity") reads recent customer interactions and pushes updates into Salesforce, so opportunity records stay current without manual data entry.

Nokori ("what remains") runs at the end of the day: it scans my calendar, reads the attached meeting transcripts, summarizes each meeting, and drafts the follow-ups, again from the same knowledge base.

Each agent runs on a schedule. A sixth agent, the Nakama's coordinator, is the fleet’s operations manager. It updates the agents’ instructions and the shared knowledge base between runs. When I want to change how an agent works, I write what I want in plain language in the Nakama’s Slack channel. Only I can post requests for changes to agents’ instructions and system prompts. The coordinator checks that channel every 15 minutes or so, picks up the request, and makes the update.

Prototyping the fleet in Claude

You don't need Managed Agents to start. I prototyped the whole fleet in Claude first, using the following pieces:

A skill per agent: the instructions for one job.

A scheduled task for each skill, so I don’t need to run it manually.

A shared folder on my laptop as the knowledge base every skill writes its learnings back into: the difference between what it drafted and what I sent, plus anything new it dug up along the way.

On Managed Agents, the skill became the agent's system prompt, the scheduled task became a schedule on the agent's deployment (opens in new tab), and the shared folder became a memory store. I still ask for changes in plain language, but now I do it all in one Slack channel, and each change to an agent's instructions is saved as a new version, so each agent keeps a numbered history of its instructions. I'd suggest starting in Claude and moving your agents to Managed Agents once you have more than you can comfortably keep track of.

Running the fleet on Claude Managed Agents

Three things I got on Managed Agents that mattered most for my workflow:

The agents can run in the background

The agents run on their schedule whether my laptop is open or not, even when it's offline. The schedule is part of each agent's deployment. I could schedule skills in Claude too, but each of those schedules was a task set up in my own app. On Managed Agents, I set the cadence and timezone in the Console, next to the deployed agent's instructions and tools, and I have no cron jobs to maintain on the side. If a run goes wrong, I can open it in the Console and see each step the agent took. And while I'm trying out a change to an agent, the scheduled runs keep using the version that’s deployed, so a half-finished edit doesn't end up in tomorrow's run.

The Nakama shares one memory and learns from my edits

Every agent reads and writes the same memory store (opens in new tab), so any agent can use the others’ learnings. The agents compare the drafts they wrote with the emails I sent, and they save each difference as a note on how I'd phrase it. They also keep whatever new information they dig up while researching an answer, from our internal docs and our official websites. I fix a phrasing once in Henji's drafts, and Sabaki and Nokori stop making the same mistake.

Credentials live in a managed vault with scoped permissions

My agents have access to my email and our Salesforce records, but since these are customer conversations and company records, I wanted that access under control. The credentials live in managed vaults (opens in new tab), which protect credentials agents use to log in to outside services, such as OAuth access and refresh tokens, API keys, and personal access tokens. Each agent’s deployment uses only the vaults its job needs, it never sees the credentials, and I can revoke access in one step.

Handing the next steps to Claude Tag

For most of what the Nakama produces, I only need to read a draft in my inbox and send it, or glance at an updated Salesforce record. But some items need a follow-up step, such as figuring out an upgrade path or a purchasing route, or escalating an issue to another team.

For those, the agents don't stop and wait for me. They hand the item to Claude Tag (opens in new tab) (in beta). Claude Tag is Claude set up as a member of our Slack workspace: anyone in a channel it has joined, a person or one of my agents, can tag @Claude with a request and it picks the request up and works on it in the thread. Once it's configured in your workspace there is nothing new to learn. You tag Claude the way you would a colleague.

In my setup it works like this. An agent posts the action item to the Nakama's Slack channel and tags Claude. Claude reads the thread, checks our rules and the terms that apply, lays out the options, and drafts what's needed. It tags me when a step needs my review or sign-off. When a customer or another team needs to reply first, Claude sets a reminder for itself to check back on a set day. In the thread below, it set a reminder for Tuesday to check whether the customer had replied and whether the deal desk had answered the ticket. When the reminder comes due, Claude checks both and posts where things stand in the same thread. If someone needs a nudge, it drafts the message and tags me to send it.

Claude also posts a morning brief of product and pricing updates. The Nakama coordinator picks up that brief and writes the necessary changes into the shared knowledge base.

What changed in my week

Now that Claude prepares inbound replies and keeps CRM records current (mostly) without my manual input, my role is to review anything that requires human judgment. A written rulebook defines each agent's lane and items like pricing questions, sensitive accounts, or ambiguous asks route to me. Every email draft from Henji, Sabaki, or Nokori arrives with a short summary at the top of what's going on, so I don't have to trace the whole thread to understand the context: I read the summary, confirm, make revisions, and send.

Looking at the weekly log of what the Nakama gets through and counting each task as the time it would have taken me to do manually, the fleet saves me around 60 hours of work. I spend the time that frees up on work that agents can't effectively do (yet): conversations with customers, outbound strategy, cross-functional projects, and helping teammates build their own fleets.

Designing agents to be more efficient

Scheduled agents run every day whether I'm watching or not, so waste can add up, in cost and reliability. Some of the most common mistakes include adding to existing instructions rather than updating them, giving agents more context than they need for their tasks, and running every job on the biggest model at the highest effort level.

Most of what keeps the agents efficient is how I designed the fleet: each agent has one job, so its instructions stay focused on that job; each working agent runs on a schedule, so it wakes up, does its pass, and stops; and the agents share memory, so a correction made once is reused everywhere.

The other big factor is which model each agent runs on. Once an agent's job is well defined, it may not need our most capable model. Furiwake and Shoudan follow a written rulebook, so they run on Sonnet, our smaller model. Sabaki, Nokori and the coordinator run on Opus, our larger model, because their work needs more judgment. The coordinator needs it most, since it edits the other agents' instructions and one bad edit would reach every agent. Henji needs as much judgment as Sabaki, because every customer's email is different, but it also runs more often than any other agent, all through the working day. Running it on Opus every time would be the most expensive option, so I use the advisor strategy (opens in new tab) in Managed Agents: Henji runs on Sonnet, and when it reaches a decision it can't make on its own, it asks Opus for advice. The advisor reads what Henji has done so far and sends back a plan, a correction, or a stop signal, and Henji then finishes the draft for my review. I also set each agent's effort level (how long the model thinks before it answers) separately from its model, and I raise it only where the reasoning is hard, as with Henji's replies.

What I learned

Three things I'd pass on to anyone building their own fleet.

You don't need a detailed prompt every time. Describe the job once, let Claude draft, fix the draft, and let it keep the fix.

The knowledge base matters more than the prompt. Every correction and past interaction is saved where all the agents can read it and write to it, so Claude takes its context from there instead of from a longer prompt. It took a few hundred cheap rounds of drafting, fixing, and saving to get the drafts to sound like me.

Give Claude more room, sooner. At first I kept doing the tasks that I assumed needed me: updating the knowledge base, or editing each agent's instructions by hand. Both worked fine once I let go of them. The agents now write what they learn into the knowledge base themselves, and the coordinator updates the other agents' instructions when I ask in plain English. I had been too cautious with work I could trust the agents to do.

Get started with Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab)

General Security News.title: A little too OpenAI.
General Security News.context: Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability.
General Security News.full_text:
An OpenAI engineer faces charges over an alleged covert recording device. Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. Aoki infostealer hunts AI credentials. Researchers uncover critical weaknesses in an AI gateway. CikaBika Bot turns Discord into a command center. Online ads deliver mercenary spyware without a click. Microsoft disrupts a massive Chinese-language phishing operation. And INTERPOL leads an international crackdown on child sexual abuse material. Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Today is Thursday October 15th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

An OpenAI engineer is charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device.

A 35-year-old OpenAI engineer has been arrested and charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed by OpenAI since July 2025, concealed an encrypted recording device inside a television’s USB port, wrapped in toilet paper. Investigators say surveillance footage placed Alfozan near the room, while chatbot queries associated with his spouse’s account included instructions for building and concealing audio recorders. Security personnel subsequently discovered a second recording device in his unattended bag. The conference room reportedly hosted sensitive discussions involving proprietary research, product development, and government relationships. Authorities have not disclosed whether any conversations were successfully intercepted. Alfozan faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

A high-severity PAN-OS firewall vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software, prompting an urgent federal response. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, allows authenticated attackers with network access to execute code with root privileges. Palo Alto Networks says exploitation has been very limited, but CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch affected systems and investigate potential compromises by October 17. The vulnerability affects PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, along with Panorama management systems. Patches are available for supported versions, but no complete workarounds exist. Researchers warn that patching alone isn’t enough. Organizations should review administrative logins, investigate suspicious configuration changes, and restrict management interfaces to trusted networks. Once attackers control a firewall, they potentially control the very device responsible for protecting the network.

CISA urges immediate patching of an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day.

CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935, allows attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely. Researchers at Volexity say an unidentified threat actor began exploiting the vulnerability October 3, chaining it with additional weaknesses to gain root access. Attackers harvested domain credentials, searched for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, and probed Active Directory. They also covered their tracks by manipulating memory and deleting logs, potentially evading Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool. Ivanti released patches October 13, though a separate privilege escalation flaw remains unpatched. CISA warns that patching alone isn’t sufficient. Organizations should investigate potential compromises, rebuild affected appliances, and rotate exposed credentials and certificates.

Aoki infostealer targets AI credentials.

A relatively new infostealer called Aoki is expanding its appetite for stolen credentials, and AI coding assistants are now on the menu. According to Symantec, newer versions of the malware target authentication tokens, session files, and API keys associated with tools including Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Gemini. Earlier versions focused primarily on browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and password managers. Researchers warn that stolen AI credentials could allow attackers to impersonate developers, run up API charges, and potentially access connected code repositories, cloud services, and development pipelines. Symantec says the malware, first observed earlier this year, remains under active development. The researchers haven’t identified the group responsible, but Aoki’s continued focus on cryptocurrency suggests its operators are financially motivated.

Researchers uncover high-risk vulnerabilities in a popular open-source gateway.

Researchers at Check Point have uncovered two high-risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, a popular open-source gateway that connects enterprise AI applications to providers including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823, could allow ordinary users to gain administrative control of the gateway. One vulnerability could enable remote code execution and potentially complete system takeover. The other could expose API keys through manipulated outbound requests. That’s particularly concerning because AI gateways often centrally manage credentials, permissions, and access to multiple AI services. Check Point says any authenticated user could potentially exploit a vulnerable deployment. The flaws affect LiteLLM versions earlier than 1.83.9, which includes fixes for both issues. Organizations are urged to update promptly.

CikaBika Bot uses Discord for command and control.

Researchers at Darktrace have uncovered a malware campaign distributing CikaBika Bot, a Rust-based remote access trojan that uses Discord for command and control. The attack begins with a document-themed lure that launches hidden PowerShell commands and attempts to bypass Windows security protections. Once installed, the malware collects system information, captures screenshots, and allows attackers to execute commands, manipulate files, and conduct surveillance. It also uses Ngrok to exfiltrate stolen data. Darktrace says the campaign illustrates how legitimate online services can support malicious operations.

A surveillance operation uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware.

Researchers at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab have uncovered a surveillance operation that uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware without requiring victims to click anything. Dubbed AdFection, the operation allegedly involves Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech, which researchers say facilitates surveillance for spyware vendors including Candiru. Citizen Lab linked the campaign to zero-click attacks targeting at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera. Discover-Tech’s ads appeared on more than 120,000 websites and 70,000 mobile apps between March and June, with activity also observed on sensitive government and international networks. Researchers also identified a related operation, dubbed DARK CARTOGRAPHER, that allegedly exploits mobile carrier vulnerabilities to connect advertising identifiers with phone numbers. Google and IAB Europe have removed Discover-Tech from their approved vendor lists. Citizen Lab warns that the findings expose fundamental security weaknesses in digital advertising, where the machinery built to target consumers can also be used to target them for surveillance.

Interpol leads an international effort against CSAM.

INTERPOL says a coordinated law enforcement operation spanning 17 countries in Latin America and Europe has resulted in 95 arrests targeting the distribution of child sexual abuse material through online messaging groups. Dubbed International Effort Confluencia, the operation involved four investigations between March and September, with authorities executing 127 search warrants. Investigators rescued a five-year-old child whose parent had allegedly been producing and selling abuse material. In Panama, police arrested the administrator of a messaging group with more than 700 members. An Argentine suspect allegedly used sextortion against girls around the world. INTERPOL warns that messaging platforms increasingly facilitate grooming, exploitation, and the commercialization of abuse material. Authorities expect evidence seized during the operation to help identify additional offenders and children at risk.

Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Character.ai’s bankruptcy offers a cautionary tale for the AI industry: attracting millions of users is one thing. Making money from them is quite another. Valued at a billion dollars in 2023, the AI companion company was spending as much as $13.8 million a month on computing costs, while subscription revenue never exceeded $2.8 million. Lawsuits involving alleged harm to users added substantial legal expenses, but the company acknowledges its business was unsustainable even without them. Character.ai tried cutting costs by simplifying its models, laying off employees, introducing advertising, and charging for additional features. Users got a diminished experience, and the company still lost eight to nine million dollars a month. The service remains operational during bankruptcy proceedings. Meanwhile, larger competitors can draw on deep-pocketed investors or established businesses to keep funding their AI ambitions. Character.ai discovered that impressive technology and enthusiastic users don’t necessarily add up to a viable business.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: Inside Arctic Wolf and Anthropic’s Trust-First Approach to the Agentic SOC
General Security News.context: Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a...
General Security News.full_text:
In the recently released 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey, nearly two out of three security professionals said they have been given AI-generated guidance that later turned out to be wrong. Not from an experimental tool off in a sandbox, but from systems built into the security stack they were told to rely on. Security teams should not have to live with that. They need to trust the systems that protect them, which is why trust had to be engineered into the foundation of our security operations platform and agentic security operations center (SOC), not bolted on afterward.

Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection

In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a pace human-led security teams were never built to match. Speed doesn’t favor both sides equally. If an attacker’s tool fails, or an AI-generated exploit produces an incorrect result, the cost to the attacker is close to zero. They try again. Defenders do not get that luxury. An AI agent that makes the wrong call inside an organization’s environment, missing a real threat or acting on a false one, can mean damage to that business, and a win for the attacker. An agentic SOC that moves fast but gets it wrong only benefits attackers.

Meeting frontline threats like these takes more than speed. It takes frontier protection, defenses built on AI capable enough to match the attacker and trustworthy enough to be allowed to act.

Why We Chose to Collaborate with Anthropic

That asymmetry is exactly why trust has to be core to what we build, and why we made the decision to collaborate with Anthropic to help us achieve that. Their mission is to ensure the world safely navigates the transition through transformative AI, and for us here at Arctic Wolf, safety and trustworthy AI are inseparable. That alignment, more than any single feature, is why working together made sense from the start.

The first result of that collaboration was the Aurora Security Assistant, which we unveiled at the RSA Conference in 2025. Built in part with Claude models, it gives customers natural language access to security insight uncovered by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them get faster answers to complex security questions via a simple, chat-based interface.

Delivering Trust and Safety from the World’s Largest Commercial Agentic SOC

Over the last 18 months, our collaboration has only deepened. Anthropic’s Claude models now run throughout the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, including the agents within the Swarm of Experts, the agentic framework that executes key functions of our SOC. That framework now supports thousands of organizations worldwide and performs more than 200,000 security investigations a week, a scale that makes the Aurora Agentic SOC the largest commercial agentic SOC in the world.

This week, at Arctic Wolf’s annual Security Operations Summit, Arctic Wolf shared the stage with Ash Alhashim, Head of Enterprise Cybersecurity GTM, Anthropic, who spoke to just how far this collaboration has come.

“Arctic Wolf’s team knows security operations deeply, and that shows in how they’ve put Claude to work,” he said from the stage. “We’ve learned a lot from working with them and we’re glad to keep building together.”

Today, the Swarm of Experts in the Aurora Agentic SOC resolves more than 60% of its investigations autonomously, with high confidence. That level of unassisted resolution comes from technology we’ve built, leveraging Anthropic’s models as part of the foundation. The same technology has also helped customers resolve cases 26% faster year over year, which means they are not just getting faster answers but better ones. The occurs because Swarm of Experts draws on real investigations across our entire customer base and on each customer’s own unique environment, so the guidance behind every investigation is tailored to their needs.

Our work together also extends to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted security teams access to Anthropic’s most capable models with reduced blocking classifiers for legitimate cyber work. Arctic Wolf is part of the program and has access at the Defense Access tier, which is built for defensive work such as security operations center and incident response tasks. It is another sign of the trust between our teams, and it helps ensure the models behind the Aurora Agentic SOC can support the demands of real defensive work.

A Collaboration That Will Keep Advancing

In under two years, Arctic Wolf and Anthropic have made incredible strides in advancing agentic security operations together. What began as a single AI security assistant has grown into the reasoning layer behind the world’s largest commercial agentic SOC, delivering faster, more accurate outcomes for thousands of customers around the globe each week.

But the best is yet to come. Arctic Wolf and Anthropic will continue to work together to find new ways to build Claude’s capabilities into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and deliver new innovations, as both the threats and the SOCs built to stop them keep moving at machine speed.

How can Aquasec help?

Aquasec monitors the real behavior of running cloud native workloads, including process activity, network connections, file changes and privilege usage. That production context shows what an application is actually doing under operating conditions rather than relying only on what was known before deployment.

Observation is only the first step. Aquasec enforces policy locally at runtime, including blocking malicious execution, preventing privilege escalation and containing attacker activity. When an attack chain accelerates, local enforcement changes what the workload is allowed to do next without waiting for a separate analysis or approval workflow.

Aquasec Compass extends that operating model into agentic investigation, containment and remediation through the Model Context Protocol, with humans retaining control over consequential decisions. Attackers are using AI to reduce the time and labor inside their operations. Defenders need automation that reduces the time from evidence to bounded action.

Runtime protection does not replace patching, recovery planning or application layer security. It addresses the interval in which an active attack turns one malicious action into the next. In an AI accelerated ransomware operation, that interval is where containment can still change the outcome.

General Security News.full_text:
TLS 1.3 introduced some major changes. It uses different cipher suite definitions to earlier TLS versions, and has different configuration options. Some implementations separate TLS 1.3 configuration from previous TLS versions. Please consult your implementation documentation to determine how to configure options specific to TLS 1.3.

The recommended profiles include both post-quantum and traditional algorithms to support the transition to PQC. The recommended symmetric cipher suites are unchanged.

The key exchange algorithms included in the recommended profiles are not the only ones the NCSC considers acceptable. All of the post-quantum key exchange algorithms currently specified for use with TLS 1.3 by the IETF offer appropriate protection for personal, enterprise and OFFICIAL-tier government information.

OpenSSL Configuration

The way preferred algorithms and cipher suites are configured varies between TLS platforms. As an example, for platforms built around the OpenSSL library, the following recommended configuration string for TLS 1.3 servers will enable a set of key exchange algorithms (or ‘supported groups’) that aims to optimise security, compatibility and performance:

*X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768:MLKEM768/SecP384r1MLKEM1024:MLKEM1024/*secp256r1:secp384r1

Client configuration for TLS 1.3

TLS clients should offer key shares and cipher suites that are most likely to be accepted by the server. The configuration of TLS clients is often outside the control of the administrator, but where it is possible to configure clients (for example within a privately hosted enterprise network), the NCSC recommends offering key shares for X25519MLKEM768 and secp256r1.

Using the recommended profiles for PQC migration

To support PQC in TLS, you should:

enable TLS 1.3 and prefer it over TLS 1.2 where possible

enable at least one of the recommended post-quantum key exchange algorithms as soon as your implementation supports them

enable the recommended traditional key exchange algorithms where you still require compatibility with systems that do not yet support PQC

In most cases, it will be appropriate to combine these activities by adopting TLS 1.3 and enabling and preferring the recommended post-quantum key exchange algorithms as a single migration activity.

Migrating the authentication methods used by TLS 1.3 to post-quantum alternatives will depend on the transition of the PKI infrastructure they rely on, and will need to wait until the relevant standards have been confirmed.

For internet-facing servers and clients, maintaining compatibility with systems that do not yet support PQC is important. As a result, support for traditional cryptography cannot be disabled until much later in the overall PQC migration.

Who’s Watching AI? The Visibility Gap Security Teams Need to Close
General Security News.context: 8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use
General Security News.full_text:
AI adoption isn't waiting for security teams.

Employees are experimenting with new tools. Business leaders are pushing teams to use AI to work faster. Applications are adding AI functionality. AI agents are accessing files, connecting to tools, and taking action as if they were employees.

This has tremendous potential.

But there's also a fundamental cybersecurity problem: Do you know what AI is doing inside your organization, or is it a growing blind spot?

That's the question at the center of a new episode of Cybercrime: From the Frontline, Who’s Watching AI? Managing Innovation Without Losing Control.

Watch or listen to the full conversation to hear Bitdefender experts explore how organizations can embrace AI innovation while managing its risks.

How Many Organizations Lack Full AI Visibility?

The 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment reveals that 44.8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use. Another roughly 3% report having no visibility at all.

The independent research surveyed 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries and shows how widespread the lack of AI visibility and control has become. And the challenge is growing because employees have powerful incentives to experiment. AI can accelerate development, automate repetitive work, analyze information, and help meet increasingly aggressive productivity expectations.

Has Shadow IT Become Shadow AI?

Shadow AI introduces similar challenges to Shadow IT, but with potentially greater consequences.

With Shadow IT, an employee installs an unauthorized application. A department adopts a cloud service without consulting IT. Someone stores corporate information in a personal file-sharing account.

With Shadow AI, an employee might use a personal AI account instead of an approved enterprise platform. Someone could paste confidential information into a free AI service. An approved application might gain new AI capabilities through an update.

In each case, sensitive information could move somewhere security teams didn't anticipate. That's particularly concerning given that data leakage into large language models ranks among the leading AI-related concerns identified in the 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment.

According to experts on the podcast episode, AI adoption often happens without IT or security oversight, making visibility an enterprise-wide responsibility.

Why Is AI Becoming an Identity Problem?

Traditional generative AI responds to requests. Agentic AI can interact with tools, access files, connect to services, write code, and take actions. During the podcast, our experts suggest thinking about these agents as non-human identities operating inside the organization.

That raises important questions:

Which agents are operating in your environment?

What data can they access?

Which tools can they use?

What actions are they permitted to take?

And what happens if an agent is manipulated?

The podcast also explores prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded within content can influence an AI system into performing unintended actions. If an agent has access to corporate systems, the question isn't simply whether you trust the AI.

What Does AI Visibility Look Like Today?

A simple inventory isn't enough. To achieve AI visibility, organizations must be able to identify the AI services and agents operating across their environments. Security teams need context on those tools, including their capabilities, permissions, connections, potential risks, and the endpoints they affect.

They also need to distinguish sanctioned AI use from unknown or potentially dangerous activity. Without that understanding, organizations risk applying blanket restrictions that frustrate employees or overlooking exposures that genuinely threaten the business.

Visibility provides the foundation for prioritizing risk and applying appropriate controls.

What Kinds of Tools Create AI Visibility and Control?

Organizations increasingly need specialized capabilities that discover AI usage, assess exposure, and translate security policies into action. One example is Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control, which helps security teams identify more than 700 AI tools, including chatbots, coding assistants, local LLMs, agents, MCP servers, and AI-enabled applications. It creates a centralized inventory and helps prioritize findings based on risk and business context.

Importantly, GravityZone goes beyond discovery. Security teams can review and investigate findings, then use integrated controls to allow, restrict, or block AI activity. For existing GravityZone customers, these capabilities operate through the same agent and console, helping organizations manage AI exposure without adding another disconnected security tool.

How Can AI Governance Keep Pace With AI Adoption?

Technology is part of the answer, but AI governance must also become part of acceptable-use policies, employee education, procurement reviews, third-party risk assessments, and conversations between security and business leaders.

Some organizations are establishing dedicated AI steering committees. Others are incorporating AI into existing security and risk governance. The structure matters less than the outcome: security needs to participate in AI adoption decisions before deploying new tools.

Can Organizations Innovate Without Losing Control?

According to the podcast episode's experts, organizations can continue AI innovation without losing control, but only with a sound strategy. Instead of putting the brakes on AI adoption, organizations should make approved AI easier to use safely, educate employees about the risks of unsanctioned tools, use technology to track where sensitive information moves, and establish controls based on actual usage.

As AI agents become more capable, organizations must also understand and constrain agent permissions, just as they would for human identities.

Together, these measures can help make AI innovation sustainable.

General Security News.title: An update on independent evaluators
General Security News.context: If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance
General Security News.full_text:
Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.

Why we work with independent evaluators

As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:

Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.

Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.

Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.

Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

What we mean by “employee-like access”

We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.1

METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)2

Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

Our other evaluator partnerships

We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

SecureBio is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.3

With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.

We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

General Security News.title: Cybersecurity: it’s AI vs AI
Penetration testing every deployment with AWS Continuum
General Security News.context: Because the gate blocks on findings that Continuum for penetration testing validated as exploitable rather than on pattern matches, a red pipeline carries a clear meaning: a...
General Security News.full_text:
Most security tooling that fits into a CI/CD pipeline—static analysis (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA), and dynamic scanners (DAST)—flags potential issues from patterns and signatures. A flagged pattern shows you where to look; penetration testing is what confirms whether something is actually exploitable. That confirmation has traditionally come from a periodic, out-of-band engagement that runs on a schedule rather than on a deploy, so deploys between engagements reach production with that confirmation still pending.

AWS Continuum for penetration testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) is a service that uses AI agents to find and confirm exploitable vulnerabilities in your running applications. In this post, we walk you through making it a post-deployment gate in your pipeline. The gate runs a penetration test that is automatically scoped to the change you just deployed, and it can block promotion to production when a finding is at or above a severity threshold you choose. Because each run tests only the change since the last passing gate rather than the whole application, it is fast and economical enough to run on every deploy. We give a high-level overview of the pattern, which can be applied on four major CI/CD platforms: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Bitbucket Pipelines, and Azure DevOps Pipelines. We then provide a specific worked example for GitHub Actions.

By the end, you will have a pipeline that deploys a change to a staging environment, runs a scoped penetration test against the deployed change, and promotes the change to production only when the gate passes.

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow. Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, then the pentest gate step authenticates to your AWS account through OpenID Connect (OIDC) and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which runs the scoped test against the staging environment. The gate waits for the result, reports the outcome back to your pipeline, and conditionally blocks promotion to production. All testing runs server-side in your AWS account, so no penetration testing logic runs on your CI/CD runner.

Figure 1: Pipeline gate architecture: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, the pentest gate authenticates via OIDC and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which returns a scope decision that gates promotion to production.

Why scoping to the change matters

What makes the gate practical to run on every deploy is that it scopes each test to the change you just deployed. Continuum for penetration testing determines the commit range—the head is the commit being gated, and the base is the previous commit the gate already cleared—and tests only what changed. Testing the change instead of the whole application is what keeps a per-deploy penetration test fast and cheap enough to belong in a pipeline rather than on a quarterly calendar.

Each run returns one of three scope decisions: in scope (the change modified the attack surface—findings are evaluated against your threshold), scoped out (the change was within scope but nothing security-relevant changed—the pipeline passes), or scope conflict (the change fell outside the configured scope and was not tested—you choose whether that blocks). The Continuum for penetration testing console records the decision and the commit range on the Scoping tab of each run. When a gate blocks, you can see exactly why. For the full mechanics of how the commit range is computed and validated, see How the pipeline integration scopes the test.

Because the gate blocks on findings that Continuum for penetration testing validated as exploitable rather than on pattern matches, a red pipeline carries a clear meaning: a reproducible vulnerability in the change, waiting to be fixed before promotion.

Setting up the gate

The gate takes three steps to set up: configure a penetration test, create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that your pipeline can assume, and add the gate step to your pipeline.

Before you start, you need an AWS account with permission to create both an IAM OIDC identity provider and an IAM role, and a staging environment the penetration test can reach.

Step 1: Configure the penetration test

Complete the one-time setup described in Before you start: verify your target domain, create a penetration test in your Agent Space, enable CI/CD mode, and connect your repository. Note the Agent Space ID (as-…) and penetration test ID (pt-…), because you pass both to the gate step in Step 3. The pipeline tests whatever this penetration test is configured to test, so its target and scope set what the gate covers.

Step 2: Create the IAM role

Authentication uses OIDC federation rather than stored keys. Your CI/CD provider issues a short-lived token identifying the pipeline, and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) exchanges it for temporary credentials when the pipeline assumes an IAM role you create. There are no long-lived AWS access keys to store as CI/CD variables, which removes the credential most often leaked from a pipeline.

The security of the gate rests on two policies: the IAM role’s trust policy (which pipelines can assume the role) and its permissions policy (what the pipeline can do once the role is assumed). For the exact policy JSON, the provider-specific OIDC URLs and audience values, and the sub claim format for each CI/CD platform, follow the reference in Scope the trust policy to your pipeline and Grant least-privilege permissions.

The following judgment calls help you decide how to scope these policies.

How tightly to scope the trust policy is the first decision. Pinning the sub claim to a single branch (for example, main) is the right default when a branch is the only one that deploys through this pipeline. If several branches or environments legitimately run the gate, scope to the environment instead of the branch where your provider’s claim supports it—and remember that not every provider carries a branch in the claim at all. On Bitbucket, the repository (and optionally a deployment environment) is as tight as it gets. Start as narrow as your deployment reality allows and widen only when a real branch or environment needs it. Note that GitHub repositories created or renamed on or after July 15, 2026 emit an immutable sub claim with numeric IDs—confirm the exact sub your pipeline emits before you write the policy.

Step 3: Add the gate step to your pipeline

The step is the same idea on every provider—the syntax differs. Pin the integration to an immutable version (a release tag, commit SHA, or pinned component version) so an upstream change can’t alter what runs in your pipeline. For the full settings reference and defaults table, see Defaults the integration ships with.

Before relying on the gate, run it once in dry-run mode. A dry run checks authentication, the Region, and that your repository resolves—without starting a scoped penetration test job. If validation fails, the step fails regardless of your error-handling settings, so a misconfiguration surfaces immediately.

A worked example: GitHub Actions

The following workflow shows the three-job topology that makes the gate work: deploy deploys to staging, security-pentest runs the gate, and deploy-prod promotes to production. Because deploy-prod declares needs: [security-pentest], GitHub skips production whenever the gate fails.

Note: The tutorials use an application with a deliberate SQL injection so the gate has a real finding to block on. Deploy it only to an isolated, non-production environment and remove it when you finish.

jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: staging steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: persist-credentials: false - run: ./deploy.sh staging security-pentest: needs: [deploy] runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write contents: write actions: read deployments: read steps: - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/my-pentest-gate-role aws-region: us-west-2 role-duration-seconds: 7200 - uses: aws-actions/aws-continuum-run-pentest@v1 with: agent-space-id: as-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx pentest-id: pt-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx severity-threshold: HIGH on-scope-conflict: block timeout-minutes: "45" deploy-prod: needs: [security-pentest] runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: persist-credentials: false - run: ./deploy.sh production

Replace the account ID, role name, Region, and the as-/pt- identifiers with your own values.

Two things in this example deserve attention. First, the contents: write permission lets the gate advance the baseline marker it keeps as a ref in your repository—without write access, every run would test a wider range than intended. Second, the role-duration-seconds: 7200 on the credential step must outlast the penetration test; AWS STS rejects a request for more than the role allows rather than reducing it, so set the role’s maximum session duration to at least (timeout + 10) x 60 seconds. A credential that expires partway through makes an otherwise-healthy run fail as though the service were at fault and leaves the cleanup unable to stop the abandoned, still-running job.

The full step-by-step tutorials for all four providers are linked at the end of this post.

Rolling out the gate: from report-only to blocking

The single most important detail before you roll this out.

Three independent settings decide whether the step fails, and each covers a different outcome: severity-threshold (what happens to findings), on-scope-conflict (what happens when the change wasn’t tested), and fail-on-infrastructure-error (what happens when the job couldn’t run). They are independent—relaxing one does not affect the others.

Most teams introduce the gate in report-only mode first—set threshold to NONE so the test runs and publishes findings without blocking anyone’s pipeline. Watch what it finds for a release or two, then tighten the threshold to HIGH. This staged rollout is sound, with one critical caveat:

A run that passes—including a report-only run—advances the baseline. The commits in that run’s range are then recorded as cleared and will not be re-tested when you later tighten the threshold. If you run report-only for a month and then switch to HIGH, the gate only assesses commits after the last report-only run—it does not go back and recheck what it already reported on.

This is by design: relaxing a setting is you accepting the outcome it allows. But if you want a stricter setting to reassess a range an earlier run cleared, override the head and base commit SHAs by setting base-commit-sha and head-commit-sha. Where the marker lives differs by provider; see What advances the baseline, and why that matters for the full matrix.

One default also deserves attention: fail-on-infrastructure-error ships as false (fail-open). For pipelines where promotion requires security sign-off, set it to true from the start.

GitLab: your committed settings are defaults, not a contract

On GitLab CI/CD, a pipeline variable overrides the value a job sets in its own variables: block. That means anyone who can run a pipeline could supply a variable that lowers the threshold, turns on dry-run, or relaxes error handling—and the gate does what the variable says, not what your .gitlab-ci.yml says. Restrict who may override variables in your project’s CI/CD settings before you rely on the gate to hold a release.

Protecting credentials on the runner

The temporary credentials and OIDC token are sensitive for the duration of the step. Three practices matter:

Keep debug and verbose tracing off for steps that handle credentials—shell-trace modes (for example, GitLab CI’s CI_DEBUG_TRACE) echo command arguments to the job log in plaintext.

Don’t persist source control credentials in the workspace—set persist-credentials: false on the checkout step so a token isn’t written to the runner’s .git configuration where a later step could read it.

Don’t expose the token to untrusted steps—grant OIDC-token permission only to the jobs that need it, and don’t run untrusted code (such as a fork build) in a job that can read the token.

Taking this to production and multiple accounts

The example uses one account for clarity. In practice, your staging and production environments are often separate AWS accounts. The pattern extends cleanly:

Create the pentest-gate IAM role in the account where the penetration test and Agent Space live—the security account. Your pipeline assumes that role via OIDC regardless of which workload account it deploys to, so you keep one well-scoped gate role rather than a copy or a set of long-lived keys in every account.

Run the gate against each pre-production environment you promote through, and gate promotion to the next stage on its result. Because the baseline advances only on a passing gate, coverage stays continuous across deploys.

Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true and restrict who can override pipeline variables once the gate is holding real releases.

Pin the integration version so upstream changes are reviewed before they run.

For broader guidance of AWS Security Agent—testing against non-production environments, validating AI-generated findings, and IAM—see Security best practices for AWS Continuum.

Cleanup

If you followed one of the provider tutorials to try the gate, complete its Clean up section to remove everything it had you create: the sample application’s staging environment, the IAM role and OIDC identity provider, and—if you created one specifically for the walkthrough—the penetration test (and dedicated Agent Spaces) in the Continuum for penetration testing console. Removing them avoids ongoing charges and takes the intentionally vulnerable sample application offline.

Conclusion

Scoping penetration tests to the deployed change is what makes them practical as a per-deploy gate rather than a quarterly exercise. The key decisions you now have are:

How strict: Start report-only (NONE), but know the baseline advances—delete the marker when you tighten.

How to fail: Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true for anything that requires security sign-off.

How to scope trust: Pin the sub claim as narrowly as your deployment reality allows.

Where to put the role: One role in a security account, assumed from workloads pipeline via OIDC.

To build the gate end to end on your platform, follow the worked tutorial for your provider:

Tutorial: Gate a GitHub Actions deployment with a scoped penetration test

Tutorial: Gate a GitLab CI/CD deployment with a scoped penetration test

Tutorial: Gate a Bitbucket Pipelines deployment with a scoped penetration test

Tutorial: Gate an Azure DevOps deployment with a scoped penetration test

For the concepts and full reference, see Run penetration tests from your CI/CD pipeline.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

Jigar Bhatt

Jigar is a Senior Software Engineer at AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing, where he builds AI-powered penetration testing capabilities helping customers find and fix exploitable vulnerabilities in their applications. Before joining the AI security space, Jigar spent several years building developer tools on AWS CodeBuild. He holds a Master of Engineering in Software Systems from BITS Pilani, India.
